question: Peter Abelard was already the star scholar of Paris, and Heloise was the brilliant young niece of a cathedral canon named Fulbert, famous across the city for her learning. By his own confession, Abelard talked his way into Fulbert's house as a paying lodger and Heloise's private tutor. What was the real reason the greatest logician in France engineered that arrangement?
answer: To be alone with Heloise, whom he meant to court and seduce.
choices: To be alone with Heloise, whom he meant to court and seduce.
To spy on Fulbert's dealings inside the cathedral chapter.
To borrow Fulbert's rare books while pretending to teach.
To win students away from Fulbert's own crowded school.
context: Abelard admits the scheme in his autobiography, the Historia Calamitatum: 'I persuaded the girl's uncle... to take me into his household... in return for the payment of a small sum.' The most celebrated logician in France used a tutoring contract as cover to seduce his own student. Source: Abelard, Historia Calamitatum (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook); Wikipedia 'Heloise'.

question: Heloise bore Peter Abelard a son, and the proud parents passed over every name of saint and king. Instead they named the boy after one of the stargazer's instruments Abelard used to chart the night sky and fix a traveler's place beneath the stars. What was their son's name?
answer: Astrolabe
choices: Astrolabe
Quadrans
Armilla
Gnomon
context: They named the child Astrolabe, after the star-charting instrument a navigator used to fix his position on Earth. Abelard later wrote him a poem of fatherly advice, the Carmen ad Astrolabium. Source: Wikipedia 'Heloise' (names Astrolabe, explains the device); Toronto DLB Abelard biography.

question: Peter Abelard, the most celebrated and arrogant logician in 12th-century Paris, wrote a book called Sic et Non ('Yes and No') on 158 disputed questions of faith. For each question he gathered quotations from Scripture and the great Church Fathers, and he deliberately chose ones that flatly contradicted each other. Why did Abelard set the saints arguing against each other on purpose?
answer: To make the student stop swallowing authority and reason it out.
choices: To make the student stop swallowing authority and reason it out.
To prove that the Church Fathers had all been frauds and liars.
To show that Scripture was too muddled to be trusted at all.
To embarrass his rivals by exposing the errors in their books.
context: Crucially, Abelard did NOT resolve the 158 contradictions himself; he left them open so the student had to reconcile them through reason. This juxtapose-the-authorities-and-think-it-through move became the engine of the scholastic method that ran the medieval universities for centuries. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and IEP (both confirm 158 questions); Wikipedia 'Sic et Non'.

question: Peter Abelard and Heloise married in secret, but her uncle Fulbert felt his family had been disgraced. One night Fulbert's kinsmen bribed Abelard's servant, broke into his lodging while he slept, and took a terrible revenge upon his body; the next morning, Abelard wrote, the whole city gathered before his door in horror. What did Fulbert's men do to Abelard?
answer: They castrated him while he slept.
choices: They castrated him while he slept.
They blinded him in both eyes.
They cut off his right hand.
They branded his face with hot iron.
context: Abelard records it plainly: 'they cut off those parts of my body with which I had done that which was the cause of their sorrow.' Of the next day he wrote that words could not describe the city's amazement. Two of the attackers were caught and were themselves blinded and castrated as punishment. Source: Abelard, Historia Calamitatum (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook); IEP and SEP confirm Fulbert ordered it.

question: After the scandal, Peter Abelard offered to marry Heloise to satisfy her furious uncle Fulbert. Astonishingly, Heloise herself argued fiercely against it, stunning everyone by fighting the very wedding meant to save her honor. What reason did Heloise give for refusing to marry the man she loved?
answer: Marriage and a home would destroy a great teacher's calling.
choices: Marriage and a home would destroy a great teacher's calling.
A wife's daily duties would always come before his students.
Her uncle would never truly forgive them, wedding or no wedding.
A secret wedding could not hold unless a bishop performed it.
context: Heloise held that a wife and household would ruin a philosopher's vocation, and that love freely given outranked any legal tie. Her lines survive: 'I preferred love to wedlock, freedom to a bond,' and 'sweeter to me is ever the word friend, or, if you be not ashamed, concubine.' She said it would be a greater dignity to be called Abelard's strumpet than the Emperor's empress. Source: Heloise's first letter to Abelard (webspace.ship.edu/cgboer/heloise.html), quotes verbatim.

question: Peter Abelard opened Sic et Non, his book of clashing Church authorities, with a line that became the credo of the questioning mind: 'By ____ we come to inquiry, and by inquiry we perceive the truth.' What word did Abelard place in that blank?
answer: doubting
choices: doubting
reasoning
reading
obeying
context: The full line in Latin: 'dubitando ad inquisitionem venimus; inquirendo veritatem percipimus.' For Abelard doubt was not the enemy of faith but the doorway to truth, and his preface praised Aristotle as the philosopher who most wanted to 'arouse this questioning spirit.' Source: web search of the Sic et Non prologue; Wikipedia 'Sic et Non'.

question: Abraham has walked three days to a mountain, obeying a command to give up his own son. He lays out the wood in silence, ties up the boy Isaac, and lifts the knife over him. At the last instant he stops, because he sees the animal God has provided to be killed in the boy's place. What does Abraham sacrifice instead of his son?
answer: A ram caught in a nearby thicket
choices: A ram caught in a nearby thicket
A bull from his own great herds
A lamb the boy had carried up
A dove released over the altar
context: This raised-knife instant is the pivot of Kierkegaard's whole book Fear and Trembling. His own retelling: 'Silently he laid the wood in order, he bound Isaac, in silence he drew the knife -- then he saw the ram which God had prepared.' In Genesis 22 the ram is caught by its horns in a thicket and offered up in Isaac's place. Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Exordium'; Genesis 22 (the Akedah).

question: Kierkegaard says the rarest hero of faith carries an inner storm no one can see. So he imagines finally meeting one in the street and is stunned: he searches the man head to toe for some sign of the infinite and finds nothing. 'Good Lord, is this the man?' he gasps. What completely ordinary figure does Kierkegaard say the man of faith looks like instead?
answer: A humble tax-collector
choices: A humble tax-collector
A wandering hermit
A devout priest
A weathered soldier
context: The famous knight-of-faith passage: 'Good Lord, is this the man? Is it really he? Why, he looks like a tax-collector!' Kierkegaard finds no 'telegraphic message from the infinite' on him -- the man walks home firm as a postman, expects a calf's-head dinner he can't afford, and smokes his pipe in the evening 'like the grocer over the way.' The storm of faith is entirely invisible. Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Preliminary Expectoration.'

question: Kierkegaard keeps returning to one detail that makes the command to kill Isaac almost unbearable: the sheer length of the wait that came before it. God had promised Abraham a son, yet he and his wife Sarah grew old in patient expectation before that one child was finally born. Roughly how long does Kierkegaard say they waited in faith for Isaac?
answer: About seventy years
choices: About seventy years
About fifteen years
About forty years
About seven years
context: Kierkegaard dwells on the age gap to sharpen the horror: 'Seventy years of faithful expectation, the brief joy at the fulfilment of faith. All was lost!' The longer the wait, the crueler the command to kill that long-awaited only son. Kierkegaard, writing at about age thirty, lingers on how old Abraham was. Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Eulogy on Abraham'; D. Anthony Storm's Commentary (sorenkierkegaard.org).

question: On the road to the mountain Abraham says nothing to Sarah, nothing to his servant, nothing to Isaac about what he means to do. Kierkegaard insists this silence is not mere secrecy but something Abraham cannot escape: the deed simply cannot be put into words. Why, on Kierkegaard's reading, is Abraham unable to explain himself to anyone?
answer: Spoken aloud, his deed could only sound like madness or murder
choices: Spoken aloud, his deed could only sound like madness or murder
He had sworn a solemn oath never to reveal God's command
He feared Sarah and Isaac would try to stop him by force
He did not yet understand the command he had been given
context: This is Problem III, and the source of the book's pen name. The moment Abraham tried to say 'God told me to kill you, son,' it would be heard as madness or murder, or not understood at all -- faith here is the thing that cannot be spoken, only enacted. Kierkegaard published under the name Johannes de Silentio, 'John of the Silence,' for exactly this reason. Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Problem III' and title page; IEP, 'Soren Kierkegaard.'

question: Kierkegaard sets Abraham beside three fathers who also gave a child to death: Agamemnon lays his daughter on the altar to free the becalmed war-fleet, Jephthah strikes down his daughter over a battlefield vow, Brutus orders his own sons put to death. We grieve for these men yet understand them, Kierkegaard says, in a way we never can with Abraham. What makes those three 'tragic heroes' understandable where Abraham is not?
answer: Each can give a reason others can weigh and accept
choices: Each can give a reason others can weigh and accept
Each was forced to it by a fate stronger than his will
Each had a god command the deed in open sight
Each wept aloud where Abraham went cold and silent
context: 'The tragic hero still remains within the ethical,' Kierkegaard writes: Agamemnon, Jephthah, and Brutus each act for an end the community recognizes, so each can give an account others can weigh and accept as justification -- and that is why we both weep for them and understand them. Abraham can give no such account: his only warrant is God's private command, which no one else can verify, so he steps outside the ethical entirely and can only be feared, not admired the same way. The rival readings miss this -- they were not compelled by fate but chose; no god commands Jephthah's vow or Brutus's law in open sight; and the point is comprehension, not whether they wept. Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Problem I'; D. Anthony Storm's Commentary (sorenkierkegaard.org).

question: Before any argument, Kierkegaard opens the book by retelling the journey four different ways, each showing an ordinary man's way of failing the test. In one version Abraham is desperate that the boy's trust in God must survive the horror of the altar, and so he plays a role that turns all of Isaac's loathing squarely onto the father himself. What does this Abraham pretend to be?
answer: A wild-eyed idolater
choices: A wild-eyed idolater
A pitiless murderer
A raving madman
A heartless stranger
context: This is the first of the four 'what if' Abrahams in the Exordium. To spare Isaac's faith, this Abraham plays the idolater so the boy will hate his father rather than hate God. The other three retellings each fail differently: one obeys but is broken and 'knew joy no more'; one torments himself begging forgiveness for having been willing at all; one lets his hand tremble so Isaac sees his despair and loses his own faith. None is the real Abraham -- each is a way an ordinary person could understand failing. Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Exordium'; D. Anthony Storm's Commentary (sorenkierkegaard.org).

question: Kierkegaard separates two heroes who both surrender the thing they love most. The 'knight of infinite resignation' lets it go forever and finds a calm peace in the loss -- and Kierkegaard says that letting-go is real and admirable, but it is only the last step BEFORE faith. The rarer 'knight of faith' makes one further move the first man cannot. What does the knight of faith do that the knight of resignation does not?
answer: He expects the loved one restored to him in this life
choices: He expects the loved one restored to him in this life
He expects the loved one restored to him in eternity
He surrenders the loved one without any pain at all
He buries his love so the loss can no longer hurt
context: This is Kierkegaard's 'double movement.' Both knights truly let go -- you must first genuinely renounce before faith is even possible -- but the knight of faith adds the absurd second move: 'I believe nevertheless that I shall get her... in virtue of the fact that with God all things are possible.' He expects Isaac back in THIS life, not merely in eternity. Infinite resignation is 'the last stage prior to faith.' Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Preliminary Expectoration.'

question: Kierkegaard states the dilemma in one razor sentence: in the language of ordinary morality Abraham WOULD MURDER his son; in the language of faith he WOULD SACRIFICE him; and the dread lives precisely in that contradiction. When Kierkegaard weighs the plain ethical charge that Abraham is simply a would-be murderer, what is his verdict on it?
answer: The honest ethical truth that only real faith could overturn
choices: The honest ethical truth that only real faith could overturn
The literal truth, full stop, that not even faith can change
A misreading the sacred story itself plainly refutes
Beside the point, since God's command settles the matter
context: Kierkegaard will not let the reader off the hook. His sentence: 'The ethical expression for what Abraham did is, that he would murder Isaac; the religious expression is, that he would sacrifice Isaac; but precisely in this contradiction consists the dread which can well make a man sleepless.' He grants that without faith 'there only remains the crude fact that Abraham wanted to murder Isaac' -- the ethical reading is the honest truth, defensible and live; only genuine faith could change that verdict. The literal-truth-that-faith-cannot-change reading is the tempting misstep: it keeps the honesty but denies the very overturning Kierkegaard's whole book is about. The bank takes no side here. Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Preliminary Expectoration.'

question: Kierkegaard poses his sharpest question: can a single individual ever rank HIGHER than the moral law that binds everyone alike? Ordinary ethics says no -- the same rule binds every person, every instant, with no exceptions. Yet faith, he argues, is the paradox that here the lone individual stands above that universal rule. Kierkegaard is blunt that if there is no such standing-above, Abraham is not the father of faith at all. How does he say the law must then regard him?
answer: As a man it must prosecute and convict of murder
choices: As a man it must prosecute and convict of murder
As a man whose deed it can neither excuse nor name
As guilty, yet beyond the reach of any human court
As innocent, since his intent was never truly his own
context: This is Problem I, the 'teleological suspension of the ethical.' 'The ethical as such is the universal,' binding everyone always; yet 'faith is this paradox, that the particular is higher than the universal.' Kierkegaard is blunt about the stakes: if there is NO such suspension, then 'Abraham is lost,' and he 'ought to be prosecuted and convicted of murder' rather than honored as the father of faith. The rival verdicts -- a deed beyond naming, guilt with no court, innocence by coerced will -- are the softening moves Kierkegaard refuses; without the suspension the law has a plain name for it. Presented as the genuine dilemma it is; the bank takes no verdict. Source: Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling (Lowrie translation), 'Problem I'; SEP, 'Soren Kierkegaard.'

question: A child reasons: 'Birds can fly. Tweety the penguin is a bird. So Tweety can fly.' Every line is something people say, yet the conclusion is false -- penguins don't fly. Where exactly does the reasoning break?
answer: 'Birds can fly' is a rule of thumb, and the penguin is the odd case it never meant to cover
choices: 'Birds can fly' is a rule of thumb, and the penguin is the odd case it never meant to cover
'Birds can fly' is plainly false, since a great many sorts of bird cannot get off the ground
The word 'bird' carries one sense in the first line and a quite different sense in the second
Calling Tweety 'a bird' quietly assumes the very thing the argument set out to prove
context: This is the fallacy of accident: applying a sound generalization to a case it was never built to reach. 'Birds can fly' is true of birds in general -- most do -- but the penguin is the accidental exception, so the rule simply doesn't stretch to it. The error is ignoring that some birds were always meant to be left out. Source: fallacyfiles.org, 'Accident'.

question: Consider this argument: 'Cutting people with knives is a crime. Surgeons cut people with knives. Therefore surgeons are criminals.' The conclusion is absurd, yet it seems to follow from two true-sounding lines. What has actually gone wrong?
answer: The rule against knife-cutting is forced onto a case -- surgery -- it was never framed to govern
choices: The rule against knife-cutting is forced onto a case -- surgery -- it was never framed to govern
The opening line is false, because cutting a person open with a knife is not in every case a crime
The word 'cut' quietly shifts its meaning between the kitchen brawl and the operating room
The argument helps itself to its conclusion, treating surgeons as criminals well before proving it
context: The classic textbook handle for the fallacy of accident. The general rule against knife-cutting is sound, but it was framed for assault, not for the operating table; the legitimate professional context is the extra feature (the 'accident') the syllogism ignores. The absurd conclusion follows from the misapplication, not from the rule. Source: en.wikipedia.org, 'Accident (fallacy)'.

question: In Plato's Republic, old Cephalus proposes that justice is simply telling the truth and returning what you've borrowed. Socrates answers with a single image: suppose you borrowed a friend's weapons, and then he loses his mind and demands them back. How does that one case break the rule?
answer: Handing the sword to a madman isn't just, so the rule was never meant to reach that case
choices: Handing the sword to a madman isn't just, so the rule was never meant to reach that case
It shows that returning what you have borrowed has nothing at all to do with being just
It shows the borrower never really owned the very weapons that he is now demanding back
It shows you are simply never required to return borrowed property to anyone who asks
context: From Republic, Book I. Socrates doesn't deny that returning what you owe is generally just -- he finds the case the rule was never built for: the borrower gone insane. Handing a weapon to a raging man is plainly not justice, so 'return what you borrowed' must carry an unstated exception. This is the fallacy of accident shown by counterexample. Source: iep.utm.edu, 'Plato: The Republic'.

question: You promised to return a borrowed knife on Friday. But by Friday its owner has become a raging maniac, raving that he'll use it on the neighbors. Someone insists: 'You must always keep your promises, so hand it over.' Why is that reasoning faulty even though keeping promises is genuinely good?
answer: 'Always keep your promises' is being pressed onto a case the rule was never built to handle
choices: 'Always keep your promises' is being pressed onto a case the rule was never built to handle
'Always keep your promises' is a false principle that a sensible person should just ignore
A promise about a knife was never a binding promise in the first place, so nothing is owed
Breaking the promise here shows that promises carry no real moral weight once they are tested
context: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's handle for the fallacy of accident: reasoning with a generalization 'as if it has no exceptions.' Keeping promises is a sound rule, but arming a maniac is exactly the abnormal case the rule's everyday scope leaves out. The fault is treating a good rule as exceptionless, not the rule itself. Source: iep.utm.edu, 'Fallacies'.

question: Aristotle's own specimen of the fallacy of accident: 'Coriscus differs from Socrates; Socrates is a man; so Coriscus differs from a man' -- and thus, absurdly, from himself, since Coriscus IS a man. Aristotle's diagnosis of why such reasoning collapses was that it makes one wrong assumption. Which one?
answer: That whatever is true of a thing must hold of every passing description of that thing too
choices: That whatever is true of a thing must hold of every passing description of that thing too
That two things which differ in one respect must therefore differ in every respect alike
That a conclusion is proven the moment no one present can think of a reply to it
That a word keeps a single fixed meaning each time it appears across the argument
context: Aristotle's structural diagnosis of why accident fails: the fallacy assumes 'some attribute belongs alike to the thing and to its accident' -- but one thing carries many accidents, so an attribute true of the thing need not transfer to every accidental description of it. 'Differs from Socrates' is just one accidental description of Coriscus, and the property doesn't carry through it. Aristotle filed accident among the non-linguistic fallacies -- the ones that fail by strict logical necessity, not by a word-trick. Source: faculty.washington.edu (Cohen on Aristotle); thenonsequitur.com.

question: In 1797 Benjamin Constant pressed Immanuel Kant on his rule that it is ALWAYS wrong to lie: then a murderer who asks where your friend is hiding must be told the truth, and your friend betrayed. Constant's sharper reply moved past the gore to a claim about who is even owed honesty. What was that claim?
answer: Truth is owed only to a person with a right to it, and the murderer has forfeited that right
choices: Truth is owed only to a person with a right to it, and the murderer has forfeited that right
Truth is owed to everyone alike, so the murderer must be answered just like any other man
Truth is owed to no one at all, so a person may say whatever happens to serve him in the moment
Truth is owed first to the friend in danger, whose claim simply outweighs the murderer's
context: Constant: 'to tell the truth is a duty only toward one who has a right to the truth.' Kant disagreed in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy,' insisting you must answer truthfully even so. The murderer is the contested 'accident' that may take the case outside the rule's scope -- and whether 'never lie' HAS a built-in exception is precisely the fight. No verdict here: the logic of rule-scope is the lesson, not who wins the ethics. Source: onlinelibrary.wiley.com, Varden on Kant.

question: A wooden bridge over the river has collapsed. A knight rides up to a peasant who is warning travelers to turn back, sneers that the peasant is 'too ugly and lowborn to know anything,' and rides on. The knight never looked at the bridge. Why is the knight's reply a bad way to settle whether the bridge is really out?
answer: What a person looks like has nothing to do with whether the bridge actually collapsed
choices: What a person looks like has nothing to do with whether the bridge actually collapsed
The peasant clearly wanted a reward, so his warning cannot be trusted at all
The knight should have mocked the peasant's courage instead of his face
A warning only counts as true if a nobleman is the one who says it
context: This move is called the ad hominem ('to the person') fallacy: attacking the character or traits of the person making a claim instead of checking the claim itself. A claim's truth does not depend on who says it. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (iep.utm.edu/fallacy/); yourlogicalfallacyis.com/ad-hominem.

question: A doctor who is herself a heavy smoker tells a patient, 'Smoking is bad for your health and you should quit.' The patient laughs and says her advice must be wrong because she smokes too. Has the patient shown that the advice is false?
answer: No — her smoking makes her a hypocrite, but it does not change whether smoking harms health
choices: No — her smoking makes her a hypocrite, but it does not change whether smoking harms health
Yes — a person who smokes cannot give true medical advice about smoking
Yes — advice only counts if the person giving it follows it perfectly
No — but only because she is a doctor and doctors are always right
context: Calling out the doctor's hypocrisy is the 'tu quoque' (Latin for 'you too') flavor of ad hominem. The habit may make her a poor role model, yet the medical claim stands or falls on the evidence, not on her behavior. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (iep.utm.edu/fallacy/); yourlogicalfallacyis.com/ad-hominem.

question: A basketball coach tells his players, 'Never skip practice if you want to win.' One player shoots back, 'But YOU skipped practice all the time when you played!' The player thinks this settles it. What has the player actually proven about whether skipping practice hurts the team?
answer: That nothing changes, since his coach once skipping does not make skipping less harmful
choices: That nothing changes, since his coach once skipping does not make skipping less harmful
That his coach lost the right to give the advice the moment he ever skipped
That skipping is harmless, since his coach skipped it and still won his games
That the rule holds true only if his coach admits he was wrong to skip
context: This is the 'tu quoque' ('you too') reply: throwing the speaker's own past back at him instead of answering his point. The coach's old habit is fair to notice, but the claim stays true no matter who makes it. Source: study.com Tu Quoque Fallacy lesson; growthtactics.net/tu-quoque-fallacy/.

question: In a town debate, one speaker dismisses a group pushing to clean up the river by announcing, 'Their plan is worthless because they're all lazy, smelly tree-huggers.' He says nothing about the plan's costs, science, or results. What is wrong with using that line to defeat the plan?
answer: It throws insults at the people instead of giving any reason the plan would fail
choices: It throws insults at the people instead of giving any reason the plan would fail
It is too polite — a real rebuttal needs even harsher words about the group
It names the group's smell, when it should have named their political party
It works fine, because a plan is only as clean as the people proposing it
context: This is the 'abusive' ad hominem: pure name-calling used to dodge the point. The insult does nothing to show whether the cleanup plan is sound. Source: scribbr.com and quillbot.com FAQ on ad hominem; iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: A city councilman argues that the town should build a new convention center downtown. An opponent replies, 'His argument is no good — he owns property nearby and would get rich if it's built.' The opponent never addresses traffic, cost, or need. The councilman's stake is worth knowing, but what has the opponent failed to do?
answer: Show that the convention center is actually a bad idea on its own merits
choices: Show that the convention center is actually a bad idea on its own merits
Prove that the councilman truly owns the nearby property he mentioned
Find a second councilman who would also profit from the project
Insult the councilman harshly enough for the crowd to turn on him
context: This is the 'circumstantial' ad hominem: rejecting a position by pointing at the arguer's self-interest. A hidden stake is a real reason to double-check his claims, but it does not by itself prove the convention center is wrong. Source: scribbr.com Ad Hominem Fallacy; quillbot.com FAQ.

question: During the 2008 U.S. presidential campaign, vice-presidential candidate Sarah Palin repeatedly attacked Barack Obama by spotlighting that he had once associated with Bill Ayers, a 1960s radical from the Weather Underground. Suppose every word about that old acquaintance were true. Why would it still leave Obama's actual policy arguments standing?
answer: Who a person once knew does not show that the arguments he makes are wrong
choices: Who a person once knew does not show that the arguments he makes are wrong
Obama could simply deny ever having met Bill Ayers in the first place
Ayers was the one running for office, so the attack landed on him instead
A candidate's old friendships are private and may never be mentioned at all
context: Going after a man through his acquaintances is 'guilt by association,' a relative of the ad hominem. Even a true and ugly connection answers none of his actual arguments. Source: Wikipedia, Ad hominem (Sarah Palin 2008 / Bill Ayers example).

question: The French writer Voltaire wanted to wound his rival Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who had argued in his famous book on education that parents ought to raise their own children rather than farm them out. In a stinging 1764 pamphlet, Voltaire anonymously exposed the truth about where Rousseau had sent his own children. Where had they gone?
answer: He had handed every one of his children to a Paris foundling hospital
choices: He had handed every one of his children to a Paris foundling hospital
He had given his children over to his publisher's family to raise
He had left his children with their grandmother back in Geneva
He had sent his children to a monastery school far outside Paris
context: Rousseau really did place all five of his children in a Paris foundling hospital, and Voltaire exposed it anonymously in 1764. The hypocrisy stained Rousseau the moralist — but it never refuted his argument that parents should raise their own kids, which stands on its own. Source: philosophy.lander.edu/logic/person.html; Wikipedia, Jean-Jacques Rousseau; Wikipedia, Emile, or On Education.

question: Two debate fouls look alike. A scientist presents an idea. In the first, a critic snaps, 'You can't trust HER — she's a known liar,' aiming squarely at the scientist. In the second, the critic ignores the scientist and sneers, 'That idea is rubbish — a crackpot cult cooked it up two centuries ago.' The first foul is the ad hominem. The second commits a different fallacy. Why does that second attack fail to show the idea is false?
answer: Where an idea first came from has no bearing on whether it is true today
choices: Where an idea first came from has no bearing on whether it is true today
An idea two centuries old has simply had too long to be disproven by now
The critic insulted the cult's members rather than the scientist who spoke
A claim can be judged false only by the expert who first proposed it
context: Rejecting the idea by its disreputable origin is the 'genetic fallacy': dismissing a claim because of where it originally came from, even when its beginnings have nothing to do with its truth. Ad hominem targets the present arguer; the genetic fallacy targets the source. Source: quillbot.com and scribbr.com FAQ on ad hominem vs genetic fallacy; iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: The English philosopher John Locke put the phrase 'argumentum ad hominem' into wide use in his 1690 'Essay Concerning Human Understanding' — but he did NOT mean a cheap insult. Locke described a legitimate debate move. Which move did he have in mind?
answer: Pressing an opponent with consequences drawn from his own stated principles
choices: Pressing an opponent with consequences drawn from his own stated principles
Calling an opponent a fool until the crowd stops listening to him
Pointing out that an opponent stands to profit from his own position
Reminding an opponent that he once held the very view he now attacks
context: For Locke, arguing 'to the man' meant showing he contradicts his OWN beliefs — a fair and powerful move. The abusive insult-sense attached to the label only later. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (plato.stanford.edu/entries/fallacies/); David Hitchcock, McMaster University.

question: A lawyer cross-examines a witness whose testimony could decide the case, and brings out that the witness has a long, documented history of lying under oath. The philosopher Douglas Walton argued this kind of credibility attack is not automatically a fallacy. Drawing only on the witness's record of dishonesty, what may the lawyer soundly conclude?
answer: That this witness should not be trusted, though not that his story is automatically false
choices: That this witness should not be trusted, though not that his story is automatically false
That the witness is probably lying now, so his testimony can be thrown out as false
That the record settles nothing, since a person's honesty cannot bear on testimony
That the witness is certainly lying about every single detail of what he saw
context: When you weigh someone's TESTIMONY, their honesty is genuinely relevant — attacking credibility differs from assuming falsehood. Concluding 'do not trust' is sound; concluding 'therefore false' overreaches into the fallacy, and treating the record as irrelevant ignores how testimony works. Source: Wikipedia, Ad hominem (Douglas N. Walton; cross-examining a witness with a history of lying); iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: Two eyewitnesses each swear they watched a robbery happen across a dark street at midnight. The defense challenges the first by proving she is severely short-sighted. It challenges the second only by proving he has cheated on his wife. One challenge is a fair reason to doubt the account and one is the fallacy. Which challenge truly weakens the witness's account of the robbery?
answer: Proving the witness is severely short-sighted, a flaw that touches the very thing she claims
choices: Proving the witness is severely short-sighted, a flaw that touches the very thing she claims
Proving the witness cheated on his wife, a flaw that touches the very thing he claims
Neither challenge, because a sworn witness may never be questioned about anything
Both challenges, because any personal flaw makes any account worthless in court
context: The whole question is relevance. Poor eyesight bears directly on whether she could have witnessed a robbery across a dark street; private misconduct does not. Attacking a trait is fair only when the trait actually touches the claim. Source: philosophy.lander.edu/logic/person.html; Federal Rules of Evidence Rule 609.

question: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that whether a personal attack is fair depends entirely on context. Picture the SAME charge — a man's immoral private conduct — raised in two arguments. In which argument does that charge actually count?
answer: When deciding whether he should hold a leadership post on the city council
choices: When deciding whether he should hold a leadership post on the city council
When deciding whether his calculations about Kepler's astronomy are correct
When deciding whether the sun rises in the east as he claims
It never counts, since private conduct is always off-limits in any debate
context: A man's private conduct is irrelevant to his math about the planets, but relevant to whether he is fit to lead a council or church. The insult itself is never the point — relevance is the whole question. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (iep.utm.edu/fallacy/).

question: You eat dinner tonight because the butcher, the brewer, and the baker each sold you what they made. Adam Smith said the real reason they feed you is NOT that they pity you or wish you well. So why, in Smith's view, do they put food on your table?
answer: Because feeding you serves their own interest
choices: Because feeding you serves their own interest
Because the law requires them to sell to you
Because they were raised to be generous folk
Because the town would shame them otherwise
context: Smith's famous line: 'It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.' Each feeds you because it serves himself, not because he pities you. Source: Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Ch. II.

question: Adam Smith watched a small pin factory. One untrained man working alone could scarcely make a single pin in a whole day, yet ten men in that same factory together made about forty-eight thousand pins in a day. Smith pointed to the single change in how they worked that produced this enormous jump. What had the ten men done differently?
answer: They each did one small step instead of making whole pins
choices: They each did one small step instead of making whole pins
They worked far longer hours than the lone man did
They used a secret machine the lone man did not have
They were simply stronger and faster as workers
context: This is Smith's 'division of labour.' A lone untrained worker 'could scarcely make one pin a day, and certainly could not make twenty'; ten men splitting the job made roughly 48,000 between them, about 4,800 each. Splitting one job into many tiny jobs multiplied output thousands of times. Source: Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Ch. I.

question: Adam Smith said the habit of trading one thing for another is found in humans and in no other animal. To make the point he imagined a swap between two animals that, he insisted, has never once happened in nature. Which exchange did Smith say no one has ever seen?
answer: Two dogs swapping one bone fairly for another
choices: Two dogs swapping one bone fairly for another
Two horses splitting a field of hay between them
Two cats trading a caught mouse for a caught fish
Two birds dividing a worm evenly down the middle
context: Smith's exact image: 'Nobody ever saw a dog make a fair and deliberate exchange of one bone for another with another dog.' He traced the whole division of labour to one human quirk, 'the propensity to truck, barter, and exchange one thing for another,' found in no other animal. Source: Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Ch. II.

question: Adam Smith was so famously lost in thought that his biographers gathered stories of his absent-mindedness. In one, he made his usual hot morning drink by absent-mindedly dropping bread and butter into the pot, then drank the result and complained it tasted poor. What drink was he trying to make?
answer: Tea
choices: Tea
Ale
Cocoa
Coffee
context: Other tales have him walking straight into a tanning pit while talking and wandering 15 miles out of town in his nightgown, lost in thought. The man who explained how the whole economy hangs together could barely make a cup of tea. Source: John Rae, Life of Adam Smith (1895), as summarized in the anecdotes about his early life.

question: Adam Smith said that when you want a shopkeeper to sell you something, begging him with how badly YOU need it is exactly the wrong approach. Smith said there is one thing you should point out to him instead that actually moves him to deal. What is that one thing?
answer: What he himself stands to gain from the deal
choices: What he himself stands to gain from the deal
That you will recommend his shop to others
That you have been a loyal customer for years
That a fair man would give you a discount
context: Smith: 'We address ourselves, not to their humanity but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our necessities but of their advantages.' The whole pitch reduces to: 'Give me that which I want, and you shall have this which you want.' Source: Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Ch. II.

question: Adam Smith visited a pin factory where the job of making a single pin was split up and shared out among many different workers, each doing just one part of it. Smith was struck by how finely the work was divided. Roughly how many separate operations did Smith count in making one pin?
answer: About eighteen
choices: About eighteen
About four
About forty
About ninety
context: Smith counts about eighteen distinct operations done by different hands: 'One man draws out the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, a fourth points it, a fifth grinds it at the top for receiving the head...' — with even whitening the pins and packing them into paper as separate trades. No one worker makes a whole pin. Source: Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Ch. I.

question: Adam Smith said that once everyone specializes in a single craft, no one stays self-sufficient: the baker cannot live on bread alone, the weaver cannot wear only cloth. Smith gave a one-word name for what each person, now leaning on everyone else, effectively becomes. What was that word?
answer: A merchant
choices: A merchant
A servant
A debtor
A landlord
context: Smith's words: 'every man thus lives by exchanging, or becomes in some measure a merchant, and the society itself grows to be what is properly a commercial society.' A baker is really a merchant of bread; a smith, a merchant of nails. Once everyone specializes, everyone ends up a trader. Source: Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Ch. IV.

question: People remember Adam Smith for cold self-interest. But seventeen years before his famous book on markets, he wrote a whole earlier book on how people tell right from wrong. Far from preaching pure selfishness, that book rests on a single claim about human nature. Which claim did Smith build it on?
answer: We naturally share in the feelings of others
choices: We naturally share in the feelings of others
We act only to serve our own advantage
We are born already knowing right from wrong
We obey morality only from fear of God
context: The earlier book is The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759). It opens with the opposite idea from cold self-interest: we feel for people by imagining ourselves in their place. The same man who said the butcher acts from self-love also wrote that 'the chief part of human happiness arises from the consciousness of being beloved.' One mind, two halves. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Adam Smith's Moral and Political Philosophy; Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759).

question: Adam Smith described a merchant who cares only about his own profit and never once aims at helping the public. Yet by chasing his private gain, the merchant ends up serving everyone around him without meaning to. Smith said such a man is led by WHAT to promote a good he never intended?
answer: An invisible hand
choices: An invisible hand
A hidden bargain
A silent partner
A guiding fortune
context: Smith's most famous phrase: the merchant is 'led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention.' He 'neither intends to promote the public interest, nor knows how much he is promoting it,' yet by pursuing his own gain he serves everyone. Order arises with no designer aiming at it. Source: Wealth of Nations (1776), Book IV, Ch. II.

question: Adam Smith asked how a person can honestly judge whether their own conduct is fair, given that we all naturally take our own side. He answered with a test you could run in your own mind. To check whether your own behavior is fair, Smith said, what should you do?
answer: Picture how a fair, well-informed stranger would judge it
choices: Picture how a fair, well-informed stranger would judge it
Consult the rules your parents taught you as a child
Ask whether the act breaks any law of the land
Notice whether you feel proud or ashamed afterward
context: Smith called this imagined fair outsider 'the impartial spectator,' and the inner judge 'the man within the breast, the great judge and arbiter' of our conduct. Your conscience, in his picture, is you watching yourself through a calm stranger's fair eyes. Source: Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part III; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Adam Smith pictured a proud, unfeeling landlord gazing across his vast fields, imagining that he alone will consume the whole harvest they produce. Smith then deflates the fantasy with a single plain observation. What did Smith point out that forces the landlord to share the harvest after all?
answer: His stomach holds no more than a poor peasant's
choices: His stomach holds no more than a poor peasant's
His fields will rot without paid guards to watch them
His title can be stripped by the king at any time
His neighbors would gather in force and seize the surplus
context: Smith's jab: 'the capacity of his stomach bears no proportion to the immensity of his desires,' so the rich must hand the rest out to the workers who grow and prepare it. This is where Smith FIRST used 'invisible hand' (in 1759, not about markets at all): the rich, feeding only their vanity, are 'led by an invisible hand' to feed everyone else 'without intending it, without knowing it.' Source: Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part IV, Ch. I.

question: Adam Smith wrote the founding book making the case for free trade and against governments taxing the flow of goods. Yet in his final years the great free-trader accepted a senior Scottish post in the Crown's own tax service, a bitter irony for the man whose book had armed merchants against the taxman. Which revenue post did Smith, of all people, take?
answer: Commissioner of customs
choices: Commissioner of customs
Comptroller of customs
Surveyor of customs
Commissioner of excise
context: Smith was appointed a Commissioner of Customs in Scotland in 1778, the very job of taxing and policing imported goods. The man whose book launched the case against trade barriers spent his last years collecting the tariffs. Source: Britannica, The life and works of Adam Smith.

question: Maya looks out at dawn and sees the lawn glistening with water. She reasons: "If it rains, the grass gets wet. The grass is wet. So it must have rained last night." But her dad just laughs and shakes his head. Where did Maya's reasoning go wrong?
answer: Rain is just one road to a wet lawn -- the sprinkler could have run, so wet grass alone can't prove it rained
choices: Rain is just one road to a wet lawn -- the sprinkler could have run, so wet grass alone can't prove it rained
Her premise is false, because rain does not actually make grass wet in the way that she had assumed it would
She needed to check the forecast first, since past weather can never be known just from looking at the wet ground
Wet grass always means rain unless a cloud is visible, and she simply forgot to look up at the morning sky overhead
context: This is the marquee defeater for affirming the consequent ('If P then Q; Q; therefore P'). The grass IS wet, but the sprinkler ran -- rain is one path to a wet lawn, not the only one (hoses, dew, a burst pipe, a kid with a bucket all end at the same wet grass). The conditional names ONE cause; the wet lawn never testifies which cause showed up. Source: Wikipedia, 'Affirming the consequent' (sprinkler / wet-grass exposition).

question: Leo announces a proof: "If an animal is a dog, then it has four legs. My cat has four legs. Therefore my cat is a dog." Everyone groans. The logic feels airtight to Leo but lands as a joke. What exactly broke?
answer: Four legs is a trait shared by cats, horses, and tables alike -- that shared trait can't back-fill the one identity 'dog'
choices: Four legs is a trait shared by cats, horses, and tables alike -- that shared trait can't back-fill the one identity 'dog'
Dogs do not really have four legs in every single case, so the opening premise that he started from was simply untrue
He should have stopped to count his cat's legs again, because the whole claim depends on that exact number being right
A cat can become a dog only if it also barks aloud, and Leo forgot to test whether his cat makes the right kind of sound
context: The same backward step as the sprinkler, but laugh-out-loud obvious: four legs is a club with many members -- cats, horses, tables, spiders-minus-four -- and dog is only one of them. A shared trait (Q) never back-fills a specific identity (P). This is affirming the consequent. Source: Wikipedia, 'Affirming the consequent' (dog / four-legs example, verbatim).

question: A detective insists: "If someone lives in San Diego, then they live in California. Joe lives in California. Therefore Joe lives in San Diego." His partner shakes her head. Granting both of the detective's sentences, why can't that conclusion follow?
answer: Living in San Diego forces you into California, but living in California runs the other way -- it leaves which city wide open
choices: Living in San Diego forces you into California, but living in California runs the other way -- it leaves which city wide open
Living in San Diego does pin you to California, so by the very same rule living in California must pin you back to San Diego
Living in California really lands Joe in the state capital instead, since that is the one city the rule was actually pointing at
Living in California tells you nothing at all about Joe, because a state line can never narrow down where a single person resides
context: The absurdity is on display: California holds millions who never saw San Diego (Los Angeles, Sacramento, Fresno). Landing inside the big set (Q, California) does not place you in the small one (P, San Diego). The fallacy is affirming the consequent -- the wide category can't collapse into the narrow one. Source: Wikipedia, 'Affirming the consequent' (San Diego / California example, verbatim).

question: At a party someone hears a woman speaking Portuguese and concludes: "If she's Brazilian, she speaks Portuguese. She speaks Portuguese. So she's Brazilian." Portugal, Angola, and Mozambique are Portuguese-speaking too. What is the most her fluency can actually establish?
answer: Only that she might well be Brazilian -- the tongue is shared by several nations, so it's a clue, never a passport stamp
choices: Only that she might well be Brazilian -- the tongue is shared by several nations, so it's a clue, never a passport stamp
That she is definitely Brazilian, since speaking the national language is what citizenship in Brazil truly requires of her
Nothing whatsoever about her, because the language that a person speaks has no bearing at all on where that person is from
That she is really from Portugal instead, as Portuguese spoken abroad will always trace back to the original home country
context: The IEP's textbook case of affirming the consequent. Portugal, Angola, and Mozambique all speak Portuguese, so hearing it makes 'Brazilian' MORE PLAUSIBLE but never PROVEN -- evidence she might be, not proof she is. Note the answer rejects both overclaiming ('definitely') and the opposite error ('nothing at all'): the language really is a clue. Source: IEP, 'Fallacies' (Affirming the Consequent entry, example verbatim).

question: "If P then Q" runs only one way: P guarantees Q, but Q does not promise P. Yet the fallacy of affirming the consequent fools sharp people constantly. A logician explains that the mind quietly does one specific thing that makes the bad step feel valid. What is the hidden move?
answer: The mind secretly swaps it for the reverse, 'If Q then P', then runs valid reasoning on a converse it never actually earned
choices: The mind secretly swaps it for the reverse, 'If Q then P', then runs valid reasoning on a converse it never actually earned
The mind forgets the original premise entirely and then invents a brand-new rule that has nothing to do with either P or Q
The mind assumes that Q is false from the very outset, which quietly poisons every single step that follows in the argument
The mind treats P and Q as the very same statement, so it simply never notices that there were two separate ideas at all
context: The deep diagnosis: the fallacy is an illegal CONVERSE. The arguer quietly upgrades the one-way 'If P then Q' into the two-way 'If Q then P' and runs perfectly valid reasoning on the swap. It only 'works' if the converse is also true (P if and only if Q) -- and usually it isn't. That silent upgrade of a one-way claim into a two-way one is why the error hides. Source: Wikipedia, 'Affirming the consequent'; FallacyFiles, 'afthecon.html'.

question: A teacher concedes that affirming the consequent isn't worthless: wet grass really does make rain more likely, and speaking Portuguese really does make 'Brazilian' more plausible. So the reasoning gives something. Where precisely does it cross from acceptable into a genuine error?
answer: When it upgrades a mere clue into a proof -- treating 'she might be Brazilian' as if it had shown 'she truly is Brazilian'
choices: When it upgrades a mere clue into a proof -- treating 'she might be Brazilian' as if it had shown 'she truly is Brazilian'
When it mentions the weather at all, since rain and wet grass are simply far too unreliable to support any real inference
When more than a single premise ever appears, because a sound argument is allowed to rest upon only one lone stated fact
When the conclusion happens to turn out to be true, because a true conclusion is the surest sign that the logic was broken
context: The honest verdict: affirming the consequent gives WEAK inductive support -- a clue, a 'maybe.' Wet grass really does make rain more plausible; Portuguese really does make 'Brazilian' more plausible. The error is the OVERCLAIM -- treating the suspicion as proof, upgrading 'she might be' into 'she is.' The fallacy is the leap from clue to certainty, not the suspicion itself. Source: IEP, 'Fallacies' (the Portuguese conclusion as 'weak inductive evidence' that fails as deduction).

question: A scientist argues: "If my theory is true, this experiment will give result E. The experiment gave E. So my theory is true." Karl Popper noticed this reasoning has the exact shape of affirming the consequent. What did Popper say science must chase instead to make real progress?
answer: A failed prediction that kills a theory outright, since a rival could also predict E, so heaping up confirmations proves nothing
choices: A failed prediction that kills a theory outright, since a rival could also predict E, so heaping up confirmations proves nothing
The same successful experiment repeated many more times, until the sheer weight of all the matching results finally proves the theory
Whichever theory happened to predict result E the earliest, because the first correct prediction has the strongest claim to being true
An escape from messy experiments entirely, reasoning from pure logic alone, since observation can only ever mislead an investigator
context: The masquerade: hypothesis testing has the shape 'If theory H, then result E; E occurred; therefore H' -- literally affirming the consequent. A confirmed prediction never PROVES a theory, because a rival theory could predict the same E. This is exactly why Popper said science advances by FALSIFICATION: a failed prediction kills H by valid modus tollens, where piling up confirmations cannot. Source: Wikipedia, 'Hypothetico-deductive model'; useofreason.wordpress.com on the scientific method and affirming the consequent.

question: "If the patient has the flu, these symptoms appear. The symptoms are here. So it's the flu." Dozens of illnesses copy flu symptoms. One documented teenage girl had a neck lump that doctor after doctor pinned on mono for years. How did her case finally turn out?
answer: A biopsy revealed a malignancy that had been quietly growing the whole time her neck lump was being pinned on mono
choices: A biopsy revealed a malignancy that had been quietly growing the whole time her neck lump was being pinned on mono
A later blood test confirmed the mono after all, vindicating every physician who had read the lump as nothing worse
The lump simply faded once the mono ran its course, proving the early reading right and the long delay harmless in the end
A fresh round of antibiotics cleared a stubborn infection that each of the earlier doctors had somehow managed to miss
context: The deadliest real-world form: dozens of illnesses copy flu symptoms, so settling on the first matching cause is affirming the consequent -- and it has a body count. In the documented case, a teenage girl's neck lump was blamed on her mono by physician after physician for years, until one finally ordered a biopsy and found a malignancy that had been growing the whole time. Source: garlikov.com, 'False Cause, Misdiagnosis, and the Fallacy of Affirming the Consequent'; Redelmeier & Shafir, 'The Fallacy of a Single Diagnosis,' Medical Decision Making (2023).

question: Touch a flame to a tuft of cotton and it blackens and crumbles to ash. Everyone says the fire burned it. The Persian thinker Al-Ghazali flatly denied that the fire was the cause at all. So on his view, what actually does the burning?
answer: God creates the blackness and the ash directly; the fire merely sits there
choices: God creates the blackness and the ash directly; the fire merely sits there
The heat inside the fire forces itself into the cotton and tears it apart
The cotton's own dryness makes it destroy itself once it is warmed
The air feeds the flame, and together they consume the cotton
context: From the Seventeenth Discussion of The Incoherence of the Philosophers: 'The one who enacts the burning by creating blackness in the cotton... is God, either through the mediation of His angels or without mediation. As for fire, which is inanimate, it has no action.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Al-Ghazali', quoting Incoherence p.167; SEP 'Causation in Arabic and Islamic Thought'.

question: Al-Ghazali argued that the bond between fire and burning 'is not necessary.' His reason was about what we can and cannot witness. No matter how closely you watch the flame meet the cotton, he said, one crucial thing is never actually given to your eyes. Which thing do we never really see?
answer: The fire forcing the cotton to burn; we see only the two arrive together
choices: The fire forcing the cotton to burn; we see only the two arrive together
The heat itself, which does the real work yet never shows up to the eye
The instant of contact, which slips past too fast to fix in the eye
The hand of God behind the flame, the true cause hidden from every sense
context: Al-Ghazali: 'The connection between what is habitually believed to be a cause and what is habitually believed to be an effect is not necessary, according to us.' Burning following fire is a HABIT God keeps, not an iron law fire carries inside itself. Roughly 650 years later the Scottish philosopher David Hume made the same move, calling causation mere 'constant conjunction.' Source: IEP 'Al-Ghazali', quoting Incoherence p.166; SEP 'Occasionalism'.

question: Al-Ghazali pressed the philosophers who insisted that fire is the true agent of burning with a single hard demand: prove it. Show me, he said, that the fire is what produces the burning. According to him, what is the ONLY evidence they could ever actually point to?
answer: Watching the burning happen right when the cotton touches the fire -- nothing more
choices: Watching the burning happen right when the cotton touches the fire -- nothing more
The ancient and unbroken agreement of every philosopher before them
The measured heat the fire gives off, which no other thing can match
The way fire spreads to anything dry, proving the power is its own
context: Al-Ghazali: 'For what proof is there that it is the agent? They have no proof other than observing the occurrence of the burning at the [juncture of] contact with the fire.' Seeing one thing follow another is not seeing one thing PRODUCE another. Source: SEP 'Causation in Arabic and Islamic Thought', quoting al-Ghazali IP p.167.

question: Al-Ghazali had a reason for denying that fire burns by its own nature: he wanted to leave room for miracles. If fire MUST burn whatever it touches, then the holy stories become impossible. The Quran tells of Abraham thrown into a roaring fire that does not harm him. On Al-Ghazali's reading, why was Abraham unburned?
answer: God, for that once, simply did not create the burning He usually creates
choices: God, for that once, simply did not create the burning He usually creates
Abraham's faith hardened his skin against the reach of any flame
The fire still burned, but God healed each wound as fast as it formed
An angel stood between Abraham and the fire and absorbed the heat
context: In the Quran (21:69) God commands the fire to be 'cool and safe' for Abraham. If fire burned by its own nature, no exception could be possible -- so Al-Ghazali's whole point was to make the miracle thinkable: not a broken law of nature, but God for once withholding the burning He normally supplies. Source: thequran.love, 'Al-Ghazali's Occasionalism as a Quranic Philosophy of Nature'; motivation corroborated by SEP 'Occasionalism'.

question: Decades after Al-Ghazali argued that fire does not truly burn, the philosopher Averroes fired back with a reply titled, point for point, The Incoherence of the Incoherence. Strip the fire of its power to burn, he insisted, and you have not saved it -- you have wrecked it. What was his argument?
answer: A fire that cannot burn is simply no longer a fire at all
choices: A fire that cannot burn is simply no longer a fire at all
A fire that cannot burn would instantly go cold and cease to exist
God would never trouble to make a fire and then forbid it to act
A fire kept from burning would shed no light, and so amount to nothing
context: Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126-1198): 'one need not therefore deny fire its burning power so long as fire keeps its name and definition.' A thing that loses its power to act loses its very identity. He further charged that denying real causes destroys knowledge itself, since to KNOW a thing is to know it by its causes. Source: SEP 'Causation in Arabic and Islamic Thought', quoting Averroes, Incoherence of the Incoherence pp.318-19.

question: Modern scholars cannot agree on how far Al-Ghazali really meant to push his fire-and-cotton argument, and they split into two camps. One camp reads him as denying that creatures have ANY real power at all -- only God acts. What does the rival camp argue he actually meant?
answer: He aimed only to defend miracles, and may let fire keep a God-given power
choices: He aimed only to defend miracles, and may let fire keep a God-given power
He was writing in jest and never believed the fire argument himself
He meant it for fire alone, and granted full power to everything else
He later retracted the whole argument in his very last writings
context: Scholars split: the 'occasionalist reading' (Marmura) takes Al-Ghazali to deny creatures any real causal power. The other reading (Frank Griffel, Perler, Rudolph) argues he meant only to defend miracles and 'leaves open the possibility of some kind of genuine secondary causality in creatures' -- fire could really have a God-given power to burn, just not one that could ever bind God's hands. Source: SEP 'Occasionalism'.

question: In 1095 al-Ghazali held the most prestigious teaching chair in the Muslim world, lecturing to hundreds of students in Baghdad. Examining his own heart, he decided that all his learning and striving was really 'for fame and reputation,' and that this left him 'on the brink of Hellfire.' What did the most celebrated scholar of the age then do about it?
answer: Walked away from the chair and slipped out of the city
choices: Walked away from the chair and slipped out of the city
Stayed in the chair but vowed to teach for nobler ends
Took on still more students to outshine his rivals
Asked the ruler to grant him a richer teaching post
context: Al-Ghazali had been appointed to the Nizamiyya of Baghdad in July 1091 by the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk. At the peak of his fame he judged his own motives corrupt and abandoned the chair, giving away his fortune (keeping only enough to support his children) and announcing a pilgrimage to Mecca while secretly resolving to settle in Syria. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: al-Ghazali; al-Ghazali, Deliverance from Error (al-Munqidh min al-Dalal).

question: As a young student, al-Ghazali was robbed on the road of his bag of study-notes. He chased the bandit chief and begged for them back. The robber laughed: 'How can you call this knowledge when it is so easily taken away?' -- then handed the notes back. According to the story, what did al-Ghazali spend the next three years doing because of that taunt?
answer: Memorizing his notes so none could be stolen
choices: Memorizing his notes so none could be stolen
Hunting down the bandits to take back his honor
Copying his notes to hide them in many places
Guarding the road so no other student was robbed
context: This episode is a traditional account (told by al-Subki in the Tabaqat al-Shafi'iyya al-Kubra, and reportedly recounted by al-Ghazali himself), so it is best treated as legend. He later called the bandit 'an oracle whom God made to speak, in order that He could guide me through him' -- the seed of his lifelong distrust of borrowed, easily-lost knowledge. Source: al-Subki, Tabaqat al-Shafi'iyya al-Kubra (cited in al-islam.org, Narratives of the Veracious, 'Story 19: Ghazali and the Thieves').

question: Al-Ghazali was the most admired lecturer of his age, but as he wrestled with abandoning his Baghdad chair the crisis turned physical: for days he could neither swallow bread nor drink water. One morning he climbed to his chair to address the packed hall as he always had. By his own account, what happened to him there in front of everyone?
answer: No words would come, and he sat there silent
choices: No words would come, and he sat there silent
His memory of the lesson went suddenly blank
His legs buckled and he had to be carried out
His sight dimmed until the faces went dark
context: In Deliverance from Error, al-Ghazali writes that God 'caused an impediment to chain my tongue and prevented me from lecturing... my mouth became dumb' -- the most celebrated lecturer of the age physically could not speak before his class. He also reports, 'I could neither swallow a morsel of bread nor drink a drop of water.' His doubt had become bodily. Source: al-Ghazali, Deliverance from Error (al-Munqidh min al-Dalal), ghazali.org/books/md/gz101.htm.

question: Al-Ghazali, the most admired lecturer of his age, lay sick and unable to keep down food, and the doctors who examined him were baffled. Then they gave a verdict drawn straight from his own teaching, naming the true seat of his sickness. Where did the doctors say the real trouble lay?
answer: In his heart, which had sickened his whole body
choices: In his heart, which had sickened his whole body
In his soul, weighed down by a sin he could not name
In his mind, worn down by too much speculation
In a melancholy humour fallen out of balance
context: The doctors gave a diagnosis straight out of al-Ghazali's own philosophy: 'The mischief is in the heart, and has communicated itself to the whole organism; there is no hope unless the cause of his grievous sadness be arrested.' His ailment was spiritual doubt made flesh -- a sickness of the heart that no medicine of the body could reach. Source: al-Ghazali, Deliverance from Error (al-Munqidh min al-Dalal), ghazali.org/books/md/gz101.htm.

question: Before he could trust anything, al-Ghazali tried to doubt everything -- first the senses, then reason itself. His sharpest tool was sleep: while it lasts, what you experience seems completely real, and only afterward do you call it baseless fancy. From this he pressed one unsettling question. What was it?
answer: Whether waking life is itself a dream, seen from some higher state
choices: Whether waking life is itself a dream, seen from some higher state
Whether two sleepers can share one dream, dreamt at the same hour
Whether a hidden deceiver plants false dreams, night after night
Whether a dream can warn of real danger, sent from somewhere beyond
context: This is the dream argument, which al-Ghazali pressed centuries before Descartes used a version of it. He asked what assurance you have 'that you may not suddenly experience a state which would have the same relation to your waking state as the latter has to your dreaming' -- a higher state (the Sufi's vision, or death) that would expose present reason as illusion, just as waking exposes a dream. He says this 'thorough-going' skepticism gripped him for about two months. Source: al-Ghazali, Deliverance from Error, ghazali.org/books/md/gz101.htm (IEP quoting p.57).

question: Al-Ghazali's doubt left him trapped: he no longer trusted reason, yet reason was the only tool he had to argue his way back. He saw that you cannot use a proof to prove that proof itself can be trusted. So when his certainty at last returned, he insisted it had not come from any argument at all. How did he say his certainty came back?
answer: As a light God cast into his heart
choices: As a light God cast into his heart
As a habit of trust rebuilt over years
As a sudden calm he could not explain
As the word of a teacher he revered
context: Al-Ghazali presents this as a serious position, not a retreat: since proof cannot certify proof, certitude need not rest on argument at all. 'I owed my deliverance, not to a concatenation of proofs and arguments, but to the light which God caused to penetrate into my heart... To suppose that certitude can be only based upon formal arguments is to limit the boundless mercy of God.' This is the heart of his claim that demonstrative reason has limits and direct knowledge of God is its own path. Source: al-Ghazali, Deliverance from Error, ghazali.org/books/md/gz101.htm (IEP quoting p.57: 'it was the effect of a light which God Most High cast into my breast').

question: Karl Marx watched factory workers produce fine goods they could never afford, then go home to cramped rented rooms. He argued this was not just bad luck or low pay. What did Marx say this scene revealed about the worker's labour itself?
answer: The same labour that builds the rich man's world of beauty builds the worker's own ruin and poverty
choices: The same labour that builds the rich man's world of beauty builds the worker's own ruin and poverty
The worker simply had not yet bargained hard enough for a fairer share of the wages
The factory was badly run, and a better-managed shop would have housed its workers well
The worker should take pride in fine work even when the fruits all go to another man
context: From Marx's most retellable passage on estranged labour: 'It produces palaces, but for the worker, hovels. It produces beauty, but for the worker, deformity... It produces intelligence, but for the worker, stupidity, cretinism.' The man who fashions beautiful things will never live among them. Source: Marx, Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, 'Estranged Labour' (marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1844/manuscripts/labour.htm).

question: Karl Marx saw a stark arithmetic in the factory and stated it as an exact proportion: as the value of the world of THINGS the worker produces keeps rising, what did Marx say happens to the worker himself?
answer: He grows ever cheaper, the more wealth he piles up, the less he is worth
choices: He grows ever cheaper, the more wealth he piles up, the less he is worth
He grows more skilled, and that rising skill slowly lifts his standing
He holds his value, since his daily wage is fixed whatever he produces
He gains the upper hand, since the boss now leans on his record output
context: Marx's lines: 'The worker becomes an ever cheaper commodity the more commodities he creates,' and 'The devaluation of the world of men is in direct proportion to the increasing value of the world of things.' The man himself is cheapened by the very abundance he produces. Source: Marx, 1844 Manuscripts, 'Estranged Labour'.

question: Karl Marx asked a simple question about factory work: when does the worker actually feel like himself? He answered that the man feels at home only when he is NOT working, and the moment he clocks in that feeling vanishes. What did Marx say this told us about the work itself?
answer: It is not freely chosen but forced, work a man does only because he must, not because it is his
choices: It is not freely chosen but forced, work a man does only because he must, not because it is his
It is honest toil that builds a man's character precisely because it is hard and unwanted
It is merely tiring, the ordinary fatigue that any real effort brings at the end of a day
It is a fair trade, unpleasant hours that a man willingly swaps for the wage they earn
context: Marx's words: 'He feels at home when he is not working, and when he is working he does not feel at home. His labour is therefore not voluntary, but coerced; it is forced labour.' This is the second alienation, from the very act of working. Source: Marx, 1844 Manuscripts, 'Estranged Labour'.

question: Karl Marx offered a test for whether a job is truly your own or really belongs to someone else: watch what the worker does the instant all compulsion is removed, no foreman, no threat, no need. If the work is genuinely his, he keeps going. Marx claimed that in the factory, the moment that pressure lifts, the worker does what?
answer: Flees the work at once, shunning it like the plague the second nothing forces him on
choices: Flees the work at once, shunning it like the plague the second nothing forces him on
Keeps working steadily on, having grown to love the very rhythm of the line
Slows down only a little, but stays at it out of plain loyalty to his workmates
Works all the harder, freed at last to show what he can really do unwatched
context: Marx: 'as soon as no physical or other compulsion exists, labour is shunned like the plague.' His chiasmus captures it: 'The worker therefore only feels himself outside his work, and in his work feels outside himself.' If you stop the second the foreman leaves, the work was never yours. Source: Marx, 1844 Manuscripts, 'Estranged Labour'.

question: Karl Marx described the first and strangest break between a worker and his job, the break from the very thing he makes. The worker pours his hours, his strength, his life into an object. Then, once it is finished and carried off to be sold, something flips in the bond between the man and his own creation. How did Marx say the finished product now stands toward the worker?
answer: As an alien, hostile power, a thing of his own making that now stands over him, no longer his
choices: As an alien, hostile power, a thing of his own making that now stands over him, no longer his
As a fading memory, soon forgotten once the next order comes rolling down the line
As a quiet trophy, proof of a hard day's skill he can still carry home with pride
As a shared possession, partly the firm's now and partly still the worker's own
context: Marx: the product of labour 'confronts it as something alien, as a power independent of the producer.' And the cruel twist: 'The worker becomes all the poorer the more wealth he produces.' The richer the world of things he makes, the poorer he himself becomes. Source: Marx, 1844 Manuscripts, 'Estranged Labour'.

question: Karl Marx drew a haunting reversal in the alienated worker. A human being, he thought, should feel most alive and most himself when creating something, for that is the human act. Yet Marx said the factory turns this upside down. WHEN, across the worker's whole day, did Marx say the man finally feels free?
answer: Only in his animal moments of eating, drinking, and resting
choices: Only in his animal moments of eating, drinking, and resting
Only when the foreman has gone and he can at last slack off and chat
Only on payday, when the wage makes the long, grinding week feel briefly worth it
Only on his one day of rest, away from the factory gates entirely
context: Marx's darkest image: 'man only feels himself freely active in his animal functions, eating, drinking, procreating... and in his human functions he no longer feels himself to be anything but an animal.' Free only when feeding and sleeping; an animal precisely at the workbench, which should be where a human is most himself. Source: Marx, 1844 Manuscripts, 'Estranged Labour'.

question: Karl Marx traced alienation outward to a fourth break, not from the product or the work, but from other people. If the thing I make is not mine, Marx reasoned, then it must belong to some other man who did not make it. Follow that logic, Marx said, and you reach a startling conclusion about the worker's tie to the man who owns what he makes. What did Marx claim the worker's own labour does to that bond?
answer: It forges the master, the worker's own toil creating the owner's very power over him
choices: It forges the master, the worker's own toil creating the owner's very power over him
It slowly levels them, each day's labour narrowing the gap between worker and owner
It makes them partners, owner and worker bound together in one shared, mutual venture
It earns the owner's debt, a gratitude the boss is bound to repay in steady work
context: In Marx's structure the worker, by his own estranged labour, 'creates the relationship' of the non-worker, the capitalist, to that labour. The worker forges the very master who then stands over him. This fourth alienation, from other men, follows logically from the first three. Source: Marx, 1844 Manuscripts, 'Estranged Labour'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx.

question: Karl Marx asked what truly separates a human worker from a spider spinning its web or a bee building its comb. The animal, he said, is fused with its task; it does not separate itself from what it does, it simply IS that activity. A human is different. According to Marx, what can a person do with his own life's activity that an animal cannot?
answer: Hold it up before his mind and choose it, stepping back to plan and freely decide how to work
choices: Hold it up before his mind and choose it, stepping back to plan and freely decide how to work
Perform it faster and far longer, outlasting any animal through sheer dogged endurance
Pass it down by teaching it, handing the skill on to the next generation in plain words
Repeat it without a single flaw, never tiring of the same motion the way an animal does
context: This rests on Marx's idea of 'species-being' (Gattungswesen): an animal 'is immediately one with its life activity. It is not distinct from that activity; it is that activity,' but 'Man makes his life activity itself an object of his will and of his consciousness.' Estranged factory labour steals exactly this, turning conscious, chosen creation into a numbing, dictated fragment. Source: Marx, 1844 Manuscripts; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx.

question: Karl Marx pointed to a second mark of truly human work, the kind the assembly line strips away. An animal, he noted, builds only when hunger or instinct drives it, and always to the one fixed pattern of its kind, a bird's nest is a bird's nest.
