The point of the scene is that no one — not Caesar, not even his own grieving son — could take from Cato the one freedom he most cared about: the freedom to end his life on his own terms. Source: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger 70 (Perrin trans., 1919), Perseus Digital Library.

question: Cato the Younger killed himself at Utica rather than accept a pardon from Julius Caesar, the man who had beaten him in war. Caesar had wanted badly to spare Cato, and to be seen as the one who spared him. When word reached Caesar that Cato had died by his own hand, he cried out a single bitter line that turned the loss back on Cato himself. What did Caesar say?
answer: O Cato, I begrudge thee thy death, for thou didst begrudge me the sparing of thy life
choices: O Cato, I begrudge thee thy death, for thou didst begrudge me the sparing of thy life
O Cato, you have robbed Rome of her last honest man, and robbed me of a friend
O Cato, even in death you call me tyrant, and even in death I cannot answer you
O Cato, the gods loved you better than Rome did, and better than I ever could
context: Caesar's words — 'O Cato, I begrudge thee thy death; for thou didst begrudge me the sparing of thy life' — prove Cato's reasoning was exactly right. Cato had died precisely so that Caesar could never claim the glory, or the right, of saving him. The mercy Caesar wanted to perform was the very thing Cato refused to let him own, and Caesar understood that he had been beaten at it. Source: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger 72 (Perrin trans., 1919), Perseus Digital Library.

question: Julius Caesar offered to pardon Cato the Younger, his defeated enemy, and let him live. Cato refused the pardon and chose death instead. He did not argue that life under Caesar would be miserable, nor that he was too proud to be spared. His reason, Plutarch reports, cut deeper: to accept the pardon would itself concede something to Caesar that Cato would never grant. What was it?
answer: That Caesar had the right to spare him, as if his life were Caesar's to give back
choices: That Caesar had the right to spare him, as if his life were Caesar's to give back
That Caesar was the lawful ruler of Rome and the war had settled the question
That Caesar deserved gratitude, which an honest enemy could not honestly feel
That Caesar might later demand a service in return that Cato could not refuse
context: In Plutarch's account Cato says he is 'unwilling to be under obligations to the tyrant for his illegal acts,' adding that Caesar 'acts illegally in saving, as if their master, those over whom he has no right at all to be the lord.' To accept a pardon is to admit the pardoner had the standing to grant it — that your life was his to give back. Cato refused to concede Caesar that ownership. For the later Stoics this made him their model: virtue alone is the true good, while life itself is only a 'preferred indifferent,' so integrity could rightly outweigh survival. Source: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger 66 (Perrin trans., 1919), Perseus Digital Library; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Stoicism.'

question: A fortune-teller points to three predictions she got exactly right and calls them proof of her gift. She has been making predictions for years. Before you believe her, what do you most need from her?
answer: Every prediction she has ever made, so you can count the ones that flopped against the ones that landed
choices: Every prediction she has ever made, so you can count the ones that flopped against the ones that landed
A fresh prediction made on the spot, since a brand-new hit would settle whether her gift is real
The names of the three people whose futures she correctly foresaw, to check that they back her story
An explanation of the method she uses, so you can judge whether her way of seeing the future is sound
context: This is the heart of cherry-picking, also called suppressed evidence: counting the hits and forgetting the misses. Three correct calls mean nothing on their own; you need the full denominator, every prediction she made, to see whether she beats chance. A record built only from the successes fakes the record. The fix is never to argue about the hits; it is to demand them all and count the flops. Source: The Skeptic's Field Guide, Observational Selection; Wikipedia, Cherry picking (psychics example).

question: A tonic-seller papers his page with glowing five-star reviews from customers who swear his remedy cured them. Every review is real and truthful. A friend says the wall of happy customers proves the tonic works. What is wrong with that?
answer: You cannot tell if it works from successes alone; you need how many tried it and how many it failed
choices: You cannot tell if it works from successes alone; you need how many tried it and how many it failed
A wall this large took years to gather, so the early reviews may describe a weaker, older formula
A crowd of cured customers this big has to mean something, so the sheer number of them settles it
The customers felt better for reasons of their own, which has nothing to do with the tonic at all
context: Each testimonial may be perfectly true, yet the wall still lies, because it is a curated slice. A pile of genuine hits with the misses filtered out is still cherry-picking. To judge a remedy you need the failures too: how many tried it and how many it did nothing for. A bouquet of success stories is not evidence that it works. Source: Wikipedia, Cherry picking (advertising/selective attention); The Skeptic's Field Guide, Observational Selection.

question: A boy keeps no record of his weekly horoscopes; he just remembers, at year-end, that they seemed to nail his mood again and again. A skeptic bets that if the boy had logged every one, the score would look like a coin flip. What flaw in relying on memory would make a worthless horoscope feel like a winner?
answer: Memory holds on to the weeks it seemed to hit and quietly drops the many weeks it plainly missed
choices: Memory holds on to the weeks it seemed to hit and quietly drops the many weeks it plainly missed
Memory rewrites the past to fit beliefs, so he recalls moods that match what he wanted to be told
Memory blurs one week into another, so a single striking hit gets spread across the whole year
Memory favors recent events, so the last few accurate weeks color how he judges all the earlier ones
context: Skeptics call this observational selection: casual readers of magazine horoscopes often see accurate predictions where none exist, because they notice the matches and forget the misses. This time the boy fools himself rather than being fooled by a seller, but it is the same move, counting the hits and forgetting the misses. Keeping a written log defeats it, because the page cannot quietly drop the failures the way memory does. Source: The Skeptic's Field Guide, Observational Selection; Wikipedia, Cherry picking.

question: Diagoras of Melos, an ancient Greek freethinker, was shown a temple wall covered with painted tablets from sailors who had prayed to the gods and then survived shipwreck. Here, his hosts said, was proof the gods answer prayers. Diagoras gave a one-line reply that gutted the whole display. What did he point out?
answer: The sailors who prayed and drowned are painted nowhere, so the wall shows only the ones who lived
choices: The sailors who prayed and drowned are painted nowhere, so the wall shows only the ones who lived
The sailors thanked the gods for luck that the sea, not any god, had handed them by sheer chance
The sailors would have survived the very same storms whether or not they had stopped to pray at all
The sailors painted those tablets themselves, so the wall proves only that grateful men like to boast
context: This story, told around the 5th century BC, is the textbook ancestor of suppressed evidence and of survivorship bias: the drowned left no tablets, so the wall was a wall of hits with every miss erased. Cicero preserves the line in De Natura Deorum, Book III, that the men who prayed and drowned are not painted anywhere. Recorded as ancient testimony about Diagoras. Source: Cicero, De Natura Deorum, Book III, via Wikipedia, Diagoras of Melos.  (Legend.)

question: Nostradamus, a 16th-century writer, left hundreds of short verses, none naming a checkable date or event. Admirers wait until after a disaster, then hold up a verse they say predicted it. A scholar grants that it can be read to fit, yet says the feat is worthless. What is the scholar seeing that the admirers are not?
answer: Hundreds of verses matched nothing and are never counted, so a stray hit among them proves no foresight at all
choices: Hundreds of verses matched nothing and are never counted, so a stray hit among them proves no foresight at all
The disaster was so large that almost any grim verse would have seemed to point toward it afterward
Reading a prophecy backward is unfair, since a real seer should be judged only on warnings given in advance
A verse written four centuries ago cannot speak to modern events the writer could never have imagined
context: This is the same hit-and-miss fraud run backwards, called postdiction: you wait for an event, then hunt hundreds of vague verses for one you can bend to match it, ignoring the thousands of lines that fit nothing. After 9/11, enthusiasts dug up quatrains they claimed foretold the attack; scholars of his text rejected every reading. A prophet who never made a checkable prediction looks uncanny only because the misses are never counted. Popular legend about his verses, not a documented prophecy. Source: Wikipedia, Nostradamus in popular culture; Discovery UK, Which Nostradamus Predictions Came True?

question: In World War II, officers studied bombers that came home riddled with bullet holes across the wings and fuselage, and wanted to bolt extra armor onto exactly those spots. The statistician Abraham Wald told them they had it backwards: armor the engines, where the returning planes showed almost no holes. Why the engines?
answer: Planes hit in the engine never made it home, so the spared spots on the survivors mark the deadly hits
choices: Planes hit in the engine never made it home, so the spared spots on the survivors mark the deadly hits
Engines are the costliest part to rebuild, so guarding them saved the air force the most money each month
A wounded engine fails slowly, giving the crew time to bail out only if the armor can buy a few minutes
The engine sits where a crew can never reach it mid-flight, so it is the one part they cannot patch in air
context: The returning bombers were a survivor-only sample, so the holes you could see marked the hits a plane could take and still fly home. As Wald saw it, the missing bullet holes were on the missing planes: the armor goes where the bullet holes aren't, on the engines. The data you don't have points to where the danger really is. Wald worked at the Statistical Research Group near Columbia University. Source: Jordan Ellenberg, How Not to Be Wrong; War History Online, Abraham Wald.

question: A swindler mails a stock tip to 1,000 strangers: half the letters predict the stock will rise, half predict it will fall. He keeps only the 500 he got right, splits them in two, and mails opposite tips again, round after round. A few marks end up having seen six correct calls in a row and now trust him completely. How is the streak fake even though every call they saw was true?
answer: Pruning the pool after each round leaves a lucky few who, by chance alone, were fed nothing but hits all along
choices: Pruning the pool after each round leaves a lucky few who, by chance alone, were fed nothing but hits all along
Beating a coin flip six straight times is so unlikely that real skill is the only way to explain the run
Six correct calls in a row is far too few to mean anything, since chance alone produces such runs all the time
The marks remember the hits more vividly than the misses, so the streak feels longer to them than it really was
context: He never predicts anything; he lets selection manufacture a winning streak. Every wrong call is mailed to someone else and quietly discarded, so each surviving mark has seen nothing but hits, then he asks for money. The streak is real to the victim and meaningless overall, because no one mark ever sees the misses that went to the others. Regulators warn about exactly this mailing scam. Source: SEC Investor Publication, Wrong Numbers and Stock Tips; Benya Clark and Paul English explainers.

question: A speaker shows a chart proving a long-rising measurement has gone flat for a decade. Every number on it is accurate. A statistician studies it and warns that an accurate chart can still be framed to tell a lie, and that this flat stretch smells like one. To catch a trick of this kind yourself, what is the first question to ask about the chart?
answer: Why does the line start in that particular year, rather than a few years before or after?
choices: Why does the line start in that particular year, rather than a few years before or after?
Were any of the plotted data points left out or quietly rounded off to smooth the line?
Did the same person both gather the measurements and decide how to draw the chart?
Is the measurement itself one that experts in the field actually trust as accurate?
context: Choosing an extreme year as your starting point can fake a trend reversal even when every number is true. The clearest documented case began the chart at one record-high year to make the following years look flat; sliding the start one year earlier or later brought the rising trend right back. The lesson is general and apolitical: a hand-picked endpoint can manufacture or erase almost any trend, so always ask why the line starts there. Source: NOAA Climate.gov, Did global warming stop in 1998?; Wikipedia, Cherry picking (endpoint example).

question: Two lawyers each leave evidence out of a closing argument. Maria omits the weather on the day of the crime, which has no bearing on who did it. Daniel omits the one eyewitness whose account points away from his client. A judge says only one of them has cheated, not both. What separates the honest cut from the dishonest one?
answer: Hiding proof that bears on the verdict and cuts against your side is the cheat; cutting what cannot sway it is not
choices: Hiding proof that bears on the verdict and cuts against your side is the cheat; cutting what cannot sway it is not
Maria cheated too, because any fact a lawyer chooses to hide is a fact the jury had a right to weigh for itself
Neither cheated, since a closing argument is meant to be one-sided and the jury hears the other lawyer anyway
Daniel cheated only because his missing fact was an eyewitness, the single most powerful kind of proof there is
context: Honest focus is not cherry-picking. The line is drawn by relevance and direction: you may set aside data that genuinely does not bear on the question, but you may not bury data that is relevant and cuts against you. This is the requirement of total evidence, a sound judgment must rest on all the relevant evidence, especially the inconvenient part, because, as Peter Suber notes, the arguments on the other side may be the stronger ones. The test: would including what they dropped change the conclusion? Then dropping it was the fallacy. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies, Suppressed Evidence; Peter Suber on one-sidedness, cited in Wikipedia, Cherry picking.

question: When Karl Marx looks at the everyday claim "this coat is worth two shirts," he says the price looks like a plain fact about the cloth, as natural a feature of the coat as its color. But Marx argues the number is secretly standing in for something the two objects hide from the shopper. What does a commodity's price actually measure?
answer: The work people put into making each item, and the human ties behind that work
choices: The work people put into making each item, and the human ties behind that work
A built-in worth the coat carries inside it, as much its own as its color or shape
An honest bargain two shoppers strike by haggling until both walk away content
A rank of rarity set by how scarce the wool and the cotton happen to be that year
context: This is Marx's idea of commodity fetishism. He wrote that 'a definite social relation between men... assumes, in their eyes, the fantastic form of a relation between things' — saying 'this coat is worth two shirts' feels like a fact about the cloth, but it is really a fact about the human labor poured into each. Marx even borrowed the word 'fetish' (Portuguese 'feitico,' a charm or made thing) from accounts of cult objects, to capture people bowing to things they themselves made. Source: Marx, Capital Vol. I, Ch. 1 sec. 4, 'The Fetishism of Commodities and the Secret Thereof' (1867), marxists.org.

question: Karl Marx's most quoted line gets hurled as a put-down: "religion is the opium of the people." Snipped from its sentence and read with today's ears, it sounds like contempt for believers. But Marx wrote in the 1840s, and the comparison turned on what "opium" meant to a reader of his day. What did the word mean then?
answer: An ordinary legal medicine of the era, taken to dull real pain
choices: An ordinary legal medicine of the era, taken to dull real pain
A banned street drug that gangs smuggled in and pushed on the poor
A rare, costly luxury that only the idle rich could ever afford
A pleasure-drug the decadent smoked in dens for an idle high
context: In the 1840s opium and laudanum were ordinary legal painkillers, so the comparison meant 'relief that dulls pain,' not 'addictive poison.' Marx did not even coin the image — he inherited it: Novalis called religion an 'opiate' in 1798, and the poet Heinrich Heine wrote of religion as 'spiritual opium' in 1840. Read in full, Marx casts faith as a comfort the suffering reach for ('the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world'), not a swindle the powerful invent. Source: Wikipedia, 'Opium of the people'; Marx, A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Introduction (1844), marxists.org.

question: Karl Marx grants that religion eases the misery of the poor, like a painkiller for real pain. Many who later marched under his banner concluded the first job was to stamp out faith itself. Marx disagreed about where to aim the blow. For Marx, what is the real cure?
answer: Heal the underlying misery itself, so the comfort it produces is no longer wanted
choices: Heal the underlying misery itself, so the comfort it produces is no longer wanted
Outlaw faith and punish those who keep clinging to it once the truth is laid bare
Protect the comfort, but expose and tear down the priests who profit from it
Give the poor a better and truer faith, one worth believing in, to hold onto
context: For Marx the painkiller is not the disease: abolishing 'religion as the illusory happiness of the people is the demand for their real happiness.' He wanted to fix the material misery underneath so the comfort would no longer be needed — the imaginary flowers are plucked off the chain not to leave a man bare, 'but so that he shall throw off the chain and pluck the living flower.' On this reading (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Karl Marx,' sec. 1.2) religion is a response to material alienation and would 'wither away' once that is emancipated. Source: Marx, A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right (1844), marxists.org; SEP, plato.stanford.edu/entries/marx/.

question: One morning Mara reaches past the coffee and pours herself tea, the way she likes it, with nobody in the room. That afternoon a robber jams a gun against her ribs and growls, 'Sign the money over.' Her hand shakes as she signs. In both moments something made her act. Which moment is the one where she did NOT act freely?
answer: The signing, because the robber forced her hand against her own will
choices: The signing, because the robber forced her hand against her own will
The tea, because her morning mood had quietly decided it for her
Both moments, because something caused each of the two actions
Neither moment, because in each one she still moved her own hand
context: The vivid handle of compatibilism: 'free' means UNFORCED and acting on your own will, not 'uncaused.' Mara's tea was caused by her own tastes, yet nobody forced her, so she chose freely; the signing was coerced, done against her will at gunpoint. The lesson: it is COERCION (the gun), not mere CAUSATION, that kills freedom. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Compatibilism' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/compatibilism/).

question: John Locke imagined a man carried into a room while fast asleep and quietly locked in. He wakes beside a dear friend he is overjoyed to see, chooses to stay and talk the whole evening, and never once tries the door, certain the whole time that he is acting freely. He never learns the door was bolted all along. Locke used the sleeper to argue that the freedom worth caring about turns on which thing?
answer: Whether he is doing the very thing he wills to do
choices: Whether he is doing the very thing he wills to do
Whether the door he sits behind is truly unlocked
Whether he could prove the room was bolted shut
Whether a friend, not a stranger, shares the room
context: Locke's locked-room intuition pump: the man genuinely chooses to stay, and he is doing exactly what he wills, so in the way that matters he acts freely, even though he COULD not have left. Locke's lesson is that the freedom we prize is doing what you will, not having the door unlocked. Source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Bk. II ch. 21 sec. 10; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Free Will' (iep.utm.edu/freewill/).

question: Thomas Hobbes wanted to strip freedom down to its barest bones, with no mystery left in it. Liberty, he wrote, is nothing but 'the absence of external impediments of motion' — a man is free whenever he meets 'no stop' in doing what he has the will or desire to do. To drive the point home Hobbes said a free man and one ordinary thing in nature are free in the very same sense. Which thing did Hobbes pick?
answer: A river running downhill
choices: A river running downhill
An arrow loosed from a bow
A stone rolling down a slope
Smoke rising from a fire
context: Hobbes gave the bluntest compatibilist line of all: a free man and a running river are free in exactly the same sense, since for each one nothing OUTSIDE blocks its motion. The river is utterly governed by causes (gravity, its banks) yet still counts as free, because for Hobbes freedom is just the absence of external impediment, not the absence of cause. Source: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, ch. 21, quoted via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Compatibilism.'

question: David Hume called free will 'the most contentious question of the most contentious science,' then claimed he could end the whole quarrel between those who say our choices are caused and those who say our choices are free. Hume's surprising diagnosis was that the centuries of fighting rested on a single confusion. What did Hume say the dispute had really been, all along?
answer: A quarrel over words, in which both sides secretly agree
choices: A quarrel over words, in which both sides secretly agree
A clash that only careful new experiments could settle
A real conflict in which one whole side was mistaken
A puzzle too deep for the human mind to ever resolve
context: Hume's 'reconciling project': he held that 'the whole dispute... has been hitherto merely verbal,' a tangle over the WORD 'liberty' rather than a real disagreement. He defined liberty as 'a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will' — once you fix the word that way, he argued, everyone secretly already agrees, and causation and freedom stop looking like rivals. Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 8 'Of Liberty and Necessity' (davidhume.org/texts/e/8; E 8.23).

question: Harry Frankfurt described two men hooked on the same drug by the very same chemistry, both helplessly craving it. The first man HATES his craving and fights it the whole way down, taking the drug only because the addiction overpowers him. The second man fully approves of his craving and would gladly take the drug even if he could shake it off. Frankfurt said only one of them takes the drug of his OWN free will. Which one, and why?
answer: The second, because the will he acts on is the very will he wants to have
choices: The second, because the will he acts on is the very will he wants to have
The first, because fighting the craving proves his will is still his own
Neither, because the same chemistry equally enslaves both of the men
Both, because each one in the end performs the same bodily action
context: Frankfurt's three-addicts case. For Frankfurt a will is FREE not when it dodges causes but when it has the right STRUCTURE: a person can step back and form a 'second-order' wish about which desire he wants to move him. The unwilling addict's will is 'not his own,' so he is unfree; the willing addict's will matches what he wants to want, so he acts freely, same chemistry, opposite freedom. A creature that never asks which craving it wants to be moved by, Frankfurt called a 'wanton.' Source: Harry Frankfurt, 'Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person,' Journal of Philosophy 68 (1971): 5-20.

question: Critics press the compatibilist hard: if the past plus the laws of nature fixed what you actually did, then you could NEVER have done otherwise, so how can the choice be free? G. E. Moore offered a rescue by re-reading what that very phrase, 'I could have done otherwise,' really claims. On Moore's reading, what does the phrase actually mean?
answer: That I would have done otherwise, if I had chosen to
choices: That I would have done otherwise, if I had chosen to
That I would have done otherwise, even with the past unchanged
That some uncaused power in me could have overridden the past
That nobody watching me could have predicted what I would do
context: This is the 'conditional analysis,' with G. E. Moore as its named defender. 'I could have done otherwise' is read as 'I WOULD have, IF I had chosen to' — and since nothing was stopping you from choosing differently in that hypothetical sense, the freedom we care about survives even if the past fixed what you in fact chose. (The second choice is the rival LIBERTARIAN reading: same past, yet a different act was genuinely open.) Daniel Dennett pushed Moore's spirit in 'Elbow Room: The Varieties of Free Will Worth Wanting' (1984): the valuable freedom is deliberating and responding to reasons, and demanding a freedom from physics on top of that is wanting magic, not liberty. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Free Will'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Compatibilism.'

question: Peter van Inwagen built the sharpest case AGAINST the compatibilist, his Consequence Argument. It runs: your acts today are the consequences of the laws of nature together with events in the remote past; you have no say over those ancient events, and no say over what the laws of nature are; so your present acts are not up to you either. A compatibilist who still wants to call you free cannot simply wave this away. To resist the argument, what must the compatibilist insist on?
answer: That having no say over the causes need not carry down to the act
choices: That having no say over the causes need not carry down to the act
That the buried past can, after all, still be reached and altered
That a fully determined choice can be neither forced nor unforced
That the laws of nature must leave a little room for pure chance
context: Van Inwagen's Consequence Argument is widely regarded as the STRONGEST objection to compatibilism, and a hard incompatibilist who accepts every step is making no mistake at all. Its engine is a transfer idea: if you lack control over the past and the laws, that lack of control flows DOWN to whatever they entail, namely your acts. The compatibilist grants determinism, so cannot deny the past or the laws; the only real foothold is to deny that 'up to you' transfers in that way, holding that freedom means acting on your own unforced will rather than controlling the laws of physics. (Reaching for 'room for chance' is the rival LIBERTARIAN escape, not the compatibilist's.) Source: Peter van Inwagen, 'The Incompatibility of Free Will and Determinism' (1975) / An Essay on Free Will (1983), via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Free Will.'

question: A new coach signs the five highest-scoring players in the league and promises the owner an unbeatable team. By the playoffs the team is a mess, beaten by clubs with lesser names. Where did the coach's reasoning slip?
answer: He assumed strengths that hold for each player must hold for the team they form
choices: He assumed strengths that hold for each player must hold for the team they form
He assumed a team plays only as well as its single weakest member allows
He assumed scoring talent matters far more than defending or passing does
He assumed five star players would mesh instantly with no time to practice
context: This is the fallacy of composition: reasoning from the parts up to the whole. Five ball-dominant stars can wreck the passing and chemistry; you want skills that COMPLEMENT each other, not five players all wanting the ball. Best individual players can make a bad team. Source: Critikid, The Composition Fallacy (critikid.com/composition-fallacy).

question: A builder argues: 'This finished wall is enormously heavy. The wall is made entirely of bricks. So each single brick in it must be enormously heavy too.' He is wrong. Why does his reasoning fail?
answer: He assumed a trait of the whole wall must belong to each brick within it
choices: He assumed a trait of the whole wall must belong to each brick within it
He assumed a trait of one brick must belong to the whole wall it helps build
He assumed many small weights can never add up into one large weight
He assumed bricks lose weight the moment they are stacked into a wall
context: This is the fallacy of division: reasoning from the whole down to its parts. Heaviness is a property the wall has by ADDING up many light bricks; it does not pass down to any single one. It is the exact mirror of composition (parts-to-whole). Source: Critikid (critikid.com/composition-fallacy); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy_of_composition.

question: A neighbor knows the Smith family is famous for being highly educated, and concludes that every single Smith must hold a Ph.D. Why is the neighbor's reasoning faulty?
answer: A reputation that fits the whole family need not fit each member of it
choices: A reputation that fits the whole family need not fit each member of it
A reputation that fits one member must always fit the whole family too
A whole family can earn a name that no single member contributed to
A family this learned would surely raise its youngest to a degree as well
context: This is the fallacy of division: a property of the WHOLE (a well-educated family) forced onto one PART (the toddler). The mirror of composition (parts-to-whole). Source: philosophyterms.com/division-fallacy-in-reasoning; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy_of_division.

question: A chemist points out that table salt is built from two parts: sodium, a metal so reactive it bursts into flame on water, and chlorine, a gas so toxic it was once used as a weapon. A child argues that salt must therefore be poisonous to eat. The chemist says the child reasoned badly. What is the error?
answer: He assumed a danger in each element must survive in the compound they form
choices: He assumed a danger in each element must survive in the compound they form
He assumed a property of the compound must survive in each element within it
He assumed bonding two elements just blends their dangers without changing them
He assumed any compound is always safer to handle than its raw elements
context: Fallacy of composition. When sodium donates an electron to chlorine, the properties change drastically: the compound (NaCl, table salt) is edible and necessary for life. 'Its parts are poisonous, so the whole is poisonous' does not follow. Source: van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/473; byjus.com.

question: Mr. Bell sees that his entire second-grade class eats a huge amount of ice cream over a year. He announces that Carlos, one boy in the class, must personally eat a huge amount of ice cream too. What is the error in Mr. Bell's reasoning?
answer: A huge total for the whole class need not mean a huge amount for each child
choices: A huge total for the whole class need not mean a huge amount for each child
A huge amount for each child is the only way a whole class total grows large
A class total can be known only by adding up every single child by name
A few heavy eaters can never lift a class total without the rest joining in
context: Fallacy of division: a property of the WHOLE (the grade's huge total) wrongly pushed down onto one PART (Carlos). A large group total can come from many members while one eats none. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy_of_division; philosophyterms.com.

question: At a packed stadium, one fan stands and suddenly sees the game better over the heads in front of him. He reasons that if standing helps him see, then everyone standing must let everyone see better. Why is his reasoning faulty?
answer: An edge that came from others sitting vanishes once everyone stands too
choices: An edge that came from others sitting vanishes once everyone stands too
An edge that helps one fan must help the whole crowd even more strongly
A standing crowd sees better than a seated one at almost every game
A taller stance lifts each fan equally, so all of them gain the same view
context: This is the composition move applied to action: an advantage that exists only by COMPARISON vanishes when everyone copies it. The seeing-better trick worked because others sat; universal standing erases the edge and adds discomfort. Presented as the logical move, not a policy claim. Source: FEE, The Fallacy of Composition (fee.org).

question: A teacher fills a glass and asks why it feels wet, even though hydrogen is not wet and oxygen is not wet. A student insists that since neither ingredient is wet, the water cannot truly be wet either. The teacher says the student misjudged how wholes work. What did the student miss?
answer: A whole can gain a fresh trait that none of its parts possessed alone
choices: A whole can gain a fresh trait that none of its parts possessed alone
A whole can show only the very traits its parts already carried into it
A trait can spread from a single part outward to fill the entire whole
A liquid feels wet only because its atoms are too small for us to see
context: This is emergence: 'the whole possesses properties not present in any of the parts.' Water is wet though neither hydrogen nor oxygen is; the same carbon atoms make soft graphite arranged one way and hard diamond arranged another. The composition fallacy assumes traits transfer up automatically; emergence is the real phenomenon that explains why they often do NOT. (Note the trap: some properties, like mass and weight, genuinely DO add up from parts to whole, so the expectation is not always wrong.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy_of_composition (emergence; carbon allotropes).

question: An education official argues: 'When ONE student earns a college degree, employers find that student more appealing. So if we make sure EVERY student earns a degree, then every student will look more appealing to employers.' Economists say the conclusion does not follow. Why not?
answer: The single graduate stood out only against others, so universal degrees erase the gap
choices: The single graduate stood out only against others, so universal degrees erase the gap
The single graduate gained real skill, so universal degrees must multiply that skill
Employers weigh a degree the same whether few or many people happen to hold one
A degree adds the same appeal to each holder no matter how common it becomes
context: Fallacy of composition. The single graduate's advantage came from STANDING OUT against non-graduates; when everyone holds a degree it just raises the baseline and the advantage disappears. Same structure as 'if one runner runs faster they win, so if all run faster they all win.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy_of_composition (degree inflation; racing runners).

question: An economist notes that for ONE family, saving more money builds a useful cushion. But she warns it is a logical leap to conclude that if EVERY family suddenly saves much more at once, the whole economy must be better off, since one household's spending is what funds another household's income. What reasoning move is she cautioning against?
answer: Assuming a habit good for one household must be good for the whole economy
choices: Assuming a habit good for one household must be good for the whole economy
Assuming a habit good for the whole economy must be good for one household
Assuming one household saving more forces every other household to save more
Assuming the spending of strangers has no effect on a single family income
context: This is the composition move (named the 'paradox of thrift'): a habit good for one saver need not be good for the whole economy, because one household's spending is another's income. It is offered as the LOGICAL point (part-to-whole need not transfer), not as an endorsement of any policy. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradox_of_thrift; AEI Carpe Diem.

question: An alchemist is certain his luck-potion works. He drinks it every single morning and his days go well -- but he has never once gone a morning WITHOUT it to see what would happen. Why does the potion feel proven beyond doubt to him?
answer: He tallies every time it seemed to work and forgets every time it didn't, so it can only ever look proven
choices: He tallies every time it seemed to work and forgets every time it didn't, so it can only ever look proven
He brewed the potion carefully and measured each ingredient, so the recipe is sound and worth repeating
He tested the potion against mornings with no potion and found the lucky mornings far outnumbered them
He asked the other townsfolk to try the potion too, and enough of them agreed that the effect is confirmed
context: This is the folk face of confirmation bias. Francis Bacon put it exactly in Novum Organum (1620, Aphorism XLVI): 'the deluded believers observe events which are fulfilled, but neglect and pass over their failure, though it be much more common.' A belief that only ever collects its hits was never really tested. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLVI.

question: A man decides early that a new neighbor is dishonest. After that, every friendly thing the neighbor does gets waved off as an act, while every small slip gets stored up as proof. No pile of kind deeds ever shakes his first verdict. Which best describes the trap he's fallen into?
answer: Once he settled on his first verdict, his mind bends each new fact to defend it instead of testing it
choices: Once he settled on his first verdict, his mind bends each new fact to defend it instead of testing it
He simply hasn't spent enough time with the neighbor yet to gather a fair sample of his behavior
He is right to weigh the bad deeds more heavily, since one betrayal can outweigh many small kindnesses
He trusts his gut over the evidence, and gut feelings about strangers are usually correct in the end
context: Francis Bacon's keystone portrait of the bias, written ~340 years before psychologists named it (Novum Organum, 1620, Aphorism XLVI): the mind, once a proposition is laid down, 'forces everything else to add fresh support and confirmation,' and though contrary instances exist, it 'does not observe... or rejects them by some distinction... rather than sacrifice the authority of its first conclusions.' Bacon filed this under his 'Idols of the Tribe.' Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLVI.

question: Many people with achy joints are certain their pain flares when rain is coming. Two researchers, Donald Redelmeier and Amos Tversky, tracked arthritis patients for over a year and found no real link between their pain and the weather at all. So why are the patients still so sure?
answer: They remember the rainy days their joints ached and skip right past the rainy days they felt fine
choices: They remember the rainy days their joints ached and skip right past the rainy days they felt fine
They keep careful daily diaries of pain and weather, so their long memory of the link is trustworthy
Their pain is real but too small for any study with so few patients to ever pick up as a pattern
They feel the change in air pressure before the rain arrives, which the researchers forgot to measure
context: Confirmation bias works on memory, not just on what you go looking for. Redelmeier and Tversky tracked 18 patients for over a year and found no statistically significant pain-weather link; in the same paper, 97 students 'saw' patterns in deliberately random numbers. You file the hits and lose the misses. Source: Redelmeier DA, Tversky A, PNAS 1996;93(7):2895-6.

question: In an ancient temple, painted tablets covered a wall, each one hung up by a sailor who had prayed in a storm and survived the shipwreck. A priest pointed to them as proof the gods answer prayers. The skeptic Diagoras looked at the wall and asked one question that undid the whole display. What did he ask?
answer: Where are the tablets of the men who prayed just as hard and drowned anyway?
choices: Where are the tablets of the men who prayed just as hard and drowned anyway?
How can you prove these sailors prayed at all, rather than simply being lucky?
Were these tablets painted by the sailors, or by priests hoping to draw a crowd?
Why should surviving one storm mean the gods will spare a man from the next?
context: The drowned men left no paintings, so the survivors' wall looks like overwhelming proof. It is confirmation bias in a single image: you only ever see the hits because the misses don't get hung up. Francis Bacon retold this anecdote about the ancient skeptic Diagoras in Novum Organum (1620). Recounted here as ancient testimony. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLVI.  (Legend.)

question: A researcher shows you the numbers 2, 4, 6 and says they follow a secret rule. To crack it, you may make up your own triples and he'll tell you whether each one fits. You guess the rule is 'goes up by two' and test 8-10-12, then 20-22-24 -- both fit, so you feel sure. But every triple you've tried already obeys your own guess. What is the one kind of triple that could actually put your guess to the test?
answer: Offered a triple you expected him to reject, like 1-2-3, to try to break your own guess
choices: Offered a triple you expected him to reject, like 1-2-3, to try to break your own guess
Offered many more triples that fit 'goes up by two' until you'd built an overwhelming case
Asked him to simply confirm whether 'goes up by two' was the rule before testing anything
Started from larger numbers like 100-102-104 to be sure the rule held across the whole range
context: This is Peter Wason's 1960 '2-4-6 task.' People test only triples that already fit their guess -- Wason called it the 'positive test strategy' -- and confirm themselves into the wrong answer. The only way to find the real rule is to risk a case that could prove you wrong. Source: Wikipedia, 'Confirmation bias' (Wason 1960, positive test strategy).

question: Picture two clues landing on a detective's desk about a suspect he already believes is guilty: one fact that fits his theory, and one fact that flatly contradicts it. Bacon warned that the human mind handles these two clues very unequally -- and that for finding the truth, this is exactly backwards. Which clue should the detective actually treat as more powerful?
answer: The single contradicting fact, since one true exception can topple what a hundred agreements cannot
choices: The single contradicting fact, since one true exception can topple what a hundred agreements cannot
The single supporting fact, since it slots neatly into a picture that is already taking clear shape
Whichever clue arrived first, since first impressions rightly set the frame for reading all the rest
Whichever clue more witnesses agree on, since weight of testimony is the surest guide to the truth
context: Bacon's mechanism, verbatim (Novum Organum, 1620, Aphorism XLVI): 'it is the peculiar and perpetual error of the human understanding to be more moved and excited by affirmatives than negatives... in establishing any true axiom the negative instance is the most powerful.' The mind craves the confirming clue; the truth lives in the disconfirming one. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLVI.

question: Two groups read the very same profile of a person -- a mix of shy, bookish moments and outgoing, talkative ones. One group was asked whether she'd suit a quiet library job; the other, whether she'd suit a high-energy sales job. Later, each group was asked to recall what they'd read. How did the two groups' memories differ?
answer: Each group mostly remembered the moments that fit the job it had in mind, and let the rest slip away
choices: Each group mostly remembered the moments that fit the job it had in mind, and let the rest slip away
Both groups remembered the profile evenly, since they had all read the identical list of moments
The library group recalled more detail overall, because a calm task makes the mind read more carefully
Each group remembered the moments that clashed with its job most sharply, because surprises stick best
context: In Snyder and Swann's experiment, readers assessing the profile for a librarian role later recalled mostly the introverted facts; those assessing for sales recalled mostly the extroverted ones. Same profile, but memory selectively served up whatever matched the expectation. Source: Wikipedia, 'Confirmation bias' (Snyder & Swann, selective memory).

question: In a Stanford study, supporters and opponents of the death penalty were each handed the identical pair of made-up studies -- one finding it deters crime, one finding it doesn't. Both camps then read the very same mixed evidence, start to finish. When researchers measured their views afterward, what had become of the two camps?
answer: Both camps left even more convinced of their original view than before they read anything
choices: Both camps left even more convinced of their original view than before they read anything
Both camps drifted toward the middle, each having now seen one study cut against it
Both camps gave up their stance, deciding the evidence was too muddled to support either side
Both camps quietly switched, each persuaded by the fresh study that opposed its old view
context: In Lord, Ross, and Lepper's 1979 study each side praised the study that agreed with it as well-run and tore the other apart -- one proponent dismissed the contrary study because it 'didn't cover a long enough period of time.' Same evidence, opposite conclusions, and deeper polarization, because each side cross-examined only the study it disliked. Source: Wikipedia, 'Confirmation bias' (Lord, Ross & Lepper 1979).

question: A man boasts that his grand theory of human nature is confirmed everywhere he looks -- every news story, every quarrel, every stranger's behavior seems to fit it perfectly. Karl Popper held that confirmations like these come far too cheaply to be impressive, and drew a sharp line between a confirmation that counts and one that doesn't. On Popper's view, what makes a confirmation actually count?
answer: It came from a risky prediction -- one the theory could easily have gotten wrong, but didn't
choices: It came from a risky prediction -- one the theory could easily have gotten wrong, but didn't
It came from a respected expert whose long experience lends the theory real authority
It is one of so many confirmations that the sheer weight of agreement now settles the matter
It fit the theory far more neatly than any rival theory could manage to fit the same case
context: Popper's exact words: 'It is easy to obtain confirmations, or verifications, for nearly every theory -- if we look for confirmations,' so 'confirmations should count only if they are the result of risky predictions.' A theory that forbids nothing and can absorb any outcome is confirmed everywhere precisely because it risks nothing. Source: Karl Popper, 'Science as Falsification' (Conjectures and Refutations, 1963).

question: Karl Popper once brought the psychologist Alfred Adler a case that didn't seem to fit Adler's theory of the mind. Adler explained it away in an instant. When Popper asked how he could be so certain, Adler said it was because of his 'thousandfold experience.' Popper's reply cut straight to the flaw. What did he say?
answer: Then with this new case it is now thousand-and-one-fold -- and no closer to being tested
choices: Then with this new case it is now thousand-and-one-fold -- and no closer to being tested
Then your thousand cases prove only that you are stubborn, not that your theory is right
Then you have explained one more case, which is exactly what any good theory ought to do
Then a thousand experiences should surely outweigh the doubts of a single young student
context: Popper's point: a theory that can explain a man who drowns a child and a man who dies saving one equally well -- as he said both Freud and Adler claimed they could -- explains nothing. Each new 'confirmation' just adds to the tally without ever risking the theory. A theory no fact could contradict isn't strong; it's empty. Source: Karl Popper, 'Science as Falsification' (Conjectures and Refutations, 1963).

question: It would be comforting to think the smartest people, being so good at reasoning, mostly escape the pull to favor evidence for their own side. Researchers who measured this 'myside bias' found that raw intelligence barely predicts who resists it. So what trait actually does the work of resisting it?
answer: Deliberately spending effort to hunt for reasons your own first idea might be wrong
choices: Deliberately spending effort to hunt for reasons your own first idea might be wrong
A confident, decisive nature that commits fully instead of second-guessing itself
A naturally calm temperament that keeps strong feelings from clouding the judgment
Wide reading across many subjects, so more facts are on hand to settle any question
context: The uncomfortable finding: being clever mostly makes you better at defending the belief you already hold. The trait that predicts resisting myside bias is 'active open-mindedness' -- deliberately searching for the case against your own view. It is a choice, not a gift of IQ. Source: Wikipedia, 'Confirmation bias' (myside bias; active open-mindedness).

question: In a witch-hunt 'swimming test,' a bound suspect was thrown into water. If she sank, she was judged innocent -- the pure water had accepted her. If she floated, she was judged a witch -- the water had rejected her. A clever villager objected that this test could never clear anyone of witchcraft. Why was he right?
answer: The one outcome that proved her innocent was drowning, so no living woman was ever cleared
choices: The one outcome that proved her innocent was drowning, so no living woman was ever cleared
The water was never blessed beforehand, so it had no real power to judge guilt or innocence
Heavy women sink and light women float, so the test merely measured a body, not a soul
A truly powerful witch could make herself sink at will, so floating proved nothing about her
context: A test with no possible disconfirming outcome proves nothing -- exactly Karl Popper's point about theories that can't be refuted. This is a cousin of confirmation bias, not the same thing: here the verdict is rigged so that no evidence could ever count against it. Recounted as historical legend. Source: History.com, '7 Bizarre Witch Trial Tests.'

question: Confucius taught that a mind needs two things held in balance, solid book-learning and your own hard thinking, and that leaning all the way to either side ruins a learner. He summed the warning up in one famous balanced line. Which line did Confucius give?
answer: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
choices: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
Reading without reflection breeds fools; reflection without reading breeds dreamers.
He who only studies stays narrow; he who only ponders strays lost.
Books fill the head with facts; thinking alone leaves the hands empty.
context: Confucius wanted both: book-learning AND your own hard thinking, each correcting the other. Memorizing without reflecting just piles up dead facts; reasoning with nothing solid underneath drifts into nonsense. Source: Analects Book 2.15 (Wei Zheng, Legge translation, ctext.org/analects/wei-zheng).

question: Confucius says that whenever he walks along with two other people, he is sure to find a teacher in them, even when one of the two behaves badly. What does Confucius say he does with whatever he sees in the people around him?
answer: He copies their good points and steers clear of their bad ones
choices: He copies their good points and steers clear of their bad ones
He praises their virtues aloud and keeps their faults a secret
He envies their strengths and quietly mocks their weaknesses
He records their wise words and forgets the foolish ones fast
context: The striking part is that the BAD example teaches too: you watch a flaw and resolve not to share it. Every person you meet becomes a lesson, one way or the other. Source: Analects Book 7.22 (Shu Er, Legge translation, ctext.org/analects/shu-er).

question: A student named Zigong asks Confucius for a single word he could practice his whole life long. The Master answers not with an abstract label but with a plain rule of conduct. Which rule did Confucius give him?
answer: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
choices: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
Always repay a kindness with a kindness twice as large.
Speak no word that you are not prepared to stand behind.
Put your family's good ahead of your own at all times.
context: Confucius offered Zigong the word 'reciprocity' (Chinese 'shu'), then unfolded it as this rule. It is the 'Golden Rule' in its negative form, given centuries before the Christian version. Notice the humble shape: not 'do good to others' but 'do not do to others what you would hate' a careful place to start. Source: Analects Book 15.24 (Wei Ling Gong, Legge translation, ctext.org/analects/wei-ling-gong).

question: Confucius is one of the most quoted teachers who ever lived, yet he never sat down and wrote the famous book of his teaching. He only spoke. So where did the Analects, the book of his sayings, actually come from?
answer: His pupils gathered his remembered sayings after he died
choices: His pupils gathered his remembered sayings after he died
He dictated it to a scribe in the last year of his life
A later emperor ordered scholars to invent it in his name
He carved it himself onto bamboo strips over many years
context: The Analects (Chinese 'Lunyu') was put together by the first and second generations of his disciples from sayings and short conversations they remembered. So the most influential teacher in Chinese history wrote no book at all his students did. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius ('compiled by first and second generation disciples of Confucius and then transmitted privately for centuries').

question: The Analects is not one flowing essay; it is a heap of short lines the teacher once spoke, gathered up one by one. Because every line quotes that same one man, almost every passage in the book opens with the exact same three-word phrase. What is that recurring opening?
answer: "The Master said"
choices: "The Master said"
"It is written"
"Long ago in Lu"
"Hear, my children"
context: Open the Analects almost anywhere and you read 'The Master said...' The book is a record of what one remembered voice taught, line after line, which is why the phrase repeats so relentlessly. Source: Analects (Legge translation, ctext.org/analects); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius.

question: Confucius did not start life as a grand sage. His father died when he was about three, and his mother raised him poor. Before he ever taught a single student, what kind of work did the young Confucius do to get by?
answer: Humble bookkeeping over granaries and livestock
choices: Humble bookkeeping over granaries and livestock
Soldiering on the borders of the state of Lu
Carving fine jade ornaments for noble houses
Sailing trade boats up and down the great rivers
context: His mother Yan Zhengzai raised him in poverty after his father Kong He died. His first jobs were lowly clerk's posts: the philosopher Mencius later names him 'Foodstuffs Scribe' and 'Scribe in the Field,' keeping granary accounts and animal records. Source: Wikipedia: Confucius; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius (Mencius's titles for his early posts).

question: A student pressed Confucius on a heavy question: how should one serve the spirits of the dead, and what comes after we die? The room waited for the Master to settle the world beyond. How did Confucius answer?
answer: You do not yet know life, so how could you know death
choices: You do not yet know life, so how could you know death
The dead watch over us and must be richly honored
Death is a long sleep from which no man ever wakes
Only Heaven knows, and Heaven has told us nothing yet
context: Confucius said, 'While you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits?' and 'While you do not know life, how can you know about death?' It is a famous refusal to speculate: master the duties of THIS life first. A philosopher who held firm views about the afterlife would not be wrong here the rung simply records how Confucius himself replied. Source: Analects Book 11.12 (Xian Jin, Legge translation, ctext.org/analects/xian-jin).

question: Travelling in the state of Qi, Confucius heard a piece of ancient ceremonial music called the Shao, and it moved him so deeply that for the next three months one ordinary pleasure of life went flat for him. He said he never dreamed music could reach such heights. What did he stop noticing for those three months?
answer: The taste of meat
choices: The taste of meat
The passing of time
The cold of winter
The need for sleep
context: 'For three months he did not know the taste of meat,' saying he never imagined music could be made so excellent. Confucius treated music as serious moral training, not mere entertainment which is why a piece of it could overwhelm his everyday senses for months. Source: Analects Book 7.13 (Legge translation; corroborated by Wikisource Chinese Classics Vol.1 Book VII).

question: For years Confucius wandered from one state to the next, Wei, Song, Chen, Cai, and Chu, going from court to court and offering each duke his counsel. He met mostly cold shoulders, and now and then real danger. What was he searching for, state after state, and never found?
answer: A ruler who would put his teaching into real practice
choices: A ruler who would put his teaching into real practice
The lost grave of an ancient king he longed to honor
A quiet province where he could retire from the world
An old rival teacher he had sworn to beat in debate
context: After leaving his home state of Lu in exile around 498 BCE, Confucius traveled the states 'looking for a ruler who might employ him but meeting instead with indifference and, occasionally, severe hardship and danger.' He never won the high office he sought yet his teaching outlasted every ruler who ignored him. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius.

question: Confucius once held a real post in his home state of Lu and meant to set it right. The neighboring state of Qi, fearing a strong and well-governed Lu, sent its duke a gift chosen on purpose to rot the court from within. The chief minister took the gift in, and the duke then skipped court three days running. What was the cunning gift that worked?
answer: A troupe of beautiful dancing girls
choices: A troupe of beautiful dancing girls
A team of swift and splendid horses
A chest of finely carved jade treasures
A fertile town on the border of Lu
context: Qi feared a strong, well-governed Lu, so it sent the distracting gift on purpose. The chief minister Ji Huan accepted the female musicians, and for three days the duke held no court. Confucius judged the court hopeless and departed beginning his long years of wandering. Source: Analects Book 18.4 (Wei Zi, Legge translation, ctext.org/analects/wei-zi).

question: Stranded between the states of Chen and Cai, Confucius and his followers ran clean out of food, and his men grew too weak to stand. His bluntest disciple, Zilu, rounded on him: does even the superior man have to suffer like this? How did Confucius say the superior man behaves when want closes in?
answer: He endures want without breaking; a lesser man runs wild
choices: He endures want without breaking; a lesser man runs wild
He prays harder than ever until Heaven sends him relief
He feels no hunger, for his mind is fixed on higher things
He turns straight back, for no teaching is worth starving for
context: Confucius replied, 'The superior man may indeed have to endure want, but the mean man, when he is in want, gives way to unbridled license.' The point is not that the noble man escapes hardship he doesn't but that hardship reveals character: he holds steady where a lesser man falls apart. Tradition says they went seven days without food. Source: Analects Book 15.1-2 (Wei Ling Gong, Legge translation, ctext.org/analects/wei-ling-gong).

question: Of all his students Confucius loved one best: Yan Hui, brilliant, humble, and poor, who seemed to grasp the Way more deeply than any other. Then Yan Hui died at about twenty-nine. The old master broke down completely, and when others said his grief went too far, what did Confucius cry?
answer: If not for this man, for whom should I mourn
choices: If not for this man, for whom should I mourn
A teacher must never weep before his pupils
He has only gone ahead of us a little while
No man should outlive the best of his students
context: At the news Confucius first cried out, 'Alas! Heaven is destroying me! Heaven is destroying me!' Told his mourning was excessive, he answered, 'If I am not to mourn bitterly for this man, for whom should I mourn?' The composed sage of the sayings shows here as a heartbroken old man who had lost his finest student. Source: Analects Book 11.9-10 (Xian Jin, Legge translation, ctext.org/analects/xian-jin); Yan Hui's death at about 29 corroborated by the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and chinaknowledge.de.

question: A new water well can go in one of two villages. The big village has 300 thirsty people; the tiny one has 12. An advisor says: 'Drill in the big village - far more people there will stop dying of thirst.' What kind of test is the advisor using to decide?
answer: Whatever brings the greatest good to the greatest number is the right choice.
choices: Whatever brings the greatest good to the greatest number is the right choice.
Whatever keeps a solemn promise once given is the right choice.
Whatever an honest, decent person would do is the right choice.
Whatever respects each single person's own rights is the right choice.
context: This is the core utilitarian move: judge a choice only by its results, picking whatever yields the greatest good for the greatest number. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes this 'greatest happiness for the greatest number' slogan is the popular summary of the view (though it calls the slogan loose). Source: SEP, 'Consequentialism'.

question: Theo gave his word he would save the last slice of cake for his sister, but four hungry friends turn up and splitting it four ways would gladden more people. A 'judge by results' thinker weighs the broken promise itself. On that view, what binding force does Theo's promise carry?
answer: None on its own; the promise binds only insofar as honoring it does the most good.
choices: None on its own; the promise binds only insofar as honoring it does the most good.
Full force whatever the tally, since a word once given holds a person to it.
Real force, since a world where promises hold tends to make more people happy.
Real force, since a man who breaks his word becomes one no one can trust.
context: To a consequentialist an act has no built-in rightness from a promise; a word given carries no weight of its own, only the weight of the happiness keeping it would produce. The rival readings are live, not dead: one holds the promise binds whatever the count (the deontologist); one keeps it because a world of reliable promises yields more happiness (the rule-consequentialist); one keeps it to stay a trustworthy person (the virtue view). The act-consequentialist move judges THIS act by THIS act's results, so for Theo the promise binds only when keeping it does the most good. The bank takes no verdict; it shows the live fork. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Consequentialism'.

question: The philosopher Philippa Foot built the most famous test of 'count the lives' thinking: a runaway trolley will kill five people unless you switch it onto a track where it kills one instead. Judith Jarvis Thomson later added a version where almost everyone refuses, though the five-for-one math is identical. What was Thomson's twist?
answer: You must shove a heavy stranger off a bridge to stop the trolley with his body.
choices: You must shove a heavy stranger off a bridge to stop the trolley with his body.
You must let all five die, since numbers can never decide a human life.
You must ask each of the five to vote first on whether to be rescued.
You must sacrifice yourself by leaping onto the track in their place.
context: The trolley problem was launched by Philippa Foot in a 1967 essay on the Doctrine of Double Effect, then named and expanded by Judith Jarvis Thomson in 1976. Her 'Fat Man' variant keeps the same arithmetic - one dies so five live - yet pushing a person to his death feels monstrous: same math, opposite gut. Source: Britannica, 'Trolley problem'.

question: A surgeon has five patients dying for lack of organs and one healthy man in for a routine checkup. By pure head-counting, cutting up the one to save five is a clear gain of lives - yet nearly everyone recoils. A thinker calls this the sharpest challenge to judging acts only by their results. Where does the challenge bite?
answer: Maximizing the total can demand using an innocent as mere material.
choices: Maximizing the total can demand using an innocent as mere material.
The totals were added wrong, since a sick life counts for less.
People's horror is just squeamishness that arithmetic should override.
The sick five gave up their claim by failing to stay healthy.
context: The 'Transplant' case is the classic challenge to act utilitarianism: the count says +4 lives, yet nearly everyone judges that butchering a healthy innocent to harvest him is forbidden - it treats a person as raw material rather than as a person. That collision between the tally and the prohibition is where the move is pressed hardest. The bank takes no verdict; it shows the live fork. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Utilitarianism, Act and Rule'.

question: John Stuart Mill compared a contented fool with a thinker who is troubled and discontented, and argued the thinker is still better off. He fixed the point in one famous line. How did Mill put it?
answer: "Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied."
choices: "Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied."
"Better a troubled Socrates than a hundred easy fools."
"Better to think and suffer than to drift and feel nothing."
"Better a restless mind than a heart that is merely full."
context: Mill's full line (Utilitarianism, ch.2) runs: 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' His point: someone who has tasted both higher and lower pleasures will never trade down - quality counts, not just quantity. Source: SEP, 'Mill's Moral and Political Philosophy' (Utilitarianism II.6).

question: Jeremy Bentham, who founded the 'judge by results' creed, opened his great 1789 book by declaring that only two things ultimately govern everything people do and everything they ought to do. He called them our two 'sovereign masters.' What did Bentham name as those two masters?
answer: Pleasure and pain.
choices: Pleasure and pain.
Reason and instinct.
Virtue and vice.
Hope and fear.
context: Bentham reduced ALL value to pleasure and pain, opening An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789): 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.' So the whole utilitarian ledger is just pleasure minus pain. Source: Bentham, IPML Ch.1 (via Wikiquote: Jeremy Bentham).

question: Jeremy Bentham compared the fine art of poetry with push-pin, a trivial children's pub game that anyone could play, and asked which of the two is more valuable. He gave a blunt, clear answer. What did Bentham conclude?
answer: Push-pin, if it gives more pleasure, is worth more than poetry.
choices: Push-pin, if it gives more pleasure, is worth more than poetry.
Poetry wins, since the pleasure it gives runs deeper and lasts longer.
The two are simply different and cannot be ranked against each other.
Push-pin is worthless beside the lasting riches of poetry.
context: In The Rationale of Reward (1830) Bentham wrote that 'the game of push-pin is of equal value with the arts and sciences of music and poetry... if the game of push-pin furnish more pleasure, it is more valuable than either.' For Bentham the SOURCE of a pleasure is irrelevant - only the quantity counts. The shocking egalitarian edge of pure head-counting. Source: Bentham, The Rationale of Reward, Bk.3 Ch.1.

question: A utilitarian is tallying the total happiness a new law would produce. A duke insists his own contentment should weigh far more heavily in the sum than a stable-boy's, since he is a man of higher station. On strict utilitarian principles, how should the duke's happiness be weighed against the stable-boy's?
answer: Exactly the same - each person's happiness counts for one, no more.
choices: Exactly the same - each person's happiness counts for one, no more.
More heavily, since a refined man feels his pleasures more deeply.
Less heavily, to correct for the privileges he already enjoys.
It cannot be compared, since their two lives are far too different.
context: Utilitarianism bakes in radical equality: when you sum happiness, a king's joy weighs no more than a beggar's. Mill credited Bentham with the dictum 'everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one' - though the exact line is not found in Bentham's own books; Mill is the source who immortalized it. Source: Mill, Utilitarianism, footnote to Ch.5.

question: Jeremy Bentham wanted to measure a pleasure the way you might measure a length, so he built a scoring system that rates each pleasure on several dimensions - its intensity, how long it lasts, how certain it is, how soon it arrives, and how many people share it. One more dimension he included is genuinely surprising. Which did Bentham also score?
answer: How likely the pleasure is to breed still more pleasures.
choices: How likely the pleasure is to breed still more pleasures.
How much money the pleasure costs a person to obtain.
How rare the pleasure is among ordinary working people.
How much the pleasure improves a person's moral character.
context: Bentham's 'felicific calculus' (or hedonic calculus) scores seven dimensions: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (how soon), fecundity (the chance it breeds MORE pleasure), purity (the chance it stays free of pain), and extent (how many are affected). The move made literal - a recipe for adding up happiness. Source: Wikipedia, 'Felicific calculus'; Bentham, IPML Ch.4.

question: Mill claimed some pleasures are higher in KIND, not merely bigger in amount - but that raises a hard question: who gets to say a poem outranks a fine meal? Mill gave one specific test for settling which of two pleasures is the higher. What was his test?
answer: Ask those who have deeply known both, and see which they prefer.
choices: Ask those who have deeply known both, and see which they prefer.
Ask a panel of trained priests which one they bless as nobler.
Ask which one more people across the world tend to choose.
Ask which one delivers the longest-lasting bodily satisfaction.
context: Mill's test is the verdict of the 'competent judges': if people 'competently acquainted with both' decisively prefer one even when it brings more discontent, that pleasure is higher in quality. This is his break from Bentham - pleasures differ in kind, not just amount. Source: SEP, 'Mill's Moral and Political Philosophy' (Utilitarianism II.5).

question: The phrase 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number' is so bound to Jeremy Bentham that he is usually credited with coining it. In truth Bentham took it from earlier writers - he even thought he had first met it in one of them. Which of these thinkers had actually used the phrase the earliest?
answer: Francis Hutcheson, in his inquiry into moral good and evil.
choices: Francis Hutcheson, in his inquiry into moral good and evil.
Joseph Priestley, in his essay on government and liberty.
Cesare Beccaria, in his treatise on crimes and punishments.
Aristotle, in his ancient lectures on ethics and the good life.
context: Bentham did NOT coin the slogan. Francis Hutcheson used it in his Inquiry Concerning Moral Good and Evil (1725) - the earliest of these; Cesare Beccaria echoed it in On Crimes and Punishments (1764); Bentham himself thought he had found it in Joseph Priestley (1768). Bentham didn't invent the formula - he drove it into the world. Source: Wikiquote: Jeremy Bentham; utilitarianism.com.

question: A critic scoffs that no one could ever live by the 'judge by results' creed - picture a shopper frozen at the checkout, tallying the total happiness of every option before he dares buy milk. Both Bentham and Mill had already answered what their happiness calculus was really meant to be. What role did they give it?
answer: A standard for what makes an act right, not a sum to run each time.
choices: A standard for what makes an act right, not a sum to run each time.
A strict procedure to be worked through in full before every choice.
A guide written only for lawmakers, never for ordinary shoppers.
A noble ideal to be admired, not a real guide to everyday choices.
context: A common caricature, but Bentham said his calculus 'should not be strictly pursued previously to every moral judgment,' and Mill called it a 'misapprehension' to think people must fix their minds on society at large each time. Utilitarianism is a standard of rightness, not a stopwatch for the checkout line - and not merely a lawmaker's tool or an unreachable ideal either. Source: SEP, 'Consequentialism'.

question: A child reasons: "All thumbs are fingers. So all fingers must be thumbs." What is the simplest way to show his second step is wrong?
answer: Show him his own index finger, which is plainly a finger but no thumb.
choices: Show him his own index finger, which is plainly a finger but no thumb.
Agree that since every thumb is a finger, most fingers must be thumbs.
Tell him "all" is too strong, so he should say "some fingers are thumbs."
Grant the flip is correct, and say the difference hardly matters anyway.
context: This is the classic handle for the CONVERSE ERROR: 'if A then B' is a one-way street, and flipping it to 'if B then A' is not promised. One counterexample (a finger that is no thumb) sinks the flip. Being a thumb is SUFFICIENT for being a finger; being a finger is only NECESSARY, not sufficient, for being a thumb. The other three moves all accept the true first sentence yet fumble the flip: one simply restates the converse error, one mistakes the real flaw for a quantifier that is too strong ('some fingers are thumbs' is still false), and one just concedes the flip. Source: Khan Academy LSAT 'If X, then Y: Sufficiency and necessity'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Necessary and Sufficient Conditions' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/necessary-sufficient).

question: A man tells himself: "Whenever I'm sick, I feel tired. Right now I feel tired, so I must be sick." Where does his reasoning go wrong?
answer: Tiredness has many causes besides sickness, so it can't prove he is sick.
choices: Tiredness has many causes besides sickness, so it can't prove he is sick.
He cannot really know he feels tired without measuring it somehow.
Nothing is wrong here; feeling tired is solid proof that he is sick.
Feeling tired should have led him to conclude he is not sick.
context: Formally this is 'affirming the consequent' (the converse error): 'If P then Q; Q is true; therefore P.' It is invalid because Q can have other causes. Tiredness comes from a hard workout, a bad night's sleep, or plain boredom, so the symptom being present does not prove the one named cause. This is the everyday form of the trap, the kind people fall into without noticing. Source: Study.com 'Affirming the Consequent'; Wikipedia 'Affirming the consequent' (illness/fatigue example).

question: Someone argues: "If it barks, it's a dog. That animal isn't barking, so it can't be a dog." What slip has he made?
answer: A dog that cannot bark, or is asleep, is still a dog.
choices: A dog that cannot bark, or is asleep, is still a dog.
Plenty of animals other than dogs are also able to bark.
He has not checked whether the animal can bark at all.
Barking is the very thing that makes an animal a dog.
context: Formally this is 'denying the antecedent' (the inverse error): 'If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q.' Also invalid. The rule only said barking guarantees dog; it never said a dog REQUIRES barking, so removing the bark removes nothing. A mute or sleeping dog is still a dog. Knocking out the named cause does not knock out the effect. Source: logicallyfallacious.com 'Denying the Antecedent'; Wikipedia 'Denying the antecedent'.

question: In Joseph Heller's war novel Catch-22, an officer accuses the chaplain of being a secret forger who signs documents "Washington Irving" because one censored letter carries that very signature right beside the chaplain's own name. His proof runs: "a name is signed here; that's your name; therefore you wrote it." Where is the gap in the officer's reasoning?
answer: A name can appear on a page without its owner writing a word.
choices: A name can appear on a page without its owner writing a word.
The censoring of the letter may have erased its true author.
The chaplain never once openly denied writing the letter.
An officer has no business reading the chaplain's private mail.
context: A textbook affirming-the-consequent trap: a signed name is the consequent, and the consequent can have another cause. In the novel, Yossarian forged the 'Washington Irving' signature, so the chaplain's name appearing on the letter proves nothing about who wrote it.
