Heller's scene is cited as a classic example of the converse error. Source: Wikipedia 'Affirming the consequent' (cites the Catch-22 chaplain/'Washington Irving' scene); Joseph Heller, Catch-22 (1961).

question: In his 1950 paper on whether machines can think, Alan Turing examines an objection: "If a man lived by a fixed set of rules, he'd be no better than a machine. But men follow no such fixed rules, so men cannot be machines." Turing dismisses this objection as plainly faulty. What is the gap in it?
answer: A man without fixed rules could still be a machine some other way.
choices: A man without fixed rules could still be a machine some other way.
Some machines very plainly do live by a fixed set of rules.
Whether men truly follow fixed rules is something no one can know.
If men really were machines, they would have to follow fixed rules.
context: This is denying the antecedent (the inverse error): the rule ran only 'fixed rules, then machine-like,' so the absence of fixed rules cannot establish 'not a machine.' Knocking out one named cause does not knock out the effect. Turing quotes the objection in the 'Argument from Informality of Behaviour' and dismisses its reasoning as faulty; in the paper he labels the flaw an 'undistributed middle,' while modern logic texts classify this same form as denying the antecedent. The rung keys only the logical flaw and takes no stand on whether minds are machines. Source: A.M. Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind 59 (1950); quoted in Wikipedia 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' and Wikipedia 'Denying the antecedent'.

question: Take the rule "If it rained last night, the grass is wet." Three of the four moves below secretly reverse that one-way rule and prove nothing. Which single move is logically airtight?
answer: The grass is dry, so it did not rain.
choices: The grass is dry, so it did not rain.
The grass is wet, so it must have rained.
It did not rain, so the grass must be dry.
The grass is wet, so it will soon rain.
context: The two flips have valid twins, and the only difference is which end you grab. Denying the CONSEQUENT ('grass is dry, so it did not rain') is valid (modus tollens) -- the airtight move here. Affirming the ANTECEDENT (rained, so wet) is also valid (modus ponens). But affirming the consequent ('wet, so it rained') and denying the antecedent ('no rain, so dry') are both invalid -- the grass could be wet from a sprinkler or dew with no rain at all. Same conditional, opposite verdict, depending on which end you grab. Source: Wikipedia 'Affirming the consequent' ('Affirming the antecedent (modus ponens) and denying the consequent (modus tollens) are valid. Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid.').

question: Cook Ding, a butcher in old China, told a lord his secret: a clumsy butcher hacks through bone and has to replace his ruined blade every month. A good one cuts cleanly and changes knives only once a year. Cook Ding then bragged about his own knife. What did he claim about it?
answer: It had carved oxen for nineteen years and was still sharp as new
choices: It had carved oxen for nineteen years and was still sharp as new
It had been blessed long ago on a sacred stone by a temple priest
It was one of a hundred knives he kept and rotated week by week
It was forged by his own hand from a meteorite that fell nearby
context: From the parable of Cook Ding (Pao Ding) in Chapter 3 of the Zhuangzi. His boast: 'A good cook changes his knife once a year, because he cuts. A mediocre cook changes his knife once a month, because he hacks. I've had this knife of mine for nineteen years and I've cut up thousands of oxen with it, and yet the blade is as good as though it had just come from the grindstone.' The point is not bragging but technique: the blade lasts because he never forces it through bone. Source: Burton Watson translation, Zhuangzi ch. 3, 'The Secret of Caring for Life.'  (Legend.)

question: Cook Ding, a butcher in ancient China, carved up a whole ox for a watching lord. His hand, his shoulder, his foot, and his knee all moved together as he worked the blade. What did onlookers say his butchering most resembled?
answer: A graceful dance set in time to music
choices: A graceful dance set in time to music
A scholar reciting a poem from memory
An archer drawing slow on a target
A potter shaping clay on a spinning wheel
context: The opening image of the parable: 'every touch of his hand, heave of his shoulder, move of his feet, thrust of his knee' went zip and zoop in perfect rhythm, 'as though he were performing the dance of the Mulberry Grove or keeping time to the Jingshou music.' Mastery looks effortless and flowing, not laborious. Source: Burton Watson translation, Zhuangzi ch. 3.  (Legend.)

question: Cook Ding, the master butcher of the Zhuangzi, kept the same knife for nineteen years and cut up thousands of oxen, yet his blade stayed sharp as new while clumsy butchers wore theirs out in a month. A lord asked his secret. How did Cook Ding say he carved without ever dulling the edge?
answer: He slipped through the gaps already in the joints and never hit bone
choices: He slipped through the gaps already in the joints and never hit bone
He swung so fast the blade never lingered long enough to wear
He soaked the blade in fine oil each night to guard its edge
He bore down with his full weight to split each joint in one stroke
context: This is the heart of the parable and a famous illustration of wu wei (acting without forcing): 'There are spaces between the joints, and the blade of the knife has really no thickness. If you insert what has no thickness into such spaces, then there's plenty of room, more than enough for the blade to play about in.' He succeeds by following the ox's natural structure (the tianli, the heaven-given grain) instead of muscling through it, so the edge never meets bone and never dulls. Source: Burton Watson translation, Zhuangzi ch. 3.  (Legend.)

question: Cook Ding, the master butcher of the Zhuangzi, told a lord how his skill had changed over the years. At first, he said, all he could see was the whole ox standing before him. Three years on, he no longer saw the whole ox at all. How did he describe his work at last, after long practice?
answer: He went at it by spirit and no longer looked with his eyes
choices: He went at it by spirit and no longer looked with his eyes
He memorized each bone so he could carve in total darkness
He counted every cut aloud to keep himself from slipping
He had an apprentice mark the joints before he ever began
context: Cook Ding's three stages of mastery: 'When I first began cutting up oxen, all I could see was the ox itself. After three years I no longer saw the whole ox. And now I go at it by spirit and don't look with my eyes. Perception and understanding have come to a stop and spirit moves where it wants.' Deep skill becomes intuitive; the deliberate, eyes-on effort of the beginner drops away. Source: Burton Watson translation, Zhuangzi ch. 3.  (Legend.)

question: Cook Ding, the butcher whose blade had carved thousands of oxen and still gleamed like new, admitted that even he sometimes reached a knotted, complicated place where the going grew hard. According to his own account, when he came to such a difficult spot, what did he do?
answer: He slowed down, watched closely, and moved the knife with great care
choices: He slowed down, watched closely, and moved the knife with great care
He struck harder and faster to break past the snag before it caught him
He set the ox aside and came back to it fresh the following morning
He called for a heavier cleaver better suited to the much tougher going
context: Even the master meets resistance, and the response is restraint, not force: 'Whenever I come to a complicated place, I size up the difficulties, tell myself to watch out and be careful, keep my eyes on what I'm doing, work very slowly, and move the knife with the greatest subtlety, until, flop! the whole thing comes apart like a clod of earth crumbling to the ground.' Effortless action is not carelessness; the hard spots get more attention, not brute strength. Source: Burton Watson translation, Zhuangzi ch. 3.  (Legend.)

question: A lord watched Cook Ding carve an ox so smoothly that he cried out in praise of the man's dazzling skill with the knife. Cook Ding laid down his blade and answered that the lord had fixed on the wrong thing. What did Cook Ding insist his butchering was really about?
answer: His skill was only the surface of a deeper way that ran past all technique
choices: His skill was only the surface of a deeper way that ran past all technique
His skill was nothing rare, just long years of dull and joyless drudgery
His skill was a gift he was simply born with and could not teach to another
His skill owed everything to a blade so keen it would slide through anything
context: Lord Wenhui exclaims, 'Ah, this is marvelous! Imagine skill reaching such heights!' Cook Ding puts down his knife and replies, 'What I care about is the Way, which goes beyond skill.' The parable draws a line between mere technique and the Dao: the dazzling butchering is only the visible surface of something deeper, a way of moving through the world by following its grain rather than forcing it. Cook Ding does not call his skill drudgery, an inborn gift, or the doing of a sharp blade; he points past the skill itself to the Way behind it. The chapter ends with the lord saying he has learned 'how to care for life.' Source: Burton Watson translation, Zhuangzi ch. 3, 'The Secret of Caring for Life.'  (Legend.)

question: Every summer in a seaside town, ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together; every winter, both fall. A worried official proposes banning ice cream to stop the drownings. What is he missing?
answer: Hot weather drives both: heat sells ice cream and sends crowds swimming, and more swimmers means more drownings
choices: Hot weather drives both: heat sells ice cream and sends crowds swimming, and more swimmers means more drownings
Ice cream weighs swimmers down, so banning it would actually push even more people to drown each summer
The drownings cause the ice-cream sales, because grieving families comfort themselves with cold sweets
The two numbers rise together every single month, which proves one of them must be feeding the other
context: This is the classic textbook case of a confounding or lurking variable. The label for the error -- 'correlation is not causation' -- goes here, off the clock. Source: Wikipedia, 'Correlation does not imply causation'; The Seattle Times, 'Ice cream doesn't cause drowning.'

question: A man notices that on the mornings he wakes up with a pounding headache, he had fallen asleep with his shoes still on the night before. He starts taking his shoes off carefully, but the headaches keep coming. What is really going on?
answer: Going to bed drunk causes both: alcohol leaves him too far gone to undress and hung over the next morning
choices: Going to bed drunk causes both: alcohol leaves him too far gone to undress and hung over the next morning
Shoes trap heat against the feet overnight, and that rising warmth is what triggers the morning headache
The headache strikes first and leaves him too dizzy at bedtime to manage his own laces and shoes
Two things that keep happening on the very same nights simply have to be feeding into each other
context: A favorite teaching example of a hidden third cause -- the drinking, not the shoes, links the two. Source: Wikipedia, 'Correlation does not imply causation' (confounder: going to bed drunk); Medium, 'Confounding, Colliding, D-Separation, and sleeping with shoes on.'

question: Across a whole grade school, the children with bigger shoe sizes turn out to be the better readers. Buying a kid larger shoes obviously won't teach him to read -- so what links big feet to strong reading?
answer: Age: older kids have both bigger feet and more years of reading practice; compare two six-year-olds and the gap vanishes
choices: Age: older kids have both bigger feet and more years of reading practice; compare two six-year-olds and the gap vanishes
Taller, bigger-footed children sit higher at their desks and see the chalkboard better, so they learn to read faster
Strong readers spend their time sitting and growing rather than running, which lets their feet grow a little larger
Two traits that climb together across a whole school must share some direct line running between the two of them
context: Statisticians like this one even better than ice cream because the trick is sneakier -- feet really do come 'attached' to reading skill through age. Source: web.ma.utexas.edu 'Mistakes in Thinking About Causality'; statistics problems on shoe size vs reading, ages 6-11.

question: Harvard law student Tyler Vigen posted the funniest near-perfect data matches he could find. Two of them: per-person cheese eating rises and falls in step with deaths from getting tangled in bedsheets, and Maine's divorce rate climbs and dips with how much margarine people eat. What do these matched-up graphs actually tell you?
answer: Nothing at all -- a gorgeous, tightly-fitting graph can turn out to be one hundred percent coincidence
choices: Nothing at all -- a gorgeous, tightly-fitting graph can turn out to be one hundred percent coincidence
That our daily food habits secretly shape household dangers and marriages in ways we rarely notice
That somewhere a single hidden cause has to be quietly driving both of the lines in each of the pairs
That cheese and margarine, being two such similar foods, must be distorting the same behaviors at once
context: Vigen collected these in a book, 'Spurious Correlations.' His point: chance alone can draw a gorgeous-looking match -- no hidden third cause needed. Maine divorce vs margarine is correlation #5,920 on his site (2000-2009). Source: Tyler Vigen, Spurious Correlations; National Geographic, 'Nick Cage Movies Vs. Drownings.'

question: Tyler Vigen's joke graph matching Nicolas Cage's yearly film count to swimming-pool drownings was no eyeball illusion: run the math and the two lines score a correlation near 0.67, passing the textbook cutoff for 'statistically significant.' Yet everyone agrees Cage drowns no one. So what does passing that significance test actually prove here?
answer: Nothing about cause -- a correlation can clear every significance test and still be utter nonsense
choices: Nothing about cause -- a correlation can clear every significance test and still be utter nonsense
That significance tests work on serious data but simply break down on silly, hand-picked pairings
That a coincidence this strong must, after all, have some hidden third cause lurking underneath it
That the cutoff for significance was set far too loose, since a real test would have rejected this
context: Vigen ran about a decade of data -- roughly 11 yearly points -- and still got r near 0.67 with a p-value around 1-in-40, 'significant' by the usual rule. The lesson hides inside the joke: significance is not causation. Source: The National, 'Nicolas Cage movies linked to drownings,' reporting Vigen's figures.

question: Look at fire after fire and a chilling pattern appears: the more firefighters who show up, the more damage the fire does. Taken at face value, the firefighters look like the arsonists. Yet send a crew to any single blaze and it plainly does help. What lurking thing makes the raw numbers slander the firefighters?
answer: How big the blaze was: a roaring inferno both summons more trucks and burns more, masking the crew's real effect
choices: How big the blaze was: a roaring inferno both summons more trucks and burns more, masking the crew's real effect
The time of day: night fires both draw larger crews and race further along before anyone even spots them
The building type: a packed warehouse both demands a huge crew and holds far more inside it to burn
How far the firehouse sat: distant stations send more trucks yet reach the blaze too late to save much
context: A confounder can do worse than hide the truth -- it can point exactly backwards, making helpers look like culprits until you control for it. Source: David M. Lane, HyperStat Online; statistics problems on firefighters and fire damage.

question: A philosophy textbook offers this deliberately silly argument: 'Loud musicians live near our low-yield cornfields. So the loud musicians must be ruining the harvest.' The joke is that someone sees two things side by side and instantly invents a cause. What is the more likely real story?
answer: Poor soil made the land cheap, so struggling musicians could afford to live there -- one cause, two effects
choices: Poor soil made the land cheap, so struggling musicians could afford to live there -- one cause, two effects
The musicians' constant noise really does stunt the corn, exactly as the careless argument first suggested
Failing crops drove the local farm prices down, which is what first lured the loud musicians to move in
Two things found right next to each other on a map have to be connected to each other one way or another
context: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy uses this to illustrate 'cum hoc, ergo propter hoc' -- 'with this, therefore because of this.' That Latin label goes here, not in the answer. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Fallacies' (quoted verbatim).

question: Every morning a rooster crows, and minutes later the sun climbs over the hill. The rooster, puffed up, concludes that his crowing hauls the sun into the sky. A logician calls this blunder 'post hoc' -- and warns that its cousin 'cum hoc' is a different trap entirely. Where exactly does the rooster's reasoning break?
answer: He treats the sun arriving later as his crowing made it happen -- yet one event following another never shows the first produced it
choices: He treats the sun arriving later as his crowing made it happen -- yet one event following another never shows the first produced it
He trusts his own groggy eyes over a careful clock, when crow and dawn may not even line up as tightly as he assumes they do
He reasons from his one hilltop alone, when the countless sunrises he has never witnessed would shatter his tidy little rule
He has mixed up a thing he badly wants to be true with a thing that he has actually gone and shown to be solidly true
context: Cum hoc = 'with this, therefore because of this' (side by side); post hoc = 'after this, therefore because of this' (in sequence). A rooster crowing before sunrise is the classic post hoc trap. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Fallacies' (Cum Hoc / Post Hoc entries).

question: In 2000 statistician Robert Matthews of Aston University plotted stork populations against human birth rates across 17 European countries and found a strong link -- so strong that chance alone would produce it only about one time in 125. By the usual rules, that 'proves' storks deliver babies. He published it anyway. What was the lurking variable?
answer: Land area: bigger countries hold more storks AND more people having babies, with no link between the two
choices: Land area: bigger countries hold more storks AND more people having babies, with no link between the two
Folklore: regions that still believe the old stork myth simply count and report their nesting birds more
Climate: the warm springs that draw nesting storks north also happen to lift the local human birth rate
Food supply: a good harvest feeds more storks and, quite separately, leads families to have more children
context: Matthews titled the paper 'Storks Deliver Babies (p = 0.008)' to mock how a tiny p-value can dress up a ridiculous claim. The same illusion shrinks to single villages in Alsace, where bigger villages mean more chimneys for nests AND more families. Source: R. Matthews, Teaching Statistics, 2000.

question: In fall 1973, UC Berkeley's graduate school admitted about 44% of men but only 35% of women, and feared a bias lawsuit. Statistician Peter Bickel then examined the admissions department by department -- and the apparent bias not only vanished but in several departments reversed, favoring women. What had hidden the real picture?
answer: Women applied more to fiercely competitive departments, men to easy-admit ones -- so the field, not sex, set the odds
choices: Women applied more to fiercely competitive departments, men to easy-admit ones -- so the field, not sex, set the odds
A few enormous departments admitted almost no one at all, dragging every single group's overall average sharply down
Men tended to reapply in far greater numbers after early rejections, inflating their final count of eventual acceptances
The university quietly raised its admission standards midway through the year, after most of the men had already applied
context: This is Simpson's Paradox: slicing the data by a hidden variable (department) can reverse the whole story. In 4 of 6 big departments women were actually admitted at a higher rate. Source: Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell, Science 1975; Statistics LibreTexts.

question: For decades doctors saw that women taking hormone replacement therapy had fewer heart attacks, concluded the hormones guarded the heart, and prescribed them to millions. Then a large randomized trial, halted in July 2002, found the hormones slightly RAISED heart attacks and strokes. Why had the original studies pointed the wrong way?
answer: The women who took the hormones were already richer and healthier, so their hearts were protected before the pills
choices: The women who took the hormones were already richer and healthier, so their hearts were protected before the pills
The early studies were simply too small to catch the harm, which only surfaced once millions had started taking it
The hormones genuinely did help at first, but their good effect quietly reversed after a woman took them for years
Doctors had prescribed the therapy mainly to women already showing signs of heart trouble, masking the true benefit
context: This is 'healthy-user bias' -- healthier people are simply more likely to be ON a treatment, so it looks protective. The randomized Women's Health Initiative trial broke the illusion. Source: Tara Parker-Pope, 'How NIH Misread Hormone Study'; WHI 2002 coverage.

question: Smoking and lung cancer were once 'just a correlation' too, and the tobacco industry used that to wave the danger away for years. In 1965 Sir Austin Bradford Hill argued one pattern is the strongest sign a link is real cause, not coincidence. Which finding below would best support that smoking actually CAUSES lung cancer?
answer: Heavier smokers get lung cancer at steadily climbing rates -- the more cigarettes a person smokes, the more cancer
choices: Heavier smokers get lung cancer at steadily climbing rates -- the more cigarettes a person smokes, the more cancer
Smokers, light or heavy, all tend to die of lung cancer at roughly the very same elevated rate as one another
Most people who developed lung cancer turned out to have taken up smoking at some point earlier in their lives
Lung cancer became far more common in the same decades that cigarettes were first sold widely to the public
context: This is Hill's 'dose-response' (biological-gradient) test: more exposure should bring more disease. His other tests include strength (smokers' lung-cancer death ran 10-30x non-smokers'), temporality (cause before effect), and consistency across studies. A correlation surviving all of them has earned the word 'cause.' Statistician Ronald Fisher argued the tobacco industry's side. Source: A. B. Hill, 1965; Bradford Hill criteria, NCBI Bookshelf.

question: In an 1897 paper for the Royal Society, the founding statistician Karl Pearson took two measurements that share nothing in common, divided each by a third number they had no reason to share, and watched a large, respectable-looking correlation rise out of thin air between them. He had manufactured a link where none existed -- and he handed the illusion a name that statisticians still reach for today. What did Pearson call it?
answer: A spurious correlation -- a falsely high number thrown up between two measurements that share no real tie
choices: A spurious correlation -- a falsely high number thrown up between two measurements that share no real tie
A confounded correlation -- a genuine link bent out of true by some hidden third cause working behind it
A nonsense correlation -- a real but meaningless overlap left by two trends that merely drift along together
A compound correlation -- a true link manufactured when several smaller measurements get stacked one on another
context: Pearson named this illusion a 'spurious correlation,' in a paper titled 'On a Form of Spurious Correlation Which May Arise When Indices Are Used in the Measurement of Organs.' He showed, over a century ago, that the coefficient alone can lie. Source: Karl Pearson, Proceedings of the Royal Society, 1897; ScienceDirect, 'Spurious Correlation.'

question: Crates of Thebes was born into one of his city's richest families. As a young man he decided to become a wandering philosopher who owned almost nothing, so he did something drastic with the whole inheritance that would have kept him rich for life. What did Crates do with his fortune?
answer: Gave it all away to his fellow citizens of Thebes
choices: Gave it all away to his fellow citizens of Thebes
Buried it in the hills outside Thebes for safekeeping
Spent it building a school to teach philosophy
Handed it to a temple to be kept by the priests
context: Diogenes Laertius reports that Crates turned his inheritance into money and distributed it among the citizens of Thebes; one tradition puts the figure at about 200 talents. He then lived as a beggar-philosopher who owned only his cloak and a knapsack. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI (Crates), trans. R.D. Hicks, LacusCurtius.

question: Hipparchia of Maroneia was a noblewoman with rich, handsome, well-born suitors lining up to marry her. Instead she fell in love with Crates, a ragged and penniless beggar-philosopher, decades older and famously ugly. When her horrified parents forbade the match, how far did Hipparchia go to marry him?
answer: She threatened to kill herself unless they let her marry him
choices: She threatened to kill herself unless they let her marry him
She ran away from her home to live in the streets with him
She begged the city magistrates to overrule her parents
She secretly wed him in a distant city far from her home
context: Hipparchia loved the discourses and the life of Crates so much that she ignored every wealthy, high-born, handsome suitor and threatened to take her own life unless her parents let her marry the beggar-philosopher. They gave in. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.96 (Hipparchia), Hicks trans., LacusCurtius; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hipparchia'.

question: The beggar-philosopher Crates of Thebes earned a strange nickname in Athens: the 'Door-opener.' He would walk uninvited straight into any house in the city, yet far from throwing him out, families were glad he came. What did Crates do once he was inside their homes?
answer: Settled their quarrels and gave the family advice
choices: Settled their quarrels and gave the family advice
Demanded a meal and a place to sleep for the night
Preached that they should give away their riches
Performed rites to bless the household and its children
context: The Greek nickname was thyrepanoiktes, 'door-opener.' The emperor Julian records that Crates entered friends' homes uninvited specifically to reconcile quarreling family members and offer counsel. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI; Julian, Orations 6.201b; Wikipedia, 'Crates of Thebes'.

question: When Hipparchia's parents begged Crates of Thebes to talk their daughter out of marrying a penniless beggar, Crates tried and failed. So he stood up, stripped off all his clothes in front of her, pointed to his bare body and ragged cloak, and said, 'This is the bridegroom, these are his possessions; choose accordingly.' What was Crates forcing Hipparchia to choose?
answer: The hard Cynic life itself, with nothing to soften or hide it
choices: The hard Cynic life itself, with nothing to soften or hide it
A husband valued for his character, not his looks or his wealth
A life of public shame, mocked by all for living like a beggar
Poverty in place of the comfortable riches she was born into
context: Crates' full words were: 'This is the bridegroom, here are his possessions; make your choice accordingly, for you will be no helpmeet of mine unless you share my pursuits.' By stripping bare in front of her, he laid out the Cynic life exactly as it was — no comfort, no status, nothing hidden — and made her choose that life itself rather than a softened picture of it. She chose him. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.96, Hicks trans., LacusCurtius.

question: Alexander the Great had razed the city of Thebes to the ground. Years later he offered its most famous son, the philosopher Crates, a magnificent gift: he would rebuild Crates' home city, stone by stone. Crates turned the conqueror down flat. What was Crates' reason for refusing to have Thebes rebuilt?
answer: Some other conqueror would only tear it down again
choices: Some other conqueror would only tear it down again
He had sworn never to accept a gift from any king
A philosopher should never set foot in a city of luxury
The Thebans had exiled him and deserved no such favor
context: Crates reasoned that any city Alexander rebuilt, some later conqueror would simply destroy again. He added a verse: 'But poverty and dear obscurity / Are what a prudent man should think his country.' Alexander had destroyed Thebes in 335 BC. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI (Crates); World History Encyclopedia, 'The Life of Crates of Thebes in Diogenes Laertius', article 742.

question: At a grand banquet, the thinker Theodorus sneered that a woman like Hipparchia had no business trading arguments with men. Hipparchia answered with a tight chain of logic: whatever Theodorus may do without blame, she may do without blame; Theodorus may strike himself without blame; so she may strike Theodorus without blame. Why couldn't Theodorus simply wave her argument away?
answer: To deny her conclusion he would have to throw out one of his own premises
choices: To deny her conclusion he would have to throw out one of his own premises
She had brought far more supporters along to the banquet than he had
No one at all was permitted to interrupt a guest at Lysimachus' table
Striking a fellow philosopher at a grand banquet was against the law
context: Hipparchia built a valid syllogism: once you grant the premises, the conclusion follows by force of logic, so the only escape is to reject a premise you have already admitted. Theodorus, unable to answer, instead yanked at her cloak to humiliate her. The exchange took place at the banquet of Lysimachus. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.97, Hicks trans., LacusCurtius; corroborated by the Suda.

question: The Greek philosopher Epicurus taught his students that a wise man should feel no dread at the prospect of his own death. Plenty of thinkers have urged calm in the face of dying, but Epicurus reached it by a peculiar route all his own. What was his reason for saying death is simply no concern of yours?
answer: Death never shares a moment with you: while you live it is not yet here, and when it comes you are gone, so it touches no one
choices: Death never shares a moment with you: while you live it is not yet here, and when it comes you are gone, so it touches no one
Death is the one event every living thing shares, so to fear it is to fear the common fate of all that breathe
Death is a doorway to judgment, so the wise prepare for the reckoning instead of wasting their days in dread
Death takes the coward and the brave alike, so a man should meet it on his feet rather than on his knees
context: Epicurus put it: 'so long as we exist, death is not with us; but when death comes, then we do not exist.' Death is never PRESENT to a subject — so you and your death never actually meet, and a thing that never reaches you cannot harm you. Source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (Cyril Bailey trans.; newepicurean.com, epicurus.net).

question: The Roman poet Lucretius offered the most vivid handle on Epicurus' idea. He pointed out that there was already an eternity of time before you were ever born, and it never troubled you for a single second. So, he said, look at that stretch of nonexistence as a mirror. A mirror of WHAT?
answer: The matching eternity of nonexistence after you die, which is the very same thing you now dread
choices: The matching eternity of nonexistence after you die, which is the very same thing you now dread
The brief candle of a human life, so small between two darknesses that grasping for more is folly
The sleep you fall into each night, from which you wake having lost nothing and feared nothing
The countless lives lived and forgotten before yours, proof that no single death is worth a tear
context: The 'symmetry argument': 'Nature holds this like a mirror up of time-to-be when we are dead and gone.' The eternity before your birth and the eternity after your death are the same nonexistence — so if the first never frightened you, why dread the second? Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura III ~830-842 (Leonard trans., classics.mit.edu/Carus).

question: Epicurus needed to explain WHY death can't harm you, and he did it with one premise about where good and bad live. He claimed that everything good or bad is ultimately something you FEEL. Death, meanwhile, is the end of all feeling. What follows for whether death can be bad for you?
answer: A thing you can never feel can be neither good nor bad for you, so death is simply nothing to you
choices: A thing you can never feel can be neither good nor bad for you, so death is simply nothing to you
Only the gods feel nothing, so by dying a man trades his small pains for their serene indifference
Since pain ends at death, dying is the greatest of pleasures and ought to be welcomed, not feared
Because feeling is the only good, a longer life is always better, and a short one is a genuine loss
context: Epicurus: 'all good and evil consists in sensation, but death is the deprivation of sensation.' If every good or bad is something felt, and death ends all feeling, then death is neither good nor bad FOR the one who dies. Source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (Cyril Bailey trans.).

question: The Stanford Encyclopedia stresses that Epicurus' line 'no one is left to be harmed' is no comforting wish but falls straight out of his physics. He held that the soul is no ghostly thing but is itself built of atoms, as bodily as anything else. So when a man dies, what becomes of those soul-atoms, and why does that leave no one for any afterlife to punish?
answer: They scatter and lose all power of sensation, so no surviving self remains to suffer reward or punishment
choices: They scatter and lose all power of sensation, so no surviving self remains to suffer reward or punishment
They rise free of the flesh at last, joining the eternal fire from which every living soul was first struck
They sink with the corpse into the ground, where in time they feed the new green life that springs above
They set into a fixed and lasting form, keeping the man's character intact for the judgment said to await him
context: The hidden engine is atomism, not hope: at death 'the soul atoms are scattered and no longer retain the capacity for sensation.' No surviving subject means no afterlife, no punishment, and nobody left to be harmed — the 'no subject' premise is built on physics. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus (plato.stanford.edu/entries/epicurus).

question: In Lucretius' poem, Nature herself rounds on a man weeping that he must die, and she scolds him with a single image drawn from a dinner party. He has had a full life, she says, with all its pleasures — so why cling to the table begging for more of the very same? Instead, she tells him, he should do WHAT?
answer: Depart the feast satisfied, like a guest who has eaten his fill and can take his rest content
choices: Depart the feast satisfied, like a guest who has eaten his fill and can take his rest content
Pour out one last cup to the gods who lent him the years, and thank them for the borrowed time
Pass his seat to the young who are still hungry, since the banquet was never his to keep
Drink deep of what remains while he still can, for the dark holds no second helping of wine
context: Nature's speech: why not 'even like a banqueter, depart the halls, laden with life? Why not, with mind content, take now, thou fool, thy unafflicted rest?' Leave the feast satisfied instead of clinging to the table for more of the same. Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura III, Speech of Nature ~931-971 (classics.mit.edu/Carus).

question: Epicurus' argument rests on one premise: if you feel nothing, you can't be harmed. The philosopher Thomas Nagel, in his 1970 essay 'Death,' attacked exactly that premise. He pointed out that a betrayal whispered behind your back harms you even though you never feel a thing. So, Nagel argued, how can death still be bad for you?
answer: It robs you of all the future goods you would otherwise have had, and a harm need not be a felt sensation
choices: It robs you of all the future goods you would otherwise have had, and a harm need not be a felt sensation
It severs every bond of love and duty you owe the living, and those broken bonds are a felt loss
It hands your enemies the victory they sought, and a defeat is real whether or not you live to see it
It ends the soul's long ascent toward wisdom, and to be halted short of the goal is the deepest harm
context: Nagel's DEPRIVATION argument — the live reply that keeps the topic contested. Death can be bad with no subject to feel it, because it deprives you of future goods; a harm needn't be a felt sensation (an unfelt betrayal still harms you). This denies Epicurus' 'no feeling = no harm' premise. No verdict — this is the open objection. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'Death' (1970); SEP: Death (plato.stanford.edu/entries/death).

question: The philosopher Derek Parfit, in his 1984 book 'Reasons and Persons,' designed a hospital case to expose why the symmetry feels wrong. You wake with amnesia, told you either ALREADY had a ten-hour agonizing operation yesterday, or are about to have a one-hour one today. Almost everyone picks one option without hesitation — and Parfit says that choice reveals a deep bias. Which option, and what bias?
answer: The past ten-hour one, revealing that we care far more about future suffering than identical past suffering
choices: The past ten-hour one, revealing that we care far more about future suffering than identical past suffering
The future one-hour one, revealing that we will always trade a long pain for a short one whatever its timing
The past ten-hour one, revealing that we would rather forget our pain than have to sit and dread it
The future one-hour one, revealing that we trust a danger we can see over a memory we cannot check
context: Parfit's 'My Past or Future Operations': almost everyone prefers the longer agony if it is safely in the past. We are deeply biased toward the future — which is exactly why an eternity of nonexistence ahead frightens us while the identical eternity behind does not. Parfit argues the bias is irrational but grants it is near-universal. Source: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984).

question: Lucretius said the eternity before your birth and the eternity after your death are mirror images, so dread the one only if you dread the other. Thomas Nagel argued the mirror is broken. The key, he said, is what would have to be true for each stretch of nonexistence to have robbed you of anything. So why is post-death nonexistence a real loss while pre-birth nonexistence is not?
answer: You can coherently imagine the same self living longer, but anyone born much earlier would simply be a different person
choices: You can coherently imagine the same self living longer, but anyone born much earlier would simply be a different person
You will be mourned by those who knew you after death, but no one could have mourned a you who was never yet conceived
You leave behind unfinished works when you die, but a later birth would have cost the world nothing it ever held
You can picture your own funeral quite clearly, but no living mind can picture the blank that came before its making
context: Nagel's textbook rebuttal of the Lucretian mirror: you cannot be deprived by a late birth, because anyone born significantly earlier would not be YOU — a different person. But you CAN coherently imagine the same self living longer. So death robs you of possible goods while pre-birth nonexistence robs you of nothing; the symmetry only LOOKS exact. No verdict — the live reply. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'Death' (1970), as summarized in SEP: Death.

question: Democritus taught that every object - a stone, a flame, the sea - is built from bits far too small to see, and he coined a Greek word for them that scientists still use 2,400 years later. He named these bits for the one thing nobody could ever do to them. What does the word 'atom' literally mean?
answer: Uncuttable - it can never be split
choices: Uncuttable - it can never be split
Unseen - it can never be observed
Unmoving - it can never be stopped
Unmade - it was never created
context: From the Greek 'atomos': a- ('not') + tomos ('cut'). Democritus named matter's smallest bits for the one thing that could never be done to them - being cut in half. (Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ancient Atomism'; ChemTeam, 'Atomic Structure - Greeks'.)

question: Democritus is remembered as the 'laughing philosopher,' set by ancient writers against Heraclitus, the 'weeping philosopher' - both faced the same human foolishness, one with laughter and one with tears. Yet Democritus wasn't mocking anyone. By his own teaching, what did he believe a good life was actually aimed at?
answer: A calm and contented mind
choices: A calm and contented mind
Endless pleasure and feasting
Fame that outlives your death
Power over other people
context: Democritus called the goal 'euthymia' - cheerfulness, a calm and contented mind. He laughed at human folly not in scorn but because he thought worry over the wrong things was itself the folly. (Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Democritus'; GreekReporter, 'Democritus the Laughing Philosopher'.)

question: Democritus prized knowledge over riches more fiercely than almost anyone. In one famous saying passed down from antiquity, he set the single thing he wanted most against 'the kingdom of the Persians' - then the wealthiest empire on earth - and said he would rather have his one thing. What was the thing he wanted that badly?
answer: To uncover the true cause of one single fact
choices: To uncover the true cause of one single fact
To be remembered and praised for a thousand years
To live a long life entirely free of trouble
To command a still greater empire of his own
context: Legend, attributed to Democritus: he would 'rather discover one causal explanation than gain the kingdom of the Persians.' Working out the true cause of a single fact beat ruling the richest empire on earth. (Source: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Democritus Fragments'; widely quoted, attribution traditional.)

question: Democritus and Leucippus claimed everything is made of bits so tiny that no one would actually see one for another 2,400 years - and they got there with no microscope, by pure reasoning. Picture cutting a piece of gold in half, then half again, on and on. What argument convinced them the cutting has to stop somewhere?
answer: Cut forever and you reach nothing, but nothing can't build a real thing
choices: Cut forever and you reach nothing, but nothing can't build a real thing
Each fresh cut takes a moment, so endless cuts could never be finished
The gods had set a sacred limit and forbade cutting any matter past it
The pieces would grow hotter with each cut until they burst into flame
context: Their reasoning: divide a real thing endlessly and you'd be left with nothing - but a real thing can't be built out of nothing, so the dividing must halt at an indivisible bit. Argument alone, ~2,400 years before anyone could see an atom. (Source: Big Think, 'How Democritus predicted the atom'; CK-12, 'Democritus's Idea of the Atom'.)

question: From an endless supply of atoms moving through endless empty space, Democritus drew a staggering conclusion: ours is not the only world. The ancient writer Hippolytus reports that Democritus taught there are countless OTHER worlds - of different sizes, some flourishing, some falling apart. What startling detail did he add about some of those worlds?
answer: Some have no sun or moon at all
choices: Some have no sun or moon at all
Some are ruled by a single great king
Some are built entirely out of fire
Some are perfect copies of our own
context: Hippolytus reports Democritus held there are innumerable worlds of different sizes - some with no sun or moon, some with suns and moons larger than ours, some with many; some thriving, some decaying, some with no living things or water at all. (Source: Hippolytus, Refutatio I.13.2f, via Encyclopedia.com, 'Leucippus and Democritus'.)

question: Democritus made a claim that still unsettles people: the sweetness you taste in honey and the blue you see in the sky are not truly out there in the honey or the sky. In one famous line he called sweet, bitter, hot, cold, and color things that hold only 'by convention.' Strip those away, he said, and what is REALLY there?
answer: The atoms and the empty void
choices: The atoms and the empty void
The four elements: earth, water, air, fire
Numbers and the ratios between them
One single unchanging whole
context: Fragment DK 68B9: 'by convention sweet, by convention bitter... but in reality, atoms and void.' Sweetness and color aren't out there - only atoms and empty space are; the rest is how atoms strike our senses. (Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Democritus', citing DK 68B9.) The rival answers are real pre-Socratic views: four elements (Empedocles), numbers (Pythagoreans), one unchanging whole (Parmenides).

question: If everything is built from the same tiny bits, how can the world hold so many DIFFERENT things - iron and water, a dog and a stone? Democritus said the bits differ in only three ways, and Aristotle illustrated it with letters: A differs from N in shape, AN differs from NA in order, and a turned letter differs in its position. What was the striking point of Aristotle's letter comparison?
answer: The same few letters spell both a tragedy and a comedy
choices: The same few letters spell both a tragedy and a comedy
The same letters in a new order make a whole new word
A mere handful of letters can write out every book ever penned
A single letter, repeated enough, can stand in for any word
context: Aristotle's point (On Generation and Corruption): just as the same alphabet spells both a tragedy and a comedy, the same atoms - differing only in shape, arrangement, and position - build every different thing in the world. (Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Democritus', citing Aristotle; Manchester PDF, 'Leucippus and Democritus'.)

question: A logic teacher tells the class: "If you trained as a knight, you carry a sword. This traveler never trained as a knight, so he must be unarmed." A merchant in the room speaks up: he never trained as a knight either, yet he bought a sword last week. What flaw has the merchant just exposed?
answer: Knight-training is only one source of a sword, so ruling it out leaves every other source untouched
choices: Knight-training is only one source of a sword, so ruling it out leaves every other source untouched
A blade does not count as a real weapon unless its owner was first formally trained to wield it well
The teacher reversed the rule, treating a man's carried sword as proof that he had trained as a knight
The opening rule was false from the very start, since plenty of trained knights carry no sword at all
context: This is the fallacy of denying the antecedent: 'If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q.' It is invalid because Q can be reached by another route entirely. Source: Wikipedia, 'Denying the antecedent'; framing handle from the topic's vivid knight example.

question: A student reasons: "If you are a ski instructor, then you have a job. This man is not a ski instructor, so he must have no job at all." The student is sure the conclusion is forced. Why is it not?
answer: Ski instructor is just one job among countless others, so ruling it out leaves every other job untouched
choices: Ski instructor is just one job among countless others, so ruling it out leaves every other job untouched
The rule secretly means the two always travel together, so missing that one job must mean missing all work
It flips the rule around, treating the man's having a job as proof that he must be a ski instructor
The opening rule is simply false to begin with, since plenty of ski instructors hold no real job at all
context: Denying the antecedent: the conditional named one job-route, and not taking that route says nothing about all the others. Maria-style cases make the same point about credentials. The second choice is the deeper trap, misreading 'if P then Q' as 'P only if Q.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Denying the antecedent'; QuillBot, 'Denying the Antecedent.'

question: A student argues: "If an animal is a mammal, it is warm-blooded. This animal is not a mammal, therefore it is not warm-blooded." Her teacher sinks the whole argument with a single living counterexample, an animal that is plainly warm-blooded yet no mammal. Which animal does the trick?
answer: A bird
choices: A bird
A snake
A frog
A lizard
context: A bird reaches 'warm-blooded' by a different door than mammals do, so it refutes 'not a mammal, therefore not warm-blooded' on the spot. Snakes, frogs, and lizards are all cold-blooded non-mammals, so none of them break the inference. The error is denying the antecedent. Source: QuillBot, 'Denying the Antecedent.'

question: In his 1950 paper on whether machines can think, Alan Turing weighs this argument: "If each man followed a fixed set of rules for living, he would be no better than a machine; but there are no such rules, so men cannot be machines." Turing refuses the conclusion. On what grounds does he reject it?
answer: Fixed rules are only one way of being a machine, so ruling them out cannot rule out being a machine
choices: Fixed rules are only one way of being a machine, so ruling them out cannot rule out being a machine
Granting that men follow no fixed rules at all already proves outright that men must indeed be machines
The argument quietly assumes its result, using the claim men are not machines to prove that very point
The opening claim is plainly false, since following fixed rules would not truly make a man machine-like
context: Turing names this as denying the antecedent: the conclusion does not follow, because 'no better than a machine' could be reached another way. Source: A. M. Turing (1950), 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' Mind 59:433-460.

question: Two bad arguments sit side by side. First: "If it rained, the pavement is wet; the pavement is wet, so it rained." Second: "If it rained, the pavement is wet; it did not rain, so the pavement is not wet." A teacher calls them mirror twins that fail for the very same reason. What is the shared blind spot?
answer: Both forget the pavement can be soaked by another cause, so ruling rain in or out settles nothing
choices: Both forget the pavement can be soaked by another cause, so ruling rain in or out settles nothing
Both mistake a conclusion that merely happens to be true sometimes for one guaranteed every single time
Both treat the conditional rule as running in only one direction when in truth it has to run in both ways
Both depend on a starting rule that is plainly false, since rain does not always leave the pavement wet
context: The first argument is affirming the consequent; the second is denying the antecedent. They are sister fallacies with the same blind spot: each ignores that the wet pavement (Q) can arise by another route. Source: Fallacy Files, 'Denying the Antecedent.'

question: A guard works from one rule: "If the bridge is safe, the warning light is off." He wants a conclusion he can fully trust. He may rule out either part, the safety or the light, but only one of these moves gives an airtight inference. Which move is the valid one?
answer: Notice the warning light is on, and conclude that the bridge cannot be safe
choices: Notice the warning light is on, and conclude that the bridge cannot be safe
Learn the bridge is not safe, and conclude the warning light must be on
Learn the bridge is not safe, and conclude the warning light must be off
Notice the warning light is off, and conclude that the bridge must be safe
context: The valid move denies the consequent (the light), not the antecedent (the safety): if the light is on, the bridge cannot be safe. Logicians call this modus tollens. The other three deny the antecedent or affirm the consequent, all invalid. One letter of difference, total collapse. Source: Fallacy Files, 'Denying the Antecedent'; Wikipedia, 'Denying the antecedent.'

question: In 1972 the creationist writer Henry Morris argued that believing in evolution is required for atheism, then concluded that rejecting atheism means rejecting evolution. A critic granted Morris that first claim and still threw out the conclusion. Why doesn't it follow?
answer: Many religious believers accept evolution too, so turning away from atheism leaves belief in evolution standing
choices: Many religious believers accept evolution too, so turning away from atheism leaves belief in evolution standing
Once atheism is set aside, every argument that ever leaned on evolution has to be set aside along with it
The argument leans on its own ending, using the claim evolution is false to prove that evolution is false
It mixes up two different groups, treating everyone who accepts evolution as though they had to be an atheist
context: Even granting Morris his premise, the inference denies the antecedent: many theistic religions accept evolution, so denying atheism never denies evolution. A famous real-world specimen. Source: Fallacy Files, 'Denying the Antecedent,' analyzing H. Morris, 'The Remarkable Birth of Planet Earth' (1972).

question: On his deathbed your grandfather makes you promise to scatter his ashes at the lake he loved. He dies. No one else knows the promise was ever made, and frankly the trip is a hassle — his ashes would do more visible good buried cheaply in the yard, and nobody would be the wiser. You feel you must go to the lake anyway. What is that pull telling you?
answer: The bond you made still holds you, even with no one left to enforce it
choices: The bond you made still holds you, even with no one left to enforce it
The bond dissolves the moment the person who heard it dies
A promise is only as good as the good that keeping it produces
A vow to the dead is a private comfort, not a debt you actually owe
context: The deathbed promise is a classic test of which moral 'move' you are running. The duty move says the promise still binds you, full stop. The rival move — judge acts by their consequences — struggles to explain why a secret promise to someone now dead should matter at all, since no one is left to be helped or hurt. That gap is exactly what makes the case a clean diagnostic. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Deontological Ethics' (promise-keeping as a perfect duty); standard ethics-textbook deathbed-promise case.

question: Two friends argue. Mara says the right choice is always whichever one brings about the most good: if framing a single innocent man would quiet a deadly riot, she would frame him and not lose sleep. Tomas is appalled and says he could never frame the innocent man. What principle is Tomas standing on?
answer: Some acts are forbidden in themselves, whatever good their results would bring
choices: Some acts are forbidden in themselves, whatever good their results would bring
Some acts are wrong because, in the long run, they lead to worse results for everyone
An act is wrong only when the person harmed by it has not agreed to it
Some acts stay forbidden only until the good at stake grows large enough
context: This is the live fork in ethics. Mara is running the consequences move (judge by outcomes), which is why she would frame an innocent man if the math favored it; Tomas is running the duty move, which forbids the framing whatever it would buy. The Stanford Encyclopedia states it exactly: 'some choices cannot be justified by their effects — that no matter how morally good their consequences, some choices are morally forbidden.' Neither side is settled here — the point is to recognize the two moves, not to crown a winner. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Deontological Ethics' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-deontological/).

question: A surgeon has five patients dying for want of organs — two need a lung, two a kidney, one a heart. A healthy young man strolls in for a routine checkup, and his blood type is a perfect match for all five. Quietly cut him up, and five people walk out alive. Almost everyone says the surgeon must NOT do it. Which principle is doing the blocking?
answer: You may not butcher one innocent person even to save a greater number
choices: You may not butcher one innocent person even to save a greater number
You may not act until you are certain all five transplants would succeed
You may not treat a patient without first getting his informed consent
You may not weigh one stranger's life against several you know better
context: This is Judith Jarvis Thomson's transplant case. The arithmetic is stark — one death buys five lives — yet the near-universal reaction is that the surgeon is forbidden to do it. That refusal is the duty move in action: it blocks the math even at five-to-one. Consent and surgical odds are real concerns, but they are not what does the deep blocking; the wrong is the deliberate butchery of an innocent. Source: Judith Jarvis Thomson, 'The Trolley Problem,' Yale Law Journal (1985); Wikipedia, Judith Jarvis Thomson.

question: In a 1797 essay Immanuel Kant takes the hardest case he can find: a killer pounds on your door and demands to know where your friend is hiding inside. Lie, and your friend likely lives. Kant's startling verdict was that you must not tell the lie at all. On his reasoning, what makes the lie wrong?
answer: Telling a deliberate lie is wrong in itself, whatever good it might secure
choices: Telling a deliberate lie is wrong in itself, whatever good it might secure
Telling a lie is wrong because the killer might see through it and attack
Telling a lie is wrong only when you cannot be sure it will save the friend
Telling a lie is wrong because it trains you into a habit of easy dishonesty
context: Kant wrote 'On a Supposed Right to Tell Lies from Benevolent Motives' (1797) in answer to Benjamin Constant, who had thrown the murderer-at-the-door case at him as a trap — surely a lie to a killer is allowed? Kant refused to flinch: the deliberate lie is wrong in itself, whatever the result. The dilemma is ancient, running back through Augustine's 'On Lying' and even Xenophon. The duty move at its starkest. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Tell Lies from Benevolent Motives' (1797); Wikipedia summary.

question: Here is the puzzle that splits people. A runaway trolley will kill five; throw a switch and it kills one on a side track instead — most people say throw it. Yet the same people refuse to let a surgeon cut up one healthy man to save five. Both trade one life for five. What is the difference that flips the verdict?
answer: In the transplant the man's body is the plan; on the track the death is a side effect
choices: In the transplant the man's body is the plan; on the track the death is a side effect
In the transplant five are saved at once; on the track the five are saved one by one
In the transplant a doctor acts; on the track an ordinary bystander acts instead
In the transplant the victim is healthy; on the track the victim was already at risk
context: This trolley-versus-transplant split is the whole puzzle. The duty move points to how the one death figures in your plan: in the transplant you USE the man — his organs ARE the rescue, so harming him is the means; on the track, the lone worker's death is an unwanted side effect of diverting the trolley, not part of how the five get saved. Whether that distinction truly carries the moral weight is itself debated. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Deontological Ethics'; Thomson, 'The Trolley Problem' (1985).

question: A challenger presses the duty view with its sharpest objection: if one murder is wrong, surely two murders are worse — so to prevent two killers from each killing, you ought to commit one murder yourself and come out ahead. The duty view bites the bullet and refuses. What is its answer to the challenge?
answer: You answer for the murder you yourself commit, not for murders other people commit
choices: You answer for the murder you yourself commit, not for murders other people commit
You should commit the one murder, since fewer total killings is plainly the better world
You may commit the one murder only once you are certain it will stop the other two
You should refuse, because committing a murder yourself rarely stops a determined killer
context: This is the 'paradox of deontology.' If wrongs are bad, why not commit one to minimize the world's total of them? The duty move answers that you are answerable for what YOU do — your own act of murder — not for keeping down the global tally of other people's wrongs. The Stanford Encyclopedia flags this as the hardest pill the view asks you to swallow, and its critics treat the refusal as a genuine cost. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Deontological Ethics' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-deontological/).

question: Bernard Williams imagined Jim stumbling on a soldier, Pedro, about to shoot twenty captives. Pedro makes an offer: shoot ONE captive yourself, and the other nineteen go free. Jim does the grim arithmetic and sees the numbers favor shooting. Williams thought something deeper was at stake than the body count. What was his objection?
answer: Pulling the trigger makes Jim the author of a killing he finds monstrous, not a bystander to Pedro's
choices: Pulling the trigger makes Jim the author of a killing he finds monstrous, not a bystander to Pedro's
Pulling the trigger hardens Jim into the kind of man who can shoot a captive on command
Pulling the trigger makes Jim a willing partner in the cruel game Pedro has set up
Pulling the trigger forces Jim to play God, picking which single captive of twenty must die
context: Bernard Williams put this case in 'Utilitarianism: For and Against' (1973) as his integrity objection. Treating the outcome as all that matters, he argued, makes a person 'a channel between the input of everyone's projects and an output of optimific decision' — alienating him from his own deepest convictions. And it is Pedro's hand on those deaths, not Jim's. The duty move keeps your own clean hands as something you need not trade away. Source: Bernard Williams, in Smart & Williams, 'Utilitarianism: For and Against' (1973); Stanford Encyclopedia, 'Bernard Williams'.

question: In 1992, when Cambridge University moved to award an honorary degree to the French philosopher Jacques Derrida, nineteen scholars — including the logician W. V. O. Quine — signed a protest letter to The Times of London. They charged that his work failed 'accepted standards of clarity and rigour,' called it 'tricks and gimmicks,' and sneered that his wordplay produced mere 'logical phallusies.' Cambridge put the honor to a full faculty vote. How did the vote come out?
answer: They awarded it anyway, 336 to 204
choices: They awarded it anyway, 336 to 204
They rejected it narrowly, 198 to 211
They rejected it in a landslide, 412 to 90
They awarded it narrowly, 270 to 264
context: Derrida was one of the most cited — and most fiercely contested — thinkers of the 20th century, and the Cambridge affair captured the split: nineteen philosophers, led by Barry Smith and the famous logician W. V. O. Quine, signed the protest published in The Times on May 9, 1992, mocking his puns as 'logical phallusies' and likening his work to the Dadaists. The faculty held a full vote and granted the degree anyway, 336 to 204. Source: Letter to The Times, 9 May 1992 (Barry Smith, Quine et al.); academia.edu/2824164, 'Revisiting the Derrida affair with Barry Smith'; Wikipedia: Searle–Derrida debate.

question: The American philosopher John Searle feuded for years with Jacques Derrida, who had argued that no author fully controls his words once they are written down — nor can he bind their meaning to whatever he originally intended. When Derrida gathered their published quarrel into a single book, Searle made one demand about his own contribution to it. What did Searle demand?
answer: That his reply be cut, since he owned the copyright to it
choices: That his reply be cut, since he owned the copyright to it
That his reply run first, ahead of anything Derrida wrote
That his name be struck from the book, to disown the project
That the publisher insert a note distancing him from the work
context: Derrida found this perfect: a man defending sole ownership and authority over his text was, to him, acting out the exact fantasy of total authorial control that deconstruction says is impossible. The feud began with Derrida's 'Signature Event Context' (1972), which argued any sign is 'iterable' — repeatable in new contexts, cut loose from its author. Derrida's book-length reply, 'Limited Inc,' even read Searle's name through 'Société à responsabilité limitée' (limited-liability company, 'Ltd'). Searle did not respond. Source: Wikipedia: Searle–Derrida debate.

question: In Plato's dialogue Phaedrus, Socrates dismisses writing as a poor substitute for living speech, and pins one Greek word on it: pharmakon. Jacques Derrida seized on that very word — because it carries two clashing meanings at once, so the term Plato chose to bury writing quietly cuts against his own tidy ranking of speech over writing. What clashing pair of meanings is hidden inside pharmakon?
answer: Remedy and poison
choices: Remedy and poison
Speech and silence
Memory and forgetting
Gift and burden
context: In Greek, pharmakon means both 'remedy' and 'poison' — so the single word Plato reaches for to dismiss writing already carries the opposite of his verdict folded inside it. Derrida treated this as the textbook case of a text undoing itself from within, using the author's own vocabulary rather than any outside attack: Plato's neat good-speech / bad-writing hierarchy collapses on its own terms. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jacques Derrida; G. Kakoliris, 'The Undecidable Pharmakon: Derrida's Reading of Plato's Phaedrus' (frenchphilosophy.gr).

question: Jacques Derrida's most quoted line, from Of Grammatology, is usually thrown into English as 'There is nothing outside the text.' It launched a thousand arguments — and, careful translators insist, just as many misreadings. Setting the careless slogans aside, which reading is the faithful one, the claim Derrida was actually making?
answer: That nothing reaches us raw; it all arrives already filtered through context
choices: That nothing reaches us raw; it all arrives already filtered through context
That the world beyond language is unreal, and only our words are truly real
That every text hides one true meaning a patient reader can dig back out
That a reader is free to make any text mean whatever he happens to want
context: The French is 'Il n'y a pas de hors-texte.' Careful translators render it not as 'there is nothing outside the text' but as 'there is no outside-of-text' — nothing free of context. It does NOT mean reality doesn't exist or that only words are real; that popular 'nothing exists but language' version is the strawman, not the claim. Derrida's point is that every experience reaches us already mediated by interpretation and contrast. Source: Of Grammatology (1967), trans. Spivak; Max Deutscher, 'Il n'y a pas de hors-texte — Once More' (philarchive.org/rec/DEUINA-2); Wikiquote: Jacques Derrida.

question: Jacques Derrida read the linguist Ferdinand de Saussure closely. In one place Saussure calls the link between a word and its meaning purely 'arbitrary' — no natural connection at all — yet elsewhere he insists on a 'natural bond' between sound and sense. Faced with a passage like this, Derrida had a signature way of working. What does his method actually do with those two claims?
answer: Read the two claims side by side and let the text unsettle its own distinction
choices: Read the two claims side by side and let the text unsettle its own distinction
Measure the text against a sounder theory of language drawn from elsewhere
Rewrite the muddled passages until the author's real intention shows through
Settle which of the two claims is correct and set the weaker one aside
context: This is deconstruction's core move: a text can quietly contradict its own neat oppositions, and the reader's task is simply to show the contradiction that is ALREADY there — never to attack from outside. Saussure insists the sign is 'arbitrary' yet also argues for a 'natural bond' between sound and sense; the two claims undercut each other inside his own framework. Derrida held that such contradictions sit in the 'neglected cornerstones' of a system, exposed rather than imposed by the critic. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jacques Derrida (iep.utm.edu/jacques-derrida).

question: Rene Descartes decides to test his beliefs with one harsh rule: any belief he can find even the smallest reason to doubt, he will throw out as if it were flat-out false. Why put himself through tearing down nearly everything he thinks he knows?
answer: To find out whether even one belief survives that cannot be doubted at all
choices: To find out whether even one belief survives that cannot be doubted at all
To prove that nothing in the world can ever really be known for certain
To memorize his beliefs in order, listing them from strongest to weakest
To win an argument against rival teachers who doubted his good sense
context: For Descartes the doubt is not despair but a search for bedrock: tear everything down, then see if anything is left standing that no doubt can shake. Source: IEP, Rene Descartes; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Descartes' Epistemology.

question: Rene Descartes points to a tall tower seen far across a field: from a distance it looks round, yet walk up close and you find it is square. What lesson does he draw from cases like this?
answer: The senses sometimes deceive us, so we cannot fully trust what they report
choices: The senses sometimes deceive us, so we cannot fully trust what they report
Towers were usually built round in his day and only later made square
Distance has no effect at all on how clearly a person sees a shape
Our eyes are flawless, and any mistake must come from a bad memory
context: This is the gentlest wave of Descartes' doubt. Because the senses slip up on distant or tiny things, he refuses to lean his whole house of belief on them. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Descartes' Epistemology; IEP, Rene Descartes.

question: To push his doubt as far as it can go, Rene Descartes imagines an enemy: not God, but a being of enormous power and cunning who pours all its energy into one task. What is this imagined being trying to do to him?
answer: Deceive him about everything, fooling him at every turn
choices: Deceive him about everything, fooling him at every turn
Steal the private notebooks where he keeps his proofs
Tempt him into laziness so he stops thinking altogether
Frighten him into agreeing with the teachers he distrusts
context: Descartes writes of 'some malicious demon of the utmost power and cunning' who 'has employed all his energies in order to deceive me.' The demon is doubt cranked to its absolute maximum. Source: Descartes, Meditations I; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Descartes' Epistemology.

question: In The Matrix, every sight, sound, and touch a person feels is secretly being piped into their mind by machines. Rene Descartes dreamed up the same nightmare around 350 years before the film, using an all-powerful deceiver instead of computers. What worry do the demon and the Matrix share?
answer: That your whole reality might be a perfect fake, fed to you from outside
choices: That your whole reality might be a perfect fake, fed to you from outside
That machines will one day grow smarter than every human combined
That a person who thinks too hard slowly loses touch with friends
That dreams are only memories the brain replays back to itself
context: The same worry powers the 'brain in a vat,' sharpened by Gilbert Harman (1973) and made famous by Hilary Putnam. Descartes got there centuries before either. Source: IEP, Brain in a Vat Argument; Wikipedia, Evil demon.

question: Rene Descartes notices something unsettling about sleep: right now he seems to be sitting by the fire in his winter dressing-gown, holding a sheet of paper, yet he has often dreamed exactly such ordinary scenes and believed them completely. What conclusion does this force on him?
answer: No sure sign tells waking apart from dreaming, so even this could be a dream
choices: No sure sign tells waking apart from dreaming, so even this could be a dream
A faint blur always marks a dream, so any sharp, clear scene must be real waking life
A person can always choose at will to wake up the instant a dream begins
Sitting beside a warm winter fire is the one scene that cannot be dreamed
context: Descartes: 'How often, asleep at night, am I convinced of just such familiar events - that I am here in my dressing-gown, sitting by the fire.' With no certain mark of waking, the whole scene falls under doubt. Source: Descartes, Meditations I; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Descartes' Epistemology.

question: Rene Descartes pictures his beliefs as a basket of apples with a few rotten ones hidden inside. He decides that pulling each apple out and checking it one by one would be foolish. What does he do with the basket instead?
answer: Tips the whole basket out, then puts back only the apples he sees are sound
choices: Tips the whole basket out, then puts back only the apples he sees are sound
Leaves every apple where it sits, trusting that most of the basket is still fine
Shoves the basket aside untouched and goes hunting for a brand-new basket
Keeps whichever apples the largest crowd of people would call good ones
context: The apple-barrel image guards against contagion: one rotten belief, left in the basket, can spread its rot to the rest, so Descartes rejects them in a heap rather than one by one and restores only the sound ones. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Descartes' Epistemology, quoting Replies 7.

question: According to the story Rene Descartes tells in his Discourse on the Method, his new way of thinking was born on a single solitary day in November 1619, while winter pinned him down near the town of Ulm. Where does he say he spent that whole day, alone with his own thoughts?
answer: Shut up by himself in a small stove-heated room
choices: Shut up by himself in a small stove-heated room
Marching in the ranks of a half-frozen winter army
Riding hard between two distant walled cities
Kneeling through long services in a stone cathedral
context: This origin is told by Descartes himself and is part legend. He recalls being 'completely free to converse with myself about my own thoughts' in a 'stove-heated room' (poele). Source: Descartes, Discourse on the Method (1637), via OUPblog and Bloomsbury, 'Descartes's Stove.'

question: Even after Rene Descartes admits he might be dreaming, a few truths still seem too plain to shake: two and three added together make five, and a square has no more than four sides. He grants these hold whether he is awake or asleep. Why does this stubborn survival trouble his whole project?
answer: If even arithmetic stands undoubted, his tearing-down of belief is not yet total
choices: If even arithmetic stands undoubted, his tearing-down of belief is not yet total
He had promised at the very outset to doubt all of mathematics before anything else
Arithmetic was the one kind of knowledge he had always quietly distrusted
Proving these simple sums true had been the single goal of his doubt all along
context: Descartes: 'whether I am awake or asleep, two and three added together are five, and a square has no more than four sides.' Because these still stand, the demolition is incomplete and he reaches for a bigger doubt. Source: Descartes, Meditations I (AT 7:20).

question: The evil demon has made Rene Descartes doubt the world, his body, even simple sums. Then he spots a crack the deceiver cannot reach: 'let him deceive me as much as he can, he will never bring it about that I am nothing so long as I think that I am something.' What keeps the thinker safe from the deception here?
answer: To be deceived at all, he must exist to be the one being fooled
choices: To be deceived at all, he must exist to be the one being fooled
The demon has sworn an oath never to lie about a person's own mind
A deceiver that powerful would find lying about him too small a task
He has caught the demon out, which strips away all its remaining power
context: This is the hinge that sets up the cogito: no deception can empty out the deceived. Even a perfect liar needs someone there to lie to. Source: Descartes, Meditations II; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Descartes' Epistemology.

question: Rene Descartes recalls how Archimedes claimed that with a single firm, immovable point he could shift the entire earth. Descartes says he hopes for something just as grand from one certainty. What is the single fixed point his whole rebuilt knowledge ends up balanced on?
answer: His own thinking - the one thing he cannot doubt while he is doing it
choices: His own thinking - the one thing he cannot doubt while he is doing it
The trustworthiness of his eyes once he checks them up close
The agreement of the wisest teachers of his own century
The rules of geometry, which the demon was never able to touch
context: Descartes: 'Archimedes used to demand just one firm and immovable point in order to shift the entire earth; so I too can hope for great things if I manage to find just one thing... that is certain and unshakeable.' That point is his own thought. Source: Descartes, Meditations II.

question: The dreaming argument could not touch arithmetic - asleep or awake, two and three make five. So Rene Descartes hands his imagined deceiver one extra, staggering power, the move that finally drags even math into doubt. What can this deceiver do that mere dreaming could not?
answer: Rig his very reasoning, so he goes wrong every time he adds two and three
choices: Rig his very reasoning, so he goes wrong every time he adds two and three
Replace the true rules of math with different rules while he sleeps
Hide the correct answer from him until he finally gives up trying
