Convince every other person that his correct sums are mistaken
context: Descartes fears the deceiver 'may have brought it about that I too go wrong every time I add two and three.' Faking math is the demon's signature power - the thing dreaming alone could never manage. Source: Descartes, Meditations I; Wikipedia, Evil demon.

question: Meditation I does not close in triumph. Rene Descartes likens himself to a prisoner who in sleep dreams he is free, then begins to suspect he is dreaming and dreads waking. What does Descartes fear waking from his doubt will mean?
answer: Being plunged back from this light into an inextricable darkness
choices: Being plunged back from this light into an inextricable darkness
Being mocked by the very teachers he had set out to surpass
Discovering that the evil demon had been entirely real all along
Forgetting every careful step of doubt he had just worked through
context: The doubt is genuinely frightening before the cogito rescues him: the prisoner 'is afraid to wake up,' fearing a return to 'inextricable darkness.' Source: Descartes, Meditations I (closing paragraph); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Descartes' Epistemology.

question: In writing, Rene Descartes called his great deceiver by the Latin genius malignus and the French malin genie - the malicious genius. He picked that figure with great care, writing in the very years when Galileo had been hauled before the Inquisition. Naming the deceiver a demon let Descartes sidestep one specific danger the censors could have pounced on. Which one?
answer: It kept him from seeming to make God himself the great deceiver
choices: It kept him from seeming to make God himself the great deceiver
It kept him from seeming to deny that the soul outlives the body
It kept him from seeming to teach that the earth circles the sun
It kept him from seeming to mock the saints the Church held holy
context: 'Evil demon' renders genius malignus / malin genie (malicious genius). By doctrine God cannot deceive, so an all-powerful liar would have to be God - a blasphemous suggestion. Writing just after Galileo's 1633 condemnation, Descartes pinned the deception on a demon instead and stayed clear of the charge. Source: Wikipedia, Evil demon; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Descartes' Epistemology.

question: People in Athens called Diogenes 'the Dog' because he lived out in the open and did his animal business in the street without shame. When someone asked him why he answered to such a name, Diogenes leaned into it with a three-part boast about how he treated people. What did he say a dog like him does?
answer: Fawns on those who give, yelps at those who refuse, and bites the wicked
choices: Fawns on those who give, yelps at those who refuse, and bites the wicked
Guards the rich man's gate and sleeps wherever a warm fire is burning
Hunts in a pack and obeys whichever master feeds it the largest meal
Begs from strangers, flatters the powerful, and runs from every fight
context: Asked why he was called a dog, Diogenes replied, 'I fawn on those who give me anything, I yelp at those who refuse, and I set my teeth in rascals.' The word 'Cynic' itself comes from the Greek kynikos, 'dog-like' (from kyon/kynos, dog) — a label earned, then embraced, by a man who lived and relieved himself in public like a shameless animal. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI.60; etymology in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and World History Encyclopedia.

question: Diogenes did things in the crowded marketplace that everyone agreed were fine to do at home behind a closed door. People were scandalized. He insisted he was proving a point, not just being filthy: the very same act drew no blame in private but disgrace in public. What was the point he claimed the stunt proved?
answer: That the shame attached to the act comes from custom, not from nature
choices: That the shame attached to the act comes from custom, not from nature
That a wise man should keep every bodily need strictly hidden from view
That city crowds are crueler judges than a man's own household ever is
That an act done openly is always braver than the same act done in secret
context: Diogenes 'made it his habit to do everything in public,' arguing that if an act is not shameful in private, doing it in public cannot make it shameful — the shame-line is drawn by nomos (convention), not physis (nature). Cynicism splits the world into nature and convention and ranks convention below; manners, etiquette, and shame were 'artificial constructs' that cut a person off from a clear view of nature. The question is presented as Diogenes' claim, not a verdict on public decency. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.69; principle stated in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Diogenes of Sinope.'

question: Plato had won applause across Athens for his definition of a human being: an animal, two-legged, and without feathers. Diogenes plucked a chicken bald, marched it into Plato's lecture hall, and set it down: 'Here is Plato's man.' Beyond the laugh, why did the bald bird actually wreck the definition?
answer: A tidy list of outer traits had captured a plucked fowl, not what a person is
choices: A tidy list of outer traits had captured a plucked fowl, not what a person is
Plato had forgotten that some humans are born with very little hair at all
A chicken and a man share too many traits for any words to tell them apart
A definition of a living thing must change the moment the creature is altered
context: Diogenes refuted Plato's celebrated formula with a single ridiculous counterexample: a featherless biped now describes a plucked chicken. The philosophical point is that a verbal definition listing outward features can perfectly fit something that is plainly not a human — so it has not grasped what a human actually is. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.40 (Perseus/Penelope text); corroborated by World History Encyclopedia, 'Diogenes of Sinope.'

question: Diogenes was run out of his home city of Sinope for tampering with coins at the mint, literally re-stamping the money. He spent the rest of his life turning that very crime into the slogan of his philosophy, and he wore it proudly. What did 'defacing the currency' come to mean for him?
answer: Stamping over the false values society passes around as if they were real
choices: Stamping over the false values society passes around as if they were real
Refusing to touch money of any kind for the rest of his wandering life
Teaching mint-workers an honest trade so no city would be cheated again
Printing his own coins stamped with the face of a barking street dog
context: 'Deface the currency' (Greek parakharattein to nomisma) was both Diogenes' literal crime and the slogan of his whole life. The pun works because nomisma (currency) shares a root with nomos (custom, law): re-stamping bad coin became re-stamping bad convention. Diogenes Laertius states the mission outright — he lived 'adulterating the currency in very truth, allowing convention no such authority as he allowed to natural right.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Britannica, 'Diogenes'; the keystone line is Lives VI.71.

question: Diogenes knew the crowds loved watching him puncture the polite lies people lived by; they cheered the show. He called himself a strange breed of hound, one that every man alive praises. What was the sting hidden in the rest of that boast?
answer: That not one of those admirers would ever go out hunting, living that bare life, beside him
choices: That not one of those admirers would ever go out hunting, living that bare life, beside him
That not one of those same men would trust a barking street dog to guard their own home
That not one of his fans could match the sharp nose he had for sniffing out a fraud
That not one of the cheering crowd had yet been bitten by him, though their turn was coming
context: Diogenes called himself 'a hound of the sort which all men praise, but no one of his admirers dared to go out hunting along with him' — everyone applauds the man who exposes false convention, but no one is willing to actually live that exposed, conventionless life alongside him. The stem withholds the 'no one dared hunt beside him' half so the player must supply it from the fact rather than decode it from the setup; the distractors offer rival readings of the 'hound' metaphor. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.33 (Perseus/Penelope text).

question: After the plucked chicken made his 'featherless two-legged animal' a laughingstock, Plato repaired the definition by tacking on three more words: a human also has broad, flat nails. Diogenes pounced on the repair itself. What did the act of patching quietly admit?
answer: That he was bolting traits onto a list with no point where the list is ever finished
choices: That he was bolting traits onto a list with no point where the list is ever finished
That he had copied the whole definition from an older thinker he refused to credit
That he had only ever watched humans from afar and never once stood close to one
That a single shared trait can tie two creatures together more tightly than ten differences
context: Stung by the plucked chicken, Plato added 'having broad nails' to fence a human off from a featherless fowl. The tell is not merely that the definition was a list — it is that he could keep amending it: bolting on one more trait shows there is no fixed point at which such a list is ever complete, so it is an open, ad-hoc tally of outer features rather than a grasp of what a human is. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.40; corroborated by World History Encyclopedia, 'Diogenes of Sinope.'

question: Diogenes of Sinope made his home inside a giant clay storage jar in the Athens marketplace and owned almost nothing, sleeping in it like a stray dog. He chose to live with so little on purpose. What was he trying to prove by stripping his life down to a single jar?
answer: That a good life needs almost nothing, so chasing more is wasted effort
choices: That a good life needs almost nothing, so chasing more is wasted effort
That poverty is a punishment the gods send to humble proud men
That a city should hand free housing to every one of its citizens
That hard work in the marketplace is the one true path to wealth
context: Diogenes the Cynic slept in a pithos, a huge clay storage jar, in the marketplace (the famous 'barrel' is a later mistranslation, since barrels did not yet exist). Stripping his possessions to nothing was the demonstration: prove by living it that virtue needs barely anything. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI; World History Encyclopedia.

question: Alexander the Great, the most powerful man in the world, sought out Diogenes and found him stretched out on the ground, basking in the warm sun. The king stood over him and offered to grant him anything in the world he desired. What did Diogenes ask the mightiest king alive to do?
answer: Step aside and stop blocking the sunlight
choices: Step aside and stop blocking the sunlight
Hand over a fortune in gold and a grand house
Make him a general in the royal army
Spare his home city from the coming war
context: 'Stand out of my light.' A truly free man wants nothing from a king, so the only thing the emperor could give him was the sunshine the emperor was himself blocking. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.38 (Hicks translation, Perseus); IEP: Diogenes of Sinope.

question: Alexander the Great met Diogenes, a beggar who lived in a jar and refused every gift the king offered him. As he walked away, the all-conquering king stunned his own followers with what he confessed about this penniless man.
answer: That were he not the king, he would rather be Diogenes
choices: That were he not the king, he would rather be Diogenes
That Diogenes was the maddest beggar in all of Greece
That he should have this Diogenes whipped for his insolence
That he pitied any man forced to live as Diogenes did
context: 'Had I not been Alexander, I should have liked to be Diogenes.' The man who conquered the world admired the man who needed nothing from it more than he admired himself. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.32 (Perseus); World History Encyclopedia.

question: Diogenes lit a lamp in the middle of a sunny day and walked through the packed marketplace, holding the flame up to one face after another as if hunting for something in the dark. He was surrounded by hundreds of people. What stinging point was this piece of street theater making?
answer: That not one person there was truly living as a real human should
choices: That not one person there was truly living as a real human should
That the crowded marketplace was too dim and needed better lighting
That he had lost something precious and begged the crowd for help
That daylight hides more than darkness, so he trusted the flame
context: His line was 'I am looking for a man' (a genuinely rational human being). Surrounded by people, he claimed none of them lived as a real human should, an insult delivered as performance art. The popular 'honest man' version is a later embellishment. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.41 (Perseus); IEP: Diogenes of Sinope.

question: Diogenes had pared his belongings down to a single wooden cup, his very last possession. Then he watched a small boy kneel at a stream and drink water straight from his cupped hands. Diogenes threw his cup away on the spot. Why did the sight of that boy make him discard his final thing?
answer: The child proved even a cup was one possession more than he needed
choices: The child proved even a cup was one possession more than he needed
The wooden cup had cracked and could no longer hold any water
He wanted the thirsty boy to have the cup far more than he did
He had vowed to copy that boy in every single thing he did
context: Every object you own is one more thing you do not actually need. A child with nothing had out-simplified him. He later threw away his bowl too, after watching a boy eat lentils from a hollowed crust of bread. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.37 (Perseus); World History Encyclopedia.

question: A vain rich man gave Diogenes a tour of his mansion, gleaming with gold and fine art, and warned him sternly not to spit on the costly floors. Diogenes cleared his throat and spat squarely in his host's face. How did he justify aiming at the one spot he chose?
answer: It was the only filthy thing he could find in the whole house
choices: It was the only filthy thing he could find in the whole house
It was the only spot where the gold would not be stained
It was the custom owed to any host who showed off his wealth
It was the nearest target when the urge to spit came on
context: Under all the gold and finery, the most worthless thing in a vain rich man's house is the vain rich man himself. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.32 (Perseus, Hicks); Wikiquote: Diogenes of Sinope.

question: The philosopher Plato won applause for defining a human being as 'an animal with two legs and no feathers.' Diogenes plucked every feather off a chicken, carried the bald bird into Plato's lecture hall, and held it up crying 'Here is Plato's man!' What was Diogenes exposing with that plucked chicken?
answer: That a tidy definition can fit perfectly yet capture nothing real
choices: That a tidy definition can fit perfectly yet capture nothing real
That chickens and humans share a surprising common ancestor
That Plato was a cruel man who enjoyed tormenting helpless animals
That no one should ever speak in public without solid evidence
context: A clever textbook definition divorced from reality is worthless; the plucked bird literally satisfied Plato's words while obviously being no man. Plato then had to add 'with broad, flat nails' to the definition. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.40 (Perseus); IEP: Diogenes of Sinope.

question: Pirates captured Diogenes and dragged him to the slave market to be sold off. When the auctioneer asked what trade he knew, Diogenes answered 'governing men,' then pointed at a rich buyer and told the crowd to announce that here stood a man who needed to purchase a master for himself. By flipping his own slave-sale into a hunt for a pupil, what was Diogenes claiming?
answer: That no master could ever own the freedom inside his mind
choices: That no master could ever own the freedom inside his mind
That the pirates would soon free him for a hefty ransom
That selling him was illegal and the buyers would be punished
That he would earn a fortune for whoever purchased him
context: Even chained on an auction block, his inner freedom was untouched; he treated being sold as merely acquiring a new pupil to command. The buyer he pointed to was named Xeniades. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.29-30 (Perseus); IEP: Diogenes of Sinope.

question: Athenians were scandalized that Diogenes did everything, eating, sleeping, and worse, right out in the open marketplace instead of behind closed doors. He shrugged off their outrage with one simple rule. By his reasoning, why was doing these things in plain view no crime at all?
answer: If an act is not shameful done in private, the public cannot make it so
choices: If an act is not shameful done in private, the public cannot make it so
The gods watch every single action, so hiding from people is pointless
A true philosopher must offend the crowd in order to earn their respect
Whatever the majority does openly becomes the rule for everyone else
context: Most of what we call 'shame' is convention, not nature. By refusing to hide what is natural, he lived entirely by nature in order to expose the difference. Source: IEP: Diogenes of Sinope (iep.utm.edu/diogenes-of-sinope); Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.

question: Plato reportedly summed up Diogenes in three words: 'a Socrates gone mad.' Socrates was the Athenian philosopher who wandered the city questioning everyone he met about how a person ought to live. What did calling Diogenes a mad version of that man capture so well?
answer: He chased the same goal but through shocking, shameless public stunts
choices: He chased the same goal but through shocking, shameless public stunts
He pursued virtue exactly as Socrates did, only far more patiently
He despised Socrates and lived only to prove the old man wrong
He copied Socrates so exactly that people could not tell them apart
context: It captures him perfectly: he chased the same goal as Socrates, a truly examined and virtuous life, but with wild, shameless, in-your-face stunts instead of polite questioning. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.54 (Perseus); Wikipedia 'Diogenes'.

question: People hurled the word 'dog' at Diogenes as an insult for his shameless, animal-like life, and from that Greek slur, kynikos, we get the very word 'Cynic.' Instead of being stung by it, Diogenes seized the name and wore it proudly. Why was being called a dog, to his mind, actually a compliment?
answer: A dog lives honestly by nature, owing no one any false shame
choices: A dog lives honestly by nature, owing no one any false shame
A dog stays loyal to one master above all other creatures
A dog is feared by thieves and guards its household well
A dog can be trained to obey far better than any man can
context: He wore the insult as a badge: living like a dog meant living honestly by nature, owing no one shame. He said a dog fawns on those who feed it, barks at those who refuse, and bites scoundrels. 'Cynic' descends directly from kynikos, dog-like. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.40, VI.60 (Perseus); Wikipedia 'Diogenes' (kynikos etymology).

question: Diogenes was driven out of his home city of Sinope for defacing its coinage, literally stamping coins so they could no longer be spent. Legend says an oracle had told him to 'deface the currency,' and he took that as the mission of his whole life. How did he reinterpret that strange command into a way of living?
answer: Stamp out society's false values the way you cancel a bad coin
choices: Stamp out society's false values the way you cancel a bad coin
Mint his own honest coins to replace the corrupt city's money
Flee from city to city so no ruler could ever tax his wealth
Teach others the hidden craft of shaping precious metals
context: The wordplay became his life's program: strike down society's counterfeit conventions the way you would cancel a bad coin. Scholars treat the oracle version as likely apocryphal or symbolic, hence its legend status, though the exile for defacing the coinage is historical. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.20-21 (Perseus); World History Encyclopedia; Britannica 'Diogenes'.

question: Mara and her brother argue about whether the dinosaurs still exist 'somewhere.' Mara says of course not -- they died out, they are gone, and only the world right now is real. Her brother pushes back with a parallel: 'Think about the word "here." You are not in Australia right now, yet Australia is no less real for that -- it is simply a place you are not standing. I say "now" works the same way: it marks where YOU sit in time, not which times are real, the way "here" marks where you stand, not which places are real.' If the brother is right that 'now' works just like 'here,' what does that make the age of the dinosaurs?
answer: Real and waiting at its own spot in time, just not the spot you occupy
choices: Real and waiting at its own spot in time, just not the spot you occupy
Real for as long as it lasted, then gone the instant its last day ended
Real only to a mind that can reach it, the way a place needs a visitor
Real only in the traces it left -- the bones and prints we dig up today
context: This is the eternalist (or 'block universe') view: every time is equally real, and 'now' is indexical -- it points at where you stand in time the way 'here' points at where you stand in space. On this picture dinosaurs are as real as Australia, and Caesar crossing the Rubicon still sits at its own place in spacetime rather than having simply stopped existing. A presentist denies all of this: the dinosaurs DID exist but do NOT exist; only the present is real. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Eternalism' (iep.utm.edu/eternalism/) -- 'now' as indexical, dinosaurs as real as Australia, Caesar tenselessly existing; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Presentism' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/presentism/).

question: Noor holds a view she calls 'the growing block': reality is like a block that keeps getting bigger, with a fresh slice of existence tacked on at every passing moment, so the sum total of what exists is always increasing. Her sister tests the idea with two things -- a fossil from the age of the dinosaurs, and a birthday that will happen next year. 'On your growing-block picture,' she asks, 'are those two equally real, equally unreal, or does it depend?' If Noor's block grows by adding each new moment onto what is already there, what should she answer about the fossil's era and next year's birthday?
answer: The dinosaur era is real and fixed, but next year's birthday is not real yet
choices: The dinosaur era is real and fixed, but next year's birthday is not real yet
Next year's birthday is real and fixed, but the dinosaur era is long gone now
Both are equally real, since a growing block can only ever add, never subtract
Both are equally unreal, since a block that grows has only its newest slice real
context: The growing-block view: the past and present are real and fixed, but the future genuinely does not exist yet -- reality keeps growing as each new 'now' is added on. C.D. Broad put it this way in 'Scientific Thought' (1923): 'The sum total of existence is always increasing, and it is this which gives the time-series a sense as well as an order.' (It contrasts with PRESENTISM, only the present is real, and ETERNALISM, every time equally real.) The view was first articulated by Samuel Alexander in 'Space, Time, and Deity' (1920) and first fully defended by Broad in 1923. Source: Wikipedia, 'Growing block universe' (Broad quote); Emily Thomas, 'The Roots of C.D. Broad's Growing Block Theory of Time' (Mind, 2019) for Alexander's 1920 priority.

question: Long before the modern fight over time, two Greek thinkers staked out the extremes. Heraclitus taught that reality is pure flux -- 'No man ever steps in the same river twice,' because the water has flowed on and so has he; everything is forever becoming. Parmenides taught the opposite: change is an illusion, and what truly IS simply is, all at once and timelessly, for 'out of nothing, nothing comes.' A student notices the two ancients map neatly onto the modern dispute over which times are real. Which modern view does Parmenides' changeless, all-at-once reality match?
answer: Every time is equally real, all of them sitting out there with no passage
choices: Every time is equally real, all of them sitting out there with no passage
Time is something the mind makes up, so nothing in it ever truly changes
Every moment exists, yet just one of them is lit up as the real present
Only the past and present are real; the future has yet to come into being
context: Heraclitus is the spirit of a flowing, becoming present -- presentism's gut feeling; Parmenides is the spirit of the changeless block where all is timelessly real -- eternalism's gut feeling. The 2,500-year-old quarrel is the same quarrel. The distractors are the other live positions, NOT mere 'change' views: 'the mind makes up time' is the McTaggart-style claim that time is unreal (J.M.E. McTaggart, 'The Unreality of Time,' Mind, 1908); 'just one moment is lit up' is the moving-spotlight picture; 'only past and present are real' is the growing block. Parmenides' POSITIVE realism -- 'what truly IS simply is, all at once' -- is what singles out eternalism among these, since a thinker holding any of the other static-flavored views would not be marked wrong merely for denying passage. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Heraclitus' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/heraclitus/) for the river fragment; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Time' (iep.utm.edu/time/) quoting Parmenides, 'Out of nothing, nothing comes'; IEP, 'McTaggart, J.M.E.' for the unreality-of-time view.

question: Leah already accepts that every moment of time is equally real -- past, present, and future all sitting out there together. But she feels something is still missing: that view leaves nothing special about RIGHT NOW. So she adds a twist with a picture. Picture the moments as a row of houses along a street, all of them equally and fully there; a policeman walks the street carrying a lantern, and at this instant its beam rests on one single house. That one lit house, Leah says, is the moment that is genuinely present. What does Leah's lantern claim that the plain 'all times are equally real' view does not?
answer: One moment is really, specially present, and which one that is keeps changing
choices: One moment is really, specially present, and which one that is keeps changing
One moment is really, specially the present, and it stays that same one forever
Each person lights a different house, so the present is only one's own viewpoint
The lantern marks nothing real in the world; it is just a manner of speaking
context: This is the 'moving spotlight' picture: all times exist (as in eternalism), but ONE of them is objectively lit as 'the present,' and that spotlight slides forward -- exactly the surplus that plain eternalism refuses to grant. For the plain eternalist, 'now' is merely where you stand, like 'here' (the 'each person lights a different house' option). The rival pictures here are all live: a present fixed forever on one absolute moment; a present that is only your own viewpoint; or no real present at all (a deflationary reading). The image and words are C.D. Broad's, from 'Scientific Thought' (1923): the present is 'like the spot of light from a policeman's bull's-eye traversing the fronts of the houses in a street.' Broad floated it as a vivid metaphor he thought ultimately explained nothing -- which is why it fits a character who PROPOSES it, not a settled answer. Source: C.D. Broad, 'Scientific Thought' (1923), via Wikipedia, 'Moving spotlight theory of time,' and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Eternalism.'

question: A skeptic presses the friend who holds that reality is a block that keeps growing, with only its newest edge counting as 'now.' 'Here's the trouble,' the skeptic says. 'On your view the whole past is just as real and solid as we are -- it never stopped existing; it only stopped being the edge. So picture Socrates, mid-conversation, dead sure that HIS moment was the live one. Every bone in him felt exactly what you feel right now. And on your view he was flatly wrong: his "now" is buried ages deep inside the finished part of the block. He is as real as you, he felt as present as you, and he was mistaken.' The friend asks what is so bad about that. What is the deepest problem the skeptic has just set up for the growing-block view?
answer: Anyone in the block could feel present yet be buried past, so no one can tell which they are
choices: Anyone in the block could feel present yet be buried past, so no one can tell which they are
Socrates must be living through his moment even now, fully awake inside the old part of the block
Nothing inside the block could ever fix which single slice is the one true growing edge
The future would have to be real already, since the edge must grow toward something there
context: This is the 'epistemic objection' to the growing block (raised by David Braddon-Mitchell, Craig Bourne, and Trenton Merricks): if past moments are fully real and everyone in them felt present, you have no evidence you occupy the live edge rather than a buried slice. Socrates was sure his moment was 'now' too -- and, on this view, was wrong. Source: Wikipedia, 'Growing block universe'; Springer, 'The Epistemic Objection' (link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-78704-6_6) -- Braddon-Mitchell, Bourne, Merricks.

question: To argue that all times are equally real, a physicist tells an unsettling little story. Two people pass each other on a sidewalk, walking in opposite directions. In his words: 'according to one of the two people, an Andromedean space fleet has already set off on its journey, while to the other, the decision as to whether or not the journey will actually take place has not yet been made.' Same two strangers, same street corner -- yet for one walker the fleet's launch is already a fixed past event, and for the other it has not even been decided. If neither walker is mistaken, what must follow about that far-off launch?
answer: It must already be real and settled, sitting out there in the block of times
choices: It must already be real and settled, sitting out there in the block of times
It cannot be real for either of them until they both come to agree it happened
It proves the future is open, since the two walkers plainly disagree about it
It shows only that the walkers measured the distance to Andromeda differently
context: If the launch is fixed-past for one walker and not-yet-decided for the other, and both are equally right, then the event must already exist 'out there' -- the block universe. (A tiny difference in motion shifts which faraway events count as happening 'now,' and across a gulf as vast as Andromeda that shift adds up to days; the story keeps the wonder and leaves the machinery out.) The scene is Roger Penrose's, in 'The Emperor's New Mind' (1989), dramatizing an argument published by C.W. Rietdijk (1966) and, independently, Hilary Putnam (1967). Source: Wikipedia, 'Rietdijk-Putnam argument.'

question: In Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, Ivan tells his younger brother Alyosha a story he calls his 'poem' - set in Seville, in the worst days of the Inquisition. How does Ivan deliver the whole tale to Alyosha?
answer: He speaks the whole poem aloud and has never written it down
choices: He speaks the whole poem aloud and has never written it down
He reads it from a worn notebook he has carried for years
He hands Alyosha the pages and waits while his brother reads
He sings it as a hymn the monks of his town had taught him
context: Ivan delivers 'The Grand Inquisitor' entirely by mouth, in a tavern, in the chapter 'Pro and Contra' - it is a poem he composed in his head and never set down on paper. Source: Constance Garnett trans., The Brothers Karamazov, Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: In Ivan's tale, Christ returns silently to Seville and stops at the cathedral steps, where a little open white coffin holds a dead child of seven. He says 'Maiden, arise!' and the girl sits up alive. At that very moment, what happens to Christ?
answer: The aged Inquisitor walks by and has his guards arrest Him
choices: The aged Inquisitor walks by and has his guards arrest Him
The grateful father falls at His feet and begs Him to stay
The crowd lifts Him onto their shoulders in joy
The cathedral bells ring out and a great feast begins
context: Christ raises the child before a gathered crowd - and in the same breath the old cardinal, the Grand Inquisitor, passing by, orders the Holy Guard to seize Him. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: In Ivan's parable the Grand Inquisitor is almost ninety, tall and erect, with a withered face and sunken eyes. A moment earlier the crowd had bowed to Christ and wept at the child He raised. When the old cardinal orders Christ seized, how does that same crowd react?
answer: It bows to the Inquisitor instead and lets his guards pass
choices: It bows to the Inquisitor instead and lets his guards pass
It surges forward and tears the prisoner from the guards
It turns on the Inquisitor and stones him in the square
It scatters in terror and flees the cathedral steps
context: Dostoevsky's crowd swings in an instant: the people who knelt to Christ now bow to the man arresting Him and clear a path for the Holy Guard - the obedience the Inquisitor counts on. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: In Ivan's parable, the Grand Inquisitor visits the silent prisoner in his cell at night. You might expect joy that Christ has come back. Instead the very first thing the old man says is a kind of accusation. What is the charge he opens with?
answer: That Christ has no right to come now and hinder the Church's work
choices: That Christ has no right to come now and hinder the Church's work
That Christ abandoned His followers for too many long centuries
That Christ failed to perform the miracles the people demanded
That Christ never truly suffered as ordinary mortals must
context: The Inquisitor's opening line is 'Why hast Thou come now to hinder us?' - to him, everything was long ago handed over to the Church, so Christ's return is an interruption, not a rescue. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: The Grand Inquisitor tells the silent Christ that His gift of freedom was a cruelty: 'Nothing has ever been more insupportable for a man than freedom.' Christ wanted people to follow Him by free love, but most cannot bear the weight of choosing. So what does the Inquisitor claim the Church has rightly done?
answer: Taken people's freedom from them so they can finally be happy
choices: Taken people's freedom from them so they can finally be happy
Multiplied people's freedom so each may seek God his own way
Left people free but added new commandments to guide them
Asked people to choose freedom or comfort and let each decide
context: This is the parable's core, presented at full strength: free people are tormented by choice, so (the Inquisitor argues) mercy means lifting that burden off them. Dostoevsky offers no verdict - readers tie it to Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and to Nietzsche's contented 'last man,' the freedom-problem at the heart of existentialism. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5; SEP, Existentialism: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/existentialism/

question: The Grand Inquisitor predicts that ordinary people, worn out by the terror of free choice, will one day come to the Church no longer asking for liberty but begging for something else entirely. What does the Inquisitor say they will cry out to the Church?
answer: 'Make us your slaves, but feed us'
choices: 'Make us your slaves, but feed us'
'Teach us the truth, whatever the cost'
'Lead us into battle against the heretics'
'Show us a sign, and we will believe'
context: The Inquisitor's wager: bread first, virtue later - 'no science will give them bread so long as they remain free.' They lay their freedom at the Church's feet for the promise of food. Scholars read this trade of liberty for security alongside Hobbes' bargain (surrender freedom to a sovereign for safety) and Tocqueville's 'soft despotism.' No verdict is imposed. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: Deep in his speech, the Grand Inquisitor reveals a secret about the Church he has served for ninety years. He says it long ago took up the sword of Caesar and 'corrected' Christ's work - and then he names whose side the Church is truly on. Whose?
answer: Christ's enemy - 'we are not with Thee, but with him'
choices: Christ's enemy - 'we are not with Thee, but with him'
Caesar's heirs, who alone can keep the peace on earth
The weak millions, whose hunger outweighs all else
His own, for he answers to no master but conscience
context: The Inquisitor's confession: to make mankind happy the Church accepted the three temptations Christ refused - miracle, mystery, and authority - and so serves the tempter, not Christ. It is offered as his sincere belief, not as the author's verdict. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: Through the Grand Inquisitor's entire towering speech, Christ does not argue back - in fact He never speaks a single word in the whole poem. When the old man finishes and waits, Christ gives His one and only reply. What does He do?
answer: He silently kisses the old man on his bloodless lips
choices: He silently kisses the old man on his bloodless lips
He presses a hand to the old man's chest and steps back
He weeps and slowly vanishes through the cell wall
He opens the cell door and walks free into the night
context: 'That was all his answer.' The kiss shakes the Inquisitor - it 'glows in his heart' - yet he sticks to his idea and tells Christ to go and never return. The frame seals it: when Ivan finishes, his brother Alyosha silently kisses Ivan on the lips exactly the same way, and Ivan laughs, 'That's plagiarism.' Dostoevsky answers the argument not with an argument but with a gesture. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5; SparkNotes: https://www.sparknotes.com/lit/brothersk/section7/

question: Tom's teacher offers him an easy deal: just say a quick sorry and he keeps his recess. Tom knows the sorry is the smart move and that skipping recess only punishes himself — yet he plants his feet and refuses, precisely BECAUSE everyone is sure he'll take the sensible way out. What is Tom mainly trying to prove?
answer: That nobody can script his choices for him
choices: That nobody can script his choices for him
That the rule punishing him is unfair
That the apology should come from the teacher first
That he never enjoyed recess to begin with
context: This is the everyday seed of Dostoevsky's 'Underground Man': a person who will harm his own position rather than do the predictable, sensible thing — just to show no one can command his choices. Dostoevsky's narrator opens by confessing 'I know better than anyone that by all this I am only injuring myself and no one else,' and does it anyway. Source: Dostoevsky, Notes from the Underground, Part I, Ch. I (Constance Garnett trans.), Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/files/600/600-h/600-h.htm

question: Dostoevsky's nameless narrator opens Notes from Underground by announcing he is sick and believes his liver is diseased — then says he will not see a doctor about it. He even admits this choice harms no one but himself. Why, he tells us, does he refuse the doctor?
answer: Out of spite, to defy what is sensible and expected
choices: Out of spite, to defy what is sensible and expected
Out of pride, to prove he needs no one's help at all
Out of fear that the news would be worse
Out of poverty, having no way to pay
context: His actual words: 'I am a sick man.... I am a spiteful man... I believe my liver is diseased' and 'No, I refuse to consult a doctor from spite.' He grants 'I know better than anyone that by all this I am only injuring myself and no one else' — the founding image of the Underground revolt: harm yourself rather than do the sensible thing a calculating world expects. Source: Dostoevsky, Notes from the Underground, Part I, Ch. I (Garnett trans.), Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/files/600/600-h/600-h.htm

question: Dostoevsky's underground narrator pictures a day when science has proved that every human choice is as fixed as the note a piano key must sound when struck. His reaction is to promise that a man would then do something perverse and ruinous on purpose. What is the narrator claiming by threatening this pointless sabotage?
answer: That a person can defy the law itself, proving he is more than a mere mechanism
choices: That a person can defy the law itself, proving he is more than a mere mechanism
That if every choice is fixed, then no one can be blamed for anything they do
That science will one day predict every choice, so freedom is only an illusion
That the wise course is to accept the proven law and live at peace with it
context: The other three are real, respectable answers in the free-will dispute — the question is only which one the narrator is making, not which is true. His move: 'even if man really were nothing but a piano-key, even if this were proved to him by natural science and mathematics, even then he would not become reasonable, but would purposely do something perverse... simply to gain his point.' The whole work of man, he says, is 'proving to himself every minute that he is a man and not a piano-key.' Source: Dostoevsky, Notes from the Underground, Part I, Ch. VIII (Garnett trans.), Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/files/600/600-h/600-h.htm

question: Dostoevsky's underground narrator turns simple arithmetic into a fight over freedom. He grants that two times two making four is an excellent, certain thing — then calls that very certainty 'a piece of insolence,' a 'pert coxcomb who stands with arms akimbo barring your path.' Against it he offers one defiant equation as 'a very charming thing,' to prove his will will not be commanded even by what is provably true. Which equation does he champion?
answer: That two times two makes five
choices: That two times two makes five
That two times two makes three
That two times two makes seven
That two times two makes one
context: His full line: 'Twice two makes four seems to me simply a piece of insolence... twice two makes four is a pert coxcomb who stands with arms akimbo barring your path.' Against it he sets the ultimate gesture of an unbowed will: 'twice two makes five is sometimes a very charming thing too.' To choose 2x2=5 is to refuse to be commanded even by what is provably true — the certainty of 2x2=4, he warns, 'is not life, gentlemen, but is the beginning of death.' Source: Dostoevsky, Notes from the Underground, Part I, Ch. IX (Garnett trans.), Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/files/600/600-h/600-h.htm

question: One of the most quoted lines in philosophy — 'If God does not exist, everything is permitted' — is almost always credited to Ivan Karamazov in Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov. But the line's history is stranger than the credit suggests. Where does that crisp wording actually come from?
answer: The wording is largely Sartre's paraphrase, not a true line in the novel
choices: The wording is largely Sartre's paraphrase, not a true line in the novel
The wording is Ivan's own outburst on the stand at his criminal trial
The wording is taken from a letter Dostoevsky sent to his publisher
The wording is Father Zosima's solemn deathbed counsel to the brothers
context: No character in the novel ever speaks that exact sentence. What Ivan actually argues is tied to the soul's immortality — that without immortality 'there is no virtue,' and so 'everything is lawful.' The familiar crisp version comes largely from Jean-Paul Sartre's 1946 lecture 'Existentialism Is a Humanism,' where he writes 'Dostoevsky once wrote: If God did not exist, everything would be permitted' and calls it 'the starting point.' The gap between what Ivan said and what everyone quotes is itself a real fact about the idea's history. Sources: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Existentialism https://iep.utm.edu/existent/ ; Andrei Volkov, 'Dostoevsky Didn't Say It' https://infidels.org/kiosk/article/dostoevsky-didnt-say-it/ ; Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Bk. II Ch. 6

question: In their third and final meeting, the servant Smerdyakov confesses to Ivan Karamazov that he, not Ivan's brother Dmitri, murdered old Fyodor Karamazov. Then Smerdyakov names the person he holds truly responsible for the killing. Whom does he name?
answer: Ivan himself, whose teaching that nothing is forbidden had freed him
choices: Ivan himself, whose teaching that nothing is forbidden had freed him
Dmitri, whose open threats against Fyodor had given him cover
old Fyodor himself, whose lifelong cruelty had finally earned it
no one but Smerdyakov, who had acted wholly alone for the money
context: Dostoevsky does not leave 'everything is lawful' as abstract talk — he shows it kill. Smerdyakov reminds Ivan he had said 'if there's no infinite God, then there's no virtue either, and no need of it at all,' and charges 'It was following your words I did it,' adding that by quietly leaving town Ivan had 'silently sanctioned' the murder. The vertigo of a lost higher ground, dramatized: the one who really believes nothing is forbidden may be the man beside you. Sources: Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Bk. XI Ch. VIII ('The Third and Last Interview with Smerdyakov'), via Owl Eyes https://www.owleyes.org/text/the-brothers-karamazov ; SparkNotes Bk. 11 https://www.sparknotes.com/lit/brothersk/section14/

question: John Duns Scotus was crowned the 'Subtle Doctor' for the finest, most penetrating reasoning of his age. But when Renaissance humanists turned against the hair-splitting of his devoted followers, they took revenge on his very name itself, turning it into an everyday insult that survives to this day. What became of this brilliant thinker's name?
answer: It became the English word for a stupid, unteachable person
choices: It became the English word for a stupid, unteachable person
It became a polite title granted to learned university scholars
It became a curse muttered against liars and false witnesses
It became a nickname for stubborn, hot-tempered hill folk
context: One of history's great ironies: the man nicknamed the SUBTLE Doctor for the most delicate, penetrating reasoning of his age became the very byword for stupidity. His followers were called 'Dunsmen' or 'Dunses'; when Renaissance humanists turned against scholastic hair-splitting, they weaponized his name into 'dunce.' The Oxford English Dictionary records 'dunce' as an insult from the mid-16th century, and the 'dunce's cap' for the slow kid in the corner is attested by 1791. The subtlest thinker of his time gave English its word for the dullest. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dunce' (citing OED 3rd ed.); Wikipedia, 'Duns Scotus.'

question: John Duns Scotus, nicknamed the Subtle Doctor, pressed a deep puzzle about what makes you uniquely YOU. Line up every quality of Socrates -- human, rational, animal, mortal -- and Plato has every one of those same qualities. So no description, however complete, can pick out which man is Socrates rather than Plato. Faced with this, Scotus asked what makes Socrates this very individual and no other. How did he answer?
answer: A bare thisness -- a further principle, beyond all qualities, fixing him as THIS one
choices: A bare thisness -- a further principle, beyond all qualities, fixing him as THIS one
His matter -- the particular stuff his body is made of is what marks him off
Nothing more is needed -- Socrates just IS his whole bundle of qualities
Nothing real at all -- being this one is only a name our minds attach
context: This is Scotus's signature move, the 'principle of individuation.' Two people can share their whole 'whatness' (their quiddity -- humanity, rationality), yet there must still be something that makes Socrates THIS one. Scotus called it a non-qualitative individuating principle: a 'thisness' that contracts the shared nature 'humanity' down to this single person after every describable property is accounted for. (One correction: Scotus himself wrote of an 'individual difference,' not the famous coined word 'haecceitas' -- his FOLLOWERS later minted that neologism for the doctrine.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Medieval Theories of Haecceity'; Wikipedia, 'Haecceity.'

question: When we call both Socrates and Plato 'human,' is the humanity they share something real out in the world, or just a word our minds apply? This is the medieval problem of universals, and John Duns Scotus, the Subtle Doctor, took one of the strongest stands on it of anyone in his century. Which account of shared natures did Scotus defend?
answer: The shared nature is real and lives right inside each individual thing
choices: The shared nature is real and lives right inside each individual thing
The shared nature is real but exists apart, in its own higher realm
The shared nature is real only as an idea in the mind, not in the world
The shared nature isn't real at all -- only the bare individuals exist
context: Scotus is the great realist counterweight to nominalism (the view, urged by thinkers like William of Ockham, that universals are merely names). He held that the common nature -- humanity, redness -- genuinely exists in the things themselves, with a 'less-than-numerical unity,' and is then 'contracted' into this-or-that individual by its thisness. The bank takes NO verdict on who is right: realism versus nominalism is a genuine, still-live fork, and a thoughtful person can defend either side. This rung only asks which side Scotus took. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Duns Scotus'; Wikipedia, 'Scotistic realism.'

question: A shopkeeper charges every customer the same fair price and never overcharges a child who wanders in not knowing what things cost. Ask him why and he admits it: a cheat's reputation would wreck his business. He has never once dealt unfairly. A philosopher watching says his honesty still falls short of real moral worth. On what ground?
answer: The deed matches what's right, but he isn't doing it because it's right — only because it pays
choices: The deed matches what's right, but he isn't doing it because it's right — only because it pays
The deed is actually wrong, since charging a child any price at all takes advantage of the young
The deed is right and his reason is too, so the philosopher has misjudged an honest, careful man
The deed is only a habit by now, and an action that runs on plain habit was never truly chosen
context: This is Immanuel Kant's honest-shopkeeper, the central scene of the whole topic. The merchant acts IN ACCORDANCE WITH duty — the outward deed is right — but NOT FROM duty, since his motive is profit. Kant says such an action has no genuine moral worth: the right thing done for self-interest only happens to line up with what's right. Kant, Groundwork (Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals), Abbott trans., Project Gutenberg #5682, First Section.

question: Immanuel Kant opens his ethics with a bold claim: of every fine thing a person could possess, only ONE is good in every case. Every other prized thing, he warns, can be turned to evil — handed to a scoundrel, it just makes his harm land harder. What did Kant name as the one exception?
answer: A will that is set on doing right, because the worth of any deed traces back to that will and not to the act it produces
choices: A will that is set on doing right, because the worth of any deed traces back to that will and not to the act it produces
A deep and settled happiness, because a life that finally has all it wants is the goal every other good is chasing after
A sharp and capable mind, because reason is the thing that lifts a person above the animals and lets them choose at all
A brave and steady nerve, because without the courage to actually act, every other virtue just sits locked up and useless
context: Kant's famous opening: 'Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.' Intelligence, courage, wealth, even happiness can all be bent to evil by a bad will, so none is good without qualification — only the good will is good in itself. The Stanford Encyclopedia spells out why it is unconditional: a good will is the very condition that makes every other good worth having (riches in a scoundrel's hands are not good), and no rational agent would trade their moral commitment away for any other good. Kant, Groundwork, Abbott trans., Gutenberg #5682, First Section, opening sentence; SEP 'Kant's Moral Philosophy', sec. 2.

question: Immanuel Kant pictures a good will struck by some cruel stroke of bad luck — try as it might, circumstances leave it unable to carry out a single one of its good aims. Kant says that even so it would still 'shine by its own light, like a jewel.' What was he insisting on with that picture?
answer: The worth of a good will sits in the willing itself and owes nothing to whatever good it does or fails to do out there
choices: The worth of a good will sits in the willing itself and owes nothing to whatever good it does or fails to do out there
The worth of a good will comes from the rightness of the goal it aimed at, so a noble target is what makes it gleam
The worth of a good will is the fine character it reveals, the steady virtue shining out through one doomed attempt
The worth of a good will is repaid beyond this world, since a higher judge credits the effort that men never saw
context: Kant: even a good will that 'by some special disfavour of fortune' is 'completely powerless to carry out its aims' would 'still shine by its own light, as a thing which has its whole value in itself' — like a jewel. The point is that moral worth lives in the willing, never in the results achieved (Groundwork 4:394). Kant, Groundwork, Abbott trans., Gutenberg #5682; quoted in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Kant's Moral Philosophy', sec. 2.

question: Immanuel Kant takes his hardest case. A man crushed by misfortune and hopeless sorrow longs for death — yet he keeps himself alive anyway, not because he still loves living and not out of any fear, but because he is convinced he is bound to go on. Beside him, Kant sets a cheerful man who clings to life simply because he naturally enjoys it. Whose holding-on did Kant say actually carries moral worth?
answer: The sorrowing man's, because he stays alive from duty alone, with no love of life left to prompt him
choices: The sorrowing man's, because he stays alive from duty alone, with no love of life left to prompt him
The cheerful man's, because a healthy delight in being alive is the most natural reason of all to go on
Both men's, because each one chooses life over death, and choosing to live is good however it is felt
Neither man's, because merely staying alive is not yet a moral act until you do some good with the time
context: One of Kant's most jarring examples: a man so crushed by 'adversity and hopeless sorrow' that he longs for death yet 'preserves his life without loving it, not from inclination or fear, but from duty.' Kant says THIS man's self-preservation finally has moral worth, while the cheerful man who clings to life merely from a natural love of living has none — because only the first acts from duty rather than feeling. Kant, Groundwork, Abbott trans., Gutenberg #5682, First Section (preservation-of-life example).

question: Immanuel Kant describes a man who once loved helping people and did it gladly, warmed by the joy he spread. Then grief of his own snuffs out every kind feeling — he no longer feels the slightest urge to help anyone. Yet he tears himself out of that cold numbness and helps a stranger anyway, with no warm feeling left at all. Of the cheerful early helper and this grieving one, which act did Kant say finally carries true moral worth, and why?
answer: The grieving man's, because he now acts purely from duty with the feeling gone — and that motive alone confers worth
choices: The grieving man's, because he now acts purely from duty with the feeling gone — and that motive alone confers worth
The cheerful helper's, because acting from genuine fellow-feeling is exactly what makes a kind deed admirable
Both equally, because the stranger is helped just the same and the man's inner state changes nothing about it
Neither one, because real moral worth needs both the right deed and a warm heart behind it together
context: Kant's cleanest illustration that moral worth needs duty, not warmth. He first grants that the cheerful philanthropist's kindness, 'however amiable it may be, has nevertheless no true moral worth' because its motive is pleasure. Then he imagines that man's sympathy 'extinguished' by his own sorrow: if he 'tears himself out of this dead insensibility, and performs the action... simply from duty, then first has his action its genuine moral worth.' Kant is NOT calling warm feeling bad — natural sympathy still 'deserves praise'; he denies only that it confers moral worth. Kant, Groundwork, Abbott trans., Gutenberg #5682, First Section (sympathy / friend-of-man example).

question: A man can save only one of two people drowning, and one of them is his wife. The philosopher Bernard Williams imagines the man's mind running 'it's my wife, AND saving one's wife is morally permitted' — and calls that pair of thoughts one thought too many. What did Williams mean was wrong with the man's thinking?
answer: His reason for saving her should simply be that she is his wife; pausing to confirm morality permits it is already the corruption Williams meant
choices: His reason for saving her should simply be that she is his wife; pausing to confirm morality permits it is already the corruption Williams meant
His thought was too thin, not too many; Williams wanted a weightier duty to a dependent in place of a bare note that saving her is allowed
His mind moved too slowly in a crisis; Williams meant that stopping to reason the matter out costs the very seconds in which she drowns
His personal pull was the real intruder; Williams meant impartial morality should decide, and 'it's my wife' is the very thought he ought to drop
context: Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' is a modern, story-shaped version of the worry that Kant's view slights love and warmth: pressing moral justification into personal love seems to spoil it. The dispute stays live, not settled — Kant's defender Barbara Herman replies that he never demanded you act from duty ALONE with no feeling present, only that the motive of duty 'would have sufficed' to carry the act if the warm feeling vanished; on her reading you may save your wife gladly, with duty merely the backstop. Bernard Williams, 'Persons, Character and Morality'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Bernard Williams'; Barbara Herman, 'On the Value of Acting from the Motive of Duty' (1981).

question: Ludwig Wittgenstein, heir to one of Europe's richest families, came home from World War I convinced he had just finished philosophy forever in one tiny book. He gave nearly his whole fortune to his siblings, calling money a hindrance to thinking. Instead of taking a university chair, what did he spend the next years doing?
answer: He taught reading and arithmetic to farm children in remote mountain villages.
choices: He taught reading and arithmetic to farm children in remote mountain villages.
He retired to run his family's great steel works and banking houses in Vienna.
He toured the European capitals lecturing the crowds on his famous new book.
He entered a monastery and took vows of silence among the cloistered monks.
context: From 1920 Wittgenstein taught six-to-ten-year-olds in tiny Austrian villages such as Trattenbach, Puchberg, and Otterthal, sleeping in the school kitchen and eating cocoa and oatmeal from a pot he never washed. He had already given away one of Europe's largest inherited fortunes, considering money a hindrance to thinking. The only other book he published in his lifetime was a children's spelling dictionary for his pupils. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Wittgenstein; openculture.com 2015 (his stint as an elementary-school teacher); iep.utm.edu/wittgens.

question: Ludwig Wittgenstein built his whole book as seven numbered sentences, each branching into smaller numbered notes. It opens grandly: 'The world is everything that is the case.' The entire book then climbs toward its seventh and final sentence, a single bare line that is the whole point. What does that last line tell the reader to do?
answer: Stop talking: about what cannot be put into words, one must say nothing.
choices: Stop talking: about what cannot be put into words, one must say nothing.
Keep asking: never accept any question as finally and fully closed.
Doubt everything: trust no claim that you have not proven yourself.
Start over: tear down the whole of philosophy and rebuild from nothing.
context: Proposition 7, the book's final line, reads in the Ogden translation: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent' (the Pears/McGuinness version: 'What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence'). The whole structure of seven propositions climbs to this one command. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tractatus_Logico-Philosophicus (lists propositions 1-7 verbatim); plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein.

question: Ludwig Wittgenstein argued that a meaningful sentence works like a picture: it shares the same logical shape as the slice of the world it describes, the way a map shares the layout of the streets it maps. A real sentence pictures a possible fact. Now suppose someone strings together grammatical words that picture no possible fact at all. On Wittgenstein's view, what has gone wrong with that string of words?
answer: It is nonsense, not merely false: no possible fact could make it true or false.
choices: It is nonsense, not merely false: no possible fact could make it true or false.
It is false, because no fact in the actual world makes it come out true.
It is true by default, because nothing in the actual world rules it out.
It is a hidden question, still awaiting the evidence to settle whether it holds.
context: This is the Tractatus' 'picture theory' of meaning: proposition 4.01 reads 'A proposition is a picture of reality.' The sharp move is that meaning equals picturing, so a string of words that pictures no possible fact is not false but literally nonsense, since there is no possible state of affairs it could be getting right or wrong. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein (proposition 4.01 of the Tractatus).

question: For Ludwig Wittgenstein, the matters you must stay silent about are the biggest of all: ethics, the meaning of life, God, the mystical. He held that they cannot be packed into sentences that picture facts, and those, he thought, are the only sentences that carry plain meaning. So on Wittgenstein's view, what becomes of these highest matters?
answer: They show themselves in how a life is lived, but can never be put into words.
choices: They show themselves in how a life is lived, but can never be put into words.
They turn out to be empty illusions, once we see they cannot be stated at all.
They belong to science, which will one day state them in fully exact terms.
They are settled by majority vote, since no plain fact can ever decide them.
context: Crucially, Wittgenstein did NOT mean these things are unreal, which is why the 'empty illusions' answer misreads him. The Stanford Encyclopedia puts his view this way: 'They make themselves manifest. They are what is mystical.' The most important things can be SHOWN but never SAID, drawing the exact line where language stops. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein (the mystical: shown not said); iep.utm.edu/wittgens.

question: Most authors stand behind every sentence they write. Ludwig Wittgenstein did something stranger: in the next-to-last line of his book, he said something startling about his own sentences. He compared reading the book to climbing a ladder, where you use his propositions as rungs to reach a clear view of the world, and then, he says, you must do one thing with the ladder itself. What does he say you must do, and what does that make his sentences?
answer: Throw the ladder away: his own sentences were nonsense, mere steps to climb past.
choices: Throw the ladder away: his own sentences were nonsense, mere steps to climb past.
Keep the ladder safe: his sentences are the eternal foundation of all of logic.
Hand the ladder on: his sentences must be taught word for word to everyone else.
Climb the ladder higher: his sentences are the first rungs of an endless tower.
context: Proposition 6.54: 'anyone who understands me eventually recognizes them as nonsensical, when he has used them, as steps, to climb beyond them. He must, so to speak, throw away the ladder after he has climbed up it.' You read the book to see the world rightly, then kick the book away. The ladder image is borrowed from Schopenhauer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wittgenstein%27s_ladder; Tractatus proposition 6.54.

question: Having declared in his book that he had found the final solution to every problem of philosophy, Ludwig Wittgenstein walked away from the subject for years. He returned to Cambridge in 1929 and submitted that very book as his doctoral thesis, judged by the same famous thinkers it had dazzled. What did Wittgenstein do with that 'finished' philosophy in the years that followed?
answer: He tore down his own picture theory, building an opposite philosophy in its place.
choices: He tore down his own picture theory, building an opposite philosophy in its place.
He defended the book unchanged for the rest of his life against all its critics.
He forbade anyone to reprint it, calling its great success a misunderstanding.
He expanded it into a vast multi-volume system covering each and every science.
context: Wittgenstein submitted the Tractatus as his PhD thesis, examined by Bertrand Russell and G.E. Moore; he ended the viva by clapping both world-famous examiners on the shoulder with 'Don't worry, I know you'll never understand it.' Moore's report read: 'I myself consider that this is a work of genius... well above the standard required for the PhD degree.' Yet by 1931 he called the early work 'dogmatic' and rejected it, demolishing the picture theory to build his completely opposite later philosophy. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Ludwig_Wittgenstein; plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein.

question: Empedocles, an ancient Greek thinker, claimed he was a god whose body would never rot but simply vanish. To prove it, legend says, he leapt into the burning crater of Mount Etna so no corpse would ever be found. But the volcano gave the trick away by spitting one thing back out of the flames. What did Etna throw up that exposed him as mortal?
answer: One of his bronze sandals
choices: One of his bronze sandals
A scrap of his burnt cloak
The golden crown from his head
A bone from his charred hand
context: Diogenes Laertius (Lives VIII.69), citing Hippobotus, reports the tale: Empedocles 'plunged into the fiery craters and disappeared,' but 'one of his slippers was thrown up in the flames; it had been his custom to wear slippers of bronze.' The single bronze sandal supposedly proved a man, not a god, had died there. This is a legend, not fact — another ancient writer, Timaeus, denied it, saying Empedocles simply left for the Peloponnese. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers VIII.69 (Wikisource).

question: Empedocles, an ancient Greek thinker, taught that every single thing in the world is built from just four basic ingredients, mixed together in different amounts like paints blended into new colors. A stone, a tree, a person, the sea: all of them, he said, are made from the same small handful of building blocks. Which four did he name as the roots of everything?
answer: Earth, water, air, and fire
choices: Earth, water, air, and fire
Salt, stone, wood, and bone
Sun, moon, sky, and sea
Blood, breath, gold, and clay
context: Empedocles called them the four 'roots' (rhizomata). This is the literal birthplace of the classical four-element scheme — earth, water, air, fire — that dominated Western thought for two thousand years; Aristotle credited him as the first to clearly single out these four as the basic elements. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Empedocles; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Empedocles.

question: Empedocles, an ancient Greek thinker, named two cosmic forces that rule the world: Love, which draws different things together, and Strife, which pulls them apart. A baby is born; a fire burns out. Most people would say new stuff has appeared and old stuff has vanished. Empedocles flatly denied it. What did he say was really going on at such moments?
answer: The same basic ingredients stay; only how they are arranged keeps changing
choices: The same basic ingredients stay; only how they are arranged keeps changing
One single basic stuff just thickens and thins into every different thing
Love and Strife themselves harden into the solid things we see
Our eyes are fooled, and nothing real is happening at all
context: This is a strikingly modern idea — a kind of conservation of matter. For Empedocles the four roots are permanent; Love and Strife only rearrange them. As Fragment B17 puts it, things come 'sometimes by Love all together into one, sometimes again each one carried off by the hatred of Strife.' Birth and death are just the same ingredients mixing and unmixing, like colors blended and then pulled apart — nothing is ever truly created or destroyed. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Empedocles, Fragment B17.

question: Empedocles, an ancient Greek thinker, told a strange story of how living things first came to be. At the start, he said, stray body parts grew up out of the earth all alone: heads with no necks, arms with no shoulders, eyes rolling about with no faces. Then Love stuck them together at random, making ox-faced people and human-faced oxen. By his account, why did horses and people end up shaped the way they are, instead of as monsters?
answer: Only the workable combinations could live and last; the rest died out
choices: Only the workable combinations could live and last; the rest died out
The gods stepped in and reshaped each monster into a proper animal
Strife smashed every creature back into parts and started over
The roots themselves remembered the correct shape for each animal
context: Empedocles' wandering body parts come from Fragments 57 and 61: 'many heads sprang up without necks, and arms wandered bare and bereft of shoulders.' Love joined them at random, and only the viable forms endured. Aristotle noted this anticipates natural selection, and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls Empedocles 'a forerunner of Darwin's theory.' Source: Wikisource, Fragments of Empedocles fr. 57 & 61; IEP and SEP on Empedocles.

question: Empedocles, an ancient Greek thinker, wrote that he himself had lived many lives before this one: 'I have been ere now a boy and a girl, a bush and a bird and a dumb fish in the sea.' He taught that one soul is reborn again and again across vast ages. Given that belief, what rule did Empedocles famously keep at every meal?
answer: He ate plants and grains only, and never any meat
choices: He ate plants and grains only, and never any meat
He ate meat, but only from beasts that had died of old age
He ate plants, but only ones he had grown himself, never wild
He ate anything, but only after a priest had blessed it aloud
context: The quoted line is Fragment 117. Empedocles taught that fallen spirits (daimones) are punished by being reincarnated through plants, animals, and humans across enormous spans of time, and can slowly purify themselves. Because any animal might house a transmigrating soul, he was a strict vegetarian — and is even said to have forbidden the eating of beans. Source: Wikisource, Fragments of Empedocles fr. 117; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Empedocles (transmigration, vegetarianism).

question: Empedocles, an ancient Greek thinker, came up with one of the first physical explanations of how an eye actually sees an object across a room. His lines on it were thought lost for over two thousand years, until April 2026, when scholars in Cairo recovered thirty of the missing verses on an ancient scroll. How did Empedocles explain the way we see a thing?
answer: The thing sheds tiny streams that slot into openings in the eye
choices: The thing sheds tiny streams that slot into openings in the eye
The eye shoots out an invisible ray that gropes for the thing
A god carries each image straight from the thing to the mind
The air between the eye and the thing simply turns clear
context: Empedocles called these streams 'effluences' and the matching gaps in our sense organs 'pores' — an ancient guess at how perception physically works. In April 2026 a papyrus from Cairo (P.Fouad inv. 218), identified by papyrologist Nathan Carlig of the University of Liege, revealed thirty previously unknown verses of his poem 'On Nature' dealing with exactly this theory of effluences and vision — the only known copy, joined to fragments already held in Strasbourg. Source: University of Liege / phys.org / EurekAlert, April 2026; SEP and IEP on the effluences-and-pores theory.

question: Maya is lost in a new city, so she stops a stranger on the street and asks him for directions. She is plainly USING him -- a tool to get where she's going. A friend says that's a bit disrespectful: people aren't tools. What's the better reply about when using a person truly wrongs them?
answer: It only wrongs them if you treat them as ONLY a tool, ignoring their own aims and choices
choices: It wrongs them whenever you fail to pay them or repay the favor somehow in return
It wrongs them a little every time, but the wrong is far too minor to worry about
It only wrongs them if you treat them as ONLY a tool, ignoring their own aims and choices
It wrongs them unless you are polite and thank them sincerely once they have helped
context: This is the load-bearing word in Kant's second formulation (the 'Humanity Formula'): treat humanity 'never as means ONLY.' Using people is constant and harmless -- a tourist uses a stranger for directions, a customer uses a waiter, a passenger uses a bus driver -- because each can still share or refuse your goal. The wrong is reducing them to a MERE instrument. Source: Kant, Groundwork 4:429 (Abbott trans.); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Treating Persons as Means.'

question: A shopkeeper keeps one fixed, fair price for everyone, so even a small child can buy from him and not get cheated. Now picture a second shopkeeper who SPOTS that a child can't count her change and shortchanges her on purpose. Both sell the same goods. What is the moral difference between them?
answer: The fair seller still respects the child he deals with; the cheat treats her as a mere mark
choices: The cheat is worse only in that he risks getting caught and losing his good name in town
The fair seller still respects the child he deals with; the cheat treats her as a mere mark
The fair seller just earns less money, so he is being foolish rather than truly virtuous
There is no real difference, since both men are only running a shop to turn a profit
context: Kant's own shopkeeper scene (Groundwork Ch. 1): a prudent merchant 'keeps a fixed general price for everyone, so that a child can buy from him as well as everyone else.' The honest dealing still treats the child as a person he is doing business with; cheating her would reduce her to nothing but a mark to exploit. (Kant adds a separate twist: if the merchant is fair ONLY to guard his reputation, he does the right thing for a merely self-interested reason.) Source: Kant, Groundwork 4:397.

question: You hand a waiter your order and a tip, using him to get your dinner -- yet nobody says you wronged him. Then a mugger in an alley uses you to get your wallet. Both 'use' you. A philosopher says the mugger crosses a line the waiter never does. What makes the mugger's kind of using the wrong kind?
answer: He forces you, so you get no chance to agree or refuse -- which a free person must keep
choices: He forces you, so you get no chance to agree or refuse -- which a free person must keep
He is a stranger, and using strangers is always worse than using the people you know
He takes something costly, while the waiter took only a small tip that you offered him
He is breaking a law, and any using that happens to break a written law is the wrong kind
context: Deception and coercion are the two paradigm ways of using someone MERELY as a means, because both shut down consent: a deceived person can't agree to what they don't know, and a coerced person can't refuse. As the philosopher Onora O'Neill puts it, the other's 'dissent is in principle ruled out.' The Stanford Encyclopedia's own example: 'Since you cannot consent to the mugger's action, the mugger is treating you merely as a means.' Source: SEP, 'Treating Persons as Means' §3.2 (citing O'Neill 1989).

question: A horse pulling a cart can't agree to the trip; you simply hitch it and go. A philosopher says THIS is exactly what separates using a horse from using a person: with a person, there is one question you must always be able to answer YES to. Which question is the test for whether you've reduced someone to a mere tool?
answer: Could this person, if they knew the whole plan, still possibly agree and make my goal theirs?
choices: Could this person, if they knew the whole plan, still possibly agree and make my goal theirs?
Does this person clearly gain more from my plan than I do, so the trade favors their side?
Have I asked this person out loud for permission, even if I went ahead before they replied?
Is this person a stranger and not a friend, since strangers may be used more freely than friends?
context: Kant's test for whether you've crossed into 'merely a means': can the other person possibly assent and share your end? On the false promise he writes that the man 'cannot possibly assent to my mode of acting towards him, and therefore cannot himself contain the end of this action.' A horse can't consent and that's fine; the point is a PERSON must be left ABLE to. Source: Kant, Groundwork 4:429-430 (Abbott trans.); SEP, 'Treating Persons as Means' §3.1.1.
