question: A philosopher draws a hard line: some things carry a PRICE, and some carry a DIGNITY. A used car has a price; a person, he says, has a dignity instead. People reach for that word 'dignity' to mean several different things. On his view, what does it actually mean to say a person has dignity rather than a price?
answer: A person has no equal, so no substitute can stand in for them as priced things do
choices: A person has no equal, so no substitute can stand in for them as priced things do
A person must always be treated gently, with courtesy and considerate, kindly manners
A person earns their standing through good deeds, and grows in worth as they achieve more
A person ranks above every animal and plant, at the very top of all living things
context: Kant: 'In the kingdom of ends everything has either a price or a dignity. What has a price can be replaced by something else as its equivalent; what is raised above all price, and therefore admits of no equivalent, has a dignity.' Priced things are swappable and tradeable; a person, having dignity, is irreplaceable and beyond exchange -- not pricier, but off the price scale entirely, so no substitute (however costly) can stand in. Source: Kant, Groundwork 4:434; Philosophy Now issue 150, 'Kant's Theory of Human Dignity.'

question: A captured enemy soldier has done genuinely terrible things, and his guards say he has thrown away any claim to be treated as anything but a thing to be used. A philosopher who treats every person as an end, never a mere tool, is asked whether the soldier still counts. On his view, what -- if anything -- does even such a wrongdoer still keep?
answer: He keeps the standing owed to any person, which no crime cancels and no merit must buy
choices: He keeps the standing owed to any person, which no crime cancels and no merit must buy
He keeps only what his captors choose to grant him, and may lose even that at their word
He keeps a portion that shrinks as his crimes grow, until the worst lose it entirely
He keeps it only if he shows remorse, since standing must be earned back by good conduct
context: On this reading the Humanity Formula demands 'recognition respect' -- regard owed simply because someone is a person -- not 'appraisal respect' earned by merit. As the philosopher Stephen Darwall frames it, 'persons cannot lose their humanity by their misdeeds.' So even a criminal or an enemy is still owed treatment as an end, never as mere material to be used up. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Kant's Moral Philosophy' §5.

question: Five patients will die tonight, each needing a different organ. In the next room sleeps one healthy visitor whose organs would match all five. A pure save-the-most-lives tally says cut up the one and save five. A philosopher who treats people as ends, not tools, calls this plainly wrong. Why does he refuse the trade?
answer: Because carving up the one to save the rest uses him as mere spare parts -- numbers buy no such right
choices: Because the five might pull through on their own, so the numbers aren't as sure as they look
Because carving up the one to save the rest uses him as mere spare parts -- numbers buy no such right
Because the surgeon could be caught, and a doctor once caught can no longer help his patients
Because the visitor is the healthy one, and healthy people deserve more protection than sick ones
context: This is the hard case philosophers use to show where the Humanity Formula bites against pure cost-benefit thinking. A surgeon who harvested one unwilling 'donor' to save five 'would be treating the donor merely as a means and thereby acting wrongly.' The favorable tally doesn't license treating a person as spare parts -- numbers can't purchase that permission. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Treating Persons as Means,' Introduction.

question: A teacher draws your head and your feet in different spots: those are your parts in different PLACES. Then she makes a bolder claim — you also have parts in different MOMENTS, so the you of yesterday and the you of today are two different parts of you, and today is just one slice. A second teacher objects that you are never split into time-parts. On the second teacher's picture, how do yesterday's you and today's you relate?
answer: Yesterday's you and today's you are one and the same whole thing, present in full on both days
choices: Yesterday's you and today's you are one and the same whole thing, present in full on both days
Yesterday's you and today's you are two smaller parts that jointly add up to the entire you
Yesterday's you has dropped clean out of existence, and only today's you is now real at all
Yesterday's you is gone, and today's you is a fresh successor that merely inherited its traits
context: This is the space-time analogy at the root of the debate. One picture says a thing has TIME-parts just as it has SPACE-parts, so 'you-yesterday' and 'you-today' are two different parts and today is one slice (the technical name, kept out of the stem, is perdurance). Its rival, endurance, denies the slicing: yesterday's you and today's you are not two parts but the very same whole thing, present in full on each day it exists. That positive identity claim is the move to recognize. The trap distractor is the time-slice view the first teacher held (two parts adding up to the whole) — the picture the second teacher rejects. The other two are real rival positions but not what the second teacher is committed to: that the past you has gone out of existence (presentism), or that today's you is a fresh successor inheriting the old traits (a successor/bundle reading). Both the time-slice and the wholly-present pictures are live among serious metaphysicians and the dispute is genuinely unresolved. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Temporal Parts' (Katherine Hawley) — 'Your spatial parts are things like your head, your feet and your nose; your temporal parts are things like you-yesterday, you-today and you-tomorrow.'

question: One picture of a banana says its whole life is a long object stretched through time, the way a film reel is one long strip; the banana's green start and yellow end are simply two cross-sections of that strip, so the object itself never really changes. A rival refuses the stretched-out strip. On the rival picture, what is it that goes from green to yellow?
answer: One whole banana, wholly there throughout, is itself green and then that very same thing is later yellow
choices: One whole banana, wholly there throughout, is itself green and then that very same thing is later yellow
Two cross-sections, a green slice and a yellow slice, that together make up the one banana's whole life
Only the banana existing right now, green or yellow; the color it had before has dropped out of being
A green banana that perishes and a fresh yellow banana that slips in to take its place under one name
context: The stretched-out picture treats every object as a four-dimensional 'worm' through spacetime, with each day a cross-section, so the worm itself never changes — it just has a green part and a yellow part (the technical name, kept out of the stem, is perdurance). Its rival, endurance, denies the worm and locates change in the thing itself: one whole banana, wholly present whenever it exists, is itself green and then that very same thing is later yellow. How a single persisting thing can bear opposite properties at different times is exactly what the endurance side owes an account of (the problem of temporary intrinsics, taken up in the poker rung). The trap distractor is the worm view the rival refuses; the others are a presentist reading (only the now-banana is real) and a perishing-successor reading (a new banana replaces the old under one name). Source: Wikipedia, 'Perdurantism' ('all objects are considered to be four-dimensional "worms"') and 'Four-dimensionalism' ('space-time worms whose temporal dimension corresponds to their career over time'); the endure/perdure labels come from David Lewis, 'On the Plurality of Worlds' (1986).

question: A philosopher poses a puzzle: one and the same poker is bent in the morning and straight by evening — so how can a single thing hold two opposite shapes without contradiction? Defenders of the time-slice picture give a clean answer that mirrors how your warm head and cold feet are no contradiction. What is their answer?
answer: An earlier time-part of the poker is bent and a later time-part is straight, so no one thing is ever both
choices: An earlier time-part of the poker is bent and a later time-part is straight, so no one thing is ever both
The poker merely seems to change shape; bentness and straightness are judgments inside the smith's own mind
Bent and straight are not genuine opposites at all, so one poker can calmly possess both of them at once
There are really two separate pokers, a bent one and a straight one, that just happen to share one name
context: This is the 'problem of temporary intrinsics' — David Lewis's name for the sharpest argument FOR time-slices. The slice answer is clean: just as warm head and cold feet are different SPATIAL parts (no contradiction), bent and straight belong to different TIME-parts. The wholly-present side must answer some other way and faces Leibniz's Law — that identical things cannot differ in their properties. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Temporal Parts'; David Lewis, 'On the Plurality of Worlds' (1986), where the banana ripe/overripe and bent/straight framing appears.

question: The old riddle: Theseus's ship has every plank slowly replaced, while someone hoards the discarded planks and rebuilds the original — so WHICH is the real ship? Defenders of the time-slice picture claim they make the riddle vanish rather than answer it. How do they dissolve it?
answer: Both ships are branches of one Y-shaped object in time, so no single ship must be crowned the survivor
choices: Both ships are branches of one Y-shaped object in time, so no single ship must be crowned the survivor
Only the continuously-repaired ship is real, because a thing must never lose its unbroken chain of use
Only the rebuilt ship is real, because the original planks always carry the true identity with them
Neither is the real ship, because the moment one plank changed the original ceased to exist forever
context: The neat trick of the time-slice picture: it dissolves the puzzle instead of answering it. The repaired ship and the reassembled ship are simply two branches of one Y-shaped four-dimensional object that shares its early temporal parts, so you never have to declare which single ship 'really' survived. The same move handles the statue/clay puzzle — 'the statue is a temporal part of the lump of clay.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Temporal Parts'; Wikipedia, 'Four-dimensionalism' (the 'Y-branching object' treatment of Theseus).

question: A third camp accepts that the world is full of time-stretched objects, but adds a twist about names: the name 'Brandon' does NOT pick out the whole ninety-year stretch — it picks out only a brief momentary slice, a different one at each instant. On this view, when you wonder what 'you' will do next week, what makes that guess true or false?
answer: How your future counterparts behave — later slices causally linked to you, not one long object that is you
choices: How your future counterparts behave — later slices causally linked to you, not one long object that is you
Nothing at all, since a guess about a week that has not yet arrived is neither true nor false until it does
Your present intentions alone, because whatever you mean to do now simply becomes what you will have done
A fixed script set into the whole stretch beforehand, which the present slice is only reading back aloud
context: This is the more radical 'stage view.' It keeps the four-dimensional world but says a name picks out a momentary STAGE, not the whole worm. So a guess about your future is made true or false by the behaviour of your future COUNTERPARTS — later stages causally linked to you — rather than by a part of one long object that is literally you. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Temporal Parts' — 'According to stage theorists, the name refers to a brief part of that ninety-year-long object... made true or false by the behaviour of your counterparts.' (Sider and Hawley are leading stage theorists.)

question: The philosopher we call Epictetus was born a slave around 55 CE, and his real birth name is lost to us. The household that took him in handed him a plain Greek word to answer to — a word that bluntly recorded his new status among them. What does the name 'Epictetus' mean?
answer: 'Acquired,' marking him as a thing that had been bought
choices: 'Acquired,' marking him as a thing that had been bought
'Servant,' marking the chores he did around the house
'Phrygian,' marking the far province he had come from
'Clever,' marking the sharp mind his teacher would praise
context: 'Epictetus' comes from the Greek epiktetos, meaning 'acquired' or 'purchased' — not a birth name but a label for the act of buying the boy. He was born around 55 CE at Hierapolis in Phrygia (modern Turkey). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus (iep.utm.edu/epictetu/).

question: Two merchants lose everything in the very same shipwreck. One is wrecked by grief; the other walks away calm. Epictetus built his entire philosophy on what this gap reveals. According to him, what is it that actually disturbs a person?
answer: Not events themselves, but the judgments a person forms about them
choices: Not events themselves, but the judgments a person forms about them
The events themselves, which wound every person with equal force
The will of the gods, who deal out grief and calm as they please
Plain bad luck, which simply falls harder on some people than others
context: This is the engine of Epictetus's whole philosophy: 'Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things' (Enchiridion 5). The event never wounds you — your judgment about it does. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Epictetus opened his handbook by splitting everything in life into two groups. In the first he put your opinions, your desires, and the things you choose to pursue or avoid. In the second he put your body, your reputation, and your property. He said only ONE of these two groups is truly ours to command. Which group did Epictetus mean?
answer: The first — our own thoughts and choices are ours; the rest is not
choices: The first — our own thoughts and choices are ours; the rest is not
The second — body, reputation, and property are ours; choices are not
Both groups, once a person has trained his mind hard enough
Neither group, since the gods command every part of a life
context: This is the 'dichotomy of control' that opens the handbook: 'Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and... whatever are our own actions' — everything else (body, reputation, property) is not ours to command (Enchiridion 1). Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: One famous tale about Epictetus, passed down by the writer Celsus, claims his master once twisted his leg out of sheer cruelty. The enslaved Epictetus neither begged nor cried out nor showed any anger at all. When the bone finally snapped under the strain, he answered with a single cool line. In the story, what did he say?
answer: 'There, did I not tell you that it would break?'
choices: 'There, did I not tell you that it would break?'
'A man may break my leg, but never my spirit.'
'You have crippled the slave and freed the sage.'
'The gods are watching every bone you shatter.'
context: LEGEND: this breaking scene is preserved by the pagan writer Celsus, quoted by the Christian Origen in Contra Celsum 7.53; the 10th-century Suda instead blames rheumatism for his lameness, so the leg-twisting is testimony, not certain fact. Either way Epictetus was lame for life. Source: Origen, Contra Celsum 7.53 (via Celsus), reported in Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus.

question: Epictetus compared a human life to a play. You are only an actor, he said, and the role you are handed — grand or humble, long or short — is not something you picked for yourself. So what did Epictetus say the actor's one real job is?
answer: To play his own part as well as he possibly can
choices: To play his own part as well as he possibly can
To judge whether the part he was handed is a good one
To hand the part back if it falls beneath his dignity
To study the whole play so he grasps the author's plan
context: 'Remember that you are an actor in a drama, of such a kind as the author pleases to make it. If short, of a short one; if long, of a long one' (Enchiridion 17). Your only job is to play your part well — and play it well whether it is short or long, grand or humble; angling for applause or for a bigger role misses the point. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 17.

question: Epictetus spent his early life as a slave inside the imperial court of the Emperor Nero. His owner was a powerful court official named Epaphroditus. There was a bitter irony in exactly who was holding Epictetus in bondage. What was startling about his master Epaphroditus?
answer: Epaphroditus had himself once been a slave before he was freed
choices: Epaphroditus had himself once been a slave before he was freed
Epaphroditus quietly taught Stoic philosophy to slaves at night
Epaphroditus was years younger than the slave-boy he had bought
Epaphroditus had been born blind and ran the household by ear
context: Epaphroditus was a rich and powerful freedman who had himself once been a slave of the Emperor Nero — so Epictetus was a slave OF a former slave, serving inside Nero's imperial court. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus (plato.stanford.edu/entries/epictetus/).

question: Epictetus is one of the most quoted teachers in all of history, yet there is a strange fact behind every saying we have from him. His words survive almost by accident, because of a gap the man himself left. What did Epictetus do about writing down his own philosophy?
answer: He wrote nothing at all; a student took down his spoken lectures
choices: He wrote nothing at all; a student took down his spoken lectures
He burned all his own books before he died, fearing his own pride
He wrote in a private code that took scholars centuries to crack
He wrote only in old Phrygian, a tongue almost no one could read
context: Epictetus wrote not a single book. Everything survives because his student Arrian of Nicomedia (later a Roman governor and general) wrote down his lectures as the Discourses and condensed them into the little handbook, the Enchiridion (Greek for 'ready-to-hand' / 'manual'). Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus.

question: Marcus Aurelius ruled the whole Roman Empire, the most powerful man alive, yet in the private journal we call the Meditations he quoted one teacher more than any other: Epictetus, who had begun life as a crippled household slave. Again and again the emperor jotted down the ex-slave's grim little reminders of how small and borrowed the self really is, copying them to steady himself. Which line is the one Marcus Aurelius took straight from Epictetus?
answer: 'You are a little soul carrying a corpse around.'
choices: 'You are a little soul carrying a corpse around.'
'You are a spark of the divine fire shut in clay.'
'You are a borrowed breath the gods will reclaim.'
'You are a shadow that the next hour may erase.'
context: The slave out-lasted the emperors. Marcus Aurelius was handed Epictetus's lecture-notes by his teacher Junius Rusticus, and Epictetus became the single most-quoted author in his private journal — including this line copied straight in: 'You are a little soul carrying a corpse around, as Epictetus used to say' (Meditations 4.41). The other three are plausible-sounding Stoic images, but only the corpse line is the one Marcus actually recorded. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.41 (quoting Epictetus); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius; World History Encyclopedia: Epictetus.

question: In Epicurus's Athens the great schools kept their doors narrow: Plato mostly taught the sons of rich Athenian families, and Aristotle tutored young nobles. Epicurus did something startling — he let people the proud schools would never seat argue philosophy as full equals in his garden. Which pair, normally kept out, did Epicurus welcome?
answer: Women and slaves
choices: Women and slaves
Merchants and sailors
Soldiers and athletes
Actors and poets
context: The Garden admitted women and slaves as equals when that was almost unheard of — noblewomen, courtesans, senators, and slaves argued philosophy side by side. Two women remembered by name are Leontion and Themista. The other schools were exclusive: Plato's Academy mostly trained sons of the Athenian elite and Aristotle tutored nobles like Alexander the Great. Sources: The Conversation, 'Long before debates over wokeness, Epicurus built a philosophy that welcomed slaves, women and outsiders'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus.

question: In Epicurus's garden school, a slave named Mys — his name meant Mouse — was not kept in the kitchen. He sat in on the lessons and studied philosophy right beside the free students. Years later, when Epicurus wrote his will, what did he do for Mys?
answer: Set him free
choices: Set him free
Left him the house
Made him head of the school
Paid for his funeral
context: Mys ('Mouse') studied philosophy in the Garden alongside the free students, and in his will Epicurus freed him along with Nicias, Lycon, and the slave-woman Phaedrium. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book X (the Will of Epicurus), via epicureanfriends.com and Wikisource.

question: Today the word epicurean means a foodie who loves rich, fancy meals — but that gets Epicurus exactly backwards. He said he was perfectly happy living on bread and water. Writing to a friend, he named one humble food he wanted sent as a special treat — his idea of a feast. What was it?
answer: Cheese
choices: Cheese
Olives
Figs
Honey
context: The popular sense of 'epicurean' inverts the man: he prized the simplest pleasures. 'Send me a pot of preserved cheese, that when I like I may have a feast,' he wrote — that was his idea of a treat, and he said he was content with bread and water. Sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives X (the cheese letter), via epicureanfriends.com; Society of Friends of Epicurus.

question: Epicurus taught that pleasure is the highest good. People hear that and picture a man chasing feasts, wine, and parties, and his rivals attacked him for it. But Epicurus said they had the very meaning of pleasure wrong. For Epicurus, the steadiest pleasure a person could reach was this. What was it?
answer: Being free of all pain and fear
choices: Being free of all pain and fear
Being full of joy every waking hour
Being lost in one thrill after another
Being praised by everyone you meet
context: Epicurus redefined 'pleasure' as two states of non-disturbance, not indulgence: aponia (absence of bodily pain) and ataraxia (absence of mental anxiety, literally 'non-disturbance'). The good life was not piling up sensations but reaching a calm, untroubled mind and body. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus; Wikipedia: Epicureanism.

question: Epicurus ranked one thing among the very greatest goods in life. He even said the most valuable part of it was not the help itself, but the steady confidence that, if you ever needed them, these people would come through for you. What did Epicurus prize this highly?
answer: Close friends
choices: Close friends
Powerful allies
Loyal servants
Wealthy patrons
context: Epicurus called friendship one of the greatest of all goods. 'Friendship dances around the world, announcing to all of us that we must wake up to blessedness,' he wrote, and he said we need the confidence that friends would help us more than we need the help itself. Source: Epicurus, Vatican Sayings 52 and 34, via newepicurean.com and the Columbia College text.

question: While ambitious Greeks chased office, honors, and a famous name, Epicurus told his students the path to a calm life ran the other way. He packed his advice into a two-word motto, lathe biosas, that became the watchword of his whole school. What did that motto tell you to do?
answer: Live unnoticed
choices: Live unnoticed
Seize the day
Know yourself
Conquer your fear
context: 'Lathe biosas' — 'live unnoticed' or 'live hidden.' Stay out of politics, fame, and the public scramble; a quiet life among friends is the path to tranquility. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus.

question: Lots of people lie awake afraid of being dead. Epicurus offered an argument meant to dissolve that fear. He pointed out that you and death never actually meet: while you are alive, death is not here; and once death has arrived, you are no longer around to experience anything at all. From this, Epicurus drew his famous conclusion about what death can never do to you. What was it?
answer: It can never hurt you
choices: It can never hurt you
It can never surprise you
It can never cheat you
It can never anger you
context: Epicurus's cure for the fear of death: 'Death is nothing to us' — while we are alive death is not here, and once death is here we no longer exist to experience it, so there is no moment when death can actually harm us. Sources: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus 124-125 (classics.mit.edu/Epicurus/menoec.html); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus.

question: Epicurus spent his final day in terrible pain from a blocked kidney, the kind of agony that breaks most people. Yet he sat down and wrote a letter to his friend Idomeneus calling it a blissful day. He said one thing was outweighing all the bodily torment and keeping his mind glad. What did Epicurus say was making his last day happy?
answer: Remembering past talks with his friends
choices: Remembering past talks with his friends
The hope of a reward after death
A drug that dulled the pain
Pride in the school he had built
context: On his deathbed, in agony from a kidney-stone blockage, Epicurus wrote to Idomeneus: 'On this blissful day, which is also the last of my life... My continual sufferings are so great that nothing could increase them; but I set above them all the gladness of mind at the memory of our past conversations.' He then asked Idomeneus to look after the children of his late friend Metrodorus. Sources: Epicurus, Letter to Idomeneus (R.D. Hicks and Cyril Bailey translations), via epicurus.net and epicureanfriends.com.

question: Epicurus's students boiled his whole philosophy into a four-line remedy they memorized like a doctor's cure: do not fear the gods; do not worry about death; what is good is easy to get; what is terrible is easy to endure. The full text was lost for centuries — until one copy turned up among scrolls in an ancient Roman town that a single disaster had sealed away in a single day, under a deep blanket of debris. What had sealed that town and saved the scroll?
answer: A volcano burying it in ash
choices: A volcano burying it in ash
A landslide sliding down on it
A sandstorm drifting over it
A flood sweeping mud across it
context: Later Epicureans compressed the philosophy into a 'four-part cure' (tetrapharmakos). It survives on a charred papyrus scroll by Philodemus recovered from Herculaneum, the Roman town buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79. Sources: Philodemus, recovered Herculaneum papyrus; Wikipedia: Tetrapharmakos; The Living Philosophy.

question: A riddle: 'A feather is light, so it isn't heavy. And whatever is light cannot be dark. So a feather cannot be dark.' The conclusion sounds airtight, but something slipped. What went wrong?
answer: 'Light' means 'not heavy' at first, then flips to 'not dark' — two senses.
choices: 'Light' means 'not heavy' at first, then flips to 'not dark' — two senses.
'Dark' is used in two ways here, once for a colour and once for evil.
It leaps from this one feather to a sweeping claim about all light things.
The opening step secretly assumes the very conclusion it is trying to prove.
context: This is the classic 'light' pun chain. The word 'light' silently switches from weight (not heavy) to brightness (not dark) — but a thing's weight tells you nothing about its colour, so the two claims never actually connect and the conclusion only LOOKS to follow. When one word is used in two senses mid-argument, logicians call it equivocation. Source: https://www.logicalfallacies.org/equivocation.html

question: A puzzle argues: 'Nothing is better than eternal happiness. A ham sandwich is better than nothing. So a ham sandwich is better than eternal happiness.' The sandwich winning is plainly absurd. Why does it fail?
answer: 'Nothing is better' makes happiness the ceiling, but 'better than nothing' only means the sandwich beats having none — different comparisons.
choices: 'Nothing is better' makes happiness the ceiling, but 'better than nothing' only means the sandwich beats having none — different comparisons.
The word 'better' means 'tastier' at first, then shifts to 'more valuable' — one word quietly doing two jobs.
It simply assumes the ham sandwich wins from the start, before it has actually shown anything at all.
It leaps from a claim about one ham sandwich to a sweeping claim about every food there could be.
context: 'Nothing is better than eternal happiness' means happiness is the highest possible value; 'a ham sandwich is better than nothing' only means the sandwich beats having none at all. The two sentences are not making the same comparison, so chaining them is a cheat — the absurd sandwich conclusion exposes the slide. The move is called equivocation. Source: https://www.fallacyfiles.org/fourterm.html

question: An argument runs: 'All rivers have banks. All banks have vaults. So all rivers have vaults.' Picture a river guarding a bank vault — clearly something broke. What broke it?
answer: 'Banks' means a river's edge in line one but a money bank in line two — two senses.
choices: 'Banks' means a river's edge in line one but a money bank in line two — two senses.
'Vaults' is used in two senses here, once for a safe and once for a leap.
The argument leaps from a few rivers to all rivers without any warrant.
Both opening claims are simply false, so the conclusion proves nothing.
context: 'Banks' is really TWO terms — river bank and money bank — disguised as one word. In syllogism terms this secretly smuggles in a fourth term (the 'fallacy of four terms'); the equivocation HIDES it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy_of_four_terms

question: A joke argues: 'Brad is a nobody. Nobody is perfect. Therefore Brad is perfect.' Brad would love this, but it is a cheat. What is the cheat?
answer: 'Nobody' means 'an unimportant person,' then flips to 'not a single person' — two senses.
choices: 'Nobody' means 'an unimportant person,' then flips to 'not a single person' — two senses.
'Perfect' is used in two ways here, once for flawless and once for complete.
It leaps from one fact about Brad to a sweeping claim covering everyone.
It assumes Brad is perfect in the premises before it ever concludes it.
context: 'Nobody' slides from 'an unimportant person' to 'not a single person.' The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy flags this exact example and warns that equivocation 'can sometimes be very difficult to detect.' Source: https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/

question: A kid argues: 'I have every right to watch this show, so it is only right that I watch it now instead of doing my homework.' It sounds clever, but the word 'right' pulled a fast one. What is the catch?
answer: 'Right' first means 'something I'm allowed to do,' then means 'the morally good choice' — two senses.
choices: 'Right' first means 'something I'm allowed to do,' then means 'the morally good choice' — two senses.
'Show' is treated as more important than homework with no reason actually given.
The argument assumes the very conclusion it is supposed to be proving.
It claims that being allowed to do something makes refusing it impossible.
context: 'Right' switches from a liberty or entitlement to 'morally good.' Having the right to do something does not make doing it the right thing — this everyday slide is equivocation. Sources: https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ and https://effectiviology.com/equivocation/

question: An argument runs: 'Noisy kids are a real headache. Two aspirin make a headache go away. So two aspirin make noisy kids go away.' The aspirin-fixes-children ending is silly. What slipped?
answer: 'Headache' is a figure of speech for an annoyance at first, then a literal pain in the head — two senses.
choices: 'Headache' is a figure of speech for an annoyance at first, then a literal pain in the head — two senses.
'Aspirin' is used in two ways here, once as a plain pill and once as a cure-all.
It assumes aspirin works on children before it has shown that it does.
It leaps from these particular noisy kids to all children everywhere.
context: 'Headache' slides from a figure of speech (an annoyance) to a literal medical headache. This is the metaphor-versus-literal flavor of equivocation. Source: https://www.txst.edu/philosophy/student-resources/informal-fallacies/equivocation.html

question: An old argument claims: 'Only man is rational. No woman is a man. So no woman is rational.' The conclusion is plainly wrong, and so is the reasoning behind it. Where is the flaw?
answer: 'Man' means humankind in the first line but a male in the second — one word, two senses.
choices: 'Man' means humankind in the first line but a male in the second — one word, two senses.
'Rational' is used in two ways here, once for calm and once for logical.
It assumes its conclusion about women before it argues for it at all.
It jumps from just a few people to a sweeping claim about everyone.
context: The first 'man' means the human species; the second means a male. The bigoted conclusion collapses the moment you notice the word switched senses. Wikipedia uses this exact case as an example of equivocation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivocation

question: Someone argues: 'Evolution is just a theory. A theory is only a hunch, and hunches aren't proven. So evolution isn't proven.' Set the topic of evolution itself aside — the reasoning leans entirely on one slippery word. Which word, and how?
answer: 'Theory' means a casual hunch at first, then a well-tested scientific framework — two very different senses.
choices: 'Theory' means a casual hunch at first, then a well-tested scientific framework — two very different senses.
'Proven' is used in two ways here, once for 'certain' and once for merely 'likely.'
It assumes evolution is unproven before it has argued the point at all.
It leaps from this one theory to a claim about every idea in science.
context: 'Theory' switches from the everyday sense (a wild guess) to the scientific sense (a well-substantiated explanation of the evidence). The flaw is the word-switch, not any verdict on evolution; sources on both sides name this as equivocation. Sources: https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/questions/jWwYiu5a/evolution_is_just_a_theory.html and https://answersingenesis.org/logic/the-fallacy-of-equivocation/

question: In Plato's dialogue Euthydemus, a sophist corners young Ctesippus: 'You own a dog? Yes. He's a father, with pups of his own? Yes. And he's yours? Yes. Then he's a father and he's yours — so he's your father, and you beat your own father!' Ctesippus is stumped. What is the trick in the argument?
answer: 'Is yours' and 'is a father' get fused into 'your father,' though each phrase keeps a different meaning.
choices: 'Is yours' and 'is a father' get fused into 'your father,' though each phrase keeps a different meaning.
It assumes Ctesippus beats the dog without ever actually proving that he does.
It leaps from this single dog to a rule covering every pet owner alive.
It goes after Ctesippus himself instead of the point he was making.
context: Plato (~380 BC) wrote this scene to mock the sophists' word-games. 'The dog is yours' and 'the dog is a father' are both true, but you cannot weld them into 'the dog is your father' — that equivocates on what 'yours' and 'father' mean together. Source: Plato, Euthydemus, Jowett translation, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/1598/1598-h/1598-h.htm

question: A speaker argues: 'Our country treasures freedom. So we should allow only state-run news, because government media keeps citizens free from foreign lies.' The case feels patriotic, but the key word does not hold still. Where is the slide?
answer: 'Freedom' starts as 'the liberty to choose' but ends as 'kept safe from a bad thing' — two senses.
choices: 'Freedom' starts as 'the liberty to choose' but ends as 'kept safe from a bad thing' — two senses.
'Country' is treated as a single person with one fixed opinion, which it is not.
The argument leaps from one example straight to a sweeping general rule.
It goes after the foreign press instead of making its own positive case.
context: 'Freedom' begins as civil liberty (not being dominated) and quietly becomes 'freed from a bad thing.' The persuasion rides entirely on the word changing sense; this is equivocation, with no verdict here on state media itself. Source: https://www.scribbr.com/fallacies/equivocation-fallacy/

question: An ad reasons: 'Soil is completely natural. Natural things are good for you. So go ahead and eat some soil.' The eat-dirt ending is obviously off, but which step actually cheats?
answer: 'Natural' first means 'found in nature,' then means 'safe and healthy' — and those are not the same.
choices: 'Natural' first means 'found in nature,' then means 'safe and healthy' — and those are not the same.
'Good' is used in two ways here, once for tasty and once for morally fine.
It jumps from this one substance to a claim about everything in nature.
It treats this as right just because nature has supposedly always done it.
context: 'Natural' switches from 'occurring in nature' to 'safe or beneficial,' which do not mean the same thing — the eat-dirt conclusion makes the hidden switch obvious. This equivocation is what unmasks a lot of 'all-natural' marketing. Source: https://www.yourdictionary.com/articles/examples-equivocation-fallacy

question: Shakespeare's Macbeth has a drunken Porter sneer at 'an equivocator... who could not equivocate to heaven.' The jab was aimed at Father Henry Garnet, a Jesuit hanged in 1606 after the Gunpowder Plot, who at his trial defended a 'doctrine of equivocation.' What did that doctrine actually permit him to do?
answer: Speak a true-sounding answer while keeping its real meaning secret in his mind, misleading without an outright lie.
choices: Speak a true-sounding answer while keeping its real meaning secret in his mind, misleading without an outright lie.
Stay completely silent and refuse to answer any question his judges put to him.
Withdraw his earlier confession by insisting it had been forced out of him under torture.
Swear a solemn oath that he secretly intended to break the moment he went free.
context: Garnet's defense was a 'secret meaning reserved in the mind' — phrasing an answer to mislead without technically lying. He was hanged, drawn and quartered, and wits joked he 'will equivocate at the gallows.' Shakespeare's Porter mocks exactly this, showing equivocation as a real moral and political scandal, not just a logic puzzle. (Legend: the Macbeth-Garnet link is the traditional, widely-told reading.) Source: https://www.shakespearesglobe.com/discover/blogs-and-features/2014/11/05/the-gunpowder-plot-and-shakespeares-macbeth/

question: A demon creeps into your loneliest hour and tells you that you must live this life again and again, forever. What does the demon say comes back each time?
answer: Every joy and every pain, in the same order, with nothing new ever added
choices: Every joy and every pain, in the same order, with nothing new ever added
Only your happiest moments, replayed while the suffering is erased
A fresh life each round, where past mistakes can finally be fixed
The same events, but each time you remember the last and grow wiser
context: This is the opening scene of Nietzsche's most famous thought experiment. The whole force of it depends on the repeat being EXACT — not a do-over, not a highlight reel, not a wiser second try. Every sigh, every grief, every small pleasure returns in the identical order, with nothing added and nothing removed. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §341 ('The Greatest Weight').

question: After the demon describes living your life over and over forever, Nietzsche says your honest reaction is the whole test. One person throws himself down, gnashes his teeth, and curses the demon. What does the other person, the one who passes, say back?
answer: "You are a god, and never have I heard anything more divine."
choices: "You are a god, and never have I heard anything more divine."
"Then I will bear it, as I have borne every other hardship."
"Prove it first, and show me the mechanism that makes it true."
"Change one thing, and then perhaps I could accept the bargain."
context: Nietzsche offers exactly two reactions, and which one is honestly yours is the test. The crushed man curses the demon; the man who has had even one moment good enough would call the news divine. Notice the trap: 'I will bear it' sounds noble, but Nietzsche wants more than gritted-teeth endurance — he wants you glad. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §341 (Walter Kaufmann translation).

question: When Nietzsche's demon tells you that your life will run again exactly as before, it reaches for one vivid image to picture how time itself moves. What image does the demon use?
answer: An eternal hourglass, turned over and over, with you a speck of dust tumbling inside
choices: An eternal hourglass, turned over and over, with you a speck of dust tumbling inside
A great wheel that grinds forward, crushing each moment beneath the next as it turns
A river that never flows the same way twice, carrying every moment out to sea
A candle burning down, its flame passed on so that no single life is ever the end
context: The exact line: 'The eternal hourglass of existence is turned over again and again, and you with it, speck of dust!' The image shrinks you to a single grain falling through the same sand for eternity. The 'river that never flows the same way twice' belongs to Heraclitus — an ancient Nietzsche admired — which is why it reads as plausible here. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §341 (Kaufmann translation).

question: Nietzsche titled the demon aphorism "The Greatest Weight." Picture the demon's question, "Do you want this life once more, and countless times more?", settling permanently onto your shoulders. According to Nietzsche, how is that question supposed to change the way you act?
answer: It bears down on every choice, pushing you to live so that you would will the whole life again
choices: It bears down on every choice, pushing you to live so that you would will the whole life again
It proves the universe must repeat, so that no single act of yours is ever truly lost
It reassures you that death is not final, since the life you have will always return
It frees you from blame, since your worst moments were fated and could never have gone otherwise
context: The aphorism is named 'The Greatest Weight' because the question is meant to press on everything you do — the heaviest weight there is. Nietzsche is explicit that this is not a claim about physics or an afterlife; it is a tool for weighing your life. If the demon's question would crush you, change how you live until it wouldn't. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §341; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Friedrich Nietzsche' (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/nietzsche/).

question: The demon's test asks whether you could will your entire life again, exactly as it was. Nietzsche says only one stance toward your life lets you answer yes, and he calls it his formula for human greatness. Toward everything that has happened to you, even the worst, what does that stance demand?
answer: Love it, and want nothing about it to be different, not forward, not backward, not ever
choices: Love it, and want nothing about it to be different, not forward, not backward, not ever
Master it, bending each hardship into fuel for the person you mean to become
Outgrow it, leaving the old wounds behind as a self you have moved past
Redeem it, telling the story so that every loss turns out to have been worth it
context: Nietzsche calls this stance amor fati — 'love of fate.' His formula for greatness: 'that one wants nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity. Not merely bear what is necessary... but love it.' It is the only attitude that can give the demon a wholehearted yes — not using your wounds, not moving past them, but loving the whole of it. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Ecce Homo ('Why I Am So Clever' §10), and The Gay Science §276 where he first names amor fati.

question: Nietzsche said the idea of eternal recurrence struck him like a revelation in August 1881, on a walk beside an Alpine lake, when he stopped at a huge pyramid-shaped boulder. He later said he scribbled the thought on a sheet that same day, and wrote across it a phrase marking how far above ordinary life he felt. What did he write?
answer: "6,000 feet beyond man and time"
choices: "6,000 feet beyond man and time"
"10,000 feet above good and evil"
"A mile above the world of men"
"Higher than any god has climbed"
context: The lake was Silvaplana near Sils-Maria in the Swiss Alps, about 6,000 feet up. In Ecce Homo, Nietzsche recalls jotting the thought on a sheet inscribed '6000 feet beyond man and time,' and calls eternal recurrence 'the fundamental conception' of Thus Spoke Zarathustra and 'the highest formula of affirmation that can possibly be attained.' Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Ecce Homo ('Thus Spoke Zarathustra' §1).

question: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, the riddle of the eternal repeat reaches its climax with a young shepherd writhing on the ground, a heavy black snake hanging from his mouth; it had crawled down his throat and bitten fast. Zarathustra screams, "Bite! Bite its head off!" The shepherd bites, spits the head away, and springs up, no longer a shepherd, no longer a man, but a transfigured, light-surrounded being — and then does the last thing you would expect from someone who had just been choking to death. What does he do?
answer: Laughs a laugh wilder than any ever heard on earth
choices: Laughs a laugh wilder than any ever heard on earth
Weeps for everything the long road behind him had cost
Throws back his head and curses the heavens that bound him
Speaks a single word that Zarathustra could never repeat
context: Nietzsche's words: the shepherd springs up 'no longer shepherd, no longer man — a transfigured being, a light-surrounded being, that LAUGHED! Never on earth laughed a man as he laughed!' The scene comes inside 'The Vision and the Enigma,' the chapter where the eternal-repeat riddle is posed — the choking horror of the thought, bitten through, turns into joy. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part III, 'The Vision and the Enigma' (Common translation).

question: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, as Zarathustra climbs with the vision of the eternal repeat, a creature he calls the Spirit of Gravity, half dwarf and half mole, rides on his shoulder weighing him down and mocking the whole vision. The dwarf shrinks it all into one contemptuous sentence. What does the dwarf sneer?
answer: "All truth is crooked; time itself is a circle."
choices: "All truth is crooked; time itself is a circle."
"Nothing matters, for all of it comes round again."
"You climb only to fall; the heights are not for men."
"There is no forward and no back, only the turning wheel."
context: The dwarf, the Spirit of Gravity, mutters it 'contemptuously': 'All truth is crooked; time itself is a circle.' The point is sharp — Nietzsche puts the glib version of his own idea ('it's all just a circle') in the mouth of the enemy who is dragging Zarathustra down. The cheap cosmological reading is the foe; the real thing is the harder, personal test of whether you would will it all again. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part III, 'The Vision and the Enigma' (Common translation).

question: A boy and his grandmother are both in a dark room where neither can see a painting. The grandmother is blind. The boy has perfectly good eyes but has them shut and could open them whenever he wants. Which of the two has actually LOST a power, rather than simply choosing to do without it?
answer: The grandmother, because her eyes truly cannot give her sight no matter what she does
choices: The boy, because by refusing to open his eyes he is the one throwing his sight away
Both of them the same, since right now not one of the two can see the painting at all
The grandmother, because her eyes truly cannot give her sight no matter what she does
Neither of them, since sitting in a dark room is nobody's fault and harms no one here
context: This is the handle behind a famous philosophical move. Blindness is not a 'thing' a person carries; it is missing sight in a creature meant to see, while the boy merely declines to use a power he still has. John of Damascus put the same idea another way: 'evil is nothing else than absence of goodness, just as darkness also is absence of light.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Absence of good'; John of Damascus.

question: A rock on the ground cannot see, and a hawk that has gone blind cannot see either. A thinker says only ONE of these counts as something having gone wrong, an evil, while the other is just the way things are. Which one is the genuine 'gone wrong' case, and why?
answer: The blind hawk, because a hawk is the kind of creature that is supposed to see and now cannot
choices: The blind hawk, because a hawk is the kind of creature that is supposed to see and now cannot
The rock, because out of the two it is the older and simpler thing yet still ends up sightless
Both alike, since at the end of the day neither the rock nor the hawk can see anything at all
Neither one, because seeing is a rare gift and going without it can never really count as a loss
context: Augustine drew exactly this line: blindness in a creature built to see is a real privation, while a stone's not-seeing is mere absence, no evil at all. Evil is not just any lack; it is a missing good that OUGHT to be there. Source: Wikipedia, 'Absence of good'; Augustine on privation.

question: A doctor heals a deep wound on a man's arm until the skin is whole again. A child asks, 'Where did the wound GO when it healed? Did it move off somewhere else?' Augustine answered this exact kind of question. What did he say happens to the wound?
answer: It stops existing entirely, because it was never a thing of its own, only missing health
choices: It travels deeper into the body and hides, waiting quietly in the blood for a later day
It breaks apart and passes off into the air, the way smoke leaves a fire that goes out
It shrinks into a tiny seed inside the scar that can later grow back the very same wound
It stops existing entirely, because it was never a thing of its own, only missing health
context: Augustine wrote that in the bodies of animals, disease and wounds 'mean nothing but the absence of health,' and when they are cured they do not flee elsewhere but 'altogether cease to exist,' because a wound was never a substance, only 'a defect in the fleshly substance.' Health is the real thing; the wound is just its hole. Source: Augustine, Enchiridion, ch. 11.

question: Rust eats away at iron; rot creeps through wood. A teacher who studies Augustine asks what such decay reveals about itself. According to Augustine, what must already be there for corruption to begin? Which answer fits best?
answer: It can only ever set to work inside something sound and good, which it then spoils and uses up
choices: It is a coating that certain objects simply come with from the start, while others are born free of it
It can only ever set to work inside something sound and good, which it then spoils and uses up
It is a small living creature, much like a mold, that is born, feeds, and dies on its own clock
It is simply the way that all matter naturally prefers to rest once nothing is left to stir it
context: Augustine pressed this point in City of God: corruption needs a good to corrupt. 'The nature it vitiates is a good,' and 'if there be no good to take away, then no injury can be done.' Rust needs iron, rot needs wood, and the more thoroughly a thing is eaten, the LESS of it remains. Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XII, ch. 3.

question: A student is troubled: if God made everything and God is good, then who made EVIL? Augustine wrestled with this puzzle for years before settling his answer. When he finally laid out what evil REALLY is, what did he say?
answer: Evil is not a thing at all, only a lack or corruption of good that has eaten into something real
choices: Evil is its own dark substance, a real stuff that exists in its own right alongside the good
Evil is a real force God lets stand, a hard trial that good people are meant to wrestle and overcome
Evil is not a thing at all, only a lack or corruption of good that has eaten into something real
Evil is a real weight sent down as punishment, laid on the world to make wrongdoers pay their debt
context: This is the heart of the position, sometimes labeled 'privation of good.' Augustine summed it up: 'For what is that which we call evil but the absence of good?' If evil is a hole rather than a stuff, the question 'who MADE it?' is like asking who manufactured the hole in a doughnut. Source: Augustine, Enchiridion, ch. 11; Confessions, Book VII.

question: For nine years Augustine followed the Manichees, who taught that evil is a vast kingdom of Darkness locked in eternal war with the Light. His friend Nebridius pressed one hard question: if that Darkness is a true rival God must forever battle and can never finish off, what does admitting such a foe force us to give up about God?
answer: Then God cannot be all-powerful, since a real competing power would hem in what God can do
choices: Then God cannot be all-good, since only a cruel god would choose to start a war with the Darkness
Then God cannot exist at all, since two eternal powers leave no room for a single creator
Then God cannot be all-knowing, since the cunning Darkness could keep its plans hidden from him
Then God cannot be all-powerful, since a real competing power would hem in what God can do
context: Nebridius's argument haunted Augustine and helped pull him away from the Manichees. If evil is a co-equal SUBSTANCE warring with God, then God has a true rival and is not omnipotent. Defining evil as a mere lack, with no substance at all, removes the rival and keeps God all-powerful. This is why the privation move is the anti-Manichee weapon. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'; Confessions, Book VII.

question: Imagine slowly stripping away every last shred of good in a thing, one scrap at a time, trying to leave behind something that is purely and only evil. Augustine asked what you would actually be holding at the very moment the final trace of good was gone. What did he say is left?
answer: Nothing whatsoever, because a thing that has lost all its good has lost its hold on existing
choices: Nothing whatsoever, because a thing that has lost all its good has lost its hold on existing
A purely evil thing, the darkest object that could exist, scrubbed clean of every last good
A thing that is now neither good nor evil, resting blankly in the middle ground between them
A thing that turns into pure good, as if total emptiness somehow loops back around to light
context: Augustine wrote in the Confessions: 'if they be deprived of all good, they will cease to be. So long, therefore, as they are, they are good; therefore whatsoever is, is good.' A wholly evil thing is a contradiction, because by the time you removed the last good, there would be nothing left to be evil in. Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book VII, ch. 12.

question: Bertrand Russell rejected the idea that evil is just a 'hole' where good ought to be, calling it too rosy. To make his case he insisted that one ordinary, miserable experience is positively REAL in its own right, with a felt quality all its own, and is not merely some good thing gone missing. Which experience did Russell choose as his example?
answer: Pain, with its own raw, stabbing feel that seems far more than just pleasure having gone absent
choices: Cold, with its biting chill that seems to seep into a room far more than warmth having drained away
Pain, with its own raw, stabbing feel that seems far more than just pleasure having gone absent
Shadow, with its dark shape on a wall that seems far more solid than light simply being blocked off
Silence, with its heavy hush over a house that seems far weightier than sound merely having stopped
context: Russell called the privation theory unwarranted optimism: 'pain and hatred and envy and cruelty are surely things that exist, and are not merely the absence of their opposites.' Philosopher Todd Calder sharpened the point: agony has its own intrinsically bad felt quality that 'lack of pleasure' fails to capture. The dispute stays open; the metaphysics is the lesson, not a verdict. Source: Russell, The Elements of Ethics; Calder, in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Augustine's escape from the Manichees leaned on the idea that evil is unreal, a corruption of good rather than a stuff. People often credit him with inventing it, but he met it in books he read around the year 386. Who first argued that evil is a privation, an idea Augustine then borrowed to defend his Christian God?
answer: Plotinus, a pagan Neoplatonist who tied evil to formless matter and the slide toward non-being
choices: Nebridius, the close friend whose sharp and probing questions kept troubling Augustine's beliefs
John of Damascus, the monk who likened evil's lack of being to darkness being a lack of light
Plotinus, a pagan Neoplatonist who tied evil to formless matter and the slide toward non-being
Thomas Aquinas, the thinker who tied a thing's very goodness to the plain fact that it exists
context: Plotinus's Enneads I.8 already argued that evil is unsubstantial, a privation or corruption of goodness tied to formless matter and non-being. Augustine read the 'books of the Platonists' around 386 CE and used their metaphysics to climb out of Manichaeism. A striking twist: a pagan philosopher supplied the bones of the Christian answer to the problem of evil. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine,' crediting Plotinus, Enneads I.8.

question: A craftsman sits down to make a paper-knife -- a slim blade for slitting open envelopes. He picks up the metal he will forge it from. Jean-Paul Sartre used this ordinary made thing to make a point about where its purpose comes from. For a paper-knife, what comes first?
answer: Its purpose and design, settled in the maker’s mind before the object exists
choices: Its purpose and design, settled in the maker’s mind before the object exists
The raw metal, which slowly suggests what the finished tool should become
The buyer’s taste, which decides afterward what the blade will be used for
Pure chance, since a craftsman rarely knows how a tool will turn out
context: Sartre's exact words: 'one cannot suppose that a man would produce a paper-knife without knowing what it was for.' The tool's purpose lives in the maker's mind before the object does. This is the hook he uses to set up his big claim about people -- who, he says, work the opposite way. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org/reference/archive/sartre/works/exist/sartre.htm.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre said a person is not like a cauliflower or a clump of moss, which simply sit there being whatever they already are. A human being, he said, works in the opposite way. In his picture, what is a person, unlike the cauliflower?
answer: A project that propels itself toward a future and is aware it is doing so
choices: A project that propels itself toward a future and is aware it is doing so
A finished object whose qualities were all fixed at the moment of birth
A creature ruled entirely by instinct, with no say over what it becomes
A blank surface that other people quietly write their own wishes onto
context: Sartre's line: a human is 'something which propels itself towards a future and is aware that it is doing so,' rather than 'a kind of moss, or a fungus or a cauliflower.' The cauliflower just is what it is; a person is always reaching ahead, planning, becoming. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre called the built-in purpose of a thing its essence, and the bare fact that it is simply here its existence. He used a paper-knife forged by a craftsman as his example. For a made tool like that, which of the two does the maker have to settle first?
answer: Its essence -- its purpose and definition, fixed in the maker's mind first
choices: Its essence -- its purpose and definition, fixed in the maker's mind first
Its existence -- the metal exists first, and its use is discovered later
Both together, arriving the very instant the blade is finally forged
Neither one, since a simple tool has no genuine purpose at all
context: Sartre: 'the essence of the paper-knife -- that is to say the sum of the formulae and the qualities which made its production and its definition possible -- precedes its existence.' 'Essence' = the what-it-is (the purpose and defining qualities); 'existence' = the bare fact that it is here. For a made tool, essence comes first: the maker conceives its purpose before the object is ever forged. The whole argument is about whether a PERSON works the same way. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre said a human being does not work like a paper-knife at all -- a person is not handed a fixed purpose at the start. So how, in his picture, does a person come to have a definite 'what-you-are' at all?
answer: They exist first with no set nature, building what they are by living
choices: They exist first with no set nature, building what they are by living
They gradually discover the one calling they were always meant for
They are mostly whatever role their family and society assign them
They are stamped for life by the habits formed in their earliest years
context: This is the slogan itself: existence precedes essence. Sartre's full sentence reads 'man first of all exists, encounters himself, surges up in the world -- and defines himself afterwards.' Unlike the knife, a human shows up with no fixed nature and only becomes a definite 'what-you-are' through living. The distractors are real rival accounts a thoughtful person might hold -- a single destined calling, a role assigned by society, or a character set by early habit -- none of which is Sartre's. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre argued that a person is not born built for a set purpose the way a paper-knife is forged for one. He summed up the consequence as the very first principle of his philosophy. According to that principle, a person is, in the end, what?
answer: Nothing but what he makes of himself through his own choices
choices: Nothing but what he makes of himself through his own choices
Mostly the product of the family and country he was born into
Whatever role society has quietly assigned him from the start
A fixed character that good upbringing simply brings to the surface
context: Sartre's exact words: 'Man is nothing else but that which he makes of himself. That is the first principle of existentialism.' Identity is an achievement built from choices and deeds, never a gift you are simply issued at birth. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre argued that because a person is not built for a set purpose, no one can blame a fixed nature for what they do -- every choice is fully theirs to answer for. He pressed this into a deliberate paradox: a person never asked to exist, was simply thrown into the world, and yet is responsible for the whole of it. How did he phrase that paradox?
answer: Man is condemned to be free
choices: Man is condemned to be free
Man is the measure of all things
Man is a wolf to his fellow man
Man is born good but turns cruel
context: Sartre's full line: 'Man is condemned to be free. Condemned, because he did not create himself, yet is nevertheless at liberty, and from the moment that he is thrown into this world he is responsible for everything he does.' Freedom here is not a gift you can decline -- it is a sentence. The distractors are other famous lines about human nature, from Protagoras, Hobbes, and the Rousseau tradition. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: A man insists that deep down he is brave and generous -- look at the fine intentions he carries and the talents he was born with, even if his life never quite showed them. Jean-Paul Sartre had no patience for this. On his account, a person amounts to exactly what?
answer: The sum of his actions -- nothing more than what his life actually is
choices: The sum of his actions -- nothing more than what his life actually is
The depth of the talents he was born with, used or not
The good intentions he held privately throughout his life
The reputation that others happen to grant him in the end
context: Sartre: a person 'is nothing else but the sum of his actions, nothing else but what his life is.' You are not your secret potential or your hopes -- only what you actually do. A coward, he insists, is made a coward by cowardly deeds, not by some inner gift gone to waste. This is the sharp edge of 'existence precedes essence': no hidden inner self to fall back on, just the record of your deeds. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: Four serious thinkers gave four different answers to one question: at birth, does a person come with a nature already, and if not, who writes the one they end up with? Aristotle, Locke, a churchman reading Genesis, and Jean-Paul Sartre would each answer differently. Which answer is the one Sartre defended?
answer: No nature at birth, and the person writes their own by the choices they make
choices: No nature at birth, and the person writes their own by the choices they make
A fixed human function present from birth, the same in everyone who is born
No nature at birth, and the world writes one by pressing in through experience
A nature drawn up beforehand by a Maker, the way a knife is planned before forging
context: The four are real rival accounts of where a person's nature comes from: Aristotle (a fixed human function, the 'rational animal,' present from the start); Locke's blank slate (born with no nature, then written on by experience -- but by the world, not by the self); the religious imago Dei view (a Creator drew up human nature beforehand, like an artisan planning a knife); and Sartre (no nature at birth, and you author your own by your choices -- existence precedes essence). The trap is Locke: he too denies a nature at birth, but for him the WORLD does the writing; only Sartre makes the SELF the author. The question asks which view is Sartre's, not which is true -- the other three remain live positions a thoughtful person might hold. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Existentialism'; Wikipedia, 'Existence precedes essence' and 'Essence'.

question: Centuries before Jean-Paul Sartre, medieval thinkers like Thomas Aquinas taught the reverse order: a thing’s essence -- its blueprint -- is settled first, and God then grants it actual existence. Sartre’s slogan was a pointed flip of exactly this teaching. For human beings, what did Sartre reverse about that older view?
answer: He put existence first, with no blueprint of human nature laid down ahead of it
choices: He put existence first, with no blueprint of human nature laid down ahead of it
He kept the blueprint first but removed God as the one who grants existence
He argued existence and essence are illusions that thinkers should drop
He claimed the blueprint is real but stays forever hidden from us
context: Aristotle and Aquinas held that essence precedes existence -- Aquinas taught that God 'bestows' existence onto a pre-existing essence (which underwrites creation from nothing). Sartre flips the order specifically for human beings: existence first, and no pre-drawn blueprint of human nature at all. The trap answer -- keep the blueprint, just delete God -- is exactly what he did NOT do. Source: Wikipedia, 'Existence precedes essence'; encyclopedia.com, 'Essence and Existence'.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre noticed that the old picture of God as creator treats God as a kind of supreme craftsman -- conceiving “human nature” in advance, just as an artisan conceives a paper-knife before making it. Sartre, an atheist, drew a blunt conclusion from rejecting that craftsman. What did he claim followed once the divine designer was removed?
answer: There is no fixed human nature, since no God conceived one in advance
choices: There is no fixed human nature, since no God conceived one in advance
Human nature survives unchanged, now grounded in biology instead
Each society simply invents whatever human nature it prefers
Human nature becomes unknowable, though it certainly still exists
context: Sartre: 'When we think of God as the creator, we are thinking of him, most of the time, as a supernal artisan' -- and 'there is no human nature, because there is no God to have a conception of it.' No divine craftsman, no blueprint. This is presented as the existentialist's position to reason about, not the bank's verdict; thoughtful people who believe in God reject the premise and so reject the conclusion. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre split the world in two. A rock or a knife is thing-like -- complete, fully and only what it is. A conscious person is the opposite -- never finished, always able to remake the meaning of their situation. Sartre gave a name to the lie of treating yourself as the first kind, a fixed thing with a set nature you cannot help. What did he call that self-deception?
answer: Bad faith
choices: Bad faith
Original sin
False consciousness
The will to power
context: Sartre's pair: being-in-itself (en-soi) is thing-like and complete -- a rock, a knife; being-for-itself (pour-soi) is consciousness, never finished, 'what it is not and not what it is.' Pretending you are a fixed in-itself -- 'I just am this way, I had no choice' -- is what Sartre calls bad faith. The distractors are real ideas from other traditions: Christian theology (original sin), Marx (false consciousness), and Nietzsche (the will to power). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Sartre: Existentialism'; Sartre, 'Being and Nothingness' (1943); iep.utm.edu/sartre-ex/.

question: As a young student, the quiet, heavyset Thomas Aquinas was so still in class that his fellow students mocked him as 'the Dumb Ox.' But his teacher Albert the Great had once heard Aquinas brilliantly defend a hard thesis, and was certain the mockery had it backwards. What did Albert predict about the boy the others were laughing at?
answer: That his bellowing in doctrine would one day resound throughout the world
choices: That his bellowing in doctrine would one day resound throughout the world
That his quiet patience would make him a model for the monks who followed
That his classmates would one day beg to study under the ox they mocked
That his slow, plodding manner in fact hid the fastest mind among them
context: Albert the Great taught Aquinas at Cologne and had himself launched the recovery of Aristotle for the Latin West, writing commentaries on every one of Aristotle's works. The 'Dumb Ox' line is a treasured legend of the order: Albert turned the insult around, since an ox bellows. Source: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), St. Thomas Aquinas (newadvent.org/cathen/14663b.htm); Dominicans (english.op.org), 'Our Brother, the Dumb Ox.'

question: In Thomas Aquinas's day, many thinkers were sure that faith and human reason were natural enemies, so that wherever one of them walked, the other had to be in the wrong. Aquinas set out to overturn this whole picture of two foes. What did he claim faith and reason actually were?
answer: Two different roads that arrive at the same single truth
choices: Two different roads that arrive at the same single truth
Two rival kingdoms locked in endless war over one land
One road, reason, that faith must always step aside for
One road, faith, that makes reason a waste of a man's hours
context: This synthesis is the heart of Aquinas. In the Summa Contra Gentiles he speaks of a 'twofold truth' about God, 'one to which the inquiry of reason can reach, the other which surpasses the whole ability of human reason.' Because all truth comes from God, the two roads can never genuinely contradict; a conclusion that clashes with faith is, he said, 'not philosophy but rather an abuse of philosophy.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Faith and Reason (iep.utm.edu/faith-re/); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Thomas Aquinas (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aquinas/).

question: Thomas Aquinas pressed his whole account of how God's grace meets the ordinary human mind into one famous Latin maxim. What was that one-line maxim?
answer: Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it
choices: Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it
Grace and nature are two names for one and the same gift
Nature climbs as high as it can, then grace alone takes over
Grace tears nature down to build something wholly new
context: In Latin, 'Gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit.' It sits in the Summa Theologiae at Prima Pars, Question 1, Article 8: 'Since therefore grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith.' Human reason is not erased by faith; it is taken up and completed by it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit'; Summa Theologiae I, q.1, a.8 ad 2.

question: Thomas Aquinas would not claim that reason could prove every Christian teaching. He sorted them instead: most rest on divine revelation and lie past what the mind can reach, but a small few, he held, human reason can demonstrate entirely on its own. Which truth did Aquinas place in that first group, as something reason can prove unaided?
answer: That God exists, the maker behind all things
choices: That God exists, the maker behind all things
That God is three persons sharing one being
That God once took on flesh and walked the earth
That the dead will rise again at the end of time
context: Aquinas called the truths reason can prove on its own the 'preambles of faith' (preambula fidei), and the existence of God was his showcase. The truths that rest on divine testimony alone he called the 'articles of faith' -- among them the Trinity and the Incarnation, the very claims offered here as distractors. The recognition: he did not pretend reason proves everything; he drew the exact line where one road ends and the other begins. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Faith and Reason (iep.utm.edu/faith-re/), on preambles vs. articles of faith.

question: Thomas Aquinas taught that faith and reason are two roads to truth, but he did not rank them as equals. Suppose a philosopher's careful argument seems to clash with a truth held on faith. According to Aquinas, which road has to give way, and how far?
answer: Reason gives way, for it can fall short or stay inconclusive, but it can never overturn a revealed truth
choices: Reason gives way, for it can fall short or stay inconclusive, but it can never overturn a revealed truth
Whichever road reaches the more certain conclusion in that case wins, and the weaker one gives way
Faith gives way, for a firm and well-argued proof of reason outranks a claim merely held on faith
Neither gives way, for each road rules its own walled-off questions and the two can never truly meet
context: Aquinas's two-fold theory of truth runs one way only: 'No contradiction can stand between these two truths. However, something can be true for faith and false (or inconclusive) in philosophy, though not the other way around.' Revealed theology is the nobler science -- greater certitude, higher dignity -- because, as he put it, 'whatever its source, truth is of the Holy Spirit.' Reason can fall short or be inconclusive; it can never overturn a revealed truth. The 'each rules its own, walled-off' distractor is the 'double truth' he rejected, linked to the Latin Averroists around Siger of Brabant. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Faith and Reason (iep.utm.edu/faith-re/), on Aquinas's two-fold theory of truth.

question: Thomas Aquinas faced a head-on clash: Aristotle had argued the universe always existed, while Scripture said God created it in time. Following the Jewish thinker Moses Maimonides, Aquinas weighed whether human reason alone could settle which side was right. What did Aquinas conclude about the world's beginning in time?
answer: That reason cannot settle it either way, so its beginning in time rests on faith
choices: That reason cannot settle it either way, so its beginning in time rests on faith
That Aristotle's eternal-world proof is airtight, so faith must give way to it
That reason proves creation in time, so faith adds nothing to the matter
That reason favors Aristotle's side, so Scripture's account must be read loosely
context: Maimonides, whom Aquinas respectfully called 'Rabbi Moses,' had judged in his Guide for the Perplexed that Aristotle's eternal-universe argument and the biblical claim of creation fight to a rational draw. Aquinas followed him exactly, citing the same Aristotelian passage to the same end: that the world began in time is held by faith, not proven by reason. He refused to fake a proof to make faith look stronger. Source: London Review of Books, Peter Adamson, 'Five Hundred Parasangs: Maimonides works it out'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Maimonides (plato.stanford.edu/entries/maimonides/).

question: A shipowner sends an old emigrant ship to sea. He has real doubts about whether she is still seaworthy, but he pushes the doubts down with warm thoughts of her past safe voyages until he feels a sincere conviction that she is sound. He never has her inspected. She sinks, and everyone aboard drowns. The philosopher W.K. Clifford uses this tale to say the shipowner did a real wrong. What is the wrong Clifford pins on him?
answer: Believing she was sound when he had not earned that belief by honest inquiry
