choices: Believing she was sound when he had not earned that belief by honest inquiry
Believing too weakly, when a captain must feel total certainty to send a ship out
The plain bad luck that this particular voyage happened to end in disaster
Failing to insure the old vessel before risking it on a long ocean crossing
context: This is the engine of evidentialism. Clifford's verdict in 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877): 'He had no right to believe on such evidence as was before him. He had acquired his belief not by honestly earning it in patient investigation, but by stifling his doubts.' The wrong is in how the belief was formed, not in the lost lives alone. Source: W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877).

question: W.K. Clifford (1845-1879), the man who declared it always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence, was no outsider sniping at science. He was a brilliant English mathematician who died of tuberculosis at just 33. Decades before Einstein, Clifford floated a startling idea about the physical world that the math of his day could barely express. What did he propose?
answer: That gravity might be nothing but the bending of the geometry of space itself
choices: That gravity might be nothing but the bending of the geometry of space itself
That time might run measurably slower for objects moving near the speed of light
That all matter might be built from tiny indivisible particles called atoms
That the whole universe might be expanding outward from a single point
context: Clifford co-founded geometric algebra (the 'Clifford algebras' carry his name) and was the first to suggest that gravity might be a bending of the geometry of space, anticipating Einstein by decades. He also wrote fairy tales for children, and died in Madeira where he had gone hoping to recover from tuberculosis. The point: the demand for evidence came from inside science, not from a foe of it. Sources: Britannica, 'William Kingdon Clifford'; Humanist Heritage.

question: Soren Kierkegaard (1813-1855) proposed to Regine Olsen in 1840, then broke off the engagement a year later. He had convinced himself he must give up the woman he loved to pursue his calling as a writer. Rather than simply tell her, Kierkegaard chose a strange and painful method to make her let go of him. What did he do?
answer: He deliberately behaved like a heartless scoundrel so that she would reject him
choices: He deliberately behaved like a heartless scoundrel so that she would reject him
He fled the country in secret without ever telling her where he had gone
He told her whole family that he had fallen in love with another woman
He sent her a long letter laying all the blame on her own parents
context: Scholars read 'Fear and Trembling' (1843) as Kierkegaard's own Abraham-and-Isaac story: he believed he had to sacrifice his own happiness to pursue his vocation, raising the knife 'on the strength of the absurd.' The abstract 'leap' was a wound he actually lived. Sources: SEP, 'Soren Kierkegaard'; D. Anthony Storm's Commentary on Fear and Trembling.

question: In W.K. Clifford's famous tale, a shipowner talks himself into believing his rickety emigrant ship is safe, skips the inspection, and sends her out, and she sinks with all aboard. Clifford then adds a hard twist. Suppose the very same ship, with the belief formed in the very same careless way, had happened to cross safely and come home. In Clifford's judgment, is the shipowner then off the hook?
answer: No, the guilt lies in how he reached the belief, and a lucky outcome cannot wash it away
choices: No, the guilt lies in how he reached the belief, and a lucky outcome cannot wash it away
Yes, since no one was harmed in the end, there was simply no wrong to answer for
Yes, because the safe arrival proves his confidence in the old ship was justified
Partly, since he is guilty of recklessness but not of any actual harm to others
context: This is the precise move that makes evidentialism more than 'did it work out?' Clifford: 'When an action is once done, it is right or wrong for ever; no accidental failure of its good or evil fruits can possibly alter that.' The shipowner is just as guilty even if the ship had come home safe, because the guilt lives in the dishonest forming of the belief, not in the luck of the result. Source: W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877).

question: Soren Kierkegaard pictured the person of faith not as someone standing on solid ground, but as someone afloat out upon the deep, over seventy thousand fathoms of water, who must stay joyful while hanging there with nothing at all underneath. By choosing this image of the abyss instead of an image of firm footing, what was Kierkegaard saying faith IS?
answer: A commitment held with full personal conviction even though its ground can never be made certain
choices: A commitment held with full personal conviction even though its ground can never be made certain
A conclusion a person reaches once the evidence has finally tipped far enough in its favor
A sense of safety that arrives the very moment a believer's last doubts have gone
A bet a person places only after working out that the odds are clearly in their favor
context: Kierkegaard's formula from the 'Concluding Unscientific Postscript' (1846): faith is 'an objective uncertainty held fast in an appropriation-process of the most passionate inwardness' - objective uncertainty held with subjective certainty. The believer must 'remain out upon the deep, over seventy thousand fathoms of water, still preserving my faith.' The risk is the whole point: 'Without risk, no faith.' This is Kierkegaard's position, presented here as one move about where evidence runs out, not as the bank's verdict. Source: Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846); SEP, 'Faith.'

question: W.K. Clifford pushed his rule about evidence further than most. Believing on weak evidence, he said, is not merely unwise, it is morally WRONG. A friend protests: 'What I choose to believe in the privacy of my own head harms no one but me.' How does Clifford answer that 'it is my own business' defense?
answer: Beliefs leak into words and deeds, so a careless believer weakens everyone's hold on the truth
choices: Beliefs leak into words and deeds, so a careless believer weakens everyone's hold on the truth
Private beliefs really are harmless, so the rule binds only the beliefs a person acts upon
The careless believer alone is harmed, yet harming oneself is still a genuine moral failing
No belief is ever truly private, because the state holds a right to police what people think
context: Clifford's reason it is never just private: 'No real belief, however trifling and fragmentary it may seem, is ever truly insignificant; it prepares us to receive more of its like.' Hence his closing rule - 'It is wrong, always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence' - and his sharpest line on character: 'The credulous man is father to the liar and the cheat.' Belief, he says, is held in trust for all mankind. Source: W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877).

question: In 'Fear and Trembling' (1843), Soren Kierkegaard fixes on Abraham, who on a three-day journey is willing to sacrifice his own son Isaac because he believes God has commanded it. The shared moral law says plainly: do not kill your son. Kierkegaard wrestles with this head-on collision rather than explaining it away. What does he claim Abraham's willingness reveals about faith?
answer: That faith can lift the single person, for a moment, past the ordinary demands of right and wrong
choices: That faith can lift the single person, for a moment, past the ordinary demands of right and wrong
That a faith worth the name will in the end never truly ask a person to do an evil thing
That Abraham must simply have misheard, since a good God would not command a real atrocity
That faith and duty are at bottom the same thing, glimpsed from two different angles
context: Kierkegaard's name for the move is the 'teleological suspension of the ethical': faith puts the single individual momentarily higher than the universal moral law. This is the move evidentialists find monstrous and Kierkegaard finds the purest faith. Note the no-verdict frame: the question asks what Kierkegaard CLAIMS, not whether Abraham was right - an evidentialist who recoils from the act would still agree this is what Kierkegaard argued. Sources: Fear and Trembling (1843), by Johannes de silentio; SEP, 'Soren Kierkegaard.'

question: Soren Kierkegaard made a claim most believers find startling: being able to PROVE God exists, the way one proves a theorem, would not strengthen faith but destroy it. For that strange claim to make any sense, what must faith essentially BE?
answer: A trust a person stakes precisely where certainty is impossible
choices: A trust a person stakes precisely where certainty is impossible
A warm private feeling that no public argument could ever hope to touch
A loyalty a person keeps to a community and its shared way of life
A hope a person leans on when the evidence is evenly balanced
context: Kierkegaard's line from the 'Postscript' (1846): 'If I am capable of grasping God objectively, I do not believe, but precisely because I cannot do this, I must believe.' If you could prove God like a theorem, there would be nothing left to have faith IN. Importantly, Kierkegaard is not a simple irrationalist: reason reaches a LIMIT - the incarnation is 'the Absolute Paradox' the understanding cannot think - and at that limit a person responds with faith or 'offense.' The leap is beyond reason, not against it. Sources: Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846); SEP, 'Soren Kierkegaard.'

question: William James answered W.K. Clifford directly. James agreed we should dread being fooled, but he argued that always refusing to believe until the evidence is in can ALSO rob a person of truths they might have had. Yet James did not throw the doors open to believing anything at all. He let a person's passions settle a question only when it met three strict conditions at once. Which three did James require?
answer: It must be a real live option, impossible to dodge, and genuinely momentous
choices: It must be a real live option, impossible to dodge, and genuinely momentous
It must be popular, long-established by tradition, and approved by respected authorities
It must be provable in principle, testable right now, and clearly useful in practice
It must be comforting to hold, harmless to other people, and pleasant to believe
context: From William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896). A 'genuine option' is LIVE (both sides are real possibilities to you), FORCED (not choosing is itself a choice), and MOMENTOUS (the stakes are serious and unique); on such questions 'our passional nature not only lawfully may, but must, decide.' James to Clifford: he is 'like a general informing his soldiers that it is better to keep out of battle forever than to risk a single wound.' This three-part test is the cleanest reasoning move on the fideist-friendly side of the fork, set against Clifford's absolute ban. Sources: William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896); SEP, 'Faith.'

question: A company executive shrugs off a 210-million-gallon ocean oil spill by saying it is 'no worse than when your neighbor drips half a liter of oil on the driveway -- both are just spilled oil.' What is wrong with the comparison?
answer: The amounts differ so enormously that calling the two spills the same erases the real harm
choices: The amounts really are equal, so the executive's comparison holds up fine
The amounts differ so enormously that calling the two spills the same erases the real harm
The driveway drip is the more serious spill, so he has the comparison backwards
Ocean oil and driveway oil are different substances, so they can't be compared
context: This is the textbook 'magnitude' case of false equivalence: both events are 'spilled oil,' but the Deepwater Horizon spill was roughly 210 million gallons against about half a liter -- orders of magnitude that calling them equivalent simply hides. The fix is to name the buried difference (scale), not to rank which spiller is the worse person. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_equivalence

question: Someone argues that a pet housecat and a pet jaguar are interchangeable, since both are cats -- members of the same animal family. What does this reasoning get wrong?
answer: The shared family is real but trivial beside all that makes one a safe pet and the other deadly
choices: The shared family is real but trivial beside all that makes one a safe pet and the other deadly
It is simply false that a housecat and a jaguar are in the same family
The jaguar is the better house pet of the two, so the claim is backwards
A housecat and a jaguar share nothing at all, so no comparison can be made
context: Housecat and jaguar do share the family Felidae -- the shared category is true, but trivial next to the difference it is being used to erase. False equivalence latches onto one real-but-minor shared trait and pretends it settles the whole comparison. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_equivalence

question: People call a bad comparison 'comparing apples and oranges.' A fair comparison and an unfair one differ in ONE crucial way. What is it?
answer: A fair comparison shares the trait that actually matters; an unfair one grabs a trait that doesn't
choices: A fair comparison shares the trait that actually matters; an unfair one grabs a trait that doesn't
A fair comparison stays inside one category; an unfair one compares across different categories
A fair comparison treats both sides as equal; an unfair one takes a side
A fair comparison is the one that most people accept as reasonable
context: False equivalence is the formal name for 'comparing apples and oranges' -- a fallacy of inconsistency. A valid analogy compares things alike in the RELEVANT respect; a false equivalence seizes an irrelevant shared trait ('both are fruit,' 'both are weapons') and acts as though that settles it. Note that 'just stay in one category' is the wrong rule: apples and oranges CAN be fairly compared on sweetness or price. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_equivalence

question: A news report describes a peaceful, lawful protest and a violent riot -- with arson and smashed windows -- using the very same phrase: 'crowds in the street.' A viewer objects that this is misleading. How should the report be fixed?
answer: Name what actually differs -- the conduct and the harm -- rather than lumping them as one crowd
choices: Name what actually differs -- the conduct and the harm -- rather than lumping them as one crowd
Decide which crowd had the more just cause and report that one as the real story
Call both events riots, since any large crowd can turn violent in the end
Drop the story, because crowds in the street are far too common to be news
context: Same surface category (a crowd), opposite substance (lawful assembly vs. arson and broken windows). The honest correction names what truly differs -- conduct and harm -- rather than pronouncing one cause righteous. Naming the buried difference is the fix; declaring a winner is not. Source: https://quillbot.com/blog/reasoning/false-equivalence-fallacy/

question: One person says the daytime sky is blue. Another insists it is yellow. A bystander, trying to be fair to both, concludes the sky must be green -- the color exactly halfway between. What went wrong?
answer: Splitting the difference between a right answer and a wrong one just invents a third wrong answer
choices: Splitting the difference between a right answer and a wrong one just invents a third wrong answer
The bystander should have picked whichever color more people in the group preferred
Green is close enough to blue that the bystander came out nearly correct anyway
Both speakers were mistaken, since the sky has no single true color to begin with
context: This is the purest illustration of the argument to moderation (Latin: argumentum ad temperantiam) -- the cousin of false equivalence. Meeting a true claim and a false one in the middle does not find truth; it manufactures a brand-new wrong answer. The error is assuming the truth ALWAYS sits between two stated positions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_to_moderation

question: You offer to sell your car for its honest value of $20,000. The buyer says it is worth $1, then smiles: 'Let's just split the difference and call it $10,000.' Why is this 'fair compromise' actually a trick?
answer: A wildly low first number drags the 'middle' down, so the compromise is just a disguised lowball
choices: A wildly low first number drags the 'middle' down, so the compromise is just a disguised lowball
The buyer's offer of one dollar was illegal and ought to be reported to someone
Splitting the difference is always the fairest possible way to settle on a price
The car's true value cannot be known until a neutral third party appraises it
context: Bo Bennett's haggling example shows how an absurd extreme weaponizes the argument to moderation: stake out a crazy position and the 'fair' midpoint slides toward you. His closer: 'There is no compromise when it comes to truth. Truth is truth.' The trap is not that compromise is always wrong -- it is assuming the middle is automatically right. Source: https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/Argument-to-Moderation

question: A debater argues that since the right to 'bear arms' protects weapons, a private citizen should be allowed to own a nuclear submarine -- after all, a rifle and a nuclear sub are both 'arms.' Where does the argument break down?
answer: Both are arms, but a rifle and a nuclear sub differ so vastly in scale that the shared word settles nothing
choices: Both are arms, but a rifle and a nuclear sub differ so vastly in scale that the shared word settles nothing
A nuclear submarine is not really a weapon, so it falls outside the meaning of 'arms'
Since both clearly count as arms, the debater's conclusion does in fact follow
The phrase 'bear arms' was never meant to cover ordinary firearms either
context: Bo Bennett stresses that false equivalence is a fallacy of DEGREE, not kind: a rifle and a nuclear sub are both 'arms,' but conflating their magnitude and regulation is the error -- 'the order of magnitude can be debated.' The reasoning move is what's recognized here; no verdict on gun policy is intended. Source: https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/False-Equivalence

question: Texas newspaperman Hubert Mewhinney mocked reporters who, when one politician says it is raining and another says it is dry, simply quote both and print the disagreement. What did Mewhinney say a reporter should do instead?
answer: Look out the window and find out which one is telling the truth
choices: Look out the window and find out which one is telling the truth
Quote a third politician to break the tie between the two
Print both claims and let the readers decide who is right
Refuse to cover the dispute until the two sides agree
context: Quote Investigator traces the famous 'look out the window' antidote to journalist Hubert Mewhinney in the late 1940s; his original named real Texas politicians -- 'If Jimmy Allred says it's raining, and W. Lee O'Daniel says it isn't raining, Texas newspapermen quote them both, and don't look out the window to see which is lying.' Equal airtime is not the journalist's job; finding the truth is. Source: https://quoteinvestigator.com/2023/11/14/rain-look/

question: A magazine prints a 'both sides' piece on the age of the Earth: one quote from a geologist who says it is billions of years old, and one from James Ussher, who in the 1600s calculated from the Bible that the world began in 4004 B.C. Why is the side-by-side misleading?
answer: It hides that the relevant experts agree, faking a 50/50 debate out of one weak source
choices: It hides that the relevant experts agree, faking a 50/50 debate out of one weak source
It should have left Ussher out, since his old date is too dated to even mention
It treated a question of faith as though it were a question of science
It quoted only two people when a fair debate truly needs many more voices
context: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy classifies false equivalence as a form of the Fallacy of Suppressed Evidence: it implies the two sides have roughly equal evidence while covering up that one side's is far weaker. The lie is not in what is printed -- it is in what is hidden (here, that the relevant experts have reached consensus). Source: https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/

question: An orator declares that a head of state who orders a military strike killing civilians is 'no different from any other mass murderer' -- both, after all, caused deaths. Setting aside which case is graver, what does this flattening bury?
answer: The differences in circumstance, responsibility, and intent that the bare word 'deaths' hides
choices: The differences in circumstance, responsibility, and intent that the bare word 'deaths' hides
Nothing of importance, since dead is dead however it came to happen
The fact that even drawing the comparison is offensive and ought to be forbidden
The reality that a head of state can never be blamed for any wartime deaths
context: This is the moral_vision's named failure mode. Bo Bennett's example equates a head of state ordering a strike with an ordinary mass murderer because both 'caused deaths' -- burying the differences in circumstance, level of responsibility, and intent. The honest move names the buried distinction; it does NOT rank which case is worse, and a careful person could weigh the two either way. Source: https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/False-Equivalence

question: After years of pairing climate scientists with skeptics for the sake of 'balance,' the BBC admitted in internal guidance that it had gotten the coverage wrong too often. What was the network's own conclusion about how to fix it?
answer: You do not need a denier on air to balance the debate
choices: You do not need a denier on air to balance the debate
Every controversial science story needs voices from both sides
Climate coverage should be dropped until the science is fully settled
Skeptics deserve more airtime, not less, to keep the network fair
context: 'False balance' is false equivalence's media-specific form, and the BBC became its famous confessor -- acknowledging climate change 'has been a difficult subject for the BBC, and we get coverage of it wrong too often.' The recognition skill is that equal airtime is not the same as equal evidence; the claim is reported as the network's own admission, not as a verdict on the underlying science. Source: https://www.snopes.com/news/2018/09/12/facing-criticism-past-climate-reporting-bbc-commits-reigning-false-balance/

question: In January 1941, almost a year before Pearl Harbor, President Franklin Roosevelt told Congress that the world should rest on four human freedoms. Two were the familiar liberties of speech and worship. But the other two pointed somewhere new: freedom from fear of war, and one more that would later grow into his whole case for guaranteeing every family a job, a home, and food. What was that fourth freedom?
answer: Freedom from want
choices: Freedom from want
Freedom from taxes
Freedom of assembly
Freedom of the press
context: In his January 1941 'Four Freedoms' address Roosevelt named speech, worship, freedom from fear, and freedom from want. The last two were economic in spirit, and 'freedom from want' became the seed he would grow, three years later, into his 1944 list of economic rights, the Second Bill of Rights. Source: FDR Presidential Library, 'FDR and the Four Freedoms Speech' (fdrlibrary.org/four-freedoms); National WWII Museum, 'The Four Freedoms'.

question: Just back from wartime conferences in Cairo and Tehran and laid up with the flu, Franklin Roosevelt did not stand before Congress to deliver his 1944 message announcing a Second Bill of Rights. He sent the text over to be read aloud and spoke to the country by radio instead. No film of the full address survives. So how do the most famous lines of the speech still exist on camera today?
answer: He re-recorded the key excerpts for the newsreel cameras afterward
choices: He re-recorded the key excerpts for the newsreel cameras afterward
A stenographer reconstructed the speech from memory for the press
Congress voted to have an actor perform the address on film
His wife Eleanor read the whole speech aloud for the radio networks
context: Sick and freshly returned from the Cairo and Tehran conferences, Roosevelt sent his 1944 State of the Union message to Congress in writing and read it to the nation as Fireside Chat 28. Afterward he read only excerpts, including the Second Bill of Rights, for the newsreel cameras. No complete film of the full speech is known to exist; its most famous lines survive only because he re-recorded them. Source: FDR Presidential Library, 1944 State of the Union (fdrlibrary.org/sotu); Miller Center, 'January 11, 1944: Fireside Chat 28'.

question: Franklin Roosevelt rested his case for economic rights on one line: 'Necessitous men are not free men.' He meant that a person can have every political liberty on paper, the vote, free speech, an open courthouse, and still not be free in any way that counts. Steel-manned at its strongest, what makes such a person unfree in Roosevelt's argument?
answer: Crushing need will force him to accept almost any terms, so his choices are not really his own
choices: Crushing need will force him to accept almost any terms, so his choices are not really his own
A written constitution never actually grants the ordinary citizen any real rights at all
Only a person who owns land or a business can ever be counted as politically free
Voting and free speech are worthless unless a court is willing to enforce them by force
context: This is Roosevelt's case at its strongest: a starving, jobless man's 'freedom' is hollow, because desperation will make him submit to whatever terms are offered. On January 11, 1944, he put it as 'We have come to a clear realization of the fact that true individual freedom cannot exist without economic security and independence.' Critics answer it (see the later rungs), but the bank presents the argument fairly first. Source: FDR Presidential Library, 1944 State of the Union Address text (fdrlibrary.org/address-text).

question: Franklin Roosevelt did not invent the phrase 'necessitous men are not free men.' He lifted it, word for word, from a ruling handed down by an English judge in 1762, repurposing a single line of old courtroom reasoning into the banner for a national argument about rights 182 years later. What kind of case had the judge been deciding when he first wrote those words?
answer: A property loan where a desperate man had pledged his land on harsh terms
choices: A property loan where a desperate man had pledged his land on harsh terms
A treason trial where a rebel had taken up arms against his own king
A theft case where a starving man had stolen bread to feed his family
A marriage suit where a young woman had been wed against her own will
context: The line comes from Lord Henley (Robert Henley, 1st Earl of Northington) in the 1762 mortgage case Vernon v Bethell: 'necessitous men are not, truly speaking, free men, but, to answer a present exigency, will submit to any terms that the crafty may impose upon them.' Henley was protecting a desperate borrower from signing away his property; Roosevelt repurposed a 182-year-old property-law line into a national rights argument. Source: Wikipedia, Vernon v Bethell (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_v_Bethell).

question: Franklin Roosevelt's Second Bill of Rights promised every family a right to medical care. A right to free speech asks others only to leave you alone and hold their tongue. A right to a doctor's care is different in kind, and critics ask exactly who or what it puts under obligation. When a sick man holds a right to a doctor's care, who or what is that right ultimately a claim upon?
answer: A doctor whose labor must be supplied on demand to answer the sick man's claim
choices: A doctor whose labor must be supplied on demand to answer the sick man's claim
A taxpayer whose earnings must be taken to cover the cost of the sick man's care
A court that stands ready to enforce the right against anyone by force
Everyone alike, who owes only a duty not to interfere with the sick man
context: This is the fork at the heart of the topic. A negative right (free speech, property) imposes on everyone else only a duty not to interfere; it costs others nothing but restraint. A positive right (food, housing, a job, medical care) imposes a duty to actively provide. A right to a doctor's care is ultimately a claim on the doctor, whose labor must answer it, and on the taxpayer who funds it; a court or a funded program may be involved, but the claim lands on someone's actual labor. The bank teaches the recognition, not a verdict. Source: Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, Santa Clara University, 'Rights' (scu.edu/ethics/ethics-resources/ethical-decision-making/rights/).

question: To test Roosevelt's dream of a guaranteed, fair spread of wealth, the philosopher Robert Nozick imagined a basketball star, Wilt Chamberlain. Start from any distribution you consider perfectly fair. Then a million fans each happily pay 25 cents to watch him play. He ends up with $250,000 and the spread is now wildly unequal, yet not one of those payments was forced. Nozick's lesson from this is blunt. What did he conclude?
answer: Keeping any fixed pattern of wealth means constantly forbidding people from freely spending their own money
choices: Keeping any fixed pattern of wealth means constantly forbidding people from freely spending their own money
A truly fair society must cap how much any single entertainer is ever allowed to earn
Voluntary trade always leaves everyone exactly as well off as they began, so wealth gaps are an illusion
Once money has changed hands enough times its original fairness can no longer be measured at all
context: From Robert Nozick, 'Anarchy, State, and Utopia' (1974). His slogan is 'liberty upsets patterns': because free choices keep reshuffling who has what, the only way to hold a guaranteed pattern of economic outcomes is to keep interfering with people spending their own money. You can have liberty or a patterned distribution, but not both. This is the bank's sharpest counter to FDR's economic-rights case; no verdict is declared. Source: Britannica, 'Wilt Chamberlain argument' (britannica.com/topic/Wilt-Chamberlain-argument); Libertarianism.org, Nozick's entitlement theory.

question: Ludwig Feuerbach spent his life on one question: when a person worships a perfect, all-loving God, what is really going on? Thinkers before him and after him gave very different answers. Which of these was Feuerbach's own answer?
answer: The believer has taken humanity's own best powers and pictured them, magnified, as a being apart.
choices: The believer has taken humanity's own best powers and pictured them, magnified, as a being apart.
The believer is in contact with a real being who exists completely apart from anything human.
The believer is honoring his society's authority, which has wrapped its rules in sacred language.
The believer is soothing his fear of death and the unknown with a comforting story.
context: This is Feuerbach's central move, which he compressed into three words: 'theology is anthropology.' When you think you are studying God, he says, you are really studying an idealized portrait of MAN. He even named the human powers involved -- 'Reason, Will, Affection': God's all-knowing is our reason, God's omnipotence our will, God's love our heart, each cranked up to infinity. The bank takes no side here on whether God exists -- this is presented as one serious position among the rivals shown (a real God; the authority of society; the fear of death), not as the verdict. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ludwig Andreas Feuerbach'; Feuerbach, The Essence of Christianity (1841), Introduction, trans. George Eliot.

question: Feuerbach offered a strange tool for sizing up ANY person: don't ask about their job or their town -- ask what sort of God they worship, and you will know the person. Look hard at someone's God, Feuerbach claimed, and you are looking straight at what?
answer: The qualities that person most admires and secretly longs to possess himself.
choices: The qualities that person most admires and secretly longs to possess himself.
The fears and dangers that person spends his whole life trying to escape.
The customs of the family and village the person simply happened to be born into.
The favors that person is hoping to win -- protection, health, good fortune.
context: Feuerbach's reading-test: 'By his God thou knowest the man, and by the man his God; the two are identical.' He continued, 'Such as are a man's thoughts and dispositions, such is his God... Consciousness of God is self-consciousness.' In plain terms: tell me your God and I will tell you exactly what you secretly admire in yourself. It is a method, not a sneer -- and it cuts both ways for any believer or unbeliever. Source: Feuerbach, The Essence of Christianity, Introduction (George Eliot trans.), Project Gutenberg #47025.

question: Ludwig Feuerbach asked a sharp question about worship: when a person praises God as having ALL wisdom, ALL power, and ALL love, what does that praise do to the person himself? Thinkers have answered in opposite directions. What did Feuerbach say happens to the worshipper himself?
answer: It empties him -- each perfection he credits to God is one he must deny is his own.
choices: It empties him -- each perfection he credits to God is one he must deny is his own.
It completes him -- by naming the highest good, he draws a share of it into himself.
It steadies him -- handing his fears to a greater power, he can finally rest.
It does nothing to him -- the worshipper and his God are simply two separate things.
context: Feuerbach gave the projection a mechanism -- a kind of zero-sum trade. He wrote: 'To enrich God, man must become poor; that God may be all, man must be nothing.' What a man withdraws from himself, he said, he then 'enjoys in an incomparably higher and richer measure in God.' Every perfection handed up to heaven is one he denies is his own. The other answers shown are real rival pictures of worship, not strawmen; the bank declares no winner. Source: Feuerbach, The Essence of Christianity, Chapter I, §2 (Eliot trans.), confirmed at marxists.org.

question: In Feuerbach's theory, God is pictured as all-wise and all-loving at once. Where, he argued, does so complete a portrait actually come from?
answer: It pools the whole species' scattered strengths into one being, each person's limits stripped away.
choices: It pools the whole species' scattered strengths into one being, each person's limits stripped away.
It copies the single greatest human who ever lived, then rounds him up to flawless.
It enlarges the worshipper's own private virtues until they fill the whole sky.
It is stitched together from random wishes, answering to nothing real in any person.
context: A crucial nuance: for Feuerbach the God-portrait is humanity's SPECIES essence, not any one person. No single human is all-loving and all-wise -- but the species' perfections, gathered up and freed from each individual's limits, get fused into a single imagined being. God, on this view, is mankind's group highlight reel attributed to one Person. Feuerbach thought only humans do this, because only a creature that can picture 'humanity-as-such, perfected' can carve that picture off and call it God. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ludwig Andreas Feuerbach.'

question: Believers had long praised God as infinitely compassionate. Ludwig Feuerbach turned that very praise into evidence for his theory. Compassion, he argued, means suffering ALONGSIDE another -- it can only belong to a being who can itself be hurt. Yet a perfect, unchanging God is said to be beyond all suffering. What did Feuerbach conclude from this about God's 'compassion'?
answer: It is a human trait, lent to God -- only a being able to suffer can pity at all.
choices: It is a human trait, lent to God -- only a being able to suffer can pity at all.
It is proof the unfeeling-God idea is wrong -- true compassion means a God who can suffer.
It is real but of a higher kind, a divine mercy that needs no suffering to be genuine.
It is a mercy too perfect for humans to invent, which is why it points to a real God.
context: This is Feuerbach's 'grammatical' attack: traditional theology makes God the subject and man the predicate, but Feuerbach flips it -- the predicates believers apply to God (compassion, mercy, love) properly belong to the human species. Since 'God as God' cannot suffer, divine compassion has to be a borrowed human trait. Note that choice C is the real reply of classical theism (God's mercy works by analogy, needing no literal suffering) -- a competent thinker can hold it; the question only asks what Feuerbach himself concluded, and the bank takes no verdict. Where this went next: the young Marx and Engels were swept up -- Engels recalled 'we all became Feuerbachians' -- and Marx built his line 'religion... is the opium of the people' on top of Feuerbach's original move that the divine is a human creation. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ludwig Andreas Feuerbach'; Engels, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy (1886).

question: In an old Chinese legend, a boy named Wang Xiang has a stepmother who dislikes him, yet in the dead of winter she craves fresh fish. The river is frozen solid. What does Wang Xiang do to get her the fish?
answer: He lies down on the ice to melt it with his own body, and two carp leap out to him
choices: He lies down on the ice to melt it with his own body, and two carp leap out to him
He trades his warm winter coat to a fisherman who has kept a catch alive in a tank
He prays beside the river all through the night until the ice cracks open on its own
He chops a hole in the ice with an axe and waits in the cold until a fish swims past
context: From The Twenty-four Filial Exemplars (Guo Jujing, Yuan dynasty), a famous collection of filial-piety legends. Wang Xiang honors even the stepmother who mistreats him -- the point is that the duty to a parent does not depend on the parent deserving it. (Legendary.)

question: In a Chinese legend, Lao Laizi is already about seventy years old himself, but his parents are extremely old and grow sad to see their own child aging. To comfort them, Lao Laizi does something deliberately silly. What is it?
answer: He dresses in bright children's clothes and tumbles about with toys, like a baby
choices: He dresses in bright children's clothes and tumbles about with toys, like a baby
He paints his grey hair jet black each morning so they forget how old he has grown
He hides all the calendars in the house so his parents lose track of the passing years
He carries his parents around the garden on his back, pretending to be their pony
context: From The Twenty-four Filial Exemplars (Guo Jujing, Yuan dynasty). Lao Laizi honors his parents by guarding their happiness, not just meeting their needs -- filial piety includes keeping a parent's heart light. (Legendary.)

question: A student named Ziyou thought filial piety just meant making sure your parents are fed. Confucius pushed back: even dogs and horses get fed and looked after. So, Confucius asked, what must a person bring to caring for parents that turns it from mere upkeep into true honoring?
answer: Reverence, a deep and genuine respect held in the heart
choices: Reverence, a deep and genuine respect held in the heart
Obedience, a readiness to do whatever they command
Hard work, the toil of earning their food yourself
Nearness, the choice to live close and never leave them
context: Analects 2.7 (Legge translation). Confucius's test for real filial piety is the inner attitude, not the chore: 'without reverence, what is there to distinguish the one support given from the other?' Mere feeding, he says, is something even animals receive.

question: In Chinese legend, Emperor Shun is the supreme model of honoring a parent: though his blind father Gusou and his stepmother tried again and again to kill him, Shun never stopped loving and serving them. The tradition says his devotion was so great it moved Heaven itself. According to the legend, how did Heaven show this?
answer: Wild elephants came to plow his fields, and birds came to pull the weeds
choices: Wild elephants came to plow his fields, and birds came to pull the weeds
A great river parted so that he could cross to safety on dry ground
His father's sight was restored the moment Shun forgave him
The sun stood still in the sky to let him finish the harvest
context: From The Twenty-four Filial Exemplars (Guo Jujing, Yuan dynasty). Shun is the tradition's hardest case for filial piety -- he honored parents who plotted his death -- and the legendary reward dramatizes how far that virtue was prized. (Legendary.)

question: Confucius told his student Zengzi that all of a person's good character grows from a single root -- the one seed every other virtue springs from. According to Confucius, where does that root first take hold?
answer: In learning to honor your own parents at home
choices: In learning to honor your own parents at home
In obeying the laws laid down by a just ruler
In studying the wise sayings of the ancient sages
In keeping your word to your friends and neighbors
context: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiaojing), ch. 1 (Legge translation): filial piety is 'the root of all virtue, and the stem out of which grows all moral teaching.' For Confucians, every other good quality grows from the respect a child first learns toward parents -- virtue starts at home, not in the law-court, the library, or the marketplace.

question: A disciple named Zai Wo complained to Confucius that mourning dead parents for a full three years was far too long, and that a single year should be plenty. Confucius defended the three years with one reason. What reason did he give?
answer: A child is not off its parents' arms until it is three years old
choices: A child is not off its parents' arms until it is three years old
Three years is simply how long honest grief is bound to last
Three years is the time a family needs to settle its affairs
The wise kings of old had fixed three years as the proper rule
context: Analects 17.21 (Legge translation). Confucius answers Zai Wo by matching the debt to the gift: you mourn parents for three years because for your own first three years they carried you. He thought a son who begrudged that had not understood the bond.

question: The Duke of She boasted to Confucius that in his land an upright young man named Gong proved his honesty by testifying in court against his own father, who had stolen a sheep. Confucius did not praise it. He said that in his own country uprightness was found in something different. What did Confucius say it was found in?
answer: A father shielding his son's wrongdoing, and a son shielding his father's
choices: A father shielding his son's wrongdoing, and a son shielding his father's
A son reporting the theft but then quietly repaying the stolen sheep
A judge weighing the family bond against the harm before he rules
A father turning himself in so his son is never forced to choose
context: Analects 13.18 (Legge translation). For Confucius, the loyalty between parent and child is not the enemy of uprightness but part of it: 'The father conceals the misconduct of the son, and the son conceals the misconduct of the father. Uprightness is to be found in this.' A real and still-debated stance on whether family loyalty can outweigh a public duty.

question: In Greek myth the giant Argus Panoptes was covered head to toe in a hundred eyes, so he could keep watch in every direction at once and never be caught fully asleep. In 1787 Jeremy Bentham borrowed the Greek word for 'all-seeing' to name a prison he had designed. What did Bentham call it?
answer: The panopticon
choices: The panopticon
The labyrinth
The colossus
The oubliette
context: 'Panopticon' is Greek for 'all-seeing,' pointing back to Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant. Jeremy Bentham coined the term in 1787 for his prison design. Source: Wikipedia, 'Panopticon'; Wiktionary, 'panopticon'.

question: Jeremy Bentham's prison was shaped like a ring of cells, with one feature standing in the middle of the empty courtyard. From that single central spot, one inspector could face inward and look straight into every cell around the ring at the same time. What stood at the centre of Bentham's prison?
answer: A tower
choices: A tower
A chapel
A fountain
A gallows
context: Foucault described the design: 'At the periphery, an annular building; at the centre, a tower; this tower is pierced with wide windows that open onto the inner side of the ring.' Each outer cell window backlit the prisoner into a perfect silhouette. Source: Foucault, 'Panopticism,' Discipline and Punish.

question: In Jeremy Bentham's ring-shaped prison, the central tower was built so the prisoners could never see whether a guard was inside it looking out. A prisoner therefore could never tell, at any given moment, whether eyes were on him right then. Since being caught misbehaving was too great a risk to take, how did each prisoner end up behaving?
answer: As if watched every moment, policing himself
choices: As if watched every moment, policing himself
Carefully only while a guard was calling orders
Recklessly, since the tower stayed dark and silent
By signalling to inmates in the cells beside him
context: This is the heart of the design. A prisoner knows only that he COULD be watched, never that he is. Unable to risk it, he behaves as though watched constantly. Foucault: 'He becomes the principle of his own subjection.' The prisoner polices himself. Source: Foucault, Discipline and Punish; SEP, 'Michel Foucault'.

question: In Jeremy Bentham's ring-shaped prison the tower often stood dark and silent, yet each prisoner still behaved as if eyes were on him every moment, never daring to risk that they weren't. Bentham boiled down the whole trick into two words for how the tower's power should work on a man. Which pair did he name?
answer: Visible and unverifiable
choices: Visible and unverifiable
Silent and merciless
Sacred and untouchable
Distant and indifferent
context: Bentham's recipe: power must be 'visible and unverifiable.' The inmate always has the tower before his eyes, yet can never confirm anyone is in it. Foucault: 'A real subjection is born mechanically from a fictitious relation' — no one even has to be in the tower. Source: Foucault, Discipline and Punish.

question: Jeremy Bentham did not dream up the ring-and-tower idea alone. His younger brother Samuel Bentham hit on the core trick while in Russia, working for Prince Potemkin and looking for a way one overseer could keep an eye on many untrained labourers at once. What kind of place was Samuel running when he first used this single-watcher idea?
answer: A workshop
choices: A workshop
A monastery
A warship
A racetrack
context: Samuel Bentham devised the 'central inspection principle' running a workshop in Russia for Prince Potemkin, so one overseer could watch many unskilled workers. Jeremy turned it into a prison blueprint and pitched it for prisons, workhouses, asylums, factories AND schools. Source: UCL Bentham Project, 'The Panopticon'.

question: Bentham's all-seeing prison was actually built once, at full scale — the Presidio Modelo in Cuba, five ring-shaped cellblocks around central watchtowers, finished around 1930. After leading the failed 1953 assault on the Moncada Barracks, a young revolutionary was locked inside it until 1955, and wrote from his cell, 'What a fantastic school this prison is!' Which prisoner wrote that?
answer: Fidel Castro
choices: Fidel Castro
Che Guevara
Augusto Pinochet
Leon Trotsky
context: Fidel Castro and his brother Raul were held in the Presidio Modelo after the 1953 Moncada attack, until 1955. Castro wrote from his cell, 'What a fantastic school this prison is!' — they ran the hospital wing as a revolutionary boot camp. Source: Wikipedia, 'Presidio Modelo'; Abandoned Spaces.

question: Jeremy Bentham sold his prison like a miracle cure, promising in one breathless line that it would reform morals, preserve health, invigorate industry and lighten the public's tax burden, 'all by a simple idea in Architecture!' For all the salesmanship, across 25 years of chasing it, what became of Bentham's prison in Britain?
answer: It was never built to his specs
choices: It was never built to his specs
It housed thousands within a decade
It spread to every county in England
It was copied across the whole Empire
context: Bentham chased his prison for 25 years and never got it built. He bought the Millbank site on the Thames for the Crown in 1799; the plan was abandoned in 1812, and Parliament paid him about 23,000 pounds in compensation in 1813. The Tate Britain art gallery now sits on the land he'd bought for his all-seeing prison. Source: UCL Bentham Project; Wikipedia, 'Millbank Prison'.

question: Foucault said the all-seeing tower was never really meant to catch every wrongdoer in the act — guards are always too few for that, and he argued that catching crooks was beside the point anyway. So what did Foucault say the prison tower was ultimately built to achieve?
answer: A discipline that runs itself, so actual watching becomes unnecessary
choices: A discipline that runs itself, so actual watching becomes unnecessary
Lower running costs, so a few guards could mind a crowd cheaply
Harsher penalties, so the fear of pain keeps every inmate in line
Bonds of trust among the inmates that quietly keep good order
context: Foucault: the design aims 'to induce in the inmate a state of conscious and permanent visibility that assures the automatic functioning of power.' The surveillance is 'permanent in its effects, even if it is discontinuous in its action,' and 'the perfection of power should tend to render its actual exercise unnecessary.' A machine that runs itself. Source: Foucault, Discipline and Punish.

question: Michel Foucault opens Discipline and Punish with a deliberate jolt. First he describes the 1757 public execution of Robert-Francois Damiens, who had scratched King Louis XV with a penknife: torn with red-hot pincers, his hand burned, his body pulled apart by four horses before a roaring crowd. Then, on the very next pages, he sets against that gruesome scene a much quieter document from 1838. What was that second document?
answer: A prison timetable scheduling every minute of an inmate's day
choices: A prison timetable scheduling every minute of an inmate's day
A royal pardon sparing a condemned man at the foot of the scaffold
A public notice announcing the end of all executions across France
A prisoner's smuggled letter begging the court to hear his innocence
context: Foucault's opening shock contrast: the 1757 torture-execution of Damiens set against a dull 1838 prison timetable that scheduled every minute of an inmate's day. Two opposite ways power works — spectacle versus schedule. Source: SEP, 'Michel Foucault'; Wikipedia, 'Discipline and Punish'; ExecutedToday.com.

question: Michel Foucault contrasts two ways power has worked. The OLD kind he calls sovereign: it punished rarely but spectacularly, carving the ruler's right to kill onto the criminal's body in public, before a crowd. The NEW kind he calls disciplinary, and says it does its real work very differently. How, according to Foucault, does disciplinary power operate?
answer: Quietly and constantly, training bodies into self-correction
choices: Quietly and constantly, training bodies into self-correction
Through rare but crushing fines that fall on a whole village
By abolishing punishment and simply trusting to people's goodwill
By handing each citizen the power to judge and punish his neighbour
context: Foucault's contrast: sovereign power punishes by spectacle, marking its right to kill on the body in public. Disciplinary power is quiet and constant, aimed at making 'docile bodies' — soldiers, workers, schoolchildren trained, scheduled, and watched into self-correction. Source: SEP, 'Michel Foucault'; Foucault, Discipline and Punish (1975).

question: A schoolboy's work is no longer just marked right or wrong; it is set beside the class average, and he is ranked somewhere from top of the form down to the dunce's corner. Foucault argues modern power leans on exactly this kind of ranking against a standard. What does ranking each pupil against the average actually do to him?
answer: It sorts people into normal and abnormal and files each one as a case
choices: It sorts people into normal and abnormal and files each one as a case
It forbids only certain acts and pays no mind to the person himself
It punishes the worst pupil in public so the rest take the warning
It leaves each pupil free to be the only judge of his own work
context: Foucault's payoff: modern power doesn't mainly FORBID, it NORMALIZES. Old law sorted acts into permitted vs. forbidden; disciplinary power ranks you against a norm and sorts people into normal vs. abnormal through three tools — hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment, and the examination. The exam fuses watching with grading ('power/knowledge') and turns a person into a documented 'case.' The move is called 'normalizing judgment.' Source: SEP, 'Michel Foucault'.

question: Foucault insists the all-seeing tower is not just a fact about old prisons and the convicts inside them. He writes that we are 'neither in the amphitheatre, nor on the stage, but in the panoptic machine,' its power reaching every one of us. What is Foucault claiming about ordinary people today?
answer: We carry the watching tower with us and police ourselves
choices: We carry the watching tower with us and police ourselves
We have finally broken free of all surveillance for good
We are watched constantly, yet it changes nothing in us
We now watch the powerful far more than they ever watch us
context: Foucault's chilling claim: we're ALL inside the machine now, not just convicts. The grade, the camera, the score — we carry the tower with us and bring its effects on ourselves. Scholars routinely read CCTV, social media, and China's Social Credit System through this lens: people self-regulate to match the norm because they might be watched and scored at any time. Source: Foucault, Discipline and Punish; ResearchGate, 'Algorithmic Panopticon' (2021).

question: Mara and Theo argue about how knowledge holds up. Mara says: "Picture a tall building. The top floors are held up by the floors below them, and those by the floors below THOSE -- but it can't be floors all the way down. At the very bottom you hit solid bedrock: there is simply nothing deeper to dig down to." In Mara's picture, what plays the role of that bedrock?
answer: A few starting beliefs that need no other belief to support them
choices: A few starting beliefs that need no other belief to support them
A few beliefs that everyone in the world happens to agree on
A few beliefs that are proved true by a longer belief above them
A few beliefs that are held up by how well they fit the others
context: Mara is describing the foundationalist picture: ordinary beliefs are upper floors supported by lower ones, but the structure ultimately rests on 'basic' beliefs that sit on bedrock and need no further belief to hold them up. Pull the foundation and the building falls -- but the foundation rests on the ground, not on another floor. It is the answer to 'where does justification finally STOP?' -- at the bedrock. Source: IEP, 'Foundationalism in Epistemology' (iep.utm.edu/foundationalism-in-epistemology) + SEP, 'Foundationalist Theories of Epistemic Justification'.

question: Theo rejects the idea that knowledge has any bottom layer at all. "Forget bedrock and forget any special bottom belief," he says. "Knowledge is more like a spider's web. No single strand is the anchor, and you could cut the whole web loose from every wall so that nothing underneath holds it up -- and yet it would not fall." On Theo's view, what makes any one belief justified?
answer: That it holds together with all the other beliefs at once
choices: That it holds together with all the other beliefs at once
That it rests at last on one unshakeable starting belief
That it can be proved true by direct observation alone
That a long chain of reasons runs on and on behind it
context: Theo is describing the coherentist picture, the opposite of the building: a web or raft that holds itself up. No plank is the special bottom plank; every belief is held in place by how well it fits with all the others, the way a web's strength comes from every strand pulling on its neighbors. Knowledge floats by hanging together, not by resting on something underneath. Source: SEP, 'Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/justep-coherence).

question: Otto Neurath gave the most famous image for a system of knowledge with no foundation underneath it. He wrote that we are like sailors out on the open sea whose wooden ship has begun to leak and rot as they sail. What is the predicament he says these sailors are stuck in?
answer: They must swap out rotten planks one at a time while afloat, never hauling the ship ashore to start clean
choices: They must swap out rotten planks one at a time while afloat, never hauling the ship ashore to start clean
They must steer the ship back to its home harbor while afloat, before any rotten plank can be replaced
They must leap from the leaking ship at once and swim for the nearest patch of dry, solid ground
They must keep the ship still in calm water and wait until a rescuer brings them fresh timber to use
context: Neurath's actual line: 'We are like sailors who on the open sea must reconstruct their ship but are never able to start afresh from the bottom.' You can replace any rotten plank one at a time while staying afloat, but you can NEVER haul the ship into dry dock, strip it bare, and rebuild from a clean foundation -- there is no dry dock, no ground to stand on outside the ship. That is coherentism: revise your beliefs piecemeal from inside the web; you never step outside and start from certified bedrock. (First used 1913; famous version in 'Anti-Spengler,' 1921; popularized by W.V.O. Quine in 'Word and Object,' 1960.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurath's_boat + SEP, 'Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification'.

question: Rene Descartes opens his Meditations vowing to demolish everything he believes and rebuild from the ground up. Recalling that Archimedes claimed he could move the whole Earth if given one fixed point to stand on, Descartes hunts for one belief so certain that not even an all-powerful deceiver fooling him about everything else could shake it. What does he land on as that one unshakeable point?
answer: That he himself exists, since he cannot be fooled about it without existing to be fooled
choices: That he himself exists, since he cannot be fooled about it without existing to be fooled
That the outside world exists, since his own senses report it to him so vividly
That a perfect God exists, since the idea of perfection had to come from somewhere
That mathematics holds true, since two and three still make five in any world
context: Descartes needs, like Archimedes, 'just one thing, however small, that is certain and unshakeable' to lever up all of knowledge. He finds it in the cogito: 'I am, I exist' is true every time he thinks it, because a deceiver can only deceive something that exists. ONE unshakeable point, and you can rebuild the world on it -- the foundationalist's dream stated at its most vivid. Source: SEP, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/descartes-epistemology) + Descartes, 'Meditations on First Philosophy' (1641), First & Second Meditation.

question: Suppose you keep asking 'and why do you believe THAT?' about every reason a person gives. A skeptic notes the answering can only go three uncomfortable ways: it runs on forever, it loops back on itself ('it's true because it's true'), or it halts at some claim the person simply refuses to back up further. Mara holds that the questioning need not run on without end -- some beliefs are simply the right place for it to come to rest. Which of the three must Mara live with?
answer: The answering halts at a few claims she owes no further reason for
choices: The answering halts at a few claims she owes no further reason for
The answering loops back so her claims end up supporting each other
The answering runs on forever, and she insists that endless chain is fine
The answering halts, but only at claims everyone in the world agrees on
context: This is Agrippa's (Munchhausen) trilemma: three exits, all uncomfortable -- infinite regress, circularity, or stopping at an unproven starting point (the dogmatic horn). The bedrock/foundationalist view bites the dogmatic horn: it stops at basic beliefs that owe nothing to any belief behind them -- and 'basic' means needing no further belief, NOT 'agreed on by everyone' (a common misreading). The web/coherentist view bites the circular horn (it embraces the loop, calling it mutual support); infinitism bites the regress horn, insisting the endless chain is fine. The kid's job is to match each view to the horn it accepts, not to crown a winner. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munchhausen_trilemma + SEP, 'Foundationalist Theories of Epistemic Justification'.

question: A critic presses the web view, the one holding that a belief is justified purely by how well it fits with all the others. "Take a well-built fairy tale," she says, "or a careful paranoid delusion. Every part can fit every other part perfectly." What is the damaging point she is driving at against judging beliefs by fit alone?
answer: A system can hang together flawlessly and still be cut off completely from reality
choices: A system can hang together flawlessly and still be cut off completely from reality
A system that hangs together is far too dull for anyone to actually believe it
A system can never really be made to hang together once it grows large enough
A system that hangs together must have hidden a secret foundation inside it all along
context: This is the isolation / alternative-systems objection: a perfectly coherent system can be totally severed from the world. A fairy tale or a delusion can be internally seamless yet false; worse, for ANY coherent web you can build a rival web that is equally coherent but says the opposite -- and if mere fit were enough, BOTH would count as justified. So coherence alone doesn't seem to connect belief to reality. (Laurence BonJour, 1985, tried to answer by giving perception-driven 'cognitively spontaneous beliefs' some weight from outside the web.) Source: SEP, 'Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification' + IEP, 'Coherentism in Epistemology'.

question: Mark is gripped by a craving for a bag of chips. At the same moment, a quieter part of him is unhappy that he craves them at all — he'd rather be the sort of person whose mouth waters for celery. A philosopher tells Mark these two pulls sit on different LEVELS. How do they differ?
answer: The first is a desire to eat; the second is a desire about a desire — it targets the craving itself
choices: The first is a desire to eat; the second is a desire about a desire — it targets the craving itself
The first is a desire to eat; the second is a belief that celery is the more sensible choice
The first is a desire to eat; the second is a memory of meals that shaped what he craves
The first is a desire to eat; the second is a sharper pang of the same hunger for chips
context: Frankfurt's hierarchy: a FIRST-ORDER desire is a desire to do something (eat the chips); a SECOND-ORDER desire is a desire ABOUT a desire (wishing you wanted celery). Wanting a particular desire to actually be your WILL — the one that moves you to act — is a second-order volition, and having the will you want is what Frankfurt calls freedom of the will. Source: Frankfurt, 'Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person' (1971); definitions confirmed in J. Speaks (nd.edu) and Holton MIT lecture notes.

question: Frankfurt imagines two addicts with the identical, unbreakable craving — neither could resist if he tried. The first HATES his addiction and wishes the craving gone, yet it drags him to the drug anyway. The second is altogether delighted with his condition: even if a cure were offered, he'd choose to keep wanting the drug just as he does. Both take it; Frankfurt says only the second takes it of his own free will. What makes the second one free?
answer: He endorses the very desire that moves him — the craving is the will he wants to have
choices: He endorses the very desire that moves him — the craving is the will he wants to have
He feels no inner conflict about the drug — his mind is calm and at peace with itself
He gets real pleasure from the drug — and doing what brings you pleasure is being free
He chose long ago to become an addict — his earlier free choice still makes this free
context: Frankfurt's central move: freedom is endorsement, not an open exit. The willing addict 'takes the drug freely and of his own free will' even though, being an addict, he could not have done otherwise — his craving is the will he WANTS. The unwilling addict's will is 'not the will he wants,' so the same outward act is not free. What separates them is not peace of mind, pleasure, or any past choice, but which desire each one endorses from above right now. Source: Frankfurt 1971; phrasing confirmed in researchgate.net 'Frankfurt's Unwilling and Willing Addicts' and plato.stanford.edu Compatibilism.

question: Frankfurt describes a strange creature: it can want the drug and want to be rid of it at the very same time, and it simply has no preference about which of those pulls wins — it doesn't care which desire ends up steering it. A beast or a small child, he says, is like this. When we ask whether such a creature acts of its own free will, Frankfurt gives a surprising verdict. Which is it?
answer: Neither free nor unfree — it never asks which desire should be its will, so the question gets no grip
choices: Neither free nor unfree — it never asks which desire should be its will, so the question gets no grip
Always free, since whichever of its desires wins, the creature ends up content either way
Never free, because a creature pulled two ways at once can never really make a choice
Free only when its gentler desire wins, and unfree whenever the baser desire prevails
context: Frankfurt calls such a creature a WANTON: one with no second-order volitions, indifferent to which of its desires moves it. Non-human animals and small children are wantons; persons are not. Freedom of the will is a matter of wanting a particular desire to be your will — and a wanton never forms that want at all, so the whole question of being free or unfree never arises for it. Source: Frankfurt 1971; 'wanton' and 'no desires about his desire; he is indifferent' confirmed verbatim in Holton MIT notes.

question: In the case of Black and Jones, the safeguard that would have forced Jones's hand never switches on — Jones acts on his own, for his own reasons, while the closed exit just sits there unused. Frankfurt argues that an exit which did no work should carry no moral weight, and rewrites the old rule by adding a single qualifying word. His repaired principle excuses a person only in one case. Which?
answer: Only when he did the act solely because he could not have done otherwise
choices: Only when he did the act solely because he could not have done otherwise
Only when he could not have foreseen that the act would cause harm
Only when someone else stood ready to do the act in his place
Only when he sincerely wished, beforehand, that he could refuse
context: Frankfurt's punchline: since Black never acted, the closed exit 'could have been subtracted from the situation without affecting what happened,' so it is 'quite gratuitous' to let it touch the verdict. His replacement principle keeps a kernel of the old rule but adds one word: 'a person is not morally responsible for what he has done if he did it ONLY because he could not have done otherwise.' If you'd have done it anyway, the locked door is irrelevant; it excuses you only if it is the whole story of why you acted. Source: Frankfurt 1969, p.837-838.

question: Critics press Frankfurt's standby case on its weakest joint: the involuntary SIGN that would have triggered Black to step in. Stare hard at that sign, say David Widerker and Robert Kane, and the case quietly defeats its own purpose against anyone who believes our choices are genuinely open. What is their charge?
answer: It must read the prior sign as already settling Jones's choice, or admit the sign leaves a real alternative open
choices: It must read the prior sign as already settling Jones's choice, or admit the sign leaves a real alternative open
It smuggles in a second agent, Black, so the blame really belongs to the manipulator and not to Jones at all
It works only when Black uses a threat — rig the brain directly and Jones is plainly no longer the true author
It quietly assumes Jones is guilty, when an innocent man caught in the same trap would be judged exactly alike
context: This is the 'dilemma defense,' raised by David Widerker, Carl Ginet, and Robert Kane — often considered the strongest objection. The two-horned fork: if the prior sign is deterministic, then to invoke it is to assume in advance that Jones has no alternative — which simply begs the question against the libertarian, who denies exactly that. But if the sign is indeterministic, then it does not settle the choice, and Jones really could still have gone the other way — so a genuine alternative survives after all. Either horn defeats the case's purpose. A related, narrower reply is the 'flicker of freedom' (associated with John Martin Fischer): the residual sign of wavering is itself the last scrap of 'could have done otherwise,' though Frankfurt's defenders answer that a flicker too thin to be a real choice cannot ground responsibility. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt_cases; plato.stanford.edu Compatibilism.

question: As a teenager, Augustine and a gang of friends raided a neighbor's pear tree late one night and hauled off heavy loads of fruit — then threw nearly all of it to the pigs, having tasted only a few. By his own account, why did he do it?
answer: He loved the wrongdoing itself, and stole simply to be bad
choices: He loved the wrongdoing itself, and stole simply to be bad
He wanted the thrill of getting away with something forbidden
He was proving to himself that he feared no punishment
He acted on a sudden craving he could not control
context: In Confessions, Book 2, Augustine dwells on this petty theft as the human face of his whole theory of evil — a will turning to a lesser good purely for the sake of the wrong. His exact words: 'It was foul, and I loved it. I loved to perish. I loved my own error — not that for which I erred, but the error itself.' The pears were poor and he already had better ones at home; the act, not the fruit, was the point. Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book 2, ch. 4.

question: Augustine, looking back on the night he and some companions stripped a neighbor's pear tree, kept asking himself what had really drawn him to so pointless a theft. What did he name as the bait that pulled him in?
answer: The sheer company of the friends he was with
choices: The sheer company of the friends he was with
The taste of the forbidden fruit itself
An old grudge against the orchard's owner
The dread of being called a coward
context: This is the social twist on Augustine's account of why we choose wrong: the disordered will is egged on by company, not only by appetite. He was blunt about it — 'Alone I would not have done it... alone I could not have done it.' The friendship itself was the bait — the pull of fellow sinners, not the fruit. It adds a vivid angle to his larger picture of evil as a will preferring a lesser good (here, the thrill of belonging) to a greater one. Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book 2, ch. 8-9.

question: Long before he changed his life, Augustine prayed what he later called a shameless prayer: 'Grant me chastity and self-control — but not yet.' What did Augustine say a prayer like this exposes about the human will?
answer: A will can want the good and refuse it at the very same time
choices: A will can want the good and refuse it at the very same time
The will is simply too weak to ever choose the good
Wanting the good is already the same as doing it
Outside temptation, not the will, is the true cause of sin
context: This is the experiential core of Augustine's account of evil: not an outside force, but a self that half-wills and half-refuses the good. In Confessions, Book 8, he describes 'my two wills, one old and the other new, one carnal, the other spiritual,' that 'contend within me; and by their discord they unstrung my soul.' Evil, for him, often looks less like a monster than a divided heart. Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book 8.

question: Augustine faced a sharp question: if God made all that exists, and made it good, how can evil be real without God being its author? Different thinkers gave different answers. Which answer was Augustine's?
answer: Evil is no substance of its own — only a corruption of something good
choices: Evil is no substance of its own — only a corruption of something good
Evil is a second eternal power, equal to good and at war with it
Evil is a real substance that God created to test human souls
Evil is only an illusion; nothing is ever truly bad at all
context: This is Augustine's 'privation' move (privatio boni): everything that exists is good insofar as God made it, so evil has no independent stuff of its own — it is a lack or corruption of good, the way darkness is the absence of light or disease the breakdown of health. The move lets him deny that evil is a created object God would be on the hook for. The rejected option about 'two equal eternal powers' is Manichaeism, the dualist religion Augustine was arguing against. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'; Augustine, De libero arbitrio (On Free Choice of the Will).

question: Augustine grants that free will is a genuinely good gift from God — yet people use it to do terrible evil. An accuser presses him: doesn't that make God, who handed out so dangerous a gift, responsible for the evil that follows? How does Augustine answer?
answer: The blame lies with the creature who misuses it, not the God who gave it
choices: The blame lies with the creature who misuses it, not the God who gave it
God shares the blame, since he chose to hand out so risky a power
The evil was fated, so neither God nor the creature can be blamed
Two warring powers, not God, planted the evil in the human heart
context: This is the heart of the free-will defense in On Free Choice of the Will. Augustine compares free will to the hands, feet, and eyes: a body part stays good even when someone turns it to a shameful act — you don't blame the eye for what it is made to look at. Free will, 'without which no one can live rightly,' is a God-given good, and 'those who misuse it are to be condemned rather than the one who gave it.' Everyone who does evil is the cause of his own evildoing. Source: Augustine, On Free Choice of the Will, Book 2; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'.

question: A challenger tells Augustine: if God knows, before you are even born, every sin you will commit, then your sins are settled in advance — so God, not you, must be their real author. What is Augustine's reply?
answer: Knowing in advance that someone will sin is not the same as causing the sin
choices: Knowing in advance that someone will sin is not the same as causing the sin
Since God foresees the sin, he must also have willed the sin to happen
God knows what we will choose only after we have already chosen it
The sinner's will is an illusion, so the whole question cannot arise
context: Augustine separates God's foreknowledge from God's causing. God's knowing in advance what you will choose does not compel the choice — the will stays genuinely free even though it is perfectly foreseen. This blocks the objection that an all-knowing God must therefore be the author of every sin he sees coming. Source: Augustine, On Free Choice of the Will, Book 3; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'.

question: The free-will defense says God permits evil as the price of real freedom. But the philosopher J.L. Mackie pressed a hard objection: there is no contradiction in a free being who always happens to choose good — so an all-powerful God could have made free creatures who never sin, getting freedom with no evil at all. Alvin Plantinga answered him. What did Plantinga argue in reply?
answer: Even God cannot guarantee that a genuinely free creature will always choose good
choices: Even God cannot guarantee that a genuinely free creature will always choose good
God could and should have created free beings who never once choose wrong
The objection dissolves, since suffering is always God's just punishment
Evil is only the absence of good, so there was nothing for God to prevent
context: This is the live, unresolved pressure point on the whole free-will defense, and it is genuinely contested — neither side is settled here. Mackie (1955) argued there is 'no logical impossibility in a free being always choosing good,' so a good, all-powerful God could have had both freedom and a sinless world. Plantinga's reply: to guarantee that a truly free creature always chooses rightly is to take away the very freedom — so not even omnipotence can do it. The dispute turns on whether real freedom requires the live possibility of choosing wrong. This rung pairs with the philosophy-of-religion problem-of-evil ladder. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Problem of Evil'; J.L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955); Alvin Plantinga, the Free Will Defense.

question: As a young man, Augustine wrote On Free Choice of the Will to argue that evil springs from the misuse of free will. Decades later — long after his own thinking had turned toward humanity's need for God's grace — the followers of Pelagius came across that early book. What did they do with it that forced Augustine to protest?
answer: They quoted it against him, to argue people are saved by free will alone
choices: They quoted it against him, to argue people are saved by free will alone
They burned it in public as a dangerous and heretical text
They rewrote it to make Augustine seem to deny free will entirely
They spread word that Augustine had secretly joined their movement
context: Augustine's own early argument came back to bite its author. The Pelagians used On Free Choice of the Will to support their claim that salvation needs only the correct use of free will, 'without any direct assistance from God.'
