The foundation below shapes the laws and beliefs above it
The beliefs above must come first before any economy can form
context: Marx: a society's economic relations 'constitute the economic structure of society, the real foundation, on which arises a legal and political superstructure.' The economy is the base; law, politics, religion, and culture are the superstructure built on top - and shaped by it. Source: Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, 1859.

question: Most people assume a man is free on the inside: he decides for himself what to value and how to live, and no outside force dictates that to him. Karl Marx insisted the opposite. He argued that a man's real place in the economy - whether he owns a mill or sweats inside one - comes first and quietly dictates the rest. In Marx's claim, what does a person's economic position reach all the way into?
answer: The very sense of what he holds to be true and right
choices: The wage that he is willing to accept for a day's work
The very sense of what he holds to be true and right
The political party that he will end up voting for
The trade that he will pass down to his own children
context: Marx: 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness.' Your economic position shapes how you think, not the other way around - the single sharpest line of the whole lens. Source: Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, 1859.

question: In Capital, Karl Marx told a hard story about how a working class first gets made. English landlords fenced off the shared common fields, turned farmland into pasture for sheep, and drove the peasants off the land they had always farmed. Marx's whole point was about what that eviction did to those peasants. Once a man can no longer grow his own food or work for himself, Marx asked, what is he finally forced to do to survive?
answer: Sell his own labor by the day to whoever owns a mill
choices: Beg the landlord for a small corner of the old field
Petition the king to restore the common land by law
Sell his own labor by the day to whoever owns a mill
Wait for the parish church to hand out charity bread
context: Marx called this 'primitive accumulation': landlords enclosed the commons, turned 'arable land into sheep-walks,' and the evicted peasants, stripped of any means to feed themselves, had nothing left to sell but their labor - which is how a working class gets manufactured. Source: Marx, Capital Vol.1, Ch.27, 1867.

question: Karl Marx's lens can explain a strike, a war, a peace, or almost any law at all by pointing back to a hidden clash of class interest. To his admirers that reach was the whole strength of the theory. The philosopher Karl Popper pointed to that very same reach and called it the theory's undoing. What was Popper's objection?
answer: That if no event could ever prove it wrong, it isn't real science
choices: That it leaned on Darwin's biology without ever once crediting him
That if no event could ever prove it wrong, it isn't real science
That it described the past well but refused to predict the future
That it rested on economics, a field still far too young to trust
context: Popper argued historical materialism is unfalsifiable: a theory flexible enough to explain any result by pointing back to class interest can never be shown wrong, and a claim nothing could refute isn't doing scientific work. The reply: a lens that reliably surfaces hidden interests can still be a real insight even if it isn't a testable prediction. No verdict is imposed here - weigh both. Source: SEP, Karl Popper; Philosophy Now, 'Popper on Marx on History.'

question: Thomas Hobbes painted a bleak picture of life with no government to keep everyone in awe: no farming, no building, no trade, no learning, and worst of all 'continual fear, and danger of violent death.' He summed up that life in five famous words. How did Hobbes say life would be?
answer: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
choices: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
Brutal, fearful, lonely, savage, and brief
Cruel, hungry, hunted, joyless, and grim
Wild, godless, violent, friendless, and doomed
context: This is the most quoted line in all of political philosophy. In Leviathan Ch. 13, Hobbes describes life with no common power to keep men in awe, listing everything that vanishes ('no Arts; no Letters; no Society') before the famous verdict. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIII, verified verbatim via Project Gutenberg (gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3207).

question: Thomas Hobbes argued that people secretly agree with his dark view of human nature, and he pointed to what they DO, not what they say: when you take a trip you arm yourself, when you go to bed you lock the doors, and you even lock your chests inside your own house. What did Hobbes say this everyday caution proves?
answer: By locking up, you accuse your fellow men just as much as he does
choices: By locking up, you accuse your fellow men just as much as he does
That laws and officers have already made people perfectly safe
That people are naturally generous but stay cautious out of habit
That fear of robbery is something only the rich ever feel
context: Hobbes notes you lock your door even though 'there bee Lawes, and publike Officers, armed, to revenge all injuries.' By your own actions you accuse mankind as much as he does with his words. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIII, verbatim via Project Gutenberg.

question: Two strangers come to blows over a single rude word. Thomas Hobbes said men fight over such trifles, 'a word, a smile, a different opinion.' Hobbes blamed one of the three things he said all men quarrel over. Which one drives a fight like this?
answer: How others see and respect them
choices: How others see and respect them
The food and the goods they own
Their safety against a first strike
Their freedom to come and go freely
context: Hobbes names three causes of quarrel built into human nature: competition (men invade for gain), diffidence or distrust (for safety), and glory (for reputation). It is glory that makes men fight over a word, a smile, or a different opinion. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIII, verbatim via Project Gutenberg + SEP, plato.stanford.edu/entries/hobbes-moral.

question: Thomas Hobbes liked to say he was born frightened. In the spring of 1588 his mother went into early labor from the shock of hearing that the Spanish Armada was sailing to invade England. In his Latin life-story, how did Hobbes describe his own birth?
answer: His mother gave birth to twins, himself and fear
choices: His mother gave birth to twins, himself and fear
He arrived already fleeing an enemy he never saw
His first cry was a warning the whole town heard
He came into a world at war and never once left it
context: In his Latin verse autobiography Hobbes wrote that his mother 'gave birth to twins: myself and fear' — a fitting origin for the man who spent his life arguing that fear of violent death is the engine that builds civilization. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Hobbes' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes) + University of York (features.york.ac.uk/philosophy/hobbes).

question: After Leviathan appeared, Thomas Hobbes was nicknamed the 'Monster of Malmesbury' and the 'Bug-bear of the Nation.' When the Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of 1666 struck London, the House of Commons reacted to his book in a way that left the old man frightened enough to burn some of his own papers. What did Parliament do?
answer: Ordered a committee to investigate the book for atheism
choices: Ordered a committee to investigate the book for atheism
Banned every printed copy and burned them in the streets
Stripped him of his royal pension and his teaching post
Summoned him to the Tower to answer for high treason
context: On 17 October 1666 a Commons committee was ordered to investigate Leviathan for atheism and blasphemy; Parliament half-blamed the book for the plague and fire, and a frightened Hobbes burned some of his papers. Source: University of York (features.york.ac.uk/philosophy/hobbes); Wikipedia 'Thomas Hobbes' citing the 17 Oct 1666 Commons order.

question: Thomas Hobbes fills the grim early chapters of Leviathan with the war of all against all, but he does not leave the reader there. From it he draws what he calls the First Law of Nature, the most basic command reason gives every single person. What does Hobbes say this First Law commands us to do?
answer: Seek peace, and follow it
choices: Seek peace, and follow it
Defend yourself by any means
Obey the ruler in all things
Do no harm to your neighbor
context: Hobbes's First Law of Nature is 'To seek Peace, and follow it.' The tempting wrong answer, 'defend yourself by any means,' is actually his Right of Nature ('By all means we can, to defend our selves') — a right, not the first law. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIV, verbatim via Project Gutenberg; IEP, iep.utm.edu/hobmoral.

question: Thomas Hobbes described the exact bargain that creates a commonwealth as a promise each person makes to every other: 'I give up my right of governing myself to this man or assembly, on condition that you give up your right to him.' What does each person get in return for giving up the right to govern himself?
answer: Peace and security for everyone alike
choices: Peace and security for everyone alike
A share of the ruler's wealth and conquered lands
The freedom to worship in whatever way he chooses
A guaranteed cut in the heavy taxes that he owes
context: This mutual surrender is, in Hobbes's words, the 'Generation of that great LEVIATHAN' — the security-for-liberty trade in a single sentence. You give up the right to govern yourself, and in return everyone else does too, which is what buys peace and defence. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XVII, verbatim via Project Gutenberg.

question: The 1651 title page of Leviathan is the whole argument drawn as one picture. A giant crowned figure rises above the countryside, gripping a sword in one hand and a bishop's staff in the other. Look closely at the giant's torso and arms and you see the book's central claim made visible. What is the giant's body actually made of?
answer: Hundreds of tiny people, all turned inward toward his head
choices: Hundreds of tiny people, all turned inward toward his head
A suit of interlocking iron plates and heavy chain mail
A detailed map of the whole kingdom that he governs
Heavy chains binding together the lands he has conquered
context: The frontispiece, engraved by Abraham Bosse and designed with Hobbes, builds the giant's entire torso and arms from over 300 tiny figures, all facing inward toward his head: the body politic is literally made of the bodies of the governed. The sword stands for earthly power, the bishop's staff (crozier) for church power. Source: Library of Social Science frontispiece analysis (libraryofsocialscience.com/ideologies/resources/hobbes-leviathan).

question: Thomas Hobbes gives the sovereign near-total power, yet he insists there is ONE right no one can ever surrender, not even to the all-powerful Leviathan. He pushes it to a shocking extreme, saying a person may use this right even in the most hopeless situation imaginable. What does Hobbes say even a condemned prisoner is still allowed to do?
answer: Fight back against his own executioner
choices: Fight back against his own executioner
Appeal his sentence to a higher court
Refuse to confess to the crime charged
Curse aloud the ruler who condemned him
context: Hobbes says a man cannot lay down 'the right of resisting them, that assault him by force, to take away his life' — because you only ever give up a right for some good to yourself, and there is no good in letting yourself be killed. So even a condemned man may fight the executioner. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIV, verbatim via Project Gutenberg; SEP confirms a right of self-defense against the sovereign (plato.stanford.edu/entries/hobbes-moral).

question: Thomas Hobbes and John Locke begin from the very same idea, imagining people with no government at all and then asking why they would ever set one up. Locke decided the people may overthrow a ruler who abuses them. What did Hobbes conclude about that same right to overthrow a ruler?
answer: They have no such right; they must obey the ruler
choices: They have no such right; they must obey the ruler
They may not revolt, but may freely leave for another land
They must revolt whenever the ruler makes taxes too heavy
They may revolt the moment a simple majority votes to do so
context: This is the bank's live Hobbes-vs-Locke debate, with no winner declared. Same premise, opposite conclusions: Hobbes's war of all against all leads him to grant the sovereign absolute power and allow no right to revolt; Locke's relatively peaceful state of nature, with natural rights, makes government rest on consent and lets the people overthrow a ruler who abuses them. Source: Britannica 'state of nature' (britannica.com/topic/state-of-nature-political-theory); American Battlefield Trust 'Hobbes, Locke, and the Social Contract'.

question: Thomas Hobbes lived through a bloody civil war and drew one firm lesson: a commonwealth must never split its power among rival branches or factions. Some thinkers want power balanced and divided to prevent abuse, but Hobbes warned that splitting a commonwealth's power amounts to one single act. To divide a commonwealth's power, Hobbes said, is really to do what to it?
answer: Dissolve it, leaving no commonwealth at all
choices: Dissolve it, leaving no commonwealth at all
Weaken it, leaving it open to its enemies
Reform it, improving the way it is governed
Shield it, guarding each part from the others
context: Having lived through the English Civil War, Hobbes judged even the most oppressive government 'scarce sensible' — barely noticeable — beside the miseries of civil war. So he held that 'to divide the power of a commonwealth' is simply 'to dissolve it,' and that any whole sovereign beats a divided one. Source: SEP 'Hobbes's Moral and Political Philosophy' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/hobbes-moral) + IEP (iep.utm.edu/hobmoral), quoting Leviathan.

question: David Hume watches one billiard ball roll across the table and strike a second ball, which then rolls away. He grants that the whole thing is plain to the eye, one event truly following the other. Yet Hume insists there is exactly ONE thing in this scene the eye never actually catches. Of the four moments below, which is the one he says we never really see?
answer: The first ball MAKING the second move — the force passing between them
choices: The first ball MAKING the second move — the force passing between them
The first ball touch the second ball — the contact at the moment of impact
The second ball begin to roll — the instant it leaves its resting spot
The first ball slow down — just as the second one speeds away from it
context: This is Hume's most famous example (Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, E 7.6, davidhume.org/texts/e/7). We see the impulse of one ball 'attended with motion in the second' — the click, then the roll. But the 'attended with' itself, the actual making, is never in view. We watch the pattern, not the power.

question: You have eaten bread a thousand times and it has nourished you every single time. David Hume points out that your eyes and hands take in the loaf easily enough, yet you eat it trusting it will feed you. Hume's claim is that one crucial thing about the bread is something neither your senses NOR your reasoning can ever actually reach. What is that thing?
answer: The secret power in it that actually turns the bread into nourishment for your body
choices: The secret power in it that actually turns the bread into nourishment for your body
The warmth you feel rising off the loaf when you first lift it out of the oven
The way the bread slowly fills your stomach and makes the hungry feeling go away
The fresh-baked smell that drifts up from the loaf the instant you tear it open
context: Hume's homely version of the billiard balls (Enquiry, Section IV, E 4.16, davidhume.org/texts/e/4): 'neither sense nor reason can ever inform us of those qualities, which fit it for the nourishment and support of a human body.' We observe that bread nourishes; the secret power doing the nourishing is never something we observe — unlike the warmth, the fullness, or the smell, which the senses take in directly.

question: David Hume imagines the very first man, with a perfect mind but not one day of experience, set before clear flowing water and bright warm fire. Hume says this man could never reason his way to the fact that the water would drown him or the fire would burn him up. Why, in Hume's account, is even a flawless reasoner stuck here — what is it about a cause that blocks him?
answer: The effect is nowhere hidden inside the cause, so no amount of thinking can draw it out
choices: The effect is nowhere hidden inside the cause, so no amount of thinking can draw it out
The man's senses are too crude to feed his perfect reason the fine details it would need
The man has too few facts before him, and a longer look would let reason crack it
The water and fire keep shifting, so reason can never pin down what they truly are
context: Hume's first-man thought experiment (Enquiry, Section IV, E 4.6, davidhume.org/texts/e/4): even a perfect reasoner 'could not have inferred from the fluidity, and transparency of water, that it would suffocate him, or from the light and warmth of fire, that it would consume him.' The block is not bad senses, too few facts, or a shifting world — it is that the effect is wholly distinct from the cause and in no way contained in it, so reason has nothing to unpack. Only experience can ever join a cause to its effect.

question: David Hume gives the line that frames his whole puzzle about causes. Picture two events where the second reliably follows the first, morning after morning, without a single exception. Hume's startling claim is that there is one thing about this pair we never once manage to catch sight of, no matter how closely we look. What is it?
answer: The first event in the very act of producing the second — we see one, then the other
choices: The first event in the very act of producing the second — we see one, then the other
Any way the first event resembles the second — they look nothing like each other
Any shared place where the two events meet — they happen far apart in the world
Any way to recall the first event clearly once the second event has happened
context: Hume's setup line (Enquiry, Section VII, E 7.26, davidhume.org/texts/e/7): 'All events seem entirely loose and separate. One event follows another; but we never can observe any tye between them.' B reliably follows A; we just never catch A in the act of making B happen.

question: Every single morning, without fail, the rooster crows and then the sun rises — a flawless, unbroken pattern. A boy decides the crowing must be what pulls the sun up. Using David Hume's distinction between a pattern we see and a power we assume, what is the sharpest reason the boy is wrong?
answer: A flawless pattern is exactly what a coincidence and a real cause share, so the pattern alone proves nothing
choices: A flawless pattern is exactly what a coincidence and a real cause share, so the pattern alone proves nothing
The boy has the order backwards, since the crow really comes a split second after the first light of dawn
The boy cannot rule out that some third hidden thing makes the rooster crow and the sun climb together
The boy should test it by silencing the rooster one morning to see whether the sun still rises on its own
context: The rooster crows because dawn is coming; the earth's rotation raises the sun. Constant conjunction is precisely what a coincidence and a genuine cause have in common, which is why conjunction alone can never prove causation. This is the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy — 'after this, therefore because of this' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_hoc_ergo_propter_hoc).

question: A man sees one ball strike one ball a single time: David Hume says he gets NO idea of any connection between them. The man then watches it happen over and over, and now calls the two events 'connected.' Hume asks what changed to give him this new idea. What is Hume's answer to what actually changed?
answer: Nothing in the balls changed — only that the man now FEELS the events linked in his mind
choices: Nothing in the balls changed — only that the man now FEELS the events linked in his mind
The balls themselves changed — slowly revealing a hidden force once struck enough times
The man's eyesight changed — finally letting him see the link clearly in the quick motion
The repeated motion left a mark — wearing a visible groove between the two events over time
context: Hume's single-instance-versus-many contrast (Enquiry, Section VII, E 7.28, davidhume.org/texts/e/7): after several instances 'he then pronounces them to be connected. What alteration has happened...? Nothing but that he now feels these events to be connected in his imagination.' The only thing that changed sits inside the observer.

question: When a cause and its effect repeat again and again, David Hume says, we come to feel a kind of 'must' between them — it seems the first event positively FORCES the second. Hume's deepest question is where that feeling of necessity actually comes from. In his own account, where does the 'must' originate?
answer: Inside our own mind as a felt expectation, which we then suppose to lie out in the objects themselves
choices: Inside our own mind as a felt expectation, which we then suppose to lie out in the objects themselves
Inside the objects as a real binding force, of which our mind forms only a faint and shadowy copy
Inside pure logic, since once we grasp the cause the effect follows by strict and unbreakable reasoning
Inside the senses directly, which plainly perceive the power passing across from the cause to the effect
context: The projectivist heart of Hume's view (Treatise of Human Nature, Book 1, Part 3, Section 14, T 1.3.14.25, davidhume.org): the mind 'spread[s] itself on external objects' and we 'suppose necessity and power to lie in the objects... not in our mind.' The 'must' is a feeling produced inside us by repetition, which we then project outward onto the world.

question: David Hume offers a definition of 'cause' and you have to spot what kind of thing it points at. He calls a cause 'an object, followed by another, and whose appearance always conveys the thought to that other.' Notice he speaks of where the THOUGHT goes. Does this definition locate a cause out in the world, or in the workings of the mind?
answer: In the mind — it is the thought's own habit of leaping to the effect the moment the cause appears
choices: In the mind — it is the thought's own habit of leaping to the effect the moment the cause appears
In the world — it is one kind of event reliably trailing after another kind, again and again
In a hidden depth of the object — a real power that reason, scrutinising hard enough, could uncover
In the contact itself — the touching in space and time of cause and effect that any eye can watch
context: This is the SECOND of Hume's two definitions of 'cause,' given back to back (Enquiry, Section VII, E 7.29, davidhume.org/texts/e/7; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume'). The first looks outward — constant conjunction in the world. This one looks inward: an object 'whose appearance always conveys the thought to that other' — the mind's trained expectation. Same relation, seen from inside the head.

question: David Hume draws a careful line between two words people throw around as if they meant the same: being CONJOINED and being CONNECTED. Picture two events that pair up, morning after morning, in all your experience. Hume says one of these two words fairly describes what you have, and the other claims far more than you could ever observe. Which word does Hume GRANT, and what does the other one wrongly claim?
answer: He grants conjoined — always FOUND paired in experience; the other wrongly claims a real power binds them, which we never see
choices: He grants conjoined — always FOUND paired in experience; the other wrongly claims a real power binds them, which we never see
He grants connected — a real power binds them in the world; the other wrongly claims they are merely found paired in experience
He grants conjoined — they strike at the very same instant; the other wrongly claims one always comes a clear moment before the other
He grants connected — careful science has proven the real link; the other wrongly claims the pairing is only a trick of the imagination
context: Hume's cleanest one-line verdict was 'They seem conjoined, but never connected' (Enquiry, Section VII, E 7.26, davidhume.org/texts/e/7). 'Conjoined' = paired in our experience, again and again — that he grants. 'Connected' would mean truly bound by a power we could observe — that we only ever assume. The pattern is in view; the power never is.

question: When you watch a struck billiard ball, you expect the next one to move — and David Hume insists this expectation is NOT a logical deduction, because there is no contradiction in imagining the second ball simply sitting still. So if the expectation is not reasoning, what does Hume say all such inferences from experience really are?
answer: Effects of custom — a trained reflex of the imagination built by seeing it happen before
choices: Effects of custom — a trained reflex of the imagination built by seeing it happen before
Effects of memory — a stored record of past cases the mind consults before each new shot
Effects of perception — a direct sight of the force as it passes from one ball to the next
Effects of instinct — a certainty about the outcome that we were simply born already having
context: Hume's verdict on inference (Enquiry, Section V, E 5.5, davidhume.org/texts/e/5): 'All inferences from experience, therefore, are effects of custom, not of reasoning.' Because the second ball staying still is no contradiction, your confidence cannot be logic — it is a habit of imagination trained by past repetition. (Memory merely stores the past cases; custom is the trained leap to the future that those cases produce.)

question: A friend swears he saw something incredible last night. David Hume says a wise man does not just react to a claim like that. How much should the friend be believed?
answer: Exactly as strongly as the evidence backs it, minus the evidence against it
choices: Exactly as strongly as the evidence backs it, minus the evidence against it
As strongly as how vividly and confidently the friend tells the story
Not at all, since wildly incredible claims almost never turn out to be true
However strongly your gut happens to react the very moment you first hear it
context: Hume's whole essay runs on this one line: 'A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence' (Enquiry 10.4). Belief is a dial, not a switch: you set it to match how strong the evidence is, then subtract whatever evidence points the other way. This is the transferable move the kid can reuse on any wild claim. Source: David Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X (E 10.4, SBN 110), davidhume.org/texts/e/10.

question: When someone told David Hume he had seen a dead man come back to life, Hume said his first move was always the same: he asked which would be the bigger stretch, that this one person lied or got fooled, or that a corpse truly revived, and he rejected whichever was harder to swallow. What is he treating the witness's possible mistake as?
answer: A small miracle of its own, to be weighed against the big one
choices: A small miracle of its own, to be weighed against the big one
Solid proof the witness is dishonest and should simply be ignored
Beside the point, since a firsthand eyewitness settles the matter
Even less likely than the amazing event the witness is reporting
context: Hume's demo: 'I weigh the one miracle against the other... and always reject the greater miracle' (E 10.13). A trustworthy person being wrong is itself unlikely, a small marvel, so you set that small marvel against the giant one and keep whichever is less of a stretch. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (E 10.13, SBN 115-116), davidhume.org/texts/e/10; cross-confirmed at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Of_Miracles.

question: David Hume defines a miracle as a one-time break in a law of nature. When a single witness reports such a break, Hume says that report does not land in an empty room. What, on his view, is already standing on the other side of the scale?
answer: Every observation that ever built the broken law in the first place
choices: Every observation that ever built the broken law in the first place
The honesty and motives of the one witness telling the tale
A short list of past wonders later unmasked as clever frauds
The trained doubt a careful listener brings to any strange story
context: By Hume's definition, 'A miracle is a violation of the laws of nature; and as a firm and unalterable experience has established these laws, the proof against a miracle... is as entire as any argument from experience can possibly be imagined' (E 10.12). Every past observation is already a vote for the law, so a single report starts buried under all of human experience. Critics say this is exactly where he loads the scales. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (E 10.12, SBN 114-115), davidhume.org/texts/e/10.

question: David Hume lays down one rule that decides every case: a witness's report of a miracle should be believed only under a single, demanding condition. When is the testimony finally strong enough to accept?
answer: When the witness being wrong would be even more miraculous than the fact
choices: When the witness being wrong would be even more miraculous than the fact
When several respectable witnesses independently agree on what they saw
When the witness has no possible motive at all to lie about it
When the event, though rare, has been reliably recorded once before
context: This is the hinge of the whole essay: 'That no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish' (E 10.13). The other three options are real tests people propose, and Hume discusses them, but his bar is higher than all of them. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (E 10.13, SBN 115-116), davidhume.org/texts/e/10.

question: The Roman emperor Vespasian, the historian Tacitus reports, healed two men in Alexandria in obedience to the god Serapis, and David Hume singled this out as one of the best-attested miracles in all of pagan history, with eyewitnesses, a learned age, and no motive to lie, and Hume STILL rejected it. By what means did Tacitus say Vespasian cured the blind man?
answer: By means of his own spittle
choices: By means of his own spittle
By the touch of his bare foot
With water drawn from the Nile
By the breath from his mouth
context: Tacitus reports Vespasian 'cured a blind man in Alexandria, by means of his spittle, and a lame man by the mere touch of his foot.' Hume picks it precisely because the testimony is gold-standard, eyewitnesses, learned age, no motive, and then rejects it anyway: that is the point, that even the best testimony loses to the prior improbability. The foot-touch was the cure for the lame man, not the blind one. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (Part II); verbatim quote confirmed at ourcivilisation.com/smartboard/shop/humed/enquiry/chap10.htm.

question: David Hume admitted his hardest case was the wave of cures reported at the tomb of the Abbe Paris in a Paris cemetery in the 1730s, the sick healed, the deaf made to hear, the blind to see, all 'proved upon the spot' before judges of integrity in a learned age, and never refuted by the Jesuits. Hume still refused. What did he say was the only thing he had to set against that 'cloud of witnesses'?
answer: The sheer impossibility of the events themselves
choices: The sheer impossibility of the events themselves
The witnesses' well-known love of wonder and surprise
The rival miracles claimed by other religions
The witnesses' motive to defend their own faith
context: Hume grants the testimony is overwhelming, then writes: 'And what have we to oppose to such a cloud of witnesses, but the absolute impossibility or miraculous nature of the events, which they relate?' The other three are genuine Humean worries he raises elsewhere, but here he leans entirely on prior impossibility, which is exactly what his critics say is question-begging. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (Part II); 'cloud of witnesses' line confirmed at ourcivilisation.com/smartboard/shop/humed/enquiry/chap10.htm; Abbe Paris context at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Of_Miracles.

question: Richard Price pushed back on David Hume in 1777, arguing Hume had quietly rigged his own scales. 'We have never seen a dead man rise,' Price granted, but that, he said, is not the same as the damning thing Hume needs it to be. What did Price say Hume wrongly treated our never having seen it as?
answer: Evidence against it, as if we had tested for it and failed
choices: Evidence against it, as if we had tested for it and failed
A reason to demand more witnesses, not fewer, before believing
A private feeling of doubt rather than a public, shared fact
A merely rare event rather than a strictly impossible one
context: Price's reply is the standard rebuttal: Hume slides from 'different from experience' to 'contrary to experience.' Never having SEEN a resurrection is just an absence in our experience; it is not the same as having tested for one and gotten a failure. An empty space in the record is not a vote against, the way a failed experiment would be. The lesson stays no-verdict: this is the live answer to Hume, not proof that miracles happen. Source: Richard Price, Four Dissertations (1777), summarized in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Miracles', plato.stanford.edu/entries/miracles.

question: Charles Babbage answered David Hume in 1837 with arithmetic. If witnesses tell the truth more often than they lie and report on their own without copying each other, Babbage proved something Hume's flat 'never' had ruled out. What did the math show enough such witnesses could do?
answer: Tip the evidence toward believing the miracle happened
choices: Tip the evidence toward believing the miracle happened
Erase any motive the witnesses might have had to lie
Turn the strange event into a perfectly natural one
Settle which religion's miracle was the genuine one
context: Babbage showed that for independent, mostly-honest witnesses you can always name a number large enough that their ALL agreeing falsely is more improbable than the miracle itself, so testimony can, in principle, win, exactly Hume's own balancing test turned against his 'never.' John Earman pressed the same probability point in a book pointedly titled 'Hume's Abject Failure.' Source: Charles Babbage, Ninth Bridgewater Treatise (1837); John Earman, Hume's Abject Failure (2000); both via plato.stanford.edu/entries/miracles.

question: David Hume tries an experiment any kid can run. He turns his attention inward and hunts for the self, the I that does all the looking and feeling, the one supposedly behind every experience. He goes in again and again, searching for it. What does Hume report his search keeps turning up?
answer: Always some particular feeling or thought, but never a self that is having them
choices: Always some particular feeling or thought, but never a self that is having them
A steady inner self that calmly watches each feeling and thought pass by
A thread of remembered moments tying one instant to the next into a person
A hidden self the feelings cover over, surfacing only in rare quiet moments
context: Hume, Treatise I.iv.6 ('Of personal identity'): 'when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other... I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception.' The watching inner self is the view Hume attacks; the thread of remembered moments is John Locke's rival answer. Source: davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6.

question: David Hume runs every idea through one test: a genuine idea has to trace back to some earlier impression, something you actually saw, felt, or sensed. No prior impression, no real idea. Then he aims the test at the permanent, unchanging self that people are sure they carry around inside, asking which impression it could ever have come from. What is Hume's verdict on that self?
answer: No impression of it ever turns up, so there is no real idea of such a self
choices: No impression of it ever turns up, so there is no real idea of such a self
It is an impression so steady and constant that it simply slips by unnoticed
It is real but grasped through pure reason rather than through any impression
Its impression is the first of all, present from birth before the rest arrive
context: This is Hume's Copy Principle: every genuine idea must copy a prior impression. He finds no impression of a permanent, simple self anywhere among the perceptions, so on his own empiricism there can be no real idea of one. The denial of the self is not asserted out of nowhere, it falls straight out of his method. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume' (Personal Identity); davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6.

question: David Hume agrees the mind is filled with perceptions racing by at incredible speed. The question that splits thinkers is what, if anything, holds those perceptions together as one mind. Hume's answer breaks from every rival before him. What does Hume say holds the perceptions together?
answer: Nothing holds them together, there is only the parade of perceptions itself
choices: Nothing holds them together, there is only the parade of perceptions itself
A single soul stays fixed in place while the perceptions pour on through it
A running memory gathers up the perceptions and stamps each one as mine
One unchanging viewpoint looks on, the place out of which they are all seen
context: Hume holds that humans are 'nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with an inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement.' The radical claim is the absence of anything that HAS the perceptions. This echoes the Buddhist no-self (anatta): in the Questions of King Milinda, the monk Nagasena argues that 'Nagasena,' like 'chariot,' is only a name for assembled parts, with no permanent owner behind them. Source: Hume, Treatise I.iv.6, davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6.

question: David Hume has a problem to answer. If there is no real self underneath, only a rush of separate perceptions, then why does each of us feel so certain we are one and the same person from yesterday to today? Hume grants the feeling is powerful and real; what he denies is that it tracks a real thing. Where does Hume say this strong sense of being one continuous self actually comes from?
answer: The perceptions resemble and cause one another, so imagination treats the chain as one
choices: The perceptions resemble and cause one another, so imagination treats the chain as one
The body stays one continuous thing, so the mind simply borrows its single identity
Memory stores a perfect record that proves the earlier self and the later are identical
Reason proves that separate perceptions must all belong to one and the same owner
context: Hume's diagnosis: because perceptions resemble and cause one another, and memory chains them, 'the whole seem[s] like the continuance of one object,' and causation stretches the belief even past what we actually remember. The unity is real as a felt effect, but the identity we ascribe to the mind is, in his words, 'only a fictitious one', a story the imagination tells rather than a thing it finds. Source: Hume, Treatise I.iv.6, davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume'.

question: David Hume offers a picture of the mind: a kind of theatre where perceptions appear, pass, re-pass, glide away, and mingle, a parade of players crossing in front of us. Then, in the very next breath, he warns that the comparison 'must not mislead us,' and takes away one thing every real theatre has. What does Hume insist the mind does NOT have?
answer: Any stage or place where the scenes are shown, the play has nowhere to happen
choices: Any stage or place where the scenes are shown, the play has nowhere to happen
Any gap between the scenes, the perceptions follow one another without a break
Any director shaping the action, the scenes are left to simply run themselves
Any players of its own, the perceptions are all borrowed from the world outside
context: Hume first writes that 'the mind is a kind of theatre, where several perceptions successively make their appearance,' then immediately undoes it: 'The comparison of the theatre must not mislead us. They are the successive perceptions only, that constitute the mind; nor have we the most distant notion of the place where these scenes are represented, or of the materials of which it is composed.' No stage, no building, no audience, the 'where' of the play does not exist. Source: Hume, Treatise I.iv.6, davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6.

question: David Hume does something rare for a philosopher: in an Appendix to his Treatise he confesses his own account of the self has broken down. He still holds two principles about how perceptions relate, and refuses to surrender either, yet admits he cannot make them fit together, and that 'all my hopes vanish.' What is the deep trouble Hume found in his own theory of the self?
answer: He had no way to say what gathers separate perceptions into one single mind
choices: He had no way to say what gathers separate perceptions into one single mind
He had proven the self is real but could not say which sense reveals it
He had shown perceptions exist yet left the outside world unaccounted for
He had let memory carry the self but memory keeps failing and leaving gaps
context: In the Treatise Appendix Hume recants. He cannot 'render consistent' two principles he refuses to abandon: (1) all distinct perceptions are distinct existences, and (2) the mind never perceives any real connection among distinct existences. With no real glue among loose, separate perceptions, he cannot explain what gathers them into a single mind, so 'all my hopes vanish.' Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume'; Hume, Treatise Appendix; Pears, 'Hume's Recantation of His Theory of Personal Identity.'

question: Two kids settle two arguments. One says a square has four sides; the other says it rained in their town last Tuesday. They notice the two were settled in very different ways. Which claim could they NOT have settled from the armchair — the one where someone first had to go out and watch the world?
answer: The rain claim — no amount of pure thinking decides it; someone had to be there to see the sky
choices: The rain claim — no amount of pure thinking decides it; someone had to be there to see the sky
The square claim — no amount of pure thinking decides it; someone had to count the sides to be sure
Both claims — each one had to be checked against the world before anyone could trust it
Neither claim — each one follows from the meaning of its own words, with nothing left to go check
context: David Hume sorted every knowable claim into two bins: 'relations of ideas' (true by the meaning of the words, like a square having four sides — settled by thought alone) and 'matters of fact' (known only by experience, like last Tuesday's weather). The square claim you can settle in your chair: the meaning of 'square' already fixes four sides. The rain claim you cannot — only somebody actually watching the sky could know. So the rain claim is the matter of fact. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume'; Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 4, Part 1.

question: David Hume picked an everyday claim almost nobody doubts — 'the sun will rise tomorrow' — to make a sharp point. He noted that 'the sun will NOT rise tomorrow' is a perfectly thinkable thing to say; nothing about it is impossible to imagine. So what did Hume conclude you CANNOT do with the sunrise?
answer: Prove it by reasoning alone, since only experience could ever settle whether it happens
choices: Prove it by reasoning alone, since only experience could ever settle whether it happens
Expect it with confidence, since every past dawn builds the habit of looking for the next
Treat it as a public fact, since a sunrise is only a private feeling and never out in the world
Count it as real knowledge, since only math and pure logic ever amount to knowing anything
context: This is Hume's own example, verbatim: 'That the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction, than the affirmation, that it will rise.' Because the opposite breaks no rule of logic, the sunrise can't be proven by reasoning alone — it's a matter of fact, settled only by experience. The distractors are all things you CAN do, dressed as limits: you can expect the sunrise (Hume says habit makes us), you can treat it as a public fact and not a private feeling, and Hume counts facts of the world as real knowledge alongside math — so the only thing the sunrise resists is proof by pure reason. Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 4, Part 1.

question: David Hume offered 'three times five equals half of thirty' as his model of one kind of truth. Imagine someone shrugs and says, 'Sure, but maybe one day we'll run into a case where it just doesn't work out.' Why is that person misunderstanding this kind of claim?
answer: A failing case would contradict what the numbers themselves mean, so none can exist
choices: A failing case would contradict what the numbers themselves mean, so none can exist
Nobody has stumbled onto a failing case yet, though one could still turn up someday
The rule has been checked on so many real groups that a failure is highly unlikely
Experts have agreed to call it true, so any failing case would simply be ignored
context: Hume gives two such samples, both verbatim: 'That three times five is equal to the half of thirty' and 'That the square of the hypothenuse is equal to the square of the two sides.' He calls these relations of ideas — 'discoverable by the mere operation of thought, without dependence on what is any where existent in the universe.' Their denial isn't merely surprising; it's contradictory, so no counterexample is even possible. Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 4, Part 1.

question: David Hume offered a blunt test for sorting real knowledge from nonsense. Pick up any book, he said, and ask two questions: Does it contain reasoning about quantity or number, like mathematics? Does it contain reasoning from experience about facts of the world? If a book passes NEITHER test, what did Hume say you should do with it?
answer: Commit it to the flames, since it can hold nothing but illusion
choices: Commit it to the flames, since it can hold nothing but illusion
Shelve it for later, since its value may simply not be obvious yet
Pass it to an expert, since a specialist might find the hidden worth
Rewrite it carefully, since the right edit could rescue its argument
context: Hume's words: 'Does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number? No. Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matter of fact and existence? No. Commit it then to the flames: For it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion.' A claim fitting neither prong of the fork, he argued, isn't knowledge at all. Note: this famous line is the closing paragraph of Section 12 of the Enquiry, not Section 4 where the fork is introduced (Wikipedia mislabels it). Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 12, Part 3.

question: David Hume reached for a striking image: even if not one circle or triangle had ever existed in nature, he wrote, the truths Euclid proved would keep their certainty and evidence forever. On Hume's view, why could no measurement of an actual drawn circle or triangle — however careful — ever overturn a single theorem of Euclid's?
answer: Its proofs run on the meanings of the ideas, so a measured shape can neither back them up nor break them
choices: Its proofs run on the meanings of the ideas, so a measured shape can neither back them up nor break them
Its proofs are really just very old measurements, so a careful enough new one could one day correct them
Its proofs describe perfect shapes in another realm, which our drawn figures can only ever approximate
Its proofs fit ideal figures alone, so real shapes obey them merely roughly and never quite exactly
context: Hume's line: 'Though there never were a circle or triangle in nature, the truths, demonstrated by Euclid, would for ever retain their certainty and evidence.' For Hume, geometry is a relation of ideas — known a priori, by thought alone — so no observation could confirm or overturn it; a sloppy real drawing reflects on the draftsman, never on the theorem. The distractors are real rival pictures Hume rejects: that math is just compressed measurement (the empiricist view), that proofs report perfect shapes in a separate Platonic realm, and that theorems only ever hold approximately of physical figures. Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 4, Part 1.

question: David Hume insisted that every claim is EITHER true by definition (like a fact of arithmetic) OR learned from experience (like a fact about the weather) — with no third option. Decades later the philosopher Immanuel Kant pushed back, arguing Hume had missed a whole category. What kind of claim did Kant insist Hume left out?
answer: Claims that truly describe the world, yet are known without checking it
choices: Claims that truly describe the world, yet are known without checking it
Claims that are true by definition, yet can only be confirmed by checking the world
Claims that describe the world, yet turn out to be neither true nor false
Claims that are learned from experience, yet could never possibly be false
context: Kant agreed with much of Hume but claimed a THIRD kind of claim the fork denied — the 'synthetic a priori': claims genuinely about the world yet knowable without observing it, such as '7 + 5 = 12' or 'every event has a cause.' This three-pronged reply is nicknamed 'Kant's pitchfork.' Source: Hume's fork, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hume's_fork (section on Kant's reply).

question: David Hume drove his fork toward an unsettling conclusion. 'The sun will rise tomorrow' isn't true by definition — its opposite is perfectly thinkable. Yet we can't simply read it off the past either: yesterday's sunrise is finished, and tomorrow is always a brand-new case. So why, Hume asked, do we still firmly expect the sun to rise?
answer: Out of habit — repeated experience breeds a custom the mind can't help following
choices: Out of habit — repeated experience breeds a custom the mind can't help following
Out of a hidden law of nature the mind directly perceives, fixing the future in advance
Out of instinct planted at birth, before any sunrise was ever observed
Out of faith that the world's Author keeps it running on a regular plan
context: Because the sunrise can be neither proven by definition nor guaranteed by past experience, Hume concludes we believe it from habit, not proof — repeated experience builds an expectation the mind follows automatically. This is his Problem of Induction. As he put it, 'Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.' The distractors name the rivals Hume rejects: a law of nature reason can directly perceive, an innate instinct, and a providential Author keeping the world regular — none of which, on his view, we actually have access to. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume'; Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 5.

question: A debate coach writes four sentences on the board and tells her students that three merely describe how the world stands, while one quietly tells you what to DO. The four: 'Water boils at 100 degrees,' 'Most families share three meals a day,' 'Honey will never spoil in the jar,' and 'You should keep the promise you made.' Which sentence is the odd one out because it lays a duty on you rather than reporting a fact?
answer: 'You should keep the promise you made'
choices: 'You should keep the promise you made'
'Honey will never spoil in the jar'
'Most families share three meals a day'
'Water boils at 100 degrees in the pot'
context: This is the is/ought distinction at its plainest. An 'is' statement describes how the world stands; an 'ought' statement tells you what to do. The first three report facts; only the last carries a duty. David Hume's claim is that a pile of is-statements, however tall and however true, never by itself entails a single ought -- you always need a value already among the premises. Source: SEP, Hume's Moral Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/hume-moral/); Wikipedia, Is-ought problem.

question: A man at a town meeting argues: 'Eating this root is completely natural, our bodies were made for it, nothing about it is artificial -- so we ought to let everyone eat it.' A girl in the back notices he never actually proved the part doing all the work. Which unproven claim is secretly holding his whole argument together?
answer: That whatever is natural is therefore good
choices: That whatever is natural is therefore good
That anything our bodies want must be good for them
That a thing with no artificial parts must be safe
That what feels natural to do is right to do
context: This is the appeal to nature: 'this is natural, therefore good.' The hidden premise -- 'whatever is natural is good' -- is itself a value claim, not a fact, and the whole argument leans on it unstated. Naming the root natural is just a fact about the root; it cannot by itself reach 'we ought to allow it.' The other three are real value-claims a smart person might mistake for the bridge, but they are not what his words assert. No verdict here on whether the root is actually fine to eat -- only that the leap needs a value the speaker never proved. Source: Wikipedia, Appeal to nature; Effectiviology, The Appeal to Nature Fallacy.

question: Two friends argue about a custom. 'Nearly everyone in the city does it, you would be the odd one out, the practice is everywhere,' one says, 'so doing it is simply the right thing.' The other grants every one of those head-count facts but says a single unspoken assumption is the only thing linking the count to the conclusion. Which assumption is it?
answer: That whatever most people do must be right
choices: That whatever most people do must be right
That the crowd is usually a safe guide to truth
That fitting in matters more than being right
That a widespread practice must be a harmless one
context: That most people do X is a head-count fact; that one OUGHT to do X is a duty. The only thing bridging them is the value premise 'whatever most people do is right' -- sometimes called the appeal to common practice. It is the same structural move as the appeal to nature, just wearing a different costume: a fact about how things ARE, dressed up as a conclusion about what we should do. The other choices are real rival values about crowds, but none of them is the specific bridge from a head-count to 'right.' Source: SEP, Hume's Moral Philosophy; Wikipedia, Appeal to nature.

question: An elder defends a practice to a newcomer: 'Our ancestors did it, everyone in this village has always done it, the custom runs back centuries -- so you ought to do it too.' The newcomer grants every fact about the past but says the conclusion leans on something the elder never stated. What unstated claim does the leap from 'always done' to 'ought to do' actually depend on?
answer: That a long-standing custom ought to continue
choices: That a long-standing custom ought to continue
That older customs are wiser than newer ones
That breaking from the village would cause harm
That what the ancestors chose must have been right
context: This is the appeal to tradition: the leap from a fact about the past ('this is how it's always been') to a duty about the present ('so we should continue'). The missing premise -- 'whatever has long been done ought to continue' -- is a value claim doing all the work while pretending to be just history. Longevity is a fact; it is not yet a reason. The other choices are genuine rival values a person might lean on, but none of them is the specific bridge from 'always done' to 'ought to do.' No verdict on the custom itself. Source: Wikipedia, Appeal to nature; Effectiviology, The Appeal to Nature Fallacy.

question: David Hume noticed something while reading book after book of morality: each author reasons calmly with 'is' and 'is not' for pages -- then, he wrote, 'of a sudden I am surprised to find' the sentences quietly change. He warns the switch is imperceptible 'but is, however, of the last consequence.' What had slipped into the argument that none of the factual sentences before it ever contained?
answer: An 'ought' no factual premise had set up
choices: An 'ought' no factual premise had set up
A hidden error in one of the earlier facts
A single word being used in two senses
Another writer quoted without any credit
context: In A Treatise of Human Nature, Book III, Hume describes the silent switch from the usual 'IS, and IS NOT' to 'an OUGHT, or an OUGHT NOT.' A new kind of claim -- a duty -- has appeared mid-argument that none of the factual premises contained. He calls the change imperceptible but 'of the last consequence' precisely because everything in a moral argument hangs on that quiet, unjustified jump. Source: Hume, Treatise III.i.1 (hume.ucdavis.edu); SEP, Hume's Moral Philosophy.

question: In a courtyard a clever speaker stacks one true fact on another -- each premise plainly about how things ARE -- and finishes, 'therefore you ought to obey me.' David Hume's challenge to exactly this move was to demand the speaker show 'how this new relation can be a deduction from others, which are entirely different from it.' What does the speaker still owe before that conclusion can stand?
answer: A value premise that his facts never gave
choices: A value premise that his facts never gave
A firm restatement of his strongest fact
Hard proof that each of his facts is true
A second witness to back all of his facts
context: Hume says the leap from is to ought 'seems altogether inconceivable' unless the speaker can show how a duty is deduced from premises 'entirely different from it.' Facts that are entirely different from a duty cannot by themselves deliver one; the speaker owes a missing value premise. Notice the answer is not 'that's the is-ought fallacy' -- naming the move is shallow. The substance is the specific thing the argument lacks. Source: Hume, Treatise III.i.1 (hume.ucdavis.edu).

question: Two thinkers fault the same claim -- that 'good' just means 'whatever people desire.' David Hume's objection is about a missing step: no duty follows from plain facts unless a value is already among the premises. G.E. Moore, in his 1903 Principia Ethica, says the error lies further back, in how the word 'good' itself is being handled. What is Moore accusing the argument of getting wrong about 'good'?
answer: That 'good' can be defined as a plain natural property
choices: That 'good' can be defined as a plain natural property
That 'good' is just a feeling dressed up as a fact
That 'good' must mean the very same for everyone
That 'good' turns out to mean nothing once examined
context: Hume's gap and Moore's 'naturalistic fallacy' are cousins, not twins. Hume's point is about inference -- you cannot validly deduce an ought from an is. Moore's point is about meaning -- trying to DEFINE 'good' as some natural property (e.g. 'good' just means 'pleasant' or 'desired') mistakes a simple, non-natural quality for a natural one. One is a gap in the logic; the other is a mistake in the dictionary. The 'feeling dressed up as a fact' choice is closer to Hume's own sentimentalism, not Moore; the other two are different confusions about the word entirely. Source: SEP, Hume's Moral Philosophy; Wikipedia, Naturalistic fallacy; Moore, Principia Ethica (1903).

question: John Searle tried to BREAK Hume's gap in a 1964 paper. He built a chain from a plain fact: Jones said the words 'I promise to pay you five dollars,' so Jones made a promise, so Jones is under an obligation, so Jones ought to pay -- a duty squeezed out of pure facts. Critics answered that one quiet value had to be assumed for the chain to move at all. Which assumed value secretly powers the jump?
answer: That any promise made ought to be kept
choices: That any promise made ought to be kept
That saying the words always makes a real promise
That being under an obligation means you must act on it
That a debt of money must always be paid
context: In 'How to Derive Ought from Is' (The Philosophical Review, 1964) Searle argued that the institution of promising is built from 'constitutive rules,' so the duty falls out of the plain facts of what was said. Critics reply that the chain only moves if you already accept a hidden norm -- 'one ought to keep promises.' So the value premise is still smuggled in, just one level down, at the institution itself. The other choices are real candidate norms in the chain, but the value critics name as the smuggled one is that promises ought to be kept. The gap reappears. Source: Searle, 'How to Derive Ought from Is' (1964); SEP and secondary discussion.

question: David Hume argued that the mind invents nothing from scratch: every idea is just a faint replay of things the senses delivered first. To prove it he points at the wildest thing you can picture — a golden mountain — and insists even THAT is secondhand. So how, on Hume's account, did the mind build a golden mountain that no eye has ever seen?
answer: It joined gold and mountain — two things the senses HAD already delivered
choices: It joined gold and mountain — two things the senses HAD already delivered
It stretched one ordinary mountain it had seen until the rock turned gold
It averaged every shiny thing and every tall thing the senses had logged
It sharpened a half-remembered mountain until the gold swam into focus
context: This is Hume's actual proof of his 'Copy Principle' — the rule that every idea is a faint copy of an earlier, livelier sense-impression. In his words: 'When we think of a golden mountain, we only join two consistent ideas, gold, and mountain, with which we were formerly acquainted.' You never SAW a golden mountain, but you saw gold and you saw a mountain; the mind only welds together pieces it already received. It does not stretch, average, or sharpen a single image into something new — it recombines whole ideas it already had. This is the very rule the missing shade of blue then breaks. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section II 'Of the Origin of Ideas', para 13 (Project Gutenberg #9662).

question: David Hume sets a trap for his OWN rule. Picture a man who has seen every shade of blue but one. Lay the blues out lightest to darkest and he spots the blank where the missing shade should sit. Hume grants that the man could probably summon that exact blue anyway. Hume's Copy Principle says every idea is a worn copy of some earlier sensation — so if the man really can picture the shade, what has it just done to that principle?
answer: Slipped one idea past it that no sensation ever stamped in
choices: Slipped one idea past it that no sensation ever stamped in
Upheld it — the man only blended the two blues flanking the blank
Sidestepped it — a hunch about the gap is not yet a real idea
Satisfied it — a sensation gave the man the shade once and he forgot
context: The man pictures a precise blue his eyes never received, so this one idea was not copied from any prior sense-impression — the mind filled it in alone. Hume concedes the case is 'a proof that the simple ideas are not always, in every instance, derived from the correspondent impressions.' His own counterexample cracks his own rule. The other answers are the live escapes a Hume-defender might try — that the mind merely interpolated from the neighboring blues, that it isn't a genuine idea at all, or that some sensation really did deliver the shade once and the man simply forgot — but each keeps the Copy Principle intact, while only the breach Hume himself admits lets an idea exist with no impression behind it. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section II, para 16 (Project Gutenberg #9662); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume', on the Copy Principle.

question: Most thinkers bury the strongest objection to their own theory. David Hume did the opposite. He raised the single sharpest counterexample to his rule — the shade of blue a man could picture without ever seeing it — set it down on the page, and then, in the very next breath, made his move on that crack in his own foundation. What was the move?
answer: He called it too singular to matter and kept building on the rule anyway
choices: He called it too singular to matter and kept building on the rule anyway
He tore the rule down and rebuilt his whole system starting from the crack
He bolted on a second rule just to cover the one case the first couldn't
He left it open, declining to say whether the rule survived the example
context: Having admitted the crack, Hume waves it away in the same breath: the exception, he says, is 'so singular, that it is scarcely worth our observing, and does not merit that for it alone we should alter our general maxim.' He spotted the hole in his own foundation, named it honestly, and just kept building on the rule. The Stanford Encyclopedia notes he 'seems unperturbed by this counterexample, and continues to build his philosophical system on the cornerstone of the Copy Principle' — betting the gap is a freak of smooth colour-gradation, not a real second source of ideas. The honesty is the point: a philosopher recording the best objection to his own theory and proceeding anyway. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section II, para 16 (Project Gutenberg #9662); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/hume/).

question: Bertrand Russell, the British philosopher, described a chicken that gets fed by the same farmer every single morning of its life. Day after day the food appears, so the bird grows completely confident it will appear again tomorrow. Russell used the chicken to make one sharp point about that confidence. What does the farmer do one morning instead of feeding it?
answer: He wrings its neck one morning instead of feeding it
choices: He wrings its neck one morning instead of feeding it
He sells it off to a neighboring farm for a profit
He stops coming one day, and the bird slowly starves
He brings it a far larger and finer meal than usual
context: Russell's exact line: 'The man who has fed the chicken every day throughout its life at last wrings its neck instead, showing that more refined views as to the uniformity of nature would have been useful to the chicken.' A thousand feedings were no guarantee of the next morning. Source: Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Ch. VI 'On Induction', ditext.com/russell/rus6.html.

question: David Hume, the Scottish philosopher, picked a homely example: bread has fed and nourished you a thousand times, so you sit down certain that today's loaf will nourish you too. Hume agreed it almost certainly will. But he asked what, strictly speaking, the long record of past loaves actually PROVES about the very next bite you are about to take.
answer: By itself, nothing at all -- the past record cannot reach forward and settle it
choices: By itself, nothing at all -- the past record cannot reach forward and settle it
That the next bite is now overwhelmingly likely, which counts as proof enough
That the next bite simply must nourish you, since nature never breaks its old habits
That bread holds a hidden power which you have now confirmed a full thousand times over
context: Hume's challenge: 'The bread, which I formerly eat, nourished me... but does it follow, that other bread must also nourish me at another time?' There is no contradiction in imagining the next loaf turning to poison -- so the past record, by itself, leaves the next bite logically open. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 2, philolibrary.crc.nd.edu/article/the-problem-of-induction/.

question: Bertrand Russell told his fable of the chicken that the farmer fed faithfully every day -- right up until the unhappy morning the farmer had other plans -- and then turned the knife: the fable, he said, is not really about birds at all. It is about us. We feel certain the sun will rise tomorrow for exactly the reason the chicken felt certain of its breakfast. What unsettling conclusion did Russell draw about our own confidence?
answer: We may be in no better a position than the chicken whose neck gets wrung
choices: We may be in no better a position than the chicken whose neck gets wrung
We reason far more carefully than any mere animal could ever manage to
Our long experience does at last make tomorrow's sunrise genuinely certain
The sunrise is perfectly safe, because the whole universe was made for us
context: Russell's words: 'Our instincts certainly cause us to believe the sun will rise to-morrow, but we may be in no better a position than the chicken which unexpectedly has its neck wrung.' The point is not that the sun WON'T rise -- it is that our certainty rests on the same footing the chicken's did. Source: Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Ch. VI, ditext.com/russell/rus6.html.

question: Some claims cannot even be denied without talking nonsense -- try saying two plus two does not make four. David Hume asked his readers to test a very different-feeling claim against that standard: 'the sun will not rise tomorrow.' He wanted to know whether denying tomorrow's sunrise lands you in the same kind of flat contradiction. What did Hume conclude about 'the sun will not rise tomorrow'?
answer: You can picture it clearly with no contradiction, so no pure logic can rule it out
choices: You can picture it clearly with no contradiction, so no pure logic can rule it out
It is flatly impossible, exactly like denying that two plus two makes four
It is meaningless, since no one could ever say what such a morning would look like
It is settled false already by the many sunrises people have recorded
context: Hume's line: 'That the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction than the affirmation, that it will rise.' A no-sunrise morning is perfectly thinkable; a world where 2+2 is not 4 is not. That gap is why no chain of pure logic can ever guarantee the future will copy the past. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 1, philolibrary.crc.nd.edu/article/the-problem-of-induction/.

question: Lightning flashes, then thunder rolls; you set a pot on the flame, then the water heats. David Hume pressed a hard question about scenes like these: what, exactly, do your eyes and ears ever actually deliver to you? He argued you never once witness the thing people assume you do. What do the senses actually show you, according to Hume?
answer: Only that one event keeps following another -- never the link that ties them
choices: Only that one event keeps following another -- never the link that ties them
The hidden force itself, passing visibly from the first event into the second
A faint glimpse of the necessity, just enough to confirm the cause is real
Nothing trustworthy at all, since the senses are simply not to be relied on
context: Hume called this bare pattern 'constant conjunction': we see flame, then heat; lightning, then thunder -- but never any wire connecting them. 'From causes which appear similar we expect similar effects. This is the sum of all our experimental conclusions.' The expectation is built from repetition alone, not from glimpsing any necessity. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 2, philolibrary.crc.nd.edu/article/the-problem-of-induction/.

question: Try to PROVE that the future will resemble the past. The only evidence anyone can offer is: 'it always has before -- every past tomorrow turned out like the days before it.' David Hume showed that this proof, which sounds like plain common sense, quietly cheats. Where is the cheat hidden?
answer: The 'so it always will' step only works if the future copies the past -- the very point at issue
choices: The 'so it always will' step only works if the future copies the past -- the very point at issue
It leans on just a small handful of past cases when far more would be needed to be sure of it
It quietly treats a claim about the natural world as though it were a claim about pure mathematics
It mistakes a strong inner feeling of certainty for a genuine step-by-step logical demonstration
context: This is Hume's marquee move. The argument 'the past has always predicted the future, therefore it will keep doing so' assumes its own conclusion: it only goes through IF the future resembles the past, which is exactly what you set out to establish. Hume's phrase: the reasoning is 'taking that for granted, which is the very point in question.' Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 2; SEP, 'The Problem of Induction', plato.stanford.edu/entries/induction-problem/.

question: David Hume watched how the mind actually works: see flame and you instantly expect heat, see snow and you expect cold, with no pause to think it through. He asked a pointed question about what FACULTY produces that instant leap from the past case to the expectation -- and his answer was not the dignified one most philosophers assumed. What did Hume say carries us across?
answer: Plain habit -- sheer repetition trains the mind to expect it, with no reasoning at all
choices: Plain habit -- sheer repetition trains the mind to expect it, with no reasoning at all
A careful logical proof that we simply run through far too quickly to notice doing
A direct inner glimpse of the necessary link that genuinely binds the two events
A deliberate calculation of the odds, which we make before we let ourselves believe
context: Hume: when flame appears 'the mind is carried by CUSTOM to expect heat... and to believe' -- 'a species of natural instincts, which no reasoning or process of the thought and understanding is able, either to produce, or to prevent.' Crucially this is no verdict that knowledge is doomed: 'Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.' The gap is real, but habit is the bridge we actually walk across. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section V Part 1, plato.stanford.edu/entries/induction-problem/.

question: Every inductive leap -- the sun will rise, bread will nourish, dropped stones will fall -- secretly rests on one sweeping assumption that can never itself be proved. David Hume and Bertrand Russell both put their finger on the same hidden bet behind all of them. What is the unprovable thing that every such leap quietly takes for granted?
answer: That nature will go on running by the same rules it always has
choices: That nature will go on running by the same rules it always has
That our senses report the outside world accurately
That every event whatsoever must have some cause
That the simplest available explanation is the likeliest to be true
context: Philosophers call this hidden bet the Uniformity of Nature -- Hume's phrase, 'that the course of nature continues always uniformly the same.' Russell framed the whole problem as 'whether there is any reason for believing in what is called the uniformity of nature.' Every prediction rides on it, yet it is precisely what cannot be established without arguing in a circle. Source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739), Book I; Russell, The Problems of Philosophy, Ch. VI, ditext.com/russell/rus6.html.

question: David Hume cornered the whole question with a dilemma. Any defense of trusting the future, he said, must come through one of just two doors: either a strict logical proof, or an argument drawn from past experience. There is no third kind of argument. Hume then maintained that he had already shut BOTH doors -- neither kind of defense can work. If that is right, what overall conclusion is forced about our leap from past to future?
answer: No reasoning of any kind can justify the leap from the past to the future
choices: No reasoning of any kind can justify the leap from the past to the future
The leap is irrational, so a careful thinker should refuse to predict at all
The future is therefore far likelier than not to break sharply from the past
The leap must rest on some proof that we have simply not yet managed to find
context: This is Hume's fork applied to induction. A demonstrative proof is out because 'it implies no contradiction that the course of nature may change'; a probable, experience-based argument is out because it 'proceed[s] upon the supposition, that the future will be conformable to the past' -- the circular move. Both doors shut, so no reasoning grounds the leap. (Hume's own answer for why we leap anyway: habit, not reason -- so this is no counsel of despair.) Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 2; SEP, plato.stanford.edu/entries/induction-problem/.

question: The philosopher Nelson Goodman invented a tricky color word: call a thing 'grue' if it is green when first seen before some future date, but blue if first seen only after that date. Every emerald examined so far is green -- and so, by the definition, every one is equally 'grue.' Goodman pressed a fresh puzzle that bites EVEN AFTER you grant that induction works. What is the difficulty he exposed?
answer: The same evidence fits two rules that predict different colors for the next emerald
choices: The same evidence fits two rules that predict different colors for the next emerald
The word 'grue' is plainly gibberish, so no real rule could ever be built out of it
Emeralds must slowly change their own color over time, which no rule can hope to track
We have simply not yet examined nearly enough emeralds to know their real true color
context: Every emerald seen so far supports BOTH 'all emeralds are green' (next one green) AND 'all emeralds are grue' (next one, seen after the date, blue) -- the identical evidence, two clashing forecasts. So even granting induction, WHICH patterns are we entitled to project? This is Goodman's 'new riddle of induction' -- his successor to Hume's problem, not Hume's original. Source: Nelson Goodman, Fact, Fiction, and Forecast (1955); SEP, 'Nelson Goodman', plato.stanford.edu/entries/goodman/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_riddle_of_induction.

question: Maya wants a new bike and tells her dad, "My friend's bike is the same brand, same model, same year as mine, and it lasted her five years -- so mine will last five years too."
