Her little brother chimes in, "My SCOOTER lasted five years, so your bike will too!" Whose prediction rests on the stronger reasoning, and why?
answer: Maya's -- the closer two things match, the more one's track record predicts the other's
choices: Maya's -- the closer two things match, the more one's track record predicts the other's
The brother's -- a scooter and a bike both have wheels, so they must wear out the same
Neither -- there is no way to predict how long a thing lasts from any other thing
Both the same -- one comparison to another object is always as good as any other
context: This is the whole engine of David Hume's reply to the design argument, stripped to a kid-sized scene. Maya's two bikes are nearly identical, so the friend's five years is real evidence; the brother's scooter shares only 'has wheels,' so it tells you almost nothing. Hume's skeptic Philo put it as a rule: 'Where-ever you depart, in the least, from the similarity of the cases, you diminish proportionably the evidence.' The strength of any 'it's like THIS, so it must have come from THAT' argument rides entirely on how close the resemblance really is. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 2 (Philo, D 2.7).

question: David Hume, writing in 1779, has his skeptic Philo grant one comparison freely: see a house, and you rightly conclude a builder made it. Yet the very thing that makes us so SURE about the house, Philo says, goes missing the moment someone points at the whole universe and infers its maker the same way. What does the house have that the universe simply does not?
answer: People have watched countless houses get built by builders, but no one ever watched a universe get built
choices: People have watched countless houses get built by builders, but no one ever watched a universe get built
A house is small and a universe is vast, and such conclusions only hold for objects of a modest size
A house is made by humans we can question, while a universe's maker could never be found or named
A house has a plain inside and outside, while a universe has no edges, so it is not really an object
context: Philo's actual words: 'If we see a house, Cleanthes, we conclude, with the greatest certainty, that it had an architect or builder; because this is precisely that species of effect, which we have experienced to proceed from that species of cause.' The house inference is strong because we have a huge track record of seeing houses being built by builders. We have NO such experience of universes being built -- we've only ever been inside one, and never watched one get made -- so the same move that nails the house has nothing to stand on for the cosmos. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 2 (Philo, D 2.8).

question: At a science fair Leo finds a strange humming device behind glass -- no label, no maker's mark, and nothing else like it anywhere. A classmate says, "It's plainly built, the same way we know a clock is built." Leo grants the clock but says THIS object slips that argument. On what does the clock verdict rest, and what is missing here?
answer: We call a thing 'built' by likening it to made things we've seen made, and nothing like this was ever seen made
choices: We call a thing 'built' by likening it to made things we've seen made, and nothing like this was ever seen made
We call a thing 'built' by how complicated it looks, and this one is too simple inside to have needed a maker
We call a thing 'built' by whether it resembles a living creature, and this one does, so it grew on its own
We call a thing 'built' only once its real maker steps forward, and no one has yet come for this device
context: This dramatizes Hume's 'unique object' objection. Design reasoning works by comparison: we call something built because it matches the many built things we've already seen made. But Philo notes the universe is 'single, individual, without parallel, or specific resemblance' -- one of a kind, with nothing to set beside it -- so he asks how the design argument 'can have place' for an object we've only ever met once. A one-off has no peers to be compared to, which is exactly the move the inference needs. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 2 (Philo, D 2.24).

question: Cleanthes argues the universe runs like a finely-made machine -- a watch, a knitting-loom -- so it must have had a machine-maker. Hume's skeptic Philo answers with a rival comparison meant to point at a totally different kind of origin. The whole world, Philo says, in fact resembles one of these far more than it resembles any watch or loom. Which comparison does Philo offer, and what would it mean?
answer: An animal or a plant, which would mean the world GREW rather than that someone built it
choices: An animal or a plant, which would mean the world GREW rather than that someone built it
A rushing river, which would mean the world simply flows along and never truly began
A roaring fire, which would mean the world feeds on itself and burns down to nothing
A turning storm, which would mean the world was thrown together by sheer blind chance
context: Philo's line: 'The world plainly resembles more an animal or a vegetable, than it does a watch or a knitting-loom.' His point is that the machine analogy isn't the only one available -- and if the world is more like a living thing, then its cause is more like GENERATION or VEGETATION than like reason or design. In other words, it may have grown or been born rather than been manufactured. The watchmaker picture only feels forced upon us because Cleanthes picked the machine comparison first. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 7 (Philo).

question: To show that loose comparisons let you spin out ANY origin tale you like, Hume's skeptic Philo cites a story he credits to the Brahmins of India: that the whole ordered world issued straight from the body of one vast creature. Philo then dares his opponent to say why a tidy world could not come from a creature's body just as well as from a mind. Which creature does the story name as the world's source?
answer: An infinite spider, who spun the whole world out of his own belly
choices: An infinite spider, who spun the whole world out of his own belly
A great serpent, who shed the whole world from his own scales
A vast whale, who breathed the whole world out of his own lungs
A sacred ox, who pressed the whole world from his own broad hide
context: This is a real legend Philo invokes (here told as legend): 'The Bramins assert, that the world arose from an infinite spider, who spun this whole complicated mass from his bowels.' His kicker to Cleanthes: 'Why an orderly system may not be spun from the belly as well as from the brain, it will be difficult for him to give a satisfactory reason.' The spider-from-the-belly is the topic's most memorable image -- once you allow any old resemblance to count, a world spun from a gut is no sillier than a world built by a mind. The serpent, whale, and ox here are foils, not part of the tale. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 7 (Philo).

question: Cleanthes argues that the order of the world points to a mind behind it, the way a ship or a city or a whole nation's government points to the mind that made it. Hume's skeptic Philo accepts the comparison -- then asks Cleanthes to picture, honestly, the kind of mind that human works on that scale really come from. Taken at face value, where does the artifact comparison actually point?
answer: Many makers working together, since the grandest human works are raised by whole teams, not by one hand
choices: Many makers working together, since the grandest human works are raised by whole teams, not by one hand
A single tireless maker, since one architect can drive a project from the first plan to the last stone
Many makers in succession, since no large human work is ever finished by the very builder who began it
No maker who can be counted at all, since a thing this vast outruns every human comparison we could draw
context: Philo turns the analogy against monotheism: 'A great number of men join in building a house or ship, in rearing a city, in framing a commonwealth: why may not several deities combine in contriving and framing a world?' If the world is like a human artifact, notice that the BIG human artifacts almost all have many makers laboring together at once. So the design analogy, taken seriously, points just as naturally to a committee of gods as to a single one -- it can't deliver the 'one supreme mind' Cleanthes wants. (Not 'makers in succession' -- Philo's point is that the great works are built by many hands joined TOGETHER, the way a crew builds a ship.) Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 5 (Philo).

question: A friend points at all the suffering and waste in the world and declares, "This proves there was no maker at all." Hume's skeptic Philo would push back -- but not by defending a perfect maker. What does Philo say a flawed world can and cannot tell us about its maker?
answer: A design clue may point to a maker, yet it cannot promise that maker is perfect, skilled, or even still living
choices: A design clue may point to a maker, yet it cannot promise that maker is perfect, skilled, or even still living
A world holding any suffering whatever is flat proof that no maker was ever mixed up in it at all
Only a flawless and undying maker could ever form a world, so the apparent flaws must be illusions
Whether the world ever had a maker is a question the evidence can fully and finally settle each way
context: Philo's vivid images: the world might be 'the work only of some dependent, inferior deity... the production of old age and dotage in some superannuated deity; and ever since his death, has run on at adventures,' and 'many worlds might have been botched and bungled, throughout an eternity, ere this system was struck out.' The move is subtle and is NOT atheism: even granting the design clue, the analogy can't certify the maker's QUALITY -- skilled or clumsy, single or many, perfect or shoddy, alive or long dead all fit the evidence equally. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 5 (Philo).

question: Cleanthes treats the world's deep order as the one thing that simply MUST point to a designer. Hume's skeptic Philo answers by reaching back to the ancient Greek atomist Epicurus and reciting his account of how such order could come about. Several origin-stories circulated among the old philosophers, but Philo revives this one in particular. Which account of the world's order does Philo borrow from Epicurus?
answer: Matter shuffles for an eternity, and only the arrangements that can hold themselves together survive
choices: Matter shuffles for an eternity, and only the arrangements that can hold themselves together survive
A single mind sets each particle into its exact place in one deliberate act at the start of all time
Matter carries a built-in upward pull that forever drives the whole cosmos toward greater perfection
A pact among several lesser gods splits the labor, each one tending and ordering his own corner
context: Philo's Epicurean hypothesis: 'A finite number of particles is only susceptible of finite transpositions: and it must happen, in an eternal duration, that every possible order or position must be tried an infinite number of times.' Given endless time, matter eventually falls into a self-sustaining order on its own -- and 'a defect in any of these particulars destroys the form,' so only the stable, self-maintaining arrangements last. We naturally find ourselves inside one of the stable ones, with no intention behind it. Scholars often read this as a striking foreshadowing of natural selection. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 8 (Philo); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume on Religion.'

question: Hume's skeptic Philo has pressed rival comparison after rival comparison against the design argument -- the world as a growing plant, as a botched first draft, as eternal shuffling matter. Cleanthes assumes such relentless doubt can only be the road to denying God. Yet when Philo finally states his own verdict on whether a maker exists, where does he land?
answer: Suspend judgment -- an analogy this weak settles nothing for OR against a maker
choices: Suspend judgment -- an analogy this weak settles nothing for OR against a maker
Deny the maker outright -- the world's many flaws have disproven any designer
Affirm the maker firmly -- the deep order of the world still demands one mind
Quit reasoning here entirely -- such questions lie wholly beyond human thought
context: The crucial point of the whole topic: Philo closes the design assault with 'A total suspense of judgement is here our only reasonable resource.' Hume's lesson is NOT that God is disproven -- it's that a weak analogy can't carry a firm verdict in EITHER direction. This is the counter-move to Paley's watchmaker, not a proof of atheism, which is why Hume aired it through a 'careless sceptic' character and only let the book be published after he died. Philo is usually taken as Hume's mouthpiece, but the dialogue form let Hume keep his own final view ambiguous -- scholars still argue over it. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 8 (Philo); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume on Religion.'

question: A girl tries to make her mind go completely blank -- to think about nothing at all. She pictures plain white, but then she is just watching the white. She tries to hear pure silence, but there is her own breathing. She even thinks the word 'nothing' -- but that is still a thought. Why can't she do it?
answer: A mind is always aimed at some thing, so it cannot aim at nothing at all.
choices: A mind is always aimed at some thing, so it cannot aim at nothing at all.
She just needs practice -- with enough training, a person can empty the mind.
The room was too distracting; in real silence her mind would have gone blank.
Part of her did not truly want to, and kept slipping thoughts back in.
context: This directedness is called intentionality: every act of the mind is consciousness OF something, so there is no such thing as a blank, objectless awareness. Edmund Husserl made it the cornerstone of phenomenology, taking the idea from his Vienna teacher Franz Brentano (1884-1886). The other answers blame focus or effort, but the lesson is about the very nature of a mind, not a skill you can train. Source: SEP, Edmund Husserl; SEP, Phenomenology ('consciousness of or about something').

question: A boy is daydreaming about a dragon -- a huge green one breathing fire. His sister laughs that he can't be thinking about anything at all, since dragons are not real and never were. Yet the boy is plainly picturing something very particular. What does his daydream show about thoughts?
answer: A thought is always about some object, even one that is not real.
choices: A thought is always about some object, even one that is not real.
A thought about something unreal is just a thought about nothing.
You can only think about things that really exist in the world.
A daydream is not a true thought, only a picture in the head.
context: Every thought is OF or ABOUT something -- its object -- and that object need not exist: you can think about a dragon, a unicorn, or the number seven. Franz Brentano, Husserl's teacher, called this the mind's power to hold an object 'within itself,' and Husserl built phenomenology on it. The wrong answers all try to deny the daydream any object at all. Source: SEP, Phenomenology; SEP, Edmund Husserl (Brentano, Vienna 1884-1886).

question: A teacher tells her class: "Notice that you can never just see. You see a face, a wall, a word. You can't fear unless there is a something you fear, or want unless there is a something you want." She says this one feature, found in every act of the mind, is what makes a mind a mind. Which claim is she making?
answer: The mind is essentially a taking-hold that always fastens onto a thing outside itself.
choices: The mind is essentially a blank surface that the world stamps its impressions onto.
The mind is essentially a machine that grinds rules over its own private symbols.
The mind is essentially a private inner show that a person sits and watches alone.
The mind is essentially a taking-hold that always fastens onto a thing outside itself.
context: This directedness is called intentionality — consciousness is always consciousness OF something. Edmund Husserl made it the cornerstone of phenomenology; he took the idea from his Vienna teacher Franz Brentano (lectures 1884-1886), who revived a medieval notion that every mental act bears its object within itself. (Source: SEP: Phenomenology, plato.stanford.edu/entries/phenomenology/; SEP: Edmund Husserl.)

question: Before Edmund Husserl founded a whole philosophy devoted to describing lived experience, he spent his twenties mastering a completely different discipline — earning a doctorate in it in 1883 under famous Berlin professors, and only afterward attending the lectures that turned him toward philosophy. In what field did Husserl earn that first doctorate?
answer: Mathematics.
choices: Medicine.
Law.
Theology.
Mathematics.
context: Husserl took his mathematics PhD in 1883, studying under the great Berlin mathematicians Karl Weierstrass and Leopold Kronecker. Only after sitting in on Franz Brentano's lectures (1884-1886) did he turn to philosophy. He also befriended Tomas Masaryk, the future first president of Czechoslovakia. (Source: SEP: Edmund Husserl, plato.stanford.edu/entries/husserl/.)

question: Edmund Husserl built his whole philosophy on a single move he called the epoche. When you look at a chair, you normally take for granted that a real chair exists out there, independent of you. Husserl said the philosopher should change just one thing about how they treat that assumption. What does the epoche have you do with it?
answer: Set its real existence aside and describe only how it shows up to you.
choices: Set out to prove the chair is really there before you trust your eyes.
Decide the chair is only an idea your own mind has thrown up.
Set its real existence aside and describe only how it shows up to you.
Throw out every belief about the chair that could possibly be false.
context: 'Epoche' is Greek for 'holding back' or abstention; Husserl borrowed it. This move is also called 'bracketing': you set the question of the chair's real existence aside and describe instead how it shows up to you, its mode of appearance. People often confuse this with Rene Descartes, who tried to DOUBT every belief that could possibly be false (option D here) — but Husserl insisted the epoche is NEITHER an affirmation NOR a denial of the world's existence. You do not doubt the chair, and you do not declare it a mere idea; you simply stop asking whether it is really out there. (Source: IEP: The Phenomenological Reduction, iep.utm.edu/phen-red/; SEP: Phenomenology.)

question: Edmund Husserl said that in everyday life — and in all of ordinary science — we live completely absorbed in the world, taking its existence for granted without a second thought. He called doing phenomenology a shift out of that absorbed stance into one where you examine how the world appears to you. Husserl reached for a striking image to capture how big that shift felt. What did he compare it to?
answer: Stepping from two-dimensional into three-dimensional life.
choices: Waking from a long dream into the daylight.
Climbing out of a dark cave toward the sun.
Turning a telescope around onto your own eye.
Stepping from two-dimensional into three-dimensional life.
context: Husserl called the everyday stance the 'natural attitude'; stepping back to examine how the world appears, and how consciousness gives it meaning, is the 'phenomenological attitude.' His own image for the shift was moving 'from two-dimensional to three-dimensional life' (Hua 6/121). This attitude is the root from which the rest of the tradition — Heidegger, Sartre, Merleau-Ponty — would grow. (Source: SEP: Edmund Husserl; IEP: The Phenomenological Reduction.)

question: Martin Heidegger had been Edmund Husserl's own student and assistant, and he dedicated his great 1927 book Being and Time to Husserl "in friendship and admiration." Then Heidegger joined the Nazi party in 1933. By the 1941 edition of that same book — with Husserl, who had Jewish ancestry, stripped of his right to teach — Heidegger had made one telling change to it. What did he do?
answer: He removed the dedication to Husserl.
choices: He added a new chapter praising the regime.
He rewrote the book to attack Husserl by name.
He withdrew the book from print entirely.
He removed the dedication to Husserl.
context: Heidegger deleted the dedication from the fifth (1941) edition. Husserl had converted to Protestantism back in 1886, but the Nazis barred him from all academic activity because of his Jewish ancestry; on 4 May 1933 he wrote that they were 'no longer to have the right to call ourselves German.' He died in Freiburg on 27 April 1938. (Source: SEP/IEP on Husserl and Heidegger.)

question: When Edmund Husserl died in 1938, he left behind roughly 40,000 unpublished pages — all written in an old German shorthand — and under Nazi rule they were in real danger of being destroyed. A young Franciscan friar named Herman Van Breda set out to rescue them, and found one ingenious way to get the whole archive safely out of Germany. How did Van Breda move the manuscripts out?
answer: He shipped them abroad as diplomatic mail from an embassy.
choices: He mailed them page by page to scholars across Europe.
He hid them in the false bottom of a monastery cart.
He microfilmed them in secret, then burned the originals.
He shipped them abroad as diplomatic mail from an embassy.
context: The pages were in Gabelsberger shorthand. On 24 September 1938 Van Breda carried them to the Belgian Embassy in Berlin in three overstuffed suitcases; with Belgian Prime Minister Paul-Henri Spaak's help they were shipped out as DIPLOMATIC documents. They founded the Husserl Archives at KU Leuven, where they remain. (Source: Husserl Archives Leuven history, hiw.kuleuven.be/hua/about/history; Wikipedia: Herman Van Breda.)

question: In a 1958 essay, an ordinary wooden pencil tells its own life story. It says its wood is cedar, cut by loggers using saws, trucks, and rope out in a far-off camp. Then the pencil makes a startling boast about the morning coffee those loggers drink while they work. What does the pencil claim about that one cup of coffee?
answer: Untold thousands of strangers had a hand in making it
choices: Untold thousands of strangers had a hand in making it
The loggers grew and roasted the coffee beans themselves
It cost the logging camp more than the saws and trucks
Without it the loggers would refuse to fell the cedar
context: Leonard E. Read, 'I, Pencil' (The Freeman, 1958). The pencil's cedar 'grows in Northern California and Oregon' and is felled by loggers; Read writes that 'untold thousands of persons had a hand in every cup of coffee the loggers drink.' The point: even a single coffee bean pulls in growers, shippers, and roasters who never met, so the pencil's own making must pull in vastly more strangers still. Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/rdPncl.html ; https://fee.org/resources/i-pencil

question: First published in 1958, 'I, Pencil' is narrated by a humble pencil who insists not one person on Earth knows how to make it from scratch. Decades later Milton Friedman waved a pencil on his TV series and the little essay reached millions. So many met it through that broadcast that its real author is often forgotten. Who actually wrote 'I, Pencil'?
answer: Leonard Read, who founded a free-market institute
choices: Leonard Read, who founded a free-market institute
Milton Friedman, who won a Nobel Prize in economics
Adam Smith, who first taught of an invisible hand
Friedrich Hayek, who showed all knowledge is scattered
context: Leonard E. Read wrote 'I, Pencil' and published it in December 1958 in The Freeman, the magazine of the Foundation for Economic Education (FEE), the free-market group he had founded. Milton Friedman only popularized it 22 years later, holding up a pencil on his 1980 PBS series 'Free to Choose.' The pencil-as-narrator is Read's; the held-up pencil on TV is Friedman's. A common mistake is to credit the essay itself to Friedman. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I,_Pencil ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Read

question: The talking pencil grants that millions of hands shape it, none of whom could make it alone. It then names a fact it calls more astounding still, more surprising even than the millions of hands. The pencil costs pennies and turns up on every desk, yet this strange fact holds. What is the fact the pencil calls the most astounding of all?
answer: No master mind plans or directs any of the work
choices: No master mind plans or directs any of the work
Each worker secretly knows every other worker's whole task
One hidden company quietly owns every step of the work
A government office hands down the plan the workers follow
context: Leonard E. Read, 'I, Pencil' (1958). Verbatim: 'There is a fact still more astounding: the absence of a master mind, of anyone dictating or forcibly directing these countless actions which bring me into being.' No CEO, planner, or committee designs the pencil, yet it turns up everywhere, cheap and abundant. This is order without a master plan, the working of Adam Smith's invisible hand. Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/rdPncl.html ; https://fee.org/resources/i-pencil

question: The young French thinker Rene Descartes spent the winter of 1619 as a soldier near Ulm, in Germany. One bitterly cold day he shut himself away, alone, and spent the whole day lost in thought, then slept and had three vivid dreams. He later traced his entire philosophy, including 'I think, therefore I am,' back to that single day. Where did Descartes shut himself away to have it?
answer: In a tiny room heated by a tile stove, away from the winter
choices: In a tiny room heated by a tile stove, away from the winter
On the deck of a ship crossing the storm-tossed North Sea
Through a long night kneeling in a great cathedral in Paris
In a packed lecture hall at one of the famous universities
context: The little stove-warmed room was called a 'poele.' Descartes reported three vivid dreams that night and read them as a calling to unify all the sciences into one rational system. The 'calling' reading is his own later telling of the story, so it is best treated as legend rather than plain fact. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Descartes Dreams the Philosopher's Dream'; Bloomsbury Literary Studies Blog, 'Descartes's Stove' (night of Nov 10, 1619, near Ulm).

question: Rene Descartes wanted to find one belief that could not possibly be wrong, so he tried to doubt everything, even his own existence. But he found there is exactly one belief that destroys itself the moment you try to deny it: 'I exist.' Why can you never successfully doubt that you yourself exist?
answer: The doubting itself needs a doubter, so something must be there to do it
choices: The doubting itself needs a doubter, so something must be there to do it
Your parents and friends can all see you, so the proof comes from them
You can feel your own heartbeat and breath, which no one can take away
Everyone simply agrees that they exist, and the whole world cannot be wrong
context: This is the move the whole 'I think, therefore I am' turns on: the harder you try to doubt your own existence, the more you prove it, because the doubting needs a doubter. It was Descartes' first certain brick after he had torn everything else down. In his words, 'I am, I exist, is necessarily true whenever it is put forward by me or conceived in my mind.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rene Descartes.'

question: Rene Descartes imagined the worst enemy a mind could have: an all-powerful evil demon straining to deceive him about everything he believes. Descartes answered the demon not with a proof but with a single defiant boast, daring it to do its very worst. What did Descartes fling back at the demon?
answer: He will never bring it about that I am nothing, while I think that I am something
choices: He will never bring it about that I am nothing, while I think that I am something
He may unmake the whole world, but never the one whom he is unmaking
He can fool my eyes and ears as he pleases, but never the clear reason in me
He may twist all my beliefs, but two and three will always make five for me
context: Descartes' exact defiant line, against the deceiver: 'let whoever can do so deceive me, he will never bring it about that I am nothing, so long as I think that I am something.' The deceiver can falsify everything I believe except the one fact that there is a 'me' here to be lied to. The other boasts pick the wrong thing the demon supposedly cannot touch: the demon really can shake the senses, the clear use of reason, and even simple sums (and in any case two and three make five, not the wrong total offered) -- only one's own existence survives. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (Meditations III, AT 7:36, CSM 2:25), direct quotation.

question: Everyone knows the slogan in its Latin dress, 'Cogito, ergo sum,' and assumes Rene Descartes wrote it that way. But when he first put the thought in print, in his 1637 Discourse on Method, he used a different language entirely. The Latin version came only years later. In what language did Descartes first publish the famous line?
answer: In French, the common tongue of the people living around him
choices: In French, the common tongue of the people living around him
In Latin, the formal language every European scholar shared
In Greek, the ancient language of Plato and the first thinkers
In Dutch, the speech of the country where he was then living
context: The line wears three different costumes. Descartes first published it in French, 'Je pense, donc je suis,' in the 1637 Discourse on Method, using the common tongue to reach a wider audience than Latin would. The Latin 'cogito, ergo sum' appeared later, in the 1644 Principles of Philosophy. His 1641 Meditations uses neither phrase, only 'I am, I exist.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Cogito, ergo sum' (Discourse on the Method, 1637; Principles of Philosophy, 1644, Part 1, art. 7).

question: Once Rene Descartes was certain THAT he existed, he asked a harder question: WHAT, exactly, is this 'I' that exists? He stripped away every feature of himself he could still call into doubt, to see what was left that he could not doubt away. Of the descriptions below, which did Descartes conclude he could be sure he is?
answer: A thing that thinks, doubts, understands, and wills
choices: A thing that thinks, doubts, understands, and wills
A body that breathes, bleeds, and grows tired and hungry
A brain that quietly makes each passing thought
A soul that lives on after the body has died
context: Descartes called it a 'thing that thinks' (res cogitans) -- 'a thing that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, is willing, is unwilling, and also imagines and has sense perceptions.' The proof does not show he has a body or a brain; only the thinking is certain. The other three choices are exactly the things he could still doubt at this stage. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (Med. 2, AT 7:28); 1000-Word Philosophy, 'Descartes: I think, therefore I am.'

question: Strangely, the words 'Cogito, ergo sum' ('I think, THEREFORE I am') never appear in Rene Descartes' greatest book, the Meditations. There he wrote only 'I am, I exist.' He deliberately left out the word 'therefore.' Why did Descartes drop that one connecting word?
answer: So no one would mistake it for a step-by-step proof instead of a truth the mind just sees
choices: So no one would mistake it for a step-by-step proof instead of a truth the mind just sees
So the short sentence would be easy for ordinary readers to memorize at a single glance
So that it would not repeat the exact wording he had already used some years before this
So the Church censors reading his book would not catch the daring claim he was making
context: When critics complained the cogito was just a sneaky syllogism ('everything that thinks exists; I think; so I exist'), Descartes shot back that he 'does not deduce existence from thought by means of a syllogism, but recognizes it as something self-evident by a simple intuition of the mind.' You do not reason your way to it -- you just see it, immediately. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (Meditations II, AT 7:25; Second Replies, AT 7:140).

question: When Rene Descartes published the cogito, readers told him a Christian bishop named Augustine had beaten him to a strikingly similar argument more than 1,200 years earlier, while battling ancient skeptics. Augustine's one-line version turned the skeptics' own favorite weapon, the worry that we are constantly fooled, back on them. What did Augustine write?
answer: If I am deceived, I exist, for one who does not exist cannot be deceived
choices: If I am deceived, I exist, for one who does not exist cannot be deceived
If I am deceived, others exist, for a lie always needs a liar to tell it
If I am doubting, I exist, for only a living mind can ever be unsure
If I am thinking, I exist, for every thought must have a thinker behind it
context: Augustine wrote it in The City of God (c. 410 AD, Book XI, ch. 26): 'Si fallor, sum' -- 'For if I am deceived, I am. For he who is not, cannot be deceived; and if I am deceived, by this same token I am.' The same self can also be reached without any doubt or deceiver at all: about 600 years before Descartes, the Persian philosopher Avicenna imagined a 'Floating Man' created in midair with no senses, who would still be certain he himself exists. Source: Augustine, City of God XI.26 (via New Advent); Peter Adamson, Philosophy Bites, 'Avicenna's Flying Man.'

question: To mock 'I think, therefore I am,' the philosopher Pierre Gassendi offered his own version: 'I WALK, therefore I am' -- surely any activity proves you exist, so why crown thinking? Rene Descartes had a sharp reply: 'I walk' actually proves your existence only through one hidden step. What did Descartes say that step was?
answer: Your own awareness that you are walking, which is itself a thought
choices: Your own awareness that you are walking, which is itself a thought
The solid ground pushing back hard against each of your footsteps
The memory of all the many other times you have walked before now
The plain fact that a cold dead corpse can never get up and walk
context: Descartes pointed out that in a dream your legs are not moving yet you seem to 'walk,' so 'I walk' proves existence only through the awareness of walking -- and that awareness is a thought. Even walking collapses back into thinking. Thought is the only activity you cannot fake having. Source: Gassendi, Fifth Objections to Descartes' Meditations, and Descartes' Replies (Cambridge Core, 'Ambulo Ergo Sum').

question: Rene Descartes thought his 'I think' proved that a single, lasting 'I' exists. Long after, the writer Georg Lichtenberg pressed a sharp objection: just as we say 'it is raining' without claiming some thing called 'it' does the raining, we should say only 'it thinks.' What did Lichtenberg argue the thinking really proves?
answer: That thinking is truly going on, but not that one steady 'I' owns it
choices: That thinking is truly going on, but not that one steady 'I' owns it
That a thinking 'I' exists, exactly as Descartes had always claimed
That no thinking can happen at all unless a body is there to do it
That every thought must be the deliberate work of some hidden god
context: Lichtenberg's charge is that Descartes smuggled in the 'I.' All the thinking actually proves is that thinking is HAPPENING, not that there is a single owner doing it -- we should say 'it thinks' the way we say 'it is lightning,' without assuming a thing behind the flash. The cogito earns 'thought exists,' but a permanent 'I' is an extra claim. The question asks only what Lichtenberg argued; a thinker who defends Descartes' lasting self is not thereby wrong. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cogito, ergo sum'; 1000-Word Philosophy, 'Descartes: I think, therefore I am.'

question: Rene Descartes was careful about exactly how much his certainty covered. He held that 'I exist' is rock-solid, but only under one strict condition about the thinking that proves it. For how long, precisely, is Descartes certain that he exists?
answer: Only at the very moment he is actually thinking it
choices: Only at the very moment he is actually thinking it
Only for as long as the thought stays fresh in his memory
For his whole life, from his birth to his death
Forever, since a soul proven real can never perish
context: The cogito comes with an expiry clause: 'I am, I exist' is guaranteed true only WHILE Descartes is actually thinking it -- in his words, 'were I totally to cease from thinking, I should totally cease to exist.' It proves existence for the present thinking moment, not that he will still be here tomorrow, nor even that the memory of the thought would keep it true. Even the worry that he might be dreaming cannot touch it, because the seeming itself still requires a seemer. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (Med. 2, AT 7:27): 'a present tense formulation is essential to the certainty of the cogito.'

question: Right after proving that he exists, Rene Descartes paused and admitted a real limit to what his proof had won him; he claimed far less than his readers expected. What did Descartes concede at that moment?
answer: That he did not yet understand what this 'I' really is
choices: That he did not yet understand what this 'I' really is
That he still could not rule out the all-powerful evil demon
That he could not prove anything outside his own mind exists
That he had not yet shown a good God exists to back him up
context: His exact words: 'I do not yet have a sufficient understanding of what this I is.' He had nailed down THAT a thinking thing exists without yet committing to it being a soul, a single substance, or the same self over time -- which is exactly the crack later objectors like Lichtenberg pried open. (The other concessions are real gaps Descartes had not yet closed at this point in the Meditations, but they are not the limit he flagged here.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (AT 7:25, CSM 2:17).

question: Ibn Khaldun, a 14th-century thinker from Tunis, built his whole science of history on one named bond — the force that drives a tough, hard-pressed group all the way to a throne, then quietly fades once they have won. He called it the basic motive force of history and gave it an Arabic name. Of these four candidate bonds, which one did Ibn Khaldun mean?
answer: A group solidarity that fuses men into one body
choices: A group solidarity that fuses men into one body
A shared religious faith uniting many strangers
Kinship and blood ties within a single family
The personal pull of one charismatic leader
context: The Arabic word is 'asabiyyah — usually translated 'group feeling,' 'solidarity,' or 'esprit de corps.' For Ibn Khaldun it is the fundamental bond of human society: the thing that makes men act as one body and put the group ahead of their own comfort. It is what carries a ruling group to power. A shared religious cause can intensify and enlarge it, but the bond itself is the group solidarity. Source: Wikipedia, 'Asabiyyah' and 'Muqaddimah.'

question: Ibn Khaldun made a bold, specific claim about how long a ruling family stays on top: a dynasty has a natural life span, like a single human body — it is born hungry, grows fat on its winnings, and dies soft, all in a fixed and surprisingly short number of generations before a new hungry group replaces it. How many generations did Ibn Khaldun say a dynasty generally lasts?
answer: Three generations
choices: Three generations
Two generations
Five generations
Ten generations
context: His most famous claim: no dynasty generally outlasts three generations, roughly 120 years. The founder is the hungry conqueror; the son maintains what he inherited; the grandson, born into privilege and never having fought for it, squanders it — and a new hungry tribe comes out of the desert. Source: Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah' and 'Asabiyyah.'

question: In 1348, when Ibn Khaldun was about seventeen, a catastrophe swept through his home city of Tunis — emptying whole streets, and reaching into his own house to take both his parents and several of his teachers in a single wave of death. Living through a disaster on that scale marked the boy who would grow up to hunt for the hidden laws behind why whole civilizations rise and rot. What was this disaster that killed his parents?
answer: The Black Death sweeping the city
choices: The Black Death sweeping the city
A famine that struck the city
A war between rival dynasties
A fire that spread through the city
context: The Black Death tore through Tunis in 1348-49, killing both of Ibn Khaldun's parents and several of his teachers when he was about 17. Witnessing a civilization-scale catastrophe shaped the boy who would later try to find the laws behind history's rise and fall. Source: Britannica, 'Ibn Khaldun'; Wikipedia, 'Ibn Khaldun.'

question: Ibn Khaldun noticed something that looks almost like a law: again and again, an empire grew strongest while its founders were still poor and hardened by struggle, then crumbled a few generations after it became rich and secure. He refused the easy answers and reached for a different kind of cause entirely. Where did Ibn Khaldun locate the true cause of the decline?
answer: In comfort itself, which quietly rots a people from within
choices: In comfort itself, which quietly rots a people from within
In the people growing sinful and being punished for it
In a stronger foreign army that happened to arrive
In sheer bad luck, since empires just end for no reason
context: This is the move that makes him arguably the first social scientist: he argued decline is STRUCTURAL, not moral. Civilizations don't fall because people became wicked — they fall because the harsh conditions that forged discipline and solidarity dissolve the moment success delivers comfort. He hunted for the laws behind the rot, not just the story. Source: cssexam.net, 'Asabiyyah'; The Fountain Magazine, 'Ibn Khaldun on Luxury.'

question: When Ibn Khaldun set out to explain the patterns he saw in dynasties and empires, he made a startling claim: he was not merely writing history but founding a science nobody had built before — with a subject all its own. He even wrote that if anyone HAD studied this subject, surely their work simply never reached him. What was the subject of Ibn Khaldun's new science?
answer: The workings of human society and civilization itself
choices: The workings of human society and civilization itself
The proper way for kings to govern their subjects
The motions of the stars that govern earthly events
The hidden meanings buried inside holy scripture
context: He named his discovery 'ilm al-'umran — the science of civilization, or human society. He believed no one before him had built it, writing that the topic was so unprecedented that perhaps others had 'written exhaustively' on it but 'their work did not reach us.' As far as he knew, he was founding it from scratch. Source: Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah.'

question: In 1401 the world-conqueror Timur — the terrifying warlord also known as Tamerlane — laid siege to Damascus while Ibn Khaldun was trapped inside the walls. Rather than wait to be slaughtered, the old scholar did something astonishing to get out and meet the conqueror face to face. He then spent weeks in Timur's camp discussing geography and his own theory. How did Ibn Khaldun get out of the besieged city?
answer: He had himself lowered over the city wall by ropes
choices: He had himself lowered over the city wall by ropes
He bribed a guard to open a side gate at night
He disguised himself as one of Timur's own soldiers
He slipped out hidden in a merchant's supply cart
context: He had himself lowered over the wall by ropes, then stayed in Timur's camp for weeks. The two discussed North Africa's geography and even Ibn Khaldun's own theory of asabiyyah; he left with deep respect for the terrifying king and wrote a long report on the Maghreb at Timur's request. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ibn Khaldun'; W. J. Fischel, 'Ibn Khaldun and Tamerlane' (1952).

question: Ibn Khaldun split human life into two worlds. In one, nomads scratch out a hard survival out in the open desert; in the other, people live settled in rich, walled cities. He had sharp things to say comparing the two — which one had the stronger bonds of loyalty, and which had the more developed crafts and arts. How did Ibn Khaldun say the rough desert tribes and the settled cities compared?
answer: Desert tribes had fierce loyalty but few crafts; cities had rich arts but soft loyalty
choices: Desert tribes had fierce loyalty but few crafts; cities had rich arts but soft loyalty
Desert tribes had rich arts but soft loyalty; cities had fierce loyalty but few crafts
Desert tribes had fierce loyalty and rich arts; cities had soft loyalty and few crafts
Desert tribes had soft loyalty and few crafts; cities had fierce loyalty and rich arts
context: Ibn Khaldun called the nomadic desert (Bedouin) phase BADAWA and the settled city phase HADARA, also called 'umran. Desert tribesmen have strong asabiyyah but few crafts; city dwellers have weak asabiyyah but highly developed arts and sciences. Badawa is the earlier, tougher phase — hadara is its luxurious destination, and its grave. Source: historiafactory.wordpress.com, 'Badawa and Hadhara'; Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah.'

question: Ibn Khaldun broke a dynasty's whole life into five stages, ending in collapse. The fourth stage is comfortable but hollow — the heirs simply enjoy and imitate what their fierce grandfathers built, fighting for nothing. Ibn Khaldun said the fifth and final stage is where the empire actually dies. What happens in that last stage?
answer: A spendthrift generation wastes and squanders everything
choices: A spendthrift generation wastes and squanders everything
A foreign people invades and conquers the territory
The ruler is assassinated and the family line ends
A plague empties the cities and the population collapses
context: Ibn Khaldun's five stages: (1) success and conquest; (2) full control, as the ruler consolidates absolute authority; (3) leisure and tranquility; (4) contentment and peaceful imitation, coasting on what was built; (5) waste, squandering, and disintegration — the spendthrift generation burns it all down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah'; philosophy-models.blog, 'Ibn Khaldun on Phases of the Civilisations.'

question: Ibn Khaldun's verdict on luxury was harsh and specific. He argued that once a people come to value material comfort above everything else, the bond that once held them together does not merely weaken — it twists into something new and is destroyed altogether. Into WHAT does Ibn Khaldun say that group loyalty turns?
answer: Individualism and factionalism, each man for himself
choices: Individualism and factionalism, each man for himself
Devotion to the ruler in place of devotion to the group
A craving for ever more luxury that consumes everything
Quiet resignation, with people simply ceasing to care
context: Ibn Khaldun wrote that the pursuit of comfort convinces a people to 'value material comfort above all else and prefer their individual interests over the interests of others' — at which point 'asabiyyah turns into individualism and factionalism' and is 'altogether destroyed.' He added that such a people even grows physically weaker and less able to survive a drought or famine. Source: The Fountain Magazine, 'Ibn Khaldun on Luxury and the Destruction of Civilizations.'

question: Ibn Khaldun spotted a pattern in taxes six hundred years before modern economists drew it on a graph. Early in a dynasty, he wrote, the rulers charge LOW rates, and the treasury still fills up handsomely. Late in a dynasty, the rulers crank the rates far HIGHER. According to Ibn Khaldun, what happens to the treasury's total take once those late rulers jack the rates up?
answer: It brings in LESS than the old low rates ever did
choices: It brings in LESS than the old low rates ever did
It brings in much more, exactly as the rulers expect
It holds perfectly steady no matter the rate
It briefly spikes upward, then settles back down
context: Ibn Khaldun anticipated supply-side / Laffer-curve thinking by 600 years: 'At the beginning of the dynasty, taxation yields a large revenue from small assessments. At the end of the dynasty, taxation yields a small revenue from large assessments.' Greedy late-stage rulers tax harder and collect less, accelerating the collapse. Source: Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah' (taxation quotation).

question: The Buddha lay dying among his monks at Kushinagar. They leaned in for one last secret. Instead, with his final breath, he gave them not comfort but a teaching and a charge -- the truth his own death was about to prove, and what to do in its light. What were his last words?
answer: Everything built up will fall apart, so strive on with care
choices: Everything built up will fall apart, so strive on with care
No comfort here can be kept, so let go of all you hold
Walk on as one road-worn band, so keep faith with each other
Treasure the years we shared, so carry the road on in me
context: His last words in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16) were 'All conditioned things are impermanent -- strive on with diligence,' spoken at Kushinagar. Even his own passing was offered as the lesson. Source: Dhamma Wiki, The Buddha's Last Words; Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16).

question: A Buddhist teacher describes samsara: a being born, then craving, suffering, dying, and born yet again, turn after turn without end. A grieving student asks who set this up and who decides each time where a soul lands next. The teacher says the student is looking for the wrong thing entirely. By the Buddha's account, what keeps this whole round turning?
answer: The being's own clinging, with no one assigning the next life
choices: The being's own clinging, with no one assigning the next life
A high god who rewards the faithful and punishes the rest
A council of judges that reviews each soul after it dies
Blind luck, which scatters every soul to a random new birth
context: Samsara is Sanskrit for 'wandering on' or 'flowing on' -- the round of birth, craving, death, and rebirth, kept turning by ignorance, craving, and karma. It is a process of becoming, not a sentence handed down by a judge; no outside power assigns the next life. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Buddha; Britannica: bhava-cakra.

question: At the very center of the Buddhist Wheel of Life, painted on temple walls, three animals chase each other in a ring, each biting the next one's tail -- and their endless spinning is what keeps the whole great wheel of birth-and-rebirth turning. A pig stands for ignorance, a snake for hatred. What is the third animal, and what does it stand for?
answer: A rooster, for grasping greed
choices: A rooster, for grasping greed
An ox, for stubborn pride
A spider, for tangled deceit
A wolf, for savage hunger
context: The pig (ignorance), snake (hatred/aversion), and rooster (greed) are the 'three poisons' at the hub of the Bhavachakra; their biting circle drives the entire wheel of rebirth. Source: Lion's Roar, What is the Wheel of Life, or Bhavacakra?

question: People often picture nirvana as a paradise the soul flies off to, a Buddhist version of heaven. The Buddha meant something quieter and stranger -- a change worked deep inside a person, the moment craving, hatred, and confusion come to their end. Which everyday picture did he choose for that moment?
answer: A flame going out once its fuel is gone
choices: A flame going out once its fuel is gone
A fever breaking and the body cooling at last
A knot in a rope finally worked loose
A caged bird flying free at the open door
context: Nirvana (Pali nibbana) literally means 'blowing out' -- nir- 'out' plus va 'to blow' -- the image of removing the fuel so a fire dies. It names the extinguishing of the three fires of craving, aversion, and delusion: a state of mind, not a place. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Buddha; Wikipedia: Nirvana (Buddhism).

question: Many imagine karma as a cosmic scoreboard that tallies good and bad deeds and pays you back later. The Buddha put it far closer to home. Picture two people: one shoves a stranger on purpose to hurt him, the other trips and knocks the same stranger down by pure accident. The Buddha taught that only the first act leaves a karmic mark at all. What is the Buddha singling out as the thing that actually makes an act karma?
answer: The will behind what a person does
choices: The will behind what a person does
The total harm or good a deed leaves behind
A ledger the gods keep of every life
The fate fixed for you before you were born
context: 'It is intention, monks, that I call action (karma). Having intended, one acts through body, speech, and mind' (AN 6.63 / A.III.415). Only willed acts make karma, and past karma never locks your fate, since the will is always free to change course -- the opposite of a fixed cosmic ledger. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Buddha, quoting A.III.415.

question: In the painted Buddhist Wheel of Life, every realm of existence -- gods, humans, animals, all of them -- is shown clenched in the fangs and claws of one fearsome figure who grips the whole turning wheel. Off to the side, outside his grasp, the Buddha is painted pointing at the moon, to say there is a way out. Who is the figure holding the entire wheel?
answer: Yama, the Lord of Death
choices: Yama, the Lord of Death
Mara, the tempter of desire
Indra, the king of the gods
Brahma, the maker of worlds
context: Yama, the Lord of Death, clutches the whole Bhavachakra in his fangs and claws -- he embodies impermanence, gripping every realm. The Buddha outside the wheel points to the moon to show the way out is real. Source: Lion's Roar, What is the Wheel of Life, or Bhavacakra?

question: A wanderer pressed the Buddha to say where an enlightened person goes after death -- does he live on, blink out, both, or neither? Rather than answer, the Buddha pointed to a small fire burning between them and asked: when this fire dies, will you be able to say it went off to the east, or west, or north, or south? The wanderer paused. Which reply fits the Buddha's point?
answer: None of those -- a fire that goes out hasn't gone anywhere at all
choices: None of those -- a fire that goes out hasn't gone anywhere at all
To the east, since that is where all flames lean as they fade
Upward, because fire by its nature always rises toward the sky
Back to the great hidden fire from which every small flame is lit
context: In the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta (MN 72) the wanderer Vacchagotta answers, 'That doesn't apply, Master Gotama.' Asking which way a freed being 'goes' is as confused as asking where an extinguished flame traveled; the liberated one is 'deep, boundless, hard to fathom, like the sea.' Source: Access to Insight, MN 72, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu.

question: A Jain monk walks across a courtyard carrying a soft broom, and before he sets his foot down or sits, he gently sweeps the ground in front of him. What is he so carefully trying to avoid?
answer: Crushing a tiny insect he cannot see
choices: Scuffing the polished temple floor
Crushing a tiny insect he cannot see
Tracking dust into the prayer hall
Slipping on the smooth stone tiles
context: Non-harm to every living thing, called ahimsa, is the first and supreme vow of Jainism. A monk carries a soft broom (the rajoharana) and sweeps the path ahead of him so he will not crush even an insect he cannot see. The principle reaches everywhere: it is why ordinary acts like lighting a fire or digging the earth are treated as acts of violence to be avoided. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahimsa_in_Jainism

question: Several blind men stand around an elephant. One feels its broad side and says it is a wall; another feels the wriggling trunk and shouts that it is a snake; a third grabs the tail and insists it is a rope. They begin to quarrel. What has each man actually gotten right?
answer: The part he touched, but not the whole animal
choices: Nothing at all, since none of them can see
The size of the beast, but not its true shape
The part he touched, but not the whole animal
Everything, because elephants are unknowable
context: The point is not that the men are stupid or lying — each is honestly reporting exactly what he felt, and each is partly right about his own piece. They quarrel only because each mistakes his single fragment for the whole. The recognition the parable teaches: everyone holds a piece of the truth and no one holds all of it, and you reach the real elephant only by putting the pieces together. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_men_and_an_elephant  (Legend.)

question: A devout Jain family keeps a strict vegetarian table, but they also refuse to serve onions, garlic, or potatoes. Their reason is the same non-harm principle that guides everything they eat. Why do these roots, in particular, cross the line?
answer: Pulling up the bulb or tuber kills the whole living plant
choices: Their strong smell is thought to cloud a calm mind
They grow underground, where the family may not dig
Their sharp taste belongs to a lower, animal appetite
Pulling up the bulb or tuber kills the whole living plant
context: Jains hold that a soul lives even in plants, so harvesting still costs a life — but a root vegetable is a special case. The bulb or tuber can still sprout, which means it is counted as alive; pulling it up kills the whole plant outright, along with the many small organisms in the soil around it. Strict Jains also eat only in daylight, finishing the last meal before sunset, and strain their drinking water to spare the creatures in it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahimsa_in_Jainism

question: A teacher tells the old story of blind men around an elephant: one grips the trunk and cries snake, one the leg and says tree-trunk, one the ear and says fan. Each honestly reports what he holds, yet each is sure the others are simply wrong, and the shouting never ends. The teacher says their quarrel could be settled in a moment. What one thing would end it?
answer: Each man letting go and feeling the parts the others hold
choices: Each man letting go and feeling the parts the others hold
Each man admitting an elephant is too strange to ever know
One wise man declaring whose single answer is the right one
Each man trusting that his own two hands could not deceive him
context: The quarrel runs not on lies but on a single move each man refuses to make: stepping past his own grip to feel what his neighbors feel. Trunk, leg, and ear are all real, so no arbiter is needed to crown one report true and the rest false, and giving up on the elephant as unknowable throws away three honest findings that already fit together. The fix is to pool the touches, not pick a winner. Jain thinkers built a whole logic on exactly this, anekantavada, the doctrine of many-sidedness: any one standpoint catches only one face of a thing, so truth is reached by gathering the standpoints, not by declaring one of them sole victor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_men_and_an_elephant  (Legend.)

question: Saxe did not leave his elephant poem as a cute fable. He aimed its last lines straight at people locked in religious and philosophical argument, who, he wrote, rail on in utter ignorance of what each other mean. What charge is Saxe leveling at all the squabblers at once?
answer: They are all describing the same thing while calling each other wrong
choices: They have never bothered to study the scriptures that they cite
They are all describing the same thing while calling each other wrong
They secretly agree but keep arguing out of their own stubborn pride
They care far more about winning the fight than about finding truth
context: Saxe's final stanza turns the parable on his own readers: the disputants 'prate about an Elephant / Not one of them has seen.' Like the blind men, the arguers are circling one and the same reality, each gripping a different part of it, each certain the others are simply mistaken. Jain thinkers used the same image for anekantavada, the doctrine of many-sidedness: reality has many aspects, and any single viewpoint, however sincere, catches only one side of it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_men_and_an_elephant  (Legend.)

question: In Jain teaching, harming any living thing is wrong, but some killings count as far worse than others. Crushing a worm is graver than uprooting a plant; killing a deer is graver still. The teaching uses one simple measure to rank how bad a given harm is. What is that measure?
answer: How many senses the injured creature has
choices: How large and long-lived the creature is
How close the creature lives to human beings
How many senses the injured creature has
How clearly the creature can feel physical pain
context: Jainism ranks living things by their number of senses. A plant has only touch (one sense); a worm adds taste (two); an ant adds smell (three); a bee adds sight (four); and animals, humans and the like have all five, adding hearing. The more senses a creature has, the worse the karmic harm of injuring it — which is why crushing a five-sensed animal weighs more heavily than uprooting a one-sensed plant. Source: https://www.hinduwebsite.com/jainism/jivas2.asp

question: Socrates wants to define justice but says it is hard to spot inside a single person -- like trying to read tiny letters from far away. The very same letters, he points out, are also written out somewhere much larger, where any eye can read them with ease. So before judging the small copy, he proposes they go study the big one. Where does Socrates say justice can be read most easily, in larger form?
answer: In a whole city, where a community lives and works together
choices: In a whole city, where a community lives and works together
In a single just deed, where justice shows in one clear act
In the written laws, where a city sets its rules down in words
In the gods, who are perfectly just and so reveal it to mortals
context: Republic 368d. Socrates argues justice is 'larger and on a larger surface' in a city than in one person, so he reads the big copy first -- the famous move that the city is the soul written large. Source: Perseus/Shorey, Republic 4.368d; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Plato: The Republic (368c-369a).

question: Plato tells of Leontius, walking up from the harbor, who passes a pile of corpses left by the executioner. He feels a sick craving to stare, and at the very same moment a disgust at himself for wanting to. For a while he covers his eyes -- then he loses, runs over, forces them wide open and snarls at himself: 'Look, you wretches, take your fill of the lovely sight!' What does Plato conclude from a man fighting his own craving like this?
answer: The soul must have more than one part, since something in him resisted
choices: The soul must have more than one part, since something in him resisted
A single desire so strong it overruled his better judgment entirely
A conscience placed there by the gods to punish shameful wishes
A memory of past wrongs that returned to torment him in the moment
context: Republic 439e-440a. The self-directed anger (spirit) wars against the craving (appetite) at the same instant, and since nothing can do opposite things at once in the same respect, the soul must have distinct parts. Source: Wikisource Jowett, Republic Book 4 (439e-440a); Perseus 439e; Psychology Today, 'Why Leontius Looked at Dead Bodies.'

question: Glaucon presses Socrates with a tale he calls a legend: a shepherd finds a ring that turns him invisible whenever he twists it. Unseen by anyone, the man strolls into the palace, seduces the queen, and murders his way onto the throne, paying no price at all. Glaucon says this is exactly the test that matters, and demands Socrates answer it head-on. What is the hard question the ring is built to force?
answer: Whether anyone would stay just once certain of never being caught
choices: Whether anyone would stay just once certain of never being caught
Whether invisible men should be punished for crimes no one saw
Whether the gods can see deeds that human eyes and laws cannot
Whether a bold shepherd deserves a throne more than a lazy king
context: The Ring of Gyges, Republic 359c-360d, told by Glaucon as legend. It forces Plato to show justice is good in itself, not merely for its rewards or for fear of getting caught. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Plato: The Republic (Glaucon's challenge, Ring of Gyges 359c-360d).

question: After many pages building his ideal city, Plato finally states his own answer to the question the whole book chases: what justice actually is. What is Plato's own definition of justice?
answer: Each person doing the one work his nature fits, and meddling in no other
choices: Each person doing the one work his nature fits, and meddling in no other
Giving back exactly what you owe, so that no debt is ever left unpaid
Helping out your friends, and doing harm to those who are your enemies
Obeying whatever the laws of the city's current rulers happen to command
context: Republic 433b: justice is 'the having and doing of what is one's own,' each doing the one job his nature best fits and meddling in no other. The distractors are real rival views from the dialogue (Cephalus's pay-your-debts, Polemarchus's help-friends/harm-enemies) and a rulers'-law account. Present this as Plato's position to weigh, not the last word on justice. Source: Wikisource Jowett, Republic Book 4 (433b); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and IEP, Republic 433a-b.

question: Early in the Republic a blunt teacher named Thrasymachus loses patience with all the high-minded talk of fairness and throws out his own hard-nosed, cynical definition of what justice REALLY is. The whole rest of the book is Plato's long campaign to demolish this one claim. What did Thrasymachus say justice really comes down to?
answer: Nothing but whatever serves the interest of the stronger party
choices: Nothing but whatever serves the interest of the stronger party
A bargain the weak invent to protect themselves from the strong
An illusion, since no one is ever truly fair when unwatched
The will of the gods, handed down for rulers to enforce below
context: Republic 338c: 'justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger.' The ruling powers make laws to suit themselves and call obeying them just; Plato's whole city-soul argument is constructed to answer this challenge. The distractors are other real theories (Glaucon's contract view, moral skepticism, divine command). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Plato: The Republic (Thrasymachus, 338c).

question: Plato has defined a just person as one in whom reason, drive, and appetite each keep to their proper role. Now he turns to the unjust person and names that broken inner condition with one vivid image. What does Plato say injustice amounts to, inside one person?
answer: A civil war among the parts of the soul, faction risen against faction
choices: A civil war among the parts of the soul, faction risen against faction
A sickness sent in from outside that infects an otherwise healthy soul
The mere absence of good habits, which steady training could supply now
A debt owed to the gods that the unjust soul has long refused to pay back
context: Republic 444b. Plato calls injustice 'a meddlesomeness, and interference, and rising up of a part of the soul against the whole' -- a faction or civil war (stasis) inside one person, the exact mirror of justice as each part keeping its place. Source: Wikisource Jowett, Republic Book 4 (444b); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, injustice as stasis/faction (444b, 444e).

question: Plato insists that being just is not really about your outward behavior at all -- a man could do every 'correct' deed and still be a wreck inside. The truly just person, he says, has set his inner life in order: he binds his reasoning, his drive, and his appetites together so they stop fighting and he becomes 'one instead of many.' To picture this ordering, Plato reaches for one familiar image of distinct things made to work as a single whole. What does he compare the well-ordered soul to?
answer: Notes of a scale brought into one harmony
choices: Notes of a scale brought into one harmony
Horses of a team pulling a chariot straight
Servants of a house obeying one master
Limbs of a body answering one command
context: Republic 443d-e. The just man 'binds together the three principles within him' and becomes 'one entirely instead of many,' tuning reason, spirit, and appetite like the high, middle, and low notes of a musical scale. The chariot-team image is also Plato's, but from the Phaedrus, not this passage. Source: Wikisource Jowett, Republic Book 4 (443d-e); Shorey translation; 'Soul Music in Plato's Republic,' voegelinview.com.

question: Penniless and stateless, Karl Marx needed a warm place to write his giant takedown of capitalism, and he found one that cost him nothing. For years he sat at the same desk in a great hall in London. Where did the exile write Das Kapital?
answer: The reading room of the British Museum
choices: The reading room of the British Museum
A rented office above a print shop
A lecture hall he taught classes in
The back room of a Soho tavern
context: Too poor to rent a study, Marx spent years in the free Reading Room of the British Museum studying political economy; the first volume of Das Kapital appeared in 1867. An English Heritage blue plaque marks the connection. Source: Wikipedia 'Karl Marx'; English Heritage 'Karl Marx' blue plaque.

question: Karl Marx ends the Communist Manifesto with a rallying cry to the workers of the world. He tells them that next to the new world they stand to win, what they risk is almost nothing -- the old order has bound them with only one thing. In that final line, what is that one thing?
answer: Their chains
choices: Their chains
Their debts
Their fear
Their borders
context: The Manifesto's closing call: 'The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win. Working Men of All Countries, Unite!' (German: 'Proletarier aller Lander, vereinigt euch!'). Source: marxists.org primary text, Communist Manifesto Ch.4.

question: Karl Marx opens the Communist Manifesto with one of the most quoted first lines in all of political writing. He turns his whole movement into a single dread image -- a spectre that has the old rulers of the continent terrified. In that opening line, what does Marx say the spectre is doing?
answer: Haunting Europe
choices: Haunting Europe
Marching on Paris
Rising from the dead
Crossing the sea
context: The Manifesto's opening line in full: 'A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of communism.' Source: marxists.org primary text, Communist Manifesto Ch.1.

question: For twenty years the man who fed Karl Marx and bankrolled the writing of Das Kapital was his friend Friedrich Engels. The joke of it is that Engels got his money from exactly the kind of business Marx spent his life attacking. Where did that money come from?
answer: His wealthy family cotton mill
choices: His wealthy family cotton mill
A country estate he had inherited
Royalties from his bestselling novels
His salary as a government minister
context: Engels, son of a wealthy cotton-mill owner, worked at the family firm Ermen & Engels in Manchester and over about twenty years funneled an estimated 3,000 to 4,000 pounds to the Marx family, effectively funding Das Kapital. In the Marx household he was nicknamed 'The General.' Source: Wikipedia 'Friedrich Engels'; Jacobin.

question: People imagine the Communist Manifesto as a lone burst of inspiration. In fact a society of revolutionary workers in London handed Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels a writing job with a deadline in December 1847. What were the two young radicals hired to produce?
answer: An official program for the movement
choices: An official program for the movement
A legal defense for arrested members
A newspaper to rally factory workers
A history of past failed revolts
context: The Communist League hired Marx and Engels to write its program; Marx drafted it in German in January 1848 (drawing on an earlier tract by Engels) and it was published anonymously in London just weeks before the French Revolution of February 1848. Marx was 29. Source: Wikipedia 'The Communist Manifesto'; History.com.

question: Karl Marx and his wife Jenny crammed into two squalid rooms on Dean Street in Soho, so broke that bailiffs once carried off their furniture and even an infant cradle. That poverty did far more than humiliate the family. What did it cost them?
answer: The lives of several of their young children
choices: The lives of several of their young children
The only manuscript of his unfinished book
Their last ties to relatives back in Prussia
Their standing in the revolutionary movement
context: Several Marx children died young in London, including baby Franziska, born at Dean Street and dead within about a year, and his son Edgar in 1855. Jenny called the Dean Street rooms 'the evil frightful rooms which encompassed all our joy and all our pain.' Source: Spartacus Educational 'Karl Marx'; English Heritage blue plaque.

question: Karl Marx opens the Communist Manifesto by naming the one hidden engine he believes has driven every society that ever existed -- a sweeping claim packed into his very first argument. According to Marx, all of history so far has really been the history of what?
answer: The struggle between social classes
choices: The struggle between social classes
The competition between rival nations
The conflict between religious faiths
The clash of great ideas and beliefs
context: The Manifesto's very first argument: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.' Source: marxists.org primary text, Communist Manifesto Ch.1.

question: For years Karl Marx wrote Das Kapital in real pain, his skin covered in agonizing boils called carbuncles. True to form, he turned even his own sickness into a jab in the class war when he wrote to Friedrich Engels about it. How did Marx brand his own illness in that letter?
answer: A truly proletarian disease
choices: A truly proletarian disease
A curse from his cruel landlords
The price of his honest labor
A fittingly bourgeois affliction
context: Marx complained to Engels that the carbuncles were 'a truly proletarian disease' and quipped, 'I hope the bourgeoisie will remember my carbuncles until their dying day.' Source: Spartacus Educational 'Karl Marx' (confidence: medium).

question: When Karl Marx died in 1883, only about a dozen mourners gathered at his graveside in Highgate Cemetery. There his friend Friedrich Engels rose to speak, and opened the eulogy by fixing the exact moment of the death with a single grand claim about the man in the grave. How did Engels begin?
answer: The greatest living thinker had ceased to think
choices: The greatest living thinker had ceased to think
The truest friend the workers ever had was gone
A fire that had lit all of Europe was now out
The bravest enemy of the rich had fallen at last
context: Engels opened his Highgate burial speech: 'On the 14th of March, at a quarter to three in the afternoon, the greatest living thinker ceased to think.' Only about a dozen mourners (estimates run from about 11 to two dozen) stood at the graveside on March 17, 1883. Source: marxists.org, Engels' burial speech.

question: Karl Marx lies under a great stone at Highgate Cemetery carved with a line that sums up his whole demand on philosophy. For ages, he said, thinkers had merely interpreted the world in various ways. According to that carved line, what is the real point instead?
answer: To change it
choices: To change it
To rule it
To endure it
To worship it
context: The back of Marx's Highgate tomb carries the close of his Theses on Feuerbach: 'The philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point however is to change it.' The Eleventh Thesis was written in Brussels in 1845 and published only after his death; the front of the tomb reads 'Workers of all lands unite.' Source: Wikipedia 'Tomb of Karl Marx'; Wikipedia 'Theses on Feuerbach'.

question: Soren Kierkegaard, the gloomy Danish thinker, got engaged to seventeen-year-old Regine Olsen, then broke it off a year later so he could pour himself into writing about how to live. To make the breakup easier on her, he did something cruel on purpose. What act did he stage?
answer: He pretended to be a cold-hearted cad so she would hate him and let go
choices: He pretended to be a cold-hearted cad so she would hate him and let go
He told her family she had been unfaithful and shamed her in public
He vanished overnight and left the city without a word of warning
He mocked her plainness to her face until she called the wedding off
context: Kierkegaard playacted the scoundrel to free Regine to move on, then poured the whole affair into his books, even writing 'The Seducer's Diary' partly to paint himself as a cad. He never married, and in his will left his whole estate to Regine 'exactly as if I had been married to her.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kierkegaard (iep.utm.edu/kierkega); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Princeton UP, The Seducer's Diary.

question: In Either/Or, Soren Kierkegaard writes a famous little riddle he jokingly calls the whole sum of philosophy: marry, and you will regret it; do not marry, you will regret that too; laugh at the world or weep over it, you regret it either way. What point is the pleasure-seeker stuck on?
answer: No clever weighing of options can hand a life its meaning
choices: No clever weighing of options can hand a life its meaning
Every real choice in life secretly comes down to money
A wise person simply picks whichever path hurts the least
Regret proves you chose wrongly and should pick again
context: This is from the 'Diapsalmata' that open Either/Or. The pleasure-seeker who weighs every option for advantage ends up paralyzed and despairing, because no calculation can give a life meaning. Source: Soren Kierkegaard, Either/Or (the 'Diapsalmata'); Stephen Hicks excerpts (stephenhicks.org); SparkNotes, Selected Works of Kierkegaard.

question: Soren Kierkegaard pictured life as three rising ways to live, each entered only by a leap of choice, never by an argument: the aesthetic life chasing pleasure and novelty until it sinks into emptiness, then the ethical life bound to duty and marriage and rules. He gave the third and highest stage a different shape entirely. What defines it?
