Confucius told Zixia, 'You have opened up my eyes!' Source: via Richard Brown -- https://brownbeat.medium.com/analects-of-confucius-book-3-new-english-translation-461a7e383e80

question: Confucius once stopped his son Boyu in the courtyard and asked whether he had yet studied ritual. When the boy admitted he had not, his father warned him that a person who never studies ritual 'will have no way to take his stand.' What did Confucius mean that the study of ritual would equip his son to do?
answer: Hold steady and act rightly even when a situation is unclear and no rule is obvious
choices: Hold steady and act rightly even when a situation is unclear and no rule is obvious
Obey his elders and superiors at once, never pausing to question what he was told
Win any dispute by out-arguing his rivals with clever and well-practiced speech
Secure a title, an office, and an inheritance that no other man could take from him
context: Analects 16.13 -- 'If you do not study ritual, you will have no way to take your stand.' Li is the ground a person stands on; it forms someone who can hold firm and act rightly, not merely win arguments or secure rank. Source: via Association for Asian Studies -- https://confucius.page/analects-16-13/

question: A teenager hears the old Stoic motto "live according to nature" and figures it means: stop overthinking, follow your gut, do whatever comes naturally. A Stoic teacher tells him that's not what the school meant at all. The Stoics argued that what makes each kind of thing what it IS is its own special nature — a plant's nature, for instance, is simply to grow. So for the Stoics, what does living "according to YOUR nature" actually require of a human being?
answer: Living by reason, the faculty that sets a human apart from plants and beasts
choices: Living by reason, the faculty that sets a human apart from plants and beasts
Living by impulse, trusting whatever urge to eat, mate, or fight comes first
Living by custom, doing as the elders of your city have always handed down
Living by love, putting the needs of the people around you ahead of your own
context: For the Stoics, "live according to nature" is the OPPOSITE of "go wild" or "follow your animal instincts." A plant's nature is to grow, an animal's is impulse and sensation — but a human's defining nature is REASON. So living by nature means living by the part that makes us human, not chasing every urge. Source: Orion Philosophy, "What do Stoics mean by nature?" (orionphilosophy.com); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism (iep.utm.edu/stoicism).

question: Diogenes the Cynic lived in a large clay jar and owned almost nothing. In ancient Greece your CITY was supposed to be the whole source of who you were — Athenian, Spartan, Theban. So when a stranger asked Diogenes where he was from, his answer shocked everyone and became one of the most famous lines in philosophy. Instead of naming his hometown of Sinope, what did Diogenes say he was?
answer: A citizen of the world
choices: A citizen of the world
A man of no city or master
A subject of the great king
A native of every harbor town
context: Diogenes' Greek word was kosmopolites — the root of "cosmopolitan." To an ancient Greek it was almost shocking, since your city was supposed to be your entire identity. The Stoics took this Cynic line and built a whole philosophy on it: the idea that the wise belong to the whole world, not just one tribe. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.63 (via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Cosmopolitanism, plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmopolitanism).

question: The Stoic Hierocles pictured all your relationships as rings drawn around you: yourself at the dead center, then your family, then relatives, neighbors, fellow citizens, and in the widest ring of all, every stranger on earth. Hierocles said the whole task of a good life is to do one particular thing with those rings. What did he say a person should work to do?
answer: Pull the outer rings inward, until a distant person feels more like your own kin
choices: Pull the outer rings inward, until a distant person feels more like your own kin
Guard the inner rings closely, keeping the outsiders at a careful, safe distance
Climb out to the widest ring alone, leaving your own family behind for humankind
Hold every ring fixed in its place, owing each exactly the duty that it is due
context: Hierocles called this widening of natural affection oikeiosis. He even gave a concrete trick for it: call your cousins "brothers" and your uncles and aunts "fathers" and "mothers," because using the warmer, closer name trains you to treat outer-circle people with inner-circle care. Source: Hierocles, fragment in Stobaeus' Anthologion (via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierocles_(Stoic); modernstoicism.com, "Oikeiosis Reimagined: The Circle of Compassion").

question: Marcus Aurelius, ruler of the entire Roman Empire and the most powerful man alive, worked through a chain of reasoning in his private notebook. If mind is common to us all, he wrote, then reason is common to us all; and if reason is common, then law is common to us all; and if law is common — then a startling conclusion follows about every other human being, peasant or king alike. What did Marcus Aurelius conclude that we all are?
answer: Fellow citizens of one single world-wide community
choices: Fellow citizens of one single world-wide community
Rival subjects of many separate and warring states
Equal servants under the rule of the Roman emperor
Distant rivals who merely happen to share one planet
context: Marcus lays the argument out step by step in Meditations 4.4: "If mind is common to us all, then also the reason... is common. If so, law also is common. If so, we are citizens... the Universe is as it were a state." A Roman emperor — the most powerful man alive — reasons his way to the conclusion that he is just one fellow-citizen of the world, the cosmopolis. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.4 (classics.mit.edu/Antoninus/meditations).

question: Two leaders of the Stoic school, Cleanthes and his successor Chrysippus, disagreed about a deep question inside their own philosophy: when a person "follows nature," exactly WHOSE nature is being followed? Chrysippus gave the answer that became the standard Stoic teaching for centuries afterward. What did Chrysippus argue a person should live in agreement with?
answer: Both the universe's nature and your own, since each self is a part of the whole
choices: Both the universe's nature and your own, since each self is a part of the whole
Only the wider universe, never the self, since one person counts for nothing
Only your own self, never the universe, since the far cosmos cannot bind you
Neither the self nor the universe, but plain reason, which outranks nature itself
context: Cleanthes had taught that you follow only the nature of the whole universe. Chrysippus, the school's third head and great systematizer, answered that you follow BOTH — the universe's nature AND your own human nature — "because our individual natures are parts of the nature of the whole." His two-part version became the standard Stoic teaching. Source: Diogenes Laertius 7.89 (via modernstoicism.com); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism (plato.stanford.edu/entries/stoicism).

question: John Locke imagines a strange morning: a prince goes to sleep, and when the cobbler across town wakes up, it is the prince's memories and awareness that open their eyes inside the cobbler's body. The cobbler's old self is simply gone. The living body in the bed is the cobbler's, but the life it remembers is the prince's. Locke asks who is now accountable for the prince's past deeds. On Locke's reasoning, which person is now lying in that bed?
answer: The prince — the self travels with the memories, not with the body
choices: The prince — the self travels with the memories, not with the body
The cobbler — the self is the living body, and that body never moved
Neither one fully — a brand-new person, with no claim on either past
It cannot be settled — selfhood is not the kind of thing that relocates
context: This is Locke's famous Prince-and-the-Cobbler case (Essay II.xxvii.15, 1694). His words: 'every one sees he would be the same PERSON with the prince, accountable only for the prince's actions: but who would say it was the same MAN?' The four choices map the four classic answers philosophers give about where the self goes: the memory view (Locke), the body/animal view, and — in the other two — the no-self view (Hume's bundle of perceptions, the Buddhist anatta tradition) which denies there is any single self to move at all. Locke's own answer is the first. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.15, quoted at textbooks.whatcom.edu/phil101hagman/chapter/the-prince-the-cobbler/.

question: John Locke imagines a prince whose inner life — his whole sense of being himself — wakes up one morning inside a cobbler's body. To the prince, he knows perfectly well he is the prince; to the whole town, who see only the familiar body at the cobbler's bench, he is plainly the cobbler. Locke refuses to leave this split hanging. He names exactly one thing that, for him, settles which PERSON a being is across time. What does Locke say fixes the person?
answer: The thread of remembered awareness he can trace back through his own past
choices: The thread of remembered awareness he can trace back through his own past
The single living body that other people have always watched and recognized
The one immaterial soul that has been housed inside him from the start
The standing record the law keeps of who each citizen has long been
context: Locke deliberately splits the outside view from the inside view (Essay II.xxvii.15): to the world the unchanged body settles who the 'man' is — 'he would be the same cobbler to every one besides himself' — but Locke's verdict is that the PERSON is fixed by something else entirely. His answer (Essay II.xxvii.9) is consciousness: the self reaches exactly as far back as you can remember being. He rejects the rival criteria the other choices name — the living body, the immaterial soul (the view of Plato and Descartes), and any external register like the law — and pins personhood to the remembered thread of awareness alone. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.15 and II.xxvii.9, quoted at textbooks.whatcom.edu/phil101hagman/chapter/the-prince-the-cobbler/ and in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: Locke imagines Socrates asleep and dreaming, then Socrates awake. Suppose waking Socrates has not the faintest memory of anything 'sleeping Socrates' thought or did in the night — a total blank. Locke then draws a sharp conclusion about blame: it would be unjust, he says, to punish the waking man for the sleeper's deeds. On Locke's reasoning, what does that blank stretch of memory cut in two?
answer: The person, even though one living man continues right through the gap
choices: The person, even though one living man continues right through the gap
The man, even though one continuous person survives right through the gap
Neither one — sleep is a mere interruption that severs nothing at all
Both the man and the person, leaving nothing of the sleeper behind
context: The sleeping/waking Socrates case (Essay II.xxvii.19). For Locke the waking and sleeping Socrates are the same MAN but — in his special sense — not the same PERSON: the PERSON reaches exactly as far as memory reaches, so a true gap in consciousness severs the person there, while the MAN, the living organism, carries on unbroken. That is why he calls it unjust to punish the waking man for what he cannot remember doing. The same logic drives his harder drunk-man case. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.19, summarized in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: John Locke asks what makes something a PERSON at all, and not merely a living creature. A dog feels and a rock sits there, but Locke says only a person can do a certain reflective thing with its own mind — a power he makes the very definition of a person, setting it apart from every animal and object. Which power does Locke pick out as the mark of a person?
answer: Being able to hold itself in mind as itself, the same thinking thing across different times
choices: Being able to hold itself in mind as itself, the same thinking thing across different times
Being inhabited by one immaterial soul that has stayed unchanged since the creature's birth
Being one continuous living body that has grown without a break from infancy onward
Being the latest link in an unbroken family line whose name and blood it carries on
context: Locke's definition of a person (Essay II.xxvii.9): 'a thinking intelligent Being, that has reason and reflection, and can consider it self as it self, the same thinking thing in different times and places.' The defining mark is not the body, the soul, or a bloodline but a reflexive power — the ability to take oneself as one's own object and recognize oneself as the same thinker across time. This is distinct from his separate claim about what FIXES that same person over time (consciousness reaching backward); here the point is what qualifies a being as a person in the first place. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.9, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: Locke raises a problem against his own theory. A man gets blackout drunk, commits a crime, and the next morning honestly recalls nothing of it. By Locke's own memory rule the sober man arguably is not the same PERSON who acted. Yet the court convicts him, and Locke says it does so justly. He could have called the verdict a mistake; instead he defends it. What grounds does Locke give an earthly court for convicting this man?
answer: No earthly judge can inspect a man's awareness, so a court must rule on the outward deed it can prove
choices: No earthly judge can inspect a man's awareness, so a court must rule on the outward deed it can prove
A blackout is no real break in awareness, so the sober man is the very same person who acted
Drinking was a choice the man made knowingly, so he owns whatever that drinking later set loose
A final reckoning will weigh his true guilt, so an earthly court need not get the verdict right
context: The drunk-man case and Locke's two-court answer (Essay II.xxvii.22). Locke grants that real moral identity tracks consciousness, but no earthly judge can see inside a skull, so courts must go by the evidence of the body. He reserves the perfect verdict for a higher court: at 'the great Day, wherein the Secrets of all Hearts shall be laid open... no one shall be made to answer for what he knows nothing of.' Earthly justice judges the body; final justice judges the consciousness. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.22, discussed in Philosophy Now issue 157, philosophynow.org/issues/157/John_Locke_and_Personal_Identity.

question: To test how far his theory will stretch, Locke runs a deliberately wild thought experiment. Imagine your little finger were cut off, and — impossibly — your entire awareness, every memory and feeling of being you, went along with the severed finger and abandoned the rest of your body. Locke says he can follow his own rule to its strange end: 'self then would have nothing to do with the rest of the body.' On Locke's reasoning, which thing would now be YOU?
answer: The little finger, because your whole consciousness departed along with it
choices: The little finger, because your whole consciousness departed along with it
The body you left behind, because that is the creature that was born and grew
Both at once, since you cannot truly be divided no matter what is cut
Neither, since a self is far too grand a thing to ride off on a finger
context: The little-finger case (Essay II.xxvii.17), verbatim: 'should this consciousness go along with the little finger, and leave the rest of the body, it is evident the little finger would be the person, the same person.' Locke is not predicting biology; he is showing that his criterion is consciousness and nothing else — wherever the awareness goes, the self goes, even somewhere absurd. The same engine drives his day-man / night-man case. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.17, quoted via the Essay text at enlightenment.supersaturated.com/johnlocke/BOOKIIChapterXXVII.html.

question: Locke imagines one body run by two minds in shifts: a waking life that owns it all day, and a separate sleeping life that takes it over all night, each with no memory whatever of the other. The day-mind never recalls the night-mind's doings, and the reverse. Locke insists these are two distinct persons — then presses one step harder, asking whether that holds even if both minds happen to belong to a single shared soul. What does Locke conclude about that case?
answer: Even one shared soul would still not make the two minds the same person
choices: Even one shared soul would still not make the two minds the same person
A single shared soul would in fact prove the two minds one and the same
Two minds can never share one soul, so the question cannot even arise
The shared body, not the soul, would settle that they are one person
context: The day-man / night-man case (Essay II.xxvii.23). Two 'distinct incommunicable consciousnesses acting the same Body' are, Locke says, 'as distinct persons as Socrates and Plato' — and crucially this holds even if they share one soul. That is the heart of his most radical move: he pries the PERSON apart from the SOUL itself, so that even the very same soul does not guarantee the same person. The intuitive rival answer — that one shared soul must make them one person — is exactly the assumption Locke is rejecting. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.23, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: Locke calls 'person' a 'forensic term' — a courtroom word. He ties it not to flesh or spirit but to being, in his words, an 'intelligent Agent capable of a Law, and Happiness and Misery.' So when Locke labors to get 'the same person' exactly right across time, what is the deep thing he is really trying to pin down?
answer: Who rightly owns a past deed, and so deserves the credit or the blame for it
choices: Who rightly owns a past deed, and so deserves the credit or the blame for it
Which invisible soul is currently housed inside a particular living body
Which personality a body displays, cheerful or gloomy, bold or shy
How long a particular human animal has managed to stay biologically alive
context: Essay II.xxvii.26: person is a 'Forensick Term, appropriating Actions and their Merit; and so belongs only to intelligent Agents capable of a Law, and Happiness and Misery.' For Locke the whole question of identity is, at bottom, about accountability — who can justly be rewarded or punished for a deed — not about metaphysical substance. That is why memory matters so much to him: you can only fairly own a deed you can own up to. The soul view he is rejecting would instead pin identity to which immaterial substance you carry. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.26, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: Thomas Reid built a trap for Locke's memory rule. A boy is flogged for robbing an orchard. Years later that same youth, now a brave young officer, captures an enemy flag in his first battle, and on that day he still keenly recalls the flogging. Decades on he is an old general who recalls taking the flag but has utterly lost every trace of the orchard and the whipping. Reid says Locke's rule, applied honestly to these three, destroys itself. What goes wrong with the rule?
answer: Locke's rule chains identity link to link, yet a chain of overlaps need not join its two far ends
choices: Locke's rule chains identity link to link, yet a chain of overlaps need not join its two far ends
Locke's rule counts only vivid memories, and a faded one is too weak to carry the self forward
Locke's rule rests on memory, and memory can be wholly invented, so no single link can be trusted
Locke's rule tracks the person while the living man runs on unbroken, so in truth nothing is severed
context: Reid's Gallant Officer objection (Essays on the Intellectual Powers, 1785). Locke says you are whoever you can remember being. The general remembers the officer, and the officer remembered the boy — so by Locke's chain general = boy. But the general cannot remember the flogging at all, so by the same rule general ≠ boy. The flaw is that overlap does not carry all the way through: A links to B and B to C, yet A need not link to C. Later philosophers patched this by replacing raw memory with unbroken 'psychological continuity.' Source: Reid 1785, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: Bishop Joseph Butler thought Locke had made a 'wonderful mistake' — an error so basic it ran the whole theory backwards. Locke says that my remembering a past deed is the very thing that MAKES that deed mine. Butler compares this to knowledge, which can reveal a truth that was already true but can never manufacture one. Run Butler's analogy through to its conclusion: what is his charge against Locke?
answer: Memory of an act already assumes the act was mine, so it cannot be what first makes the self the same
choices: Memory of an act already assumes the act was mine, so it cannot be what first makes the self the same
Memory is too dim and patchy, so it cannot carry the whole weight of the self that Locke rests on it
Memory is locked inside one mind, so no outside judge could ever confirm who a person really is
Memory is a trait of the body, so Locke fastened the self to the wrong part of what we are
context: Butler's 'wonderful mistake' objection (1736), verbatim: 'consciousness of personal identity PRESUPPOSES, and therefore cannot CONSTITUTE, personal identity; any more than knowledge, in any other case, can constitute truth.' The worry is circularity: to remember doing a thing already means it was you who did it, so memory can report identity but cannot be what identity is built out of. It remains one of the two classic attacks on the memory theory, alongside Reid's. Source: Butler 1736, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: John Locke asks us to imagine a baby's mind at the very moment of birth, before the child has seen, heard, or done anything at all. Which picture matches how Locke said that newborn mind begins?
answer: A sheet of blank white paper, waiting for life to write on it
choices: A sheet of blank white paper, waiting for life to write on it
A full storehouse already stocked with every idea it will ever need
A clay tablet pressed at birth with the rules the child must obey
A flame that flickers out unless the world keeps feeding it fuel
context: This is the image later nicknamed the "blank slate" or tabula rasa, though Locke himself never wrote that Latin phrase. His real words ask us to suppose the mind "white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas," then ask how it ever comes to be furnished. The storehouse stands for the rival view (innate ideas) that Locke is arguing against. The slate is not infinitely blank, and Locke knew the nature-and-nurture question runs deeper than this one image; the bank takes no verdict on it. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Ch. I, sec. 2.

question: John Locke wanted to explain where every idea a person ever holds comes from: colors, words, numbers, all of it. He traced the whole lot back to one source that, he said, furnishes the empty mind. What did Locke name as that single source?
answer: From experience: everything a person lives through writes the ideas in
choices: From experience: everything a person lives through writes the ideas in
From reason working alone, with no help at all from the world outside
From teachers and tradition, handing down what earlier minds had learned
From sudden flashes of insight that arrive from nowhere we can name
context: Locke answers in one word: "experience." He writes that in experience "all our knowledge is founded, and from that it ultimately derives itself." The rival answer ("from reason alone") names the opposing tradition Locke set himself against. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Ch. I, sec. 2.

question: John Locke said every idea is fed by two "fountains." The first is plain enough: the five senses pouring in colors, sounds, and smells from the world outside. But Locke insisted on a SECOND fountain that owes nothing to the five senses. What was Locke's second source of ideas?
answer: The mind turning its gaze inward to watch its own thinking, doubting, and willing
choices: The mind turning its gaze inward to watch its own thinking, doubting, and willing
Ideas built into the soul before birth, needing no experience at all to appear
Memories handed down in the blood from a person's long-dead ancestors
Truths revealed all at once by God to the waiting, newly made mind
context: Locke named his two fountains SENSATION (the senses bringing in the outside world) and REFLECTION (the mind noticing its own inner workings: perceiving, thinking, doubting, willing). Both are still kinds of experience, so neither breaks the rule that nothing is born already written. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Ch. I, secs. 2 to 4.

question: Some thinkers said certain truths, like "a thing cannot both be and not be," are branded on every human soul at birth, so each of us secretly knows them from the very start. John Locke thought up a simple test to check whether any truth is really inborn. What was Locke's test?
answer: If a truth were branded on us at birth, infants and the unschooled would show it most clearly, yet they show no trace of it
choices: If a truth were branded on us at birth, infants and the unschooled would show it most clearly, yet they show no trace of it
If a truth were truly important, every wise teacher across all of history would have written it down in the very same words
If a truth were branded on us at birth, only the cleverest of scholars could ever dig down deep enough to uncover it at last
If a truth were real, then people everywhere would surely have invented the very same words to express it on their own
context: Locke argued that if logic-truths were stamped on every soul, they would be plainest in the people with the least schooling: "children, idiots, savages, and the grossly illiterate." Yet ask a baby whether "it is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be" and you get a blank stare, so the stamp is not there. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book I, Ch. II.

question: A friend handed John Locke a riddle. Picture a man blind from birth who has learned, by touch alone, to tell a metal sphere from a metal cube. One day his sight is cured, and the two shapes sit before him on a table, untouched. Locke and his friend agreed on the answer to a single question: could the man now tell which shape is the sphere using his EYES alone, before laying a finger on either?
answer: No: sight is a brand-new sense, and his mind has not yet learned to match what he sees to what he once felt
choices: No: sight is a brand-new sense, and his mind has not yet learned to match what he sees to what he once felt
Yes: a sphere and a cube look so plainly different that anyone with working eyes would name them at once
Yes: the shapes he learned by touch were waiting in his memory, ready for his new eyes to recognize
No: the fresh cure would leave his sight too blurred to make out any shape at all for many weeks
context: This is the famous Molyneux Problem. William Molyneux first mailed the blind-man puzzle to Locke in 1688; Locke later loved it ("Your ingenious problem will deserve to be published to the world") and slipped it into the 1694 second edition of the Essay. Both men answered NO: sight is a separate fountain the slate has not yet linked to touch. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Molyneux's Problem; Locke, Essay, Book II, Ch. IX (2nd ed.).

question: John Locke set out to disprove the idea that any moral rule is stamped on us at birth, so that we are all born knowing right from wrong. As his proof, he pointed to whole peoples in history who, he said, abandoned their own newborns in open fields to die of hunger or wild beasts, and felt no guilt at all. What did Locke conclude from it?
answer: That even "do not kill your child" cannot be inborn, since a whole people felt free to ignore it
choices: That even "do not kill your child" cannot be inborn, since a whole people felt free to ignore it
That those peoples were simply wicked, while the rest of mankind kept the rule God had written on them
That moral rules grow strong only when a harsh and hungry land forces a people to live by them
That children must be taught kindness early, before cruelty has any chance to take root in them
context: Locke used the horror to cut against "universal conscience": if even "do not kill your baby" were branded on every heart, no whole nation could have shrugged it off. Note this is LOCKE'S argument, not a settled verdict; Leibniz and later Kant held that morality does spring from something inborn, and the second choice is roughly their reply. The bank takes no side. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book I, Ch. III.

question: John Locke pictured the newborn mind as a blank sheet of paper, written on only by experience. Gottfried Leibniz rejected that picture and answered Locke with a famous rival image of the mind. Which image of the mind was Leibniz's?
answer: A block of veined marble whose grain already leans toward one statue hidden inside it
choices: A block of veined marble whose grain already leans toward one statue hidden inside it
A still pond that simply mirrors whatever happens to drift across its surface
A seed that will grow into one fixed plant no matter what soil it happens to meet
A lantern whose own flame lights up the things standing around it in the dark
context: Leibniz said the mind is not blank paper but a block of marble whose veins already trace the shape of Hercules; the statue is "in a way innate" in the stone, and experience is just the chisel that frees what the grain was already leaning toward. For Leibniz the inborn part is not finished facts but LEANINGS ("inclinations, dispositions, habits"); you are not born knowing 2+2=4, you are born built to grasp it. The seed (a fixed outcome no matter what) overstates his view and is the trap. Source: Leibniz, New Essays on Human Understanding, Preface.

question: John Locke said the state you're born into, before any king or police exist, isn't lawless chaos — it has one rule everyone is bound by: no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions. A traveler argues he owes this only where a sheriff might catch him. How does Locke answer the traveler?
answer: It binds you as a duty you owe others even when no one is watching to enforce it
choices: It binds you as a duty you owe others even when no one is watching to enforce it
It binds you only once you've signed an agreement promising to keep the peace
It binds you only while a stronger neighbor could plausibly punish you for breaking it
It binds you only after a government has written it down and made it the law
context: Locke, Second Treatise of Government §6 (Project Gutenberg #7370). Locke's state of nature is governed by a law of nature whose single razor-sharp rule is a DUTY owed to others, not merely a right you claim for yourself — which is what separates it from Hobbes's war of all against all.

question: A fountain in a town square runs with water free for everyone — it belongs to no one. A man dips his pitcher, fills it, and carries it home. John Locke used exactly this picture to settle a hard question: once the pitcher is full, whose water is it?
answer: It is his alone, because his own labor is what drew it out of the common fountain
choices: It is his alone, because his own labor is what drew it out of the common fountain
It stays everyone's, since the fountain it came from was free to the whole town
It belongs to whoever in the town happens to be thirstiest at that moment
It belongs to the town as a group, to be shared out by whoever governs them
context: Locke, Second Treatise §29 (Project Gutenberg #7370): the water 'in the pitcher is his only who drew it out.' The act of drawing the water — your labor — is what turns common water into private property. It is Locke's most vivid image for how work creates ownership.

question: A man boasts that being truly free means he can do absolutely anything he pleases — no rules, no limits, total liberty. John Locke flatly disagreed. What did Locke say real freedom actually is?
answer: Ordering your own life and goods as you wish, within laws that shield everyone from each other's violence
choices: Ordering your own life and goods as you wish, within laws that shield everyone from each other's violence
Doing whatever you have the strength and cunning to get away with, answering to no one
Obeying every command a ruler issues, since submitting to authority is the whole of freedom
Living entirely apart from other people, where no rule could ever reach or bind you
context: Locke, Second Treatise §57: freedom is not 'a liberty for every man to do what he lists,' and 'where there is no law, there is no freedom.' Locke separates liberty from license — law is what makes you free (by protecting you from others' violence), not what chains you, and freedom is not mere obedience to a ruler's will either.

question: John Locke argued that you carry the rights to life, liberty, and property with you BEFORE any government exists. Thomas Jefferson borrowed this triad almost word for word for the Declaration of Independence — but he dropped Locke's third right and wrote a different one in its place. Which phrase did Jefferson put where Locke had 'property'?
answer: the pursuit of Happiness
choices: the pursuit of Happiness
the security of the realm
the consent of the governed
the common good of all
context: johnlocke.org and the Bill of Rights Institute on Locke's influence on the Declaration. Jefferson kept Locke's 'life' and 'liberty' but swapped 'property' (or 'estate') for 'the pursuit of Happiness' — the word property never appears in the Declaration.

question: The earth, John Locke said, was given to all of mankind in common — so how could a single apple, or a field, ever become one person's PRIVATE property without first getting everyone's permission? Locke built his whole answer on one thing he says you own before you own anything else. What does Locke say you start out owning?
answer: Your own person and the labor of your body, which you join to whatever you work on
choices: Your own person and the labor of your body, which you join to whatever you work on
The first patch of ground you spot and claim aloud before any of your neighbors
Whatever share of the common earth a ruler has marked out and granted to you
Only what the rest of mankind has agreed in advance to let you call your own
context: Locke, Second Treatise §27 (UChicago Founders' Constitution): 'The labour of his body, and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his.' When you mix your labor with something unowned, you join something of your own to it — your work is what makes the world yours.

question: John Locke asks a blunt question: if free people already enjoyed life, liberty, and property in the state of nature, why on earth would they ever hand themselves over to a government? Rival thinkers gave rival answers. What did Locke say government is actually FOR?
answer: To supply a settled known law, an impartial judge, and the power to enforce a verdict
choices: To supply a settled known law, an impartial judge, and the power to enforce a verdict
To make its people good, holy, and worthy of the rights they hold
To rescue people from fear, want, and the war of all against all
To pass down the rule, the lands, and the authority first granted to Adam
context: Locke, Second Treatise §123–125. In the state of nature three things are missing: a settled written law, an impartial judge, and the power to back a verdict. Government is just those three fixes — not (against Hobbes) an escape from total war, and not (against Filmer) inherited Adamic authority.

question: Three thinkers gave three rival answers to 'why should I obey the government?' Robert Filmer and Thomas Hobbes were two of them; John Locke was the third. Filmer rooted all power in God's original grant to Adam. Setting Filmer's view aside, what was Locke's own answer about where governing power comes from and whether the people can ever reclaim it?
answer: It rises from the people by their consent, and they can take it back
choices: It rises from the people by their consent, and they can take it back
It is loaned by God to whichever ruler can keep firm order
It belongs to whoever holds the land and the wealth of the realm
It is fixed forever once the first generation agrees to obey
context: IEP: John Locke; SEP: Locke's Political Philosophy. Filmer traced power down from Adam; Hobbes made the sovereign absolute and irrevocable; Locke said power rises FROM the people, by consent, and can be reclaimed. Rights come first; government is a trustee.

question: John Locke had a problem: hardly anyone ever signs a document agreeing to obey their government, so how can he claim they consented at all? Rather than drop the idea of consent, Locke argued that a much smaller, everyday act is already enough to count as agreeing. In Locke's account, what is enough to count as consenting to obey?
answer: Enjoying the government's protection — even just using its roads — counts as agreeing
choices: Enjoying the government's protection — even just using its roads — counts as agreeing
Being born inside the country's borders binds you to obey for the rest of your life
Letting most of your neighbors vote, since their majority decides for everyone
Falling under a ruler's power by conquest obliges you to obey whoever rules you
context: Locke, Second Treatise §119; SEP (Simmons critique). Locke called this 'tacit consent': express consent is openly agreeing to join, but tacit consent is given merely by enjoying a government's protection — Locke reached so far for it that he counted even 'barely travelling freely on the highway' as proof. Critics like A. John Simmons argue this makes consent so easy it stops meaning anything.

question: John Locke insisted that a legislature does not OWN its power but only holds it for the people, the way a steward manages money that belongs to someone else. So what did Locke say becomes of that power the instant rulers turn it against the very people it was meant to serve?
answer: It is forfeited on the spot, because power held for an end is lost once that end is betrayed
choices: It is forfeited on the spot, because power held for an end is lost once that end is betrayed
It still binds the people, because power once handed over can never lawfully be undone
It passes to whichever official happens to stand next in line to take command
It must be endured until the rulers themselves decide to hand it back of their own will
context: Locke, Second Treatise §149: the legislature is 'only a fiduciary power to act for certain ends' — power held in TRUST, like money managed on someone else's behalf, not power the ruler owns. It is forfeited the instant the end is 'manifestly neglected, or opposed,' and the people keep a supreme power to remove or alter it.

question: John Locke didn't think everyone should grab as much land as they could — he attached a single limit to the very rule that lets your labor make land yours. What was Locke's condition before you could carve property out of the common ground?
answer: Only where there is enough, and as good, still left in common for others
choices: Only where there is enough, and as good, still left in common for others
Only where a ruler has first marked out and approved your particular claim
Only where every one of your neighbors has consented in advance to your claim
Only where the land has lain unused and unclaimed for many years before you
context: Locke, Second Treatise §27 — the 'enough-and-as-good' proviso. You can't fence off the whole river and leave your neighbor thirsty. Notably Locke does NOT require everyone's prior consent — your labor itself makes the thing yours, so long as enough and as good remains. He also added a spoilage limit (§31): take only what you can use before it rots.

question: John Locke set a limit on hoarding: take only what you can use before it rots, since letting your share spoil robs someone who'd have eaten it. Yet Locke also showed how a man could honestly 'heap up' great wealth without breaking this rule. What did Locke point to as the honest escape from the spoilage limit?
answer: Money, since durable gold and silver never rot the way food does
choices: Money, since durable gold and silver never rot the way food does
Charity, since giving the surplus away leaves nothing of yours to spoil
Conquest, since a larger realm can absorb whatever one man cannot use
Inheritance, since wealth passed to heirs is consumed across the generations
context: Locke, Second Treatise §46–49. Because gold and silver don't spoil, men tacitly agreed to put value on durable money and so could accumulate honestly. Locke's vivid line for the land-rich pre-money world (§49): 'in the beginning all the world was America.'

question: John Locke is famous for justifying revolution — yet he warned that people must NOT rise up over every bad law or small abuse, which 'will be born by the people, without mutiny or murmur.' He set a much higher bar before revolt becomes legitimate, and the American Declaration of Independence later echoed his very phrase. What did Locke say it takes?
answer: A long train of abuses revealing a deliberate design against the people's rights
choices: A long train of abuses revealing a deliberate design against the people's rights
A single act of cruelty severe enough to outrage the conscience of the nation
A majority vote of the people formally declaring that they withdraw their obedience
A foreign power willing to recognize and support the people's new government
context: Locke, Second Treatise §225. Revolution becomes legitimate only after 'a long train of abuses, prevarications, and artifices' — a phrase Jefferson echoed almost word for word in the Declaration ('a long train of abuses'). Locke is no hothead; ordinary bad laws must be endured.

question: When a ruler tears up the people's rights and tries to reduce them to slavery under his arbitrary power, common sense calls the people who then resist him 'rebels.' John Locke turned that word completely around. In Locke's account, who is truly guilty of rebellion?
answer: The ruler, who by breaking his trust brings back the state of war against his people
choices: The ruler, who by breaking his trust brings back the state of war against his people
The people, who by taking up arms have shattered the lawful peace of the realm
Both sides equally, since any resort to force makes a rebel of whoever uses it
Neither side, since in such a clash there is no longer any law to be guilty under
context: Locke, Second Treatise §226–227. The Latin rebellare means 'to bring back the state of war' — and it is the tyrant who does that. When rulers use the force in their hands to invade the people's liberties, THEY are 'guilty of rebellion,' not the people defending their rights (§222).

question: John Locke asks who is entitled to judge that a ruler has betrayed his charge and to remove him -- the ruler having no judge set over him on earth. His blunt answer overturns the assumption that a king answers to no one. Who holds that power of judgment?
answer: Those who handed him the job in the first place
choices: A council of the oldest and wisest judges
Those who handed him the job in the first place
The ruler himself, by weighing his own record
Whoever commands the largest army at the time
context: Locke, Second Treatise §240: 'who shall be judge whether his trustee or deputy acts well... but he who deputes him, and must... have still a power to discard him, when he fails in his trust?' The one who hires keeps the power to fire. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §240 (let.rug.nl / constitution.org).

question: Critics warned John Locke that letting people resist their rulers would spark revolt over every little grievance. Locke disagreed: people put up with plenty of mistakes without rising. He argued that a people only rouses itself to throw off a government under one specific condition. What is it?
answer: A long train of abuses all pointing the same way
choices: A single law that a large faction finds unjust
A long train of abuses all pointing the same way
A foreign king offering them a better bargain
A famine or plague that the ruler failed to stop
context: Locke replies that 'Great mistakes... will be born by the people without mutiny or murmur. But if a long train of abuses, prevarications and artifices, all tending the same way, make the design visible to the people,' then they act — it takes a visible pattern of tyranny, not one bad law. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §225 (let.rug.nl / constitution.org).

question: John Locke imagines a king who once governed under the law but now rules by naked force, brushing the law aside whenever it suits him. The people answer with arms of their own. Both sides are now fighting in earnest. Locke insists one side has earned a name the other has not -- the name 'rebel.' Which side is it, and why?
answer: The king -- by bringing back war, he is the true rebel
choices: The king -- by bringing back war, he is the true rebel
The people, the moment they first raised a weapon
Neither side, since both now wage open war as equals
The foreign powers who armed and funded the uprising
context: Those who 'set up force again in opposition to the laws, do rebellare -- that is, bring back again the state of war, and are properly rebels.' The Latin re-bellare means 'to bring back war,' so whoever re-introduces force, even a king, is the true rebel. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §§226-227 (let.rug.nl); etymology confirmed via VoegelinView, 'Redefining Rebellion.'

question: John Locke and the defenders of the throne fought over a single question: where does a ruler's power come from, and whose is it in the end? They gave their answers; Locke gave his. On Locke's account, what IS a ruler's power?
answer: A power held for the people, to be returned to them
choices: A power handed down from God to the king alone
A power won by the sword and held by force
A power inherited from Adam down the bloodline
A power held for the people, to be returned to them
context: Locke calls government a 'fiduciary' power — a 'Fiduciary Power to act for certain ends.' A fiduciary holds something in trust for someone else, the way a guardian or trustee does; because the power is conditional, 'there remains still in the People a Supream Power to remove or alter the Legislative' when it acts against the trust given them, and when the trust is broken the power 'devolves to the people.' Legitimacy is a loan held in trust, not a possession. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §149, §222, via University of Chicago Founders' Constitution.

question: Defenders of absolute monarchy argued that a people could simply consent to obey a king in everything, surrendering themselves completely. John Locke answered that one thing can never be handed over by any agreement, no matter how willingly. What can no contract give away?
answer: A people's right to preserve their own lives
choices: A people's right to preserve their own lives
A people's claim to a share of the common land
A people's freedom to worship as they choose
A people's voice in choosing their representatives
context: 'No Man, or Society of Men, having a Power to deliver up their Preservation... to the Absolute Will and arbitrary Dominion of another.' You cannot consent to your own enslavement, so no contract can make tyranny legitimate. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §220, via University of Chicago Founders' Constitution.

question: John Locke faces the hardest case: the people say their ruler has betrayed them, the ruler denies it, and no court on earth stands above them both to settle it. Locke borrows a phrase from the story of the biblical judge Jephthah for what the people may do as a last resort. What is that final remedy?
answer: To appeal to Heaven by taking up arms
choices: To submit and wait for the ruler to repent
To petition a neighboring Christian prince
To draw lots and abide by the outcome
To appeal to Heaven by taking up arms
context: With 'no Judge on Earth,' the people may 'appeal to Heaven' -- literally, take up arms and let God judge by the outcome who is in the right. Locke draws the image from the judge Jephthah facing the Ammonites. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §168, §241 (Founders' Constitution); Jephthah link via academia.edu, 'Jephthah, the Hebrew Bible, and John Locke's Second Treatise.'

question: John Locke answers the objection that his right of revolution would make governments unstable, forever trembling on the edge of revolt. He argues the opposite: granting the people this power actually makes revolution LESS likely. What is his reasoning for that paradox?
answer: A ruler who can be lawfully removed takes more care not to be
choices: A ruler who can be lawfully removed takes more care not to be
People who may revolt grow content and lose the appetite for it
The power is so rarely used that rulers soon forget it exists
Other nations will step in before any revolt can succeed
context: This power in the people 'is the best fence against rebellion, and the probable means to hinder it.' A ruler who knows the people may lawfully remove him is the ruler least likely to be removed -- the threat itself is the deterrent. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §226 (let.rug.nl).

question: A circle of scientists and philosophers meeting in 1920s Vienna proposed one ruthless rule for sorting real claims from fake ones: a sentence carries genuine meaning only if it is true by definition, the way a math equation is, OR you could check it against experience, at least in principle. They then turned the rule on a claim like 'an unseen soul survives the death of the body.' How did the Vienna rule classify that claim?
answer: As meaningless, saying nothing one could test either way
choices: As meaningless, saying nothing one could test either way
As a bold conjecture that future science will likely settle
As false, since no good reason supports believing it is real
As true, a matter of faith beyond the reach of evidence
context: The Vienna Circle's verifiability criterion of meaning: a statement is literally meaningful only if it is analytic (true by definition, like math or logic) OR empirically testable in principle. Anything failing both isn't false -- it is cognitively meaningless 'nonsense.' In one stroke that binned whole stretches of metaphysics, normative ethics, and theology, not as wrong but as saying nothing at all. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Vienna Circle' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/vienna-circle/).

question: Moritz Schlick founded and led the Vienna Circle, the group that branded most of old philosophy meaningless because no test could check it. On the morning of 22 June 1936 he was climbing the marble staircase of the University of Vienna, on his way up to give a lecture. The man who had tried to scrub metaphysics out of philosophy never reached the hall above. What ended Schlick's life on that staircase?
answer: A gunman waiting on the steps shot him dead where he stood
choices: A gunman waiting on the steps shot him dead where he stood
A failing heart gave out as he labored up the long stairs
A loose marble slab broke free and sent him crashing down
A rival blocked his path and shoved him hard down the steps
context: At about 9:20 a.m. on 22 June 1936 Schlick was shot four times with a 6.35mm pistol on the main marble staircase and died at the scene. The philosopher who had tried to rid the world of metaphysics was murdered as he climbed to teach. Source: Wikipedia, 'Moritz Schlick'; David Edmonds, 'The Murder of Professor Schlick' (Princeton University Press).

question: Rudolf Carnap of the Vienna Circle hunted for a perfect specimen of a sentence that sounds profound but, by his testing rule, states nothing whatever. He found one in the philosopher Martin Heidegger: 'The Nothing itself noths.' Carnap refused to call the line false. He called it nonsense dressed as a deep truth. What exact mistake did Carnap charge it with?
answer: It mistakes the word 'nothing,' which names no object, for the name of a thing
choices: It mistakes the word 'nothing,' which names no object, for the name of a thing
It mistakes a private feeling for a fact that holds true for everyone
It mistakes a circular restatement for a real step in an argument
It mistakes one sense of a word for another and slides between them
context: In his 1932 essay 'The Elimination of Metaphysics Through Logical Analysis of Language,' Carnap held up Heidegger's 1929 line 'Das Nichts selbst nichtet' as the model 'pseudo-statement': Heidegger had invented a verb 'to nothing' and treated 'Nothing' as if it named an object that could do something. Not false, said Carnap -- nonsense. In the same essay he called metaphysicians 'musicians without musical ability.' Source: Carnap, 'The Elimination of Metaphysics...' (1932); Aeon, 'Heidegger v Carnap.'

question: Otto Neurath of the Vienna Circle wanted to show how people actually improve what they know, and offered a famous picture. We are, he said, like sailors far out at sea, far from any harbor, whose ship has sprung leaks and needs rebuilding. In Neurath's image, how do the sailors rebuild the ship?
answer: By swapping in one fresh plank at a time, never leaving the water
choices: By swapping in one fresh plank at a time, never leaving the water
By steering to dry land and rebuilding the whole hull from the keel
By drafting a flawless design before they touch a single board
By abandoning the leaky ship and assembling a new one alongside
context: Neurath rejected the dream of resting all human knowledge on some perfectly certain bedrock; his boat is why. 'We are like sailors who on the open sea must reconstruct their ship but are never able to start afresh from the bottom. Where a beam is taken away a new one must at once be put there, and for this the rest of the ship is used as support.' No dry dock, no bedrock -- you rebuild knowledge while still floating on it. Quine later made the image famous in 'Word and Object' (1960). Source: Wikipedia, 'Neurath's boat'; Neurath, 'Anti-Spengler' (1921).

question: The Vienna Circle's program rested on a single rule: a statement is meaningful only if it is true by definition or testable against experience; anything else is nonsense. A critic then aimed the rule back at itself and pressed the awkward question -- does the rule pass its own test? Which response is the one that undoes the whole program?
answer: The rule fails its own test and so is meaningless by its own verdict
choices: The rule fails its own test and so is meaningless by its own verdict
The rule counts as true by definition and needs no test of its own
The rule is a practical recommendation, not a claim that could be tested
The rule proves itself each time a meaningless claim is rightly discarded
context: Here is the self-destruct: 'only definitions and testable statements are meaningful' is itself neither a definition nor empirically testable -- so by its own law it is meaningless nonsense, sawing off the branch it sits on. A.J. Ayer himself later conceded the strict form was 'self-stultifying.' Source: SEP, 'A.J. Ayer' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ayer/); Wikipedia, 'Language, Truth, and Logic.'

question: A.J. Ayer became the loudest English champion of the Vienna Circle's ideas, declaring at just 24 that talk of God, or of right and wrong, was not false but flatly meaningless. Decades later an interviewer asked the elderly Ayer what, in the end, had been the chief thing wrong with the whole movement he once preached. What was Ayer's answer?
answer: That nearly all of it had turned out to be false
choices: That nearly all of it had turned out to be false
That it had been far too cautious in its claims
That its critics had never genuinely grasped it
That it still stood up better than any rival did
context: Asked decades later what was chiefly wrong with logical positivism, Ayer replied, 'Well, I suppose the most important defect was that nearly all of it was false.' He also said flatly, 'Logical Positivism died a long time ago. I do not think much of Language, Truth and Logic is true... it is full of mistakes.' The movement's loudest English champion pronounced its death. Source: SEP, 'A.J. Ayer'; Wikipedia, 'Language, Truth, and Logic' (later-life interview quotes).

question: The Roman poet Lucretius wrote his whole philosophy of atoms and void as a grand epic poem — and he admitted exactly why. A doctor, he said, smears sweet honey around the rim of a cup so a sick child will drink the bitter medicine inside. In Lucretius's comparison, which part of his book is the honey?
answer: Its beautiful poetry
choices: Its beautiful poetry
Its theory of atoms
Its arguments against the gods
Its claim that death is nothing
context: Lucretius calls the medicine inside the cup bitter wormwood — his hard Epicurean physics — and the honey on the rim his sweet verse, the lure that gets the reader to swallow the lesson. By his own admission the poetry is the bait, not the teaching. Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.936-950 (the honey-and-wormwood simile); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius.

question: The Roman poet Lucretius retold a grim scene from the Trojan War to make a point about religion. The Greek king Agamemnon stands by while priests lead his own veiled daughter to the altar and kill her — a human sacrifice offered so the gods will free his becalmed war-fleet to sail. Lucretius caps the scene with one of the most biting lines in Latin, blaming a single force for the whole atrocity. What does he blame?
answer: Religious fear, which can drive people to do monstrous things
choices: Religious fear, which can drive people to do monstrous things
The gods themselves, who genuinely demanded the girl's blood
Agamemnon's cowardice in not defying his own priests
The long war with Troy, which had hardened everyone's heart
context: The daughter is Iphigenia, sacrificed at Aulis. Lucretius ends the scene with 'Tantum religio potuit suadere malorum' — 'So much evil could religion persuade.' His move: it is superstition, not piety, that pushes people to atrocity. Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.80-101 (line 101).

question: The Roman poet Lucretius reasoned his way to the existence of particles far too small for any eye to see — roughly two thousand years before anyone built a microscope. He started from one rule he thought undeniable: nothing ever springs from pure nothing, and nothing is ever ground away into pure nothing. What did that force him to conclude about the world's basic building blocks?
answer: They can never be destroyed and have always existed
choices: They can never be destroyed and have always existed
The gods keep creating fresh matter all the time
The world is one smooth stuff with no smallest parts
Any bit can be split forever into ever-tinier pieces
context: His foundational rule was 'nothing comes from nothing' (nil posse creari de nilo). Because nothing is ever made out of pure nothing AND nothing is ever ground away into pure nothing, the building blocks of the world must be indestructible and eternal — atoms. Reasoning purely from everyday observation, Lucretius arrived at particles far too small to see roughly two thousand years before anyone built a microscope. Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.149-264; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius.

question: The Roman poet Lucretius set out to cure people of the fear of death. His key claim was physical: the mind and soul are themselves made of atoms — fine particles knitted into the living body. From that single claim, how did he argue that death is nothing to fear?
answer: When the body dissolves the soul scatters too, so no one is left to suffer
choices: When the body dissolves the soul scatters too, so no one is left to suffer
The soul flies free of the body and lives on in a better place
The gods reward a brave death and punish a fearful one
Death is a long dreamless sleep from which the soul later wakes
context: Lucretius closes Book 3 with 'Nil igitur mors est ad nos' — 'death is nothing to us.' The reasoning move: if the mind is MATERIAL, it cannot outlive the matter it depends on, so there is no one left to experience any afterlife. (Cross-reference: this materialist soul pairs with the swerve, his account of free will.) Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 3 (esp. 3.830); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius.

question: In Lucretius's universe, atoms pour straight down through the empty void, every one of them falling at the exact same speed. Into this steady downpour he introduces the 'swerve' — at no fixed time or place, an atom tips a tiny bit off its straight path. Lucretius insists that without this minute veer, no world of any kind could ever take shape. Why not?
answer: Without it, the atoms would fall forever without ever meeting to collide
choices: Without it, the atoms would fall forever without ever meeting to collide
Without it, the atoms would drift apart and the world would thin into void
Without it, the atoms would lock in place and nothing could ever change
Without it, the atoms would scatter wildly and no shapes could ever hold
context: Students often think the swerve is ONLY about free will, but it also solves a physics problem: atoms falling like rain at equal speed would never touch, so they could never clump or build a world. The minimal sideways veer starts the very first collisions. (Pairs with the swerve's other job — leaving room for free will.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius; De Rerum Natura 2.216-293.

question: Lucretius feared his own physics had trapped him. If every atom moves only by being shoved by the atom before it, in one unbroken chain of cause and effect, then everything you will ever do was already locked in at the beginning of time — pure fate, no free will. His escape was the 'swerve': atoms tip slightly off the straight fall, at no set time or place. Why does adding the swerve let Lucretius keep free will?
answer: It adds a touch of real chance, so the future is not fully fixed in advance
choices: It adds a touch of real chance, so the future is not fully fixed in advance
A random veer is just luck, so it makes actions accidental, not freely chosen
It removes cause and effect entirely, so nothing about anyone is predictable
A person can decide by sheer will exactly when one of their atoms swerves
context: Without the swerve, Lucretius argues, atoms in fixed causal chains would leave no living thing able to originate a new motion of its own; the unpredictable veer 'snaps the bonds of fate.' The move to recognize is that a tiny built-in indeterminacy is what rescues choice from strict determinism — not the Latin label 'clinamen.' Note the rival readings: critics object that a purely random veer would make actions merely accidental rather than freely chosen, and others over-read the swerve as either total chaos or as minds commanding atoms on demand — Lucretius needs just a little indeterminacy, not those extremes. (Cross-references the free-will strand; the same swerve also starts the first atomic collisions.) Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 2.251-293; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius.

question: A regime promises its people one glorious final society and insists that history is marching there inevitably -- the end is fixed, only a matter of time. Jean-Francois Lyotard taught his children to be suspicious of exactly this shape of story. What is the danger he warns about when rulers tell a sweeping tale of a guaranteed wonderful future?
answer: The promised future becomes a blank check used to excuse harsh deeds in the present
choices: The promised future becomes a blank check used to excuse harsh deeds in the present
It cannot be tested or proven, so believing it is just an unscientific leap of faith
It quietly borrows its hopeful tone from older religions and is disguised theology
It is too tangled for ordinary people to follow without years of special schooling
context: This is the steel-manned reason Lyotard distrusts a 'metanarrative': a story that guarantees a glorious universal end-state can be used to license almost anything done in its name now. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that for Lyotard the demand to fold everyone into one Whole -- 'totality' -- 'produces terror through exclusion,' his central example of an unspeakable wrong being Auschwitz (which he analyzes as a 'differend,' a wrong the available language cannot present). The recognition skill, not the label: a sweeping 'history is inevitably heading toward X' tale can mask and enable atrocity in the name of the promised X. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Postmodernism'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Lyotard'.

question: Jean-Francois Lyotard argued that the one big story claiming to explain all of history and everyone's place in it had lost its grip. But he did not think this left people with nothing to believe. In his picture, what takes the place of the single all-explaining story?
answer: A crowd of small, local stories, each true enough for its own community and none claiming to fit all
choices: A crowd of small, local stories, each true enough for its own community and none claiming to fit all
A single better story, more carefully argued, that finally explains history correctly for all
Pure science alone, since only measurable facts survive once the storytelling has been stripped away
A return to ancient myths, retold word for word as the only tales worth a serious person's trust
context: Lyotard's terms are 'grands recits' (grand narratives) versus 'petits recits' (little narratives). What replaces the toppled big story is not nothing but a swarm of modest, local stories: Wikipedia frames it as 'a plurality of small narratives that compete with each other, replacing the totalitarianism of grand narratives,' and the Stanford Encyclopedia describes 'little or regional narratives at odds with one another.' Each one is valid for its own community without claiming to explain the universe. Sources: Wikipedia, 'The Postmodern Condition'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Jean-Francois Lyotard'.

question: Jean-Francois Lyotard noticed that once people stopped trusting the grand story that knowledge serves humanity's march toward freedom and truth, the old question 'but is it true?' quietly lost its authority in the universities. A different test slipped into its place. By what new measure, he warned, does a piece of knowledge then earn a place in the university?
answer: By whether it runs the system efficiently and can be packaged, sold, and put to work
choices: By whether it runs the system efficiently and can be packaged, sold, and put to work
By whether the wisest and most learned experts in the field have agreed to vouch for it
By whether it fits neatly with the picture of the world we already hold
By whether it can be defended in open debate against the strongest objections
context: Lyotard calls this new yardstick 'performativity' -- knowledge judged not by truth but by efficiency, its input-output ratio, and whether it can be sold. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy puts it bluntly: students 'no longer ask if something is true, but what use it is,' and knowledge 'is produced in order to be sold, and is consumed in order to fuel a new production.' Truth gets quietly swapped for usefulness-to-the-system. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Postmodernism'; Wikipedia, 'The Postmodern Condition' (truth 'replaced by performativity and efficiency in the service of capital or the state').

question: When the fanatical Almohad sect captured Cordoba in 1148, they gave the city's Jews a brutal choice: convert to Islam, flee, or be killed. Among the city's Jews was a boy of about thirteen, Moses Maimonides, who would one day be remembered as the greatest Jewish thinker of the Middle Ages. What did that conquest turn the rest of his younger life into?
answer: Long years as a refugee, wandering Spain and North Africa
choices: Long years as a refugee, wandering Spain and North Africa
A quiet life of study back home in his native Cordoba
A forced conversion to Islam he could never undo
A single swift voyage to a safe new home in Egypt
context: Maimonides (born c.1138) spent years on the move through Spain and North Africa -- Fez, then a stop in the land of Israel -- before finally settling in Fostat (Old Cairo). The Almohads gave conquered Jews no room to live openly as Jews. Source: Britannica, 'Moses Maimonides'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides' (iep.utm.edu/maimonid/).

question: Moses Maimonides made a strict rule of never taking money for teaching Torah, so his family lived on the trade of his younger brother David, a jewel merchant who carried their whole fortune on his voyages. Around 1171 David's ship sank in the Indian Ocean; David drowned, and the fortune sank with him. Maimonides fell into nearly a year of grief and illness. With the family's income gone, what did he turn to in order to make a living?
answer: He took up medicine and made his living as a physician
choices: He took up medicine and made his living as a physician
He at last accepted payment for teaching the Torah
He took over his drowned brother's jewel business
He sailed off to Spain to live on wealthy patrons
context: Maimonides wrote of David that 'whenever I see his handwriting or one of his letters, my heart turns over.' Only after the drowning did he take up the physician's trade that would consume the rest of his days. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides'; Chabad, 'Maimonides: His Life and Works' (chabad.org).

question: Maimonides wrote his great book, the Guide for the Perplexed, for one particular reader: a man of real faith who had ALSO mastered the philosophy of Aristotle, and was now torn in two. Scripture spoke of God having a hand, a throne, a face, and bursts of anger; Aristotle's reason said God must be bodiless and unchanging. Maimonides' whole answer to this reader rests on a single claim about where the conflict between them actually lies. What did he argue?
answer: The clash lives only in reading word-pictures literally
choices: The clash lives only in reading word-pictures literally
Reason must always give way to the plain text of Scripture
Scripture must always give way to the findings of reason
Faith and philosophy describe two unrelated worlds
context: There is no real war between Torah and Aristotle, Maimonides held: the verses that give God a body are figurative, and the perplexity dissolves once they are read that way. It is the mirror image of the move the Muslim philosopher Averroes made for the Qur'an. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/maimonides/).

question: To explain how he thinks we come to know God, Maimonides tells a story. A man has heard the word 'ship' and knows it names something real, but has never seen one. People tell him only what a ship is NOT: not an event, not a mineral, not a plant, not flat like a board, not a ball, not solid. They give him roughly ten such denials and nothing else -- no one ever tells him what a ship IS. Maimonides says our talk of God works the very same way. By this picture, what is he claiming about how we can know God?
answer: Stacking up true denials carries us genuinely nearer God
choices: Stacking up true denials carries us genuinely nearer God
Only a positive description could carry us nearer God
Denials clear away errors yet bring us no nearer God
Knowing the word for God is what carries us nearer Him
context: This is Maimonides' famous via negativa, or negative theology (Guide 1:60). We can never say what God IS, only what He is not -- and he insists each true denial is a real step CLOSER, not an empty subtraction: 'the more you can prove inapplicable to God, the better' (Guide 1:59). So he rejects the skeptic's reading (denials add no knowledge), the word-dependency objection, and the shortcut of positive description alike. Source: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed I:59-60, Friedlaender translation (ccel.org).

question: Scripture calls God merciful, gracious, and at times angry. But Maimonides denies that God has any such feelings, since feelings would change Him. So he reads those words a different way. Think of a single fire, he says: the same fire makes wax soft and clay hard. When Scripture says God 'is merciful,' Maimonides argues it really means which of these?
answer: God brings about what a merciful person would bring about
choices: God brings about what a merciful person would bring about
God's mercy and anger are two truly different states in Him
Mercy and anger are one act felt differently by those it meets
God's mercy is another name for His justice, not any act
context: Maimonides called these 'attributes of action' rather than attributes of essence: 'Every attribute found in the books of the deity is an attribute of His action and not an attribute of His essence' (Guide 1:53). One fire is not itself 'soft' and 'hard'; it merely produces those effects on different things. So 'God is merciful' names an effect God produces in the world, not an emotion God has, two states He holds, or a secret synonym for justice. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides' (fire/wax analogy).

question: Maimonides paints a parable: a king sits deep inside his palace, and every kind of person is placed by where they stand in relation to him. Some are out beyond the city walls, some stand in the city itself, some walk the road toward the palace, some have reached its outer wall and circle it, some wait in the antechamber, and a few stand in the inner court WITH the king. Maimonides says one single thing decides how near to the king -- and so to God -- each person stands. What is that one thing?
answer: How deeply they truly understand what God is
choices: How deeply they truly understand what God is
How strictly they obey every last commandment
How freely they give their wealth to the poor
How many long hours they pour into prayer
context: In the Parable of the Palace (Guide 3:51), the dutiful law-keepers reach the gate but only those who have demonstrated what can be proved about God enter the inner court with the king. Nearness to God is depth of understanding, not piety alone. Source: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed III:51, Friedlaender translation (sacred-texts.com/jud/gfp).

question: Maimonides insisted that 'good' and 'wise,' said of God, can only mean God LACKS no good and no wisdom -- pure denial, since any real likeness to human goodness would drag God down to our scale. A century later Thomas Aquinas studied this. He agreed the crude literal attributes fail and that God is perfectly simple, but he rejected Maimonides' move of bare denial and gave his own account of how 'good' and 'wise' relate to God. What account did Aquinas give?
answer: They fit God by analogy, a real but unequal likeness
choices: They fit God by analogy, a real but unequal likeness
They fit God in the very same sense they fit people
They fit God only as a faint borrowed word-picture
They fit only God's effects, never God's own being
context: Three thinkers, three answers to one problem. The Muslim philosopher Avicenna and then Maimonides chose negation: God is described 'only by negation.' Aquinas chose analogy -- 'good' is said of God and of people by a scaled, genuine resemblance, neither identical nor merely a word. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides'; Marquette, 'Maimonides and Aquinas on Divine Attributes' (epublications.marquette.edu).

question: Aristotle watched people everywhere forming towns and cities, and asked a deep question: why do humans gather together at all, instead of living scattered and alone? On Aristotle's view, why do humans live in communities?
answer: We are by nature built for shared life; community completes a human
choices: We are by nature built for shared life; community completes a human
We strike a deal to guard our property and trade our goods in safety
We cluster only because rulers herd scattered people into walled towns
We gather by habit, the way chance travelers come to share one road
context: This is the heart of Aristotle's famous claim that 'man is by nature a political animal' (Greek: zoon politikon). He held that the polis, or city, is a creation of nature, not merely a handy convenience: we don't just live NEAR each other, we are made for shared community life, and the impulse toward it is implanted in us. The other choices are real rival theories of why people associate (a contract for property and trade, force from rulers, or mere habit), but Aristotle grounds community in human nature itself. Politics Book I, ch. 2, Bekker 1253a. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Aristotle, Politics 1253a (Rackham trans., Harvard Univ. Press 1944); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Political Theory.'

question: Aristotle argued that needing a community is woven into being human, so a being who could live with NO community at all, perfectly self-sufficient and needing no one, would not really be a man at all. Such a creature, he wrote, must be one of two things. Which pair did he name?
answer: A beast or a god
choices: A beast or a god
A monster or an angel
A demon or a spirit
A brute or a titan
context: Aristotle's point: needing others is part of being HUMAN, so anyone who truly needed no community would have to fall outside humanity entirely, either below it or above it. Jowett (1885) renders the line 'he must be either a beast or a god'; Rackham (1944) has 'a lower animal or a god.' Bekker line 1253a27, Politics Book I, ch. 2. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Politics 1253a (Rackham); cross-checked MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett 1885).

question: Aristotle agreed that people first band together just to STAY ALIVE, finding food and safety in numbers. But mere survival, he insisted, is not the real point of a city. Once it exists, a true community aims at something higher. What did Aristotle say the city is really for?
answer: To help its members live WELL, in a flourishing life
choices: To help its members live WELL, in a flourishing life
To grow as rich and as powerful as it possibly can
