A princess, not a professor, framed the question that still defines the field. The other three choices are genuine criticisms later aimed at Descartes' system, but they were not the line Elisabeth herself took. Source: SEP, Elisabeth, Princess of Bohemia; MIT Press Reader, 'Descartes and the Discovery of the Mind-Body Problem.'

question: Pressing Rene Descartes in June 1643, Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia made a startling admission. After turning his account of how the soul moves the body over and over, she found she simply could not believe it. She told him there was one wild-sounding belief she would find EASIER to accept than his account - and named it outright. Which belief did Princess Elisabeth say she would sooner accept?
answer: That the soul has size and takes up space, the way matter does
choices: That the soul has size and takes up space, the way matter does
That the body, and not the soul, is what truly does our thinking
That the soul and the body never interact and only seem to
That God moves our limbs for us at the moment we decide to
context: Her letter of 10 June 1643: 'I admit that it would be easier for me to concede matter and extension to the soul than to concede the capacity to move a body and to be moved by it to an immaterial thing.' She'd sooner believe the soul is physical than swallow that a no-size, no-place thing can shove matter. The other three options are genuine historical escape routes from the interaction problem. Source: Modern Reformation, 'Elisabeth of the Palatinate and the Mind-Body Problem'; SEP, Elisabeth, Princess of Bohemia.

question: Rene Descartes' theory needed the pineal gland to swing to and fro in the brain's fluid, so the soul could rock it like a tiny lever and steer the body. In 1669 the anatomist Nicolas Steno carefully dissected the gland and reported what he actually saw under the knife - and what he saw quietly demolished Descartes' whole mechanism. What did Steno find when he opened the brain?
answer: The gland sits firmly anchored in place and is ringed about by veins
choices: The gland sits firmly anchored in place and is ringed about by veins
The gland can be rocked, but by the pulse of the blood, not by the soul
The gland is fed by great arteries that pump right through it
The gland comes paired, one half mirroring the other across the brain
context: Descartes claimed the gland dangled freely in the fluid-filled ventricles so it could swing, bathed by arteries. Nicolas Steno (Steensen) showed in 1669 that the pineal is firmly anchored, not suspended, and surrounded by veins, not arteries - so it physically cannot tilt and steer the 'spirits' the way the theory required. Source: SEP, Descartes and the Pineal Gland, citing Steensen 1669.

question: A herald struts into a tavern of ten ordinary drinkers, each earning about fifty thousand a year, and announces that the AVERAGE fortune in the room is now beyond a king's. He is not lying: moments earlier the richest man alive, with a billion-a-year income, sat at the bar, and adding his pile to the ten and dividing by eleven really does make the 'average' a hundred million apiece. A patron wants to tell a newcomer what a typical drinker here actually earns. Which figure should she give him?
answer: Report the earnings of the middle person once all are lined up by income, still about fifty thousand
choices: Report the earnings of the middle person once all are lined up by income, still about fifty thousand
Report the average the herald gave, since the arithmetic of adding up every income and then dividing is correct
Report the figure halfway between the poorest and richest earner, splitting the gap down the middle
Report the income that more people in the room earn than any other, since it is the most common one
context: This is the median versus the mean. The single huge outlier (the richest man) drags the mean up to a figure no actual drinker matches, while the median — the middle person once everyone is lined up by income — still reports the true typical earner. The 'average' that misleads here is called a misleading average. Source: 'When Bill Gates Walks Into a Bar' (introductorystats.wordpress.com): mean leaps to ~$100M while the median patron is unchanged at about $50,000.

question: A town crier proclaims that assaults in the village have surged 'a full hundred percent' over last year, and panic spreads through the market. The constable, who keeps the actual ledger, is unimpressed. He says the alarming percentage is true yet tells the villagers almost nothing about their real danger. What single fact in his ledger drains the scare of its force?
answer: Last year the ledger recorded one assault, and this year it recorded two
choices: Last year the ledger recorded one assault, and this year it recorded two
Last year the ledger recorded two hundred assaults, and this year four hundred
Last year the ledger recorded ninety assaults, and this year one hundred eighty
Last year the ledger recorded a thousand assaults, and this year two thousand
context: A percentage with no baseline is nearly empty: every choice here is a +100% rise, but a jump from one case to two is a triviality while two hundred to four hundred is a real emergency. The scary percent says nothing until you know the raw base. The fix is to demand the raw counts and a real baseline (such as cases per 100,000 people), not the bare percent. Source: gitnux.org misleading crime statistics and the UCI Kubrin analysis ('more than 1,000% increase' from a baseline of almost zero).

question: A merchant wants the council to believe his guild's output is exploding, though it has crept up barely one percent. He keeps every true number exactly as recorded and changes nothing in the data, yet draws a chart whose line rockets up like a cliff-face. A rival accuses him of a trick of the eye. What did the merchant do to the chart itself to make a gentle rise look like a surge?
answer: He cut the bottom off the vertical axis so it no longer begins at zero
choices: He cut the bottom off the vertical axis so it no longer begins at zero
He widened the gaps between the gridlines near the top of the chart
He squeezed the chart narrow so the same climb rose over a shorter width
He tilted the whole chart on the page so the line leaned more steeply
context: Darrell Huff named this the 'gee-whiz graph.' The numbers stay perfectly honest; the deception lives entirely in where the axis begins and how it is scaled. Chop the bottom off the vertical axis so it no longer starts at zero, and a true one-percent rise looks like a vertical cliff. Source: Darrell Huff, How to Lie with Statistics, ch. 5 'The Gee-Whiz Graph' (truncated/non-zero y-axis).

question: A pamphlet roars that a full third of the women at Johns Hopkins had married faculty members, and readers picture a scandal of professors hunting students. A statistician asks for the raw count behind the percentage and the scandal evaporates at once. The true number, he shows, makes the headline almost meaningless. What did the raw count reveal?
answer: Only three women were enrolled, and exactly one of the three had married a faculty member
choices: Only three women were enrolled, and exactly one of the three had married a faculty member
Three hundred women were enrolled, and a full hundred of them had married a faculty member
Ninety women were enrolled, and a solid thirty of them had married a faculty member
Thirty women were enrolled, and a clear ten of them had married a faculty member
context: A big-sounding percentage on a tiny base means almost nothing. Every choice here works out to the same one-third, but a third of three hundred is an ordinary fact while a third of three is one marriage — the figure is true and the impression is a lie. Always ask for the raw count and who was included before being moved by a percent. Source: Darrell Huff, How to Lie with Statistics (the Johns Hopkins example: 3 women, 1 married = 33⅓%).

question: A man waves away the Surgeon General's report linking tobacco to lung disease with a single story: his Uncle Harry smoked for forty years and died hale at ninety. The vivid tale feels more convincing to him than a stack of dry mortality tables drawn from millions of smokers. A careful thinker grants that Uncle Harry is real, yet says the story cannot overturn the report. What is the flaw in trading the tables for the tale?
answer: One survivor cannot move a rate measured across millions; he is the rare exception the tables already counted
choices: One survivor cannot move a rate measured across millions; he is the rare exception the tables already counted
The Surgeon General's tables ought to be trusted absolutely, since careful official reports do not contain real errors
Personal stories carry no weight whatsoever and so should never be allowed to enter a discussion about health
Uncle Harry must have had some hidden habit that quietly protected him, which the man relating the tale simply failed to notice
context: The move of leaning on one vivid anecdote against solid aggregate data is the fallacy of misleading vividness. A rate measured across millions of people already includes the lucky survivors; a single memorable exception does not change the rate — it is exactly the kind of case the data has already weighed. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (Misleading Vividness; the Uncle Harry / Surgeon General illustration).

question: In 1936 a great magazine mailed ten million ballots and counted nearly two and a half million back, the largest political poll ever taken, and declared Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt then swept every state but two. A young pollster named George Gallup, asking only fifty thousand people, had called the landslide nearly to the point. Why did the magazine's enormous sample fail so spectacularly?
answer: Its ballots went only to car and telephone owners, the well-off who leaned against Roosevelt
choices: Its ballots went only to car and telephone owners, the well-off who leaned against Roosevelt
Its tally counted only the eager few who bothered to mail a ballot back, a self-picked slice of the nation
Its readers deliberately lied on the ballots they returned in order to embarrass the magazine they disliked
Its young rival George Gallup had merely guessed luckily, as any small poll sometimes happens to do
context: This is the biased-sample fallacy: a huge but skewed sample loses to a small representative one. The Literary Digest drew its names from car owners, telephone subscribers, and its own readers — the well-off, who skewed anti-Roosevelt during the Depression. Gallup polled only ~50,000 but chose them to mirror the country, and was right within about one percent. The poll was so wrong it helped kill the magazine. Source: Wikipedia, Literary Digest (2.38M responses, predicted Landon ~57%, actual FDR landslide; all states but Maine and Vermont).

question: An accountant reports a single company's single year two ways to two different audiences. To the shareholders he announces 'profits up forty percent'; to the tax board he sighs that profits are 'down sixty percent.' Both statements are perfectly accurate and describe the very same year's very same earnings, with no figure invented or changed. How can one true year of profit be honestly called both a rise and a fall?
answer: Each percentage is measured against a different past year, so the same profit grows from one and falls from another
choices: Each percentage is measured against a different past year, so the same profit grows from one and falls from another
He has blurred the profit with the profit margin, two different quantities, between the two separate reports
He swapped the kind of average he relied on, giving the mean to one audience and the median to the other audience
He measured the change one way as plain growth and the other way as growth corrected for the year's inflation
context: Huff showed one set of profit numbers can be honestly reported five different ways — the same year was both 'an increase of 40 percent (compared with the 1935–39 average)' and 'a decrease of 60 percent from last year.' Every figure is accurate; the chooser just selects the baseline that serves the story. A percentage is meaningless until you know percent OF WHAT. Source: Darrell Huff, How to Lie with Statistics (the five framings of one profit figure).

question: After two of Sally Clark's babies died in their cribs, an expert witness told the 1999 jury that the chance of two such deaths striking one family was 'one in seventy-three million.' He reached the number by taking the odds of a single crib death, about one in eight thousand, and multiplying that figure by itself. The Royal Statistical Society later declared the calculation had no statistical basis, and her conviction was overturned. What was wrong with multiplying the two chances together?
answer: The two deaths are not independent, since shared genes and home make a second far likelier once the first has occurred
choices: The two deaths are not independent, since shared genes and home make a second far likelier once the first has occurred
The odds of a single crib death were really far longer than one in eight thousand, throwing off the entire sum
Multiplying any two probabilities is forbidden in mathematics, so the witness ought to have added them instead
A jury cannot be given any numerical odds at all, because plain people are quite unable to weigh probabilities
context: You may multiply two probabilities only when the events are independent — like separate coin flips. Two crib deaths in one family are not: shared genes and home conditions make a second death far likelier once one has happened, so squaring the single-death odds (about 1 in 8,543, giving ~1 in 73 million) was invalid. The Royal Statistical Society said the figure had 'no statistical basis'; Clark's 2003 acquittal followed, and the expert was struck off. Multiplying probabilities that aren't independent had helped jail an innocent mother. Source: Wikipedia, Sally Clark.

question: A castle has one rule: if the drawbridge is down, a knight on horseback can ride across. A scout gallops back with word that the drawbridge is, in fact, down right now. The captain says the knight can definitely cross — no need to go watch the gate himself. What makes him so sure, before anyone has even seen the knight cross?
answer: Grant the rule, confirm its trigger truly happened, and the result it promises must hold
choices: Grant the rule, confirm its trigger truly happened, and the result it promises must hold
Drawbridges are usually left down, so crossing is the safe bet in almost every such case
Watching the knight reach the far bank would be the only way to truly know it is possible
A scout's report all by itself counts as solid proof of whatever he happens to claim
context: This is modus ponens (Latin 'modus ponendo ponens,' 'the mode that by affirming, affirms'): grant 'if P then Q,' confirm P, and Q is locked in — the conclusion cannot escape. Source: philosophyalevel.com (If P then Q); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modus_ponens.

question: A village lives by one rule: if the volcano is about to erupt, the warning bell in the tower rings. One quiet morning the bell has stayed silent. The elder tells everyone to relax and stand down, without climbing up to inspect the crater himself. Granting that same rule, how can a bell that never rang justify the elder in standing the village down?
answer: The rule promises a ringing bell whenever the danger is real; the absence of that ring rules the danger out
choices: The rule promises a ringing bell whenever the danger is real; the absence of that ring rules the danger out
A bell that stays silent settles nothing, since the rule only ever described what a ringing bell would mean
Danger could be looming all the same, since no rule tying a bell to a mountain can be trusted to hold
Nothing short of the elder climbing up and eyeing the quiet crater himself could justify standing down
context: This is MODUS TOLLENS, modus ponens's valid backward-running cousin: 'If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.' Ponens fires the rule forward from a true trigger; tollens fires it in reverse from a missing result. (Don't confuse it with the INVALID 'denying the antecedent,' which switches off the trigger — here the missing RESULT is what does the work.) Source: quillbot.com/blog/reasoning/modus-tollens; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modus_tollens.

question: A scout reports to the king: if the eastern pass is clear, the army can march at dawn. Word comes that the eastern pass is indeed clear. The general means to hand his officers the one-word command 'March!' But an aide objects that he cannot give that order without restating the whole 'if the pass is clear' rule right beside it. Granting the rule and the scout's report, who has it right?
answer: The general: once the trigger is confirmed, the conclusion is settled and travels on its own
choices: The general: once the trigger is confirmed, the conclusion is settled and travels on its own
The aide: a conclusion keeps its force only while the rule that yields it rides alongside
The aide: until the conclusion is spoken aloud it has not yet been made true at all
The general: an officer of his rank may issue any command he likes, rule or no rule
context: Because it pulls the consequent loose from the conditional once the antecedent fires, modus ponens is also called the LAW OF DETACHMENT (rule of detachment): you detach Q and keep it on its own. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modus_ponens.

question: Everyone agrees on the castle's rule: if the enemy is marching on them tonight, the watch lights the war-beacon on the hill. After dark, a guard spots the war-beacon blazing and cries out that the enemy must be marching on them right now. Granting the very rule everyone accepts, why does the lit beacon fail to prove the enemy is on the march?
answer: A beacon can be lit for more than one reason, so its blaze proves nothing certain about the enemy
choices: A beacon can be lit for more than one reason, so its blaze proves nothing certain about the enemy
The rule plainly runs both ways, so a blazing beacon guarantees a marching enemy in return
The watch would never light that beacon except for a real attack, so the guard read it right
Only a scout sent right up to the enemy's camp could ever settle whether they are marching
context: This broken backward move ('Q is true, therefore P') is the fallacy called affirming the consequent. The rule only runs one way; a beacon can be lit by a careless watchman or a drill, not just a real attack. Source: quillbot.com/blog/reasoning/modus-ponens; fallacyfiles.org/afthecon.html.

question: A teacher writes the class rule on the board: if you finish the quiz early, you may read at your desk. A student who is still working insists that this means he is now forbidden to read, since he did not finish early. Granting the very rule on the board, why is the student wrong to think not finishing early shuts the reading door on him?
answer: The rule only says what early finishers may do; it never claimed they are the only readers allowed
choices: The rule only says what early finishers may do; it never claimed they are the only readers allowed
The teacher surely meant to let the whole class read, so the rule as written can simply be set aside
He can always finish early next time, so the rule never really blocks his reading at all
Finishing early and being allowed to read go hand in hand, so missing one means missing the other
context: Switching off the trigger does not switch off the result — this is the fallacy of denying the antecedent ('if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q'). The rule never promised Q comes ONLY from P. Source: quillbot.com/blog/reasoning/denying-the-antecedent; philosophyalevel.com.

question: Two builders look at an argument shaped 'if the gate is locked, the dog stays in the yard; the gate is locked; so the dog stays in.' The first says it just tends to work out in practice. The second insists on something stronger: with THIS argument, there is simply no way to grant both starting claims and still deny the ending. What does the second builder think delivers that ironclad guarantee?
answer: The bare pattern it follows, which would hold up no matter what the argument was about
choices: The bare pattern it follows, which would hold up no matter what the argument was about
A long run of real yards where this very conclusion was checked and held up
The plain fact that its starting claims happen to be true in this case
The homely subject matter, familiar enough that few would ever dispute it
context: A valid argument 'takes a form that makes it impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion nevertheless to be false.' Validity lives in the FORM, not in the topic or a track record. Source: IEP, Validity and Soundness (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: A logician offers a deliberately ridiculous argument: 'All toasters are made of gold; all gold things are time-travel devices; so all toasters are time-travel devices.' He then insists it is a flawless, valid argument anyway. A student protests that the conclusion is obviously nonsense. The logician agrees the conclusion is false in the real world — yet stands by calling the argument valid. On what grounds can he?
answer: Were those false claims somehow true, the conclusion would be forced — that is all validity asks
choices: Were those false claims somehow true, the conclusion would be forced — that is all validity asks
A conclusion that is plainly false in real life is enough to prove the whole argument valid
An argument counts as valid the moment every one of its starting claims is actually true
Validity is just another name for an argument whose conclusion the audience finds convincing
context: Validity is about form, not real-world truth: IF the premises were true the conclusion would have to follow. A valid argument whose premises are ALSO actually true is called SOUND. This one is valid but not sound. Source: IEP, Validity and Soundness (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: Lewis Carroll, the logician who wrote Alice in Wonderland, published a teasing little dialogue in 1895 called 'What the Tortoise Said to Achilles.' The Tortoise happily grants both starting facts of an argument but flatly refuses to accept the conclusion they force. Each time Achilles writes the connecting rule down as one more agreed premise, the Tortoise nods, accepts that too — and still won't budge to the conclusion, demanding yet another rule, forever. What was Carroll showing with this endless stalling?
answer: An inference rule must be allowed to ACT, not just be stacked on as one more premise
choices: An inference rule must be allowed to ACT, not just be stacked on as one more premise
Achilles simply had not yet written down enough premises to finish the argument off
The Tortoise had quietly spotted a real hidden flaw lurking in the original argument
Two true starting facts can never actually force any conclusion at all on their own
context: Carroll's tale (Mind, 1895) shows modus ponens can't be reduced to 'just one more premise' — try, and you fall into infinite regress (premise C, then D, then E...). The rule has to be permitted to detach the conclusion. The title nods to Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the tortoise. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_the_Tortoise_Said_to_Achilles.

question: A guard dog barks whenever it senses an intruder. One night it stays completely silent. A detective reasons backward from that silence. Which conclusion does the silence actually guarantee?
answer: No intruder came near — a real intruder would have forced a bark, so silence rules one out.
choices: No intruder came near — a real intruder would have forced a bark, so silence rules one out.
An intruder came but the dog failed — the silence proves the dog was defective tonight.
Nothing can be concluded — a silent dog simply tells you nothing either way.
An intruder probably came — a silenced dog is exactly what a clever burglar arranges.
context: This is the valid form logicians call modus tollens (Latin modus tollendo tollens, 'the mode that by denying denies'), also called denying the consequent. The rule 'if intruder, then bark' guarantees the bark; so a MISSING bark works backward to rule the intruder out completely. It is the same trick Sherlock Holmes uses with 'the dog that did nothing in the night-time' — the silence itself is the clue. Source: Wikipedia, Modus tollens (dog/intruder example).

question: In chemistry class you learn that any acid will turn blue litmus paper red. You dip the paper into a mystery liquid and it stays blue. Your lab partner shrugs, 'that proves nothing.' Why is your partner wrong — what can you firmly conclude?
answer: It is not an acid — the missing red rules acid out completely.
choices: It is not an acid — the missing red rules acid out completely.
It must be a base — blue is the telltale sign of a base.
It is probably water — only plain water leaves litmus blue.
Nothing is settled — a longer dip might still redden it.
context: An everyday lab use of modus tollens: 'if acid, then red; the paper is NOT red; therefore not an acid.' Because the conditional promises that EVERY acid reddens the paper, the absent red color, read backward, conclusively rules 'acid' out. Notice you cannot conclude what the liquid IS — only what it is not. Source: quillbot.com, What Is Modus Tollens (litmus/acid example).

question: Everyone agrees: if it is snowing, then it is cold out. Mara argues 'it is NOT cold today — so it is not snowing.' Jonah argues 'it is NOT snowing today — so it is not cold.' Whose reasoning is logically airtight?
answer: Mara's only — snow always brings cold, so no cold means no snow; no snow leaves cold's other causes open.
choices: Mara's only — snow always brings cold, so no cold means no snow; no snow leaves cold's other causes open.
Jonah's only — snow is the cause of cold, so once the snow is gone the cold must be gone too.
Both are airtight — when either snow or cold goes missing, the other one is cancelled along with it.
Neither is airtight — you can never run an argument from one 'not' across to another 'not.'
context: The valid move and its fake twin look almost identical — the difference is WHICH part you deny. Mara denies the THEN-part (the consequent): valid modus tollens. Jonah denies the IF-part (the antecedent): the invalid fallacy called 'denying the antecedent' — it fails because it could be freezing cold with no snow at all, for entirely other reasons. Source: quillbot.com, denying the antecedent (snow/cold example).

question: A knight reasons: 'If a dragon were in this cave, the walls would be scorched black. The walls are cold and damp. So no dragon is here.' His squire objects that he never even looked for the dragon — only at the walls. Why is the knight's conclusion still completely certain?
answer: Because the rule makes scorching unavoidable — cold walls are flat-out impossible with a dragon there, so it is ruled out.
choices: Because the rule makes scorching unavoidable — cold walls are flat-out impossible with a dragon there, so it is ruled out.
Because dragons are genuinely rare creatures — cold walls make one very unlikely here, though not strictly impossible.
Because he checked the walls first — reading the strongest clue settles it without facing the beast.
Because a missing sign always proves a missing thing — no scorching simply means no dragon in sight.
context: The dragon is a made-up illustration, not a legend. The point: a TRUE conditional guarantees the effect always follows the cause, so a missing effect doesn't merely make the cause unlikely — it makes it impossible, a CERTAIN conclusion, not a probable one. That guaranteed link is exactly what separates valid modus tollens from a mere good guess. Source: queue framing_note + philosophyalevel.com (If P then Q / dragon-cave example).

question: After a dry night with no rain, Theo finds the lawn soaking wet and insists 'that's impossible — it didn't rain, so the grass cannot be wet.' His reasoning has a specific hole. What exactly is the flaw in 'no rain, therefore no wet grass'?
answer: Rain is only one cause of wet grass — dew or a sprinkler could soak it, so no rain still allows wet grass.
choices: Rain is only one cause of wet grass — dew or a sprinkler could soak it, so no rain still allows wet grass.
He flipped the rule backward — wet grass would show it rained, but a dry sky shows nothing about the grass.
Rain never really wets grass at all — the supposed link between them was a mistake from the start.
He skipped checking the weather report — without the forecast he cannot say a thing about the wet lawn.
context: Theo commits the fallacy that imitates modus tollens: denying the antecedent. It fails because an effect can have MORE than one cause — ruling out one possible cause (rain) does not rule out the effect (wet grass), since dew, a sprinkler, or a burst pipe could do it. Real modus tollens never makes this error: a true conditional promises the effect happens whenever the cause does, so a MISSING effect cleanly kills the cause. Source: quillbot.com, denying the antecedent (grass/rain example).

question: A logician claims that 'If it is a rose, then it is a flower' and 'If it is NOT a flower, then it is NOT a rose' are not two facts but ONE fact said two ways — flip both halves and swap them, and the meaning is identical. If she is right, what does that reveal about reasoning backward from a missing result ('not a flower, so not a rose')?
answer: It is the forward rule in disguise, run on the mirror sentence — so the backward step is equally airtight.
choices: It is the forward rule in disguise, run on the mirror sentence — so the backward step is equally airtight.
It is a weaker, riskier cousin of the forward rule — the backward step can only suggest, never fully prove.
It is a separate new rule of its own, needing its own justification apart from the forward one.
It works only for roses and flowers, cases where one whole category sits neatly inside a larger one.
context: The mirror sentence is called the contrapositive, and 'If P then Q' is logically identical to 'If not-Q then not-P.' That hidden equivalence is the entire engine of modus tollens: denying the consequent is really just the forward rule (modus ponens) run on the contrapositive — which is why working backward from a missing result is exactly as valid as reasoning forward. Source: quillbot.com (how modus tollens relates to contrapositives) + Wikipedia, Modus tollens (contrapositive equivalence).

question: Karl Popper argued that a real scientific theory must stick its neck out and predict that some specific thing WILL be observed. He built his whole picture of scientific progress on what happens to that prediction. In Popper's account, how does science actually move forward?
answer: By making risky predictions and killing the theories whose predictions fail — progress is ruling the false ones out.
choices: By making risky predictions and killing the theories whose predictions fail — progress is ruling the false ones out.
By making predictions that come true and proving theories correct once confirmed — progress is stacking up successes.
By building agreement until enough experts accept a theory as settled — progress is growing consensus.
By keeping whatever theories prove useful in practice — progress is holding on to what works.
context: Popper built his entire theory of science on modus tollens: if a theory is true then THIS will be seen; if it is NOT seen, the theory is dead. Science advances not by proving theories true but by working backward from failed predictions to eliminate false ones. The 1919 solar-eclipse test was a live example — IF general relativity is true, THEN starlight grazing the Sun bends by a set amount; had the bending been absent, Einstein's theory would have been falsified. Eddington's expeditions measured the deflection during the eclipse, so it survived. Source: bertie.ccsu.edu (Popper, Confirmation and Refutation); royalsocietypublishing.org (the 1919 eclipse results).

question: Mohandas Gandhi set out to break an unjust British law that forced every Indian family to buy taxed government salt, though salt lay free along the coast for the taking. He led a 24-day march to the sea, and when he reached the shore he broke the law with one quiet act. What did he do?
answer: He bent down and lifted a lump of salt
choices: He bent down and lifted a lump of salt
He poured the king's salt back into the sea
He dumped a sack of taxed salt on the sand
He smashed the salt-works gate with the crowd
context: On the morning of 6 April 1930, at the seaside village of Dandi, Gandhi bent down and raised a lump of natural salt from the beach, illegal under the 1882 British Salt Act. He declared, 'With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire.' He had walked roughly 240 miles over 24 days from the Sabarmati Ashram, setting out with 78 volunteers as crowds swelled the column. The satyagraha point is in the choice: he did not destroy or seize anything, he simply made his own free salt. Source: Wikipedia, 'Salt March' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March).

question: At the Dharasana Salt Works in 1930, roughly 2,500 of Mohandas Gandhi's followers walked in columns straight toward a line of police holding steel-tipped clubs. The police clubbed them on the head and shoulders. A reporter watching wrote that the marchers 'went down like ten-pins.' What did the marchers do as the blows landed?
answer: They took the beating and never lifted a hand
choices: They took the beating and never lifted a hand
They charged the police and seized the clubs
They turned and fled back into the watching crowd
They hurled stones to drive the police back
context: The Dharasana raid (21 May 1930) is the purest illustration of satyagraha. Eyewitness reporter Webb Miller wrote: 'Not one of the marchers even raised an arm to fend off the blows. They went down like ten-pins.' Leading them in, the poet Sarojini Naidu had ordered: 'You must not use any violence under any circumstances. You will be beaten, but you must not resist.' This is the core move of a satyagrahi, in Gandhi's words: vindicating truth 'not by infliction of suffering on the opponent, but on oneself.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Dharasana Satyagraha' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharasana_Satyagraha).

question: Critics filed Mohandas Gandhi's whole movement under one dismissive phrase: 'passive resistance.' The word 'passive' made it sound limp, soft, and easy, a tactic for people with no fight in them. Gandhi was insulted by it and threw the phrase out, calling his method instead a 'weapon of the strong.' Why did he insist on the word 'strong'?
answer: Because his method demands more nerve than fighting does
choices: Because his method demands more nerve than fighting does
Because he kept a hidden army ready to fight if needed
Because it only works against a weak, crumbling enemy
Because winners are always called strong by history
context: Gandhi deliberately rejected the phrase 'passive resistance,' saying it 'has admitted of violence' and was 'a weapon of the weak,' whereas 'Satyagraha is a weapon of the strong.' The recognition the bank teaches: refusing to hit back, standing unarmed in front of the clubs, takes more strength than hitting back, not less. Satyagraha means 'truth-force' (Sanskrit satya, 'truth,' plus agraha, 'firm holding'); Gandhi rooted it in ahimsa, the active refusal to harm. Method presented straight, no hagiography. Source: Wikipedia, 'Satyagraha' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyagraha).

question: Mo Di - Master Mo, or Mozi - lived in China just after Confucius, and tradition says he rose from the artisans, a man who worked with his hands building fortifications. He was first schooled by teachers of Confucius's own tradition. What did he do with that training?
answer: Broke with his teachers and founded the first school to rival the Confucians
choices: Broke with his teachers and founded the first school to rival the Confucians
Refined Confucius's teachings into the settled official doctrine of the court
Abandoned philosophy to serve as a war-general for the great state of Chu
Withdrew from public life to live alone as a hermit working with his hands
context: Mozi (Master Mo / Mo Di) flourished in the late 5th to early 4th century BCE, roughly between Confucius and Mencius. By tradition he first studied under Confucian teachers, then rebelled and founded the first organized rival school. Many sources hold he came from the artisan/craftsman class, which fits his hands-on expertise in fortification and siege defense. Source: iep.utm.edu/mozi; plato.stanford.edu/entries/mohism.

question: The engineer Gongshu Ban had built new cloud-ladders and siege towers so the great state of Chu could crush tiny Song. Mozi challenged him to a mock battle at the Chu court - a whole siege fought on a tabletop. To stand in for the besieged city's wall, what did Mozi use?
answer: His own leather belt, unfastened and laid down flat
choices: His own leather belt, unfastened and laid down flat
A folded court map weighted down at its four corners
A long line of bronze wine cups set end to end
A long wooden measuring-ruler from the engineer's own kit
context: Mozi laid his unfastened leather belt down as the city wall and used small sticks or wooden tablets as the weapons. Gongshu Ban (Lu Ban) set up nine different machines of attack; Mozi repelled all nine. In the text's words, 'Gong Shu Ban was at an end with his machines of attack while Mozi was far from being exhausted in defence.' Source: Mozi, Book 50 'Gong Shu'; ctext.org/mozi/gong-shu (W.P. Mei translation).

question: When the great lords of the Warring States cast giant bronze bells and drums and staged grand musical performances at court, most thinkers saw dignity and high culture. Mozi saw a wrong being done. His objection was not that the music sounded bad - he granted it was pleasant. What was his actual complaint against the lords' music?
answer: Its cost came out of the people's food and cloth and pulled them off their fields and looms
choices: Its cost came out of the people's food and cloth and pulled them off their fields and looms
Its grand sound drowned out the simpler work-songs that the farmers sang in the open fields
Its performance broke the ancient rites of mourning that the sage-kings had handed down
Its sweet pleasure made the rulers idle and careless of the defence of their own states
context: In 'Against Music,' Mozi argued that when great lords cast giant bronze bells and drums and stage performances, the food and cloth come out of the people's mouths, plowmen are pulled off the fields, and the women hired to play 'must abandon their work of spinning, weaving, and sewing.' He targeted court ceremony, not the work-songs sung in the fields. Source: Mozi, Book 32 'Against Music' (Ivanhoe, 'A Condemnation of Musical Performances').

question: Mozi pressed a hard question on the warlords of his day: a man who murders one innocent person is put to death and called a criminal by all, yet a king who kills ten thousand in a war of conquest is honoured as righteous, his deed written down for later ages to admire. What was Mozi's charge against that way of judging?
answer: It praises a great crime while it punishes a small one, so it cannot tell right from wrong
choices: It praises a great crime while it punishes a small one, so it cannot tell right from wrong
It lets kings who act for the many be judged by a far gentler rule than common men are
It shows that war is a different matter entirely, outside the rules that govern private men
It proves the people are simply too cowardly to hold a powerful king to any account at all
context: Mozi turned ordinary moral sense against generals: murdering one innocent man earns universal condemnation, yet a king who slaughters ten thousand in aggressive war is praised and recorded for posterity. In his words, 'To hold a principle that forbids the killing of few but allows that of many cannot be said to be understanding the fundamental categories.' Source: Mozi, Book 5 'Condemnation of Offensive War' and Book 50 'Gong Shu' (W.P. Mei translation).

question: Mozi taught that every cruelty in the world - the strong crushing the weak, the rich mocking the poor - grows from one root: partiality, the way people care far more for their own. He called his cure jian ai. What did this cure actually require a person to do?
answer: Weigh a stranger's household exactly as your own, and weigh his life as your own
choices: Weigh a stranger's household exactly as your own, and weigh his life as your own
Love your own household first, and then let that love reach outward as far as it can
Deal fairly with every person you meet, but keep your deepest love for your own
Return love for love and harm for harm, matching exactly what each person gives you
context: Jian ai is usually rendered 'impartial care.' Mozi's rule: 'regard the state of others as one's own, the houses of others as one's own, the persons of others as one's self' (W.P. Mei). His diagnosis of all the world's harms was one word - partiality (bie): when nobody loves any other, 'the strong will overpower the weak, the many will oppress the few, the wealthy will mock the poor.' The cure was to replace partiality with impartiality (jian). Source: Mozi, Book 4 'Universal Love II / III.'

question: Mozi broke with the thinkers who defended a custom by appealing to the past. For him the age of a custom proved nothing - a funeral, a court ceremony, even a war had to justify itself by something else before it could stand. By what measure did Mozi say a custom should finally be judged?
answer: By whether it brings a real benefit to the common people who must live under it
choices: By whether it brings a real benefit to the common people who must live under it
By whether it has been handed down unbroken since the most ancient of times
By whether the refined and the educated find it dignified, proper, and fitting
By whether it flows along with the natural, spontaneous way of all things
context: Mozi's test was the three fa (gnomon-standards): its ROOT (does it accord with the ancient sage-kings), its SOURCE (can ordinary people actually see and hear it confirmed), and its USE (put into practice, does it benefit the state and the common people). Tradition alone was no justification; benefit was the measure. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/mohism (the three fa: Root, Source, Use).

question: Mozi demanded that we weigh every person's family as heavily as our own. His critic Wumazi pushed back with a confession: 'I love the people of the next district more than those of a far province, my own district's people more than the next district's, and my own family most of all.' Wumazi was not boasting of a flaw - he meant this as the natural and right shape of human love. What principle was Wumazi defending against Mozi?
answer: Love rightly runs strongest for those closest to you and fainter with distance
choices: Love rightly runs strongest for those closest to you and fainter with distance
Love is owed equally to every person, and any favouring of one's own is a fault
Love should be spent only on oneself, since no one ever truly looks after another
Love should be measured out to each person in exact return for what they give you
context: Wumazi's concentric circles of love are the natural human objection to impartial care, posed inside the Mozi itself (Book 46 'Geng Zhu'). The Confucian side escalated in Mencius (3B:9): Mencius charged that Mozi's 'love everyone equally' denies the special duty a son owes his father, and that 'to acknowledge neither king nor father is to be in the state of the beast.' At the opposite extreme stood Yang Zhu's 'each for himself,' which Mencius said denies the ruler. These are competing Warring-States positions, presented without a modern verdict. Sources: Mozi, Book 46 'Geng Zhu'; Mencius 3B:9 (Legge); plato.stanford.edu/entries/mohism.

question: A reformer says the cure for a tyrant is to find a wise and good ruler and put him in charge. The French thinker Montesquieu disagrees: he says every man handed power is apt to abuse it, so you must not bet liberty on one person staying good. What does Montesquieu trust instead of the ruler's virtue?
answer: A design where power is set up to check power, so no one hand can run wild
choices: A design where power is set up to check power, so no one hand can run wild
Frequent elections, so a ruler who turns bad can be voted out
A written charter of rights the government swears never to cross
Splitting the country into small regions, each ruling its own local affairs
context: Montesquieu's rule: 'To prevent the abuse of power, it is necessary that by the very disposition of things power should be a check to power,' because 'constant experience shews us, that every man invested with power is apt to abuse it.' The safeguard distrusts ALL rulers by structure, not the virtue of any one. The distractors are real but different safeguards: regular elections still leave power concentrated between them, a charter of rights is an external limit on paper, and dividing the land into small regions disperses power geographically rather than making the branches inside one government restrain each other. Montesquieu's specific fix is power restraining power from WITHIN the design. Source: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws, Book XI, Ch. 6 (1758 Nugent translation, Wikisource).

question: Montesquieu sorts the work of any government into three kinds of task: making the laws, carrying them out while handling war and peace, and judging crimes and the quarrels between people. He cares far less about that list than about ONE rule binding it. What is the rule he insists on?
answer: Keep the three jobs in different hands, never all held by one
choices: Keep the three jobs in different hands, never all held by one
Write the three jobs down plainly so the people can read them
Rank the three jobs so the lawmakers always outrank the rest
Bind the three jobs tightly together so they always act as one
context: Montesquieu names the legislative (enacts, amends, or abrogates laws), the executive (makes peace or war, sends or receives embassies, guards against invasion), and the judiciary (punishes criminals and decides disputes). The move the bank prizes is keeping the three in different hands, not memorizing the list. Source: The Spirit of the Laws, Bk XI, Ch. 6; National Constitution Center primary-source page.

question: Montesquieu spent about twenty years writing The Spirit of the Laws, the book that taught the modern world to split up government power. By the time he died in Paris in 1755, something had befallen the man behind that work. What had become of Montesquieu?
answer: He had gone completely blind, the map of free government drawn by a man who could not see
choices: He had gone completely blind, the map of free government drawn by a man who could not see
He had been cast out of France, his great book printed only in distant foreign cities
He had been ruined and left penniless, having spent his whole fortune on the printing
He had been locked in the king's prison, his manuscript smuggled out of the cell by friends
context: Montesquieu spent roughly twenty years on The Spirit of the Laws (published 1748); failing cataracts left him nearly blind by the time he finished, and he died fully blind in Paris on 10 February 1755. The map of separated powers that shaped modern constitutions was completed by a man losing his sight. Source: PubMed, 'Montesquieu visually impaired, then blind (January 1689-February 1755),' PMID 25230527.

question: Montesquieu warns of a first deadly mix: when the same person or body both MAKES the laws AND carries them out, he says there can be no liberty. Spell out exactly why joining those two jobs in one hand kills freedom.
answer: The same hand could pass tyrannical laws and then enforce them tyrannically
choices: The same hand could pass tyrannical laws and then enforce them tyrannically
The lawmakers would grow lazy, knowing that someone else must apply their work
The people would lose all track of whom to blame whenever a bad law is passed
The two jobs need different talents, so one person is bound to do both poorly
context: Montesquieu: 'When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty,' because the same hand could enact tyrannical laws and then execute them in a tyrannical manner. The one who makes the rule must not be the one who enforces it. Source: The Spirit of the Laws, Bk XI, Ch. 6 (Wikisource).

question: Montesquieu says liberty also dies if the power of JUDGING is not kept apart from making and enforcing laws. If the same person were both lawmaker and judge, he warns, a subject's life and liberty would lie under arbitrary control. What is the precise danger when judge and lawmaker are one?
answer: The judge could invent the rule and the verdict at once, against anyone he chose
choices: The judge could invent the rule and the verdict at once, against anyone he chose
The judge would be overworked and rush through the cases without any proper care
The judge would copy the lawmaker's own mistakes straight into his court rulings
The judge would lose the respect of the people, who prize a truly impartial court
context: Montesquieu: 'there is no liberty, if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers.' Joined to the legislative, the judge would BE the legislator, inventing the rule and the verdict together, exposing life and liberty to arbitrary control. Source: The Spirit of the Laws, Bk XI, Ch. 6 (Wikisource).

question: Montesquieu builds to a climax: there would be an END of everything, he says, if one and the same hand held the power to make laws, to enforce them, and to judge under them. He insists one detail does NOT save you from this ruin. Which detail makes no difference at all?
answer: Whether that single hand is one man, a few nobles, or the whole people
choices: Whether that single hand is one man, a few nobles, or the whole people
Whether the ruler seized power by force or instead won it in a fair vote
Whether the laws happen to be just and gentle at this particular moment
Whether the nation is large and mighty or small enough to watch closely
context: Montesquieu: 'There would be an end of every thing, were the same man, or the same body whether of the nobles or of the people, to exercise those three powers.' Concentration itself is the tyranny, whether the hand is a king, an elite, or a majority. Source: The Spirit of the Laws, Bk XI, Ch. 6 (Wikisource).

question: When the American founders argued for splitting up government, James Madison leaned on Montesquieu as 'the oracle who is always consulted' on the subject. In Federalist No. 47 (1788) Madison gives a one-line definition of tyranny itself. According to Madison, the very definition of tyranny is what?
answer: Gathering all the lawmaking, enforcing, and judging power into the same hands
choices: Gathering all the lawmaking, enforcing, and judging power into the same hands
Ruling a whole people by the will of a single king who answers to no court
Taking a nation's property and liberty without the consent of the governed
Silencing every rival voice so that no one may question the ruler's command
context: Madison, Federalist No. 47 (1788): 'The accumulation of all powers legislative, executive and judiciary in the same hands... may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.' Madison called Montesquieu 'the oracle who is always consulted and cited on this subject... the celebrated Montesquieu.' Source: Founders' Constitution (Univ. of Chicago).

question: Montesquieu did not want his three powers walled off as strangers that never deal with one another; he gave the branches a working relationship instead. The whole point of that relationship was to stop any one branch from swallowing the rest. How did Montesquieu set the branches to relate?
answer: Each branch can block the others, halting a move it judges an overreach
choices: Each branch can block the others, halting a move it judges an overreach
Each branch answers to the people alone, who settle their clashes at the ballot
Each branch must give consent before any single act of state can take effect
Each branch takes a strict turn at power, leading the whole state for a season
context: Separation is not isolation: Montesquieu linked the powers so they 'are forced to move, and forced to move in concert.' The mechanism is mutual restraint — the two legislative houses 'check one another by the mutual privilege of rejecting,' and the executive can 'prevent the encroachments of the legislature on its authority.' Power restrains power: each branch can halt the others rather than rule alone, share the work by thirds, defer to the ballot, or answer to a fourth referee. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Montesquieu and the Separation of Powers' (quoting Bk XI, Ch. 6).

question: A philosopher giving a public lecture claimed he could prove, on the spot, that the everyday world is really there and not just a dream in his head. He reached for no chalkboard and no chain of logic. What did he do to make his case?
answer: Raised his two hands, one then the other, saying 'Here is one hand, and here is another'
choices: Raised his two hands, one then the other, saying 'Here is one hand, and here is another'
Pinched himself hard on the forearm to show that he could feel real, sharp pain
Threw a stick of chalk clear across the room so the whole audience watched it fall
Told everyone to shut their eyes, then to describe the door they had just been seeing
context: This is G.E. Moore in his 1939 British Academy lecture 'Proof of an External World.' Verbatim: 'I can prove now... that two human hands exist. How? By holding up my two hands, and saying... "Here is one hand"... "and here is another".' He claimed that gesture alone proved that things outside the mind exist. Source: G.E. Moore, 'Proof of an External World' (1939), reprinted in G.E. Moore: Selected Writings, p.165-166.

question: Pressed hard, G.E. Moore made a striking admission: if a skeptic demands that he PROVE he isn't merely dreaming, he confesses he simply cannot do it. Yet he flatly refused to take the next step the skeptic wanted. What did Moore insist, even while granting he had no such proof?
answer: That he could still KNOW he had hands, even with no proof he wasn't dreaming
choices: That he could still KNOW he had hands, even with no proof he wasn't dreaming
That a real proof would surface later, once philosophers worked out the details
That proof and knowledge are really one thing, so without the one he lacked both
That nothing at all can be known until every last possible doubt is ruled out
context: Moore's closing line: 'I can know things, which I cannot prove; and among things which I certainly did know, even if (as I think) I could not prove them, were the premisses of my two proofs.' Knowing and being-able-to-prove come apart — you can genuinely know something you have no way to prove. Source: G.E. Moore, 'Proof of an External World' (1939), closing paragraph.

question: A skeptic builds a tidy argument: 'If you truly knew you had hands, you'd know you weren't merely dreaming. But you can't be sure you aren't dreaming. So you don't really know you have hands.' A philosopher answers that he is far MORE certain he has hands than he could be of any single step in that argument. Which move does that greater certainty push him toward?
answer: Keep the argument's logic but run it backward: he DOES know he isn't merely dreaming
choices: Keep the argument's logic but run it backward: he DOES know he isn't merely dreaming
Accept the skeptic's conclusion, and grant that his hands might be an illusion after all
Drop the whole dispute as meaningless, since neither side could ever truly win it
Concede that he knows nothing for sure, not his hands and not anything else either
context: This is the 'Moorean shift.' The skeptic reasons: knowing hands implies knowing you're not dreaming; you can't know you're not dreaming; therefore no hands-knowledge. Moore accepts the logic but, being surer of his hands than of any premise, runs the same chain in reverse: I DO know I have hands, so I must know I'm not merely dreaming. Same logic, conclusion flipped (the skeptic's modus tollens becomes Moore's modus ponens). Sources: Wikipedia, 'Here is one hand'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'George Edward Moore.'

question: G.E. Moore opened his famous lecture by quoting Immanuel Kant, who decades earlier had pointed to one long-standing embarrassment and named it 'a scandal to philosophy.' According to Kant, what was the thing philosophers ought to be ashamed they had never managed?
answer: To prove that a world outside our own minds exists, rather than just assume it
choices: To prove that a world outside our own minds exists, rather than just assume it
To agree on what makes an action right, rather than each thinker insisting on his own
To explain how mere lifeless matter could ever give rise to a thinking mind
To settle whether the universe had a first beginning or stretches back forever
context: Kant wrote that it is 'a scandal to philosophy... that the existence of things outside of us... must be accepted merely on faith, and that, if anyone thinks good to doubt their existence, we are unable to counter his doubts by any satisfactory proof' (Critique of Pure Reason, 2nd ed. preface, 1787). Moore set out to END that scandal by supplying the very proof Kant said was missing. Source: Moore, 'Proof of an External World' (1939), opening lines, quoting Kant's B-preface (1787).

question: Critics charged that G.E. Moore's hand-proof quietly cheats. Moore holds up his hands and says he KNOWS he has them. But a skeptic who doubts that anything exists outside the mind says Moore helps himself to too much before he even begins. What is the thing Moore takes for granted that the skeptic will not grant him?
answer: That his own eyes and hands are reporting a real world out there, not staging a private show
choices: That his own eyes and hands are reporting a real world out there, not staging a private show
That holding a thing up in plain view is the kind of act that can settle a question of fact
That his listeners will trust their senses about the hands exactly as readily as he trusts his
That whatever feels this certain to him must, for that reason, be something he genuinely knows
context: The standard objection is 'begging the question' (or 'transmission failure'): to trust his senses is already to presuppose an external world feeding them, so the proof leans on the very thing in dispute. Moore's reply isn't to repair the logic but to deny the burden — he knows the premise even if he can't prove it non-circularly. Source: 1000-Word Philosophy, 'G.E. Moore's Proof of an External World: Responding to External World Skepticism.'

question: Moore's two raised hands haunted Ludwig Wittgenstein. In the last eighteen months of his life he filled notebooks wrestling with them and reached a surprising verdict: when Moore says 'I know I have hands,' the word KNOW is misused. Such certainties, Wittgenstein argued, play a wholly different role. What did he compare them to?
answer: The hinges a door needs: they stay put precisely so everything else can swing and be questioned
choices: The hinges a door needs: they stay put precisely so everything else can swing and be questioned
An instinct hard-wired since birth: fixed for life, yet a quirk of biology we never reasoned our way into
A law of logic, true in every possible world: unshakable, but proven by argument rather than just held
The foundation stones of a house: solid, yet able to be dug up and inspected one by one
context: Prompted by Norman Malcolm in 1949 to reconsider Moore's proof, Wittgenstein wrote the remarks published as 'On Certainty' (composed April 1950 to April 27, 1951 — two days before he died; published 1969). His verdict: Moore's hand-propositions aren't things we KNOW but 'hinges.' As he put it, 'If I want the door to turn, the hinges must stay put' — some certainties can't be doubted because they are what makes doubting possible at all. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy & Philopedia, 'On Certainty'; EBSCO Research Starters, 'On Certainty by Ludwig Wittgenstein.'

question: Thomas Nagel pictures a driver who skipped his last brake check, with no reason to suspect anything wrong. A child darts into the road, the worn brakes fail, and the child dies. Nagel says this man will not merely feel terrible the way anyone would after a tragic accident. How does Nagel say the driver responds to the death?
answer: Blame himself for the child's death
choices: Blame himself for the child's death
Grieve deeply but place the fault on the child who darted out
Accept it as a tragic accident no one could have prevented
Report the faulty brakes and move on
context: This is Thomas Nagel's own version of the case ("Moral Luck," 1979, in Mortal Questions). Nagel's words: if the driver was guilty of even a minor negligence, failing to have the brakes checked, and that negligence contributes to the child's death, he will not merely feel terrible, he will blame himself for the death. Had no child run out, the very same unchecked brakes make him merely a normal driver. The negligence is identical; only luck differs. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'Moral Luck' (1979); quoted at provisionalsignificance (2017) and academicweb.nd.edu.

question: Bernard Williams describes a lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, runs over and kills a child who ran out in front of him. Everyone agrees the driver is blameless. Williams insists that even so, the driver is left with something a witness on the sidewalk, however horrified and sorry, never carries. What marks the driver's response?
answer: A pull to seek out the family and make amends
choices: A pull to seek out the family and make amends
A calm that, being blameless, the matter is closed for him
A guilt indistinguishable from a driver truly at fault
A relief that fate, not his choosing, did the harm
context: Bernard Williams named this feeling 'agent-regret.' His words: we feel sorry for the driver, but that sentiment co-exists with, indeed presupposes, that there is something special about his relation to this happening, which cannot be eliminated by the thought that it was not his fault. Agent-regret typically includes the urge to make amends, and it shows that even we feel the outcome attaches to the agent who acted. Being blameless does not settle whether amends are owed, and it is not the same as the guilt of a driver who really was at fault. Source: Bernard Williams, 'Moral Luck' (1981), on the lorry-driver; quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Moral Luck.'

question: Two men each fire a gun meaning to kill. One bullet strikes home and the victim dies; the other shot is spoiled at the last instant when the intended victim happens to trip and fall. The first man is tried for murder, the second only for attempted murder, a lesser crime and a lighter sentence. Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams point to pairs like this to name a single unsettling fact about how we judge people. What is that fact?
answer: How guilty we hold someone can hinge on luck, not choice
choices: How guilty we hold someone can hinge on luck, not choice
Both men are equally guilty, whatever the law decides
Intentions weigh far more with us than the actual harm
The law can never measure what a person truly deserves
context: This is the phenomenon called 'moral luck,' named in a 1976 Aristotelian Society symposium where Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel each gave a paper by that title. Nagel's definition: where a significant aspect of what someone does depends on factors beyond his control, yet we treat him as an object of moral judgment, it can be called moral luck. The murderer/attempted-murderer pair (the spoiled shot, the victim who 'unexpectedly tripped and fell') is the bloodless twin of the driver case. The answer describes how we DO judge, not a verdict that it is justified. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Moral Luck.'

question: Bernard Williams tells of the painter Paul Gauguin, who in 1891 left his wife and children to sail for Tahiti and paint. Williams says no reasoning at the moment of leaving could settle whether Gauguin was justified, that the verdict had to wait. On Williams's view, what would end up deciding whether the desertion was justified?
answer: Whether his talent succeeded, so the gamble paid off
choices: Whether his talent succeeded, so the gamble paid off
Whether the canvases he painted there sold well in his lifetime
Whether he suffered enough hardship to pay for it
Whether history judged him a kind and decent man
context: Gauguin is Bernard Williams's signature example of moral luck. Williams's claim: nothing could justify the abandonment in advance; only success could, retrospectively. If Gauguin becomes a master, the gamble is 'justified by results'; if his talent had failed, the same act stands condemned. The criterion is artistic success, not mere sales in his lifetime or later fame as a decent man. Whether he gets that justification depends on talent and luck he cannot command at the moment of choosing. Source: Bernard Williams, 'Moral Luck' (1976/1981); summarized in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A follower of Immanuel Kant says the moral worth of an act lies in the will behind it alone, that a good will would still shine by itself like a jewel, however things happen to turn out. Now put two equally reckless drivers before him: one killed a child in the road, the other found the road empty. What must he say about their guilt?
answer: They are equally guilty; the outcome was luck, not will
choices: They are equally guilty; the outcome was luck, not will
The killer is guiltier; a will that brings death answers for more
Neither is guilty; neither one meant a child to die
Only the killer is guilty; guilt must land on a real victim
context: This is the 'equal guilt' answer, resting on the Control Principle: we are morally assessable only to the extent that what we are assessed for depends on factors under our control. Kant supplies its purest voice. The good will is good in itself; like a jewel it would still shine by itself, and usefulness or fruitlessness can neither add to nor take from its worth. On this view the dead child adds nothing to the reckless driver's guilt and the empty road subtracts nothing. A philosopher who holds that outcomes DO matter is not thereby wrong; the question asks only what the Kantian must conclude. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Moral Luck,' and Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785).

question: Thomas Nagel takes the rule that we should not blame people for what lies beyond their control and follows it carefully. Strip away the luck in how things turned out, then the luck of the situations you faced, then the luck of the very temperament you were born with, none of which you chose. Where does Nagel say this leaves the self that can be blamed?
answer: Nothing is left to blame, only events to deplore or celebrate
choices: Nothing is left to blame, only events to deplore or celebrate
Your chosen acts still belong to you, even if your character does not
A core self that endorses or resists its temperament stays answerable
Blame simply shifts to whoever shaped you into who you are
context: This is the skeptical position: luck is everywhere, and pushed all the way it threatens blame entirely. Nagel's words: eventually nothing remains which can be ascribed to the responsible self, and we are left with nothing but a portion of the larger sequence of events, which can be deplored or celebrated, but not blamed or praised. The other choices are real rivals a philosopher might press, that your chosen acts stay yours, or that a core self answers for how it handles its temperament, but the question asks where Nagel's own regress ends. Nagel sorts luck into four kinds the regress runs through: resultant (how things turn out), circumstantial (the situations you face), constitutive (the temperament you were born with), and causal (how prior causes determined you, which collapses into the free-will problem). Source: Thomas Nagel, 'Moral Luck' (1979); quoted at provisionalsignificance (2017); taxonomy from the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A boy says, 'There's really no such thing as right or wrong -- it's just whatever each family decides for itself.' His sister asks: so if the neighbors decided it was fine to torture their cat for fun, that would be perfectly OK? The boy goes quiet. What is his hesitation pointing at?
answer: Some things are wrong no matter who decides they are fine.
choices: Some things are wrong no matter who decides they are fine.
He should have picked a less upsetting example to argue with.
Families ought to talk things over before setting their house rules.
Whatever upsets you the most is what the word 'wrong' really means.
context: The everyday handle for MORAL REALISM -- the view that some acts are really wrong, not merely disapproved of. The boy's gut refusal to bless cat-torture-for-fun is the realist intuition the bank shares: 'there's no real right or wrong' sounds open-minded until it has to call an obvious cruelty just 'someone's opinion.' Source: standard intro-ethics framing; cf. James Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy.

question: A traveler argues that since customs differ everywhere, nothing is really right or wrong -- it's all just what your people happen to approve. A friend replies that he is more certain that torturing a small child purely for amusement is wrong than he is of any clever argument built to deny it. How is that reply meant to work?
answer: If careful reasoning concludes the act is not truly wrong, that counts against the reasoning.
choices: If careful reasoning concludes the act is not truly wrong, that counts against the reasoning.
If most cultures forbid the act, then a head-count of societies is what makes it wrong.
If the act merely feels wrong to him, then his own private disgust is all 'wrong' can mean.
If the act can't be proven wrong by strict logic, then calling it wrong is just loose talk.
context: The realist's Moorean move: G.E. Moore answered a skeptic who doubted the outside world by holding up his hand -- 'Here is one hand' -- being surer he had a hand than of any premise in the skeptic's argument. Run the same play in ethics: I am surer that torturing a child for fun is wrong than of any premise concluding nothing is really wrong, so the premise is what gives way. Source: G.E. Moore, 'Proof of an External World'; Tristram McPherson, 'Moorean Arguments and Moral Revisionism.'

question: King Darius tested custom: he asked Greeks what would make them EAT their dead fathers, and they recoiled in horror; he asked the Callatiae, who honored their dead by eating them, what would make them BURN their fathers instead, and they recoiled too. Each was disgusted by the other's funeral. What does this story honestly establish?
answer: That funeral customs truly vary, each one feeling obvious to the people inside it.
choices: That funeral customs truly vary, each one feeling obvious to the people inside it.
That right and wrong are merely whatever one's own society happens to approve.
That no society's way of honoring its dead is any better or worse than another's.
That moral disgust is all the words 'right' and 'wrong' have ever really meant.
context: From Herodotus (Histories 3.38), relativism's oldest and strongest piece of evidence -- and the bank grants it fully: customs DO differ, each self-evident from within. That is the honest steel-man. But the relativist's LEAP, from 'funeral customs differ' to 'so nothing is really right or wrong,' is the invalid step (next rung). Variation in etiquette is no more evidence against moral truth than flat-earth belief was evidence against a round earth. Source: Herodotus 3.38; James Rachels.

question: Frederick Douglass and the abolitionists fought to end slavery while their own society overwhelmingly approved of it. A relativist holds that 'right' just means 'whatever your society approves.' A student notices this hands down a strange verdict on reformers. What does relativism force her to say about people who oppose their society's approved customs?
answer: That such reformers are, by definition, in the WRONG -- they reject what their society calls right.
choices: That such reformers are, by definition, in the WRONG -- they reject what their society calls right.
That such reformers are right, because a later society came around to agreeing with them.
That such reformers are right, because every society secretly knows the real truth already.
That such reformers are neither right nor wrong until the society's law itself finally changes.
context: This is the REFORMER'S DILEMMA, the classic refutation of cultural relativism. If 'right' just means 'approved by your society,' then anyone who fights an approved evil -- the abolitionists, the suffragists, the anti-apartheid movement -- is automatically in the wrong, and genuine moral PROGRESS becomes impossible (you could only ever match your society, never improve on it). Since we know the abolitionists were heroes, the premise that brands them wrong must be false. Source: James Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, 'The Challenge of Cultural Relativism.'

question: The philosopher James Rachels examined a popular argument: different societies have different moral codes, therefore there is no objective right or wrong. He granted the premise -- societies really do differ -- yet called the argument broken. To show the flaw he pointed at geography: some peoples once believed the earth flat, others that it was round. What does that parallel expose?
answer: A conclusion about what is really so cannot follow merely from what various people believe.
choices: A conclusion about what is really so cannot follow merely from what various people believe.
The societies that believed wrongly had simply not yet gathered enough careful evidence.
Disagreement always means the truth must lie somewhere in the middle of the rival views.
Once the experts settle a question, every society is then obliged to adopt the answer.
context: Rachels calls this the 'Cultural Differences Argument' and shows it is INVALID: the conclusion (there is no objective right or wrong) does not follow from the premise (codes differ). His geography analogy makes it vivid -- some societies thought the earth flat, others round, but that disagreement plainly did not make the earth's shape a matter of opinion. Likewise, moral disagreement does not by itself prove there is no moral truth. Source: James Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy.

question: Gilbert Harman defended relativism at full strength: of a man like Hitler, raised (he supposed) wholly outside our moral world, Harman said it sounds strictly odd to tell him 'you ought not to have done it.' Even Harman did not think the genocide was acceptable. A critic answers that this very example is the strongest case AGAINST Harman's view. Why?
answer: A view that cannot say Hitler ought not to have done it gives up more than it could ever prove.
choices: A view that cannot say Hitler ought not to have done it gives up more than it could ever prove.
Harman never established that Hitler was truly raised outside every moral agreement at all.
Hitler plainly did share in our moral agreement, so Harman had simply got his history wrong.
Once a man throws off every rule we live by, our words can't reach him, so nothing is lost.
context: Harman ('Moral Relativism Defended,' 1975) made 'ought' relative to a shared agreement, so a flat 'ought' supposedly can't reach someone outside it -- a serious, sophisticated position the bank presents at full strength, not as mush. But this is the realist's decisive reply, the Moorean move again: we are far MORE certain that Hitler ought not to have murdered millions than we could ever be of any premise concluding we can't say so -- so the premise, not the certainty, is what must give way. Source: SEP 'Moral Relativism' (Harman 1975); G.E. Moore, 'Proof of an External World.'

question: The thinker Nagarjuna lays one stick on the table and calls it long. Then he sets a longer stick beside it, and now the first stick is the short one, though nobody touched it or changed it. The wood is identical; only its company changed. Nagarjuna asks his students: so what was the longness of that stick, really?
answer: Something it had only by standing beside a shorter stick, not on its own
choices: Something it had only by standing beside a shorter stick, not on its own
A real long-essence in the wood, briefly outweighed by the longer stick
A label the students pinned on it that the new stick made them peel off
Its plain measured length, the same before and after the second stick
context: This is Nagarjuna's plainest handle on emptiness (sunyata): 'long' and 'short' are a relational pair with no essence of their own. A stick has no 'long-essence' inside it; it is long only in dependence on a shorter one. The same dissolving move applies to fire and fuel, cause and effect, action and agent. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Madhyamaka Buddhist Philosophy' (iep.utm.edu/madhyamaka-buddhist-philosophy/).

question: Nagarjuna, a Buddhist monk of southern India around 150 to 250 CE, was so revered that later followers called him the greatest Buddhist thinker after the Buddha himself. Scholars warn that almost nothing certain is known of his actual life, so the most famous tale about him is told as legend, not history. What does that legend say he did?
answer: Dove beneath the sea to recover lost wisdom-scriptures guarded by serpent-beings
choices: Dove beneath the sea to recover lost wisdom-scriptures guarded by serpent-beings
Received the lost scriptures from a glowing god who appeared to him in a long dream
Lived six full centuries by brewing a secret elixir that quietly halted his aging
Tamed a wild mountain dragon that then carried the scriptures to him on its back
context: The legend says Nagarjuna retrieved the Perfection of Wisdom sutras from the underwater realm of the nagas (serpent-beings). The Stanford Encyclopedia stresses this is myth, not biography: 'very little can be said precisely about Nagarjuna's life.' His philosophy of the Middle Way (madhyamaka) shaped Indian philosophical debate for a thousand years. The three rival options are invented legend-foils, not sourced claims. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nagarjuna' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/nagarjuna/).

question: Nagarjuna goes hunting for the chariot itself, the thing that makes a chariot a chariot. He takes it apart, lays out every wheel, the axle, the pole, the frame, and searches for the chariot among them. He never finds it anywhere in the pile, yet people ride chariots every day and the word works fine. So what, in the end, is a chariot?
answer: A handy name we give to the parts once they are fitted together and working
choices: A handy name we give to the parts once they are fitted together and working
