context: Williams' 'one thought too many': the impartial justification is itself a kind of betrayal, because a loving husband simply dives for his wife. Behind it lies his integrity objection, that a person is made of 'ground projects,' the loves that give a life meaning, and an ethics forcing every choice through impartial maximizing severs the self that was supposed to be good. Presented as a position, not a verdict. Sources: Bernard Williams, 'Persons, Character and Morality,' in Moral Luck (1981); SEP entry on Bernard Williams.

question: Socrates wandered the Athens marketplace barefoot, in one ragged cloak, talking philosophy with anyone who would listen. Other teachers in the city, the Sophists, charged hefty fees to teach the sons of the rich. What did Socrates do about payment for his conversations?
answer: He refused to take any money for them at all
choices: He refused to take any money for them at all
He charged a small fee that the poor could afford
He took payment only from students who became famous
He asked for a share of his students future earnings
context: Socrates embraced poverty deliberately and never took a coin for his talk, which set him apart from the paid Sophists who sold their teaching. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates (iep.utm.edu/socrates); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates.

question: Athenians prided themselves on refined beauty and fine dress. Into this city walked Socrates: barefoot in every season, unwashed, wearing the same single cloak by day and by night, carrying a plain stick. What was most remarkable about how Socrates lived?
answer: He owned almost nothing and never cared to
choices: He owned almost nothing and never cared to
He hid great wealth beneath his shabby clothes
He changed his rough appearance for important men
He begged in the streets for his daily bread
context: Sources describe Socrates as barefoot and unwashed, in the same cloak and sandals through day and evening, carrying a stick, and ignoring wealth entirely. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates.

question: Socrates shaped the whole course of Western philosophy, yet when scholars go looking for his writings, they find a strange gap. Everything we know of him survives only because his students Plato and Xenophon and others wrote it down. Why must we rely on what others recorded?
answer: Socrates himself never wrote down a single line
choices: Socrates himself never wrote down a single line
Socrates wrote in a code no one could later read
Socrates ordered his own writings burned at his death
Socrates only ever wrote in languages now lost
context: Socrates left not one written line of his own; the man who shaped Western thought is known only secondhand from Plato, Xenophon, the playwright Aristophanes, and later Aristotle. Scholars call this 'the Socratic problem.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates.

question: On trial for his life, Socrates would not apologize for pestering Athens with hard questions. He compared the city to a great and noble horse, grown slow and heavy from its very size. What did Socrates call himself, in that image?
answer: The gadfly clinging to the drowsy beast all day
choices: The gadfly clinging to the drowsy beast all day
The rider who alone could mount the great beast
The groom who fed and brushed the great beast
The trainer who put the great beast through its paces
context: In Plato's Apology, Socrates called himself 'that gadfly which God has attached to the state... all day long... arousing and persuading and reproaching you,' the state being 'a great and noble steed who is tardy in his motions owing to his very size.' Source: Plato, Apology (Jowett translation), classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html.

question: At his trial Socrates was practically offered his life back if he would only stop questioning everything and live quietly. He refused, saying a certain kind of life was no life worth living at all. He was put to death soon after by drinking hemlock. What did Socrates say was not worth living?
answer: A life that is never examined
choices: A life that is never examined
A life spent chasing after wealth
A life lived in fear of the gods
A life without a single true friend
context: Defending the philosophic life, Socrates declared that 'the life which is unexamined is not worth living' and would rather die than stop questioning; he was executed with hemlock. Source: Plato, Apology (Jowett translation), classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Socrates.

question: Socrates married Xanthippe, a woman remembered for her fiery temper. One day, after shouting herself out scolding him, she emptied a pitcher of water over his head. Socrates did not lose his temper, but answered with a quip. What did Socrates say?
answer: Did I not say her thunder would end in rain?
choices: Did I not say her thunder would end in rain?
Would a wise man not learn to swim at home?
Do the gods not send storms upon the just?
Does a cold head not make for clear thought?
context: Diogenes Laertius reports that after Xanthippe scolded Socrates and dumped water on him, he quipped, 'Did I not say that Xanthippe's thunder would end in rain?' He claimed living with her trained him to handle anyone. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book II.37, via perseus.tufts.edu.

question: When the oracle at Delphi declared no man wiser than Socrates, he was stunned, for how could that be true? He spent years cross-examining the citys celebrated wise men, and finally grasped what the god must have meant. What did Socrates conclude the oracle meant?
answer: He alone knew the true extent of his own ignorance
choices: He alone knew the true extent of his own ignorance
He had been chosen by the gods for some great deed
He would one day become the wisest of all the Greeks
He must teach his hard-won wisdom to all of Athens
context: Socrates' friend Chaerephon asked the Pythian priestess whether anyone was wiser than Socrates; she said no one was. Cross-examining 'wise' men to disprove her, Socrates concluded the god meant he alone knew how little he truly knew. Source: Plato, Apology (Jowett translation), classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html.

question: Socrates mother Phaenarete worked as a midwife, helping mothers bring their babies into the world. Socrates claimed his own work was just the same as hers, though plainly he birthed no infants. When Socrates called himself a midwife, what did he mean he did?
answer: Helped people give birth to truths already inside them
choices: Helped people give birth to truths already inside them
Eased the sharp pain of learning hard and bitter truths
Drew the most promising young minds out into public life
Knew which budding ideas to keep and which to discard
context: Echoing his mother Phaenarete's trade, Socrates called himself a midwife of ideas: he insisted he taught nothing and 'gave' no one knowledge, only helping people give birth to the truth already within them by asking questions. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; History.com: Socrates.

question: On campaign at Potidaea, Socrates fell to pondering some hard problem and simply stopped, rooted to one spot. His fellow soldiers grew so amazed that some dragged their bedding outside to watch him through the night. How long did Socrates stand there lost in thought?
answer: From one dawn straight through to the next
choices: From one dawn straight through to the next
For the length of a single evening
Until the enemy attack forced him to move
For three days without food or water
context: Alcibiades tells in Plato's Symposium that at Potidaea Socrates stood fixed on one spot from one dawn to the next, a full day and night; at sunrise he offered a prayer to the sun and walked away. Source: Plato, Symposium 220c-d (Jowett translation), gutenberg.org/files/1600/1600-h/1600-h.htm.

question: At a drinking party, a tipsy Alcibiades stood to praise Socrates and reached for the perfect comparison. He pointed to the little carved Silenus figures sold in shops, the kind that look like one thing on the outside but split open to reveal another within. What did Alcibiades say cracking Socrates open would reveal?
answer: A little golden god hidden inside
choices: A little golden god hidden inside
A hollow shell with nothing inside
A second ugly face uglier than the first
A coiled serpent ready to strike
context: In Plato's Symposium the drunken Alcibiades likens Socrates to a Silenus statue, grotesque outside but cracking open to reveal little golden gods within: ugly outside, divine within. Source: Plato, Symposium 215a-b; Cambridge Core, 'For Love of a Statue: A Reading of Plato's Symposium 215A-B'.

question: Everyone quotes Socrates as saying I know that I know nothing, four neat words of humble wisdom. But scholars point out he never said it in that snappy form anywhere in Plato. What Socrates actually claimed in his trial was something subtler. What did Socrates really say?
answer: I neither know, nor think that I know
choices: I neither know, nor think that I know
I know one thing, that I know nothing
The wise man knows the limits of his knowing
Only a fool believes that he knows anything
context: LEGEND-FLAG: the snappy 'I know that I know nothing' is folklore that, scholars note, 'occurs nowhere in Plato's works.' In the Apology (21d) Socrates says the humbler thing: 'I neither know nor think I know,' reckoning himself wiser only in not thinking he knows what he doesn't. Source: Plato, Apology 21d; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_know_that_I_know_nothing.

question: Years before the trial, the comic playwright Aristophanes put Socrates on the Athenian stage in a comedy called The Clouds, running a school for clever nonsense. The crowd roared at his very first entrance, an absurd sight that Aristophanes dreamed up just for the laugh. How did Socrates first appear in the play?
answer: Dangling in a hanging basket, treading the air
choices: Dangling in a hanging basket, treading the air
Riding a donkey backward through the market
Wrapped head to toe as a talking Egyptian mummy
Sprouting feathers and crowing like a rooster
context: In Aristophanes' The Clouds (423 BCE) the character Socrates runs a 'Thinkery' and first appears dangling overhead in a hanging basket, 'treading the air and contemplating the sun' — a prop Aristophanes invented. Plato later blamed this comedy for turning Athens against Socrates. Source: Aristophanes, The Clouds (423 BCE); greatbooksguy.com on Clouds.

question: Socrates loved to trap a man who bragged he was an expert. He would say he knew nothing himself and humbly beg to be taught — then a few gentle, simple-sounding questions tied the expert in knots until it was clear the man had never understood his own claim. What was Socrates up to?
answer: Pretending to be the clueless one so the expert would talk himself into a corner
choices: Pretending to be the clueless one so the expert would talk himself into a corner
Sincerely confessing he was lost and hoping the expert could finally settle the matter
Buttering up the expert so the flattered man would let slip a closely guarded secret
Killing time politely because he had not yet thought of a sharp objection to raise
context: This is the move called Socratic irony — from the Greek 'eironeia,' meaning feigned ignorance or shamming. Socrates feigns ignorance as part of a strategy for exposing the ignorance of the person he is questioning; the pretended confusion is the tactic, not real bewilderment. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Socrates' (iep.utm.edu/socrates).

question: Euthyphro is so sure he understands holiness that he has come to court to prosecute his own father for a killing. Socrates greets him, says he knows nothing of holiness himself, and asks Euthyphro to teach him so he might become his pupil. Five attempts at a definition later, Euthyphro abruptly claims he is late and hurries away. Why had Socrates asked to be Euthyphro's student?
answer: He was setting a trap to push Euthyphro into trying and failing to define holiness plainly
choices: He was setting a trap to push Euthyphro into trying and failing to define holiness plainly
He honestly needed Euthyphro's expertise to judge whether the father truly deserved prosecuting
He hoped that a friendly chat might persuade Euthyphro to drop the case against his own father
He wanted to delay the hearing long enough for his own accusers to lose interest in his case
context: In Plato's 'Euthyphro' (5a-b) Socrates says he 'can learn from him and will become his pupil' — the meek-pupil pose was the trap. After five failed definitions of holiness, Euthyphro 'abruptly ends the conversation and walks away, pretending to be late.' Sources: IEP, 'Socrates' (Euthyphro 5a-b); LitCharts, 'Euthyphro' summary.

question: Thomas Sowell's most-quoted line, from a 2005 TV interview, is: "There are no solutions, there are only trade-offs." Imagine a friend says a new rule will "solve" the litter in your park. Taking Sowell's line seriously, which worry would he most want you to raise?
answer: Some cost lands on people you will never see or count.
choices: Some cost lands on people you will never see or count.
A good enough rule can wipe a problem out entirely.
The loudest complainers should set what the rule does.
A plan is fine as long as its first results look good.
context: Sowell's point is that every choice spends something - there is no free fix, only a better-or-worse exchange. The perfection worry ("wipe it out entirely?") chases a fantasy; letting the loudest voices decide is a different mistake; judging by the first visible results stops at "Stage One," the immediate price. His move presses past all of that to the cost that does NOT show up in front of you - the people who quietly pay and never get counted. Source: Sowell, 2005 Fox News interview with Fred Barnes (https://www.aei.org/carpe-diem/video-thomas-sowells-most-profound-economic-insight-and-his-three-questions-for-the-left/).

question: Thomas Sowell taught a three-word question he said would deflate most arguments he disagreed with: "Compared to what?" A town council is judging a flawed bus plan. One member calls it a failure because it isn't perfect. By Sowell's move, what should the plan actually be measured against?
answer: The best real alternative the town could choose instead.
choices: The best real alternative the town could choose instead.
A perfect plan with no flaws that anyone can imagine.
The hopes the council had when they first proposed it.
Whether every single rider ends up completely satisfied.
context: Sowell's error to catch is comparing a real thing to a fantasy. A plan can have ugly downsides and still be the best option on the table; a "perfect-sounding" plan can be worse than the messy one it replaces. You judge against the next-best real choice, not against perfection. Source: https://www.aei.org/carpe-diem/video-thomas-sowells-most-profound-economic-insight-and-his-three-questions-for-the-left/ ; https://blog.acton.org/archives/83316-3-questions-to-counter-arguments-from-the-economic-left.html

question: Thomas Sowell, born in 1930 in the segregated South and raised in Harlem after his father died before he was born, dropped out of an elite high school and served as a Marine Corps photographer before reaching Harvard. As a young man he held one strong political conviction that he would later spend his career attacking. What was it?
answer: He was a committed Marxist who believed in the system.
choices: He was a committed Marxist who believed in the system.
He was a devoted free-market believer who trusted the market.
He was a firm pacifist who opposed every kind of war.
He was a strict traditionalist who distrusted all change.
context: Sowell graduated Harvard magna cum laude at 28 and earned his economics PhD at the University of Chicago in 1968. He began a committed Marxist and became one of Marxism's sharpest critics - a reversal driven by what he found in the data, not by changing crowds. Sources: https://reason.com/2021/06/12/the-conversion-of-thomas-sowell/ ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Thomas-Sowell ; https://manhattan.institute/article/thomas-sowells-harlem-years

question: In his 2003 book "Applied Economics," Thomas Sowell warns against stopping your thinking at "Stage One" - the immediate, visible result of a policy. He says many politicians can't see past it because they don't think beyond the next election. How does Sowell say you should judge a policy instead?
answer: Trace it to its later effects, which can reverse the first one.
choices: Trace it to its later effects, which can reverse the first one.
Judge it by whether the immediate, visible result looks good.
Judge it by how good the intentions behind it clearly are.
Judge it by whether the right experts endorse its design.
context: The trap is treating the first visible result as the whole story - exactly what the second choice does. Intentions and expert approval are not the test either. Sowell's later stages often run opposite to Stage One, so you follow a policy through to its repercussions. The book's subtitle is literally "Thinking Beyond Stage One." Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_Economics:_Thinking_Beyond_Stage_One

question: Thomas Sowell gives a plain example of stopping your thinking too early: a state raises taxes on a business. In Stage One, the visible win, the state collects more money. But Sowell says that if you keep tracing it through later stages, the result can flip. What does he say tends to happen next?
answer: The business moves parts of itself and builds elsewhere.
choices: The business moves parts of itself and builds elsewhere.
The business happily pays and the revenue keeps climbing.
Every other business in the state lowers its own prices.
The state's voters immediately demand even higher taxes.
context: New factories get built in other states, and over time the state can end up with LESS revenue, not more - the opposite of the Stage One win. The lesson is that stopping at the first result is the trap. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_Economics:_Thinking_Beyond_Stage_One

question: In the summer of 1960, the young Marxist Thomas Sowell interned at the U.S. Labor Department studying the minimum wage in Puerto Rico's sugar industry, and found that as the wage rose, employment FELL. But the detail that shook him most was about the agency itself. What did Sowell realize about the Labor Department?
answer: It had little reason to find the harm, since the program funded it.
choices: It had little reason to find the harm, since the program funded it.
It was secretly run by the sugar companies it claimed to police.
It had quietly published his exact finding years before he arrived.
It already planned to raise the wage even higher the very next year.
context: Administering the minimum wage was a big part of the Labor Department's budget and staff, so the agency benefited from NOT finding the damage. That insight - that the people running a policy can have an incentive to stay blind to its costs - is the seed of Sowell's whole later critique. Source: https://reason.com/2021/06/12/the-conversion-of-thomas-sowell/

question: Thomas Sowell set a strict bar for the word "solution": he said you have reached one only when it is no longer necessary to make a trade-off at all. A friend insists a new law has finally "solved" a problem for good. By that strict bar, why would Sowell say the thing your friend is describing almost never qualifies?
answer: Picking it still means accepting a real cost somewhere.
choices: Picking it still means accepting a real cost somewhere.
The right experts were never put in charge of building it.
Most people are simply too lazy to finish the real job.
A true fix exists, but officials keep it hidden from us.
context: Sowell's strict definition: "A solution is achieved when it is no longer necessary to make a trade-off." Almost every real choice still forces you to bear a cost on one side to gain something on the other, so it never clears that bar - what people call a "solution" is usually just a trade-off in disguise, not a job left unfinished, not a missing expert, not a hidden cure. Source: Sowell, A Conflict of Visions (1987), quoted at https://holisticinvestor.substack.com/p/there-are-no-solutions-only-trade

question: In "A Conflict of Visions" (1987), Thomas Sowell splits political thinkers by a single question: WHY does evil exist in the world? One camp, which includes Jean-Jacques Rousseau, blames bad institutions and people's foolish or immoral choices - all of it fixable. Sowell's other camp gives a very different answer about where evil comes from. What does that camp say?
answer: It comes from the permanent flaws built into every human being.
choices: It comes from the permanent flaws built into every human being.
It comes from a few uniquely wicked people who must be removed.
It comes from ignorance that the right education would erase.
It comes from material scarcity that real abundance would dissolve.
context: Sowell calls Rousseau's camp the UNCONSTRAINED vision: evils are fixable, so an ideal solution exists. The other camp is the CONSTRAINED vision (Adam Smith, Edmund Burke, Hobbes), which traces evil to the "inherent moral and intellectual limitations of human beings" - not a few wicked individuals, not curable ignorance, not scarcity, but a flaw universal and permanent in everyone, so the most you get is a prudent trade-off, never a cure. Steven Pinker later renamed the pair the "utopian" and the "tragic" visions. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Conflict_of_Visions ; https://theindependentwhig.wordpress.com/haidt-passages/sowell-constrained-and-unconstrained-visions/sowell-the-unconstrained-vision/

question: When Amsterdam's Talmud Torah elders pronounced their fearsome herem against the 23-year-old Baruch Spinoza in 1656, theirs stood apart from every other ban the community ever issued in one striking way. What made this curse extraordinary?
answer: It was never lifted
choices: It was never lifted
It was read out in Latin
It named his father as well
It was to last exactly one year
context: A herem is the Jewish ban of excommunication. Spinoza's was the harshest his congregation ever issued, and uniquely it was never lifted: 'Cursed be he by day and cursed by night... cursed in his going forth, and cursed in his coming in.' It forbade anyone to speak with him, do business with him, come near him, or read a word he wrote. Source: NEH, Why Spinoza Was Excommunicated; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza; the congregation's Book of Ordinances (Livro dos Acordos da Nacao e Ascamot).

question: Baruch Spinoza turned down professorships and fame to earn his bread at a quiet, skilled craft. The same trade most likely killed him at 44 in 1677, his lungs scarred by years of breathing the fine dust it threw off. What was the craft that paid his way and ruined his lungs?
answer: Grinding optical lenses
choices: Grinding optical lenses
Setting printer's type
Cutting diamond gems
Blowing window glass
context: Spinoza ground lenses for microscopes and telescopes. He died February 21, 1677, of consumption (pulmonary tuberculosis), his lungs believed to have been damaged by years of inhaled glass dust. Source: World History Encyclopedia: Baruch Spinoza; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza.

question: Baruch Spinoza knew his ideas were dangerous, so he sealed his letters with a signet ring carved with a thorny rose and a single Latin word. He chose it for a world he judged was not ready for him. What was the word on the ring?
answer: Caute
choices: Caute
Cogito
Veritas
Libertas
context: 'Caute' is Latin for 'be careful' or 'beware.' Spinoza's signet ring paired it with a thorny rose, the motto of a thinker who knew the world was not ready for him. (Cogito = 'I think', from Descartes; Veritas = 'truth'; Libertas = 'freedom'.) Source: kvond.wordpress.com, 'Spinoza's Rose' (2008); Streets of Israel, 13 Things About Baruch Spinoza.

question: After Amsterdam's Jewish community cursed and expelled Baruch Spinoza, the young philosopher stopped signing himself with that Hebrew given name, Baruch, and began using the Latin form instead. Strikingly, the two names carry the very same meaning. What name did he take, and what do both names mean?
answer: Benedictus, meaning blessed
choices: Benedictus, meaning blessed
Maledictus, meaning cursed
Sapiens, meaning wise
Solitarius, meaning alone
context: Both 'Baruch' (Hebrew) and 'Benedictus' (Latin) mean 'blessed.' After the ban he set aside Baruch and signed himself Benedictus. Among the charges that got him expelled: denying the soul's immortality, rejecting a transcendent God, and holding that the Torah was not literally handed down by God. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza.

question: The charge that got Baruch Spinoza cursed and expelled at 23 was, in part, his idea about God. He would soon build a whole philosophy out of it, captured in a Latin phrase historians still quote. Setting aside whether he was right, what was Spinoza's actual claim about God and the natural world?
answer: God and Nature are one and the same thing
choices: God and Nature are one and the same thing
God is a perfect mind who designed Nature
God is the moral law written into Nature
God speaks to us through signs in Nature
context: Spinoza's marquee move, summed up in his phrase 'Deus, sive Natura' ('God, or Nature'): the natural world is not a power separate from and below God but one and the same with divine power, with no separate creator standing outside it. The question is the identification itself, not a verdict on whether it is true. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza; Spinoza, Ethics IV Preface.

question: Baruch Spinoza argued there is only ONE thing that truly exists in its own right, needing nothing else in order to exist: a single infinite, eternal substance he called God, or Nature. So what, in his system, is every rock, mind, and person you can point to?
answer: A passing modification of that one substance
choices: A passing modification of that one substance
A thing God created to exist on its own
A separate soul on loan from the divine
A copy of an eternal form beyond the world
context: For Spinoza everything other than the one substance is a 'mode,' a passing modification of it. As the Ethics puts it: 'Whatever is, is in God, and nothing can be or be conceived without God' (Ip15). ('Substance' = that which exists in itself and needs nothing else in order to exist.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza; Spinoza, Ethics Ip15.

question: Baruch Spinoza cast his masterwork, the Ethics, in a startling form for a book about God and human freedom: he wrote it the way Euclid wrote geometry, sealing each step with Q.E.D. as though God and the human mind were theorems. Most readers would expect a religious work to plead, preach, or console. Why would Spinoza reach for the cold machinery of mathematics instead?
answer: To force his conclusions on anyone who granted his opening handful of self-evident truths
choices: To force his conclusions on anyone who granted his opening handful of self-evident truths
To dress dangerous heresies in a form too forbidding for hostile outsiders to follow
To borrow mathematics' prestige and make daring claims look already settled and safe
To slip the whole work past Church censors who were watching only for plain preaching
context: Spinoza wrote the Ethics 'in geometrical order,' aiming to deduce God, mind, and human freedom as strict consequences: grant the opening definitions and axioms and you are logically compelled to grant everything that follows. His goal was demonstrative force, not disguise or borrowed authority. Its last line: 'All things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Spinoza; Spinoza, Ethics Vp42 scholium.

question: In 1673 the University of Heidelberg offered Baruch Spinoza its chair of philosophy. The letter promised him ample freedom to teach as he pleased, adding only that the prince trusted he would not use it to disturb the publicly established religion. To most scholars this was a dream post. Spinoza weighed that single clause and declined. What had he seen in it?
answer: A permission whose one condition quietly cancelled the permission
choices: A permission whose one condition quietly cancelled the permission
An oath of loyalty he could sign in good conscience
A limit only on public preaching, not on teaching
A routine formality that every professor accepted
context: Johann Ludwig Fabritius, writing for Karl Ludwig, Elector Palatine, promised 'the most ample freedom in philosophical teaching, which the prince is confident you will not misuse, to disturb the religion publicly established.' Spinoza read the catch and politely refused: the one condition took back the very freedom the chair offered. Source: Correspondence of Spinoza, Letters LIII and LIV; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Spinoza.

question: Baruch Spinoza ground optical lenses for a living rather than chase fame, and his glass was good enough that he kept company with Europe's leading astronomers. In 1665 the famous Christiaan Huygens, who ground his own lenses, joined Spinoza at a thirty-foot telescope for a single remarkable night of stargazing. Which world did the two of them turn it on?
answer: The planet Jupiter
choices: The planet Jupiter
The planet Saturn
The planet Mars
The planet Venus
context: In 1665 Spinoza joined Christiaan Huygens to observe Jupiter through a thirty-foot telescope. Even the Huygens brothers, who ground their own lenses, rated Spinoza's the best they could get, yet he chose to keep his quiet craftsman's life rather than pursue fame. Source: Britannica: Benedict de Spinoza; kvond.wordpress.com, 'Spinoza's Foci' optics articles.

question: Baruch Spinoza held that nothing in Nature is merely possible or contingent; every event was bound to happen, following from the nature of God-or-Nature as necessarily as a triangle's three angles follow from what a triangle is. A reader presses him: then what about a miracle, an event that suspends the ordinary course of Nature? On Spinoza's own principles, how must he answer?
answer: Nothing can ever run contrary to Nature, so no true miracle is possible
choices: Nothing can ever run contrary to Nature, so no true miracle is possible
God can step in to overrule Nature whenever He means to reward the faithful
What looks miraculous is a real event whose natural cause we have simply not yet grasped
A real miracle can occur but lies forever beyond what human reason can explain
context: 'In nature there is nothing contingent, but all things have been determined from the necessity of the divine nature to exist and produce an effect in a certain way' (Ip29). God does not choose by free will or aim at goals; everything follows from God's nature the way a triangle's angles follow from its definition. A miracle would mean something contrary to Nature, but for Spinoza nothing can be contrary to Nature, so he denies the category outright, not merely our knowledge of its causes. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza; Spinoza, Ethics Ip29.

question: Baruch Spinoza accepted only one substance, God-or-Nature, knowable in countless ways. Most thinkers of his day puzzled over how a mind and a body manage to push each other around, how a decision moves an arm, how a wound troubles the soul. Spinoza rejected the whole question as wrongly put. In his view, how do a person's mind and body actually relate?
answer: They are a single reality described two ways, neither one ever pushing the other
choices: They are a single reality described two ways, neither one ever pushing the other
The mind steers the body from within the way a pilot steers his ship
The body acts and the soul merely looks on, powerless to move it
Two created things God yokes together to act in perfect concert
context: For Spinoza a thing and the idea of that thing are not two items but one reality seen two ways: 'a mode of extension and the idea of that mode are one and the same thing, but expressed in two ways' (IIp7s). Because mind and body are one reality under two descriptions, they never causally push each other, and the old puzzle of how they interact dissolves. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza; Spinoza, Ethics IIp7 scholium.

question: For Baruch Spinoza the highest human good was not pleasure, power, or even being spared death, but something he called the intellectual love of God: the joy of a mind that truly understands Nature, whose ideas come to mirror the deepest order of God-or-Nature itself. In Spinoza's view, what does a mind gain by reaching this understanding?
answer: It comes to share in eternity
choices: It comes to share in eternity
It earns a place in the afterlife
It wins power over other people
It escapes the body altogether
context: This is the 'amor Dei intellectualis.' When the mind understands Nature, its ideas mirror God's eternal order and so 'participate in eternity.' Spinoza adds a startling identity: God's love toward man and the mind's intellectual love toward God are one and the same love. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza; Spinoza, Ethics Part V.

question: Benedict de Spinoza wrote a whole book of ethics the way Euclid wrote his geometry. He believed how to live could be worked out as rigorously as a math proof. How did he actually build the book?
answer: He began from self-evident definitions and axioms, then proved each new claim only from ones already established before it.
choices: He began from self-evident definitions and axioms, then proved each new claim only from ones already established before it.
He gathered wise sayings out of many old traditions and carefully arranged the whole collection by theme.
He told vivid parables and let the moral of each one quietly emerge from the unfolding story itself.
He set down long back-and-forth dialogues, testing every single claim by patient question and answer.
context: Each of the Ethics' five parts opens with definitions and axioms (truths assumed self-evident, needing no proof), then grinds out a chain of propositions, each proved only from what came before — exactly Euclid's structure. The full title says it outright: 'Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order' (Ethica, ordine geometrico demonstrata). The audacious claim was that how to live could be deduced step by step, the way you deduce a triangle's angles. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Geometrical Method'; Wikipedia, 'Spinoza's Ethics'.

question: Benedict de Spinoza ended each of his moral proofs about God, the mind, and freedom the way Euclid signs off a proven theorem in geometry: with the geometer's proof-mark, Q.E.D. — quod erat demonstrandum, which was to be demonstrated. By stamping a conclusion about God with the very mark that closes a proof about a triangle, what was he asserting?
answer: Reason by itself had reached the conclusion, with no appeal to scripture, authority, or revelation.
choices: Reason by itself had reached the conclusion, with no appeal to scripture, authority, or revelation.
The conclusion was offered humbly as one man’s guess, open to revision by any later reader.
The matter was a sacred mystery that argument could gesture toward but never finally settle.
The point rested on faith first, and the proof was added afterward to comfort the doubtful.
context: Q.E.D. is short for the Latin 'quod erat demonstrandum' — 'which was to be demonstrated' — the mark a geometer writes to close a finished proof. By signing off a conclusion about God or human freedom with the exact mark used for proving a triangle, Spinoza was making the audacious claim of the whole project: reason alone had reached the conclusion — no preaching, no scripture, no appeal to authority. The distractor stances were precisely what the geometric method refused: not a tentative personal guess, not a mystery left to faith, not a conclusion propped up by belief after the fact. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Baruch Spinoza'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Geometrical Method'.

question: In the third part of his Ethics, Benedict de Spinoza turned his geometric method on the passions — love, hate, jealousy, fear. He vowed to treat them as if he were dealing with lines, planes, and solids, aiming not to mock or condemn human actions but to understand them. What stance toward the emotions did this commit him to?
answer: They arise from their own causes by strict necessity, so they ask to be explained like any other effect.
choices: They arise from their own causes by strict necessity, so they ask to be explained like any other effect.
They are failures of a weak will, which a person must repent of and slowly learn to master.
They lie private and beyond all reason, so philosophy is wise to simply leave them well alone.
They are unreal illusions, and the truly wise person learns in the end to feel nothing at all.
context: In the Part III preface Spinoza wrote that he would 'consider human actions and desires in exactly the same manner as though I were concerned with lines, planes, and solids' — a geometry of the emotions, treating feelings as effects that follow from causes by necessity rather than as sins to be scolded. His stated aim was 'not to mock, lament, or execrate human actions, but to understand them.' Source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part III Preface (quoted in EBSCO Research Starters and Wikiquote, 'Baruch Spinoza').

question: A campus sidewalk bends around the corner of a lawn. Over a few weeks a bare dirt trail appears straight across the grass, cutting the corner the pavement ignored. A new student asks where the trail came from. Which answer is true?
answer: One footstep at a time, as each passer-by took the shortest way across
choices: One footstep at a time, as each passer-by took the shortest way across
A groundskeeper marked it out as the lawn's one official walking route
The campus architect drew it on the master plan but left it unpaved
The grass simply died along that strip, unrelated to anyone walking
context: This is a 'desire path' (or desire line): the route people actually walk, worn one step at a time with no designer. It can appear after as few as about fifteen crossings, and once a faint track shows, others spot it and follow - so it reinforces itself. It is order with no plan behind it. Source: 99% Invisible, 'Least Resistance: How Desire Paths Can Lead to Better Design'; Wikipedia, 'Desire path'.

question: English has firm rules - add an 's' for more than one, keep the words in a certain order - and almost everyone follows them. A child asks how those rules got set. Which account is true of how the grammar of a living language actually arose?
answer: It grew on its own over centuries as people talked and were understood
choices: It grew on its own over centuries as people talked and were understood
A council of scholars wrote the full rules and the public then adopted them
A single celebrated author fixed the grammar in one settled rulebook
A king decreed the grammar and made his subjects speak exactly that way
context: Nobody invented language; no one wrote the rules of English first and handed them out. The grammar grew up by itself as generations kept speaking. Hayek used language as his favorite example of a refined, useful order that had no inventor. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: In 1887 a young eye doctor named L. L. Zamenhof built a whole language from scratch with just sixteen grammar rules, and signed it with the pen name 'Doktoro Esperanto' - 'one who hopes.' Many such invented languages are tried; almost all die unspoken. What became of Zamenhof's?
answer: It became the most successful invented language in human history
choices: It became the most successful invented language in human history
It was banned by his government and survived only in old letters
It stayed a private code shared among a handful of his friends
It was slowly absorbed into German until nothing of it remained
context: Esperanto - the language took its name from his pen name - is the most successful made-from-scratch language, the deliberate opposite of a tongue that grew on its own. The twist Hayek's followers love: even Esperanto began growing on its own once real people used it, coining new words and shifting usage. A designed thing can sprout a grown order inside it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Esperanto' (Unua Libro, July 26, 1887).

question: Barter has a built-in wall: to trade, you each have to want what the other has. The economist Carl Menger set out to explain how humanity first broke through that wall and got money, back in the earliest days of trade. Which origin story did Menger argue for?
answer: Traders kept taking the most tradeable good until one quietly became money
choices: Traders kept taking the most tradeable good until one quietly became money
A wise king studied all his markets and declared one metal the realm's coin
Merchants gathered in a great congress and voted on a good all would take
A temple grew rich, then issued the first tokens and lent them to traders
context: Menger argued no king or committee invented money: each trader independently accepted whichever good was 'most saleable,' everyone drifted to the same one, and it became money - solving barter's 'double coincidence of wants' with no one aiming to. He summed it up: money 'has not been generated by law. In its origin it is a social, and not a state-institution.' Source: Carl Menger, 'On the Origin of Money' (1892); FEE; Mises Institute.

question: The Scottish thinker Adam Ferguson, writing in 1767, asked how nations come by their laws, customs, and whole way of life. He compressed his answer into one line so sharp it became the seed of a big idea. Which line is Ferguson's?
answer: They are the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design
choices: They are the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design
They are the gift of wise founders who clearly foresaw the whole future ahead
They are pure accidents of fortune in which deliberate human effort plays no part
They are the standing commands of rulers, obeyed only until a stronger ruler comes
context: Ferguson wrote that 'nations stumble upon establishments, which are indeed the result of human action, but not the execution of any human design.' His picture: 'Every step and every movement of the multitude... are made with equal blindness to the future,' yet lasting institutions appear anyway. This line is the seed the whole idea of spontaneous order grows from. Source: Adam Ferguson, An Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767); Online Library of Liberty.

question: A boy sees that everyone in his town greets each other the same odd way and asks his grandfather how the custom came to be. The grandfather says any custom you ever meet sorts cleanly into the same three boxes, and the trick is keeping all three open. Which trio of boxes is he handing the boy?
answer: Someone designed it, or it grew with no designer, or it was sheer chance
choices: Someone designed it, or it grew with no designer, or it was sheer chance
A leader ordered it, the townsfolk chose it together, or an old habit held on
Neighbors were copied, it was invented at home, or travelers carried it in
It began as a joke, stiffened into a rule, then hardened into something sacred
context: There are really three answers to 'why is it this way?': someone designed it (a watch), it grew with no designer (a footpath, money, language), or it was blind luck. The skill is not assuming 'designed' the moment you see order - much of the best order grew, and some apparent order is plain chance. Source: synthesis of Hayek, Law, Legislation and Liberty, and Adam Ferguson, via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Friedrich Hayek'.

question: Friedrich Hayek said it makes plain sense to ask what an army is FOR: a commander drew it up to win a battle. But he insisted the very same question misleads you the moment you aim it at a market. Why, in Hayek's view, does asking 'what is it for?' fit the army yet mislead you about the market?
answer: The army was built to win; the market was built by no one, so it holds no aim
choices: The army was built to win; the market was built by no one, so it holds no aim
The army answers to one commander; the market to millions, so its aim is theirs combined
The army can lose and disband; the market never ends, so its aim outlasts any one goal
The army serves its general; the market serves the richest, so its aim is whoever holds power
context: Hayek borrowed two Greek words for the split: TAXIS, a made order (literally troops arranged by a commander), versus KOSMOS, a grown order. A made order always has the goal its maker gave it; a grown order can have none of its own, even when it is hugely useful to those inside it. So 'what is it for?' is fair of an army but misleads you when aimed at a language or a market. Source: Allen Mendenhall, 'Taxis and Cosmos: A Clarifying Table' (quoting Hayek); F. A. Hayek, Law, Legislation and Liberty.

question: Maria's brother makes a quick, sloppy argument for a later curfew. Maria wants to win the disagreement for good. Instead of pouncing on his clumsy wording, she first rebuilds his case into the strongest, most reasonable version she can — better than he actually said — and answers THAT. What is the point of beating the strongest version rather than the weak one?
answer: Defeating his clumsy wording proves nothing, since he can just say he meant something better
choices: Defeating his clumsy wording proves nothing, since he can just say he meant something better
Restating his case fairly is only good manners and changes nothing about who is right
Winning against a weak version embarrasses him enough that he drops the whole demand
Agreeing with his best points first means she no longer has to disagree at all
context: This is the 'steel man,' the deliberate opposite of the straw man: instead of attacking the flimsiest phrasing, you build the most robust version of the other side — one even harder to defeat than what they actually said — and answer that. The metaphor is exact: straw is easy to knock down, steel stands up. Source: Wiktionary, 'steelman'; Chana Messinger, 'The Merely Real' (2012).

question: In a debate club, Theo crushes the weakest, silliest form of his opponent's position and declares victory. His opponent calmly replies that Theo just knocked down something nobody actually believes. Why has Theo settled nothing, even though he 'won'?
answer: He beat a version his opponent never held, so his opponent simply says 'that's not what I meant'
choices: He beat a version his opponent never held, so his opponent simply says 'that's not what I meant'
He was rude while winning, and rudeness always cancels out a real victory
He forgot to list the points he agreed with before he started attacking
He argued too long, so the audience stopped paying attention to his case
context: Beating a straw man proves nothing — the opponent just disowns it. Only by demolishing the strongest, most charitable version do you earn a victory that actually settles the question. Source: synthesis of 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (steelman as anti-straw-man) and Chana Messinger, 'The Merely Real' (2012).

question: Aisha disagrees with a classmate, but before she argues back she restates his view aloud. He lights up and says, 'Thanks — I wish I'd thought of putting it that way.' Many things could lie behind that 'thanks.' What did his reaction actually prove Aisha had done?
answer: She put his own view into words so good that he himself would gladly use them
choices: She put his own view into words so good that he himself would gladly use them
She buttered him up with praise, so his thanks was really just him being flattered
She uncovered a hidden assumption beneath his view that he had never noticed
She pushed him into conceding the point, and the thanks was his way of giving in
context: This is Rapoport's first rule, presented by Daniel Dennett in 'Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking' (2013) and credited to game theorist Anatol Rapoport: re-express the target's view 'so clearly, vividly, and fairly that your target says, "Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way."' The 'thanks' is not flattery, a confession, or surrender — it certifies that she captured HIS position in words he would himself endorse. If you can only describe their view in terms they'd reject, you're arguing with a version that exists only in your own head. Source: Dennett (2013); The Marginalian (2014).

question: Devon notices a habit in himself: whenever he argues, he quietly skips the hardest version of the other side and only takes on the weak forms he's sure he can beat. A friend tells him this dodge actually reveals something about Devon's own confidence. What does always avoiding the strong version reveal?
answer: That he is secretly afraid the strong version might be right, and won't face it
choices: That he is secretly afraid the strong version might be right, and won't face it
That he is too polite to embarrass an opponent with the full force of his case
That he has already studied the strong version and found it not worth repeating
That he prefers short arguments and the strong version simply takes too long
context: Chana Messinger framed facing the strongest version as what real confidence looks like: it shows 'you know exactly what your opponents are up to, and that if it was good you'd reconsider, but it's not, so you won't.' Refusing to face the strong version is the tell that you're afraid of it. Source: Chana Messinger, "'Charity' Is Totally Badass Activism," The Merely Real, Dec 29 2012.

question: The game theorist Anatol Rapoport laid out four steps for criticizing someone well, and he put the criticism deliberately LAST: first restate their view so well they thank you, then list every point you agree with, then say what you learned from them. Only after all three are you permitted a word of rebuttal. Why does this recipe hold criticism until the end?
answer: Because doing the first three steps turns your opponent into a receptive audience for your criticism
choices: Because doing the first three steps turns your opponent into a receptive audience for your criticism
Because the rules forbid any criticism at all until both sides fully agree
Because listing agreements long enough usually makes the disagreement disappear on its own
Because the person who speaks last in a debate is the one judged to have won
context: Daniel Dennett presents 'Rapoport's Rules' in 'Intuition Pumps' (2013) and is blunt that it's a winning tactic, not just good manners: proving you understood disarms your opponent before you ever swing, making them 'a receptive audience' for the rebuttal. Source: Dennett (2013); The Marginalian, 'How to Criticize with Kindness' (2014).

question: John Stuart Mill argued in 'On Liberty' (1859) that it is not enough to hear your opponents' views filtered through your own teachers' refutations — you must hear those views 'from persons who actually believe them,' in their most plausible and persuasive form. Mill drove the warning home with a single famous line about the person who never bothers to do this. Which line was it?
answer: 'He who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that'
choices: 'He who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that'
'A person does not say things for naught'
'Assertions startlingly false are likely to turn on differences of language'
'The strong man will soon morph into a steel man'
context: Mill wrote the steelman two centuries before the word existed: it is not enough to hear opponents refuted by your own teachers — you must meet their case in its strongest, most sincerely held form. The distractor lines are real maxims from elsewhere in this same tradition — Rabbi Meir on not dismissing others, Quine on charity in translation, and the 2003 joke that coined 'steel man' — but only the keyed line is Mill's, and only it is about the cost of knowing just your own side. Source: John Stuart Mill, 'On Liberty' (1859), Chapter 2.

question: On August 8, 2003, in an online discussion, Paul C. Anagnostopoulos tossed off a joke about an opponent's overblown argument: 'this straw man is so big and so strong that he'll soon morph into a steel man.' It is the earliest known use of the term — and the thinkers who picked it up did something unexpected with the insult. What became of Anagnostopoulos's throwaway jab?
answer: The insult flipped into a virtue — a name for building your opponent's argument at its strongest
choices: The insult flipped into a virtue — a name for building your opponent's argument at its strongest
The insult was forgotten, and the term was independently coined decades later by philosophers
The insult became a formal fallacy, the name for any argument made too strong to be fair
The insult stuck as mockery, used ever since for opponents who exaggerate their own case
context: The earliest written use of 'steel man' as an argument term was a joke — and the jab flipped into the name for one of reasoning's great virtues. Source: Wordspy, 'steel man' (earliest citation: Paul C. Anagnostopoulos, Aug 8 2003).

question: John Stuart Mill pressed a harder point in 'On Liberty' (1859): suppose your opinion is actually true, and no one has ever refuted it — yet you yourself cannot answer the strongest objections the other side could raise. Mill says that in this case you have 'no ground for preferring either opinion.' On Mill's reasoning, what is wrong with holding a true belief you cannot defend against its best challenge?
answer: It is luck, not knowledge — you happen to be right without being able to show why
choices: It is luck, not knowledge — you happen to be right without being able to show why
It is dishonest, since a belief you can't defend should always be abandoned
It is harmless, because a belief that is true needs no defense to count as knowledge
It is arrogant, because only experts are entitled to hold opinions on hard questions
context: Mill's deeper case for steelmanning: even a true belief, held by someone who cannot meet the strongest opposing reasons, rests on luck rather than understanding. Knowing why the best objection fails is what turns a lucky guess into knowledge. Source: John Stuart Mill, 'On Liberty' (1859), Chapter 2.

question: Neil L. Wilson, in a 1959 paper, named the rule philosophers now call the 'principle of charity' — the very rule that steelmanning puts into practice. Imagine a new student blurts out, 'Nobody passed the test,' even though three of her classmates clearly did pass. Wilson's rule tells you how to read a clumsy, ambiguous claim like hers. Which reading does it tell you to choose?
answer: That she meant only her own study group, the reading that keeps most of her words true
choices: That she meant only her own study group, the reading that keeps most of her words true
That literally not one single student in the entire class actually managed to pass the test
That she was secretly sneering at the three who passed, to erase what they had done
That she meant whichever twisted version is the easiest one for you to argue against
context: This is the 'principle of charity,' named by Neil L. Wilson in 'Substances without Substrata' (1959). His test: when someone's words are ambiguous, read them so as to make the largest possible number of their statements come out true — here, that she meant her own group, not the whole class. It is the underlying rule that steelmanning puts into practice. Source: Wilson (1959), The Review of Metaphysics; summarized at Effectiviology, 'The Principle of Charity.'

question: W.V.O. Quine, working out how anyone could translate a foreign language from scratch in 'Word and Object' (1960), reached a rule for what to do when a translation makes a speaker sound absurd: 'assertions startlingly false on the face of them are likely to turn on hidden differences of language.' When your reading makes someone sound ridiculous, what does Quine say is the more likely explanation?
answer: You have mistranslated them, since deep silliness is less likely than a bad translation
choices: You have mistranslated them, since deep silliness is less likely than a bad translation
They are in fact being ridiculous, and you should report exactly what they said
They are joking, and a startling claim should always be read as humor first
They hold a foreign belief that no careful translation could ever capture
context: Quine built charity into the heart of translation: his punchline was that 'one's interlocutor's silliness, beyond a certain point, is less likely than bad translation.' If a reading makes someone sound absurd, suspect the reading first. Source: W.V.O. Quine, 'Word and Object' (1960).

question: Donald Davidson pushed the principle of charity further than anyone before him: he argued it is not a favor you may choose to grant or withhold, but — in his words — 'a presupposition of any interpretation whatsoever,' something built into the very act of interpreting another person. He called charity 'not optional.' If Davidson is right about that, what follows for someone who tries to drop it?
answer: He can no longer make sense of them as a speaker at all
choices: He can no longer make sense of them as a speaker at all
He still understands them perfectly, having dropped only a kindness
He fairly judges them mistaken whenever they really are mistaken
He understands them fine but cannot hope to change their mind
context: Davidson turned charity from a courtesy into a precondition of understanding anyone at all — his rule was to 'optimise agreement between ourselves and those we interpret,' which he also called 'rational accommodation.' Charity, he held, is 'not optional': unless you assume the other side holds mostly true beliefs and reasons soundly, you could not make sense of their words as words at all — they would be mere noise to you. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Donald Davidson.'

question: Long before philosophers named the principle of charity, an early-third-century Jewish sage, Rabbi Meir, is credited (by tradition) with a maxim that captures its spirit: 'a person does not say things for naught.' The saying tells you how to treat another person's words even before you decide whether you agree. How does Rabbi Meir's maxim tell you to treat what someone says?
answer: Assume their words carry rational intent worth taking seriously, not nonsense to dismiss
choices: Assume their words carry rational intent worth taking seriously, not nonsense to dismiss
Assume their words are true until someone proves otherwise beyond doubt
Repeat their words back exactly before you are allowed to respond at all
Treat their words as binding promises they must later be held to keep
context: An ancient ancestor of the principle of charity, attributed by tradition to the sage Rabbi Meir (early 3rd century CE) — labeled here as legend, since the attribution is traditional. Source: cited in Effectiviology, 'The Principle of Charity.'

question: A museum case is full of gorgeous medieval swords, centuries old, still gleaming. A visitor concludes, "They don't make blades like they used to — every medieval smith must have been a master." What is the flaw in that conclusion?
answer: The weak and badly-forged blades broke or rusted away long ago, so only the finest ones survived to be displayed
choices: The weak and badly-forged blades broke or rusted away long ago, so only the finest ones survived to be displayed
The visitor compares two eras unfairly, since modern blades are made to serve very different purposes
Medieval smiths guarded secret forging techniques that were lost and never written down for us
The museum chose only its finest pieces for display, while the ordinary ones sit in storage unseen
context: This is survivorship bias: we judge a whole population by the handful that made it through a brutal filter. The clumsy, brittle, badly-forged medieval blades snapped, rusted to nothing, or were melted down for scrap; only the toughest, best-preserved, or purely ceremonial pieces lasted to reach a display case. So the surviving swords aren't a fair sample of average medieval work — they're the ones that survived. Source: Hackaday (2025), 'Medieval Iron, Survivorship Bias And Modern Metallurgy'; Statology, 'Survivorship Bias' (Royal Armouries example).

question: "Bill Gates and Steve Jobs both dropped out of college and became billionaires — so dropping out is a smart bet." A friend repeats this as career advice. What is wrong with the reasoning?
answer: You only hear about the few dropouts who struck it rich; the many who dropped out and struggled left no trace
choices: You only hear about the few dropouts who struck it rich; the many who dropped out and struggled left no trace
Gates and Jobs were unusually gifted, so their results say almost nothing about what anyone else should do
Dropping out merely came before their wealth; it does not follow that dropping out is what caused it
Two examples is far too small a sample to support any general rule about dropping out at all
context: Each of the other replies names a real flaw, but the specific trap here is survivorship bias. The dropout billionaires are famous precisely because they won; the vastly larger crowd who dropped out and struggled never got a magazine cover or a stage, so they vanish from view. Counting only the visible winners makes a long-shot path look like a sure thing. The fix is always to ask: who didn't survive to be in front of me? Source: Britannica, 'Survivorship bias'; MasterClass, 'Survivorship Bias Explained: 4 Examples.'

question: A coach brags that his training method works, since every athlete he still coaches has gotten faster. A skeptic wants to test the claim honestly. Which question best exposes whether the method truly works?
answer: What happened to the athletes who quit or were cut, and might the method have failed them?
choices: What happened to the athletes who quit or were cut, and might the method have failed them?
How much faster did each remaining athlete get compared with the previous season?
Did the athletes improve because of the method, or simply because they grew older?
How does this coach's method compare with the methods used by rival coaches?
context: This is the core survivorship-bias skill in everyday clothes. The coach is only counting the athletes who stayed — the survivors of his program. The ones the method failed may have quit or been cut, dropping out of the very evidence he's pointing to. Measuring how fast the remaining athletes got still looks only inside the filtered group. The honest move is always to hunt for the missing data: who or what didn't survive to be counted? Source: Britannica, 'Survivorship bias'; Wikipedia, 'Survivorship bias.'

question: Abraham Wald, who would later teach the U.S. military how to study its bombers, grew up in a devout Jewish family in Kolozsvar. As a boy he could not attend the local schools at all. What kept him out?
answer: The schools held classes on Saturday, the day his family kept for rest
choices: The schools held classes on Saturday, the day his family kept for rest
The schools turned away Jewish children, refusing to enroll them at all
The schools charged fees his father could not afford to pay
The schools sat too far from his home for a young boy to reach each day
context: Abraham Wald was born 31 October 1902 in Kolozsvár (now Cluj, Romania) into a deeply observant Orthodox Jewish family — his grandfather a rabbi, his father a kosher baker. Because the local schools required pupils to attend on Saturday, the Jewish Sabbath, he was largely taught at home, yet still went on to study mathematics at the University of Vienna under Karl Menger. The boy locked out of ordinary school grew into the statistician who taught armies how to count what they couldn't see. Source: MacTutor Biography of Abraham Wald (mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk); Jordan Ellenberg, 'How Not to Be Wrong.'

question: In 1943, Allied officers studied bombers that returned from Germany riddled with bullet holes and prepared to bolt extra armor onto the most-damaged sections. Statistician Abraham Wald stopped them, insisting the heaviest armor belonged on a different part entirely. Which part did Wald say to protect?
answer: The engines, buried deep in the wings and nose
choices: The engines, buried deep in the wings and nose
The fuselage, the plane's long central body
The fuel tanks, holding the volatile gasoline
The tail, which steered the bomber in flight
context: As Ellenberg puts it, 'The armor doesn't go where the bullet holes are. It goes where the bullet holes aren't: on the engines.' The returning planes were peppered everywhere except the engines — and that was exactly the clue. Planes hit in the engines tended to crash and never come home, so the survivors that flooded the data had clean engines. The few holes there marked the most fatal place to be struck. This is the founding tale of 'survivorship bias.' Source: Jordan Ellenberg, 'How Not to Be Wrong' (Penguin Press excerpt); AMS Feature Column, 'The Legend of Abraham Wald.'

question: People admire centuries-old medieval ironwork — armor, blades, the fittings of grand old buildings — as proof that medieval smiths built things to last. But when modern experts examined these surviving pieces up close, the "built to last" story took a hit. What did they find?
answer: The surviving ironwork was quietly rotting from within — corroding away even where it sat sheltered indoors
choices: The surviving ironwork was quietly rotting from within — corroding away even where it sat sheltered indoors
The surviving ironwork had secretly been repaired many times over with far newer metal
The surviving ironwork was machine-made, exposing the celebrated pieces as modern forgeries
The surviving ironwork matched modern steel almost exactly in its strength and purity
context: Survivorship bias hides twice here. First, the flimsy medieval buildings and blades long ago collapsed, burned, or rusted to nothing, so the survivors aren't a fair sample. Second, even the survivors aren't holding up as well as they look: 13th-century iron rebar in Bourges Cathedral was found 'decidedly rusting away' even indoors, and a gilded medieval Spanish spur was 'largely falling apart' after centuries buried. The admired pieces are the ones that survived — not proof that everything was made to last. Source: Hackaday (2025), 'Medieval Iron, Survivorship Bias And Modern Metallurgy'; Statology, 'Survivorship Bias.'

question: Abraham Wald, the statistician who had taught the Allies how to study damage on their bombers, was killed in 1950, aged 48. He and his wife were crossing southern India on a mathematics lecture tour, there at the personal invitation of the Indian government. How did Wald die?
answer: His plane crashed into a mountain range, killing him and his wife
choices: His plane crashed into a mountain range, killing him and his wife
A sudden illness took him during the long voyage between his lectures
A car carried him off a mountain road, killing him and his wife
He drowned when a crowded ferry capsized crossing a river in the south
context: A grim irony: the man whose fame rests on planes that don't come back died in one. On 13 December 1950, Wald and his wife were killed when their Air India DC-3 slammed into the Nilgiri Mountains of southern India (near the Rangaswamy Pillar, in the Travancore region). They had come at the personal invitation of the Indian government for a lecture tour. Source: Wikipedia, 'Abraham Wald'; MacTutor Biography (mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk).

question: When officers charted the bullet holes on returning bombers, the engines showed the fewest hits of any section — 1.11 holes per square foot, against 1.73 on the fuselage. Most read the low engine number as good news. Abraham Wald read it as proof the engines were the deadliest place to be hit. How could the fewest holes mean the greatest danger?
answer: Engine-hit bombers went down and never returned, so their damage never reached the chart
choices: Engine-hit bombers went down and never returned, so their damage never reached the chart
The engines sat so deep that only a rare, fatal shot could punch through the frame to reach them
One engine hit doomed the plane, so few such hits were needed to bring a bomber down
The engines were so cramped that a single hit there wrecked far more than a hit in the wing
context: The full counts were fuselage 1.73, rest of the plane 1.8, fuel system 1.55 — and the engine just 1.11, the lowest reading anywhere. Wald argued the gunfire actually struck the whole plane roughly evenly; the engine count looked low only because engine-hit planes went down and were removed from the sample. The dip in the data marked the deadliest spot. Wald's guiding question was 'Where are the missing holes?' Source: weeklymaths.wordpress.com, 'Abraham Wald and the bullet holes' (reproducing Ellenberg's table from 'How Not to Be Wrong').

question: Abraham Wald faced a problem that looked impossible: he needed to know which parts of a bomber were most fatal to lose, yet the planes that would prove it — the ones shot down — lay at the bottom of the sea or scattered over Germany, beyond any inspection. All he had were the bombers that limped home. How did Wald crack it?
answer: He treated the holes on returning planes as a sample and back-calculated, square foot by square foot, how often a hit in each spot was fatal
choices: He treated the holes on returning planes as a sample and back-calculated, square foot by square foot, how often a hit in each spot was fatal
He ordered armor bolted onto every section that arrived torn up, trusting the worst-hit spots on survivors to reveal the danger
He ranked each part by how badly the worst-hit survivors were torn up when they limped home
He counted how often the surviving crews recalled watching other bombers take fire there
context: Wald didn't just notice the bias — he built a method to measure each part's vulnerability using only the damaged survivors, mathematically reconstructing the fate of the planes nobody could examine. Treating the holes on returning bombers as a sample, he worked back to how often a hit in each spot was fatal. His 1943 work, now treated as a founding example of operational research (using mathematics to make real wartime decisions), turned the absence of evidence into the evidence itself. Note that simply armoring the worst-hit survivor spots is the officers' naive mistake Wald rejected, not his method. Source: Wikipedia, 'Survivorship bias' ('seminal in the then-nascent discipline of operational research'); Wald, 1943, 'A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors.'

question: A 1987 veterinary study found something baffling: cats that fell from more than six stories reached the vet with FEWER injuries, on average, than cats that fell from just a few floors up — as though falling farther were safer. In 1996 a statistician offered a cleaner reason for the strange pattern. What did he propose?
answer: Cats killed outright by the longest falls never reached the vet, so only the high-fall survivors were recorded
choices: Cats killed outright by the longest falls never reached the vet, so only the high-fall survivors were recorded
Cats falling farther had more time to right themselves and land squarely on all four paws
Owners of the worst-hurt cats delayed the trip, which hid how severe those injuries really were
Cats from the higher floors were generally younger and more agile than the ground-floor cats
context: The 1987 'high-rise syndrome' data really did show lower-fall cats arriving more injured. One proposed reason was terminal velocity at about five stories, after which a relaxed cat spreads out like a parachute. But the 1996 reanalysis offered something simpler: survivorship bias. Cats killed outright by very high falls were never carried to a vet, so they vanished from the records — making high falls look survivable when the worst outcomes had simply been filtered out. (The righting-reflex idea is real too, but it isn't what the dataset alone proves.) Source: Wikipedia, 'Survivorship bias' (1987 high-rise syndrome study; 1996 reinterpretation).

question: Abraham Wald escaped Europe for the United States in 1938 and went on to teach the Allies how to account for the bombers that never came back. He had left family behind in Europe. Of the nine relatives he could not bring out, what became of them under the Nazis?
answer: The Nazis murdered all but one of them in the gas chambers at Auschwitz
choices: The Nazis murdered all but one of them in the gas chambers at Auschwitz
The Nazis imprisoned most of them, though nearly all of them survived the war
They scattered across Europe and slowly lost all contact with Wald for good
They followed Wald to America within just a few years of his own escape
context: A wrenching shadow over the famous story. Wald, a Romanian-Hungarian Jew who had fled the Nazis — and who had earlier been barred from an academic post in Austria for being Jewish — built his fame teaching the Allies to count the missing planes. Yet of the nine family members he left behind in 1938, all but one were murdered in the gas chambers at Auschwitz. The man who taught the world to count the cases it couldn't see lost almost his entire family to the cases the world refused to count. Source: MacTutor Biography of Abraham Wald (mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk): 'all but one of the nine members of his family left behind died in the gas chambers of the Nazi concentration camp at Auschwitz.'

question: The famous story of Abraham Wald and the bullet-riddled bombers has grown over the years, and historians at the American Mathematical Society warn that some of its most dramatic touches cannot be verified. Of the following, which one is solidly documented rather than part of the embellished legend?
answer: His 1943 report laying out a method to judge a plane's weak spots from the damage on the survivors
choices: His 1943 report laying out a method to judge a plane's weak spots from the damage on the survivors
A surviving wartime worksheet in which Wald personally tallied the bullet holes on each returning bomber
The tense meeting where Wald personally argued down a room full of skeptical generals
The iconic diagram of a bomber speckled with red bullet-holes, drawn in his own wartime files
context: A nice twist for a topic about telling real evidence from a flattering picture. The AMS notes that the vivid version — Wald dramatically arguing down a room of generals — is partly embellished and unverifiable, the iconic red-dotted bomber silhouette is a modern illustration rather than a wartime drawing of his, and no such personally-tallied worksheet is part of the documented record. What IS documented is his real report, 'A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors' (1943) — eight technical memoranda, with memo five laying out the survivor-based method. Source: AMS Feature Column, 'The Legend of Abraham Wald' (ams.org); Wikipedia, 'Survivorship bias.'

question: An investment company boasts that its family of mutual funds grew about 10.8% a year over the past decade. But that figure counts only the funds still open today; funds the company shut down during those years were quietly dropped from the list before the average was taken. What does that practice tell us about which funds get shut down?
answer: The funds that did worst are the ones companies close, so dropping them lifts the average that remains
choices: The funds that did worst are the ones companies close, so dropping them lifts the average that remains
Companies close their strongest funds first, to lock in the gains before any downturn can erase them
The closed funds were simply the newest ones, which had not yet had the time they needed to grow
Companies pick funds to close at random, so leaving them out does not tilt the average up or down
context: Mutual-fund track records are quietly inflated by survivorship bias. Ellenberg describes a fund class that 'grew an average of 178.4% between 1995 and 2004 — a healthy 10.8% per year,' but once you add back the funds that did so badly they were shut down and erased from the list, the real return drops to about 8.9% a year. The failures get deleted, so the surviving funds flatter the whole industry. The same fix applies as with the bombers: ask what's missing from the list. Source: Jordan Ellenberg, 'How Not to Be Wrong' (Penguin Press excerpt, medium.com/@penguinpress).

question: Aristotle pointed to a single acorn and said it was already 'aiming' at something, all on its own, with nothing pushing it from outside. The goal, he taught, sits hidden inside the seed itself, waiting to unfold. Of these, which is the end the acorn is aiming at?
answer: The mature oak it will slowly grow into
choices: The mature oak it will slowly grow into
The biggest crop of acorns it can scatter
The cool patch of shade it can cast for animals
The soil and sunlight it draws upon to live
context: Aristotle's classic image of an IMMANENT end: the goal is not pushed in from outside but already contained in the seed's own form. The acorn's end is the grown organism itself, not its later seed-crop (its 'generation' serves the adult, not the reverse) nor any use it gives others. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Biology'; Physics II.8.

question: Aristotle leaned on one short slogan again and again -- in his books on animals, on their parts, on their movements -- as the bedrock under his whole study of living things. Generations later it became the line people quote to capture how he saw living things. What was the slogan?
answer: Nature does nothing in vain
choices: Nature does nothing in vain
Only the strongest creatures last
Every creature is a craftsman's work
Living things bend to their surroundings
context: Greek: he phusis ouden poiei maten. Every part of a creature exists for some job; nothing is built without a reason. In Parts of Animals he adds 'nature does nothing superfluous.' The rival slogans here belong to Darwin, to design, and to Lamarck -- not to Aristotle. Source: Aristotle, On the Movement of Animals VIII & Parts of Animals IV.

question: Aristotle's favorite proof that nature works toward ends was teeth. In every animal, he noted, the front and back teeth come in two distinct kinds, and always the same way round -- reliably, never by fluke. Each kind, he insisted, was shaped for its own job. Which jobs did he pair with the front teeth and the back?
answer: Tearing in front, grinding in back
choices: Tearing in front, grinding in back
Gripping in front, slicing in back
Cutting in front, crushing in back
Piercing in front, holding in back
context: Aristotle argued that a pattern which ALWAYS serves the animal's good demands a purpose, not luck: teeth grow that way 'for biting and chewing.' Sharp front teeth tear; broad flat molars grind. Regularity that reliably helps the creature is his telltale sign of an end at work. Source: Aristotle, Physics II.8 (198b23-32).
