So the active ingredient was none of those: it was the tempting profile. Strip the vivid detail and the illusion that a fuller description is likelier simply vanishes. Source: Tversky & Kahneman 1983, Psychological Review 90(4), p.305.

question: Practicing internists were asked to rank a patient's likely symptoms. One option was hemiparesis -- weakness on one side of the body, a fairly unusual sign here. Another was hemiparesis TOGETHER WITH dyspnea -- that same rare weakness plus shortness of breath, which is common. Across five such problems the doctors rated the pair more likely than the rare symptom alone between 73% and 100% of the time. Why is ranking the pair higher impossible?
answer: Every patient who has both symptoms already has the rare one, so the pair can never show up in any more patients than the rare symptom alone
choices: Every patient who has both symptoms already has the rare one, so the pair can never show up in any more patients than the rare symptom alone
Two symptoms occurring together always trace back to one single illness, so a matching pair is rarer than either sign and the doctors had it backwards
The common symptom adds almost nothing at all, so the pair and the rare symptom alone are effectively equal and cannot honestly be ranked apart
A rare symptom plus a common one averages out to a middling chance, so the pair really should sit between the two, and never above the rare one
context: Even trained doctors fell hardest of all -- the violation rate averaged 91%. Tacking a likely symptom onto an unlikely one made the PAIR feel more probable than the unlikely one alone, which is impossible: the pair is a subset of the rare symptom. Source: Tversky & Kahneman 1983, Psychological Review 90(4), pp.301-302.

question: Decades after Linda, Ralph Hertwig and Gerd Gigerenzer argued the trap leans partly on the slippery word 'probable.' They reran it as a head-count: 'Of 100 women who fit Linda's description, how many are bank tellers? How many are bank tellers AND feminists?' Framed that way, the fallacy fell from 50-90% down to 0-25%. Why does counting heads cure what asking 'how probable' did not?
answer: Once you are counting people, nobody claims a smaller group holds more members than the larger group it sits inside, so the subset rule turns obvious
choices: Once you are counting people, nobody claims a smaller group holds more members than the larger group it sits inside, so the subset rule turns obvious
Counting forces people to estimate exact percentages, and the slow arithmetic of working out real numbers leaves no room for any gut feeling to intrude
Counting makes people picture concrete women, and a vivid mental scene quiets the gut and lets cold logic take the wheel where a bare word could not
Round numbers like 100 make every estimate feel like a wild guess, so people stop trusting Linda's profile and fall back on pure coin-flip odds
context: Hertwig & Gigerenzer (1999) mount the strongest defense of ordinary people, not the fallacy: the word 'probable' is genuinely ambiguous, and the head-count framing is the cure that proves the underlying logic is sound -- a subset cannot outnumber its set. Source: Hertwig & Gigerenzer 1999, J. Behavioral Decision Making 12(4):275.

question: A smuggler, Mr. P., is under investigation, and people rank how likely various suspicions are. One suspicion read 'Mr. P. killed one of his employees.' Swapping it for 'Mr. P. killed one of his employees TO STOP HIM TALKING TO THE POLICE' made the killing feel MORE likely -- the motive fit the smuggling so well. But Mr. P. could have killed for revenge, in a panic, in self-defense, or for no clear reason. So what does naming that one motive do to the odds?
answer: It can only lower them, because a killing for that one motive is just a slice of all the killings he might have done for any reason at all
choices: It can only lower them, because a killing for that one motive is just a slice of all the killings he might have done for any reason at all
It can only raise them, because a killing that has a clear smuggling motive is exactly the kind of killing a smuggler is most likely to commit
It leaves them unchanged, because supplying a motive explains why he might kill but does not alter whether the killing itself ever took place
It raises them only if the motive is true, so the ranking is right whenever Mr. P. really did fear his employee would talk to the police
context: The dark courtroom version of the conjunction fallacy. A believable motive is a DETAIL, and details that fit always feel more probable -- yet specifying one motive can only narrow the set of possible killings, never widen it. Source: Tversky & Kahneman 1983, Psychological Review 90(4), pp.306-307.

question: No one can name the exact instant when day becomes night - dusk slides from light to dark with no sharp dividing line. A clever debater says: 'Since you can't point to the precise second it happens, day and night must really be the same thing.' What's wrong with his reasoning?
answer: A missing sharp cutoff does nothing to erase the obvious gap between noon and midnight
choices: A missing sharp cutoff does nothing to erase the obvious gap between noon and midnight
He assumes time moves in discrete jumps rather than flowing smoothly from one moment to the next
He forgets that the boundary between day and night shifts with the seasons and your latitude
He confuses what we can measure precisely with what actually exists out in the world
context: This is the continuum fallacy in its plainest form: the inability to fix the boundary does not melt the two states into one. Noon and midnight are unmistakably different even though no instant is THE switch. Source: LogicalFallacies.org, 'Continuum Fallacy'.

question: There is no single hair whose loss tips a man from hairy to bald - pull them out one at a time and you can never name THE hair that did it. From this, someone concludes that 'bald' is a meaningless label. Yet Patrick Stewart is plainly bald and a young Conan O'Brien plainly is not. What does that pair of clear cases show?
answer: A word can mark a real difference at its extremes even when its middle has fuzzy borderline cases
choices: A word can mark a real difference at its extremes even when its middle has fuzzy borderline cases
A word is only meaningful if every single case it covers can be sorted with total certainty
A word's meaning is decided purely by how most people happen to use it day to day
A word that has any unclear cases at all should be thrown out and replaced with a number
context: Borderline cases exist, but so do plenty of obvious clear cases at each end - which is exactly why 'no sharp line' fails to prove 'no difference.' The ancient Greeks called this bald-man puzzle the 'phalakros.' Source: Humanities LibreTexts, 'Critical Reasoning: A User's Manual' (Southworth & Swoyer), 11.3 'Drawing the Line'; Wikipedia, 'Sorites paradox'.

question: A puzzle runs like this: a single grain of sand isn't a heap; and adding just one more grain can never turn a non-heap into a heap; therefore - step by harmless step - there are no heaps of sand at all. Each step looks true, but the conclusion is plainly absurd. Where does the trick go wrong?
answer: Piling up tiny differences that each seem to change nothing can still add up to a genuine change
choices: Piling up tiny differences that each seem to change nothing can still add up to a genuine change
The very first step is false, because one grain of sand really is a very small heap
The argument secretly assumes heaps exist in order to prove that they don't
Sand grains are too small to count, so the word 'heap' can never apply to them
context: This is the classic 'sorites' (Greek 'soros,' heap). Every individual step is harmless, yet the accumulation crosses a real line - which is precisely the move the fallacy hides. Source: The Fallacy Files, 'Logical Fallacy: The Fallacy of the Heap' (fallacyfiles.org/fallheap.html).

question: Across all its forms - the heap, the beard, the bald man - the same bad argument keeps surfacing: because there's no exact point where a little becomes a lot, the two ends supposedly can't really differ. Philosophers have a one-line answer to the whole family. Which line is it?
answer: A difference in degree is still a difference, and a big enough one becomes a difference in kind
choices: A difference in degree is still a difference, and a big enough one becomes a difference in kind
Any word that lacks a precise definition should be banned from careful and serious reasoning
If you cannot measure a thing exactly, you have no business claiming that it is real
Two things only count as different when a clear rule separates every case between them
context: The fallacy goes by many names - continuum fallacy, fallacy of the beard, line-drawing fallacy, bald-man fallacy, sorites fallacy, fallacy of grey - but this single sentence answers them all. A fuzzy border between two things does not abolish the genuine difference between the clear cases at each end. Source: The Fallacy Files, 'The Fallacy of the Heap'; Wikipedia, 'Continuum fallacy'.

question: The Stoic Chrysippus had a plan for surviving the heap riddle. As the questioner counted upward - is three many? is four? is five? - Chrysippus meant to escape the trap, just before the borderline, by doing one particular thing the Greeks called 'hesuchazein'. What was his actual tactic?
answer: Falling silent and refusing to answer once the questions neared the fuzzy boundary
choices: Falling silent and refusing to answer once the questions neared the fuzzy boundary
Conceding that the heap has no real existence and abandoning the word entirely
Demanding the questioner first define the exact number of grains that makes a heap
Answering every question 'yes' so that even a single grain counted as a heap
context: 'Hesuchazein' meant to keep quiet or rest. It was the ancient world's most famous dodge of a vague boundary: stop answering before the question forces you to name the impossible cutoff. Source: Cicero, Academica (Lucullus) II, secs ~91-98, as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Sorites Paradox.'

question: When the Stoic Chrysippus tried to escape the heap riddle by simply falling silent near the borderline, the skeptic Carneades mocked the dodge with a joke Cicero wrote down: 'Rest and welcome; you may even snore, for all I care. But what good does it do?' Why, in Carneades' jab, does staying silent solve nothing?
answer: The next questioner just asks the very next number, and the same problem is right back
choices: The next questioner just asks the very next number, and the same problem is right back
A sleeping philosopher has plainly lost the argument by refusing to defend his view
Silence is itself an answer, and it quietly concedes that the heap does not exist
Snoring breaks the rules of debate, so Chrysippus forfeits the contest on a technicality
context: Cicero records Carneades verbatim: 'for one follows who will waken you from sleep, and question you in the same manner.' You can go quiet, but the vague boundary doesn't go away - it waits at the next grain. Source: Cicero, Academica (Lucullus) II, quoted in Epicureanfriends.com thread 4345.

question: A debater argues: 'You can't point to the single day a child becomes an adult, so setting any drinking age or voting age is purely arbitrary - the lines are meaningless.' A functioning society draws exactly such lines: ages for driving, prison terms scaled to crimes, speed limits. What does the debater get wrong about those cutoffs?
answer: The exact line is partly a choice, yet the gap it tracks between a child and an adult is entirely real
choices: The exact line is partly a choice, yet the gap it tracks between a child and an adult is entirely real
The lines aren't arbitrary at all, because lawmakers can prove each one is the single correct cutoff
Society should drop fixed ages and instead test each person individually before granting any right
Since no cutoff is ever perfect, the fairest rule is to pick every legal boundary by a coin flip
context: This is the line-drawing fallacy where it does real damage in public argument. The cutoffs are partly arbitrary, but the differences they track - a child versus an adult, safe versus reckless speed - are entirely real. Source: Critical Thinking Academy, 'The Line-Drawing Fallacy'; Humanities LibreTexts, 11.3 'Drawing the Line.'

question: Doctors call blood pressure 'high' above roughly 140 over 90 - a number that was chosen, not handed down by nature, and a reading a hair below it is barely different from one a hair above. A skeptic seizes on this: 'Since the cutoff is admittedly arbitrary, high blood pressure isn't a real thing.' What's the flaw in that leap?
answer: An arbitrary line can still flag a real danger, since a very high reading harms you whatever number we picked
choices: An arbitrary line can still flag a real danger, since a very high reading harms you whatever number we picked
The cutoff isn't arbitrary at all, since 140 over 90 is the exact reading where the harm suddenly begins
Blood pressure can't really be 'high' or 'low', because it changes constantly throughout an ordinary day
Doctors ought to abandon fixed numbers and judge each patient's pressure purely by how the patient feels
context: Medicine leans on admittedly chosen cutoffs that still mark something real. Denying that high blood pressure exists because no single reading is THE boundary is a textbook line-drawing fallacy. Source: Critical Thinking Academy, 'The Line-Drawing Fallacy' (criticalthinkingacademy.net).

question: Watch Mars night after night and it usually drifts one way across the sky — then for a few weeks it slows, stops, and crawls BACKWARD, before resuming its march. Copernicus insisted Mars never truly reverses at all. If the planet really keeps moving forward the whole time, why does it APPEAR to back up?
answer: The faster Earth, on its inside track, overtakes the slower Mars, so it then seems to slip backward as we pass by.
choices: The faster Earth, on its inside track, overtakes the slower Mars, so it then seems to slip backward as we pass by.
The faster Mars briefly swings closer to Earth, and that nearness makes its motion look reversed to us for a while.
The slower Mars dips below its usual path, and from Earth that sideways sag can look much like a backward slide.
The light from Mars bends through Earth's air at certain seasons, painting a false backward path against the stars.
context: These backward 'retrograde' loops were the showpiece of Copernicus's model. The old Earth-centered system of Ptolemy explained them with extra circles-upon-circles bolted onto each planet's path; Copernicus made them a mere trick of perspective. A faster inner Earth overtakes a slower outer Mars the way a fast car passes a slow one — from inside the speeding car, the slow car seems to drift backward, though it never stops moving forward. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicolaus Copernicus'; people.highline.edu/iglozman/classes/astronotes/retrograde.htm.

question: Aristotle offered what felt like proof the Earth stands still: if it spun eastward at huge speed, a stone dropped from a tower should land far to the WEST, since the ground would slide east as the stone fell. Yet it lands at the tower's base. Galileo answered with a ship: drop a ball from the mast of a smoothly sailing ship, and where does the ball land?
answer: At the foot of the mast, because the ball already shares in the ship's motion and keeps it as it falls.
choices: At the foot of the mast, because the ball already shares in the ship's motion and keeps it as it falls.
Well behind the mast, since the ship sails on ahead while the dropped ball hangs briefly in the open air.
Off to one side of the mast, as the ball is flung outward the instant it parts from the moving rigging.
Wherever the wind sends it, for a ball in open air has no fixed share in the motion of the ship below.
context: This is Galileo's famous ship thought-experiment, his reply to the 'Tower Argument.' The dropped stone, like the ball, already shares the motion of the ground (or the ship) and carries that motion with it as it falls, so it lands directly below — a spinning Earth would feel exactly as still as the cabin of a smoothly moving ship. Galileo could not PROVE the Earth moves, but he dismantled the old proof that it does not. Source: 'Galileo's ship', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo's_ship; web.stanford.edu/class/phil61/section1027.text.

question: Before Copernicus, Earth was the fixed hub of everything — the one unmoving point the entire cosmos wheeled around. Copernicus's real leap was not an arithmetic tweak to the star charts; it was a jolt to where humanity imagines it sits. What did he ask people to believe about the very ground beneath their feet?
answer: That it is just one ordinary planet among many, itself adrift in motion around the Sun.
choices: That it is just one ordinary planet among many, itself adrift in motion around the Sun.
That it sits a touch off the true center, still the anchor the cosmos is built around.
That it spins in place at the very hub while the Sun alone circles it once each day.
That it floats at the far outer rim, beneath the older and crowded heavens overhead.
context: This is the unsettling sting of the Copernican revolution, and it is a philosophical jolt, not merely an astronomy detail: the place we stand is not the still middle that the whole cosmos honors with its motion — it is itself moving, an ordinary planet circling the Sun. The reasoning leap was demoting Earth from THE hub to just one body among many. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicolaus Copernicus'.

question: Smart astronomers fought the sun-centered idea with real evidence, not mere stubbornness. They reasoned: if Earth truly circles the Sun, then over a year a nearby star should appear to shift back and forth as we view it from changing positions — yet no such shift could be seen. From that one missing observation, what could a careful skeptic conclude?
answer: Either Earth does not move at all, or the stars must lie at unimaginably vast distances from us.
choices: Either Earth does not move at all, or the stars must lie at unimaginably vast distances from us.
Either the star itself is drifting, or Earth's orbit is far smaller than Copernicus had supposed.
Either the eye is too weak to catch the shift, or the heavens still wheel around a fixed Earth.
Either the star sits far closer than thought, or the Sun, not the Earth, is the body on the move.
context: This back-and-forth shift is called parallax, and the absence of any visible parallax was the strongest scientific case against Copernicus. The logic was sound and left only two options, both seeming absurd at the time: a motionless Earth, or stars so staggeringly far away that the shift was too tiny to detect across a huge empty gap. Faced with that choice, careful skeptics bet on the still Earth as the safer guess. Source: Scientific American, 'The Case against Copernicus'; scientus.org/Copernicus-Stellar-Parallax.html.

question: The famous lesson is that Copernicus HUMBLED us — knocking proud humanity out of the place of honor at the center. But the historian Dennis Danielson points to what medieval thinkers actually believed about that center: Pico della Mirandola called Earth's core the 'filthy' bottom of the world, and Dante put Hell at the dead center of it. Given THAT, how should the move be read?
answer: As a promotion: it lifted Earth up out of the cosmic basement to join the circling heavens.
choices: As a promotion: it lifted Earth up out of the cosmic basement to join the circling heavens.
As a demotion: it cast Earth down from its proud seat into the lowly company of mere planets.
As a wash: shifting Earth's place changed nothing about the rank that thinkers gave to it.
As a riddle: with Hell at the center, no one of that age could say where honor truly lay.
context: Historian Dennis Danielson named this reversal 'The Great Copernican Cliche' (Am. J. Phys., 2001). In the old picture the center was not the seat of honor but the cosmic basement — Pico della Mirandola called Earth's core 'the excrementary and filthy parts of the lower world,' and Dante put Hell at the very center of the Earth. By that logic, sending Earth up to join the circling heavens was a step UP, not a humbling. The 'demotion' reading came later. Source: Dennis Danielson, 'The Great Copernican Cliche' (Am. J. Phys. 2001); Physics Today, 'The Copernican myths'.

question: For nearly 300 years after Copernicus, no one could directly PROVE the Earth moves — the back-and-forth star shift his theory demanded was simply never seen. In 1838 Friedrich Bessel finally trained his instruments on the star 61 Cygni and caught the long-sought wobble at last. How big was the shift that settled the centuries-old question?
answer: About a third of an arcsecond, the width of a coin seen from miles off, placing the star ten light-years away.
choices: About a third of an arcsecond, the width of a coin seen from miles off, placing the star ten light-years away.
About a tenth of an arcsecond, a twitch so faint that it set the star a good fifty light-years away from us.
A bit over a full arcsecond, the closest stellar case yet found, though still far too fine for the naked eye.
Barely a few hundredths of an arcsecond, a tremor so slight it set the star many hundreds of light-years off.
context: Bessel measured the parallax of 61 Cygni in 1838 as roughly 0.31 arcseconds, fixing its distance at about ten light-years. The skeptics' 'impossible' option had been right all along: the stars really are unimaginably far away, AND the Earth really does swing around the Sun — both at once. Direct proof arrived nearly three centuries after Copernicus first dared to move the Earth. Source: phys.org, 'Resolving long-standing mysteries about the first parallaxes'; Britannica, '61 Cygni'.

question: Two students stare at the same starry sky. The first says the order she sees -- each star at its distance, one event before another in time, the first causing the next -- is simply OUT THERE, and her mind just takes a faithful picture of it. Immanuel Kant tells her she has it backwards. On Kant's view, that order is not something her mind FINDS. What is it instead?
answer: Something her own mind supplies, the very structure it brings to whatever it meets
choices: Something her own mind supplies, the very structure it brings to whatever it meets
Something the world hands her complete, which her mind only receives and records
Something she invents whole, so the stars themselves would vanish if she looked away
Something forever hidden from her, since the real sky stays beyond anyone's reach
context: This is the heart of Kant's reversal. Naive realism says the mind passively copies a ready-made world; Kant rejects that. The dispute is not whether a real world exists -- it is whether the ORDER (space, time, cause) is found in the world or contributed by the viewer. Kant's answer: partly contributed by the viewer. Distractor 2 is naive realism, distractor 3 is the stronger claim that nothing exists apart from being seen (which Kant does NOT make -- he keeps a mind-independent reality), distractor 4 is skepticism. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Kant: Transcendental Idealism' (iep.utm.edu/kant-transcendental-idealism/), section contrasting Kant with naive realism.

question: Immanuel Kant offers a small test about space and time. Try to picture a single object -- a coin, a stone -- with no space around it and no moment it sits in. You cannot. Now try the reverse: picture empty space, or empty time, with nothing in it at all. That, Kant says, you CAN do. From this asymmetry, what does Kant conclude about space and time?
answer: They are the frame the mind brings first, into which every object must be poured
choices: They are the frame the mind brings first, into which every object must be poured
They are the largest objects of all, the containers physics will someday measure
They are properties each object carries, the way it carries its weight or color
They are illusions, so neither the object nor its setting is ever really there
context: From the Transcendental Aesthetic. Because you can imagine empty space and empty time but cannot imagine an object stripped of them, space and time must come first -- they are the form our own sensibility brings TO the world, not features we find in it. Kant: 'space represents no property at all of any things in themselves' (A26/B42). They are, in his phrase, transcendentally ideal yet empirically real. Distractor 2 is roughly Newton's absolute space; distractor 3 is roughly Leibniz's relational view -- both real rivals Kant rejects. Source: IEP, 'Kant: Transcendental Idealism', citing Critique A26/B42, A32/B49.

question: Immanuel Kant named his great reversal after Copernicus, and meant it exactly. Copernicus had been stuck: he could make no sense of the heavens while assuming the sun and stars wheeled around the watcher. So he tried the opposite -- he let the heavens hold still and set the WATCHER moving instead, on a spinning Earth. Kant says he ran the identical trick on human knowledge. What did Kant set in motion that everyone before had assumed held still?
answer: The knower, whose own structure shapes the order we seem to find in things
choices: The knower, whose own structure shapes the order we seem to find in things
The objects, which he proved are racing past us faster than the eye can follow
The stars, which he fixed to points lying far behind the slowly moving sun
The senses, which he showed must deceive us about every motion we perceive
context: Kant's own words, B Preface: 'We here propose to do just what Copernicus did... he reversed the process, and tried the experiment of assuming that the SPECTATOR revolved, while the stars remained at rest.' The vivid image: Copernicus stopped the sky and spun the watcher; Kant spins the knower and lets the world hold still. In both, something taken to be 'out there in the object' turns out to be a condition of the observer. Source: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, B Preface (~Bxvi-Bxvii), full text at marxists.org; SEP 'Kant's Account of Reason' on the analogy.

question: David Hume pressed a hard point: watch one billiard ball strike another and you never actually SEE the first MAKE the second move. You see one ball, then the other moving -- and habit quietly adds the word 'must.' Hume concluded the necessary connection is nowhere in the world. Immanuel Kant agreed you will never find it in the world, yet insisted the necessity is real. Where did Kant locate the source of that 'must'?
answer: In the understanding, which orders every experience by cause and effect
choices: In the understanding, which orders every experience by cause and effect
In the balls themselves, in a force too quick to see yet plain to instruments
In long habit alone, exactly as Hume said, with no real necessity behind it
In a standing decree of God, who fixes each collision the instant before it lands
context: Cause, for Kant, is one of the mind's built-in lenses, not something read off the world. Hume could not find the connection in nature; Kant's reply is that the necessity is real but supplied by the understanding, which structures every experience through the category of cause-and-effect. So the link Hume couldn't find in the world was there all along -- in the knower. Distractor 4 is occasionalism (Malebranche), a genuine historical rival. Source: IEP, 'Kant: Transcendental Idealism', citing Critique A129-130/B163-165; SEP 'Kant's Critique of Metaphysics'.

question: Immanuel Kant's reversal comes with a bill. If your own mind dresses everything you meet in its space, its time, its causes BEFORE you ever experience it, then a strange consequence follows about the naked thing underneath -- reality as it is in itself, with no human costume on it. According to Kant, what is our standing toward that thing-in-itself?
answer: We can never know it, meeting the world only after our own forms have shaped it
choices: We can never know it, meeting the world only after our own forms have shaped it
We know it best of all, since stripping away appearance is just what reason does
We reach it through science, whose instruments slowly remove the mind's distortions
We half-know it, glimpsing the bare thing whenever the forms briefly fall away
context: The price of the turn. Because our minds shape everything we experience, we only ever know things as they APPEAR (phenomena), never as they are in themselves (the noumenon). Kant: things in themselves 'are beyond our epistemic reach and cannot be an object of cognition.' We see the world dressed in our own space, time, and cause, and can never take the costume off to check the naked thing underneath. Source: SEP 'Kant's Critique of Metaphysics' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-metaphysics/); IEP 'Kant: Transcendental Idealism'.

question: Teachers often picture Immanuel Kant's view with tinted glasses you can never remove: everything you see is colored by them, and you cannot step outside to check the world un-tinted. It is a handy image -- yet Kant scholars such as Sebastian Gardner reject it as a misreading. Their objection rests on one real difference between Kant's mental forms and a pair of glasses. What is that difference?
answer: Glasses only distort a world you could see without them, while the forms make any experience possible at all
choices: Glasses only distort a world you could see without them, while the forms make any experience possible at all
Glasses can be swapped for a clearer pair, while Kant held the forms must stay identical in everyone forever
Glasses sit before the eye, while Kant placed the forms behind it, deep in a brain that light never enters
Glasses are ground by human hands, while Kant taught that God sets the forms in the mind at the hour of birth
context: The 'tinted glasses' picture is a teaching aid, NOT Kant's own metaphor, and serious scholars (Sebastian Gardner, Matthew Altman) reject it as misleading. Glasses merely distort a world you could in principle see without them; for Kant the forms (space, time, cause) are the very condition of there being any experience at all -- take them away and there is no view to correct, not a clearer one. A good intuition pump, a bad literal reading. Source: scholarship on transcendental idealism discussing the colored-glasses analogy and its rejection by Gardner and Altman.

question: A magician seems to pull a rabbit out of an empty hat, and a child asks her grandfather how the creature could possibly have gotten there. He laughs that every trick hides a real rabbit somewhere, and says the whole cosmological argument leans on one stubborn old rule the magician only seems to defy. Which rule is he describing?
answer: Out of nothing, nothing can come to be.
choices: Out of nothing, nothing can come to be.
Out of disorder, order will always emerge.
The simplest explanation is usually the right one.
Whatever can go wrong eventually will.
context: This is the ancient maxim 'ex nihilo nihil fit' (out of nothing, nothing comes): something cannot pop into being from absolutely nothing. It is the everyday intuition underneath the cosmological argument, whose spine is that everything that exists has a cause, that there cannot be an infinite chain of causes, and so there must be a first, uncaused cause. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cosmological Argument (plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmological-argument/).

question: Thomas Aquinas argued that whatever is moving was set moving by something else, and that this chain of movers cannot run backward forever. There must be a first mover that nothing else set going. To make the idea vivid, he reached for one homely everyday object. What was his image?
answer: A staff, which moves only because a hand pushes it.
choices: A staff, which moves only because a hand pushes it.
A river, which flows only because the rain feeds it.
A candle, which burns only because a flame lights it.
A clock, which ticks only because a spring drives it.
context: From Aquinas' First Way: 'Whatever is in motion must be put in motion by another... as the staff moves only because it is put in motion by the hand.' Trace the movers back; it cannot go to infinity 'because then there would be no first mover.' Each of the Five Ways ends by naming the stopping point, the First Way closing 'this everyone understands to be God.' Source: Aquinas, Summa Theologica I, Q.2, A.3 (newadvent.org/summa/1002.htm).

question: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz thought the cosmological argument was really chasing one enormous question, the deepest he believed anyone could ask. He held that nothing is ever a brute accident: everything real must have a sufficient reason behind it. Boiled down to a single line, what was that great question?
answer: Why is there something rather than nothing at all?
choices: Why is there something rather than nothing at all?
How can we know that anything truly exists?
What is the smallest thing the world is made of?
Does the world have a purpose or only chance?
context: Leibniz's engine for the question is his Principle of Sufficient Reason. In the Monadology, section 32: 'no fact can be real or existing and no statement true without a sufficient reason for its being so and not otherwise.' If every fact needs a reason, then the universe as a whole needs one too. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cosmological Argument; Leibniz, Monadology section 32.

question: In a 1948 BBC radio debate, the Jesuit priest Frederick Copleston pressed Bertrand Russell to grant that the universe must have an explanation beyond itself, a being holding the reason for its own existence. Russell would not grant it. Pushed on where the universe ultimately comes from, what was his famously blunt reply?
answer: The universe is just there, and that is all.
choices: The universe is just there, and that is all.
The universe will reveal its cause to science one day.
The universe is too vast for human minds to judge.
The universe rests on laws that need no maker.
context: Copleston had defined the target as a being 'that must and cannot not exist,' one 'which contains within itself the reason for its own existence.' Russell's full line was 'I should say that the universe is just there, and that's all,' and he rejected the demand outright: 'I see no reason whatsoever to suppose that the total has any cause whatsoever.' Source: Copleston-Russell BBC debate transcript, 28 Jan 1948 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copleston-Russell_debate).

question: Almost everyone who first hears the cosmological argument fires back the same objection: if everything needs a cause, then what caused God? Defenders answer that the objection misreads the very first premise, because the argument never claimed that simply everything has a cause. What did the premise actually say needs a cause?
answer: Only what begins to exist at some moment needs a cause.
choices: Only what begins to exist at some moment needs a cause.
Only what can be seen and measured needs a cause.
Only what changes or moves from one state to another needs a cause.
Only what depends on smaller parts to hold together needs a cause.
context: The kalam premise is only that everything that BEGINS to exist has a cause; the contingency version only that CONTINGENT things (those that could have not-existed) need one. A necessary, beginningless being falls outside the rule by definition, so asking for its cause is a category mistake rather than special pleading. The SEP calls Hawking's 'Who created God?' question 'out of place.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cosmological Argument.

question: Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, proposed in the late 1920s that the whole universe expanded outward from a single ultra-dense starting point he called the primeval atom, the seed of what became the Big Bang. Many were eager to say his physics had proven the religious idea of creation. What did Lemaitre himself insist about that connection?
answer: That a beginning in the equations does not by itself prove a creator.
choices: That a beginning in the equations does not by itself prove a creator.
That his equations had at last placed creation on solid proof.
That only a priest could correctly interpret what the physics meant.
That the universe must therefore be exactly six thousand years old.
context: Lemaitre called his origin point 'the primeval atom,' poetically 'a day without yesterday.' Yet he warned AGAINST equating his physics with the theological idea of creation, even quietly passing that message to the Pope. A beginning in the equations does not by itself settle who or what, if anything, caused it. This is exactly the gap a cosmological argument must still bridge. Source: Britannica, Georges Lemaitre; American Museum of Natural History, Georges Lemaitre, Father of the Big Bang (amnh.org).

question: Bertrand Russell granted that every single thing inside the universe has a cause, yet denied that the universe as a whole must have one. To probe that leap, he noted that every human being has a mother, while the human race itself does not have one. Russell said his opponent's argument committed a specific reasoning error. Which error was it?
answer: Assuming a whole must share a trait just because each of its parts has it.
choices: Assuming a whole must share a trait just because each of its parts has it.
Assuming each part must share a trait just because the whole has it.
Assuming one part's trait must belong to every other part too.
Assuming a collection must share a trait simply because it is large.
context: This is the fallacy of composition. Russell's words: 'Every man who exists has a mother, and it seems to me your argument is that therefore the human race must have a mother, but obviously the human race hasn't a mother, that's a different logical sphere.' Composition wrongly carries a trait from each part up to the whole; the reverse error (whole to each part) is division. Even if every thing in the universe has a cause, it does not follow that the universe as a whole does. Source: Copleston-Russell BBC debate transcript, 28 Jan 1948.

question: Defenders of the kalam argument argue the past cannot stretch back infinitely, because an actual infinity would produce absurd results. Their favorite illustration is a hotel with infinitely many rooms, every single one already full. A new guest then walks up to the desk. What surprising thing does the puzzle say the manager can do?
answer: Free up a room by moving each guest up one, leaving room 1 open.
choices: Free up a room by moving each guest up one, leaving room 1 open.
Fit infinitely many new guests, but never just one more.
Double his money by charging every guest twice over.
Empty the whole hotel by moving guests down one each.
context: This is Hilbert's Hotel. By shifting every guest up one room, the 'full' infinite hotel still has space, which William Lane Craig argues is absurd, concluding that an actually-infinite past cannot be real and the universe must have a finite beginning. Critics reply that this is just the defining weirdness of infinite sets, not a real contradiction. Craig revived the kalam argument in his 1979 book The Kalam Cosmological Argument. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cosmological Argument; reasonablefaith.org.

question: Immanuel Kant lived his whole quiet life in the town of Konigsberg, and he kept to one habit so faithfully that his neighbors built a saying around it. What did the townspeople claim they could do, thanks to how regular Kant was?
answer: Set their clocks by his afternoon walk
choices: Set their clocks by his afternoon walk
Guess the weather from his choice of coat
Tell the season by the books he carried
Find his house by the crowd of students
context: Kant's daily afternoon walk was so punctual that the people of Konigsberg were said to set their clocks by him, nicknaming him 'the Konigsberg clock'; he walked the same lime-tree avenue, which became known as 'The Philosopher's Walk.' Told as a town legend (likely embroidered, but rooted in his real, famous discipline). Source: Verso Books, 'Immanuel Kant the Walker?'; University of Bonn, 'Kant's Enlightenment Project.'

question: Immanuel Kant gave the whole Enlightenment its motto in two Latin words, 'Sapere aude.' He insisted that most grown people stay childishly dependent on others to think for them not because they are stupid, but because they lack one thing. By Kant's account, what do they lack?
answer: The courage to use their own minds
choices: The courage to use their own minds
The leisure that real study demands
The teachers who could guide them
The books that would inform them
context: 'Sapere aude' means 'Dare to know' (literally 'dare to be wise'). In 'An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?' (1784), Kant defines enlightenment as a person's emergence from 'self-incurred' immaturity, blaming not lack of understanding but 'lack of resolution and courage' -- so the motto becomes 'Have courage to make use of your own understanding!' Source: Kant, 'What Is Enlightenment?' (1784), marxists.org; Wikipedia, 'Sapere aude.'

question: Immanuel Kant closed his great book on ethics with one famous sentence, naming two things that filled his mind with ever-increasing awe the more steadily he reflected on them. What two things did he pair as the sources of that awe?
answer: The starry heavens above and the moral law within
choices: The starry heavens above and the moral law within
The boundless ocean far off and the bold will within
The vast turning seasons and the calm conscience within
The endless heavens above and the keen reason within
context: The line closes the Critique of Practical Reason (1788): 'Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe... the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me.' One source of wonder he found by looking outward at the cosmos, the other by looking inward at conscience; the same words were later carved on his tomb in Konigsberg. Source: Kant, Critique of Practical Reason (1788), Conclusion; quoted at Smithsonian American Art Museum and Goodreads.

question: Diogenes the Cynic owned almost nothing, but he still carried one wooden cup to drink from. One day he watched a boy kneel at a stream and scoop water with his bare cupped hands. Diogenes threw his cup away on the spot. Why was he glad to lose his last possession?
answer: Every want he gave up was one less thing luck could ever take from him
choices: Every want he gave up was one less thing luck could ever take from him
A gift freely shared with a stranger is worth more than any object kept
A wise man should own only what he can carry on his own two shoulders
A tool made by human hands can never be as honest as the bare body
context: 'A child has beaten me in plainness of living,' Diogenes said. The cup is the gateway image of the Cynic idea (autarkeia, self-sufficiency): every desire you drop is one less handle fortune has on you. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI.37.  (Legend.)

question: Diogenes the Cynic lay stretched out in the sun one morning when Alexander the Great, the most powerful man alive, stood over him and offered to grant him absolutely anything he wished. Diogenes looked up at the conqueror and made a single odd request. What did he ask the king for?
answer: "Stand a little out of my sunshine."
choices: "Stand a little out of my sunshine."
"Give me a hundred talents of gold."
"Make me the governor of this city."
"Set free every slave in your army."
context: The man who owned the world had nothing Diogenes needed. Walking off, Alexander told his laughing courtiers, 'If I were not Alexander, I would wish to be Diogenes' -- the conqueror envying the beggar. Source: Diogenes Laertius VI.38; Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14.  (Legend.)

question: Diogenes the Cynic lit a lamp in the middle of a bright sunny morning and carried it through the crowded marketplace, peering into face after face as if hunting for something he could not find. When people asked what he was doing, what did he say he was looking for?
answer: A single honest human being
choices: A single honest human being
An exit out of the noisy city
A master worthy of his service
A coin some thief had dropped
context: 'I am looking for a human being,' he said -- his theatrical complaint that, surrounded by people chasing money and status, he could find almost no one actually living a rational, natural life. Source: Diogenes Laertius VI.41.  (Legend.)

question: Plato's famous school in Athens defined a human being as 'a featherless two-legged animal,' and the scholars were proud of the clever phrase. Diogenes the Cynic thought such bookish definitions were empty, so he answered the school not with an argument but with a single mocking stunt. What did he do?
answer: He plucked a chicken bare and set it loose among the scholars
choices: He plucked a chicken bare and set it loose among the scholars
He shaved a monkey smooth and stood it up at the lectern
He plucked a goose naked and perched it on the speaker's chair
He stripped a stork of its feathers and stood it by the lectern
context: 'Behold, Plato's human being!' he announced. The school had to amend its definition to add 'with broad flat nails.' The move: deflate abstract, bookish philosophy with one concrete prop -- live the argument instead of defining it. Source: Diogenes Laertius VI.40.  (Legend.)

question: In ancient Greece a man was expected to put loyalty to his home city first, with its own laws, gods, and feuds. Asked plainly which city he came from, Diogenes the Cynic refused to name any single one and instead claimed a belonging that bound him only to nature and to reason. What did he call himself?
answer: A citizen of the whole world
choices: A citizen of the whole world
A free man who serves no city
An exile with no home at all
A subject of the gods alone
context: The Greek was kosmopolites -- the moment the word 'cosmopolitan' was coined. The move: refuse the parochial loyalty everyone assumes you must have, and owe allegiance to humanity at large instead. Source: Diogenes Laertius VI.63; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Cosmopolitanism.'

question: Diogenes the Cynic did odd things on purpose. One day people watched him walk up to a cold stone statue and beg it for coins, again and again, though of course a statue can give nothing. When they asked, why did he say he did it?
answer: To practice being refused, so real rejection could never wound him
choices: To practice being refused, so real rejection could never wound him
To shame the rich men who gave him less than a statue would
To prove that a carved god hears prayers no better than stone
To beg from one thing that would never judge him for his poverty
context: The Cynics called this askesis, training. He also rolled in scorching sand in summer and hugged snow-covered bronze in winter -- courting discomfort on purpose so that a real blow of fortune could not move him. Source: Diogenes Laertius VI.49; IEP, 'Cynics.'  (Legend.)

question: The word 'Cynic' comes from a Greek word meaning 'dog-like,' and people first used it to insult Diogenes. Rather than take offense, he embraced the name, arguing that a stray dog actually lives more honestly than most so-called civilized people. What did he say a dog does better than humans?
answer: It eats anything, sleeps anywhere, and feels no shame about its body
choices: It eats anything, sleeps anywhere, and feels no shame about its body
It guards the house, obeys its master, and asks for nothing in return
It hunts in a pack, defends its young, and mourns a fallen companion
It greets every stranger, forgives each beating, and never holds a grudge
context: To the Cynic, the dog's shamelessness (anaideia) is honesty: if a thing isn't wrong to do at home, the public square doesn't make it wrong -- the blush is mere convention, not nature. So 'Cynic' meant living like a dog on purpose. Source: IEP, 'Cynics'; Diogenes Laertius VI.60-61.

question: Diogenes the Cynic had literally been exiled from his home city after a scandal over tampered coins, and he took that very crime as his lifelong motto: deface the currency. But he meant it as a philosophy, not a confession. Read as his whole program for how to live, what was the slogan telling him to do?
answer: Expose the customs everyone treats as solid gold as counterfeit
choices: Expose the customs everyone treats as solid gold as counterfeit
Mint a set of honest new values and impose them on a corrupt world
Abandon money altogether, since coins breed greed and endless quarrels
Obey his city's laws in public while privately despising them as fake
context: The Greek was parakharattein to nomisma, and nomisma meant both 'coin' and 'custom' or 'accepted convention' -- so 'deface the currency' became his philosophy: show society's settled customs to be counterfeit, the way a forger's coin is exposed as fake. His program in one line: 'to fortune oppose courage, to convention nature, to passion reason.' His pupil Crates taught Zeno, who carried 'live according to nature' forward into Stoicism. Source: IEP, 'Diogenes of Sinope'; Diogenes Laertius VI.20-21, VI.38.

question: A teacher asks her class for a tight, final definition of 'a game' — one that fits hide-and-seek, chess, solitaire, and a video game you cannot lose. Every definition a student offers, a classmate breaks with a game it leaves out or a non-game it lets in. What is the teacher trying to show about pinning a big, living idea down in one neat label?
answer: The label can quietly shrink it, fencing off the whole and losing part of it
choices: The label captures it perfectly, since any real thing fits in one good sentence
The label proves the thing was never real, since only what we can define exists
The label can quietly shrink it, fencing off the whole and losing part of it
The label makes the word useless, since no one else will accept your meaning
context: This is the opening move of Daoism. The Daodejing (Tao Te Ching) begins: 'The tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao. The name that can be named is not the eternal Name.' The Dao is the nameless source and pattern running through everything; the instant you slap a fixed label on the Way, you've already lost the real thing. (Stephen Mitchell, Tao Te Ching Ch.1, terebess.hu; IEP: Daoist Philosophy, iep.utm.edu/daoism)

question: Daoism has a homely picture for natural wholeness and simplicity — the world as it just is. Of these four everyday images, which one did the old Daoist teachers actually reach for?
answer: A block of plain wood nobody has carved or shaped yet
choices: A flowing river that never holds the same shape twice
A block of plain wood nobody has carved or shaped yet
A bronze mirror polished until it reflects the world exactly
A full granary holding every kind of seed at once
context: The term is 'pu' (樸), 'the uncarved block' (also rendered uncarved wood or unhewn log). It stands for natural wholeness and simplicity that exists BEFORE we shape and label things. The word appears six times in the Daodejing (chapters 15, 19, 28, 32, 37, 57). (IEP: Daoist Philosophy, iep.utm.edu/daoism; egreenway.com/taoism Ch.28)

question: Daoism pictures the world before we sort it as one whole, unshaped block of wood. The Daodejing's Chapter 32 turns to what happens once people take a knife to that block and start carving it up. A student asks what the carving itself is meant to stand for. What is the best answer?
answer: Naming the world, since each cut marks off one more thing and pins a word to it
choices: Destroying the wood, since a block once cut can never again be made truly whole
Selling the wood, since a plain useless lump becomes tools that people will pay for
Naming the world, since each cut marks off one more thing and pins a word to it
Hiding the wood, since carving and shaping disguise the plain true nature underneath
context: Chapter 32: the Dao is forever nameless and 'small' like uncarved wood, but 'when the whole uncarved block is divided, the pieces become instruments and in need of their names.' Carving = creating named parts; naming is how the one whole gets cut into separate labeled pieces. Mitchell renders the caution: 'When you have names and forms, know that they are provisional.' (egreenway.com/taoism Ch.32; Stephen Mitchell Ch.32, terebess.hu)

question: Two friends argue about the Daoist Way. The old Daoist teachers famously compared the Way to one everyday thing, and that single picture decides everything about how the Way guides a person who follows it. Each friend names a different everyday thing. Which one did the Daoists actually reach for?
answer: A map of the land, showing the open routes you find and walk yourself
choices: A rulebook that lists, step by step, the one correct move to make
A map of the land, showing the open routes you find and walk yourself
A prize at the finish, handed to whoever pushes hardest to reach it
A single straight road that carries everyone to the very same place
context: The Stanford Encyclopedia stresses the Dao is 'more like a map than a formula, rule or law.' It marks natural possibilities you can walk, the way water finds its way downhill without forcing — the model for 'wu-wei,' acting without forcing. The Way shows permissible paths; it doesn't bark commands. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Daoism, plato.stanford.edu/entries/daoism)

question: Ask most people where real power lies and they point to whatever is hardest and strongest. The Daodejing makes the opposite claim: the deepest, most unbeatable power belongs to what is soft and yielding. To prove it, the old text holds up one soft, ordinary thing above all the rest. Which soft thing did the Daodejing crown as its great emblem?
answer: Water, soft enough to take the shape of whatever holds it
choices: The reed, soft enough to bend flat in a gale yet spring back up
Water, soft enough to take the shape of whatever holds it
Breath, soft enough to slip through gaps no wall can close
Fresh snow, soft enough to settle without a sound on the field
context: Chapter 78: 'There is nothing in the world as soft and weak as water. But to erode the hard and strong, nothing can surpass it... The weak can overcome the strong; the soft can overcome the hard.' Of all soft things the Daodejing crowns water — given time it wears away even the hardest stone. Yielding, not forcing, is where the real power is — the Daoist counter-move to brute strength. (Daodejing Ch.78, egreenway.com/taoism; taoistic.com/taoteching-78; SEP: Daoism, plato.stanford.edu/entries/daoism)

question: The Daoist thinker Zhuang Zhou (Zhuangzi) told of waking from a dream of being a butterfly, fluttering happily about — then said he couldn't be sure whether he was a man who had dreamt he was a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming he was a man. He told this little tale to shake loose one comfortable assumption. Which one was he aiming at?
answer: That the neat boxes we sort the world into hold firm no matter what we find
choices: That a hidden message is waiting inside every dream for us to find and decode
That one fixed self carries on unbroken from falling asleep to waking again
That the neat boxes we sort the world into hold firm no matter what we find
That a vivid enough dream can leave a person shaken for the rest of the day
context: Zhuangzi (Zhuang Zhou, c.369-286 BCE): 'I dreamt I was a butterfly... I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.' The settled categories we name the world with may be far less solid than we assume — the same Daoist suspicion of fixed labels, dramatized. Told as a famous parable. (Zhuangzi, Inner Chapters; theconversation.com Zhuangzi explainer 196215)  (Legend.)

question: Socrates sat in an Athens prison in 399 BCE, condemned to die. Before dawn his wealthy friend Crito slipped into the cell: he had already bribed the guards and rented a safe house in distant Thessaly, and he begged Socrates to run. What did Socrates do?
answer: Refused, and drank the poison hemlock when the day came
choices: Refused, and drank the poison hemlock when the day came
Slipped out at dawn and lived out his years in Thessaly
Appealed to the jury one last time to overturn the sentence
Asked the guards for one more month to settle his affairs
context: This is the heart of the legend: Socrates genuinely could have fled. In Plato's Crito, his rich friend Crito reports he has bribed the guards and arranged a refuge in Thessaly, and pleads with him to escape. Socrates refuses and stays to drink the hemlock. Source: Plato, Crito; Wikipedia 'Crito' ('Crito has planned to bribe all of the guards'; 'Socrates would be taken to a home in Thessaly').

question: The jailer handed Socrates the cup of hemlock and the moment everyone dreaded had come. His friends expected him to tremble or beg for a little more time. Instead, Plato tells us, how did Socrates take the poison?
answer: Quite readily and cheerfully, draining it without flinching
choices: Quite readily and cheerfully, draining it without flinching
With shaking hands, spilling part of it on the floor
Only after a long silence, his face gone pale and rigid
Slowly, sip by sip, putting it off as long as he could
context: The calm itself is the famous detail. Plato writes that 'holding the cup to his lips, quite readily and cheerfully he drank off the poison' with no change of color or expression. Source: Plato, Phaedo 117c, Jowett translation.

question: As Socrates drank the hemlock, his friends in the cell could not hold back their grief, the excitable Apollodorus loudest of all. Socrates rebuked them, reminding them why he had earlier sent the women out of the room. What did he say he wanted?
answer: To die in peace, which their outburst was spoiling
choices: To die in peace, which their outburst was spoiling
To spend his last hour teaching, not comforting them
To prove that a good man can face death unafraid
To be remembered for his calm, not for their tears
context: Socrates scolded them: 'What is this strange outcry? I sent away the women mainly in order that they might not offend in this way, for I have heard that a man should die in peace. Be quiet, then, and have patience.' Source: Plato, Phaedo 117d-e, Jowett translation; Wikiquote Socrates.

question: On the morning of his execution Socrates' wife Xanthippe sat beside him in the cell, weeping and holding their baby. Before the long final conversation with his friends began, Socrates made one quiet request to spare them both the scene. What did he ask?
answer: That someone take Xanthippe and the child home
choices: That someone take Xanthippe and the child home
That Xanthippe be allowed to stay until the very end
That his friends find a wet-nurse for the baby
That a message be carried to his grown sons
context: Xanthippe was sitting by him holding their child and weeping; to spare them both, Socrates quietly turned to Crito and asked that someone take her home before the philosophical conversation began. Source: Plato, Phaedo 60a; CliffsNotes Phaedo summary.

question: The man whose job was to bring Socrates the cup of poison came in weeping, said his goodbye, and turned away. Even this executioner could not hold back his tears. As he left, what did the jailer call Socrates?
answer: The noblest and gentlest and best ever to come there
choices: The noblest and gentlest and best ever to come there
A danger to Athens he was sorry to have to kill
A stubborn old man who could have saved himself
The wisest of the Greeks, whom the gods would judge
context: The jailer who had to deliver the poison wept and said goodbye, calling Socrates 'the noblest and gentlest and best of all who ever came to this place'; Socrates praised the man's kindness in return. Source: Plato, Phaedo 116c, Jowett translation.

question: After Socrates drank the hemlock, the jailer told him to walk about until his legs felt heavy, then lie down. An attendant pressed hard on his foot and asked if he felt it; Socrates said no. The cold numbness was creeping up his body. What did the attendant say would happen when it reached a certain point?
answer: When it reaches his heart, that would be the end
choices: When it reaches his heart, that would be the end
When it reaches his chest, he would stop breathing
When it reaches his head, he would lose his wits
When it reaches his stomach, the pain would begin
context: The hemlock killed Socrates from the feet upward. The attendant pressed his foot, found it numb, and explained: 'When the poison reaches the heart, that will be the end.' Source: Plato, Phaedo 117e-118a, Jowett translation.

question: Before drinking the poison, Socrates asked to take a bath and washed himself carefully in his cell. It was not about feeling clean for his last hours. He gave a practical, considerate reason for bathing first. What was it?
answer: So the women would not have to wash his corpse
choices: So the women would not have to wash his corpse
So he could meet death dressed in fresh clothes
So he might pray to the gods with a pure body
So the poison would work faster on clean skin
context: Socrates bathed himself before drinking the hemlock partly so that the women would not have to wash his corpse after he died, one more small act of consideration. Source: Plato, Phaedo 115a; SparkNotes Phaedo 115b-118a summary.

question: As the cold numbness from the hemlock climbed up his body, Socrates uncovered his face one last time and spoke a few quiet words to his friend Crito. Then he said no more. What were these famous last words of Socrates?
answer: 'Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius; do not forget to pay it'
choices: 'Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius; do not forget to pay it'
'Crito, return the lamp I borrowed from our friend Phaedo'
'Crito, see that the boy who served my meals is set free'
'Crito, share out the bread that is left among the guards'
context: Socrates' eerie last words: he uncovered his face and said, 'Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?' Crito answered 'The debt shall be paid' and there was no answer. The other choices are invented errands, not anything Socrates said. Source: Plato, Phaedo 118a, Jowett translation.

question: Socrates was condemned to die, yet about a month passed before the sentence was carried out. The delay had nothing to do with appeals or mercy. Athens forbade any execution while one of its holy ships was away on a yearly voyage, and contrary winds kept it out thirty days. Where had the ship been sent?
answer: To the island of Delos, on the voyage honoring Apollo
choices: To the island of Delos, on the voyage honoring Apollo
To the oracle at Delphi, to ask whether he should die
To Crete, where the charges against him were first judged
To Sparta, to seek terms in the long war with Athens
context: Athens had sent its sacred ship to the island of Delos (sacred to Apollo) on the annual voyage commemorating Theseus saving the fourteen youths from Crete; no executions were allowed in the city until it returned, and contrary winds made the trip take thirty days. Source: Plato, Phaedo 58a-c; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Socrates' ('While the sacred ship was on its journey to Delos, no executions were allowed in the city').

question: In his cell Socrates admits that Athens has wronged him with an unjust verdict. Crito argues that this very wrong frees him to break the law and escape. Socrates disagrees, and his refusal rests on a principle that has nothing to do with whether escape is possible. What principle does he stand on?
answer: One must never repay a wrong with a wrong, whatever was done to him
choices: One must never repay a wrong with a wrong, whatever was done to him
Escaping would only confirm to Athens that he was guilty all along
A philosopher must obey whatever the majority of citizens decide
The gods, not men, should decide when his life is to end
context: This is a genuine ethical fork, and Socrates' move is the heart of the Crito. He grants that Athens wronged him, but holds that 'we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him' — two wrongs do not make a right, so an unjust verdict does not license him to break the law in return. A thinker who held that state injustice forfeits a citizen's obedience would simply be taking the other side of a real dispute. Source: Plato, Crito 49; SparkNotes Crito 50a-51c.

question: Socrates' dying words asked Crito to pay a debt of one rooster to Asclepius. Here is the haunting part: Asclepius was the god of healing, and people who recovered from an illness sacrificed a rooster to thank him for the cure. Read that way, what was Socrates quietly saying about his own death?
answer: That death was the cure, freeing his soul from the body at last
choices: That death was the cure, freeing his soul from the body at last
That he had fallen ill in prison and the gods had healed him
That he forgave the city the way a healed patient forgives
That Crito should pray to Asclepius to spare his life
context: Because the sick sacrificed a cock to Asclepius after being cured, Socrates' dying request is read as treating death itself as the cure — the soul finally healed of, and released from, the body. Source: Plato, Phaedo; Wilson Quarterly 'Socrates' Last Words' ('Socrates apparently meant that death is a cure for the ills of life'); CliffsNotes Phaedo.

question: In the Crito, Socrates imagines the Laws of Athens themselves arguing with him. They point out that for seventy years he was free to pack up and leave the city if he disliked how it was run, yet he chose to stay his whole life. Crito insists an unjust verdict cancels any duty to obey. The Laws draw a conclusion from those seventy years. What do they argue Socrates' lifelong staying amounts to?
answer: A standing agreement to live by the city's laws, binding even now
choices: A standing agreement to live by the city's laws, binding even now
A habit too comfortable to break, but no real duty at all
Proof only that no better city existed for him to flee to
A debt of gratitude he could repay by escaping and teaching abroad
context: This is the famous social-contract argument, and it is a real fork with thinkers on both sides — does a citizen owe the laws obedience even when wronged? The Laws say Socrates had seventy years to leave if their rule displeased him, so by staying he made an implied agreement to obey them; fleeing now would betray that covenant and help destroy the city. The bank takes no side; Crito's view that injustice voids the agreement is the live rival position. Source: Plato, Crito ('seventy years to think of them, during which time you were at liberty to leave the city').

question: In the Crito, Socrates has the Laws of Athens come to life and scold him like a stern family member. To prove he owes them everything, they make a startling claim about his very birth: they insist he would not exist at all without them. On what grounds do the Laws claim credit for his existence?
answer: His father married his mother under their authority
choices: His father married his mother under their authority
They had spared his father's life in an old war
They had blessed the marriage at a temple altar
They had paid the bride-price that sealed the match
context: Socrates personifies the Laws as parents: 'Did we not bring you into existence? Your father married your mother by our aid and begat you.' They argue they made his birth, raising, and education possible, so fleeing would be like a child striking the parent who reared him. Source: Plato, Crito, the personified Laws passage.

question: William Paley says that if you kicked a stone on a heath and someone asked how it got there, you could answer that it had simply lain there forever and sound a little foolish but not absurd. But if you found a watch lying in the grass, that same answer suddenly won't do. What is it about the watch, and not the stone, that blocks the easy answer?
answer: Its many parts are shaped and fitted together to do a job
choices: Its many parts are shaped and fitted together to do a job
It is a far smaller and much heavier object than the stone
It is made of worked metal rather than of ordinary rough rock
It is a rare and valuable thing to find lying there in the grass
context: Paley opens Natural Theology with the heath: a stone you might dismiss, but the watch's fitted parts demand a maker. The difference is contrivance, not mere existence. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I (Lumen Learning transcription).

question: Looking closer at the watch he found, William Paley sees it is packed with springs, wheels, and a coiled chain. A friend says the watch must have a maker simply because it is such a complicated object. Paley thinks the friend has named the wrong feature. What does Paley say is the true mark of a made thing?
answer: That its several parts cooperate to bring about one result
choices: That its several parts cooperate to bring about one result
That it is made of finely polished metal rather than rough stone
That a skilled craftsman could sell it for a very high price
That its hands move on their own once the spring is wound up
context: Paley: we perceive that the watch's 'several parts are framed and put together for a purpose,' so that they point the hour. Parts cooperating toward an end is the design-marker, not complexity alone. The rewritten distractors offer real rival markers (material, value, self-motion) that the 'complexity is wrong' premise does not eliminate. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I (Lumen Learning transcription).

question: Granting that the watch was plainly built for some purpose, William Paley says one conclusion is now unavoidable. He does not claim to know the craftsman's name, where the workshop stood, or when the work was done. What is the move Paley says we are forced to make?
answer: From what we plainly see in the thing, to a maker we never saw
choices: From what we plainly see in the thing, to a maker we never saw
From the small thing we hold, to the very person who once owned it
From the tool in our hand, to the rare skill its maker must have had
From the thing we found, to the exact use it was surely meant to serve
context: Paley: the inference is 'inevitable, that the watch must have had a maker.' The move runs from observed contrivance to an unobserved contriver, not to the maker's identity. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I (Lumen Learning transcription).

question: William Paley carries his watch reasoning over to the human eye. He says there is precisely the same proof that the eye was made for seeing as there is that a telescope was made to help us see. A telescope is plainly a made instrument. What does Paley point to in the eye that, he argues, licenses the very same conclusion?
answer: That it is built on the very same laws of light a telescope uses
choices: That it is built on the very same laws of light a telescope uses
That it is more delicate and far more beautiful than a glass lens
That nobody has ever once watched a working eye being assembled
That it can fail and slowly go blind just as a telescope can break
context: Paley's prize exhibit. Eye and telescope are built on the same optical principles (the refraction of light), so the artifact inference transfers straight to the organ. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. III (quod.lib.umich.edu).

question: As a young student, Charles Darwin read William Paley's Natural Theology and said he had hardly ever admired a book more, that its reasoning gave him as much delight as Euclid's geometry. Years later this same man would discover the idea that toppled Paley's central claim. What was the young Darwin's relationship to the design argument?
answer: He took its starting points on trust and was charmed and convinced
choices: He took its starting points on trust and was charmed and convinced
He enjoyed it greatly as elegant work yet was never actually persuaded
He admired it yet already saw the very gap he would one day exploit
He admired its polished style but rejected its conclusion straight away
context: Darwin's Autobiography: 'I do not think I hardly ever admired a book more... gave me as much delight as did Euclid.' He took the premises on trust and was 'charmed and convinced' by the argument he would later overturn. Source: Charles Darwin, Autobiography (monadnock.net transcription).

question: Someone hands William Paley a watch that runs badly: it gains time, the hands stick, and a few of its parts seem to do nothing he can make out. Surely, they say, a thing this faulty and puzzling cannot be the work of any maker. Paley is unmoved. What does Paley say a flawed, partly mysterious watch still shows?
answer: That it was plainly still built for a purpose, despite its flaws
choices: That it was plainly still built for a purpose, despite its flaws
That it must have slowly come together by accident, with no maker
That it is now far too broken for anyone to tell whether it was made
That its flaws prove many hands made it, working against each other
context: Paley lists objections that don't weaken the inference: you needn't have seen a watch made, know who made it, or make one yourself; a watch going wrong or having parts you can't explain is still obviously made. This pre-empts 'but the eye has flaws.' Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I (objections I-VII).

question: William Paley raises a strange new case: suppose the watch you found could make another watch just like itself, carrying inside it the moulds and tools to do the job. A bystander says this at last removes any need for a maker, since the watch now turns out watches on its own. What does Paley conclude about the self-copying watch?
answer: That it still leaves the design of the first watch wholly unexplained
choices: That it still leaves the design of the first watch wholly unexplained
That it finally proves no maker was ever needed in the first place
That it must therefore have slowly grown up from a seed like a plant
That it is far too strange a device to be worth discussing at all
context: Paley (Ch. II): a watch that makes watches still cries out for a contriver. 'Contrivance is still unaccounted for. We still want a contriver. A designing mind is neither supplied by this supposition nor dispensed with.' This anticipates the reply that heredity explains living design. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. II (joelvelasco.net).

question: In 1986 Richard Dawkins answered Paley with a book whose title turned Paley's own image against him. Living things really do look built for their jobs, Dawkins grants, so what does the building when no mind is at work? He points to the slow process Darwin had uncovered. On Dawkins's account, how does that process end up producing parts that look designed?
answer: By keeping whatever happens to work and scrapping the rest, with no aim
choices: By keeping whatever happens to work and scrapping the rest, with no aim
By a hidden mind that quietly plans out each living creature in advance
By a single stroke of luck, with all the parts falling into place at once
By a striving deep inside living things to better themselves over the ages
context: Dawkins titled his reply The Blind Watchmaker (1986): the process Darwin found 'has no purpose in mind' yet is 'essentially nonrandom.' It is not a planner and not luck, but a blind, cumulative filter. Source: Richard Dawkins, The Blind Watchmaker (1986).

question: A critic tells William Paley that the watch needs no maker: it is merely one of the many shapes that matter can fall into, thrown up by the laws of metallic nature and a built-in principle of order in things. Paley answers that this is no real explanation at all. Why does Paley say naming such a law settles nothing?
answer: Because it merely relabels the very ordered thing we set out to explain
choices: Because it merely relabels the very ordered thing we set out to explain
Because the laws of nature are far too weak to push metal into a shape
Because no real law of nature has ever once been written down by anyone
Because a principle of order would make every object identical, not varied
context: Paley rejects the 'unknown law' dodge: calling the watch 'one out of possible combinations,' or crediting 'a principle of order' or 'the laws of metallic nature,' names the thing to be explained instead of explaining it. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I, objections IV-VI.

question: In later life Charles Darwin wrote that Paley's old argument, once so convincing to him, now failed. We can no longer insist, he said, that the beautiful hinge of a clam shell must have been made by an intelligent being, the way the hinge of a door was made by a man. What had Darwin found that, in his view, knocked the support out from under Paley's argument?
answer: Natural selection, which can build fitted parts with no designer at all
choices: Natural selection, which can build fitted parts with no designer at all
Inherited striving, where a creature passes on the traits it strains to gain
A built-in drive, which pushes living things up toward ever higher forms
Blind chance alone, which throws fitted parts together over the long ages
context: Darwin's Autobiography: 'The old argument of design in nature, as given by Paley... fails, now that the law of natural selection has been discovered.' The clam-shell hinge no longer needs a maker the way a door-hinge does. Source: Charles Darwin, Autobiography (monadnock.net); also plato.stanford.edu/entries/teleological-arguments/.

question: Writing before Paley, David Hume grants that finding a watch we never saw made still lets us infer a watchmaker. Cleanthes then wants to run the same move from the orderly universe to a world-maker. Hume presses on one difference between the two cases that makes the second leap shakier. What is that difference?
answer: We have seen watches built many times, but never a whole world made
choices: We have seen watches built many times, but never a whole world made
The universe is surely too large for any single maker to have built it
A watch and a world are made of completely different sorts of stuff
A world might have grown from a seed, while a watch is plainly built
context: Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), written 23 years before Paley: the watch inference rests on repeated experience of watches being made ('a thousand and a thousand times'); the cosmos is 'single, individual, without parallel,' so there is no track record of world-making to generalize from. The conclusion is pulled out of the stem so the answer must be known, not echoed; distractor D ('grown from a seed') is Hume's own rival analogy from Part VII, a live wrong pick rather than a contradiction of the granted premise. This sets up the next topic, Hume's reply. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part II (and Part VII for the seed/vegetation analogy).

question: A farmer wakes to find a downpour has flattened his ripe wheat the night before harvest. He is wretched all day. His neighbor, whose field was hit just as hard, shrugs and starts again.
