Epictetus, a former slave who taught how to keep your peace, would point out that both men met the very same weather -- so what made only the first one miserable?
answer: His own verdict that this was a catastrophe
choices: His own verdict that this was a catastrophe
The rain, a plainly real and ruinous misfortune
His failure to bring the harvest in a day sooner
The gods, who flood the fields of careless farmers
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: 'Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views they take of them.' The rain is just rain; the misery is the judgment laid on top. The neighbor met the same weather and added no such verdict. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: A girl spends the morning before a long-planned picnic furious that it is raining, certain the day is ruined. Epictetus, the Stoic teacher, taught that you cannot order the weather to obey you. What did he say is the path to a steady, contented life instead?
answer: Wish for things to happen the way they actually do
choices: Wish for things to happen the way they actually do
Demand loudly until events bend to the way you wish
Feel nothing at all, so no event can ever touch you
Plan so carefully that nothing is left to go wrong
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 8: 'Don't demand that things happen as you wish, but wish that they happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.' It is not numb resignation -- it is aiming your wanting at reality instead of fighting it. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 8 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Epictetus became one of the ancient world's greatest teachers of inner freedom -- the freedom no one can take from your own mind. Yet his early life under Epaphroditus, a rich official in the household of the emperor Nero, was the very opposite of free. What was Epictetus's station in those early years?
answer: He was a slave in another man's household
choices: He was a slave in another man's household
He was a soldier in one of Nero's legions
He was a merchant who later lost his fortune
He was a tutor to the children of senators
context: Epictetus was born a slave around 50-55 CE and owned by Epaphroditus, a freedman who served as secretary to the emperor Nero. The man who taught that your will can never be enslaved had once been a slave himself. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu).

question: Epictetus taught his students to change one word when something is taken from them. Instead of saying 'I have lost it' when a possession -- or even a person -- is gone, what did he tell them to say, on the grounds that the thing was never truly theirs to keep?
answer: I have given it back
choices: I have given it back
I have been robbed
I will earn it again
I never wanted it
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 11: 'Never say of anything, I have lost it; but, I have given it back. Is your child dead? It is given back.' Externals -- property, even loved ones -- are on loan, not owned; death is the lender calling them home. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 11 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Ancient sources tell that when Epictetus was still a slave, his master began twisting his leg for cruel sport. Quietly the enslaved man warned, 'You will break it.' The master kept on until the bone snapped -- and Epictetus, who would limp for the rest of his life, spoke a single line that became the emblem of his whole teaching. According to the story, what did he say?
answer: There, did I not tell you that it would break?
choices: There, did I not tell you that it would break?
Strike again, for a slave feels nothing at all.
Now I am free of you; a cripple has no master.
The leg is yours to break; the rest is not.
context: Reported by Origen citing Celsus. Whether or not it happened exactly so, the story became the emblem of his teaching: the master could break the leg -- a thing 'not up to' Epictetus -- but not his composure, which was. He was lame the rest of his life. (Told as legend.) Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu).

question: Epictetus opens his little handbook by sorting everything in life into two bins: things that are 'up to us' and things that are not. On the 'NOT up to us' side he names your body and your property -- and then a third thing, one most people are sure they own and would fight hardest to keep. What is that third item on Epictetus's list?
answer: Your reputation
choices: Your reputation
Your friends
Your homeland
Your good luck
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: NOT up to us are 'the body, property, reputation, and public office.' Reputation is the surprising one -- it is built and held inside other minds, so it can never be 'up to you.' Friends, homeland, and fortune are also outside your control, but they are not the word Epictetus names third on his list. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Epictetus himself never published a single line, yet his teaching survives in full -- a set of lectures and a famous pocket handbook meant to be carried and used. One devoted follower wrote it all down from his words and gave it to the world. Whose pen preserved the teaching of Epictetus?
answer: Arrian, who also wrote a history of Alexander's campaigns
choices: Arrian, who also wrote a history of Alexander's campaigns
Seneca, who penned long Stoic letters of his own
Plutarch, who filled volumes with the lives of great men
Diogenes Laertius, who collected the lives of the philosophers
context: Flavius Arrianus (Arrian) studied under Epictetus, then set down the Discourses and distilled them into the Enchiridion ('handbook') around 104-107 CE -- a manual meant to be carried, not just admired. The same Arrian wrote the Anabasis of Alexander, the great history of Alexander's campaigns, and served Rome as governor of Cappadocia. Without him, Epictetus would be a name and nothing more. (Seneca's Letters, Plutarch's Lives, and Diogenes Laertius's Lives of the Philosophers are all real works by real authors -- offered as plausible-wrong distractors.) Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu).

question: Epictetus gave a startling piece of advice about loving the people closest to you. When you kiss your own child or your spouse goodnight, he said, quietly remind yourself of one plain fact about them -- a fact that keeps the love steady and unafraid. What did he tell you to remember in that tender moment?
answer: That you are kissing a mortal human being
choices: That you are kissing a mortal human being
That you love them more than your own life
That the gods may grow jealous of your joy
That they belong to you and to no one else
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 3: 'When you kiss your child or your wife, say to yourself that you are kissing a human being; then you will not be disturbed if they die.' Not cold detachment -- love fully, but hold without the lie that they are yours to keep forever. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 3 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Epictetus pointed to ball-players to show how to live. They sprint, dive, and strain every muscle to catch a ball that, in itself, is a worthless scrap of leather they will toss back a moment later. What lesson did he draw from how hard they try over a thing that does not matter?
answer: Throw yourself into playing well, hold the outcome loosely
choices: Throw yourself into playing well, hold the outcome loosely
Care only about the score, since winning is the whole point
Guard your heart by never wanting the ball in the first place
Treat every contest as a grave matter of life and death
context: From the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Epictetus: good players run flat-out to catch a ball they know is worthless in itself -- the effort goes into playing WELL (up to them), not into owning the ball (not up to them). Full commitment to the action, open hands on the result. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/epictetus).

question: Epictetus admitted that some things in life truly cannot be escaped: 'I must die. I must be imprisoned. I must go into exile.' Yet he insisted that even when the event is fixed and forced upon you, one thing about it is still entirely yours to decide. According to him, what remains in your hands?
answer: The manner in which you meet it -- groaning, or serene
choices: The manner in which you meet it -- groaning, or serene
Whether the sentence is just enough to be obeyed
How long the gods will permit the hardship to last
Which of your friends will be punished alongside you
context: Epictetus, Discourses 1.1: 'I must die. But must I die groaning? I must go into exile -- can anyone stop me from going with a smile, cheerful and serene?' The event is forced; the bearing is chosen. Source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.1 (George Long trans.; en.wikisource.org).

question: A young athlete trains for years and wants, more than anything, for the crowd to love him. Epictetus would warn that he has staked his peace on the one thing he can never control. He can master his own training and his own conduct -- but the cheering itself, Epictetus argued, can never be 'up to him.' Why not?
answer: What others think of him is decided inside their minds, not his
choices: What others think of him is decided inside their minds, not his
Crowds are fickle and will always turn on a winner in time
Seeking applause is shameful, so the wish is wrong to begin with
No athlete is ever truly skilled enough to deserve the cheers
context: Per the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Epictetus: 'Our reputations must be decided by what other people think of us, and what they think is up to them.' He can govern his effort and character; he cannot reach into the spectators and make them cheer. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu).

question: Here is a hard case in Epictetus's teaching. We assume nothing is more 'ours' than our own body -- yet he put even the body on the 'NOT up to us' side, calling it borrowed clay, a 'little donkey' we are merely lent. On what grounds did he deny that your body is fully within your power?
answer: It can be chained, sickened, or broken by forces outside your will
choices: It can be chained, sickened, or broken by forces outside your will
It is an illusion that the wise learn to see straight through
It belongs by right to the emperor, who may claim it in war
It is evil and corrupt, fit only to be starved and punished
context: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Epictetus (citing Discourses 1.1.10, 1.3.5): he calls the body 'pathetic little flesh,' molded clay, a borrowed 'little donkey.' God could make the WILL unhampered but not the body -- so the body, hostage to sickness and chains, sits on the 'not up to us' side. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/epictetus).

question: A cruel tyrant drags a man before him in chains and gloats that he now holds the man's fate entirely in his hands, free to ruin him however he pleases. Epictetus would answer that the tyrant, for all his power, has overreached: there is one thing about this man no chain and no executioner can touch. What is it?
answer: Whether he turns into a worse man -- that descent is his alone to make, not the tyrant's
choices: Whether he turns into a worse man -- that descent is his alone to make, not the tyrant's
Whether he keeps his calm and contentment -- that peace is his to hold, not the tyrant's
Whether his body lives to see another dawn -- that breath is his to keep, not the tyrant's
Whether he holds his rank and good name -- that standing is his to keep, not the tyrant's
context: Epictetus locates all good and evil in the prohairesis -- the faculty of choice. A tyrant can chain your leg, seize your goods, ruin your name, even take your life; what he cannot do is reach into the part that chooses and make you vicious -- only your own assent can do that. Note the trap: your felt calm is the fruit of right judgment and can be shaken, but your moral character is yours alone to corrupt or keep. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Epictetus'.

question: A soldier sees a live grenade land among his sleeping comrades. With no time to throw it clear, he flings his own body on top of it and smothers the blast. He dies; his friends live. A man who shoots himself in despair also brings about his own death on purpose -- yet we call the soldier a hero and the other a suicide. Which feature of the soldier's act, if it were missing, would make us call him a suicide too?
answer: His death is something he would gladly have avoided had any way to save the others let him live.
choices: His death is something he would gladly have avoided had any way to save the others let him live.
His death was forced on him by the desperate moment, and a death forced like that is not his own fault.
His death served a worthy cause, and a death in a worthy cause is never the kind of thing we call suicide.
His death wounded nobody at all but himself, while a real suicide always scars the people left behind.
context: The grenade-jumper is the gentle mirror of the doctrine of double effect. A man who throws himself on a grenade FORESEES his own death but does not INTEND it -- if he could shield his friends and live, he gladly would. That is the opposite of suicide, where death is the very thing aimed at. The same intend-versus-foresee line that can excuse a harm also explains why we honor a death knowingly caused but not sought. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect,' self-sacrifice discussion.)

question: Two wartime pilots each fly a mission that ends the same number of civilian lives. The first is ordered to break the enemy's will to fight, and aims his bombs squarely at the crowded tenement quarter to do it. The second is ordered to wreck a munitions plant; his bombs flatten it, and the same number die in the houses pressed up against its wall. Lawyers of war call the first a murderer and the second perhaps blameless. What makes the killing different?
answer: For the first, the dead are the thing his plan runs on; for the second, they are rubble his plan steps over.
choices: For the first, the dead are the thing his plan runs on; for the second, they are rubble his plan steps over.
The first could have won the war by gentler means, while the second had no other way to reach the plant.
The first dropped his bombs out of hatred, while the second dropped his from cold and lawful soldier's duty.
The first struck homes that had no defences, while the second struck a target the laws of war plainly allow.
context: This terror-bomber / tactical-bomber pair is what the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls the 'least controversial' illustration of the doctrine of double effect. Identical body count, identical certainty of death -- yet for the terror bomber the civilian deaths ARE the means (frighten the enemy by killing them), while for the tactical bomber they are an unwanted side-effect of destroying the factory. The intend-versus-foresee line, not the death toll, is doing the moral work. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect.')

question: A man walking home is set upon by a killer bent on murdering him. He fights back to save his own life, and in the struggle the attacker is killed. A medieval thinker used exactly this scene to argue the defender does no wrong -- because, he said, a single act can produce two effects, one the man reaches for and one that falls outside what he reaches for. Two effects flow from his struggle: he keeps his own life, and his attacker dies. Which does the thinker place OUTSIDE the man's intention?
answer: The attacker's death, which he accepts as the cost but would just as soon have spared if he safely could.
choices: The attacker's death, which he accepts as the cost but would just as soon have spared if he safely could.
The keeping of his own life, which is merely a lucky result of the blows he was forced to throw.
Both effects equally, since once he chooses to fight he must own everything the fight brings about.
Neither effect, since a man who lifts his hand against another plainly means whatever follows from it.
context: The thinker is Thomas Aquinas, who first stated the doctrine of double effect in the Summa Theologiae (II-II, Q.64, A.7) while defending the right to kill an attacker in self-defense. His exact words: 'Nothing hinders one act from having two effects, only one of which is intended, while the other is beside the intention.' Of the two effects the act produces, the man INTENDS to preserve his own life; the aggressor's death is the one that is beside that intention -- and because of that, the act is lawful. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect,' quoting Summa Theologiae II-II Q.64 A.7.)

question: Thomas Aquinas argued that a man fighting off a murderer may lawfully kill the attacker to save his own life. But he refused to leave that permission open-ended. In the very same passage he added a sharp brake: the defense is lawful only up to a point, beyond which it becomes wrong even though the original threat was real. What was the limit Aquinas set?
answer: He may use no more force than the danger requires; excess violence makes it unlawful.
choices: He may use no more force than the danger requires; excess violence makes it unlawful.
He may strike only if he first warns the attacker and gives him a chance to flee.
He may defend himself only against a foe who is plainly the stronger of the two.
He may act only while a witness is present to vouch that he did not start the fight.
context: Even Aquinas, the founder of the doctrine, built in proportionality. The same article runs: 'if a man, in self-defense, uses more than necessary violence, it will be unlawful, whereas if he repel force with moderation, his defense will be lawful.' Killing to stop a killer can be fine; going on stabbing after he is disarmed is not -- the foreseen harm is tolerable only when the force matches the threat. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect,' quoting Summa Theologiae II-II Q.64 A.7.)

question: A doctor tends a dying patient in unbearable pain. She keeps raising the morphine until the agony loosens its grip, knowing a dose this high may also bring the end sooner. A second doctor, facing the same suffering, administers a single dose he knows full well is past any patient's power to survive. Both patients die the same evening. Many call the first doctor's act right and the second's wrong, though the drug and the death look alike. Where does that difference lie?
answer: The first wants the suffering gone and will live with the death; the second wants the patient gone.
choices: The first wants the suffering gone and will live with the death; the second wants the patient gone.
The first gives the smaller dose of the drug, while the second deliberately gives a far larger one.
The first cannot be sure the drug will kill, while the second leaves the outcome in no doubt at all.
The first keeps to accepted practice, while the second breaks the standing law against taking a life.
context: This is the doctrine of double effect's most familiar modern home. A doctor who gives escalating morphine to relieve agony, foreseeing it MIGHT shorten life, is widely held to act permissibly because she aims at easing pain, not at death; a doctor who gives a lethal dose AIMING at death fails the test, even though the patient dies the same way. The intention splits the verdict. (A footnote worth knowing: many palliative-care physicians now argue that properly dosed morphine almost never actually hastens death, so the textbook example may rest on a medical myth.) (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect'; BMC Medical Ethics, 'Goods, causes and intentions.')

question: Doctors once drew a fine line in two grim cases. To save a mother whose unborn child cannot be delivered, crushing the child's skull to free it was called forbidden; removing a cancer-ridden womb to save her, with the child dying as a result, was called permitted. The defenders' reason was that the first death is aimed at and the second merely foreseen. Critics like Jonathan Bennett pressed back hard. What was their objection?
answer: The surgeon could claim to intend only the crushing and not the death, so the line is too fine to be real.
choices: The surgeon could claim to intend only the crushing and not the death, so the line is too fine to be real.
Both procedures kill the child for certain, so a doctor is bound to refuse to perform either one of them.
The mother's life cannot outrank the child's, so saving her can never justify the loss of the child.
A merely foreseen death is just a disguised intended one, so the doctrine has to forbid both cases alike.
context: This obstetric pair -- craniotomy forbidden, cancer-hysterectomy permitted -- founded the doctrine of double effect in Catholic moral theology and is its hardest test, the 'problem of closeness.' Jonathan Bennett and Warren Quinn argued the line is drawn too finely: 'one can intend the crushing without intending the death,' so a clever surgeon could redescribe the craniotomy as merely-foreseen too, and the supposed moral gap vanishes. The bank takes no verdict; this is a live, unresolved objection. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect,' Problem of Closeness.)

question: Caleb is sure he is wide awake. To prove it he pinches his own arm — it hurts, so this must be real life, not a dream. His sister tells him the pinch proves nothing. Why does a painful pinch fail to prove you are awake?
answer: A dream can make a pinch hurt just as much, so the pain settles nothing
choices: A dream can make a pinch hurt just as much, so the pain settles nothing
Pain is really an emotion, and emotions are never reliable evidence about anything
He should have pinched much harder, since a soft pinch can still be felt in sleep
A pinch only tests the skin, so it can say nothing about what the mind is doing
context: This is the classic kid-level version of Descartes' dream doubt. Your brain simulates body-sensations in a dream, so a dreamed pinch can hurt — and you can even dream of pinching your nose shut and still 'breathe' through it. Any test you can run, you can also dream running, which is exactly Descartes' point that the senses can't certify themselves. Source: Reality Checks for Lucid Dreaming, Oneironauts; Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy I.

question: Every kid has woken from a dream so vivid that, while it was happening, it felt completely real — you were certain you were awake inside it. So when a friend insists, "But I just KNOW I am awake right now," why does that feeling of certainty fail to prove it?
answer: A dreaming you would feel that very same certainty, so the feeling cannot tell the two apart
choices: A dreaming you would feel that very same certainty, so the feeling cannot tell the two apart
Certainty is only a strong emotion, and strong emotions are usually wrong about the world
You can be certain only of things you see, and dreams are things you merely imagine
Feeling awake is good proof by morning but fails late at night once you are tired
context: This is the opening move of Rene Descartes' dream argument: from the inside, a vivid dream feels exactly like waking life, so the bare feeling 'I'm definitely awake' proves nothing — a dreaming you would feel the identical certainty. Source: Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy I; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (the 'Now Dreaming Doubt').

question: Rene Descartes sat by his fire in his winter dressing-gown, holding a sheet of paper, hunting for one thing he could not possibly doubt. Then a memory stopped him: on many past nights he had been just as sure he was sitting by that fire — when really he was lying undressed in bed, fast asleep. Granting that, why could he no longer be certain he was awake at THIS moment?
answer: This very moment by the fire might itself be one of those dreams, with no way to tell
choices: This very moment by the fire might itself be one of those dreams, with no way to tell
He must have dozed off in his chair, so the paper he was holding had to be imaginary
He could not recall sitting down, and a missing memory is a clear sign you are dreaming
The firelight looked too vivid to be real, and dreams are always the most vivid scenes
context: Descartes' own words: he recalls being 'convinced of just such familiar events — that I am sitting by the fire in my dressing-gown — when in fact I am lying undressed in bed.' Because a past dream had copied the waking scene perfectly, the very scene in front of him could be a dream too. He even shakes his head and feels his hand to check, then notes he has been 'tricked by exactly similar thoughts while asleep.' Source: Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy I (Cottingham translation).

question: An old Chinese story, told of the sage Zhuangzi around 300 BC, says he dreamed he was a butterfly — drifting happily from flower to flower, completely sure he was a butterfly. Then he woke as a man. The tale ends on a jolt that matches a famous doubt about dreams. What unsettling thought did it leave him with?
answer: Maybe he was not a man who dreamed he was a butterfly, but a butterfly now dreaming it was a man
choices: Maybe he was not a man who dreamed he was a butterfly, but a butterfly now dreaming it was a man
Maybe butterflies have real thoughts of their own, since he had truly felt like one of them
Maybe the dream was a warning he was meant to obey, not a riddle he was meant to solve
Maybe a happy dream is worth more than a dull waking life, however real the waking feels
context: Often retold as a legend, 'The Butterfly Dream' (Zhuangzi, ch. 2) lands the same 'which side is real?' jolt as Descartes — centuries earlier and a world away. Zhuang Zhou awakes and cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it is Zhuang Zhou. Source: Zhuangzi, 'The Butterfly Dream'; discussed in Philosophy Now, Issue 76.

question: Rene Descartes pushed his dream doubt to a sharp point: there are, he wrote, no sure signs by which being awake can be told apart from being asleep. But the dream was only a tool — he was aiming at something bigger. If no test can prove you are awake rather than dreaming, what did he decide you can no longer fully trust?
answer: Anything your senses report, since any sight, sound, or touch could be a dream instead
choices: Anything your senses report, since any sight, sound, or touch could be a dream instead
Your own memories, since a person who is dreaming can recall nothing from real life
Other people, since only you could ever know whether you are awake or asleep
Your imagination, since the same power that builds dreams also builds daydreams
context: The real target of the dream argument is the senses. Since no test reliably tells waking from dreaming, anything you believe purely because your eyes, ears, or hands reported it could be a dream's report — so the senses can't be the bedrock of knowledge. As the IEP puts it, 'since there is no principled way of distinguishing waking life from dreams, any belief based on sensation has been shown to be doubtful.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rene Descartes'; Descartes, Meditations I.

question: Rene Descartes pushed the dream doubt hard: maybe everything in front of him was only a dream. Yet he insisted that one kind of truth would still hold firm even if his whole life were a dream. Which sort of fact did he say the dream doubt cannot touch?
answer: Truths of arithmetic and geometry, like that 2+3=5, which hold whether or not any object is real
choices: Truths of arithmetic and geometry, like that 2+3=5, which hold whether or not any object is real
Vivid memories of his past, since he could picture them as sharply as anything before his eyes
Facts that nearly everyone agrees on, since so many people cannot all be mistaken at once
Things he had checked many times before, since a careful re-check rules out any mistake
context: The dream doubt has a limit — it doesn't sink everything. Descartes reasons that whether he is awake or dreaming, 'two and three added together are five, and a square has no more than four sides.' Painted dream-castles might be fake, but the math the painter used to make them stays true — such truths don't depend on any object actually existing. Sense-facts fall; pure arithmetic and geometry survive this wave of doubt (the next wave — the all-powerful deceiver — is built to knock down even those). Source: Descartes, Meditations I; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology'.

question: The dream doubt has a modern descendant. Picture a living brain kept alive in a vat of fluid, wired to a computer that feeds it electrical signals — signals that produce the full experience of an ordinary life: a job, friends, lunch. The 1999 film The Matrix put this picture on screen for everyone. Why is this brain-in-a-vat exactly the puzzle Descartes raised?
answer: From the inside the fed-in life would feel just like the real thing, so you could never tell
choices: From the inside the fed-in life would feel just like the real thing, so you could never tell
A brain in a vat would slowly lose its real memories, the way a dreamer forgets waking life
The computer could replay only experiences it had recorded, so the brain would relive its past
A real brain still needs a real body, so the vat must eventually fail and break the spell
context: Same crack, new costume. The 'brain in a vat' was made famous in Hilary Putnam's 1981 book Reason, Truth and History: a brain fed wired-in signals would have experiences identical to a real life, so from the inside it could never tell. The Matrix (1999) put the idea on screen for everybody. (Cross-link: this pairs with the Brain-in-a-Vat / Matrix topic.) Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Brain in a Vat Argument'; Hilary Putnam, Reason, Truth and History (1981), ch. 1.

question: A boy says he is sure the back of his own head has hair on it, though he has never seen it. His sister keeps pressing -- not why it is likely, but how he could really KNOW it. Which reply gives him a true ground to KNOW it, rather than just a reason the belief is a safe bet?
answer: "I have felt it with my hands and seen it in a mirror, so it comes from what I touched and saw"
choices: "I have felt it with my hands and seen it in a mirror, so it comes from what I touched and saw"
"It simply has to be true, since a head that was bald only on the back would be a strange one"
"Everyone agrees boys have hair there, and that many people surely cannot all be wrong at once"
"I have just always believed it, as far back as I can recall, so it has to have been true"
context: This is the empiricist test in its plainest form -- a way of settling where knowledge comes from, not a word to memorize: trace any idea back to something you actually saw, heard, or touched. If you can point to the sight or the touch it came from, it counts; reasoning that it 'must' be so, or that everyone says so, or that you have simply always believed it, does not trace back to experience. The motto goes back to Aristotle and was repeated by Aquinas as 'there is nothing in the mind that was not first in the senses.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'British Empiricism' (iep.utm.edu/british-empiricism/).

question: John Locke asked his readers to picture a just-born baby's mind as a sheet of white paper, not one word or mark on it yet. Then came the real question: where does that empty mind get ALL its later stock of reasoning and knowledge? Locke answered in a single word. What was his one-word answer?
answer: Experience -- every last bit flows in from what the person later senses and notices
choices: Experience -- every last bit flows in from what the person later senses and notices
Reason -- the mind spins out its knowledge by pure thought, with no help from the world
Instinct -- the useful truths are bred into the body and surface on their own in time
Teaching -- the knowledge is poured in by parents and tutors who already hold it
context: From Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690): 'Let us then suppose the mind to be, as we say, white paper void of all characters, without any ideas... Whence has it all the materials of reason and knowledge? To this I answer, in one word, from EXPERIENCE.' The white-paper image was later Latinized as the 'tabula rasa,' the blank slate, and it is the opening shot of empiricism: nothing is written on the mind until the world writes it there. Source: John Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Ch. 1 (via age-of-the-sage.org/philosophy/john_locke_tabula_rasa.html).

question: A girl insists she carries a perfectly clear idea of a brand-new color -- one no one has ever seen and no light could ever make -- and she is certain it counts as something she truly knows. An empiricist following Locke's rule has a single blunt test for whether an idea like hers counts as real knowledge. What is that test?
answer: Whether the idea can be traced back to some particular thing she once sensed; if not, it is empty
choices: Whether the idea can be traced back to some particular thing she once sensed; if not, it is empty
Whether other people happen to share the very same idea when she carefully describes it to them
Whether the idea stays steady and vivid in her mind over time instead of fading or shifting on her
Whether she can reason the idea out step by step without ever once contradicting herself along the way
context: The Internet Encyclopedia calls this the 'Lockean Axiom': 'There is no idea in the mind that cannot be traced back to some particular experience.' The empiricist demand is concrete -- point to the sight, sound, or touch the idea came from. An idea that floats free, tied to no experience at all, fails the test no matter how clear or steady it feels. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'British Empiricism' (iep.utm.edu/british-empiricism/).

question: Rene Descartes pointed to your idea of a perfect triangle -- three perfectly straight sides, perfectly meeting. Every triangle you have ever actually seen, drawn or printed, is a little crooked, never truly perfect; yet you grasp the perfect one exactly. From this gap, Descartes drew a conclusion that cut against the whole 'all knowledge from the senses' idea. What did he conclude?
answer: The idea of the perfect triangle was in the mind already, not copied from any triangle you saw
choices: The idea of the perfect triangle was in the mind already, not copied from any triangle you saw
The idea of the perfect triangle is a blurred average of the many crooked triangles you have seen
There is no real idea of a perfect triangle, only a vague wish for one we can never truly form
The idea of the perfect triangle is learned from teachers who hand the perfect version down to us
context: This is the rationalist counter-move, and Descartes is its sharpest voice: some ideas are 'innate,' stamped in the mind at birth rather than learned. He sorted all ideas into three kinds -- arriving through the senses, made up by the imagination, and innate (placed in the mind, he said, by God) -- and his examples of the innate ones were the idea of God and the idea of a perfect triangle. A competent empiricist would answer differently; the bank takes no side on who is right. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rationalism vs. Empiricism' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/rationalism-empiricism/); philosophy.institute, 'Descartes' Classification of Ideas.'

question: Some thinkers claimed a few truths are branded on every human mind from birth -- truths like 'whatever exists, exists' and 'nothing can both be and not be at the same time.' John Locke fired back with one plain observation about young children to argue these truths were never branded in at all. What did Locke point out about children?
answer: They show not the least grasp of those truths, so no truth that everyone supposedly shares is in them
choices: They show not the least grasp of those truths, so no truth that everyone supposedly shares is in them
They believe whatever a grown-up tells them, proving the mind starts out trusting rather than knowing
They learn to speak long before they can reason, so words must come into the mind before ideas do
They forget almost everything from their earliest years, so any truths born in them are simply lost
context: Locke's argument from the lack of universal assent: if such truths were stamped on the mind at birth, everyone would recognize them instantly -- yet, in his words, 'all children and idiots have not the least apprehension or thought of them' ('idiots' being his period's word for the severely cognitively disabled). Since the supposed universal truths get no universal recognition, Locke concludes they were never branded in; they have to be learned. Source: John Locke, Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book I, Ch. 2 (earlymoderntexts.com); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'British Empiricism.'

question: David Hume split everything in the mind into two kinds: the forceful, lively perception you get the moment you actually see, hear, or feel a thing, and the fainter version of it that drifts back later in memory and imagination. He then offered a way to test any hazy idea for whether it is real or empty. What did Hume say to do with a hazy idea?
answer: Hunt for the earlier first-hand perception it sprang from; if there is none, the idea is empty
choices: Hunt for the earlier first-hand perception it sprang from; if there is none, the idea is empty
Hold it firmly in mind and see whether it grows sharper the longer you keep your attention on it
Break it down into smaller ideas, since a true idea can always be split while a false one cannot
Compare it against what other careful people report, trusting the version most of them agree upon
context: Hume named the two kinds 'impressions' (the forceful, first-hand perceptions) and 'ideas' (their fainter copies in memory and imagination). His 'Copy Principle' holds that every simple idea is just a faded copy of an earlier impression: 'all our simple ideas in their first appearance are derived from simple impressions, which are correspondent to them.' So to test a fuzzy idea, hunt for the impression it came from -- and if there is none, the idea is empty. Source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, Book I (via philosophyalevel.com; hume.ucdavis.edu).

question: Socrates stands in the King-Archon's court as the DEFENDANT, charged with impiety. Waiting there too is Euthyphro, who has come to the same court as a PROSECUTOR. The shocking part is WHO Euthyphro is prosecuting for murder. Who is it?
answer: His own father
choices: His own father
A rival priest
The man who accused Socrates
A foreign general
context: The whole dialogue on holiness happens between two religious court cases. A hired laborer on Naxos had killed a household slave in a drunken brawl; Euthyphro's father bound the laborer hand and foot, threw him in a ditch, and sent to Athens to ask a priest what to do — and the bound man died of hunger and cold before the answer came back. Euthyphro is so certain of his own piety that he is taking his father to court over it. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Jowett trans.), standardebooks.org/ebooks/plato/dialogues/benjamin-jowett/text/euthyphro.

question: Every time Socrates and Euthyphro pin down a definition of holiness, it slips loose and the argument circles back on itself. Socrates jokes that his words behave like the statues his mythical ancestor Daedalus was said to carve. What was special about those statues?
answer: They came alive and ran off
choices: They came alive and ran off
They wept real tears
They could foretell the future
They turned onlookers to stone
context: Euthyphro complains that 'our arguments... seem to turn round and walk away from us.' Socrates teases that the runaway definitions are like the moving statues of Daedalus — adding, 'he only made his own inventions move; I move those of other people as well.' The image is a definition that refuses to sit still. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Jowett trans.), standardebooks.org/ebooks/plato/dialogues/benjamin-jowett/text/euthyphro.  (Legend.)

question: After a long back-and-forth hunting for what holiness IS, Socrates still has no answer and asks Euthyphro one last time to teach him. How does Euthyphro end the conversation?
answer: He suddenly remembers an appointment and hurries off
choices: He suddenly remembers an appointment and hurries off
He admits at last that he was wrong all along
He angrily storms out of the court shouting
He finally gives a clear definition of holiness
context: Cornered, Euthyphro says, 'Another time, Socrates; for I am in a hurry, and must go now,' and walks off. Socrates is left lamenting, 'will you leave me in despair? I was hoping that you would instruct me in the nature of piety.' The man prosecuting his own father over holiness cannot say what holiness is — and the dialogue ends with no answer. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Jowett trans.), standardebooks.org/ebooks/plato/dialogues/benjamin-jowett/text/euthyphro.

question: Leibniz attacked the idea that a thing is good ONLY because God wills it, with no standard of goodness lying behind the choice. He pressed a sharp question: why praise God for what he has done, if he would have been just as praiseworthy had he done the very opposite? What did Leibniz conclude this shows?
answer: The word 'good' would tell us nothing, since it would fit whatever God willed
choices: The word 'good' would tell us nothing, since it would fit whatever God willed
We could never be sure which acts God has actually commanded
God could never reverse one of his own commands once issued
Each person must settle good and evil privately for himself
context: This is Leibniz's shot at the 'good because commanded' branch (Discourse on Metaphysics, section 2): if things are good only by God's bare will and not by any standard of goodness, then 'why praise him for what he has done, if he would be equally praiseworthy in doing the contrary?' On that view, calling God good says nothing — and justice collapses into mere 'tyrants' justice': whatever pleases the most powerful. Source: Leibniz, Discourse on Metaphysics, section 2; afterall.net/quotes/leibniz-on-the-divine-command-theory/.

question: Take the first branch: a thing is good ONLY because God commands it, with no deeper reason behind the command. A philosopher presses the believer on this branch — what uncomfortable thing follows if goodness is purely whatever God happens to will?
answer: Cruelty could have been good, had God chosen to command it
choices: Cruelty could have been good, had God chosen to command it
Goodness would turn out to be something humans simply invented
Praise and blame would have to be decided by a vote of priests
Right and wrong would depend on the strongest human ruler
context: This is the arbitrariness horn — the one that makes the believer flinch. If a thing is good only because it was commanded, goodness becomes a coin-flip of divine will rather than anything real, and God could just as easily have made cruelty good. Source: Christian Miller (Wake Forest), 'The Euthyphro Dilemma', users.wfu.edu/millerc/Euthyphro.pdf; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Religion and Morality', plato.stanford.edu/entries/religion-morality/.

question: Now take the second branch: God commands a thing because it is ALREADY good. A philosopher warns the believer that this branch costs something too. What does it seem to do to God's standing?
answer: It puts goodness above God, as a standard he must consult
choices: It puts goodness above God, as a standard he must consult
It proves that God does not exist
It makes God the inventor of cruelty
It means God can never command anything new
context: This is the sovereignty horn — the one that makes the believer flinch the OTHER way. If God commands a thing because it is already good, then goodness is a standard standing ABOVE God, which he consults like a rule-book; he becomes morality's subject rather than its source. So one horn seems to make morality groundless, the other seems to dethrone God. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Religion and Morality', plato.stanford.edu/entries/religion-morality/; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Divine Command Theory', iep.utm.edu/divine-command-theory/.

question: Faced with the two horns, some philosophers refuse the fork entirely and say goodness is NEITHER an arbitrary command NOR a rule sitting above God. Robert Adams offered the best-known version of this third move. Where did he locate goodness so it could be neither?
answer: In God's own loving nature, so cruelty contradicts who God is
choices: In God's own loving nature, so cruelty contradicts who God is
In the rewards and punishments God attaches to our acts
In the private conscience each person is born already holding
In the balance of pleasure and pain that an act produces
context: This is the 'split the horns' move — deny the fork is real. Goodness just IS God's own character. On Adams' modified divine command theory, grounded in the commands of a LOVING God, cruelty being commanded is only a LOGICAL possibility, never a real one, because it would contradict who God is. So goodness comes out neither arbitrary nor external. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Divine Command Theory', iep.utm.edu/divine-command-theory/.

question: Most defenders of the first branch soften it, but William of Ockham bit down hard. He insisted the ONLY limit on God's will is that it cannot be self-contradictory. Which startling thing did Ockham say WOULD be good, even obligatory, if God commanded it?
answer: Hatred of God himself
choices: Hatred of God himself
Worship of two gods
Silence about God forever
Doubt that God exists
context: Ockham (d. 1347) held that theft, adultery, and even hatred of God would be meritorious and obligatory if God commanded them — since the only limit on God's will is the law of non-contradiction. For Ockham, saying God COULDN'T command such things was itself an insult to his omnipotence. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Divine Command Theory', iep.utm.edu/divine-command-theory/; philosophy.institute/ethics/ockhams-voluntarism-primacy-gods-will-ethics/.

question: The very same fork split Islamic thinkers long before Europe debated it. Two great schools, the Mu'tazila and the Ash'aris, fought over a single question: where do good and evil actually come from? The Ash'aris, whose answer eventually won out across much of Sunni theology, took one definite side. What did the Ash'aris hold makes an act good?
answer: That God commanded it, and nothing in the act counts as good before that
choices: That God commanded it, and nothing in the act counts as good before that
That its own nature is good, which human reason can grasp without revelation
That the community's most learned teachers have agreed it is good
That it brings people more benefit than harm in their life together
context: The Mu'tazila took the 'commanded because good' side — good and evil are real, knowable by reason. The Ash'aris (and al-Ghazali) took the 'good because commanded' side: nothing is good or bad in itself; an act is good ONLY because God's law says so. The Ash'ari command-side eventually won out in Sunni theology, the same horn Ockham would later bite in the West. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Religion and Morality', plato.stanford.edu/entries/religion-morality/; al-islam.org/history-muslim-philosophy-volume-1-book-3/chapter-11-asharism.

question: Socrates climbs the steps of the Athenian court, summoned to stand trial for impiety — failing to honor the gods. There he meets Euthyphro, who boasts that he is an expert on holiness and knows exactly what counts as pious. What does Socrates do with this self-styled expert?
answer: He asks the expert to define holiness
choices: He asks the expert to define holiness
He asks the expert to defend him at his trial
He charges the expert with impiety in return
He asks the expert to pray for him
context: The dramatic irony of the whole dialogue: a man accused of impiety meets a man who claims to be an expert in piety, and proceeds to prove the expert cannot even define the word. Socrates was executed for impiety in 399 BC. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates.

question: Euthyphro meets Socrates outside the Athenian court, proud and certain he is doing the holy thing. He has come to bring a charge of murder. Whom is Euthyphro prosecuting?
answer: His own father
choices: His own father
His own brother
His own uncle
His own cousin
context: Euthyphro is so sure that prosecuting a wrongdoer is pious that he will haul his own father before a judge — and that very certainty is what Socrates dismantles with a single question. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642); IEP: Socrates.

question: On the island of Naxos, a hired laborer killed a household servant in a drunken quarrel. The laborer's master bound him hand and foot, threw him in a ditch, and sent a messenger to Athens to ask a priest how to proceed. What became of the bound man before the messenger returned?
answer: He died of cold, hunger, and his chains
choices: He died of cold, hunger, and his chains
He broke free and fled the island
He was hanged on the master's order
He was set loose once he sobered up
context: The man who bound the killer was Euthyphro's own father — and this is the death Euthyphro has now come to prosecute him over, certain that doing so is holy. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642), opening narration.

question: After Socrates picks apart every answer Euthyphro gives about holiness and asks him to try once more, Euthyphro — cornered and out of replies — does what?
answer: He says he is in a hurry and leaves
choices: He says he is in a hurry and leaves
He admits that holiness cannot be defined
He offers yet another definition to try
He accuses Socrates of twisting his words
context: The dialogue's famous non-ending: Euthyphro blurts 'Another time, Socrates; for I am in a hurry, and must go now,' and bolts. Socrates: 'Alas! my companion, and will you leave me in despair?' Plato's early dialogues end this way on purpose — with no answer reached (aporia). Source: Plato, Euthyphro, closing lines (Project Gutenberg #1642); IEP: Socrates.

question: Pressed again and again, Euthyphro offers his last definition: holiness is knowing how to pray and sacrifice rightly — knowing how to please the gods. Socrates immediately recasts this as something that sounds far less holy. As what?
answer: A kind of trade or bargaining with the gods
choices: A kind of trade or bargaining with the gods
A kind of flattery aimed at the gods
A kind of fear dressed up as devotion
A kind of guesswork about the gods' wishes
context: Socrates exposes 'knowing how to please the gods in word and deed' as a kind of commerce: we hand over prayers and offerings expecting benefits back. It is the last of five definitions Euthyphro tries — and like the others, it falls apart. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642); IEP: Socrates.

question: Euthyphro defends dragging his own father to court by pointing to the gods: Zeus, he says, the best and most righteous of the gods, once bound his OWN father for a monstrous crime — so why may a mortal not punish his father too? What had Zeus's father done to deserve being bound?
answer: He had devoured his own children as they were born
choices: He had devoured his own children as they were born
He had stolen fire from the gods for mankind
He had tricked the gods with a false sacrifice
He had loosed a great flood to drown mankind
context: In the legend Euthyphro invokes, Zeus bound his father Cronos for swallowing his children — and Cronos had earlier castrated and overthrown his own father, Uranus. Euthyphro's logic: if the gods punish their fathers, so may I. Told here as the Greek myth it is. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642).

question: Euthyphro finally settles on a definition: holiness is simply 'what the gods love.' Socrates accepts the words, then asks the one question philosophers have argued over ever since. Which question does he ask?
answer: Do the gods love holy things because they are holy, or are things holy only because the gods love them?
choices: Do the gods love holy things because they are holy, or are things holy only because the gods love them?
Do all the gods love the very same things, or do different gods love different things?
Do the gods love a thing for being useful, or do they love it for being beautiful?
Do the gods love holy things truly, or do they only pretend to love them?
context: Plato, Euthyphro around 10a: 'Is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it pious because it is loved by the gods?' One question, two doors — and Western philosophy has been choosing between them for 2,400 years. Source: Plato, Euthyphro ~10a (Project Gutenberg #1642); IEP: Divine Command Theory.

question: Take the first answer to Socrates' question: a thing is holy only because the gods love it, with no reason lying behind their choice. Socrates asks what would follow if the gods had instead loved cruelty. On this view, what follows about cruelty?
answer: Cruelty would then be holy, and goodness merely a matter of divine whim
choices: Cruelty would then be holy, and goodness merely a matter of divine whim
The gods would become evil, and so no longer worthy of worship
Cruelty would be allowed but never holy, since the gods only permit it
Holiness would shift from god to god, since the gods rarely agree
context: This is the cost of the first horn: if goodness is whatever the gods happen to command, then had they commanded cruelty, cruelty would be holy — goodness becomes arbitrary, a coin-flip of divine will. A defender of divine command accepts this; a critic calls it the horn's fatal flaw. The bank takes no side. Source: IEP: Divine Command Theory.

question: Take the second answer to Socrates' question: the gods love a holy thing because it is already good, not the other way around. Socrates asks what that leaves for the gods to add. On this view, what do the gods do about goodness?
answer: They register a goodness already there, contributing nothing to its being good
choices: They register a goodness already there, contributing nothing to its being good
They enforce a goodness they did not create, and punish those who defy it
They guarantee that goodness and reward line up in the end
They reveal goodness to mortals who could not find it on their own
context: This is the cost of the second horn: if the gods love things because those things are already good, then goodness stands on its own and divine approval adds nothing to what makes it good — the gods are like inspectors passing what was already sound. So neither horn lets the gods' love be the SOURCE of goodness. Source: IEP: Divine Command Theory; Plato, Euthyphro ~10a.

question: Socrates offers a proof that 'holy' and 'loved by the gods' cannot mean the same thing. Take a plainer pair, he says: a thing gets carried because someone carries it, and gets seen because someone looks at it. Now apply the same test to holiness and being loved by the gods — which way does the explanation run?
answer: A thing is loved by the gods because it is holy; being loved follows from holiness
choices: A thing is loved by the gods because it is holy; being loved follows from holiness
A thing is holy because the gods love it; their love is what makes it holy
Holiness and being loved arise together, and neither one explains the other
A thing is holy and loved for one shared reason too deep for us to name
context: Socrates' point (Euthyphro 10a-11b): a thing is carried because someone carries it, seen because someone sees it — the state follows the act, never the reverse. So the holy is loved BECAUSE it is holy; being god-loved is a consequence of holiness, not its essence. A divine-command theorist genuinely disputes this, holding the gods' love is what makes a thing holy — which is why the direction, not the wording, is the whole fight. Source: Plato, Euthyphro 10a-11b; Yale Historical Review, 'The Socratic Elenchus on Piety in the Euthyphro.'

question: Centuries after Socrates, the Franciscan friar William of Ockham embraced the dilemma's first horn — that an act is good because God commands it. He pressed it harder than anyone, asking what would hold if God commanded theft, adultery, even hatred of God himself. How far did Ockham go?
answer: He said that on God's command, even those acts could be done meritoriously
choices: He said that on God's command, even those acts could be done meritoriously
He said God would never command such acts, so the question is idle
He said such acts stay evil, marking the one limit on God's commands
He said the faithful must refuse them, even if God himself commands
context: William of Ockham (c.1287-1347) held that if God commanded theft, adultery, even hatred of God, those acts 'can even be performed meritoriously' — they would become good simply because God commanded them. The purest form of 'the good is whatever is commanded.' Source: IEP: William of Ockham, quoting Opera Theologica V, p. 352.

question: Gottfried Leibniz attacked the view that calls a thing good simply because the strongest being wills it. If that were so, he argued, then praising God for his goodness would be empty — he 'would be equally praiseworthy in doing the contrary.' On such a view, Leibniz asked, what does justice come down to?
answer: A tyrant's whim — justice as whatever the ruler pleases to call just
choices: A tyrant's whim — justice as whatever the ruler pleases to call just
A standing decree — justice as whatever has been laid down, obeyed unquestioned
A perfect measure — justice as whatever the wisest will is sure to choose
A hollow name — justice as a word with no fixed meaning behind it
context: Leibniz, Discourse on Metaphysics §2: if good is only what the most powerful wills, you are left with 'a certain despotic power' where, 'according to the definition of tyrants, justice consists in whatever pleases the most powerful.' His objection to making the command itself the source of goodness. Source: Leibniz, Discourse on Metaphysics §2; afterall.net/quotes/leibniz-on-the-divine-command-theory.

question: Socrates told the jury that Athens was like a great and noble horse that had grown fat and slow, and that the god had set HIM upon the city to keep stirring it all day long, never letting it settle into its complacency. Kill him, he warned, and the city would simply doze off again. What creature did Socrates say he was?
answer: A gadfly that keeps stinging the horse
choices: A gadfly that keeps stinging the horse
A bridle that holds the horse in check
A hound that runs beside the horse
A sparrow that nests above the horse
context: Socrates calls himself a 'gadfly' the god has fastened onto Athens: the city is 'a great and noble steed who is tardy in his motions... and requires to be stirred into life,' and he is the biting fly that all day long keeps 'arousing and persuading and reproaching' the citizens out of their complacency. The image explains WHY he questioned everyone — and why he warned that killing him would just leave the horse asleep. Source: Plato, Apology 30e-31a, trans. Benjamin Jowett (MIT Internet Classics Archive, classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Socrates traced his lifelong habit of questioning everyone to a riddle from the oracle at Delphi: asked whether any man was wiser than Socrates, the priestess answered that no one was. Socrates, who was sure he possessed no special wisdom, puzzled over it for years and finally decided the god meant he was wisest in one strange respect. What was it?
answer: He alone did not imagine he knew what he did not
choices: He alone did not imagine he knew what he did not
He alone had been picked to lead the city
He alone had studied under the finest teachers
He alone could defeat any man in argument
context: Socrates' friend Chaerephon asked the Delphic oracle if anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the priestess said no one was. Baffled — since he felt he knew nothing — Socrates cross-examined Athens' reputed wise men and concluded the oracle meant only this: he was wisest because, unlike them, 'I neither know nor think that I know.' The questioning was his way of testing the god's word. Source: Plato, Apology 21a-23b, trans. Jowett (MIT Internet Classics Archive); iep.utm.edu/socrates.

question: On trial for his life, Socrates was invited to name a punishment mild enough to spare him. Instead he told the court what he believed the single best thing a human being can do — the activity he prized above staying alive, and the very thing they wanted him to stop. What did he say that best thing was?
answer: To talk through what makes a person good, every day
choices: To talk through what makes a person good, every day
To win honor and high office in the city
To grow wealthy enough to never work again
To obey the laws of Athens without question
context: Socrates names the thing he values above his own life in plain words: 'the greatest good of man is daily to converse about virtue, and all that concerning which you hear me examining myself and others.' This is the positive heart of the maxim — not just that the unexamined life is empty, but that talking through what makes a person good, every single day, is the best thing a human being can do. Source: Plato, Apology 38a, trans. Jowett (MIT Internet Classics Archive, classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Athenian law let a condemned man propose his own punishment as an alternative to death — the expected move was to suggest exile or a fine and hope the jury chose mercy. Socrates, claiming a poor man who spent his days trying to make the city good had earned an honor, not a penalty, proposed something outrageous instead. What did he demand for himself?
answer: To be fed free meals for life in the city dining hall
choices: To be fed free meals for life in the city dining hall
To have a bronze statue raised in the marketplace
To be given supreme command of the Athenian army
To be granted a lifelong seat on the ruling council
context: Required to propose his own punishment, Socrates instead proposed a REWARD: free meals for life in the Prytaneum, the public dining hall — an honor Athens reserved for Olympic victors and war heroes. He argued that a poor man who spends his days trying to make the city good deserves to be fed like a champion, not punished. One historian writes that he 'acts more like a picador trying to enrage a bull than a defendant trying to mollify a jury.' Source: Plato, Apology 36d-37a (MIT Internet Classics Archive); Douglas Linder, 'The Trial of Socrates' (famous-trials.com/socrates/833-home).

question: Condemned to death, Socrates could have proposed prison or exile instead and very likely lived. He refused even to ask. Other men in his place might have reasoned in any number of ways. Which reasoning is the one Socrates actually gave for refusing to bargain his sentence down?
answer: I will not take a sure evil on to dodge one no one can prove
choices: I will not take a sure evil on to dodge one no one can prove
I will not defy a sentence the city has lawfully imposed
I will not give my friends cause to call me a coward
I will not die crawling when I could die on my feet
context: Socrates refused to propose any punishment, because that would mean admitting he had done wrong: 'I will not say of myself that I deserve any evil, or propose any penalty.' His reasoning: he does not know whether death is good or bad — so why trade his life for exile or prison, which he KNOWS to be evils, to flee a death that might not be one? Choosing a known evil to dodge an unknown is, to him, the unexamined move. Source: Plato, Apology 37b-38b, trans. Jowett (MIT Internet Classics Archive, classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Socrates told the court he did not actually fear death. He said the common attitude toward death is really a false confidence dressed up as wisdom — a claim to know something no living person can know, the very pretence he had spent his life puncturing in others. Below are four confident beliefs people hold about death. Which one is the false confidence Socrates singled out?
answer: Being certain that death is an evil to be escaped
choices: Being certain that death is an evil to be escaped
Being certain that the gods fix each person's hour of death
Being certain that the soul lives on once the body dies
Being certain that a good life earns a man a gentle death
context: In Socrates' words: 'this fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being the appearance of knowing the unknown; since no one knows whether death... may not be the greatest good.' To dread death as a thing to be escaped is to treat it as a KNOWN evil — to claim a knowledge you do not have, the same false confidence he spent his life puncturing in others. The rival claims here (that the gods set each man's hour, that the soul outlives the body, that a good life earns a gentle death) are confident beliefs about death too — things a careful person might wonder about — but the precise pretence Socrates singled out at his trial was being sure death itself is an evil, when no one can know that. Source: Plato, Apology 29a, trans. Jowett (MIT Internet Classics Archive, classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Alex argues: all foxes have tails; this animal has a tail; so it must be a fox. That reasoning is broken — having a tail proves nothing, since dogs and cats have tails too. Bob pounces: 'Your logic is garbage, so this animal is definitely NOT a fox.' Why is Bob now the one reasoning badly?
answer: Alex only failed to prove it is a fox; the animal could still perfectly well be one
choices: Alex only failed to prove it is a fox; the animal could still perfectly well be one
A flawed argument always reverses, so the true conclusion is the exact opposite
Bob cannot judge the logic until he has personally examined the animal himself
Two broken arguments cancel out, leaving the original question fully undecided
context: Alex's argument commits 'affirming the consequent' — a real flaw. But Bob's leap from 'bad argument' to 'opposite conclusion' is the fallacy fallacy itself: a failed proof that something is a fox does not show it isn't one. Source: Effectiviology, 'The Fallacy Fallacy'; Wikipedia, 'Argument from fallacy'.

question: A knight defends a verdict with a sloppy reason that falls apart the moment his rival pokes at it. The rival grins: 'Your reason is rubbish — therefore the verdict you defended is WRONG.' A wise onlooker says the rival has overreached. What did knocking down the knight's reason actually prove?
answer: Only that this one argument failed; the verdict itself might still be right on other grounds
choices: Only that this one argument failed; the verdict itself might still be right on other grounds
That the verdict is false, since a defense that collapses takes its conclusion down with it
That the knight lied, because no honest person offers an argument that falls apart so fast
That the matter is settled for the rival, who needs no argument of his own to win the point
context: This is the core of the fallacy fallacy: refuting an argument is not the same as refuting its conclusion. A bad reason FOR a claim leaves the claim's truth wide open — it may be true for some other reason no one has yet given. Source: Effectiviology, 'The Fallacy Fallacy'; The Fallacy Files, 'Fallacy Fallacy'.

question: A clock stopped dead at 3:48 is a hopeless way to tell time — its hands never move and its 'reasoning' comes from nothing. Yet twice a day it displays the exact correct time. A thinker offers this stopped clock as a picture of one tempting mistake. Which mistake does the dead-but-occasionally-right clock warn against?
answer: Assuming a true result must mean the method was good — a broken process can still land on the truth
choices: Assuming a true result must mean the method was good — a broken process can still land on the truth
Assuming a stopped clock is useless — in fact it beats a clock that runs a few minutes slow
Assuming time can be known at all, when every measuring device fails in some way or another
Assuming that being right twice is enough, when a good method must be right far more often
context: 'Even a stopped clock is right twice a day' is the folk version of the fallacy fallacy: a hopeless process (right about 1/720 of the time, ~0.14%) can still produce a true output by accident. So a true answer never proves the reasoning behind it was sound. Source: RationalWiki, 'Stopped clock' / 'Fallacy fallacy'.

question: Two friends mix up two different things. One insists 'her argument commits a fallacy, so her claim must be false.' A logic teacher stops them: a fallacy and a falsehood are not the same kind of failure at all. Where does each of those two failures actually live?
answer: A fallacy is a defect in the reasoning linking premises to a claim; truth or falsity belongs to the claim
choices: A fallacy is a defect in the reasoning linking premises to a claim; truth or falsity belongs to the claim
A fallacy and a falsehood both live in the claim, so spotting either one is enough to reject what was said
A fallacy lives in the speaker's honesty while falsity lives in the claim; the two must be checked separately
A fallacy is simply a falsehood dressed up in formal language to make it that much harder to detect
context: The line that names the whole confusion: 'Fallacies are errors in reasoning, not errors about truth or falsity.' Truth belongs to claims; fallacies are defects in the reasoning that links premises to a claim. Mixing 'this argument fails' with 'this claim is false' is the entire mistake. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Fallacies'; Effectiviology, 'The Fallacy Fallacy'.

question: You catch a real flaw in someone's argument for a claim, and you are tempted to announce that you have therefore disproved the claim. A careful reasoner tells you to be precise about what that flaw actually buys you. What have you actually won by exposing the flaw?
answer: The right to throw out that argument and demand a better one — not a proof that the claim is false
choices: The right to throw out that argument and demand a better one — not a proof that the claim is false
A proof that the claim is false, since an argument and the claim it defends stand or fall together
Nothing at all, because pointing out flaws is merely negative and never advances a discussion
The right to assume the claim is true, since a defender who argues badly clearly has weak opponents
context: The corrective slogan: 'reject the argument, not the conclusion.' Catching a fallacy earns you the right to discard that argument and ask for a better one — not to declare the opposite proven. To actually refute the claim you must bring separate evidence that it is false. Source: The Logic of Science, 'The fallacy fallacy: Reject the argument not the conclusion' (2017).

question: A debater spots a weak, fallacious argument that someone gave for a position, and treats catching it as a serious blow against the position itself. A logician shrugs and says the catch barely counts against the position at all. Why is one bad defense such weak evidence against a position?
answer: Fallacious arguments are easy to make for almost any position, true or false, so finding one tells you only that this defender argued poorly
choices: Fallacious arguments are easy to make for almost any position, true or false, so finding one tells you only that this defender argued poorly
Fallacious arguments are extremely rare, so the presence of even one is a strong sign the whole position was built on confusion
Fallacious arguments can only be made for false positions, which is exactly why catching one settles the matter against it
Fallacious arguments are impossible to make for true positions, so a flawed defense reveals the position must be false underneath
context: Why the move is so tempting and so worth guarding against: it is easy to cook up a fallacious argument for any proposition, true or false, while a genuinely sound argument can be hard to find even for true claims. So one weak defense of a position is completely ordinary and tells you nothing about whether the position is right. Source: The Fallacy Files, 'Fallacy Fallacy'.

question: For over 350 years, the greatest mathematicians tried to prove Fermat's Last Theorem and kept failing. Gabriel Lame announced a triumphant proof; Joseph Liouville quietly wrecked it by showing Lame had assumed a property of numbers that fails in some systems. Wreck after wreck piled up. A bystander watching the centuries of collapsing proofs concluded 'so the theorem must be FALSE.' What was wrong with that conclusion?
answer: Each broken proof showed only that one argument failed; the theorem could still be true and simply await a sound proof
choices: Each broken proof showed only that one argument failed; the theorem could still be true and simply await a sound proof
Each broken proof was fresh evidence the theorem is false, since a true theorem would have yielded to proof long ago
The bystander should have deferred to a vote among mathematicians rather than judging any of the proofs himself
The bystander mixed up Lame with Liouville, when it was really Liouville whose own flawed proof first raised the doubt
context: The capstone gem: Fermat's Last Theorem was true the whole time. Lame had assumed unique prime factorization holds in number systems where it fails; others published invalid proof after invalid proof. Anyone who concluded 'therefore false' from the wreckage committed the fallacy fallacy — Andrew Wiles proved it true in 1994. Source: The Fallacy Files (Fermat case); Wikipedia, 'Fermat's Last Theorem' and 'Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem'.

question: In a heated debate, one side stops engaging with the other's points and instead just shouts the names of fallacies — 'Strawman!' 'Ad hominem!' — as if naming a move automatically wins the exchange and proves their own side. A philosopher warns that this trick is itself a dodge. Why does merely shouting a fallacy's name fail to settle anything?
answer: Imputing a fallacy without showing the actual reasoning error proves nothing, and a pile of labels can derail thinking instead of doing it
choices: Imputing a fallacy without showing the actual reasoning error proves nothing, and a pile of labels can derail thinking instead of doing it
Imputing a fallacy is always false, because trained debaters are careful never to commit any of the recognized fallacies in public
Imputing a fallacy automatically proves the opposite claim, so the label-shouter has in fact already won the argument outright
Imputing a fallacy only works if the name is the correct Latin term, so an English label leaves the original point standing
context: This is why the fallacy fallacy guards the whole fallacy ladder: learning a list of fallacy NAMES tempts people to shout 'strawman!' or 'ad hominem!' as if the label ends the matter. Simply imputing a fallacy — without demonstrating the real error — is itself a dodge, and a stack of labels can be used to derail rather than to think. Source: Wikipedia, 'Argument from fallacy' (citing philosopher William Lycan); The Logic of Science (2017).

question: A dad tells his son, 'You either love me or you hate me — and if you loved me, you would eat your broccoli.' Where does the dad's reasoning go wrong?
answer: He pretends love and hate are the only two feelings, ignoring annoyed or just-not-hungry.
choices: He pretends love and hate are the only two feelings, ignoring annoyed or just-not-hungry.
He claims the broccoli is good for the boy but never offers him any real proof of it.
He goes after his son's character instead of making any case for the broccoli at all.
He insists that every other kid the boy's age already happily eats their vegetables.
context: This is the classic dinner-table form of the false dilemma: forcing a pick between two feelings when a third was quietly left off — you can be neutral, annoyed, or just not in the mood for broccoli. The name 'false dilemma' goes here, not in the answer; what matters is spotting the missing middle. Source: IEP, Fallacies (False Dilemma entry), iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: At a cookout, your uncle holds up two bottles and asks, 'Do you want ketchup or mustard on your hot dog?' Picking from just those two feels forced. What did the question quietly leave out?
answer: That 'or' need not mean only those two — both, neither, or something else all count.
choices: That 'or' need not mean only those two — both, neither, or something else all count.
That a real choice always needs at least three options on offer, and never just two.
That ketchup and mustard actually taste completely different from one another anyway.
That his uncle never once said the hot dog on the grill was even meant for him.
context: Why not both? Or neither? Or a salad instead? The question pretends its two named options are the only possibilities. The tell to teach a kid: whenever you hear 'either/or' language, put your guard up and ask 'are there other choices?' Note the trap is NOT that two is too few — a two-option question can be perfectly fair; the error is falsely closing off the others. Source: logicallyfallacious.com (False Dilemma) + scribbr.com/fallacies/false-dilemma-fallacy + critikid.com/false-dilemma.

question: A coach tells a teenager, 'You can either go to college, or be a failure in life.' What is the flaw buried in that warning?
answer: It crushes a wide range of real paths — a trade, the army, a business — into two extremes.
choices: It crushes a wide range of real paths — a trade, the army, a business — into two extremes.
It quietly assumes that college costs the very same amount for every family out there.
It promises sure success at college while never admitting that plenty of students drop out.
It treats the teenager as far too young and foolish to make any real choice at all.
context: The fallacy works by collapsing a whole spectrum of good roads — a trade, an apprenticeship, starting a business, the military — down to exactly two extremes. Once you name even one hidden road, the trap springs open. Source: owl.excelsior.edu (False Dilemma Fallacy) + scribbr.com/fallacies/false-dilemma-fallacy.

question: 'You're either with us, or against us' is the most famous form of the false either/or. A friend who refuses to pick a side hears it as a threat. What real option does the slogan erase?
answer: That you might stay neutral, back the goal but not the method, or just not have picked yet.
choices: That you might stay neutral, back the goal but not the method, or just not have picked yet.
That you might in fact already secretly belong to the other side this whole entire time.
That you might honestly be far too uninformed to follow the heart of the argument at all.
