True, justified, validly reasoned — still not knowledge. Source: Gettier (1963), Case II, fitelson.org/proseminar/gettier.pdf.

question: Henry is driving through the countryside, points at a building by the road, and thinks 'that's a barn.' And it genuinely is a barn — a real one. What Henry has no idea about is that this county is packed with fake barns: flat wooden FRONTS propped up to look exactly like barns from the road. He just happened to point at one of the few real ones. Henry believes nothing false at any step. So why does he still not KNOW it's a barn?
answer: He could so easily have pointed at a fake and thought the very same thing — being right was luck.
choices: He could so easily have pointed at a fake and thought the very same thing — being right was luck.
He never once confirmed the building was a barn by walking up to inspect the back of it.
A structure seen so briefly from a fast-moving car can't support any belief about it at all.
The whole county set out to deceive its drivers, and that deceit poisons every belief formed there.
context: Alvin Goldman made this fake-barn case famous in 1976, crediting Carl Ginet. It's the hardest test for any repair to the knowledge puzzle: Henry's reasoning has no false step in it, yet he still doesn't know — because in this county he could so easily have been fooled by a fake. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/knowledge-analysis; philarchive.org/archive/TURKAI.

question: After Gettier, philosophers tried an obvious fix: a belief counts as knowledge only if you didn't pass through any FALSE step to reach it. It works on the ten-coins case, whose reasoning ran straight through a falsehood. But Henry — who looks at a real barn while unknowingly surrounded by fake barn fronts — reasons through NOTHING false, and still doesn't know. What does Henry's barn fail to drive out of this 'no false steps' fix?
answer: It fails to remove the luck that made Henry right in the first place.
choices: It fails to remove the luck that made Henry right in the first place.
It fails to make Henry feel certain, leaving real doubt in his mind.
It fails to handle any case beyond the very one it was built for.
It fails to stop people from trusting too readily in what they see.
context: The 'no false lemmas' patch says a belief is knowledge only if it wasn't inferred from a falsehood. It handles the ten-coins case (Smith reasoned through the false 'Jones will get the job'), but the fake-barn case defeats it: Henry infers nothing false, yet luck still makes him right. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/knowledge-analysis.

question: One modern repair to the knowledge puzzle is called the SAFETY rule: you only KNOW something if you couldn't EASILY have ended up believing it while being wrong. Test it on the stopped clock — the man who glanced at a dead clock that happened to read the right time. By the safety rule, why does his belief fall short?
answer: Glancing a minute earlier or later, he'd have read a wrong time and believed it just as readily.
choices: Glancing a minute earlier or later, he'd have read a wrong time and believed it just as readily.
He believed the time without ever feeling the full certainty that real knowledge requires of us.
He leaned on one single clock, when knowledge plainly demands at least two independent sources.
He could not prove the clock had stopped at all, so his belief secretly rested on an unknown.
context: This is the SAFETY condition, associated with Ernest Sosa, Timothy Williamson, and Duncan Pritchard. A true belief is 'safe' only if, in nearby situations where you'd believe the same way, you'd still be right. The stopped clock fails badly — the tiniest change in when you looked flips you to a falsehood. Source: iep.utm.edu/safety-c.

question: A rival repair, from Robert Nozick, says real knowledge must TRACK the truth: if the thing you believe were FALSE, you would stop believing it — your belief flips off the moment the fact flips off. Hold the stopped clock up to this rule. How does the man's belief fail the tracking test?
answer: Even if it weren't two o'clock, the dead clock would still read two — so his belief wouldn't budge.
choices: Even if it weren't two o'clock, the dead clock would still read two — so his belief wouldn't budge.
He keeps right on believing it's two even after a passerby warns him the clock has stopped.
His belief shifts around so constantly that it never settles long enough to track anything real.
He follows the clock's hands closely but ignores the position of the sun outside his window.
context: This is Nozick's SENSITIVITY or 'truth-tracking' condition, a rival to the safety rule; the two come apart in tricky cases, which is why epistemologists still argue over them. The stopped clock fails tracking because a dead clock's reading is frozen: it would say 'two o'clock' whether or not it actually is. Source: iep.utm.edu/safety-c.

question: Some twelve hundred years before Edmund Gettier, an 8th-century Buddhist philosopher in Kashmir named Dharmottara dreamed up the very same trap. In his scene a cook has just lit a fire to roast meat, but it hasn't sent up any smoke yet. Far off, a traveler sees a dark shape hanging in the air just above the spot and concludes 'there's a fire over there.' He's right — there IS a fire. But the dark shape he saw wasn't smoke at all. What was it?
answer: A swarm of dark insects, drawn by the smell of the roasting meat and mistaken for smoke.
choices: A swarm of dark insects, drawn by the smell of the roasting meat and mistaken for smoke.
A storm cloud gathering over the hills, with no real connection to the fire down below.
Smoke drifting over from a different, older fire smouldering somewhere else nearby.
A flock of birds circling above the meat, too far off for the traveler to make out.
context: Dharmottara (c. 740-800 AD), commenting on Dharmakirti's work, built this fire-and-insects case roughly twelve centuries before Gettier's 1963 paper. The traveler reaches a TRUE belief through the wrong cause: a swarm of bugs he mistook for smoke. Scholars like Jonathan Stoltz note Dharmottara held that justification must be foolproof, so it's a striking anticipation rather than an identical problem. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettier_problem; Stoltz on Indo-Tibetan epistemology.

question: In a timed debate, one side fires off twenty shaky claims in a single breath -- far more than the other side can check before time runs out. Most go unanswered. The crowd, counting the claims left standing, decides the fast-talking side won. What does that pile of unanswered claims actually prove?
answer: That a claim left unanswered merely for lack of time was never thereby shown to be true
choices: That a claim left unanswered merely for lack of time was never thereby shown to be true
That the faster side argued the better case, since a strong case throws off more points
That the slower side has silently conceded each claim it could not find the time to address
That the claims must be sound, or surely the other side would have found time to rebut them
context: This firehose tactic is called the 'Gish Gallop.' The recognition skill is seeing that the SHEER NUMBER of claims is not evidence for any of them -- quantity is being smuggled in as if it were quality, and a claim left unanswered for lack of time has not been shown true. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gish gallop'; Bo Bennett, Logically Fallacious.

question: Duane Gish held a real Ph.D. in biochemistry from UC Berkeley and boasted of more than 300 public debates against biologists, talking fast and with total confidence as he buried each opponent under more claims than anyone could answer. Even his critics granted the degree was genuine. So what did his credential and his confidence actually establish about the flood of claims he fired?
answer: That a real degree and a confident delivery never make a flood of claims correct
choices: That a real degree and a confident delivery never make a flood of claims correct
That his claims deserved the benefit of the doubt, given his training in the field
That his confidence was earned, since no amateur could out-debate biologists so often
That his expertise made his rapid claims more reliable than a nervous rival's
context: The Gish Gallop is named for Duane Gish (1921-2013), whom Eugenie Scott called the technique's 'most avid practitioner.' His real biochemistry Ph.D. and confident delivery were part of the staging; they did nothing to make the cherry-picked factoids and non-sequiturs correct. Source: NCSE obituary, 'Duane T. Gish dies'; Scientific American, 'Trump's Gish Gallop Debate Tactic Comes from Creationists.'

question: A debater's flood of claims is built from individually weak pieces -- vague assertions, anecdotes passed off as data, real facts twisted out of context, flat falsehoods, points beside the question, and jargon thrown in for show. The flood arrives too fast for the other side to chase every item. Why does picking just ONE claim and examining it slowly tend to break the whole tactic?
answer: Each piece is a bluff that collapses the moment someone actually stops to test it
choices: Each piece is a bluff that collapses the moment someone actually stops to test it
Debaters always lead with their strongest claim, so the very first one topples easiest
Disproving one claim forces the speaker to formally withdraw every one of the others
One claim is all any audience remembers, so the rest of the flood never mattered anyway
context: The ingredients of a Gish Gallop -- unsubstantiated claims, anecdotes as data, facts twisted out of context, lies, irrelevancies, and dense jargon -- are each individually weak and were never meant to be examined one at a time. Slowing down to pick one up and look at it is exactly what defeats the pile. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gish gallop'; Effectiviology, 'Gish Gallop.'

question: In a live debate one speaker rattles off false claim after false claim. The opponent knows each is false, but properly dismantling even one would take a patient, detailed explanation -- and while she gives it, the speaker has already moved on to five more. The longer she stops to set the record straight, the fewer of his points she covers. Why does she, the honest one, end up looking slow or evasive?
answer: A lie is cheap to throw out but costly to clean up, so the clock punishes the honest side
choices: A lie is cheap to throw out but costly to clean up, so the clock punishes the honest side
The crowd assumes anyone who slows down has just been caught lying and is now stalling
Pausing to correct a claim concedes that it was worth answering, handing over the point
Judges always penalize whichever speaker ends up using the smallest share of the time
context: It is far easier to ASSERT a false thing than to REFUTE it: a one-sentence falsehood costs three seconds, while dismantling it can take minutes the format won't allow. The asymmetry of effort -- not the strength of the claims -- is doing the work; the side that 'said more' is exploiting the clock, not winning the argument. Source: Effectiviology, 'Gish Gallop'; Wikipedia, 'Gish gallop.'

question: In 1994 Eugenie Scott, who led the National Center for Science Education, kept watching a creationist win over live crowds against trained biologists -- not because his claims were true, but because he fired so many of them, so fast and so confidently, that the crowd came away impressed. She coined a name for the trap. When Scott asked WHY he kept looking persuasive, what did she point to?
answer: The debate format itself, whose lopsided airtime let error outrun any possible reply
choices: The debate format itself, whose lopsided airtime let error outrun any possible reply
The audience, who came in already convinced and simply cheered the side they favored
The two debaters' charisma, since a crowd always rewards whichever speaker is likable
The creationist's calm, forceful delivery, which read to viewers as quiet authority
context: Anthropologist Eugenie Scott, founding director of the NCSE, coined the phrase 'Gish Gallop' in a July 1994 post to the TalkOrigins Archive, objecting to a format where the creationist could 'spew forth torrents of error that the evolutionist hasn't a prayer of refuting' in the time given. The structural insight: the FORMAT, not the truth of the claims, decided who looked persuasive. Source: Wordorigins.org, 'Gish gallop' (original 1994 Scott quote); Wikipedia, 'Gish gallop.'

question: Steven Novella describes a mirror-image trick: instead of flooding you, your opponent waits for your careful answer and pounces on one tiny slip -- you said 'clip' when you meant 'magazine' -- then treats that single word as proof your whole gun-safety argument collapses. What is wrong with declaring the entire argument dead over that one slip?
answer: A true conclusion can outlast a small slip in a detail, so one stray error never sinks it
choices: A true conclusion can outlast a small slip in a detail, so one stray error never sinks it
A careful speaker should never misspeak, so any slip proves the rest was just as careless
Word choice is the foundation of an argument, so the wrong term voids everything built on it
The slip shifts the burden of proof, so the speaker must now re-prove every earlier claim
context: Neuroscientist Steven Novella calls this the 'reverse Gish gallop' or 'weaponized pedantry' -- and treating one irrelevant flaw as if it sinks an entire argument is itself a fallacy (the 'fallacy fallacy'). His stock example is dismissing a gun-safety point because the speaker said 'clip' instead of 'magazine.' Source: Steven Novella, NeuroLogica Blog, 'Weaponized Pedantry and Reverse Gish Gallop'; Wikipedia, 'Gish gallop.'

question: A 'squid ink' barrage is the Gish gallop's strange cousin: where a Gish flood is stitched from falsehoods, every point in a squid-ink dump is rock-solid TRUE -- yet the opponent still drowns. If each fact really is true, what makes the dump dishonest all the same?
answer: Not one of the true facts actually bears on the question at issue, so they bury it unanswered
choices: Not one of the true facts actually bears on the question at issue, so they bury it unanswered
Each true fact, fired off so fast, gives the listener no time to weigh how much it matters
The speaker keeps the strongest true fact hidden, padding the dump out with weaker ones
The true facts are common knowledge, so reciting them adds nothing the audience lacked
context: 'Squid ink' is a close cousin of the Gish Gallop: both overwhelm rather than illuminate, but squid ink piles up accurate, true-but-IRRELEVANT information while the Gish Gallop is built from lies and half-truths. That is the trap to recognize -- every statement can check out as true and the dump can still be dishonest, because none of it touches the actual question; truth is not the same as relevance. Source: Wordorigins.org, 'Gish gallop' (distinction from 'squid ink'); Political Dictionary, 'Gish Gallop.'

question: A village is terrorized by a dragon. One knight, shaking with fear, gallops away and abandons the people. Another knight, drunk on his own daring, charges the beast alone and is burned to ash. Aristotle would praise neither. What does the truly brave knight do instead?
answer: Stands his ground and fights only when he has a real chance to win
choices: Stands his ground and fights only when he has a real chance to win
Runs from the dragon, since survival matters more than the village
Charges the dragon at once to prove that he is not afraid
Refuses to feel any fear at all before facing the dragon
context: This is Aristotle's marquee example of the mean. Courage sits between the coward, who feels too much fear and flees, and the rash man, who feels too little and charges into danger he cannot handle. Bravery is not the absence of fear but feeling the right amount and acting well. Aristotle even notes that a man who fears literally nothing has no name in common speech, and is almost a madman. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II and Bk III ch.7 (F.H. Peters trans.).

question: Aristotle says giving money away can go wrong in two opposite directions. A miser hoards every coin and never helps anyone. A spendthrift hurls his whole purse at flatterers and strangers and is soon broke. Between these two, what does the genuinely generous person do?
answer: Gives a sensible amount to those who genuinely need his help
choices: Gives a sensible amount to those who genuinely need his help
Keeps almost all of his money so he is never left with nothing
Gives away everything that he has as fast as he possibly can
Refuses to think about money at all so it never troubles his mind
context: Generosity (liberality) is the mean between stinginess, which clutches money and gives too little, and wastefulness (prodigality), which throws money at the wrong people. The generous person gives the right amount, to the right people, at the right time. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II and Bk IV ch.1 (F.H. Peters trans.).

question: Aristotle admits anyone can get angry, and that part is easy. The hard part, he says, is getting angry well, which means doing it under several conditions at once. Which set of conditions does Aristotle name?
answer: The right person, the right amount, the right time, the right aim, and the right way
choices: The right person, the right amount, the right time, the right aim, and the right way
The right words, the right reason, the right place, the right cost, and the right goal
The right person, the right feeling, the right cause, the right limit, and the right outcome
The right time, the right intention, the right witness, the right degree, and the right excuse
context: Aristotle's famous line: 'Anyone can be angry, that is easy; anyone can give money away. But to do these things to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right object, and in the right manner, that is not what everybody can do, and is by no means easy.' The mean is not just feeling less; it is hitting all the targets at once: person, extent, time, object, manner. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II ch.9 (F.H. Peters trans.).

question: A boy watches a bully shove and rob a smaller child right in front of him. The boy feels nothing, no flash of anger and no urge to step in, and just walks on. Some might call him calm and unbothered. What would Aristotle say about a person who never gets angry even at a real wrong?
answer: His failure to feel anger is itself a flaw, not a virtue
choices: His failure to feel anger is itself a flaw, not a virtue
His calm under provocation is the highest form of virtue
He has perfectly mastered his temper and should be admired
He proves that anger is always a weakness to be avoided
context: Good temper (gentleness) is the mean about anger, between the hot-tempered man who flares too easily and the 'wrathless' man who will not get angry even when he should. Aristotle says the man who is not angry at the right things is thought a fool: failing to feel anger can itself be a vice. The deficiency, not only the excess, misses the mean. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II and Bk IV ch.5 (F.H. Peters trans.).

question: Aristotle insists that being bad is easy while being good is hard. He compares it to shooting at a target. Why, on his view, is missing so much easier than hitting the mark?
answer: There are countless ways to overshoot or fall short, but only one mark hits home
choices: There are countless ways to overshoot or fall short, but only one mark hits home
A skilled archer can always hit the center, so virtue takes only steady practice
The target keeps moving about, so no one can ever truly know where it is
Hitting the outer edge counts as much as the center, so near enough is fine
context: Aristotle: 'It is possible to fail in many ways, but to succeed in only one, which is why one is easy and the other hard, easy to miss the mark, hard to hit it.' Vice can overshoot or undershoot in endless directions; virtue is one bullseye. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II ch.6 (F.H. Peters and Chase trans.).

question: Temperance, for Aristotle, sits between chasing every bodily pleasure and feeling almost none. The person who overdoes pleasure is easy to spot and easy to name: the glutton, the drunkard. But Aristotle notes something odd about the opposite failing, the person who takes no pleasure in anything at all. What does he say about that deficient extreme?
answer: It is so rare among people that it barely even has a name
choices: It is so rare among people that it barely even has a name
It is the safest condition and the one closest to true virtue
It is far more common and more dangerous than overindulgence
It is impossible, since every living person enjoys some pleasure
context: Temperance is the mean about bodily pleasures, between the self-indulgent person who chases every pleasure and the 'insensible' person who feels none. Aristotle observes that caring too little for pleasure is so uncommon it barely has a name, just as the man who fears nothing has no name. The rare deficiencies expose how lopsided our vices usually are. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II (F.H. Peters trans.); SEP, Aristotle's Ethics.

question: Aristotle treats honesty about yourself as a balance. The braggart who claims more than he is misses it on one side. But the person who downplays himself, who pretends to know less or be less than he truly is, the way Socrates pretended to know nothing, also misses the mark. Why does Aristotle count false modesty as a failing too?
answer: Understating your worth is just as untrue as overstating it
choices: Understating your worth is just as untrue as overstating it
Downplaying yourself is really a sly way of fishing for praise
A modest person can never be trusted to lead other people
Pretending to know nothing is an insult to one's own teachers
context: Truthfulness about oneself is the mean between the boaster, who claims more than he is, and the falsely modest or 'ironical' man, who understates himself. Aristotle's example of the ironical type points to Socrates, who pretended to know nothing. Even self-deprecation is an extreme, not a virtue, because it departs from the plain truth about who you are. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II and Bk IV ch.7 (F.H. Peters trans.).

question: Aristotle admits that hitting the exact middle between two vices is genuinely hard, so he gives practical advice. Notice which fault you personally lean toward, he says, whether you are naturally a coward or naturally a hothead, then deliberately pull yourself the opposite way, as men straighten a bent stick. What is the point of bending yourself the other way?
answer: Over-correcting against your own worst tendency lands you nearer the middle
choices: Over-correcting against your own worst tendency lands you nearer the middle
Switching over to the opposite vice is better than staying in your current one
Once bent the other way, a person's character can never spring back again
The middle does not really matter, so long as you keep changing direction
context: Because the exact middle is so hard to find, Aristotle says to 'take the least of the evils' and to pull hard away from the extreme you personally lean toward, 'as we straighten a bent stick by bending it the other way.' Know your own warp and over-correct against it; aiming a bit past center is how you actually end up near it. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II ch.9 (F.H. Peters and Chase trans.).

question: Aristotle says courage shows itself most fully against the most terrifying thing of all, death, and above all death faced in battle for a noble cause. He draws a sharp contrast between the truly brave man and the merely rash one in how each acts around real danger. According to Aristotle, how does the rash man give himself away?
answer: He talks big about danger beforehand but shrinks back when it actually arrives
choices: He talks big about danger beforehand but shrinks back when it actually arrives
He refuses to fight at all unless someone is watching there to praise him
He feels the same terror as everyone else around him but hides it perfectly
He charges first into every single fight and is always the last to leave it
context: Aristotle holds that courage is shown most fully in facing death, and most properly death in battle for a noble cause. The rash man often boasts of danger beforehand but draws back when the real terror arrives, while the brave man is quiet beforehand and keen in the moment of action. The tell of false courage is loud talk that collapses under real fear. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk III ch.6-7 (Loeb/Ross trans.).

question: Aristotle warns that one thing above all drags us off the balanced middle, and we can scarcely judge it fairly: pleasure. He reaches for a famous scene from the Trojan War, where the old counsellors of Troy looked upon Helen, whose beauty had launched the war, and reached a verdict. What does Aristotle say we should do with pleasure, following their example?
answer: Admit honestly that it is lovely, and then send it away
choices: Admit honestly that it is lovely, and then send it away
Deny that it holds any real beauty or pull at all
Surrender to it fully, since no one can resist it anyway
Lock it away and pretend that it was never there
context: Aristotle: 'We must be especially on our guard against pleasure, for we can scarcely judge her impartially.' He says to treat pleasure the way the old counsellors of Troy treated Helen, admit she is lovely, then send her away, 'for so, by sending it away, we shall err the less.' Honest dismissal, not denial and not repression, keeps us nearer the mean. The Helen scene is drawn from the legend of the Trojan War. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II ch.9 (F.H. Peters and Chase trans.).

question: A wrestling coach must set how much food a fighter eats each day. Ten pounds is plainly too much, and two pounds plainly too little. A confident student declares the rule simple: split the difference, order six pounds, and feed every fighter that same amount. On Aristotle's account of the mean, what is the flaw in the student's tidy rule?
answer: The right amount tracks the particular eater, so no single ration fits all
choices: The right amount tracks the particular eater, so no single ration fits all
An average of the two extremes is the balanced mean, so six pounds is right
Six pounds errs high, so the coach should default to the smaller ration
A trained body adjusts to any ration, so the exact figure scarcely matters
context: This is the heart of Aristotle's twist: the mean is 'relative to us,' not the arithmetic average. 'If ten pounds is too much and two too little, it does not follow that the trainer will order six; for that also may be too much or too little, too little for Milo, too much for the beginner.' Milo of Croton was a legendary champion wrestler who ate enormously; six pounds that starves him would overstuff a novice. The right amount tracks the person and the situation, never a fixed midpoint. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II ch.6 (F.H. Peters and Chase trans.).

question: A clever student tells Aristotle: If every virtue is a balance between too much and too little, then there must be a right amount of everything, a right time to steal, a right way to murder, the proper person to betray. Aristotle flatly rejects this. Where does the student go wrong?
answer: Some acts are wrong in the very doing, with no good amount or occasion
choices: Some acts are wrong in the very doing, with no good amount or occasion
Those acts are fine in small doses but become harmful when taken too far
Whether they are wrong depends entirely on the exact situation you face
They are wrong only because society has agreed together to forbid them
context: Aristotle says the doctrine of the mean does NOT mean 'everything in moderation.' Adultery, theft, and murder, and feelings like spite and envy, are 'bad in themselves, not because of too much or too little.' There is no right amount of murder and no committing adultery 'with the right person at the right time in the right way.' Some acts are already wrong in the mere doing of them. Source: Nicomachean Ethics Bk II ch.6 (Chase and F.H. Peters trans.).

question: Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi stroll along the dam of the Hao River. Zhuangzi points at the water: "See how the minnows dart about wherever they please — that's what fish really enjoy!" Huizi, the sharpest logician of his day, shoots back a single objection. What does he say?
answer: "You're not a fish, so you have no way to know what a fish enjoys."
choices: "You're not a fish, so you have no way to know what a fish enjoys."
"Fish feel nothing at all, so there's no enjoyment there to know."
"You're only seeing your own good mood reflected back in the water."
"Darting that fast is fright, not joy — you've read it backwards."
context: From the Zhuangzi, ch. 17 'Autumn Floods' (Burton Watson trans.). Huizi raises the problem of other minds: you cannot cross the gap between species to know another creature's inner experience. Thomas Nagel made the same worry famous in 1974 with 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' — a bat's echolocating world is so alien that no human can know what it is like to be one. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi ch. 17; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zhuangzi'.

question: On the bridge over the Hao River, Huizi tells Zhuangzi, "You're not a fish, so you can't know what fish enjoy." Zhuangzi answers not with evidence about fish but with a single question that flips Huizi's own rule around. What does Zhuangzi ask?
answer: "You're not me — so how do you know that I don't know what fish enjoy?"
choices: "You're not me — so how do you know that I don't know what fish enjoy?"
"You're not these fish — so how do you know that they take no joy at all?"
"You're not the river — so how do you know what does or doesn't stir below?"
"You're not my eyes — so how do you know what years of watching taught me?"
context: Zhuangzi's move (Zhuangzi ch. 17, Watson trans.): rather than defend his reading of the fish, he turns Huizi's own principle back on him. If no one can know another mind, then Huizi can't know what is inside Zhuangzi's head either — so the rule that forbids all cross-mind knowledge defeats itself. Logicians call this throwing an opponent's premise back at him; the name matters less than seeing that the skeptic's rule saws off the branch he's sitting on. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi ch. 17; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zhuangzi'.

question: On the Hao bridge, Huizi presses one last time: "You're certainly not a fish, so how do you know what fish enjoy?" Zhuangzi has the last word, and he wins it by seizing on the very first word of Huizi's question rather than saying anything new about the fish. How does he close it?
answer: He hears Huizi's question of how he knows as a question of where, and answers that he knows it from right where he stands.
choices: He hears Huizi's question of how he knows as a question of where, and answers that he knows it from right where he stands.
He admits that he was only speaking in fun, and grants that he never really knew the inner life of the fish.
He allows that the two of them can never settle it, and lets the whole stubborn question quietly dissolve.
He stands by his first claim, and holds that watching a creature closely is, all by itself, a full way to know it.
context: Zhuangzi wins with a pun, not a proof. He treats Huizi's word for 'how' (whence) as if it meant 'from where' — so 'How do you know?' becomes 'From where do you know?', and his answer is simply: from this spot on the bridge. The Stanford Encyclopedia notes he 'bests him by switching between senses of the word whence.' The humor IS the philosophy: strict logic pushed too far traps the logician, and Zhuangzi's real point is that knowledge always comes from somewhere — here, above the Hao — never from nowhere. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi ch. 17; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'School of Names' (Life of Hui Shi).

question: A small child is lost and frightened in a dark forest, crying out for her mother. J.L. Schellenberg uses this picture to ask what love requires: a mother who hears her child and can come would come. He says the same should hold for a loving, all-powerful God who hears a sincere seeker. Why, on this analogy, is divine silence a puzzle?
answer: For a loving mother, only something past her own power could keep her silent, yet nothing is past God's.
choices: For a loving mother, only something past her own power could keep her silent, yet nothing is past God's.
A loving mother sometimes stays silent on purpose, to teach her frightened child to be brave on its own.
The child may be crying in some way that a loving mother standing nearby cannot recognize as a real call.
A human mother's love is small and limited, so stretching the comparison up to a perfect God just breaks down.
context: This lost-child-in-the-forest image is Schellenberg's signature analogy. A loving mother able to answer would answer; only something beyond her power could keep her silent. For an all-powerful God, nothing is beyond His power, so His silence toward a sincere seeker has no such excuse. The other choices are real replies people make (faith-building, a call He doesn't recognize, the comparison failing), but they are not the force of Schellenberg's analogy. Paraphrase of the 'loving mother' analogy from 'Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason' (1993); see Realseekerministries summary + Wikipedia, 'Argument from nonbelief.'

question: J.L. Schellenberg points to the shape of who believes what. A child born in Thailand grows up Buddhist, a child born in Saudi Arabia grows up Muslim, and hundreds of millions across the secular West believe nothing at all. Why does he think this pattern counts against a loving God who would show Himself to every open heart?
answer: What a person ends up believing tracks their surroundings, not how honestly they sought the truth.
choices: What a person ends up believing tracks their surroundings, not how honestly they sought the truth.
It shows that most religions must be false, since at most one of them can be the truly correct one.
It proves that people only ever come to believe whatever their own parents first told them to believe.
It shows a loving God simply chooses to reveal Himself in a different way to each separate culture.
context: Schellenberg argues the map of belief looks like an accident of birth, not a record of who searched sincerely. A God who 'shows up' for the open-hearted, he says, wouldn't produce a pattern that tracks culture and upbringing instead of honesty. The distractors are different morals people draw from the same fact (one religion is right, parents determine belief, a pluralist God) but none is Schellenberg's point. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hiddenness of God' (demographics of belief; Thailand / Saudi Arabia, secular West) - plato.stanford.edu/entries/divine-hiddenness/

question: Long before modern philosophy, the prophet Isaiah cried, 'Truly, you are a God who hides himself' - the line Latin writers called Deus absconditus, which Martin Luther returned to again and again, and which echoes in the mystics' 'dark night of the soul.' Centuries later J.L. Schellenberg took up this ancient theme. What was his distinctive move with it?
answer: He turned an old cry of longing into a precise, step-by-step argument against a loving God.
choices: He turned an old cry of longing into a precise, step-by-step argument against a loving God.
He set out to prove, once and for all, that no god of any kind could possibly exist.
He traced the ancient complaint carefully back through scripture to its earliest written sources.
He argued the long silence is plainly a deliberate test, meant to strengthen a seeker's faith.
context: The ache of God's hiddenness is ancient (Isaiah 45:15, Luther's Deus absconditus in his Genesis lectures, the mystics' dark night, Jesus's cry of dereliction). Schellenberg's novelty was not noticing the silence but converting that lament into a tight, premise-by-premise deductive argument. Note: choice four ('a test of faith') is actually one of the later REPLIES, not Schellenberg's own move. The mystic and dereliction framing is treated as legend/tradition here. Wikipedia 'Deus absconditus' + Cambridge 'Vere tu es Deus absconditus' (Luther) + Stanford Encyclopedia, 'Hiddenness of God.'

question: Some defenders of God answer J.L. Schellenberg by saying God keeps His distance on purpose, so that people can grow - building faith, humility, and the deep longing that comes only from searching for something not simply handed to you. Schellenberg grants these can be real goods, yet presses one sharp objection in reply. What is it?
answer: None of those goods seems worth leaving a sincere seeker entirely cut off from the relationship itself.
choices: None of those goods seems worth leaving a sincere seeker entirely cut off from the relationship itself.
A short stretch of distance would already secure those goods; a whole life of silence asks far more.
No sincere seeker ever agreed to be kept in the dark as the price of growing those very virtues.
Those goods land on some seekers and skip others entirely, which a loving God would not permit.
context: This is the soul-making / 'epistemic distance' reply, rooted in John Hick: God stays hidden so virtues like faith, humility, and longing can develop. Schellenberg grants the goods are real, then presses sufficiency: no such good looks weighty enough to justify leaving a sincere seeker completely shut out of the relationship that was supposedly the whole point. The other three also grant the goods are real but attack on different ground (the amount of distance needed, the seeker's lack of consent, the uneven distribution of the goods) - each a live objection, but the keyed one is Schellenberg's stated reply. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy + Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Hick's soul-making / epistemic-distance reply) - iep.utm.edu/divine-hiddenness-argument-against-gods-existence/

question: It would be easy to assume the philosopher behind the strongest modern argument against God must be a triumphant atheist who thinks nothing lies beyond the physical world. Yet J.L. Schellenberg calls his own outlook 'skeptical religion.' What does he say his hiddenness argument actually refutes?
answer: Only the personal, loving God of theism, leaving an impersonal Ultimate an open possibility.
choices: Only the personal, loving God of theism, leaving an impersonal Ultimate an open possibility.
Every theistic religion alike, since each one rests its hopes on a personal creator-god.
Any personal God who acts in the world, whether that God is loving or stern and distant.
Only those religions that demand belief while offering no real evidence for it at all.
context: Schellenberg is not a hostile atheist. He builds his view around 'ultimism' - the idea that SOMETHING ultimate may exist in the nature of things, worth imagining even if unproven - and calls his stance 'skeptical religion.' He holds that the hiddenness argument refutes the personal, loving God of theism while leaving an impersonal Ultimate fully open. The argument's engine is specifically God's LOVE, so it does not touch a stern or distant deity, an impersonal Ultimate, or every theistic tradition wholesale - those are the over-broad readings in the distractors. Wikipedia, 'J. L. Schellenberg' + Cambridge 'Religious Studies' on ultimism + Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews of 'The Wisdom to Doubt.'

question: J.L. Schellenberg lays his hiddenness argument out in steps: a perfectly loving God would always be open to relationship with anyone willing; you cannot consciously relate to someone unless you believe they exist; some people sincerely seek and still find no such belief; so no perfectly loving God exists. Critics who reject the conclusion zero in on a single step. Which one do they dispute?
answer: On whether perfect love really must translate into making belief available to every sincere person.
choices: On whether perfect love really must translate into making belief available to every sincere person.
On whether relating to God at all truly requires first believing that God exists.
On whether anyone really seeks sincerely without somehow resisting or hiding from the truth.
On whether the existence of honest nonbelievers can settle, by itself, that no God exists.
context: A common misread is that the fight is over whether God is 'really hiding' or whether God exists. Schellenberg's critics almost never deny that sincere, non-resisting nonbelievers exist; the disputed step is the inferential BRIDGE from God's perfect love to the claim that belief would then be available to every sincere seeker. ('Non-resisting' means a seeker not engaged in self-deception or refusing to look at the evidence.) The other steps - the belief-precondition for relationship, the existence of non-resisting seekers, and the final leap to no God - are each genuine parts of the argument a thinker might probe, but locating the contested love-to-belief inference is the recognition this rung tests. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hiddenness of God' (the disputed inferential step) - plato.stanford.edu/entries/divine-hiddenness/

question: When the Western Roman Empire fell, most of Aristotle's writings and Greek science disappeared from Latin Europe for centuries. Hundreds of years later, Europeans got Aristotle back. By what unlikely route did his philosophy return to the West?
answer: Scholars in Baghdad had translated it into Arabic, and Europeans later turned that Arabic into Latin
choices: Scholars in Baghdad had translated it into Arabic, and Europeans later turned that Arabic into Latin
Monks in Ireland had quietly copied the Greek scrolls and carried them back across the sea
Byzantine emperors had locked the originals away and at last shipped them west as a gift
Traders coming home from India had hauled the lost Greek books back in their saddlebags
context: The most memorable payoff of the whole movement: Aristotle came home to the West dressed in Arabic. Abbasid scholars translated Greek works in the 800s and 900s; that Arabic learning later flowed back into Europe through Latin translation. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy'; SEP 'al-Kindi'.

question: Hunayn ibn Ishaq was the master translator of Baghdad's great movement to save Greek learning. His finished translations were so prized that the biographer Ibn Abi Usaybi'a records he was paid for a completed book in the strangest measure. How was Hunayn paid?
answer: In gold equal to the weight of the book itself, weight for weight
choices: In gold equal to the weight of the book itself, weight for weight
With a house and a servant for every text he completed
In silver coins counted out by the number of pages he filled
With a share of every student's fee at the city's schools
context: Hunayn ibn Ishaq (d. 873) catalogued about 129 works of the physician Galen alone that he had translated. The 'weight for weight' figure traces to the medieval biographer Ibn Abi Usaybi'a and is treated as testimony rather than hard fact. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'Hunayn the Translator' (quoting Ibn Abi Usaybi'a).

question: Baghdad's translation movement belonged to no single tribe: Hunayn ibn Ishaq was a Christian, Thabit ibn Qurra was a pagan star-worshipper, and their paymasters were Muslim caliphs. A student asks what this strange mix shows about how learning actually travels between peoples. Which claim holds up?
answer: Learning crosses between strangers and rivals, not down one people's bloodline
choices: Learning crosses between strangers and rivals, not down one people's bloodline
Learning lasts mainly through the institutions, not the people, that house it
Learning moves fastest only when one shared tongue unites every scholar
Learning takes root only where rulers grow rich enough to fund it
context: Hunayn ibn Ishaq was a Nestorian Christian; Thabit ibn Qurra was a Sabian, from the Harran star-cult; their patrons were Muslim caliphs and viziers. No single tribe could claim the translation movement: the learning passed between strangers and rivals of different faiths, not down one people's bloodline. Source: SEP 'Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy'; Britannica 'Thabit ibn Qurrah'; Dimitri Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture'.

question: Thabit ibn Qurra became one of the great translators and mathematicians of Baghdad, revising the Arabic Euclid and rendering Archimedes and Ptolemy. But the eldest Banu Musa brother first found him doing ordinary work in the market town of Harran. What was Thabit doing when he was discovered?
answer: Working as a money-changer, changing coins for a fee
choices: Working as a money-changer, changing coins for a fee
Teaching village children their letters for coins
Copying out prayer books in the city mosque
Selling star-maps he had drawn from memory
context: Muhammad, the eldest Banu Musa brother, passed through Harran, noticed Thabit's rare command of Syriac, Greek, and Arabic, and brought him to Baghdad. He went on to revise the Arabic Euclid and translate Archimedes, Apollonius, and Ptolemy. Source: Britannica 'Thabit ibn Qurrah'; MacTutor 'Al-Sabi Thabit ibn Qurra al-Harrani'.

question: We often picture Baghdad's translation movement as a project paid for by caliphs alone. But three rich brothers, the Banu Musa, personally funded much of it, paying scholars hundreds of dinars a month. To stock the work, what did they send their agents abroad to do?
answer: Buy up old Greek manuscripts deep in Byzantine territory
choices: Buy up old Greek manuscripts deep in Byzantine territory
Recruit Greek-speaking scholars willing to move to Baghdad
Study how Byzantine schools trained their young copyists
Carry gifts to the emperor to keep the borders peaceful
context: The Banu Musa paid scholars such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq and Thabit ibn Qurra roughly 500 dinars a month and sent agents into Byzantine lands to purchase Greek manuscripts. It was a privately funded operation, not just a royal one. Source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Banu Musa brothers'.

question: For centuries, scholars in the Arabic world and later in Europe studied a profound book of metaphysics they believed Aristotle had written, called 'The Theology of Aristotle.' Historians later uncovered an awkward truth about it. What was actually wrong?
answer: It was not Aristotle at all, but a reworked piece of the later pagan thinker Plotinus
choices: It was not Aristotle at all, but a reworked piece of the later pagan thinker Plotinus
It was a forgery written in Baghdad to flatter a caliph who admired Aristotle
It was Aristotle's work, but a clumsy translation had reversed his real meaning
It was a student's lecture notes mistaken for the master's own finished book
context: A reworked chunk of the Neoplatonist Plotinus's Enneads circulated under the title 'The Theology of Aristotle,' and a piece of Proclus traveled as 'Aristotle on the Pure Good' (the later Latin Liber de Causis). A translation mix-up shaped centuries of metaphysics in both Islam and Christendom. Source: SEP 'Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy'; SEP 'al-Kindi'.

question: Popular books describe the 'House of Wisdom' as a grand university humming with translators under one roof. The Yale scholar Dimitri Gutas argues this picture is mostly a modern legend. What does he say the Bayt al-Hikma more likely was?
answer: A palace library or records office, not a teaching school
choices: A palace library or records office, not a teaching school
A school for caliphs' sons that later added some translators
A workshop that copied books but translated none of them
A myth invented whole, no such building ever stood in Baghdad
context: Dimitri Gutas argues Bayt al-Hikma was closer to a palace library or records office (the name may even derive from khizana, a storehouse); the real translating happened across a scattered network of private homes and patrons. Source: Dimitri Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture' (1998), as discussed in Wikipedia 'House of Wisdom' and SEP 'Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy'.

question: A famous story says the caliph al-Ma'mun launched Baghdad's whole translation movement after Aristotle came to him in a dream and told him Greek reason and Islamic faith were no enemies. A student wants to know what really set the movement going. Which explanation does the historical record actually back?
answer: Decades of broad demand and money from many rival patrons carried the work
choices: Decades of broad demand and money from many rival patrons carried the work
One ruler's dream set off a movement that no one had wanted before he came
The Banu Musa brothers' private fortune alone is what carried the whole effort
Persian scholars already at court drove it long before any Greek text arrived
context: Legend, framed as legend. The dream tale is told in the sources but treated by historians as embellishment that gives one caliph too much credit; the movement was really driven by decades of broad social demand and money from many patrons (the Banu Musa funded it privately, and the work continued well after al-Ma'mun died in 833 -- Hunayn ibn Ishaq worked on to 873). Source: Dimitri Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture' (1998); SEP 'Greek Sources in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy'.

question: A sculptor carves a twisting knot of teak, sets it on a pedestal, and announces that it symbolizes Human Destiny. Visitors stare and stare but find nothing of destiny in the curling grain — it is just a beautiful piece of wood. Can the sculptor's announcement, by itself, make the carving actually mean Human Destiny?
answer: No — saying so cannot pour a meaning into a work that the work itself will not carry
choices: No — saying so cannot pour a meaning into a work that the work itself will not carry
Yes — the maker's word is final, so anyone can make anything mean anything by declaring it
Yes — a viewer who feels nothing has simply failed to study the work hard enough
No — a carving can never mean anything beyond the literal wood it is made of
context: This is Monroe Beardsley's 'twisted teak' thought experiment from Aesthetics (1958). His point: 'anyone can make anything symbolize anything just by saying it does' is absurd — a declared intention cannot inject a meaning the work won't bear. (The view that a maker's stated aim is not the final word on a work's meaning is, in literary criticism, called the intentional fallacy.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Beardsley's Aesthetics', plato.stanford.edu/entries/beardsley-aesthetics/.

question: A critic reads a streak of irony into one of A.E. Housman's poems. Housman — the very man who wrote it — flatly denies intending any irony at all. The poet swears to one reading; a careful reader of the page swears to another. When the maker of a poem and its readers clash like this, where does the poem's meaning finally rest?
answer: In the public conventions of the language we all share, which can hold more than the maker meant
choices: In the public conventions of the language we all share, which can hold more than the maker meant
In the private feeling of the author, since only he knows what he truly meant to say in each line
In suspense and unsettled, until the author himself steps in and declares which reading he wants
In the verdict of the skilled reader, who now stands as the one true judge of what the poem says
context: Beardsley used Housman as his cleanest case: the poet denied an irony his own words plainly carry, because sentence-meaning rests on 'public conventions of usage,' not on 'the whim of the individual, and his mental vagaries.' Even the maker can misread the made thing — and Wimsatt and Beardsley were equally clear the poem 'is not the critic's own' either. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Beardsley's Aesthetics', plato.stanford.edu/entries/beardsley-aesthetics/.

question: In 1702 readers split violently over Daniel Defoe's pamphlet 'The Shortest Way with the Dissenters,' whose calm proposal to crush religious dissenters some took as a sincere call and others as savage mockery of that very cruelty. A philosopher uses the quarrel to press the anti-intentionalists, who hold that a text's meaning lives in its words alone. What is the sharpest worry the case raises for that view?
answer: Telling sincere from ironic can hang on the author's aim, so intention may help fix meaning after all
choices: Telling sincere from ironic can hang on the author's aim, so intention may help fix meaning after all
Internal cues in the prose alone settle whether it is ironic, so the words by themselves suffice
The era's public conventions of usage settle the reading, so no appeal to the author is needed
The readers' own reactions settle what it means, so a furious audience makes the cruel sense correct
context: This is the intentionalists' strongest reply to Wimsatt and Beardsley. With Defoe — and Jonathan Swift's 'A Modest Proposal,' also read as literal — 'the only ground for saying that the pamphlet is ironic seems to be Defoe's intention.' Serious philosophers (E.D. Hirsch; in a moderate form Noel Carroll) hold that intention does real work in fixing meaning, so the dispute is genuinely open — no verdict here. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Art and Interpretation', iep.utm.edu/art-and-interpretation/.

question: In 1689 John Locke imagined two people who agree on every color word: both call ripe tomatoes 'red,' both stop at red lights, both pass every color test. Yet, Locke supposed, the inner experience one of them has looking at a violet might be the very experience the other has looking at a marigold. Locke decided this swap would have one strange feature. What was it?
answer: No one could ever catch it, since no person can climb inside another's mind to compare
choices: No one could ever catch it, since no person can climb inside another's mind to compare
No one could ignore it, since it would secretly change which colors each person finds lovely
No one could share it, since two people could never end up swapped in the very same way
No one could cause it, since the colors a person sees are fixed for life at birth
context: Locke gave the first explicit inverted-spectrum scenario (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Ch. xxxii, Sec. 15), using a violet and a marigold. His own verdict: the swap 'could never be known: because one Man's Mind could not pass into another Man's Body, to perceive, what Appearances were produced by those Organs.' He raised the most haunting version of the puzzle and then shrugged it off as harmless -- since no test could detect it, it changes nothing about how we talk or live. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Inverted Qualia,' quoting Locke Essay II.xxxii.15; https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qualia-inverted/

question: People long assumed a perfect color-swap could never be caught: flip someone's whole spectrum and their behavior would look identical to ours. But the range of colors we see is lopsided, not a tidy mirror. The clinching example is what happens when you darken one particular color: it turns into a wholly different-feeling color, one a swapped person would suddenly report seeing where a normal person never would. Darken which color, and you get brown?
answer: Yellow
choices: Yellow
Blue
Green
Red
context: The color solid isn't symmetric, so a true 180-degree swap would actually show up. The clincher: 'Dark yellow is brown' -- a qualitatively different color -- 'whereas dark blue is blue.' Yellow also reaches its maximum saturation at a higher lightness than red or blue. So if you really rotated someone's colors, their darkened yellows would turn brown while a normal person's would not, and the supposedly undetectable inversion betrays itself. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Inverted Qualia' (color-space asymmetry; cf. C.L. Hardin); https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qualia-inverted/

question: The color-swap puzzle says the inner red you see might be the inner green I see, yet we behave alike and pass every color test the same way. Four philosophers weigh in. One of them is a member of the Vienna Circle. Hearing 'maybe your red is my green,' how does she rule on it?
answer: The sentence only looks like a claim; underneath, there is no fact to be right or wrong about
choices: The sentence only looks like a claim; underneath, there is no fact to be right or wrong about
The sentence states a real fact about us, one that no possible test could ever reach
The sentence states a plain truth, since each of us plainly carries his own private colors
The sentence sets a real task for science, which will one day measure the true answer
context: This is the killer reply, called verificationism: a difference that no test could ever detect, even in principle, is no difference at all. The logical positivists of the Vienna Circle tested every claim by asking whether any observation could in principle confirm or deny it, and on that standard they dismissed the inverted spectrum as a meaningless, unverifiable claim; on the Frege-Schlick view, comparing one person's inner color to another's simply 'do[es] not make sense' -- it is an empty sentence dressed up as a deep mystery. Note the contrast with Locke (the 'real but undetectable' distractor): Locke granted the same undetectability yet still treated the swap as a real hidden fact -- the positivist denies there is any fact there to hide. The 'task for science' reply is a further trap: the positivist is not deferring the question to future instruments; she holds there is nothing there to measure. No verdict is imposed here; this is one live position among rivals. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Inverted Qualia' (Frege-Schlick view; logical positivist treatment); https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qualia-inverted/

question: A man is sure a mineral supplement cures cancer. One study found it works; twenty found nothing. He throws out all twenty, saying those trials were too small, biased, and fished for results. He never asks whether those same flaws sit in the single study he loves. Granting his criticisms name real problems that can wreck a study, why does his argument still fail?
answer: He aims his doubt only at the twenty studies he dislikes and never at the one he likes, so it filters out unwelcome evidence rather than testing truth
choices: He aims his doubt only at the twenty studies he dislikes and never at the one he likes, so it filters out unwelcome evidence rather than testing truth
Twenty studies always outweigh one study, so the majority verdict settles the question no matter how any single trial happened to be run
Small samples, bias, and result-fishing are myths invented to discredit findings, so not one of his three objections names anything real
A cure either works or it does not, so running more than a single trial on the same mineral can never add anything genuinely worth knowing
context: Scott Alexander's selenium example: a believer points to one study and waves away twenty by invoking p-hacking, bias, and small samples — but only against the inconvenient twenty. 'Maybe these things happened in each of the twenty studies that disagree with you. Or maybe they happened in the one contrarian study you are getting so excited about.' The methodological doubt is real and valid in the abstract; the cheat is aiming it in only one direction. Source: Scott Alexander, 'Beware Isolated Demands For Rigor,' Slate Star Codex, 2014.

question: A diner posts a strict 'no animals allowed' rule. A blind woman walks in with a guide dog and is let in; the rule has a real, fair exception for her. Later a regular shows up with his pet and insists he should be let in too, his only reason being that he is a beloved regular and the rule should bend for him. Both ask to skip the same rule. What makes the woman's exception fair and the regular's a cheat?
answer: Her dog meets a need the rule was never meant to block, while his only reason is that the rule is inconvenient for him personally
choices: Her dog meets a need the rule was never meant to block, while his only reason is that the rule is inconvenient for him personally
She asked a manager first and filled out the proper request, while the regular simply walked in without getting anyone's permission
A blind person counts as disabled and a regular does not, so disability alone always overrides any posted rule a business makes
Her dog is trained and well behaved, while his pet might bark or bite, so the danger of the animal is what decides each case
context: This is the family the isolated demand for rigor belongs to: special pleading, a double standard. A legitimate exception needs a RELEVANT difference that addresses the rule's purpose (a service animal answers a disability-accommodation need). A bogus exception offers a difference with no relevant justification — the only special thing about the favored case is that it's yours. Source: Gary Curtis, 'Logical Fallacy: Special Pleading,' FallacyFiles.org; framing from Scott Alexander (2014).

question: A commentator opposes a proposed military strike, so he insists it first prove itself by an exact dollars-per-life-saved standard, measured against the cost of mosquito nets that prevent malaria. He never holds a domestic program he favors, like public broadcasting, to anything close to that punishing test. Why is this a rigged contest rather than honest budgeting?
answer: He points a standard nothing real could ever satisfy at the one option he already opposes, and spares the option he likes
choices: He points a standard nothing real could ever satisfy at the one option he already opposes, and spares the option he likes
Military strikes and mosquito nets save lives in different ways, so putting a single dollar price on either one is impossible
Public broadcasting plainly saves more lives per dollar than any airstrike, which is why he is right to spare it the test
Government should never weigh dollars against human lives at all, so any cost-per-life standard is offensive from the start
context: Scott Alexander's even-handed example (drawn from a Matt Yglesias column): 'If for political reasons he doesn't support air strikes, suddenly that plan has to justify itself according to rigorous criteria that no government program that exists could possibly pass.' A bar no real program could clear, applied only to the disfavored option, isn't rigor — it's a rigged contest. The method here stays neutral on whether the strike is actually wise. Source: Scott Alexander, 'Beware Isolated Demands For Rigor' (2014).

question: A Science Czar reviews a study finding the minimum wage helps workers. He says correlation is not enough and demands stronger proof; they deliver it. He demands a tougher significance level; they deliver. He demands a full randomized trial; they run it, and it still shows a benefit, so he raises the risk of publication bias. Then a different team finds, in six restaurants in one small town, a faint and statistically meaningless hint that the wage hurt slightly. He instantly declares the matter closed. What gives him away?
answer: The same man who needed a randomized trial to believe one result accepts six restaurants and no significance to believe the opposite
choices: The same man who needed a randomized trial to believe one result accepts six restaurants and no significance to believe the opposite
He never proposes a single fixed standard of proof in advance, which is the only correct way to run any serious scientific review
Studies of six restaurants are worthless, so his real mistake is paying any attention to the small-town finding at all
Randomized trials are the gold standard, so he was right to demand one and simply got unlucky with conflicting results
context: The essay's marquee scene. The tell is not that any single demand was wrong — RCTs really are strong evidence — but that the standard of proof collapsed the instant the conclusion flipped to the one he wanted. As Scott Alexander puts it, such a person 'is not trying to create a revolutionary new scientific regime, he's taking pot shots.' Source: Scott Alexander, 'Beware Isolated Demands For Rigor' (2014).

question: A councilor judges every proposed plan by a brutally demanding standard of proof, and plenty of weak plans fail under it. A watching clerk wants to tell whether his rigor is honest inquiry or a weapon dressed as inquiry. She decides one feature alone settles the question. What should she watch for?
answer: Whether he turns the demand back on his own favored plans too, or aims it only ever at everyone else's
choices: Whether he turns the demand back on his own favored plans too, or aims it only ever at everyone else's
Whether the standard of proof he picks is set high enough to actually catch a genuinely bad plan
Whether the councilor is personally honest and sincerely believes the strict standard he is enforcing
Whether the rival plans truly deserve to fail once the demanding standard is finally applied to them
context: This is the whole distinction: directionality. Scott Alexander notes a fair use of rigor 'would prevent both Heraclitus and his victims from owning property' — a universal bar, high or low, is honest. The fallacy is a bar 'applied by Heraclitus to other people but never the other way around,' which 'would merely give Heraclitus an unfair advantage.' A standard that SWITCHES based on whose claim it is, is the cheat — not the height of the bar, and not the sincerity of the person holding it. Source: Scott Alexander, 'Beware Isolated Demands For Rigor' (2014).

question: Heraclitus taught that nothing ever stays the same; everything is in constant flux, so nothing is truly the same thing from one moment to the next. Then a rustler walks off with an ox Heraclitus had bought and paid for, arguing the beast has changed and so is not the same ox he bought and is up for grabs. At that, Heraclitus suddenly drops his grand doctrine and clings to the plain, ordinary sense of 'the same ox.' What does his sudden switch expose about how he was using his philosophy?
answer: He demands constant flux when it undercuts other people's claims, but quietly keeps stable identity the moment his own property is at stake
choices: He demands constant flux when it undercuts other people's claims, but quietly keeps stable identity the moment his own property is at stake
He never really believed in flux at all, since a thinker who meant his own doctrine would gladly have surrendered the ox without complaint
His doctrine of flux was simply mistaken, because the rustler's clever argument proves an ox really does become a different ox over time
He should have argued that an ox changes far more slowly than a river, so flux is true of water but plainly false of livestock
context: The essay's seed image. The instant his property is at stake, Heraclitus 'accepts the watered-down vulgar sense of identity like everyone else' — flux for your claims, stable identity for his own. Scott Alexander credits the framing to John Perry's 'A Dialogue on Personal Identity and Immortality' (Hackett, 1978). Source: Scott Alexander, 'Beware Isolated Demands For Rigor' (2014).

question: In Scott Alexander's playful tale, the ancient Greek thinkers face off in a Wild West shoot-out. Protagoras boasts that he was never once tempted to abandon his own position, because he held that his self-interest simply determined what was true, so the truth always conveniently matched whatever suited him. Socrates, gun drawn, answers him with a single line that turns Protagoras's boast of flawless consistency into a grim joke. What does Socrates say?
answer: The only truly consistent people are the dead, Protagoras
choices: The only truly consistent people are the dead, Protagoras
A man who never doubts himself has simply stopped thinking, Protagoras
Truth that always flatters you was never truth at all, Protagoras
He who makes himself the measure measures nothing real, Protagoras
context: The essay's closing gag (a legendary, invented scene, not history). Protagoras — the relativist who said his self-interest 'determined truth, and so never suffered any temptation to depart from my position' — takes Socrates' last bullet and last word. The joke carries the real point: perfectly consistent rigor is nearly impossible for the living, which is exactly why selectively demanding it of others is such an effective weapon. Source: Scott Alexander, 'Beware Isolated Demands For Rigor' (2014).

question: Across his essay, Scott Alexander gives one plain test for spotting this trap, however it is dressed up. Someone holds a rival's claim to a punishing standard of proof, yet never turns that same standard on his own claim; the skepticism only ever points one way. Each time he catches this move, he lands the same blunt, slightly absurd one-line verdict, accusing the person of plain theft rather than careful thought. What is his recurring verdict?
answer: Applied inconsistently, you are just stealing cows again
choices: Applied inconsistently, you are just stealing cows again
Spare your own claim and you are merely pickpocketing again
Dodge the bar yourself and you are simply robbing the till
Aim doubt one way and you are quietly looting the argument
context: The diagnostic punchline of the whole piece. One-directional skepticism isn't carefulness; it's a way to win without arguing, so the verdict is theft: 'Applied inconsistently, you're just stealing cows again.' The recognition skill: ask whether the SAME standard is being aimed back at the demander's own position. Source: Scott Alexander, 'Beware Isolated Demands For Rigor' (2014).

question: Confucius watched two men hear of the same chance to make easy money. He said one was a junzi, a person of real character, and the other a 'small' or petty man. What set them apart was the very first question each one asked himself about the chance. What was that telltale first question?
answer: The junzi asked whether it was the right thing to do; the petty man asked what he would gain from it
choices: The junzi asked whether it was the right thing to do; the petty man asked what he would gain from it
The junzi asked whether it carried real danger; the petty man asked whether it took much effort
The junzi asked whether the law allowed it; the petty man asked whether it could be done quickly
The junzi asked whether others would approve of it; the petty man asked whether others would find out
context: Analects 4.16 (Legge): 'The mind of the superior man is conversant with righteousness; the mind of the mean man is conversant with gain.' For Confucius the dividing line is what you reach for first when a chance appears: the good, or the gain. Source: Analects 4.16, James Legge translation, Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/analects/li-ren).

question: Confucius said you can tell a junzi, a person of cultivated character, from a petty man by watching where each one looks the moment a plan falls apart. The two react in opposite directions. Where does the junzi look first when something goes wrong?
answer: Inward, to ask where he himself fell short
choices: Inward, to ask where he himself fell short
Around him, to find whoever else is to blame
Away, to slip off before anyone has noticed
Ahead, to reach for the quickest excuse he can
context: Analects 15.21 (Legge): 'What the superior man seeks, is in himself. What the mean man seeks, is in others.' This is the verse behind the saying that the junzi blames himself while the petty man blames others. Source: Analects 15.21, James Legge translation, Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/analects/wei-ling-gong).

question: Confucius drew a picture of how a junzi, a person of real character, carries himself through hard times, and set it against how a petty man carries himself through the very same hardship. The junzi's whole bearing is the opposite of the petty man's. How does Confucius say the junzi goes through trouble?
answer: Settled and at ease, broad and unhurried
choices: Settled and at ease, broad and unhurried
Loud and boastful, sure he can fix it
Frozen and silent, hoping it passes
Always anxious and fretting, never at rest
context: Analects 7.36 (Legge): 'The superior man is satisfied and composed; the mean man is always full of distress' (junzi tan dangdang, xiaoren chang qiqi). The same hardship lands on both; the junzi stays calm and broad, the petty man frets without end. Source: Analects 7.36, James Legge translation, Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/analects/shu-er).

question: In Confucius's day the word 'junzi' literally meant 'son of a lord' — you counted as one only if you were born into a ruling family, by bloodline alone. Confucius took that word and aimed it somewhere completely different, and later scholars called the result an 'aristocracy of merit.' What did Confucius change about who gets to be a junzi?
answer: You now earn it by cultivating your own character, and anyone of any birth can
choices: You now earn it by cultivating your own character, and anyone of any birth can
You now win it by passing the hardest of the empire's official examinations
You now receive it only when the reigning king grants it for great service
You now seize it by the courage and feats you show on the battlefield
context: Confucius hijacked a birth-word: a junzi is now anyone who behaves like one, through learning and self-cultivation, regardless of family. Scholars call him an 'ethical aristocrat' and the system an 'aristocracy of merit.' Sources: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius (iep.utm.edu/confucius); Yuri Pines, 'Confucius' Elitism: The Concepts of junzi and xiaoren'; Britannica: Junzi.

question: A ruler asked Confucius whether he should execute the wicked to scare everyone else into being good. Confucius told him no — become virtuous yourself instead — and reached for an image to explain how a leader's character spreads to ordinary people without any force at all. What was the image he used?
answer: Wind blowing across grass, which bends whichever way the wind goes
choices: Wind blowing across grass, which bends whichever way the wind goes
A struck bell that keeps on ringing long after the blow has landed
A single lamp passed from hand to hand, lighting one dark room after another
A patient river that carves its own shape into the hardest standing stone
context: Analects 12.19 (Legge): 'The relation between superiors and inferiors is like that between the wind and the grass. The grass must bend, when the wind blows across it.' The junzi leads by the pull of his goodness, not by killing. Sources: Analects 12.19, James Legge translation; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius (iep.utm.edu/confucius).

question: Confucius said a junzi and a petty man have opposite effects on the people around them — that you can spot each by what comes out in others when that person is in the room. The two effects are exact mirror images. What does Confucius say happens in people when a junzi is among them?
answer: Their best qualities are drawn out and brought to completion
choices: Their best qualities are drawn out and brought to completion
Their worst impulses are quietly fed and encouraged along
Their flaws are noted and reported to whoever is in charge
Their worth is weighed, and the useless ones are set aside
context: Analects 12.16 (Legge): 'The superior man seeks to perfect the admirable qualities of men, and does not seek to perfect their bad qualities. The mean man does the opposite.' The junzi helps others become their best self; the petty man feeds their worst. Source: Analects 12.16, James Legge translation, Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/analects/yan-yuan).

question: Two men of high standing walk into a crowded room. Confucius said one carries himself like a junzi and the other like a petty man, and the whole difference lies in how poise and pride combine in each. The junzi has the one without the other; the petty man has the reverse. How does Confucius describe the junzi's bearing?
answer: Dignified and at ease with himself, but with no arrogance in it
choices: Dignified and at ease with himself, but with no arrogance in it
Arrogant and looking down on others, but with no real ease
Commanding and proud, and dignified enough to carry it off
Meek and self-effacing, with neither pride nor any real dignity
context: Analects 13.26 (Legge): 'The superior man has a dignified ease without pride. The mean man has pride without a dignified ease.' One is self-possessed and puts others at ease; the other struts and looks down on people. Source: Analects 13.26, James Legge translation, Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/analects/zi-lu).

question: Confucius sat in on a group thrashing out a hard decision together. He watched two agreeable-seeming men and said only one of them was building any real harmony in the room, though both nodded along and neither caused a fuss. The agreeable one who was actually a junzi, Confucius said, differed from the other in a single thing. What was the junzi doing that the other man was not?
answer: Saying plainly where he still disagreed, and working with the others anyway
choices: Saying plainly where he still disagreed, and working with the others anyway
Smoothing every difference over so the group could reach a quick agreement
Matching his stated opinion to whichever way the room was already leaning
Praising each idea warmly so that no one in the room would feel slighted
context: Analects 13.23 (Legge): 'The superior man is affable, but not adulatory; the mean man is adulatory, but not affable' — commonly rendered as harmonizing without echoing. Real harmony keeps each voice intact; the petty man just agrees to fit in and creates no harmony at all. Source: Analects 13.23, James Legge translation, Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/analects/zi-lu).

question: Confucius said a junzi and a petty man are judged in opposite ways. You can hand a junzi your single gravest, weightiest responsibility and trust him with it completely. What did Confucius say is true of the petty man instead?
answer: He can shine at a small job, yet cannot be trusted with what truly matters
choices: He can shine at a small job, yet cannot be trusted with what truly matters
He turns down small jobs as beneath him, and waits only for great ones
He can be trusted with the greatest things, yet bungles every small one
He handles every task in the same way, whether it is small or great
context: Analects 15.34 (Legge): 'The superior man cannot be known in little matters; but he may be intrusted with great concerns. The small man may not be intrusted with great concerns, but he may be known in little matters.' Source: Analects 15.34, James Legge translation, Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/analects/wei-ling-gong).

question: Adam Smith, back in 1776, stared at a puzzle that would haunt economics: water keeps you alive yet trades for almost nothing, while a diamond does nothing for you yet trades for a fortune. To make sense of it, Smith drew a line between two different things a single good can have. Which split did he draw?
answer: He split a good's value in USE — how useful it is — from its value in EXCHANGE — what it trades for.
choices: He split a good's value in USE — how useful it is — from its value in EXCHANGE — what it trades for.
He split a good's COST to make from its PRICE in the market, blaming the gap on greedy middlemen.
