He split a good's SUPPLY from the DEMAND for it, and said the larger of the two always sets the price.
He split what a person NEEDS from what a person merely WANTS, and ranked needs as always worth more.
context: This is the diamond-water paradox. Adam Smith named it in The Wealth of Nations (1776, Book 1, Ch. 4): 'Nothing is more useful than water: but it will purchase scarce any thing... A diamond, on the contrary, has scarce any value in use; but a very great quantity of other goods may frequently be had in exchange for it.' He split 'value in use' from 'value in exchange' but could not explain WHAT drives the gap between them — the puzzle the marginalists would later crack. Source: Adam Smith, Wealth of Nations, Bk 1 Ch 4 (1776).

question: A merchant is baffled: water keeps you alive yet costs almost nothing, while a diamond does nothing for you yet costs a fortune. A young economist says he can resolve the puzzle without any contradiction. Which explanation does he give?
answer: What you pay tracks the worth of the NEXT unit, not the whole supply: water is everywhere, so one more glass is worth almost nothing.
choices: What you pay tracks the worth of the NEXT unit, not the whole supply: water is everywhere, so one more glass is worth almost nothing.
What you pay tracks the labor inside a thing: a diamond is dug from deep mines, while water costs no one any real toil to gather.
What you pay tracks how rare a thing is alone: diamonds are scarce and water is common, and scarcity by itself fixes every price.
What you pay tracks how badly people need a thing: since no one truly needs diamonds, their high price must be a temporary craze.
context: This is the marginalist move — value lives in the last unit you'd give up (the 'margin'), not in total usefulness or hours of labor. Water has immense total utility but, being everywhere, low MARGINAL utility; one more glass is worth little. Diamonds have trivial total utility but high marginal worth because they are scarce. Source: Wikipedia: Paradox of value / Marginalism; Study.com: Diamond-Water Paradox.

question: To test the idea that hard work is what makes a thing valuable, picture two cases side by side: a craftsman pours weeks of backbreaking effort into giant, beautifully shaped MUD PIES that not one person on earth wants to buy; meanwhile a hiker bends down and, with no effort at all, pockets a diamond worth a fortune. Taken together, what do the two cases show?
answer: Effort is neither needed nor enough for value; a buyer's desire decides it, so all that labor in the pies yields nothing.
choices: Effort is neither needed nor enough for value; a buyer's desire decides it, so all that labor in the pies yields nothing.
Effort still sets value in the long run; the mud pies will find a buyer once people grasp how much labor they hold.
Effort sets value only for made goods; found things like the diamond are a special exception that proves the broader rule.
Effort sets value once it is skilled; the craftsman simply chose a foolish product, but his real error was poor planning.
context: The 'mud pies' image is the marginalist case against the labor theory in one picture: weeks of congealed labor in something no one wants produce zero value (effort isn't SUFFICIENT), while a stooped-for diamond commands a fortune with almost no labor in it (effort isn't NECESSARY). Value is decided by the buyer's wants, not the maker's sweat. Source: Mises Institute: Marxism's Fragile Foundation — The Labor Theory of Value.

question: Karl Marx argued that what fixes a commodity's value is the labor poured into making it. But a sharp objection follows at once: would a lazy worker who dawdles all day then produce a MORE valuable shirt, since he sank more hours into it? Marx had a precise answer that closed this hole. What did he say actually counts?
answer: Only the labor SOCIALLY NECESSARY to make it — the hours an average worker needs at the normal skill and pace of the day.
choices: Only the labor SOCIALLY NECESSARY to make it — the hours an average worker needs at the normal skill and pace of the day.
Only the labor of the FASTEST worker available — the fewest hours any skilled hand could manage under perfect conditions.
Only the labor the BUYER believes went in — the hours a customer imagines were spent, whether or not they truly were.
Only the labor that the OWNER personally paid for — the hours he covered in wages, setting aside any unpaid overtime worked.
context: Marx's term is 'socially necessary labour-time.' Capital Vol. 1, Ch. 1: what determines a thing's value is 'the amount of labour socially necessary... for its production,' meaning the labour 'required to produce an article under the normal conditions of production, and with the average degree of skill and intensity prevalent at the time.' So dawdling earns no extra value — only the average needed hours count. Source: Marx, Capital Vol. 1, Ch. 1 (marxists.org).

question: In Capital, Karl Marx reached for a monster image to dramatize the dread he felt at the factory: the machines and stockpiles that past workers built, he said, were merely DEAD labor set against the worker still toiling at the bench. What creature did he say capital itself is?
answer: A vampire, that lives only by sucking living labor and lives the more, the more labor it sucks.
choices: A vampire, that lives only by sucking living labor and lives the more, the more labor it sucks.
A serpent, that lives only by swallowing living labor whole and grows the more, the more it downs.
A spider, that lives only by draining living labor dry and swells the more, the more it traps.
A wolf, that lives only by tearing living labor apart and gorges the more, the more it runs down.
context: Marx's line, Capital Vol. 1, Ch. 10: 'Capital is dead labour, that, vampire-like, only lives by sucking living labour, and lives the more, the more labour it sucks.' 'Dead labour' is the machines and stockpiles past workers built; 'living labour' is today's worker. He also wrote of capital's 'werewolf hunger for surplus-labour.' Source: Marx, Capital Vol. 1, Ch. 10 (marxists.org).

question: In 1896 the economist Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk set out to refute Karl Marx, and he pressed one charge above all. Marx, he said, was like a man who, desperate to draw a WHITE ball from an urn, makes sure of it by filling the urn with white balls only. What flaw was Bohm-Bawerk accusing Marx of?
answer: Marx had defined value as labor at the start, then treated his conclusion that value comes from labor as a discovery.
choices: Marx had defined value as labor at the start, then treated his conclusion that value comes from labor as a discovery.
Marx had drawn sweeping laws from a single factory he studied, then claimed they held for every trade on earth.
Marx had leaned on figures from old records he could not check, then built his whole system on those shaky sums.
Marx had assumed all workers labor at one fixed pace, then ignored every craftsman who worked faster or slower.
context: The fallacy is begging the question — assuming the very thing you set out to prove. Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk made the charge in 'Karl Marx and the Close of His System' (1896): Marx 'acts as one who, urgently desiring to bring a white ball out of an urn, takes care to secure this result by putting in white balls only.' His harder empirical point: real commodities do NOT trade in proportion to labor content — 'of necessity and permanently' — because competition equalizes profit rates across capital-heavy and labor-heavy industries. Source: Bohm-Bawerk, Karl Marx and the Close of His System (1896); Mises Institute.

question: In Plato's Symposium, the great philosopher Socrates takes his turn to speak in praise of love before the other guests at the party. But Socrates does something unexpected with his big moment. Rather than lecture the room as the wise expert, how does he present what he is about to say?
answer: As a lesson he was taught by a wise woman, which he only repeats
choices: As a lesson he was taught by a wise woman, which he only repeats
As the hard-won conclusion of his own years of careful reasoning
As a secret revealed to him directly in a dream by the god Eros
As the common wisdom that every Athenian already knows by heart
context: Socrates says he is merely relaying what Diotima of Mantinea, 'my instructress in the art of love,' once taught him (Symposium 201d, 211d). The most celebrated philosopher in Athens casts himself not as the expert but as the pupil who had to be taught about love -- by a woman. Source: Plato, Symposium 201d, 211d; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/plato-friendship); Jowett translation (gutenberg.org/files/1600).

question: The priestess Diotima describes love as a climb, and the climb begins when a young person is first drawn to one single beautiful body. That first crush is real and powerful, she grants. But in Diotima's teaching, what is this first attraction to one beautiful body actually meant to be?
answer: A first step to climb past, not a place to stay
choices: A first step to climb past, not a place to stay
The truest love a person will ever hope to find
A trap to flee and renounce as a shameful desire
Proof the body matters far more than the mind does
context: Diotima warns that a love resting on one body alone is 'shallow and fleeting': the desire for one beautiful body is only the lowest rung -- a real beginning, but one the lover must 'use as a step' and move beyond, not a final home and not something to be ashamed of (Symposium 210a). Source: Plato, Symposium 210a; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/plato-friendship); philosophybreak.com/articles/plato-scala-amoris.

question: The priestess Diotima presses Socrates with a hard question: what is love really FOR? It is not the beautiful thing itself we want, she says, but 'birth in beauty' -- we long to bring forth babies, or to bring forth grand ideas and noble deeds. In Diotima's answer, what deep human longing is love at bottom?
answer: A mortal creature's reach for immortality
choices: A mortal creature's reach for immortality
A bargain struck for comfort and protection
A sickness of the mind that must be cured
A debt that is owed to the one who is loved
context: Diotima defines love as 'the principle of immortality in a mortal creature' (Symposium 206b-207a): we beget children and noble works to leave a trace of ourselves behind, so at bottom love is the mortal's reach for the eternal. The rival views -- love as bargain, sickness, or debt -- are real positions other thinkers have held. Source: Plato, Symposium 206b-207a; Jowett translation (gutenberg.org/files/1600); LitCharts (litcharts.com/lit/the-symposium/204d-209e).

question: Diotima lays out love's climb as an ordered ascent. The lover starts with one beautiful body, then sees that all beautiful bodies share the same beauty. Once the lover has come to love every beautiful body, what does Diotima say is the very next, higher thing he should learn to love?
answer: The beauty of people's souls and minds
choices: The beauty of people's souls and minds
The beauty of music, art, and poetry
The beauty of gold and fine possessions
The beauty of one's own city and family
context: Diotima's order of ascent: one body, then all bodies, then beautiful SOULS, then beautiful laws and customs, then knowledge, and finally Beauty itself -- each lower rung 'used as a step only' toward the next (Symposium 210a-211c). After bodies, the lover learns to prize a fine soul above a fine face. Source: Plato, Symposium 210a-211c; LitCharts (litcharts.com/lit/the-symposium/210a-212a); Jowett translation (gutenberg.org/files/1600).

question: At the very top of love's climb, Diotima says, the lover at last glimpses Beauty itself -- and it turns out to be unlike every beautiful thing he admired on the way up to it. According to Diotima, what is the one quality that sets Beauty itself apart from every beautiful face, law, or idea below it?
answer: It is everlasting and the same, never fair one way then foul the next
choices: It is everlasting and the same, never fair one way then foul the next
It is the most beautiful living body any mortal will ever lay eyes on
It is a beauty that grows richer and fuller with each passing season
It is whatever a person's own city agrees is most beautiful and good
context: A beautiful face fades; a law admired in one city is scorned in another. By contrast Diotima calls Beauty itself 'beauty absolute, separate, simple, and everlasting' -- not waxing or waning, not fair at one time and foul at another, not fair to one person and foul to another (Symposium 211a-b). Unlike a face or a custom, it never changes and is not relative to anyone. Source: Plato, Symposium 211a-b; Jowett translation (gutenberg.org/files/1600); philosophybreak.com/articles/plato-scala-amoris.

question: For centuries Diotima's ascent of love has been nicknamed the 'ladder of love' -- the scala amoris in Latin -- and pictured as rungs climbing toward Beauty itself. Yet scholars point out something surprising about that famous nickname when set against Plato's actual Greek text. What is it?
answer: The word 'ladder' never actually appears in Plato's Greek
choices: The word 'ladder' never actually appears in Plato's Greek
Plato drew the ladder himself in the margin of the page
Plato borrowed the whole ladder image from an Egyptian rite
The ladder originally had exactly seven labeled rungs
context: The passage is traditionally called the 'scala amoris' (Latin for 'ladder of love'), but the literal word 'ladder' never appears in Plato's Greek -- the image is built from his metaphor of mounting 'as on steps' toward Beauty. The nickname is later readers' shorthand for his stair-climbing picture. Source: Academia.edu 'The Rites of Love: Scala Amoris' (academia.edu/14183570); LitCharts (litcharts.com/lit/the-symposium/symbols/ladder-staircase-ascent); philosophybreak.com/articles/plato-scala-amoris.

question: In Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, the prophet Zarathustra describes a future nobody he calls the "last man" -- so cozy, so shrunken, that the great questions no longer move him. Zarathustra hurls them at him anyway: What is love? What is creation? What is longing? What is a star? The last man has only one small response to all of it. What does he do?
answer: He blinks.
choices: He blinks.
He shrugs.
He yawns.
He smiles.
context: This is Nietzsche's signature image of the last man -- a soul so shrunk that wonder no longer registers, only a dull flutter of the eyelids. The text: "'What is love? What is creation? What is longing? What is a star?'--so asketh the last man, and blinketh." The blink IS the whole portrait. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Thomas Common translation), Zarathustra's Prologue Section 5 (Project Gutenberg).

question: In Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, the comfortable little "last man" boasts, "We have discovered happiness." He is proud of it -- he thinks he has solved how to live. Nietzsche says it back to him with contempt. By Nietzsche's account, how did the last man arrive at this happiness?
answer: He shrank what he wants until nothing is left to reach for
choices: He shrank what he wants until nothing is left to reach for
He learned to want only whatever the crowd around him wants
He filled his days with small pleasures so no hour felt empty
He numbed himself to pain until almost nothing could touch him
context: "'We have discovered happiness'--say the last men, and blink thereby." Nietzsche's point is that the last man did not win happiness by striving for it -- he manufactured it by lowering the target until there was nothing left to reach for, then declared victory. Trading every future greatness for being warm and safe right now. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Thomas Common translation), Zarathustra's Prologue Section 5 (Project Gutenberg).

question: In Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Zarathustra hangs a brutal label on the cozy, contented "last man": "the most despicable man." Yet this man is no tyrant and breaks no laws -- by his own lights he is doing just fine. So what is it about this satisfied little soul that Nietzsche finds so contemptible?
answer: He is so pleased with himself that he wishes to be nothing more
choices: He is so pleased with himself that he wishes to be nothing more
He is so afraid of any risk that he will never leave his comfort
He is so fond of his ease that he leaves the hard work to others
He is so sure he is right that he will not hear another argument
context: "There cometh the time of the most despicable man, who can no longer despise himself." Nietzsche's warning: the danger is not being bad, it is being so cozily satisfied that you have lost even the wish to be better -- a creature with no contempt left for its own smallness, and so no drive to surpass it. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Thomas Common translation), Zarathustra's Prologue Section 5 (Project Gutenberg).

question: On the 1651 cover of Thomas Hobbes' book Leviathan, a giant crowned king towers over a whole walled town, sword in hand. Look closely and his entire torso and arms are built out of more than three hundred tiny people, packed together like scales into one enormous body. Hobbes meant this picture to answer one question before you read a single word: where does the king's power come from?
answer: It rises up out of the people themselves, who make the ruler by joining together.
choices: It rises up out of the people themselves, who make the ruler by joining together.
It is handed down from God, who owes nothing to the people below.
It is seized by the strongest family, who hold the land by force.
It is inherited from an ancient order the people are simply born into.
context: This is Hobbes' social contract drawn as one image: the many literally merged into one sovereign body, the giant rising out of the very people he rules. The whole commonwealth answers 'what is a state?' before a word is read. Source: Wikipedia, 'Leviathan (Hobbes book)' — 'The torso and arms of the figure are composed of over three hundred persons'; the giant emerges from the landscape.

question: On the cover of Thomas Hobbes' Leviathan, the giant sovereign grips two things at once: a sword in one hand, and in the other a crosier, the curved staff a bishop carries. Most pictures of a king show only a sword or a sceptre. Hobbes put a fighting weapon and a holy staff in the same pair of hands on purpose. What was he claiming by that?
answer: One ruler must hold both worldly and holy power, so no church can stand against the king.
choices: One ruler must hold both worldly and holy power, so no church can stand against the king.
A wise king should guard the church but leave its rule to the bishops alone.
The sword is meant for foreign enemies and the staff for shepherding the poor.
Making war and keeping peace are the only two real duties a king ever has.
context: For Hobbes the sovereign alone commands earthly AND spiritual authority — there is no separate church power allowed to rival him. The page below the giant even splits into matching columns: castle versus church, crown versus a bishop's mitre, cannon versus the thunderbolts of excommunication. Source: Wikipedia, 'Leviathan (Hobbes book)' — 'the union of secular, and spiritual in the sovereign.'

question: Thomas Hobbes had a special copy of Leviathan made by hand on fine vellum as a gift for the future King Charles II, and its cover differs from the printed one. In the common printed book, every tiny person making up the giant's body turns away from us, facing up toward the king's head. In the king's private copy, those little bodies are drawn a strikingly different way. How?
answer: They are made of faces instead, every one looking outward straight at the viewer.
choices: They are made of faces instead, every one looking outward straight at the viewer.
They are made of soldiers instead, every one kneeling in toward the king.
They are made of skeletons instead, packed tightly beneath his great crown.
They are made of children instead, climbing in a chain up both his arms.
context: In the printed edition only the giant's own face looks out at you; the crowd shows their backs. In the 1651 manuscript Hobbes had prepared for Charles II, the body is composed of many faces, all gazing outward with a range of expressions — the people looking back at the reader. Source: Wikipedia, 'Leviathan (Hobbes book)' — the Charles II manuscript's 'body is also composed of many faces, all looking outwards from the body and with a range of expressions.'

question: Write down the sentence 'This sentence is false,' then try to settle whether it is true or false. What is the trouble?
answer: It settles at neither value, since claiming one forces it to be the other one
choices: It settles at neither value, since claiming one forces it to be the other one
It settles at true, the way most sentences we write down turn out to be true
It settles at false, no worse than any other plainly mistaken everyday claim
It settles at no value at all, since it is empty noise that asserts nothing
context: This is the Liar paradox, the sentence that talks about itself. As the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy puts it: if it is true, then it is false; conversely, if it is false, then it is true. Because each guess flips into the other, the sentence can be neither true nor false without immediately overturning itself. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Liar Paradox' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/liar-paradox/).

question: In 1913 Philip Jourdain printed two sentences on a card. On the front: 'The sentence on the OTHER side of this card is true.' On the back: 'The sentence on the other side is false.' Flip back and forth and you can never pin down which one is true. How can two such ordinary sentences spring the same trap as 'This sentence is false'?
answer: A ring of sentences each pointing to the next springs it, with none naming itself
choices: A ring of sentences each pointing to the next springs it, with none naming itself
One of the two cards must really be pointing at its own self after all this
The clash springs only from the reader muddling up which side is which
Printing the words onto a card is what makes those words stop being true
context: Jourdain's 'card paradox' shows the Liar does not need direct self-reference; a circle of references does the same job. Neither sentence refers to itself, yet together they form the same self-swallowing loop. Source: 'Card paradox' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_paradox), citing Philip Jourdain, 1913 — 'Neither of the sentences employs direct self-reference; instead this is a case of circular reference.'

question: Where the Liar says 'This sentence is false,' Kurt Goedel in 1931 built a mathematical statement that effectively says 'This statement has no proof.' He proved that no consistent system of arithmetic can ever prove this particular statement. So what must be true of any consistent system big enough to do arithmetic?
answer: Some statements it cannot prove are nonetheless true
choices: Some statements it cannot prove are nonetheless true
Every statement it cannot prove must be simply false
A new rule supplying the missing proof repairs the gap
A larger, stronger system could prove all of its truths
context: This is Goedel's first incompleteness theorem, and he built it on the very self-reference trick behind the Liar. Goedel wrote that 'there is also a close relationship with the "liar" antinomy... we are therefore confronted with a proposition that asserts its own unprovability.' Any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic must contain truths it can never prove. Source: Goedel, 'On Formally Undecidable Propositions...' (1931), quoted via Cambridge Core, Bulletin of Symbolic Logic, 'Goedel, Tarski, Church, and The Liar.'

question: A teacher leans over Marcus's desk and asks, "Have you stopped cheating on your tests?" Marcus has never cheated in his life, yet he freezes, unsure how to answer safely. What makes this question a trap?
answer: Whether he says yes or no, he admits he cheated at some point.
choices: The teacher already has proof, so any answer will convict him.
Whether he says yes or no, he admits he cheated at some point.
The question is too vague for any honest student to answer.
The teacher is angry and will not believe his reply either way.
context: This is the classic 'loaded' (or 'complex') question. The trick isn't in any answer — it's smuggled into the question itself before you open your mouth. Both 'yes' (I used to and stopped) and 'no' (I still do) concede the thing that was never proven: that he cheated at all. The textbook version is 'Have you stopped beating your wife?', where yes and no both admit you have a wife and once beat her. Source: fallacyfiles.org, 'Loaded Question'; Wikipedia, 'Loaded question'.

question: Lena is innocent, but her older brother grins and asks, "Have you stopped sneaking my snacks?" If she says "yes" she admits she used to; if she says "no" she admits she still does. What is her best reply?
answer: "I have never touched your snacks."
choices: "No, and you can't prove that I did."
"Yes, I promise I quit doing that."
"I have never touched your snacks."
"That is honestly none of your business."
context: The right move against a loaded question is to REJECT the hidden premise, not to answer it. fallacyfiles.org puts it exactly: the proper response is 'not to answer it directly, but to either refuse to answer or to explicitly reject the question.' Saying yes or no walks into the trap; 'you can't prove it' still concedes she does it; 'none of your business' sounds like hiding. Denying the smuggled assumption is the only reply that escapes. Source: fallacyfiles.org, 'Loaded Question'; Wikipedia, 'Loaded question'.

question: A prosecutor turns to the defendant and asks, "Did you smirk when you kicked the man?" The defendant never kicked anyone, but a plain "no" sounds like he only denies the smirk. His lawyer stands to object. What is the lawyer objecting to?
answer: The question treats the kick, which was never proven, as already established.
choices: The prosecutor is badgering the defendant with a hostile tone of voice.
The question asks about private feelings rather than about plain facts.
The prosecutor is asking about an act the whole jury already witnessed.
The question treats the kick, which was never proven, as already established.
context: In court the loaded question is the prosecutor's weapon, and the countermove is the objection 'assumes facts not in evidence' — the legal name for refusing a question's smuggled premise. 'Did you smirk when you kicked him?' can't be answered yes or no if you never kicked anyone at all. Source: ABA, 'How Courts Work: Cross Examination' (americanbar.org); corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Loaded question'.

question: An innkeeper eyes a traveler and demands, "Where did you hide the gold you stole?" The traveler stole nothing. The clever move is to break the demand into the separate questions hiding inside it. Which breakdown exposes the trick?
answer: Was any gold stolen? Did I take it? Where did I put it?
choices: Are you the innkeeper? Do you own gold? Why ask me?
Was any gold stolen? Did I take it? Where did I put it?
Is the gold valuable? Was it locked away? Who saw it?
Am I a traveler? Did I stay here? Will I pay you?
context: A loaded question is really several questions crammed into one and disguised so you can't answer them separately — its Latin name, 'plurium interrogationum', means 'of many questions.' The parliamentary defense is to 'divide the question': split the rigged single question back into the separate questions it was hiding, then answer or reject each on its own. The right split surfaces the smuggled claims (gold was stolen; the traveler took it); the others chase harmless side-points. Source: fallacyfiles.org, 'Loaded Question'; Wikipedia, 'Loaded question'.

question: Around 300 BC the philosopher Alexinus tried to trap Menedemus by asking whether he had stopped beating his father. Menedemus would not pick "yes" or "no." What did he actually reply?
answer: "I was not beating him and have not left off."
choices: "First prove that I ever once beat him."
"My father lives and is well, go ask him."
"I was not beating him and have not left off."
"A son's discipline is no crime to confess."
context: Recorded by Diogenes Laertius (Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, Book II.17), this is the oldest known person to spot and refuse a loaded question. By denying BOTH halves at once — he wasn't beating his father AND hadn't left off — Menedemus rejected the whole smuggled premise instead of choosing a side of the trap. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book II.17 (Perseus Digital Library).

question: In the 2000 South Carolina primary, callers posing as pollsters asked voters whether they would be less likely to back John McCain if they knew he had fathered an illegitimate black child. McCain had done no such thing. What did the fake poll actually accomplish?
answer: It planted a smear by phrasing a lie as a settled fact.
choices: It measured how many voters already distrusted McCain.
It planted a smear by phrasing a lie as a settled fact.
It gathered honest opinions about McCain's family life.
It was research to find McCain's real weak spots.
context: This is a 'push poll' — a fake survey meant to plant a smear, not measure opinion — and it works by loading a question. The 'fact' was a lie (it twisted McCain's adopted daughter from Bangladesh), but asking whether it would change your vote made it sound already established. Source: Ballotpedia, 'Push polling'; corroborated by Wikipedia, 'Loaded question'.

question: Asking "Did you enjoy the cake?" assumes you ate cake, yet nobody calls it a dirty trick. Asking "Have you stopped lying to me?" of an honest person clearly is one. What separates the fair question from the foul one?
answer: The hidden assumption is one the person being asked actually disputes.
choices: The foul question is the one that is phrased as a yes-or-no question.
The foul question is the one asked by someone who wants to win.
The fair question is the one about a smaller and lighter subject.
The hidden assumption is one the person being asked actually disputes.
context: A question that presupposes something is NOT automatically a fallacy. Wikipedia: 'Only when some of these presuppositions are not necessarily agreed to by the person who is asked the question does the argument containing them become fallacious.' If everyone agrees you ate cake, the assumption is harmless; the trap only springs when the smuggled claim is one you'd contest. Source: Wikipedia, 'Loaded question'.

question: A reporter asks a mayor, "Will you keep wasting our taxes on this project?" The mayor, who denies the project is waste, refuses the question and challenges the word "wasting." The reporter immediately tells viewers the mayor "dodged the question." Why is that accusation what makes the tactic so effective?
answer: Refusing the smuggled premise can be spun to look like guilty evasion.
choices: The mayor should have simply answered yes or no to stay credible.
Reporters are allowed to ask anything, so refusing one looks rude.
Refusing the smuggled premise can be spun to look like guilty evasion.
The mayor admitted the waste the moment he repeated the reporter's word.
context: There's a built-in counter-trap. Wikipedia notes 'the asker may respond to a challenge by accusing the one who answers of dodging the question' — so the correct move (rejecting the loaded premise) can be made to LOOK like evasion, which is exactly why the tactic is effective. Calling the spending 'wasting' is itself the smuggled, unproven judgment, a form the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy classes under begging the question. Source: Wikipedia, 'Loaded question'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Fallacies'.

question: A town runs a fair raffle: 1,000 tickets, exactly one winner. You hold ticket #738. The odds it loses are 999 to 1, so it seems reasonable to just believe, flat out, that yours loses. But the SAME reasoning works for every ticket: each holder may believe their own loses. What goes wrong once you line up all 1,000 of those individually-reasonable beliefs side by side?
answer: Together they claim no ticket wins at all, though one of them must
choices: Together they claim no ticket wins at all, though one of them must
Together they prove the raffle was rigged against every player at once
Each one quietly assumes the holder peeked at the winning number early
Each one ignores that the true odds shift after the first ticket is drawn
context: This is the Lottery Paradox. Each belief 'this ticket loses' is overwhelmingly likely and looks rational on its own, but together they say no ticket wins, contradicting what you already know: one must. Henry E. Kyburg Jr. introduced it in his 1961 book 'Probability and the Logic of Rational Belief', using a fair 1,000-ticket lottery. His deeper point is general: pick any 'very likely' threshold and a big enough lottery breaks it. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemic Paradoxes'; Wikipedia, 'Lottery paradox' (Kyburg 1961).

question: A scholar finishes a long book. She has checked every sentence and believes each one is true. Yet in the preface she writes the familiar line: any mistakes that remain are mine alone. She means it, too: across hundreds of pages, she is sure at least one error slipped through somewhere. So she believes every single sentence, and also believes the book as a whole is not error-free. How do those two beliefs stand together?
answer: Each is reasonable, yet the two cannot both be fully true
choices: Each is reasonable, yet the two cannot both be fully true
Each is false, since a careful scholar makes no errors at all
One must be a lie, because nobody really believes their own book
One quietly cancels the other, leaving no real belief at all
context: This is the Preface Paradox, named by D.C. Makinson in 'The Paradox of the Preface' (Analysis, 1965). It is the Lottery's quieter twin and arguably sharper, since it needs no lottery and no probability rule at all: ordinary scholarly humility alone produces the clash. The humble disclaimer is the mark of an honest scholar, yet it is exactly what makes her beliefs formally inconsistent. Makinson built it from Raymond Wilder's 1952 'Introduction to the Foundations of Mathematics'; its 1982 reprint carried three pages of errata, vindicating Wilder's humility. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemic Paradoxes'; Wikipedia, 'Preface paradox'.

question: Faced with the raffle puzzle, where a stack of reasonable beliefs about single tickets somehow piles up into a flat contradiction, one philosopher offered a bold fix. He said you may keep believing, one at a time, that ticket #1 loses, that ticket #2 loses, and so on through all 1,000, and stay perfectly rational. The price is one tempting step you must always refuse. Which step is it?
answer: Merging the separate beliefs into a single all-in-one belief
choices: Merging the separate beliefs into a single all-in-one belief
Treating any of those very likely beliefs as something you flatly know
Letting a belief about one ticket raise your confidence in the next
Updating the odds each time another losing ticket gets revealed
context: The philosopher is Henry E. Kyburg Jr. The puzzle is really a forced choice among three rules that all feel right: accept what is very likely true; never accept what you know is contradictory; and if you accept two things separately, you may accept them bundled together. The lottery shows all three cannot stand. Kyburg rejected the bundling rule (the 'conjunction' or agglomeration step) and chose to tolerate joint inconsistency: a rational mind may hold a pile of beliefs that can't all be true, so long as it never combines them into one self-contradicting belief. Other escapes in the literature include paraconsistent logics, which hold a contradiction without it 'exploding', and probabilistic restatements (Lacey & New) that recast beliefs as degrees of confidence. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemic Paradoxes'; Wikipedia, 'Lottery paradox' and 'Preface paradox'.

question: Ancient Chinese thinkers held that Heaven grants a ruler the right to rule — but only on one condition. As long as a king governs justly, Heaven backs him. The radical twist in this doctrine, the Mandate of Heaven, concerned what happens when a king turns cruel. What follows?
answer: Heaven withdraws its backing, and the people then have the right to overthrow him
choices: Heaven withdraws its backing, and the people then have the right to overthrow him
Heaven sends a flood to drown his lands but leaves his throne untouched
Heaven strips his eldest son of the crown but lets the king himself rule on
Heaven curses his family line so his grandsons are born sickly and weak
context: Tianming ('Heaven's command') made legitimacy CONDITIONAL: a tyrant forfeits Heaven's backing and the people may rightfully remove him. It is one of history's earliest 'right of revolution' ideas, predating Western versions by over two thousand years. Source: Wikipedia, Mandate of Heaven (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandate_of_Heaven); Britannica, Tianming (britannica.com/topic/tianming).

question: Under the Mandate of Heaven, a Chinese king governed knowing that the natural world reported on his virtue. A famine, a flood, a drought, an earthquake — each could be read by his people not as bad luck but as a verdict. What were such disasters taken to mean?
answer: A sign that Heaven was displeased and the king might be losing the mandate
choices: A sign that Heaven was displeased and the king might be losing the mandate
A sign that the king should marry again to bring new fortune to the realm
A sign that the harvest gods wanted a grander temple built in their honor
A sign that the dead kings of old wished for fresh offerings at their tombs
context: Famines, floods, droughts, earthquakes and especially solar eclipses were read as omens that Heaven was displeased — early warnings the mandate was slipping. This tied a king's personal virtue directly to the welfare of the realm and gave the people a recognized signal that rebellion might now be righteous. Source: Britannica, Tianming (britannica.com/topic/tianming); World History Encyclopedia, Mandate of Heaven (worldhistory.org/Mandate_of_Heaven/).

question: In the legends of how the last Shang king, Di Xin, lost Heaven's favor, his appetites grew monstrous. Storytellers gave him one unforgettable indulgence built on his palace grounds — and in 1999 archaeologists at Yanshi unearthed a great structure matching the tale. What did the legend say he built?
answer: A reservoir of wine with trees of hung roasted meat, where he floated drinking in canoes
choices: A reservoir of wine with trees of hung roasted meat, where he floated drinking in canoes
A tower of solid gold so tall that its peak was said to scrape the underside of the clouds
A maze of bronze mirrors in which he trapped and starved the ministers who dared defy him
A vast walled park of rare beasts brought from every corner of the realm for him to hunt
context: The 'wine pool and meat forest' (jiuchi roulin): a stone pool filled with wine, an island of roasted-meat skewers hung on trees, where Di Xin and his concubine Daji floated in canoes drinking straight from the pool. Strikingly, a large stone pool matching the description was excavated at Yanshi, Henan in 1999. Told here as legend. Source: Wikipedia, Di Xin (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Di_Xin); Ancient Origins (ancient-origins.net/history/chinese-emperor-built-lake-wine-and-forest-meat-0010076).

question: The Mandate of Heaven raised a hard question: if Heaven decides who may rule, how does Heaven announce that a king has lost its favor? Heaven never speaks aloud. Mencius answered by quoting an old line from the Book of Documents that located Heaven's voice in one place. Where?
answer: In the people: Heaven sees as the people see, and Heaven hears as the people hear
choices: In the people: Heaven sees as the people see, and Heaven hears as the people hear
In the stars: Heaven writes its judgment in the comets that cross the night sky
In the priests: Heaven whispers its will to the diviners who read the cracked bones
In the dreams: Heaven warns the king himself through visions sent in his sleep
context: Mencius quoted the Great Declaration: 'Heaven sees as my people see; Heaven hears as my people hear.' Heaven has no separate voice — popular suffering, revolt and famine ARE Heaven speaking, which made the people the instrument by which Heaven transfers the mandate. The quoted scriptural line is traditional/legendary. Source: Mencius 5A.5 quoting the Shujing (Book of Documents), Tai Shi chapter; IEP (iep.utm.edu/mencius/).

question: At the Battle of Muye around 1046 BC, King Wu of Zhou marched on the Shang capital with the smaller army. The tyrant Di Xin had far more soldiers — but he had armed roughly 170,000 slaves and conscripts who loathed him. As the two hosts met, those troops did something that doomed their own king. What?
answer: They turned their spears upside-down and defected, opening a clear path to the capital
choices: They turned their spears upside-down and defected, opening a clear path to the capital
They threw down their weapons and fled into the hills before a single blow was struck
They demanded more gold to fight and stood idle once the king's treasury had run dry
They begged the oncoming invaders for mercy and were cut down where they knelt to die
context: Rather than fight, many of Di Xin's own conscripts turned their spears upside-down and defected mid-battle, opening a path to the capital. The mass desertion of his own troops became the perfect image of a tyrant whom even his soldiers knew Heaven had abandoned. Battle details are traditional. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Muye (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Muye).  (Legend.)

question: When his army collapsed at Muye, the Shang tyrant Di Xin fled back to his treasure-tower, the Deer Terrace. Cornered and certain of capture, he made a final choice meant to deny his enemy the prize of his person. Robed in his finest jewels, what did he do?
answer: He set the tower alight and burned himself alive among his hoarded treasures
choices: He set the tower alight and burned himself alive among his hoarded treasures
He swallowed a draught of poison and was found slumped upon his golden throne
He flung the royal seals into the river so no conqueror could ever claim them
He surrendered and knelt before King Wu, begging to be spared as a common man
context: Di Xin draped himself in his finest jewels and robes on the Deer Terrace (Lutai) and burned himself alive rather than be captured. King Wu then opened the royal granaries to feed the starving people and redistributed the tyrant's hoarded wealth — Heaven's mandate visibly passing to the merciful. Told as legend. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Muye and Di Xin (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Di_Xin).

question: Mencius, a court philosopher in 4th-century-BC China, ranked the three parts of a state — the common people, the state's own altars of grain and soil, and the ruler — from most precious to least. His order would have stunned the kings who heard it, for it put their throne in a place no king expected. Which order did he give?
answer: The people are worth most, the altars of the state next, and the ruler counts for least
choices: The people are worth most, the altars of the state next, and the ruler counts for least
The ruler is worth most, the people of the land next, and the altars count for least
The altars are worth most, the ruler of the realm next, and the people count for least
The ruler is worth most, the altars of the state next, and the people count for least
context: Mencius 7B.14: 'The people are to be valued most, the altars of grain and soil next, and the ruler least' (min wei gui, sheji ci zhi, jun wei qing). For a court philosopher to put the common people ABOVE the king was the heart of the conditional-legitimacy idea — the throne exists to serve the people, not the reverse. Source: Mencius 7B.14, via IEP (iep.utm.edu/mencius/).

question: Mencius argued that a cruel king is not just wicked but self-defeating, and he reached for images from nature to prove it. He said the people turn to a kind ruler the way water flows in one direction, and that tyrants actually drive subjects into a rival's arms — as a hunting otter or hawk drives its prey toward cover. Which way did he say the water flows?
answer: Downward — the people flow to a benevolent ruler as surely as water runs downhill
choices: Downward — the people flow to a benevolent ruler as surely as water runs downhill
Upward — a great king draws his people to him as the sun draws the morning mist
Outward — the people scatter from a kingdom the way a river spreads into the sea
In circles — the people return to a just king as a stream winds back to its spring
context: Mencius 4A.9: 'The people turn to a benevolent ruler as water flows downward.' His twist: tyrants like Jie and Zhou actually HELPED the virtuous kings who replaced them, 'as the otter drives the fish into deep water, and the hawk drives the little birds into the thickets.' A cruel ruler herds his own people straight into a rival's arms — misrule is self-defeating. Source: Mencius 4A.9 (nothingistic.org/library/mencius/mencius26.html).

question: In 1394 the founder of the Ming dynasty, Zhu Yuanzhang — himself a peasant who had rebelled his way to the throne — read Mencius's passages defending the overthrow of tyrants and grew alarmed. Fearing the ideas could be turned against him, he ordered a drastic act against the long-dead philosopher's legacy. What did he do?
answer: He had Mencius's tablet pulled from the Confucian temple and the dangerous passages cut
choices: He had Mencius's tablet pulled from the Confucian temple and the dangerous passages cut
He banned the teaching of Mencius in every school across the empire on pain of death
He had every copy of Mencius's writings gathered into the palace square and burned
He declared himself the rightful heir of Mencius and ordered shrines built in his name
context: Zhu Yuanzhang ordered Mencius's spirit-tablet removed from the imperial Confucian temple and commissioned an expurgated 'Mengzi jiewen' cutting about 85 passages — including 'the people are most important' (7B.14) and the 'mere fellow' regicide line (1B.8). The censorship didn't last; the full text outlived the abridgement. Source: Satyori, Mencius (satyori.com/historical-figures/mencius/); University of Washington Manifold, The Scholar and the State.

question: King Xuan of Qi tried to trap the philosopher Mencius: the founders Tang and King Wu KILLED their own kings, the tyrants Jie and Zhou — is it not monstrous for a subject to murder his sovereign? Mencius refused the framing. By what argument did he answer?
answer: A man who outrages benevolence and righteousness is no longer a king but a mere robber and ruffian, so striking him down is execution, not the killing of a sovereign
choices: A man who outrages benevolence and righteousness is no longer a king but a mere robber and ruffian, so striking him down is execution, not the killing of a sovereign
A subject owes total obedience to his sovereign no matter how cruel, and must endure tyranny while petitioning Heaven for mercy rather than ever taking up arms
A king once crowned keeps his title for life, so the only lawful remedy against a tyrant is to flee his lands and let Heaven punish him in its own time
A ruler and his subjects are bound by a contract both sign, and either side may dissolve it the moment the other breaks a written term of the bargain
context: Mencius 1B.8: 'He who outrages benevolence is called a robber; he who outrages righteousness is called a ruffian... I have heard of the cutting off of the FELLOW Zhou, but I have NOT heard of the putting a sovereign to death.' The move: a tyrant has stopped being a king at all — just a criminal — so killing him is execution, not regicide. Source: Mencius 1B.8, via Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/mengzi/liang-hui-wang-ii) and IEP (iep.utm.edu/mencius/).

question: A student asked Mencius whether the sage-king Yao had simply GIVEN the empire to his worthy successor Shun, the way a man hands a gift to a friend. Mencius said no — a throne is not a private possession one ruler can bestow on another by personal favor. So who, he insisted, actually conferred the empire on Shun?
answer: Heaven conferred it, and human beings conferred it — never Yao by his own private gift
choices: Heaven conferred it, and human beings conferred it — never Yao by his own private gift
Yao conferred it by royal decree, for the empire was his alone to bestow as he pleased
The ministers of the court conferred it after weighing every claimant's fitness to rule
Shun conferred it upon himself by seizing the throne once the old king had grown weak
context: Mencius 5A.5: asked whether Yao 'gave' the empire to Shun, Mencius answered 'HEAVEN gave it to him; HUMAN BEINGS gave it to him.' No ruler can hand the throne to a successor by personal whim; legitimacy must be ratified by Heaven AND accepted by the people. Power is a trust, never private property. Source: Mencius 5A.5, via IEP (iep.utm.edu/mencius/).

question: John Stuart Mill asked a hard question: when may a free society rightly use force to make a grown person stop doing something? Picture a town council that bans a pamphlet simply because its argument deeply offends and upsets many residents. Mill would say the council had no right to ban it. By Mill's rule, what is the ONLY thing that can justify using force against a person against their will?
answer: Preventing that person from harming other people.
choices: Preventing that person from harming other people.
Protecting the community from arguments it finds offensive.
Shielding widely shared beliefs from public ridicule.
Stopping the spread of ideas that the majority rejects.
context: This is Mill's 'harm principle,' the frame around his whole book On Liberty: 'the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.' Merely offending or persuading people is not 'harm' in this sense, which is exactly why opinion gets the widest protection of all. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 1; Wikipedia: On Liberty (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Liberty).

question: When the Roman Catholic Church considers declaring someone a saint, it does not simply let the praise pile up. By long tradition it appoints an official whose entire job is to argue AGAINST the candidate, digging up every doubt and objection before the honor can be granted. John Stuart Mill pointed to this as proof that even the highest claims should face a designated opponent. What is this appointed objector traditionally called?
answer: the devil's advocate
choices: the devil's advocate
the keeper of the seal
the grand inquisitor
the public censor
context: Mill wrote that 'the most intolerant of churches, the Roman Catholic Church, even at the canonisation of a saint, admits, and listens patiently to, a devil's advocate.' The Latin name for the office was advocatus diaboli, and this real Church role is the literal origin of the everyday phrase 'to play devil's advocate.' Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).  (Legend.)

question: John Stuart Mill imagined the most lopsided disagreement possible: every single person in the world holds one opinion, except for ONE lone individual who disagrees. Surely, you might think, the whole of humanity may simply silence that one stubborn dissenter. Mill said no. The size of the majority, he argued, changes nothing about the matter. Why may the many not rightfully silence the one?
answer: Humanity has no more right to silence the one than the one would have to silence humanity.
choices: Humanity has no more right to silence the one than the one would have to silence humanity.
The lone dissenter is more likely than the whole crowd to be right.
Silencing a single person is far too trivial a matter to bother with.
One quiet voice is far too weak to endanger what everyone believes.
context: Mill's exact words: 'If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind.' The right to speak does not depend on being in the majority, or even on turning out to be correct. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: John Stuart Mill made a claim that surprises people: even an opinion that is FALSE is worth letting people hear and argue for. Suppose a community could painlessly erase one mistaken idea, so no one ever encountered it again. Mill insisted this would still be a loss, because keeping a false view alive and openly argued actually does something FOR the truth. What does Mill say a living, openly-argued falsehood does for the truth?
answer: It forces the truth to be defended, keeping its meaning sharp and clearly understood.
choices: It forces the truth to be defended, keeping its meaning sharp and clearly understood.
It distracts attention away from the truth, so the truth is gradually forgotten.
It makes the truth seem more certain by comparison, ending all further debate.
It has no effect on the truth at all, which stands firm whether challenged or not.
context: This is Mill's most counter-intuitive move. He argued that silencing even an error robs us of 'the clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error.' A truth with no live opponent goes soft; the false view, by forcing a defense, keeps the true one understood rather than merely repeated. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: John Stuart Mill examined what happens to a TRUE belief that everyone accepts and no one ever has to defend. Picture a community where a correct idea is so settled that arguing against it feels pointless: the schools teach it, but no student ever meets anyone who really opposes it. Mill asked what becomes of such a belief over the years. According to Mill, what happens to a true belief that is never tested against a live opponent?
answer: It hardens into a dead slogan that people repeat but can no longer actually defend.
choices: It hardens into a dead slogan that people repeat but can no longer actually defend.
It grows stronger and more certain, since no one is left to doubt it at all.
It quietly changes into a different belief better suited to the new times.
It stays exactly as powerful as a belief that people once had to fight for.
context: Mill's signature contrast: 'However true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.' He even said an unexamined belief falls into 'the deep slumber of a decided opinion' -- a sleeping truth that has no real power over how anyone actually lives. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: The phrase 'the marketplace of ideas' is how Americans name the principle that truth should win by open argument, not by force. People often credit it to Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, who defended the idea powerfully in a famous 1919 Supreme Court dissent, writing that the best test of truth is its 'power... to get itself accepted in the competition of the market.' But there is a catch about that famous phrase itself. What is the surprising truth about the words 'the marketplace of ideas'?
answer: Holmes never actually wrote them; later judges coined the exact phrase decades afterward.
choices: Holmes never actually wrote them; later judges coined the exact phrase decades afterward.
Holmes wrote them, but only in a private letter that he never published.
John Stuart Mill wrote them first, and Holmes copied the phrase word for word.
They first appeared in the very law that Holmes was arguing against.
context: Holmes (dissenting in Abrams v. United States, 1919) wrote 'free trade in ideas' and 'competition of the market,' echoing Mill sixty years later -- but never the exact words 'marketplace of ideas.' That phrase shows up in later Supreme Court opinions, such as Justice Brennan in Lamont v. Postmaster General (1965): 'It would be a barren marketplace of ideas that had only sellers and no buyers.' The famous name is younger than the idea. Source: MTSU First Amendment Encyclopedia, 'Marketplace of Ideas' and 'Lamont v. Postmaster General' (firstamendment.mtsu.edu).

question: John Stuart Mill noticed that every time authorities ban an opinion on the grounds that it is simply false, they are quietly assuming something about THEMSELVES that they have no way to prove. Mill called this the fatal flaw in all censorship: to forbid a view as too false to be heard, the censor must be taking for granted a certain thing about his own mind. What, according to Mill, is the censor secretly assuming about himself?
answer: That his own judgment could never be mistaken.
choices: That his own judgment could never be mistaken.
That he alone is wise enough to choose for everyone else.
That his power gives him the right to decide what is true.
That he has already heard the strongest case for the other side.
context: Scholars call this Mill's 'infallibility argument.' To forbid an opinion as false, you must be certain you could never yourself be wrong about it -- and no human being or government actually has that certainty. The catch is that the censor almost never notices he is making such a sweeping claim about his own mind. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Stuart Mill (plato.stanford.edu/entries/mill/); J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2.

question: John Stuart Mill reminded his readers of two men whom history honors among its greatest moral teachers: Socrates, condemned by an Athenian court as an impious 'corrupter of youth,' and a teacher put to death on a hill called Calvary as a 'blasphemer.' Mill pointed to these two executions to make an unsettling claim about the kind of people who carry out such killings. What did Mill say was true of the authorities who condemned both Socrates and the man at Calvary?
answer: They were respectable men who sincerely believed they were doing right.
choices: They were respectable men who sincerely believed they were doing right.
They were cruel tyrants who knew full well the charges were false.
They acted in secret, afraid that the public would try to stop them.
They were foreign occupiers indifferent to the local faith and law.
context: Mill's point is more disturbing than 'bad men did a bad thing.' He wrote that 'mankind can hardly be too often reminded, that there was once a man named Socrates,' lawfully convicted by his own countrymen, and he paired it with 'the event which took place on Calvary' -- a man put to death 'as a blasphemer.' Both were killed by sincere, law-abiding authorities who were certain of their own righteousness, which is exactly why suppression is so dangerous. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: A knight points at a masked stranger and reasons: "I know my own brother. This masked man I do not recognize. Therefore this masked man is not my brother." In truth the stranger IS his brother behind the mask, so both starting claims hold true while the conclusion comes out false. Where exactly does the reasoning break?
answer: Not recognizing the man is a fact about what is going on in his own head, not about who the person there really is
choices: Not recognizing the man is a fact about what is going on in his own head, not about who the person there really is
Claiming to know his own brother overreaches, since no one knows a face so well they could never once be fooled
Leaping from not knowing the man right now to his never being the brother trades a passing blank for a fixed fact
Reading the man through a mask that hides his face argues from missing evidence as though it were the whole picture
context: This is the masked-man fallacy (the label belongs here in context, not in the answer). The slip: a fact about what you RECOGNIZE or KNOW got smuggled in as a fact about the man HIMSELF. What you believe about a thing is not a property OF the thing, so it cannot be substituted into claims about who the thing is — the masked man and the brother can be one and the same person; the difference lives only in the knower's head. Source: Wikipedia, 'Masked-man fallacy' (opening definition; 'The premises may be true, yet the conclusion is false if Claus is the masked man and the speaker does not know that').

question: Lois Lane is certain Superman can fly and just as certain Clark Kent cannot — yet Superman and Clark are the same man. Someone wants to argue from her two beliefs to a conclusion. Only ONE conclusion is actually valid here. Which is it?
answer: Lois believes Superman is not Clark Kent
choices: Lois believes Superman is not Clark Kent
Superman and Clark Kent must be two different people
Lois is simply mistaken that Clark Kent cannot fly
Whether Clark can fly has no fixed answer at all
context: It does NOT follow that Superman and Clark are different people — they're the same man. The only thing that validly follows keeps Lois on the OUTSIDE: 'Lois believes Superman is not Clark.' The fix is to never reach inside someone's belief and swap one name for another that happens to refer to the same thing — belief is referentially opaque, which is exactly where the masked man hides. Source: Wikipedia, 'Masked-man fallacy' (Superman/Clark Kent example; invalid 'Therefore, Superman and Clark Kent are not the same person' vs. the only consistent conclusion, the belief with Lois kept outside).

question: René Descartes argued: "I can doubt that my body exists, but I cannot doubt that my mind exists; therefore my mind is not my body." Critics say his reasoning rests on the very same slip behind the masked man. What is the flaw they point to?
answer: Being doubtable by Descartes is a fact about his own mind, not a genuine feature of the body it could pry loose
choices: Being doubtable by Descartes is a fact about his own mind, not a genuine feature of the body it could pry loose
He never actually established that his own mind exists, so the whole argument rests on nothing
Doubt and certainty are mere feelings, and feelings have no place inside a serious philosophical proof
Anyone who can doubt that a body exists is equally able to doubt that any mind exists at all
context: The sound rule he leaned on is Leibniz's Law (the indiscernibility of identicals): if two things are identical, they share all their REAL properties. 'Being doubtable by Descartes' is not a real property of the body — it's a state of the observer — so feeding it into Leibniz's Law to separate mind from body is the masked-man fallacy wearing a metaphysical robe. Strip out the doubting and the argument that mind ≠ body collapses. Source: Wikipedia, 'Identity of indiscernibles' (notes the masked-man problem 'creates a problem for Descartes' argument'; the standard intensional-property objection to mind-body dualism via doubt).

question: The philosopher Hegel imagines two strangers meeting for the first time, each demanding the other admit he matters. Neither will back down, and the standoff turns violent. Hegel's surprising claim is that a single trait settles who walks away the master. According to Hegel, the master is which of these?
answer: The one who will risk his life rather than yield
choices: The one who will risk his life rather than yield
The one who strikes the hardest and the fastest
The one who stays the coldest and most calculating
The one who has the most to gain from winning
context: For Hegel the whole hierarchy is born from who was willing to risk dying: the one who fears death submits and becomes the bondsman (slave); the one willing to die becomes the lord (master). 'It is only through staking one's life that freedom is won' (Phenomenology of Spirit, trans. A.V. Miller, 'Lordship and Bondage,' paragraph 187).

question: In 1833 a sixteen-year-old enslaved boy named Frederick Douglass had been beaten for months by a slave-breaker, Edward Covey. One morning Douglass refused to take it and fought back, and the two grappled for nearly two hours. Douglass later wrote that something happened to Covey during that fight that no one expected of the powerful master. What did Covey do?
answer: He trembled like a leaf in Douglass's grip
choices: He trembled like a leaf in Douglass's grip
He called three other men over to help him
He sold Douglass off to a far worse plantation
He pretended afterward that nothing had happened
context: It is a real-life echo of Hegel's reversal: Hegel said it would be the slave who trembled in mortal fear, yet here the MASTER 'trembled like a leaf.' Douglass introduces the scene, 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man,' and for the six months after, Covey 'never laid the weight of his finger upon me in anger.' (Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845, Ch. X, Project Gutenberg.)

question: A master sits back and is waited on, while the slave he owns does all the labor: growing the food, building the house, making every tool the master uses. The master never learns to do any of it himself. Over the years, who has quietly become dependent on whom?
answer: The master depends on the slave for everything he has
choices: The master depends on the slave for everything he has
Neither one really depends on the other at all
The slave depends on the master for protection and orders
Both depend equally on the land they happen to share
context: This is the heart of Hegel's dialectic, and its great twist: the master wins, but he comes to depend on the slave for both labor AND recognition, while the slave, forced to WORK on the world, builds real skill and grows toward genuine independence. Who depends on whom gets flipped. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraphs 190-196.)

question: The philosopher Hegel argues that you cannot really become a full self all by yourself on a desert island. To be certain of who you are, he says, you need one specific thing that only another person can give you. What is the thing he says a self can only get from another self?
answer: To be recognized and acknowledged as someone who matters
choices: To be recognized and acknowledged as someone who matters
To be given enough food, shelter, and basic safety
To be taught a language so it can finally think clearly
To be protected from the constant fear of being alone
context: This is why the encounter has to become a struggle in the first place. Hegel: 'Self-consciousness exists in and for itself... it exists only in being acknowledged,' and at its fullest, 'They recognize themselves as mutually recognizing one another.' Identity is something two people do to each other. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraphs 178 and 184.)

question: A king forces a servant he considers worthless to bow and call him great. The king wanted to feel truly important, and the servant does exactly as told. Yet the king feels strangely empty afterward. Why does this forced praise fail to satisfy the very thing the king was after?
answer: Praise only satisfies when it comes from a respected equal
choices: Praise only satisfies when it comes from a respected equal
The servant clearly did not mean a single word of it
The king should have wanted to be feared, not praised
No amount of praise is ever enough for a proud man
context: Hegel's exact verdict on the master's prize is that it is 'a recognition that is one-sided and unequal' (paragraph 191). Because the acknowledgment is forced and given by someone the master treats as a non-person, it can never meet his deepest need, to be recognized by an equal. The master is trapped: the only one who could give him real recognition is the equal he just turned into a slave.

question: Hegel compares two people facing a block of wood. The master simply burns it for warmth, uses it up, and moves on to the next thing. The slave is made to carve it into a chair, holding back the urge to just use it up. Hegel says the slave gains something from this that the master never can. What does the slave gain by shaping the wood instead of consuming it?
answer: His own will becomes stamped permanently into the world
choices: His own will becomes stamped permanently into the world
A clever carving trade he can keep hidden from the master
A short, welcome rest from his master's constant demands
The simple warmth of having done an honest day's labor
context: Hegel calls the slave's work 'desire held in check': instead of devouring the object, he forms and shapes it, so his will gets pressed into something that lasts. 'Work forms and shapes the thing,' and through it 'consciousness, qua worker, comes to see in the independent being of the object its own independence.' The master only consumes and is left with nothing. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraph 195.)

question: Hegel borrows a famous line, 'the fear of the lord is the beginning of wisdom,' but he twists its meaning. By 'lord' he means death itself, which the slave faced in terror during the struggle. Hegel argues this raw terror was not simply cowardice in the slave. What does he claim that fear actually did for the slave?
answer: It shook everything fixed in him loose, making real change possible
choices: It shook everything fixed in him loose, making real change possible
It hardened him into someone who could endure almost any suffering
It woke a burning hatred that would one day fuel an open revolt
It taught him the cool patience to outlast a far stronger master
context: Hegel redirects the line from Proverbs: the slave 'has experienced the fear of death, the absolute Lord. In that experience it has been quite unmanned, has trembled in every fibre of its being, and everything solid and stable has been shaken to its foundations.' That total dissolution of everything he took for granted is, paradoxically, the seed of his freedom. Fear plus work together are what free him. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraphs 194-195.)

question: Hegel works through the master-and-slave scene to its shocking conclusion. The master thought he was the independent, essential one and the slave was nothing. But Hegel says the master's real nature, his hidden truth, turns out to lie somewhere he would never expect. Whose existence does Hegel say the master's truth actually turns out to be?
answer: The slave's, whose worked-on world the master secretly leans on
choices: The slave's, whose worked-on world the master secretly leans on
His own, confirmed at last by finally winning the fight
The other masters', who alone can see him as a true equal
No one's, since a master answers to nobody but himself
context: Hegel's words are devastating: the master's supposed truth collapses, since 'his truth is in reality the unessential consciousness,' and then, 'The truth of the independent consciousness is accordingly the servile consciousness of the bondsman.' The truth of the master is the slave. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraphs 192-193.) Through his work the slave 'acquires a mind of his own' (paragraph 196).

question: After Frederick Douglass fought off the slave-breaker Covey, Covey never raised a hand against him again, though Douglass remained legally enslaved for years more. Douglass called that fight the turning point of his life. In his own words, the day had passed forever when he could be a slave in a particular sense. In which sense did Douglass say he could never again be a slave?
answer: A slave in fact, however long he stayed one in form
choices: A slave in fact, however long he stayed one in form
A slave in chains, now that he had learned to fight
A slave in name, having earned the master's respect
A slave in danger, having proven he could fight back
context: The lived version of Hegel's reversal, won by refusing to be a mere thing. Douglass: 'This battle with Mr. Covey was the turning-point in my career as a slave. It rekindled the few expiring embers of freedom... I now resolved that, however long I might remain a slave in form, the day had passed forever when I could be a slave in fact.' (Narrative, 1845, Ch. X, Project Gutenberg.)

question: The French thinker Alexandre Kojeve, lecturing in 1930s Paris, said the master-slave fight is not like animals fighting over food or territory. He argued the two humans risk their lives for something no animal would ever want, and that wanting it is what first makes them human rather than beasts. According to Kojeve, what are the two fighters actually risking death to win?
answer: Recognition from the other, valued above life itself
choices: Recognition from the other, valued above life itself
The right to give the orders from that day on
Freedom from ever having to do hard labor again
Revenge for an old wrong one had done the other
context: Kojeve called it a 'fight to the death for pure prestige.' What makes the combatants human is that they desire something no animal desires, the desire of the other (to be recognized); risking biological life for mere recognition is the first truly human act. His 1933-39 lectures shaped Sartre, Lacan, and many others. (Alexandre Kojeve, Introduction to the Reading of Hegel.)

question: Alexandre Kojeve drew a bold conclusion from Hegel's scene and used it to read the whole of history. He asked which of the two figures, the master or the slave, could actually change and develop over time, and he built his entire reading of history on that answer. From which side did Kojeve say all real historical progress comes?
answer: From the slave's side, through the work that transforms the world
choices: From the slave's side, through the work that transforms the world
From the master's side, through his freedom to command others
From neither side, since the two stay locked in place forever
From a third party who finally frees the slave from above
context: Kojeve called mastery an 'existential impasse': the master cannot develop, so all real progress comes from the slave's labor that transforms nature and the self. This was the bridge to Marx. In the 1844 Manuscripts Marx praised Hegel for grasping 'the essence of labour' and seeing 'objective man... as the outcome of their own labour,' then recast master and slave as the class struggle of owners and workers. The same passage later seeded de Beauvoir on man-as-Subject and woman-as-Other, and Fanon on colonizer and colonized. (Kojeve, Introduction to the Reading of Hegel; Marx, Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844.)

question: Leo Tolstoy had just written Anna Karenina and was rich, famous, and admired across Russia. Yet each night he undressed alone in his room, and he had quietly taken one ordinary object out of it - something he was frightened he would use on himself. What had he removed?
answer: The cord he could hang himself with
choices: The cord he could hang himself with
The razor he could cut himself with
The pistol he could shoot himself with
The poison he could swallow himself
context: In A Confession (1882) Tolstoy wrote of being 'a fortunate man, carrying a rope from my room... so that I would not hang myself from the beam,' and he also stopped hunting with a gun 'so that I would not be too easily tempted to rid myself of life.' At the height of his fame, he was hiding the means of his own death from himself. Source: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession (1882), archive.org/stream/TolstoyConfession-English-LeoTolstoy.

question: Leo Tolstoy was no broken man when despair seized him: a loving wife, fine children, a vast estate, and a body that could swing a scythe beside his peasants all day. His misery came from no loss at all, but from one question he could not answer. Which question?
answer: Is there any meaning in my life that death will not destroy?
choices: Is there any meaning in my life that death will not destroy?
Have I been a good husband and father to my family?
Does God exist, and can a person ever truly know it?
Why do the poor suffer while the rich do not?
context: Tolstoy's own words: 'I had a good, loving and beloved wife, fine children, and a large estate... Physically, I could keep up with the peasants... mentally, I could work eight and ten hours at a stretch.' And the question that stopped him: 'Is there any meaning in my life that will not be destroyed by my inevitably approaching death?' He called his life 'some kind of stupid and evil practical joke that someone is playing on me.' Source: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession (1882).

question: To show how it feels to live while knowing you must die, Leo Tolstoy retold an old fable. A traveler flees a beast and drops into a dry well - but a dragon waits at the bottom, jaws open. He catches a bush in the wall and hangs there while two mice, one white and one black, gnaw the branch in turns. Doomed either way, the man sees something on the leaves and stretches out his tongue. What did he reach for?
answer: Drops of honey
choices: Drops of honey
Drops of cool dew
Drops of sweet sap
Drops of fresh rain
context: The two mice are night and day, gnawing away the branch of your life; the honey is the small pleasures that distract us from the dragon below. Tolstoy's point: once he saw the dragon clearly, 'I tried to lick the honey which formerly consoled me, but the honey no longer gave me pleasure.' He labels it an old Eastern fable. Source: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession (1882), Ch. IV; online-literature.com/tolstoy/a-confession/4.  (Legend.)

question: Albert Camus opened his book The Myth of Sisyphus, written in France under Nazi occupation, by declaring that there is only ONE truly serious problem in all of philosophy. Everything else - whether the world has three dimensions, how the mind works - comes afterward. What did Camus say that one problem was?
answer: Whether to go on living, or to end your life
choices: Whether to go on living, or to end your life
Whether God exists and rules over us
Whether the soul outlasts the body
Whether anyone truly has free will
context: The famous opening line: 'There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide. Judging whether life is or is not worth living amounts to answering the fundamental question of philosophy.' Everything else, Camus says, comes after you have decided to keep living. Source: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942).

question: In Greek myth, King Sisyphus became the only mortal ever to cheat death twice. When Zeus sent Thanatos - Death in person - to seize Sisyphus and haul him down to the underworld, Sisyphus pulled off an astonishing reversal. What did he do to Thanatos?
answer: Chained Death up himself
choices: Chained Death up himself
Poisoned Death with wine
Outran Death on foot
Bribed Death with gold
context: While Death sat helpless in those chains, no one on earth could die - until the war-god Ares finally freed him. This was the first of Sisyphus's two escapes from death, and the gods' eventual answer was the endless boulder. Told as legend. Source: Sisyphus myth, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisyphus (citing Homer, Iliad VI and Odyssey XI); worldhistory.org/sisyphus.
