question: Dragged to the underworld at last, King Sisyphus still had one trick left. Before dying he had given his wife a strange instruction about his body. Down among the dead he then used what she had done to win a chance to return to the surface - and once there, he simply refused to go back. What had he ordered his wife to do?
answer: Leave his corpse unburied in the open square
choices: Leave his corpse unburied in the open square
Burn his body without any funeral rites
Bury him in secret beneath the house
Throw his body in the river at night
context: With his body lying disrespected and unburied, Sisyphus complained to Persephone, queen of the dead, and won her permission to go back and scold his wife for it - then refused to return. Only then did the gods drag him back for good and set him to the stone. Told as legend. Source: Sisyphus myth, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisyphus; greekmyths-greekmythology.com/the-myth-of-sisyphus.

question: Albert Camus took the image of Sisyphus - condemned forever to heave a boulder up a mountain only to watch it roll back down - and ended his book with one famous instruction. The moment that interests him, Camus said, is not the straining climb but the walk back down to the fallen rock, the one moment Sisyphus owns his fate. Camus tells us we must picture Sisyphus how?
answer: Happy
choices: Happy
Defiant
At peace
Triumphant
context: Camus's closing words: 'The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' It is in the lucid walk back down - owning a fate he cannot change - that Sisyphus rises above his punishment. Source: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942).

question: Thomas Nagel said life feels absurd because of a clash between how seriously we take ourselves and how shaky it all looks from outside - the very clash in small mortifying moments. He gave two examples of that everyday absurd. One was pouring out a heartfelt declaration of love to a telephone recording. What was his other example?
answer: Your pants fall down as you are being knighted
choices: Your pants fall down as you are being knighted
Your voice cracks as you accept a great award
You forget your lines while addressing the king
You sneeze on the bride at a royal wedding
context: Nagel called the absurd 'a conspicuous discrepancy between pretension or aspiration and reality.' A mouse's life is not absurd, he noted, precisely because a mouse cannot step back and judge itself - absurdity is the price of self-awareness. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'The Absurd', Journal of Philosophy (1971), philosophy.as.uky.edu.

question: Albert Camus said the absurd - our hunger for meaning meeting a silent universe - must NOT be answered by suicide, which is plain surrender. But he ALSO rejected the religious leap of faith, naming it a kind of cheating he called philosophical suicide, because it escapes the absurd by inventing hope. If neither the bullet nor the leap is honest, what did Camus say the one honest response was?
answer: To keep living it fully, eyes open, in revolt
choices: To keep living it fully, eyes open, in revolt
To find a smaller, private meaning to live for
To chase what pleasure you can before the end
To treat the whole question as beneath you
context: Camus aimed 'philosophical suicide' at Kierkegaard and Shestov, who he thought fled the absurd into religious hope. His answer was revolt: to hold the tension open, refusing both the bullet and the leap, and to live the absurd fully with eyes open. A thinker who disagrees and takes the leap is not thereby foolish - this is Camus's stance, not a verdict. Source: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942).

question: Thomas Nagel agreed that human life is absurd: we can always step back and judge ourselves under the aspect of eternity, and from there nothing we do ultimately matters. But Nagel thought both the heroic answer and the despairing answer overshot. His own move was the deflationary one: if nothing matters, then it does not even matter that nothing matters. So he said we can meet our absurd lives with what attitude?
answer: A gentle irony
choices: A gentle irony
A calm religious faith
A bottomless grief
A cheerful indifference
context: Nagel's line in full: 'If sub specie aeternitatis there is no reason to believe that anything matters, then that doesn't matter either, and we can approach our absurd lives with irony instead of heroism or despair.' The 'too romantic and slightly self-pitying' thinker he had in mind was Camus. This is Nagel's verdict, offered against Tolstoy's faith and Camus's defiance - the bank takes no side. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'The Absurd' (1971).

question: The philosopher Richard Taylor imagined the gods showing Sisyphus one mercy: not freeing him, but reaching into him and altering him, so that the endless boulder now fills him with deep purpose and he is wholly absorbed in his task. The rock and the hill are exactly as before. Taylor said his existence is now utterly transformed. According to Taylor, where does the meaning come from?
answer: From the man's own will within him
choices: From the man's own will within him
From the labour being truly worthwhile
From the gods who reshaped his heart
From fulfilling what he was made for
context: Nothing about the rock or the hill changed - the boulder still rolls back forever, the labour still finishes nothing - yet from the inside Sisyphus's existence is now full of mission. Taylor's conclusion: 'The meaning of life is from within us, it is not bestowed from without, and it far exceeds in both beauty and permanence any heaven of which men have ever dreamed.' He thought the whole living world - birds rebuilding the same nests, creatures repeating endless cycles - is Sisyphus, and that 'the day was sufficient to itself, and so was the life.' This is Taylor's view; Susan Wolf's rival reply (that the object must really be worth loving) is presented separately. Source: Richard Taylor, 'The Meaning of Life' (1970), rintintin.colorado.edu/~vancecd/phil150/Taylor.pdf.

question: Philosophers split the question two ways: does the universe hold a cosmic purpose (the meaning OF life), and separately, can THIS one person's life matter (meaning IN life)? On the second, Susan Wolf offered a famous test. A life can be utterly absorbing - say, devoted to growing the world's largest ball of string - and still sit empty. So Wolf argued a meaningful life needs two things at once. Which two?
answer: Loving something that is genuinely worth loving
choices: Loving something that is genuinely worth loving
Wanting something and finally achieving it
Feeling happy and being useful to others
Believing in God and living by his rules
context: Wolf's formula: meaning arises when 'subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness' - you genuinely love something that is genuinely worth loving. Passion alone is not enough. She drove the point home with silly cases: a life devoted to keeping exactly 3,732 hairs on your head, or to long-distance spitting, can fully satisfy you yet stay empty, because the object lacks real worth. This is Wolf's account, set against Taylor's pure 'meaning is the wanting.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Meaning of Life', plato.stanford.edu/entries/life-meaning (Wolf 2015).

question: A mousetrap can be built from a wooden plank with a snapping metal bar, or a sticky glue pad, or a tipping box, or a dab of poison. None of these is made of the same stuff or works the same way, yet we call every one of them a mousetrap. So what is it that actually makes a thing count as a mousetrap?
answer: That it catches mice, whatever it is built from
choices: That it catches mice, whatever it is built from
That a person built it on purpose to do that very job
That people have agreed to call that kind of object a mousetrap
That it is small enough to sit unnoticed against a wall
context: This is the functionalist move: a thing is what it DOES, not what it is made of. Pain, a functionalist says, is likewise whatever state gets caused by injury and makes a creature wince and pull away -- in a human, an alien, or a robot. (Contrast a diamond, which IS its physical stuff: cubic zirconia does the same job but still isn't a diamond.) Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Functionalism; David Lewis (1972); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Functionalism.

question: A visitor is given a full tour of a famous university: every college, every library, the laboratories, the playing fields, the dormitories. At the end the visitor frowns and asks, "This is all very fine, but where is the UNIVERSITY itself?" The thinker Gilbert Ryle says the visitor has gone wrong. What mistake has the visitor made?
answer: Looking for the university as one more thing beside its parts, when it just IS those parts together
choices: Looking for the university as one more thing beside its parts, when it just IS those parts together
Failing to ask which one of all the many fine buildings was the earliest to be constructed
Forgetting that a real university is its students far more than it is any of its stone walls
Assuming that a single short afternoon tour could ever take in so large and sprawling a place
context: Ryle (1949) called this a 'category mistake.' He aimed it at Descartes' picture of the mind as a 'ghost in the machine' -- a spooky extra substance hiding inside the body. The mind, Ryle argued, is not one more thing alongside the body's workings; it just IS those workings, organized a certain way. Source: Gilbert Ryle, The Concept of Mind (1949).

question: A boy insists his toothache cannot possibly be the same thing as some buzz of activity in his brain, because the ACHE feels like nothing at all when you describe firing cells. His sister replies that two different descriptions can still turn out to name one single thing. Which pair below is a real case of that?
answer: The Morning Star and the Evening Star are both the one planet Venus
choices: The Morning Star and the Evening Star are both the one planet Venus
The Morning Star and the Evening Star are both the planet Mercury
The North Star and the Evening Star are both the one same star
The Morning Star and the Evening Star are both our Moon, seen twice
context: Identity theorists used exactly this reply. 'The Morning Star' and 'The Evening Star' sound like two objects but are both the planet Venus; 'water' and 'H2O' mean different things but name one substance. So 'my toothache' and 'this brain process' can be one single event even though the words feel worlds apart. (The other three pairs are real near-misses: the morning and evening apparitions are Venus, not Mercury; the North Star is Polaris, a different star from the Evening Star; and neither is our Moon.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Mind/Brain Identity Theory; J.J.C. Smart, 'Sensations and Brain Processes' (1959).

question: Rene Descartes set out to doubt everything he possibly could. He found he could imagine that his own body did not exist at all, perhaps the trick of some deceiver. But he could NOT doubt that he, the one doing the doubting, existed -- a thing that thinks must be there to do the thinking. From this gap between body and thinker, Descartes drew a famous conclusion. What did he conclude about the mind and the body?
answer: That the mind and the body are two entirely different kinds of thing
choices: That the mind and the body are two entirely different kinds of thing
That the mind is simply better known to us than the body ever is
That the body is only a tool that the mind owns and steers about
That thinking is the one activity a mere body could never perform
context: Descartes called the mind a 'thinking thing' whose whole essence is thought, and the body an 'extended thing' whose essence is to take up space. Because he could doubt the one but not the other, he judged them two different substances -- a substance being, for him, 'something that can exist by itself.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Dualism; Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation II.

question: Rene Descartes noticed that a body can always be divided -- cut into halves, into quarters, into ever smaller pieces. Then he turned to the mind and asked whether a thinking self could be carved up that very same way. What did Descartes claim about a mind here?
answer: You could never split a mind in two, however hard you tried to cut
choices: You could never split a mind in two, however hard you tried to cut
You could split a mind in two, and get a smaller mind in each half
You could split a mind only where one thought gives way to the next
You could split a mind just as far down as you can split a body itself
context: In Meditation VI Descartes wrote that 'the body is by its very nature always divisible, while the mind is utterly indivisible.' You cannot cut a self into half a self at all -- not into smaller minds, not along any seam -- and since one thing is divisible and the other is not, they cannot be the same thing. This is often called the cleanest single argument for dualism. Source: Descartes, Meditations, Meditation VI (via Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes' Mind-Body Distinction).

question: Some thinkers say a sensation is not merely CAUSED by something in the brain -- it literally IS a brain process, one single event described two different ways. To argue this is no stranger than discoveries we already accept, U.T. Place reached for a famous case from the study of storms and the sky, where science found that two things people once kept apart are really one and the same. Which of these is the discovery Place actually reached for?
answer: Lightning is really nothing but a flow of electric charge
choices: Lightning is really nothing but a flow of electric charge
Thunder is really the air clapping shut after lightning rips it open
A shooting star is really a speck of rock burning up as it falls
The aurora's glow is really the Sun's wind striking the high air
context: In 'Is Consciousness a Brain Process?' (1956), U.T. Place argued a sensation IS a brain process, the very same thing under two descriptions -- no more mysterious than 'lightning IS an electric discharge.' The other three are also genuine 'two-things-found-to-be-one' discoveries (thunder is air violently expanding off the lightning's heat; a shooting star is a burning meteoroid; the aurora is solar wind striking the upper air) -- but the case Place himself reached for was lightning and electricity. We learn such identities by science, he said, not by armchair logic; and the same may go for mind and brain. Source: U.T. Place (1956); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Mind/Brain Identity Theory.

question: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, just twenty-four years old, wrote to Rene Descartes with a problem he could never answer. Descartes had taught that each of us is an immaterial soul joined to a body, the soul steering the body about as we choose to act. Elisabeth granted his whole picture and then pressed him on the one thing it left dark. What did she press him to explain?
answer: How a soul with no size at all could ever push a body into motion
choices: How a soul with no size at all could ever push a body into motion
How the body's own pushes could ever reach a soul that has no size
How a soul could feel a body's pains when the two are so unalike
How a soul could know which body among many is its own to steer
context: Elisabeth wrote (1643) that 'it would be easier for me to concede matter and extension to the soul than to concede the capacity to move a body... to an immaterial thing.' Her point: in the mechanical world bodies move only by being pushed, and pushing takes contact and extension (taking up space) -- but a mind with no extension cannot push anything. Descartes' famous reply was to point at the tiny pineal gland deep in the brain as 'the principal seat of the soul,' yet he never gave her a satisfying account of HOW something with no size could nudge it. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Elisabeth, Princess of Bohemia; Descartes-Elisabeth Correspondence (1643).

question: Suppose someone declared that pain is exactly one particular state of the HUMAN brain -- a certain bundle of nerve fibres firing -- and could be nothing else. Hilary Putnam answered by pointing to an octopus, a creature whose body is built on a wholly different plan from ours, yet which recoils and guards a wound when it is hurt. From this case Putnam drew a lesson about what pain IS. What did he conclude?
answer: That no one fixed brain state could ever be what pain is
choices: That no one fixed brain state could ever be what pain is
That pain is whatever each creature happens to call its own hurt
That only creatures fairly like us can truly be in pain at all
That pain is a private feeling no outside study could ever reach
context: Putnam (1967) noted that humans, mammals, birds, reptiles, and even an octopus all seem to feel pain, though their brains are built completely differently. So pain can't be ONE specific brain-state like 'C-fibres firing' -- insisting it was would be a kind of 'chauvinism' that wrongly denies the octopus its pain. This 'multiple realizability' point broke strict identity theory and pointed toward functionalism. Source: Hilary Putnam, 'The Nature of Mental States' (1967); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Multiple Realizability.

question: A medieval lord raises a fort in two parts. One part is a broad, sunny walled courtyard, pleasant enough that you would happily make your home there. The other is a cramped, dank stone tower perched on a steep mound, miserable to be stuck in but hard for any attacker to storm. A philosopher borrows this fort to picture one dishonest way of arguing. Which way of arguing does the fort picture?
answer: Make the exciting claim, but slip back to the safe, dull one the moment a challenger appears
choices: Make the exciting claim, but slip back to the safe, dull one the moment a challenger appears
Make the exciting claim and stand on it head-on, never giving a challenger any ground at all
Give up the exciting claim for good the first time a challenger lands a real hit on it
Go after the challenger first, so the exciting claim is never actually put to any test
context: This is the "motte-and-bailey" trap. The bailey is the bold claim you actually want; the motte is the boring, near-undeniable fallback. You live in the bailey and retreat to the motte only when an attacker shows up. Nicholas Shackel coined the name; he wrote that "the only reason for [the Motte's] existence is the desirability of the Bailey." Source: Nicholas Shackel, "Motte and Bailey Doctrines," Practical Ethics blog, University of Oxford, Sept 5 2014.

question: A merchant in the market makes a wild, exciting claim. The moment a passerby challenges him, he swaps to a mild, almost-undeniable version and says that is all he ever meant, so the challenger looks foolish. The passerby shrugs and walks off. What does the merchant do once the challenger is gone, the move that exposes the whole trick?
answer: He slides right back into the wild claim, which he never actually gave up
choices: He slides right back into the wild claim, which he never actually gave up
He sticks with the mild version from then on, having truly changed his mind
He admits aloud that the wild claim was wrong and apologizes to the crowd
He falls silent on both versions and refuses to argue the point any further
context: Writer Scott Alexander popularized this three-step description in 2014: "You make a bold, controversial statement. Then when somebody challenges you, you retreat to an obvious, uncontroversial statement... Then when the argument is over you go back to making the bold, controversial statement." Returning to the bold claim is the tell of the motte-and-bailey. Source: Scott Alexander, "All In All, Another Brick In The Motte," Slate Star Codex, Nov 3 2014.

question: A speaker says, "Morality is socially constructed." Pressed by a challenger, he insists he only means our BELIEFS about right and wrong are shaped by the culture we grow up in, which the challenger can hardly deny. Yet the claim he keeps reaching for is far bolder. What bold claim was that one sentence quietly carrying?
answer: That there is, in the end, no such thing as right and wrong at all
choices: That there is, in the end, no such thing as right and wrong at all
That whatever a given culture approves of is thereby right
That morality is a tool the powerful made to keep people in line
That no one is ever entitled to judge another culture’s customs
context: This is the single most famous worked example of a motte-and-bailey. One sentence carries both claims: the easy motte (beliefs are shaped by culture) and the bold bailey (there is no right or wrong at all). Challenge the bold reading and the speaker insists he only ever meant the boring one. Source: Nicholas Shackel, Practical Ethics blog 2014; Wikipedia, "Motte-and-bailey fallacy."

question: A believer preaches a God who builds universes, makes a woman from a man’s rib, parts seas, and heals the sick. A skeptic objects that none of this can be shown. The believer answers that he only means God is another name for the beauty and order in the universe, which is hard to argue with, and there he digs in. What is wrong with the believer’s move?
answer: He argues only for the gentle claim, yet still believes the miracle-worker he never defended
choices: He argues only for the gentle claim, yet still believes the miracle-worker he never defended
He has honestly swapped the miracle-worker for the gentler idea of beauty and order
He contradicts himself, since beauty and order would rule out any creator at all
He attacks the skeptic’s character instead of answering the objection that was raised
context: Scott Alexander's God example of the motte-and-bailey: the bailey is "a supernatural creator who builds universes, creates people out of other people's ribs, parts seas, and heals the sick"; the retreat motte is "God is just another name for the beauty and order in the Universe." He argues only for the motte, then keeps preaching the literal bailey. The question is never whether God exists, but whether the move is honest. Source: Scott Alexander, Slate Star Codex, Nov 3 2014.

question: A writer once quipped that feminism is simply "the radical notion that women are people." A speaker leans on that line, yet the feminism he actually presses for is a bundle of specific, contestable political stands. Challenged on those stands, he retreats to the quip and treats the matter as settled. Why does that quip make such a good place to retreat to?
answer: It commits to so little that a critic can find nothing at all to push against
choices: It commits to so little that a critic can find nothing at all to push against
It quietly proves the contested stands by tying them to a much-admired writer
It brands anyone who rejects the stands as denying that women are people
It narrows feminism so tightly that the contested stands fall outside it
context: Scott Alexander used this as a motte-and-bailey: the undeniable slogan is the motte, the specific political commitments are the bailey. Its safety as a retreat is the whole point — the slogan is so hard to deny that an attacker has nothing to push against, which lets the speaker shelter the contestable stands behind it and then return to them. The slogan traces to writer Marie Shear, who in a 1986 book review wrote "Feminism is the radical notion that women are people." The bank takes no side on the commitments themselves; it teaches you to see the slogan being used as a shield. Source: Scott Alexander, Slate Star Codex, Nov 3 2014; Marie Shear, New Directions for Women, 1986.

question: In Lewis Carroll’s tale, Humpty Dumpty boasts, "When I use a word, it means just what I choose it to mean." A philosopher names this trick after the egg: a single word secretly carries two different claims at once, an easy meaning and a hard one. How does an arguer cash that in?
answer: He proves the easy meaning, then acts as if he has proven the hard one
choices: He proves the easy meaning, then acts as if he has proven the hard one
He proves the hard meaning first, then the easy one follows for free
He keeps both meanings vague so neither can ever be pinned down
He picks one meaning openly and defends only that one to the end
context: Nicholas Shackel calls this "Humpty Dumptying," after Lewis Carroll's egg in Through the Looking-Glass. It is the engine of the motte-and-bailey: the easy meaning (the motte) shields the hard meaning (the bailey), so proving the easy claim is passed off as proving the hard one. Source: Wikipedia, "Motte-and-bailey fallacy"; Nicholas Shackel, "The Vacuity of Postmodernist Methodology," Metaphilosophy 36 (2005).

question: Nicholas Shackel insists this trap is a real cheat, not mere sloppiness. A defender might protest that he was only redefining his words, and a soft-hearted critic might let him off on that basis. Shackel says letting him off there misses the essential dishonesty. What is wrong with the "I was only redefining my words" defense?
answer: It excuses the swap without touching it: he still argues the modest claim as a case for the bold one
choices: It excuses the swap without touching it: he still argues the modest claim as a case for the bold one
It overstates the matter, since a thinker is never genuinely free to redefine any of his own terms
It misses that the modest and bold meanings were really the same claim worded two different ways
It concedes too much, treating the harmless act of redefining as if it were the whole of the cheat
context: The redefinition defense is beside the point. Shackel's exact charge against the motte-and-bailey is "offering the arguments for doctrines in the Motte as if they were arguments for the doctrines in the Bailey" — so the dishonesty is in passing off the case for the modest claim as a case for the bold one. Of his target Foucault he wrote that defending the speaker on the redefinition alone "is missing the essential dishonesty of what he is doing." The redefinition is real; it just is not where the cheat lives. Source: Nicholas Shackel, Practical Ethics blog, Oxford, 2014.

question: In a 2005 paper, Nicholas Shackel aimed this charge at the French thinker Michel Foucault over the word "truth." Foucault, he says, defends a modest point that what a society accepts as true is shaped by who holds power, then trades on it to push a far bolder claim about truth itself. What was the bold claim hiding behind the modest one?
answer: That truth, when you get down to it, is nothing but power
choices: That truth, when you get down to it, is nothing but power
That the powerful tend to lie about what is really true
That only the powerless are able to discover the truth
That power and truth in fact have nothing to do with each other
context: Shackel coined "motte-and-bailey" in "The Vacuity of Postmodernist Methodology" (Metaphilosophy vol. 36, 2005), aimed squarely at postmodernist philosophers. Foucault was his marquee target: the bold bailey is that truth just IS power; the safe motte is the trivial point that what gets accepted as true is shaped by who holds power. Source: Nicholas Shackel, Metaphilosophy 36 (2005), pp. 295-320.

question: Shackel turns the same charge on the sociologist David Bloor and his "strong programme" for studying science. Bloor leans on a bland observation, that what a community calls knowledge is simply what it happens to agree on. But the startling claim he reaches for is bolder. What was that bolder claim about scientific knowledge?
answer: That it is just one more believed-in thing, its truth no part of why we hold it
choices: That it is just one more believed-in thing, its truth no part of why we hold it
That scientists routinely fake their results to keep the grant money flowing in
That its experiments never genuinely test anything about the real world at all
That it springs from lone geniuses working in defiance of their whole community
context: A second scholarly motte-and-bailey Shackel dissects: David Bloor's "strong programme" in the sociology of science. The bailey is the startling claim that scientific knowledge is no different from any other accepted belief and that truth plays no role in why we hold it; the motte is the bland "what we call knowledge is just what is commonly accepted as such." Source: Wikipedia, "Motte-and-bailey fallacy," summarizing Shackel 2005.

question: This trap is a special kind of equivocation, swapping one concept for another mid-argument. But ordinary equivocation leans on meanings that are only subtly different, while here the two meanings are obviously distinct, which should make the swap easy to catch. What lets the arguer get away with it anyway?
answer: He first dresses the double-meaning phrase up as profound, so the swap feels like insight
choices: He first dresses the double-meaning phrase up as profound, so the swap feels like insight
He states both meanings out in the open and lets the listener pick whichever one suits
He picks two plainly different words so that nobody notices they point the very same way
He rushes the argument along so fast that the listener cannot weigh either meaning at all
context: The motte-and-bailey is a form of equivocation called concept-swapping. What makes it sneakier than ordinary equivocation is that the two meanings are not subtly different but obviously distinct; the trick first "softens up the audience" by presenting the dual-meaning phrase as something deep, so the swap feels like insight rather than a switch. Source: Wikipedia, "Motte-and-bailey fallacy."

question: A killer pounds on your door, hunting a friend he means to murder. He asks you straight: is your friend inside? Your friend really is hidden in your house. One bystander says the right choice depends only on which answer leads to fewer deaths. Which response follows that way of deciding -- weighing the act by the results it produces?
answer: Lie that he is not there, because a saved friend beats a kept rule
choices: Lie that he is not there, because a saved friend beats a kept rule
Tell the truth, because an honest tongue matters more than any result
Tell the truth, because betraying a friend can never once be excused
Lie that he is not there, because loyalty to a friend is a sacred bond
context: This is Kant's 'murderer at the door,' the textbook collision between doing the rule and getting the best result. Deciding by which answer leads to fewer deaths -- a lie that saves a life is good -- is the consequentialist instinct; Kant's rival side judges the act by the rule itself, regardless of how it turns out. The truth-telling distractor reaches the same act for a non-results reason. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Moral Philosophy; Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: Benjamin Constant, a French liberal writer, attacked the harsh view that you must not even lie to a killer hunting your friend. He argued from a principle about who is owed honesty at all. Which principle did Constant use to argue you may lie to the murderer?
answer: No one has a right to a truth that would harm others, and the killer has no such right
choices: No one has a right to a truth that would harm others, and the killer has no such right
A lie is wrong only when some written law has already forbidden that exact act
Honesty is owed to everyone alike, so the killer is owed just what a friend is owed
The truth belongs to whoever can pay for it, and the killer has offered you nothing
context: Constant (1767-1830), author of the novel 'Adolphe,' wrote in 1796 that 'to tell the truth is a duty only with regard to one who has a right to the truth -- but no one has a right to a truth that harms others.' His reasoning: a duty in one man matches a right in another, and the murderer has no right, so you owe him nothing. Source: Kant quoting Constant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: Confronted with the killer at the door, Benjamin Constant said you may lie to save your friend. Immanuel Kant answered him with a verdict most people find shocking. What did Kant say you must do when the murderer asks where your friend is hidden?
answer: Answer him truthfully, even though this betrays your friend's hiding place
choices: Answer him truthfully, even though this betrays your friend's hiding place
Lie boldly to him, since saving an innocent life cancels the wrong of lying
Strike him down first, because a hunter of the innocent has forfeited his claims
Bargain with him for time, telling neither a clean truth nor a clean lie
context: Kant held that even to this killer you must answer truthfully -- even when a 'bold and confident lie' is the only thing that might save the friend's life. This is the position the whole case strains against. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Benjamin Constant said the killer has no RIGHT to the truth, so you may lie to him. Immanuel Kant rejected the whole way of talking about a 'right to truth,' calling the phrase meaningless. How did Kant reframe what the real question at the door is?
answer: Whether you are permitted to make yourself into a liar, not what the killer deserves
choices: Whether you are permitted to make yourself into a liar, not what the killer deserves
Whether the killer can be trusted to keep any promise he might make back to you
Whether the friend ever gave you leave to speak about his hiding place at all
Whether a court would later convict you for the exact words you chose to say
context: Kant argued a man has a right only to his own truthfulness -- truth in his own person -- because whether a statement is true or false is not something anyone owns or demands like property. So the question is never what the murderer deserves; it is whether YOU are permitted to make yourself a liar. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: Immanuel Kant insisted a lie is wrong even when it harms no particular person -- even a kindly lie told to protect a friend. He grounded this in a harm that reaches past the person you are speaking to. According to Kant, whom does every lie ultimately wrong?
answer: Humanity in general, because a lie corrupts the very source of trust all dealings rest on
choices: Humanity in general, because a lie corrupts the very source of trust all dealings rest on
The liar himself alone, since the deceit stains only the soul of the one who tells it
Just the friend, who is now bound to a falsehood that he never agreed to be part of
No one at all, as long as the lie is never discovered by anybody else afterward
context: Kant wrote that 'a lie always harms another; if not some other human being, then it nevertheless does harm to humanity in general, inasmuch as it vitiates the very source of right.' Every lie chips at the foundation of trust on which all contracts and declarations depend. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: Immanuel Kant pressed a strange twist to argue the liar must answer for everything that follows from the lie. Suppose you tell the killer your friend is NOT inside -- but unknown to you the friend had already slipped out the back. In Kant's own version of the story, what does your lie actually set in motion?
answer: The killer leaves, meets your friend out on the road, and murders him there
choices: The killer leaves, meets your friend out on the road, and murders him there
The killer leaves, gives up the whole hunt, and your friend lives on for years
The killer leaves, is caught by neighbors down the lane, and harms no one
The killer leaves, doubles back to seize you, and forces the real truth out
context: In Kant's hypothetical the friend had 'gone out unobserved'; the killer, sent away by your lie, runs into him on the road and kills him. Had you told the truth, neighbors rushing in might have caught the killer mid-search and prevented the deed. So the liar, Kant argues, must answer for whatever follows. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: Twentieth-century critics gave Kant's puzzle its most disturbing form to argue an absolute no-lying rule must be wrong. Each kept the same shape -- an armed pursuer at the door asking after a person you have hidden to save -- but one swap made the case feel unanswerable to most readers. Which pursuer made this the famous knock-down version against Kant?
answer: A Gestapo officer asking whether you are hiding Jews in the house
choices: A Gestapo officer asking whether you are hiding Jews in the house
A slave-catcher asking whether a runaway is hidden on your land
An inquisitor asking whether a fleeing heretic shelters with you
A warlord's soldier asking whether a deserter is hiding under your roof
context: The 'Anne Frank' reframing replaces the murderer with a Nazi officer asking whether you hide Jews. If Kant is right that you must never lie, you would have to give them up -- which most people find a decisive reason to reject a rigid no-lying rule. This became the standard knock-down case against absolute deontology. The distractors are real hider's-dilemma scenes, but the Gestapo swap is the one critics made infamous. Source: Helga Varden, 'Kant and Lying to the Murderer at the Door' (2010).

question: Around the 8th century a student named Wasil ibn Ata studied under al-Hasan al-Basri. The two clashed over how to judge a Muslim guilty of a grave sin, and Wasil set up his own circle of students in opposition. al-Hasan reacted with a single phrase that became the name for Wasil's whole school. What did he say?
answer: "Wasil has withdrawn from us" — so they were called the ones who withdraw
choices: "Wasil has withdrawn from us" — so they were called the ones who withdraw
"Wasil has betrayed us" — so they were called the ones who turn traitor
"Wasil has surpassed us" — so they were called the ones who go beyond
"Wasil has silenced us" — so they were called the ones who hush debate
context: Al-Hasan reportedly said "Wasil has withdrawn from us" (i'tazila 'anna), and the name stuck: "Mu'tazila" literally means "those who withdraw" or "those who secede." The whole rationalist school of Islamic theology is named after a man walking away from his teacher's circle (Wasil ibn Ata, 700-748). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Mu'tazilism'; muslimphilosophy.com Routledge Encyclopedia (H052).

question: Al-Ash'ari was raised among the rationalist theologians and studied under al-Jubba'i, the head of their school at Basra — by some accounts his own stepfather. He learned their whole system of defending God's justice through human reason. Then, around the age of forty, al-Ash'ari did something that stunned his teacher's circle. What was it?
answer: He renounced the school in public and founded the tradition that became its fiercest rival
choices: He renounced the school in public and founded the tradition that became its fiercest rival
He inherited the school and led it to its greatest influence across the whole empire
He abandoned theology for good and lived out his years as a wandering desert merchant
He fled the city in secret and never wrote a single word of doctrine ever again
context: The man who built the most formidable case AGAINST rationalist theology was trained by its leading rationalist. Around age 40, al-Ash'ari publicly broke with al-Jubba'i (d. 915), head of the Basran Mu'tazila, and founded the rival Ash'ari tradition — which, not Mu'tazilism, became mainstream Sunni theology. Source: muslimphilosophy.com Routledge Encyclopedia (H052); ebsco.com Research Starters 'al-Ash'ari'.

question: In 833 the caliph al-Ma'mun launched an inquisition called the Mihna, forcing scholars to swear in public that the Quran had been created in time rather than being eternal. The jurist Ahmad ibn Hanbal stood before the authorities and refused to swear it. What happened to Ibn Hanbal because he would not say the words?
answer: He was imprisoned and flogged, and held out until the policy was reversed
choices: He was imprisoned and flogged, and held out until the policy was reversed
He was honored at court and rewarded for the depth of his learning
He was sent into comfortable exile to teach in a distant province
He was quietly pardoned once he agreed to stop preaching in public
context: The created-Quran was the Mu'tazila position (an eternal Quran would be a second eternal thing beside God). Ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and flogged; caliph al-Mutawakkil reversed the policy around 851. Decades later the Qadiri Creed (1017) declared anyone calling the Quran created an infidel — and Ash'arism, not Mu'tazilism, won out. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Mu'tazilism'; Cato Institute, 'An Early Islamic Debate on Faith and Reason Is Worth Examining'.

question: As the story is told, al-Ash'ari put a case to his teacher al-Jubba'i. Three brothers die: one pious (Paradise), one wicked (Hell), one a child (neither). The child asks God why he was not allowed to live and earn Paradise; al-Jubba'i answers that God foresaw the child would have sinned, so taking him early was best for him. Al-Ash'ari then sprang a single question that left al-Jubba'i silent. What did the brother in Hell get to cry out?
answer: "Then why did You not take me as a child too, before I could ever sin?"
choices: "Then why did You not take me as a child too, before I could ever sin?"
"Then why did You not warn me of the torment that my sins would earn?"
"Then why did You not make my pious brother strong enough to save me?"
"Then why did You not grant me the long life my pious brother enjoyed?"
context: Legend: this exchange is the dispute that allegedly broke al-Ash'ari from the Mu'tazila. The trap targets the Mu'tazila claim that God is bound to always do what is BEST for each person (aslah): if so, the man in Hell has a fair grievance — God should have taken him as a child too. Al-Jubba'i fell silent. Source: abuidris.com, 'The Three Brothers Question to the Mu'tazilah'; en.wikibooks.org 'History of Islam/The Mutazilites-Asharites debate'.

question: The thinker Ibrahim al-Nazzam argued that God would never punish children, because to punish those who have done no wrong would make God an oppressor — and He is not one. Pressed on how he could be so sure of this, al-Nazzam gave the answer that defined his whole school. Which answer did he give?
answer: Our minds can see on their own that harming the innocent is unjust, so a just God will not do it
choices: Our minds can see on their own that harming the innocent is unjust, so a just God will not do it
Only scripture can reveal that harming the innocent is unjust, so we trust the texts that forbid it
Whatever God decrees toward the innocent counts as just by the very fact that He decreed it
No mind can weigh such matters at all, so we must withhold all judgment about what God will do
context: Ibrahim al-Nazzam (c. 775-845) was a leading Mu'tazila thinker. The school held that reason can know good and evil ON ITS OWN, before revelation; from there they argued a just God simply will not do what reason already condemns. The opposing Ash'ari reply (distractor two) was that we know such acts are wrong ONLY because revelation says so. Source: Cato Institute, 'An Early Islamic Debate on Faith and Reason Is Worth Examining'.

question: An Ash'ari theologian is challenged: if burning the innocent is wrong, then surely even God is bound by that rule. He answers that this gets things exactly backward. On his view, what goes wrong the instant you set a moral standard over God's will?
answer: He would no longer author what is right but merely answer to it, like any creature under a law
choices: He would no longer author what is right but merely answer to it, like any creature under a law
He would lose the power to forgive a sinner He had already condemned under that same law
He would be unable to work the miracles that suspend the ordinary order of nature
He would owe each creature the exact reward its own deeds had earned, with no mercy beyond
context: This is the Ash'ari position at full strength — not stubbornness. If good and evil were standards above God that bound His will, He would be subject to a law outside Himself and not be truly omnipotent; "external purpose would put a limit to God's omnipotence." So to keep God supreme, morality must come FROM His command. al-Ash'ari: whatever God decrees is just precisely because He decreed it. Source: al-Islam.org, 'A History of Muslim Philosophy, Ch. 11: Ash'arism'; muslimphilosophy.com Routledge Encyclopedia (H052).

question: Two theologians are asked the same hard question: if God Himself commanded you to burn an innocent person alive, would obeying be the right thing to do? The first answers flatly NO — he would refuse, and he insists the deed would be a wrong no command could turn into a right. The second answers YES — the moment God commanded it, obeying would become exactly what is good. The first theologian's refusal commits him to which underlying claim about right and wrong?
answer: Right and wrong are fixed in the nature of acts, and a human mind can know them on its own
choices: Right and wrong are fixed in the nature of acts, and a human mind can know them on its own
Right and wrong wait upon God's command, and a human mind learns them only once He speaks
Right and wrong are not real at all, so the command settles a question that had no answer
Right and wrong shift with each people's custom, so a new command can simply overturn them
context: This is the live fork at full strength, with no verdict: the first thinker's view is the Mu'tazila one — acts are good or evil in their own nature and reason can see it (Qadi Abd al-Jabbar, d. 1025, argued God knows the immorality of all unethical acts and, being self-sufficient, would never command them). The second is the Ash'ari view — good simply IS whatever God wills, so His command defines justice. It is the Euthyphro dilemma of Plato in Islamic dress: is a thing good because God wills it, or does God will it because it is good? Same dilemma, 1,200 years and a different civilization later, argued in a mosque instead of an Athenian street. Source: Cato Institute, 'An Early Islamic Debate on Faith and Reason Is Worth Examining'; academia.edu 'Theories of ethics in Islamic thought'; muslimphilosophy.com Routledge Encyclopedia (H052).

question: Plato ends the Republic with a soldier named Er, killed in battle, whose body lay among the slain for ten full days without rotting. On the twelfth day his comrades laid him on the funeral pyre to burn the corpse. What happened next?
answer: He came back to life and began to speak.
choices: He came back to life and began to speak.
The flames bent away and refused to touch him.
His body crumbled all at once into ash.
A voice spoke out of the smoke above him.
context: Er revived on his own funeral pyre and reported everything he had seen of the world beyond. Plato invented this whole vision as a teaching tale, not as a doctrine he claimed was literally true; it is the frame for the Republic's closing message about how we live. Source: Plato, Republic X (Jowett trans.), classics.mit.edu/Plato/republic.11.x.html -- 'on the twelfth day, as he was lying on the funeral pile, returned to life and told them what he had seen in the other world.'  (Legend.)

question: In Er's report, each dead soul had to choose its next earthly life from a heap of sample lives scattered on the ground. Odysseus, the hero of the long voyage home, drew the very last lot of all. Remembering every hardship his old life had cost him, he searched a long while and then gladly chose which life?
answer: The quiet life of a man with no cares at all.
choices: The quiet life of a man with no cares at all.
The throne of a great and much-feared king.
A new voyage even grander than his first.
The body of a powerful and noble lion.
context: Cured by the memory of his old toils of all love of fame, Odysseus hunted a long time for the life of an ordinary private man with no cares, found it lying neglected in a corner, and took it gladly -- saying he would have chosen the same even if his lot had been first. Plato's point: suffering had taught him wisdom, so he chose by judgment, not greed. Source: Plato, Republic X (Jowett trans.), classics.mit.edu/Plato/republic.11.x.html -- 'the recollection of former toils had disenchanted him of ambition... the life of a private man who had no cares... he would have done the same had his lot been first instead of last.'  (Legend.)

question: Plato did not write Er's vision as a mere ghost story. As the dead gathered to pick their next lives, his prophet flung lots on the ground and called out the single lesson the whole tale was built to teach. The prophet's words name exactly who is to blame when a soul ends up with a wretched life. On whom does Plato place that responsibility?
answer: On the soul that does the choosing.
choices: On the soul that does the choosing.
On the gods who shape each destiny.
On the turning spindle of the heavens.
On the luck of which lot is drawn.
context: This is the whole reason Plato crafted the myth -- to argue that our fate is our own doing. The prophet proclaims Lachesis's word: 'Your genius will not be allotted to you, but you will choose your genius... Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser -- God is justified.' Plato offers it as a teaching tale about responsibility, not as a creed. Source: Plato, Republic X (Jowett trans.), classics.mit.edu/Plato/republic.11.x.html.  (Legend.)

question: Friedrich Nietzsche had a private nickname for his sister Elisabeth, who had married into Germany's antisemitic movement. He picked a stubborn beast of burden, saying it 'fit her well,' and later wrote of her as his pet animal gone among the antisemites. Which animal did Nietzsche call his sister?
answer: The Llama
choices: The Llama
The Camel
The Mule
The Donkey
context: He called Elisabeth 'the Llama' on purpose, fitting the load-bearing, saliva-spitting, stubborn animal to her, and later wrote of his llama gone among the antisemites. The vivid insult marks how completely he had broken from her. Source: Wikipedia, Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche; LRB, Jenny Diski, 'It wasn't him, it was her' (2003).

question: In January 1889, in a Turin street, Friedrich Nietzsche's mind broke for good, and he would spend his last years unable to speak for himself or correct a word printed in his name. Legend says that as he collapsed, he flung his arms around what?
answer: A flogged carthorse
choices: A flogged carthorse
A weeping stranger
A marble statue
A stray dog
context: By legend Nietzsche collapsed in Turin on 3 January 1889 with his arms around a horse being flogged, then sent friends a flurry of deranged letters. He never recovered, which is exactly why he could not stop what his sister did next with his papers. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: In 1887 Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche and her husband Bernhard sailed to the jungle of Paraguay to found a colony called Nueva Germania, and Friedrich Nietzsche mocked the whole scheme. What kind of colony was it built to be?
answer: An 'Aryan,' Jew-free settlement for pure Germans
choices: An 'Aryan,' Jew-free settlement for pure Germans
A Christian mission to convert the natives
A socialist commune sharing all property
A trading post for German merchants
context: Nueva Germania, on land about 300 km north of Asuncion, was open only to Germans 'of pure Aryan ancestry.' Bernhard Forster had co-launched the 1880 Antisemites' Petition and called Jews 'a parasite on the German body.' This was the movement Nietzsche refused to be joined to. Source: Wikipedia, Nueva Germania and Bernhard Forster; The Forward.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche, in a letter breaking with his sister, wrote that it was 'a matter of honor' for him to be 'absolutely clean and unequivocal' on a single point -- one his own books, he said, already proved. On what point was Nietzsche so insistent?
answer: A firm opponent of anti-Semitism
choices: A firm opponent of anti-Semitism
A loyal German nationalist
A defender of the Christian faith
A free spirit loyal to no party
context: In the December 1887 draft letter to his sister Elisabeth, Nietzsche wrote that it was a matter of honor to be 'absolutely clean and unequivocal in relation to anti-Semitism, namely OPPOSED to it, as I am in my writings.' He was breaking with her over her marriage into the antisemitic movement. The nationalism and the Christian piety the other choices name are precisely the false Nietzsche the Nazis later built, and he was no party-man at all. Source: Wikiquote, Friedrich Nietzsche; Holub, Nietzsche's Jewish Problem (Princeton UP).

question: The book the Nazis prized as Nietzsche's crowning work, 'The Will to Power,' has a strange secret: Friedrich Nietzsche himself abandoned a project under that title in 1888, before his collapse. So where did the famous 'book' actually come from?
answer: His sister and Peter Gast assembled it from leftover notes
choices: His sister and Peter Gast assembled it from leftover notes
A publisher reprinted his early lectures under one cover
An editor expanded his published essays into a book
A rival scholar wrote it and forged his signature
context: Nietzsche had abandoned the project by August 1888; after he could no longer object, Elisabeth and Peter Gast built the 'book' out of leftover notebook scraps. She published 483 sections in 1901, then padded it to 1,067 by 1906, more than double. Source: Wikipedia, The Will to Power (manuscript); Montinari and Colli critical-edition scholarship; LRB, Jenny Diski (2003).

question: Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche built 'The Will to Power' from her dead brother's notebooks, raiding them for whatever she fancied 'entirely out of context.' One detail proves she ignored his intent: many passages she printed were ones Friedrich Nietzsche had personally marked a certain way. How had he marked them?
answer: He had crossed them out
choices: He had crossed them out
He had marked them for a friend
He had labeled them as fiction
He had dated them as juvenilia
context: As the LRB put it, she 'took what she fancied entirely out of context and whether or not it had been CROSSED OUT, and knitted together a book.' The scholars Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari, who produced the authoritative critical edition, branded the result a 'historic forgery.' Source: LRB, Jenny Diski (2003); Wikipedia, The Will to Power (manuscript), citing Colli and Montinari.

question: Editors who later untangled the Nietzsche Archive found that Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche had forged roughly thirty letters and rewritten passages to flip her brother's meaning. Friedrich Nietzsche had savaged Christianity for years, so how did his sister's doctored text recast his stance toward Jesus?
answer: A tender love for the founder of Christianity
choices: A tender love for the founder of Christianity
A reverent admiration for Jesus as a moral teacher
A late deathbed return to the faith of his father
A grudging respect for Christ's compassion
context: Scholars say Elisabeth dressed his fierce anti-Christianity as a 'tender love for the founder of Christianity,' just as she recast his anti-nationalism as patriotism. She courted the fascists from the Archive she founded in 1894; when she died in 1935, Hitler attended her funeral. Source: Britannica and Encyclopedia.com, Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche; LRB, Jenny Diski (2003).

question: Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, kept a private journal where he wrote: 'The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.' NFL teams later took the line up as a slogan. He is not promising the wall in your path is secretly nice. What is the move he describes?
answer: The thing blocking you is itself the material you now act on — patience, ingenuity, or courage worked on the hard case
choices: The thing blocking you is itself the material you now act on — patience, ingenuity, or courage worked on the hard case
If you refuse to admit the wall is there at all, it loses its power to stop you and quietly disappears on its own
Every wall has a hidden door somewhere, so the real task is to search the obstacle until you find a way around it
Hardship is sent to punish your bad choices, so a blocked path is a sure signal that you took the wrong road back there
context: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20 (Gregory Hays' 2002 translation): 'The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.' The reframe is not that the obstacle is good — it's that the obstacle is the raw material your response acts on: blocked from one thing, you act on another (patience on the rude person, ingenuity on the dead end). Ryan Holiday's 2014 bestseller 'The Obstacle Is the Way' lifts its title straight from this line; it spread through pro sports, adopted by teams including the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks. Source: Wikiquote, Marcus Aurelius (Meditations V.20) — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius ; Wikipedia, The Obstacle Is the Way — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Obstacle_Is_the_Way

question: Epictetus, once a slave and later a teacher, gave his students an image: a dog is leashed to a moving cart. It can fight the rope and be dragged along scraped and furious, or it can trot beside the cart and take in the view. The cart goes where it goes either way. According to Epictetus, where is the obstacle actually located?
answer: In your own resistance — the rope and the cart you cannot change, but how you meet them is yours
choices: In your own resistance — the rope and the cart you cannot change, but how you meet them is yours
In the rope itself, which is the one cruel thing that ought to be cut so the dog runs free
In the cart's destination, since a wiser driver would steer somewhere the dog prefers to go
In the dog's weakness, because a stronger animal could simply drag the cart the other way
context: The dog-and-cart is Epictetus' image for the Stoic 'discipline of desire' — to desire what the universe allows and not pursue what it does not. The cart's path (the external event) is fixed; the suffering comes from fighting it rather than from the rope. This keeps the obstacle reframe from being mere denial: you don't pretend the cart isn't moving — you keep your agency by choosing how to go along. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Stoicism (discipline of desire; Epictetus' dog-and-cart) — https://iep.utm.edu/stoicism/

question: A coach tells two injured players the same thing: 'It isn't the injury that's wrecking you — it's your story that the season is over.' The line echoes Epictetus, born a slave and later a famed teacher in Rome, who built a whole philosophy out of meeting hardship. Both players face the identical injury. What does the Stoic say turns it from a plain defeat into a discipline?
answer: You meet it as the very rep you were preparing for, working patience and nerve on the one hard case now in front of you
choices: You meet it as the very rep you were preparing for, working patience and nerve on the one hard case now in front of you
You school yourself to feel calm about it, since reaching a settled, untroubled mind is the whole of what the philosophy asks
You stop wanting anything from it at all and simply wait it out, since a setback is fate's business and none of yours to work
You out-muscle it by sheer effort of will, since a hard enough push can drive almost any setback back the way it came
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: 'Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.' The Stoic guardrail against toxic positivity: the obstacle isn't reframed by pretending it's good (that's the 'good news in disguise' trap) — it's reframed by changing your judgment about what it's for. The wall stays real; what you control is your verdict on it. Epictetus elsewhere casts hardship as the rep you trained for: a philosopher meeting trouble should think, 'It was for this that I've been training myself, it was for this that I was practising' (Discourses III.10.7); 'It is difficulties that show what men are' (Discourses I.24.1). Source: Wikiquote, Epictetus (Enchiridion 5; Discourses III.10.7; I.24.1) — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Epictetus

question: Anselm of Canterbury believed he could prove that God exists without ever stepping outside to look at the world. He would not point at the stars, or at living creatures, or at anything he could see. Instead the whole proof would be unpacked from one idea he started with. What did Anselm choose as that one starting idea?
answer: A definition of God as the greatest thing anyone could conceive
choices: A definition of God as the greatest thing anyone could conceive
The whole list of perfections that everyone agrees God must possess
The meaning given to the word "God" in the pages of Scripture
The deep, restless longing for God that Anselm felt in his own heart
context: This is what makes Anselm's argument so strange and famous: it is purely 'a-priori' — squeezed out of a single definition without ever pointing at the world. His exact phrase was 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' (Latin: aliquid quo nihil maius cogitari possit). The other three are real armchair starting points thinkers HAVE used (a checklist of divine perfections, the meaning of a sacred word, a felt longing for God) — but none was Anselm's move, which begins from the definition of the GREATEST conceivable thing. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ontological Arguments.'

question: Anselm of Canterbury already believed in God completely before he wrote a single line of his proof. For him the proof was an act of devotion — a way to explore a faith he already held, not a debate he was trying to win. Anselm summed up his approach in a motto about the order of believing and understanding. What did his motto say?
answer: "I believe so that I may understand"
choices: "I believe so that I may understand"
"I understand so that I may choose to believe"
"I believe only what I have already understood"
"I understand, and so I have no need to believe"
context: Anselm (c.1033-1109), Archbishop-to-be of Canterbury, wrote the work between 1077 and 1078 and first titled it 'Fides Quaerens Intellectum' — 'Faith Seeking Understanding.' His full line: 'I do not seek to understand in order that I may believe, but rather, I believe in order that I may understand.' That order is the reverse of the modern instinct ('prove it first, THEN I'll believe') — which is why the other three options are tempting but wrong. Source: Britannica, 'Saint Anselm of Canterbury'; Wikipedia, 'Proslogion' / 'Fides quaerens intellectum.'

question: Anselm of Canterbury aimed his proof at 'the fool' from the Psalms — the man who says in his heart, 'There is no God.' Anselm claimed he could catch the fool with words alone: the instant the fool hears the phrase 'a being greater than anything that could be imagined,' Anselm says, the fool is already trapped. What did Anselm say that one act of hearing accomplished?
answer: It placed the being in the fool's mind as an idea he now holds
choices: It placed the being in the fool's mind as an idea he now holds
It proved straight away that the being exists in the real world
It showed the phrase was empty noise that pointed to nothing
It forced the fool to admit he had been wrong to deny God
context: The 'fool' is from Psalm 14:1. Anselm's trick is that even a denier who HEARS and follows the phrase has, just by understanding it, let the being into his mind as an idea — it now exists at least in his understanding. That is only the first step (the real-world leap comes later), which is why jumping straight to 'it exists in the real world' is the wrong choice here. Source: Anselm, Proslogion Ch. II (Deane 1903 translation); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ontological Arguments.'

question: Once Anselm of Canterbury has the fool merely considering the idea of "a being greater than anything that could be imagined," he springs his trap. Anselm argues this being cannot live ONLY in the mind. To show why, he asks the fool to compare the mind-only being against a rival being he could just as easily conceive. Which rival did Anselm say would outrank a being that exists in the mind alone?
answer: The very same being, except that it also exists out in reality
choices: The very same being, except that it also exists out in reality
The very same being, except picked out by a far longer list of perfections
The very same being, except imagined far more vividly and in sharper detail
The very same being, except held in the minds of far more people at once
context: This is the engine of the whole argument (Proslogion II). A being existing only in the mind can't be the greatest, because you could always conceive a greater one — namely the SAME being existing in reality too. So 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' would absurdly be a thing than which a greater CAN be conceived. The contradiction, Anselm says, forces the being to exist in reality. The wrong choices name other ways you might dress up the rival (more perfections, more vivid, more widely held in mind), but for Anselm none of those is what makes a thing greater — existing in reality is. Source: Anselm, Proslogion Ch. II (Deane 1903); SEP, 'Ontological Arguments' ('if it is even in the understanding alone, it can be conceived to exist in reality also, which is greater').

question: A monk named Gaunilo, living in Anselm of Canterbury's own time, was not convinced. Rather than deny that God exists, Gaunilo answered with his own example: imagine the most excellent island possible, richer and more perfect than any real land. Run Anselm's exact reasoning on that island, Gaunilo said, and it leads somewhere absurd. What absurd conclusion was Gaunilo driving at?
answer: The same reasoning proves a perfect island is real, so the reasoning breaks
choices: The same reasoning proves a perfect island is real, so the reasoning breaks
The same reasoning proves the island beats God, so God is not the greatest
The same reasoning proves the island is only in the mind, so Anselm was right
The same reasoning proves God is just an island, so the two are one thing
context: Gaunilo was a fellow Benedictine, of Marmoutiers Abbey near Tours, France, and wrote his reply 'On Behalf of the Fool' (Pro Insipiente, c.1078) — deliberately taking the side of the Psalm-fool Anselm had mocked. His move is a parody (a reductio): if Anselm's form can 'prove' a lost island 'more excellent than all other countries' must exist somewhere just because you can imagine it, then the form proves nonsense and must be broken. The wrong choices misread where the absurdity lands — Gaunilo's point is not that the island outranks God, nor that it vindicates Anselm, but that the FORM itself is faulty. He even twisted the knife: of anyone convinced by it, 'I should find it hard to decide which of us I ought to judge the bigger fool.' Source: Britannica, 'Gaunilo'; Gaunilo, Pro Insipiente (Lost Island passage); IEP, 'Anselm's Ontological Argument.'

question: Immanuel Kant attacked arguments like Anselm's with a famous money example. Picture a hundred coins you actually hold, and a hundred coins you only imagine. Kant insisted the two are spelled out in exactly the same terms, yet he admitted there is plainly SOME difference between having real coins and merely imagining them. Where, for Kant, does that difference lie?
answer: In what your real coins let you do, like actually spending them
choices: In what your real coins let you do, like actually spending them
In the proud feeling that holding real coins in your hand gives you
In how other people start to treat you once you are truly rich
In the safety of knowing real coins can never be taken from you
context: Kant's words: 'A hundred real thalers do not contain the least coin more than a hundred possible thalers' — the concept is identical. But he adds: 'My financial position is, however, affected very differently by a hundred real thalers than... the mere concept of them.' The point: being real changes your actual situation in the world — what you can do, what you can spend — not the DESCRIPTION of the coins. The wrong choices name real consequences too (pride, how others treat you, security), so 'same terms' alone can't rule them out — but Kant's example is specifically that real money changes your circumstances, your power to act, not merely your feelings or reputation. Source: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (hundred-thalers passage); Philosophy Now, Issue 152.

question: Immanuel Kant thought he had found the deep flaw in every argument shaped like Anselm's. The trick, Kant said, was to slip "exists" into a list of a thing's qualities, right beside genuine ones like being all-knowing or all-powerful, and then claim the greatest thing must have that one too. Kant denied that "exists" works like the others. What was Kant's reason for treating "exists" differently from "all-knowing"?
answer: Saying a thing exists adds nothing to what the thing is actually like
choices: Saying a thing exists adds nothing to what the thing is actually like
Saying a thing exists is the one claim about it that can never be doubted
Existence is what every other quality depends on, so it must come first
Existence is something only the greatest of all beings could truly have
context: This is Kant's famous line, in plain dress: 'Being is evidently not a real predicate' (a 'predicate' just means a quality you attach to a subject). His REASON: describe a thing as fully as you like, and then saying it exists adds NOTHING to that description — it only posits that the already-described thing is actual. So Anselm cheated by treating 'exists' as a great-making feature like 'all-knowing,' when it isn't that kind of feature at all. The wrong choices are live-sounding rivals — that existence is undoubtable, or the ground of every other quality, or a divine privilege — but Kant's specific complaint is that asserting existence describes the thing no further. Source: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, 'The Impossibility of an Ontological Proof'; SEP, 'Ontological Arguments.'

question: Anselm of Canterbury was not satisfied with merely proving God exists. In a second move, he argued the greatest conceivable being must exist in an even stronger way than ordinary things do. A rock or a star happens to exist, yet you can easily imagine it gone. The greatest being, Anselm claimed, could not even be imagined away. Why did Anselm think a being you can picture as gone must fall short of being the greatest?
answer: Because a being you can picture as gone might just as well be absent for real
choices: Because a being you can picture as gone might just as well be absent for real
Because a being you can picture as gone has clearly been thought of before
Because a being you can picture as gone is one you grasp too easily to revere
Because a being you can picture as gone leaves room for a greater you cannot
context: This is Anselm's second step (Proslogion III), upgrading from plain existence to NECESSARY existence: 'it assuredly exists so truly, that it cannot be conceived not to exist.' His reasoning: a thing whose absence you can even picture might really be absent, so it is outranked by a being whose absence you cannot picture at all — the greatest must be that unthinkable-to-remove kind. The wrong choices also fasten on picturing the being as gone, but pin greatness on the wrong feature (novelty, ease of grasp, or merely leaving room for a greater); for Anselm the flaw is that conceivable absence means the being could really fail to exist. This step later became his shield against Gaunilo's island: any island can always be coherently imagined gone, so it never qualifies. Source: Anselm, Proslogion Ch. III (Deane 1903); SEP, 'Ontological Arguments'; IEP, 'Anselm's Ontological Argument.'

question: Socrates is told by the oracle at Delphi that no man alive is wiser than he is. Instead of feeling proud, Socrates is baffled - he is sure he is not wise at all. What does he do about it?
answer: He sets out to find a wiser man and prove the oracle wrong
choices: He sets out to find a wiser man and prove the oracle wrong
He thanks the gods and accepts the honor with a feast
He stops asking questions, certain he already knows enough
He travels the land repeating the praise to everyone he meets
context: Hearing the verdict, Socrates would not believe it: 'When I heard the answer, I said to myself, What can the god mean? ... for I know that I have no wisdom, small or great.' So he set out to PROVE THE GOD WRONG - to find one clearly wiser man and parade him before the oracle as a counter-example. A man told he is the wisest alive, who immediately tries to disprove it. Source: Plato, Apology 21b (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Socrates had a strange habit when he wanted to swear an oath and truly mean it. Most Athenians swore by the great gods - by Zeus, by Apollo. Socrates, telling a hard truth in court, would instead swear by a common animal. By what did Socrates swear?
answer: By the dog
choices: By the dog
By the goat
By the ox
By the goose
context: Mid-trial, insisting he was telling the unflattering truth about Athens's famous men, Socrates let fly his trademark oath: 'I swear to you, Athenians, by the dog I swear!' - his odd habit of swearing 'by the dog' rather than by the gods. Source: Plato, Apology 22a (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Socrates never went to Delphi to ask whether he was the wisest man alive - he would have thought the question absurd. The whole thing started when an Athenian acquaintance made the journey to Delphi and put the question to the oracle without telling Socrates. Who was it that got Socrates the famous verdict?
answer: A close friend of his
choices: A close friend of his
A rival from the assembly
A pupil from his circle
A herald of the city
context: It was Socrates's impetuous friend Chaerephon who marched up to Delphi and 'boldly asked the oracle to tell him whether there was anyone wiser' than Socrates - and the Pythian prophetess answered that there was no man wiser. Socrates never sought the title; a friend went and got it for him. (Chaerephon was a famous Athenian eccentric - pale and gaunt, Aristophanes nicknamed him 'the bat.') Source: Plato, Apology 21a (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html; gutenberg.org/files/1656).

question: The temple at Delphi that handed Socrates his strange verdict carried a famous command carved over its entrance, so that every visitor walked in beneath it. Tradition holds it was a two-word order, and Socrates seemed to spend his whole life obeying it. What did the carving command?
answer: Know thyself
choices: Know thyself
Honor gods
Conquer death
Seek wealth
context: At the entrance (pronaos) of Apollo's temple at Delphi stood the maxim GNOTHI SEAUTON - 'Know Thyself' (alongside 'Nothing in excess'). Socrates's whole quest is that command in action: the wise man is the one who knows what he is - and isn't. Labeled legend: the placement of the maxim is preserved by tradition. Source: Wikipedia: Delphic maxims; New World Encyclopedia: Delphi.

question: Socrates questioned a politician with a towering reputation for wisdom, sure he had finally found a man wiser than himself. Instead he came away holding one small edge. On the great questions, Socrates judged, both of them were equally ignorant - so what was his only advantage over the man?
answer: The man believed he knew things he did not, while Socrates claimed nothing
choices: The man believed he knew things he did not, while Socrates claimed nothing
The man had read fewer of the old books than Socrates had
The man argued far more clumsily in public than Socrates did
The man honored the wrong gods, while Socrates honored Apollo
context: This is the resolution of the whole riddle. After cross-examining the reputedly wise politician - the obvious place to look for a smart man - Socrates concluded: 'I am better off than he is - for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.' His ONLY edge is that he does not fake knowledge he lacks. Source: Plato, Apology 21b-d (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Socrates found that the skilled craftsmen of Athens really did know their crafts - the shoemaker knew shoes, the smith knew iron. Yet Socrates judged that this true skill became a trap that overshadowed their wisdom. What was the trap their real expertise led them into?
answer: Knowing one craft well, they each thought they knew all great matters too
choices: Knowing one craft well, they each thought they knew all great matters too
Knowing one craft, they refused to ever learn a second trade
Knowing their work, they charged the city far too much for it
Knowing their tools, they grew too proud to teach an apprentice
context: The craftsmen genuinely knew their trades - and that was exactly their trap. 'Because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters,' and this conceit, Socrates says, 'overshadowed their wisdom.' Real expertise in one thing fooled them into faking expertise in everything. Source: Plato, Apology 22d-e (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Two of Socrates's own students wrote down what the Delphic oracle said about him, and the two reports do not match. In Plato's account the oracle says no man is wiser than Socrates. In the other student's account the oracle praises something else about him entirely. What did that second version say the oracle called Socrates?
answer: No man more free, more just, and more moderate than he
choices: No man more free, more just, and more moderate than he
No man more clever, more eloquent, and more learned
No man more pious, more humble, and more devout
No man more bold, more cunning, and more daring
context: There are two surviving versions of what the oracle said. Plato has the Pythia declare 'no one is wiser than Socrates,' but Xenophon's Apology gives a different verdict - that no man was 'more free, more just, and more moderate' than Socrates. Same oracle, two reports from two students. Source: iep.utm.edu/socrates (citing Plato, Apology 21a and Xenophon, Apology 14).

question: You grip the armrest as a monster stalks the heroine across the screen. Your heart pounds and your stomach knots as it closes in. Philosophers call your state here a genuine puzzle, not just a quirk — an inconsistent knot at the heart of why fiction moves us at all. Which description pins down that knot?
answer: You feel fear toward a monster you are completely sure does not exist
choices: You feel fear toward a monster you are completely sure does not exist
You feel fear that drains away the instant the film cuts to credits
You feel fear much fainter than a real intruder would ever provoke
You feel fear yet lift not one finger to protect the heroine onscreen
context: This is the 'paradox of fiction.' It is usually laid out as three claims that each look obviously true but can't all be true at once (an 'inconsistent triad'): (1) we really do have emotions at the movies; (2) we don't believe the characters exist; (3) we can only have a real emotion about something we believe exists.
