question: Theo argues that since nobody can name the exact grain that turns a pile into a heap -- or the exact day a boy becomes a man, or the exact dollar that makes someone rich -- there is really no difference at all between a heap and one lonely grain. A friend insists Theo has gone wrong somewhere. What is the flaw in Theo's reasoning?
answer: A blurry borderline still leaves the two far ends plainly different
choices: A blurry borderline still leaves the two far ends plainly different
There really is an exact grain, and Theo simply failed to find it
Heaps and grains are the same, so Theo is right and the friend is wrong
Counting is impossible, so no question about heaps can be answered
context: This is the everyday 'line-drawing fallacy': because you can't mark the EXACT cutoff, it's tempting to conclude there's no real difference between the extremes -- but a heap and a single grain are obviously different even though the border between them is fuzzy. A vague boundary blurs the middle; it does not erase the ends. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Sorites Paradox' (line-drawing problem).

question: The heap paradox is built from two claims that each look perfectly innocent on their own. The first: a million grains piled together is a heap. Yet it is the SECOND claim that smuggles in all the trouble and traps you. Which of these is that dangerous second claim?
answer: A heap with one grain taken away is still a heap
choices: A heap with one grain taken away is still a heap
A heap must contain at least a thousand grains
A heap stops being a heap once you can count it
A heap and a pile are really just two words for one thing
context: Logicians call the first claim the 'base step' and the second the 'inductive step.' Each is wildly plausible on its own -- who would deny that removing one grain leaves a heap? -- but accept both and apply the second a million times over, and you are forced to conclude that one lonely grain is a heap. The whole paradox lives in that second, endlessly repeatable premise. Source: Wikipedia, 'Sorites paradox'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (induction form).

question: Eubulides of Miletus, a 4th-century-BC philosopher, spent his days hurling logic puzzles at Aristotle, his great rival. The heap was only one of four traps he is famous for. Another runs: 'What I am now saying is false.' Why did this little sentence drive logicians to despair?
answer: If it is true then it is false, and if false then it is true
choices: If it is true then it is false, and if false then it is true
It can never be spoken aloud without instantly becoming true
It quietly proves that Aristotle himself must have been lying
It is far too short a line to count as a real argument at all
context: This is the Liar paradox, the most famous of Eubulides' four (the others being the heap, the Horned Man, and the Masked Man). Eubulides belonged to the Megarian school and, per Diogenes Laertius, was 'constantly attacking' Aristotle; he reputedly taught the great orator Demosthenes. The Liar still spawns research today because no simple true-or-false answer survives it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Eubulides'; OUP Blog, 'Eubulides and his paradoxes.'

question: Four friends sort grains and argue about what 'heap' really means. Rhea says: 'There is one exact grain that turns the pile into a heap -- but no one alive could ever find out which.' Cleon says: 'No single grain is the one that turns it; you could fairly draw the line in lots of different spots.' Ada says: 'Right at the border I'd call a pile two-thirds of the way to being a heap.' Bran says: 'Take a vote -- a pile counts as a heap once more than half the room would call it one.' On whose view alone is a pile right at the border still, as a plain matter of fact, either a heap or not?
answer: Rhea's view, that one hidden grain turns the pile
choices: Rhea's view, that one hidden grain turns the pile
Cleon's view, that the line could fall in many spots
Ada's view, that a pile can be partway to a heap
Bran's view, that a show of hands settles it
context: Rhea's view is 'epistemicism,' defended by Timothy Williamson and Roy Sorensen: a precise grain really does turn non-heap into heap (and a precise hair turns a man bald) -- the line exists, we just cannot KNOW it. Because a sharp line really exists, every statement stays plainly true or false. The rivals all surrender that crisp true/false: Cleon's gap view (in the spirit of Kit Fine and Bas van Fraassen's supervaluationism) says borderline piles have no truth-value; Ada's degree or 'fuzzy' logic (built on Lotfi Zadeh's fuzzy sets, 1965) makes truth a matter of degree; Bran's crowd test leaves it wobbling with opinion. The question asks only which view keeps ordinary true-or-false, not which is correct. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Sorites Paradox' (epistemicism, supervaluationism, degree theory).

question: Most thinkers try to SAVE the word 'heap' from the paradox. The philosopher Peter Unger took the wildest road instead: he agreed that 'heap' has no real boundary, and then refused to flinch from where that leads. What jaw-dropping conclusion did Unger draw and defend?
answer: That there are, strictly, no heaps -- nor clouds, tables, or rocks
choices: That there are, strictly, no heaps -- nor clouds, tables, or rocks
That a heap is just a private picture, unique to each separate mind
That a heap, a cloud, and a rock are all secretly one single object
That a heap pops into being only on the day someone first names it
context: Unger bit the hardest bullet: if 'heap' has no genuine boundary then strictly there are no heaps -- and the same reasoning wipes out clouds, tables, rocks, and even people. He published papers titled 'There Are No Ordinary Things,' 'Why There Are No People,' and even 'I Do Not Exist.' His cloud example: a cloud has no exact edge, so any 'cloud' is really countless overlapping cloud-candidates, and none of them is THE cloud. Source: Information Philosopher, Peter Unger; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Problem of the Many).

question: Even in a city with police and courts, a man bolts his front door at night and locks his money in a chest inside his own house. Thomas Hobbes pointed at this ordinary habit to argue that people already half-believe his grim view of human nature. What does Hobbes say locking your door secretly admits?
answer: That you expect neighbors to rob you the instant it was safe
choices: That you trust the law to guard you while you sleep peacefully
That you expect neighbors to rob you the instant it was safe
That property is theft and that ownership breeds crime
That fear of God alone is what restrains wicked men
context: Hobbes' rebuttal to 'when did this war ever happen?' He noted that even under law a man 'armes himselfe' for a journey, 'locks his dores,' and 'locks his chests' inside his own house: everyday distrust proves his point. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch.13 (Wikisource).

question: Jean-Jacques Rousseau imagined the very first humans, long before towns or farms or kings: people who wandered the forest alone, ate what grew within reach, and never compared their lives to anyone else. He insisted this earliest human was neither a violent brute nor a hero. How did Rousseau say this wandering forest-dweller actually felt?
answer: Healthy and free, his few wants easily met by the woods
choices: Terrified, sleeping with one eye open against night attackers
Lonely, forever aching for the comfort of a tribe
Healthy and free, his few wants easily met by the woods
Ashamed, sensing something was missing from his life
context: Rousseau's 'savage man' was solitary, healthy, wandering and content, with 'no idea of mine and thine' and no need to rank himself against others; nature easily met his few wants. The diagnosis is lost innocence, not Hobbes' terror. Source: Rousseau, Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755), Part 1; IEP 'Rousseau'.

question: Thomas Hobbes traced his anxious temperament to the very day he was born. In 1588 his pregnant mother heard that the Spanish Armada was sailing to invade England, and the shock brought him into the world too early. Looking back, Hobbes joked about the curious pair his mother delivered that day. What did Hobbes say his mother gave birth to?
answer: Himself and Fear, born together as twins
choices: Himself and Fear, born together as twins
Himself and Sorrow, weeping from his first breath
Himself and Genius, marked out for greatness
Himself and Sickness, never to know a healthy day
context: Hobbes told the story as a joke: his mother 'gave birth to twins, Me and Fear' (also remembered as 'fear and I were born twins together'). The man who made fear of violent death the base of all politics claimed he was literally born of fear. Source: Britannica & Wikipedia 'Thomas Hobbes'; History Today, 'Birth of Thomas Hobbes'.  (Legend.)

question: Thomas Hobbes ran a thought-experiment: strip away every government, law, and police force, and ask what is left of human life. His answer became the single most quoted line in all of political philosophy. In that lawless condition, Hobbes wrote, the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and ___.
answer: short
choices: cruel
short
savage
doomed
context: The full line from Leviathan describes the 'warre of every man against every man,' where life is 'solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short.' It is the gateway picture of the whole debate: no rules at all means terror. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch.13 (Wikisource).

question: John Locke pictured humans with no government very differently from Hobbes. Everyone there is perfectly free and equal, Locke agreed, with no one ruling over anyone else, yet he flatly denied that this freedom let a person do whatever he pleased. In Locke's picture, what holds people back even where there is no king or police?
answer: A moral law, knowable by reason, that forbids harming another
choices: A moral law, knowable by reason, that forbids harming another
The fear of revenge from the victim's family and friends
The will of whoever happens to be strongest at the moment
An inborn pity that makes deliberate cruelty feel unbearable
context: Locke: 'though this be a state of liberty, yet it is not a state of licence.' A law of nature, read off reason itself, already obliges everyone that 'no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions' (the pity answer is Rousseau's; might-makes-right and feud-fear are rival accounts of restraint). Source: Locke, Second Treatise (1689), Sec.4-6; Bill of Rights Institute.

question: Almost everyone credits Jean-Jacques Rousseau with the phrase noble savage, picturing him praising primitive man as a pure-hearted hero. But scholars who checked his writings found he never used those words at all; the phrase was coined a century earlier by the poet John Dryden. Why do experts say Rousseau was, in effect, framed for it?
answer: He called early man content and pre-moral, not a noble hero
choices: He called early man content and pre-moral, not a noble hero
He had quietly stolen the whole idea from Dryden
He used the phrase once, in a letter later burned
He praised savages in public while mocking them in private
context: Rousseau never wrote 'noble savage'; Dryden coined it in his 1672 play The Conquest of Granada. Anthropologist Ter Ellingson argued Rousseau was 'framed': he described natural man as content and pre-moral, not as a noble hero. A famous thinker remembered for words he never wrote. Source: Britannica 'Noble savage'; Ter Ellingson, The Myth of the Noble Savage (2001).  (Legend.)

question: Thomas Hobbes argued that what makes life without government so dangerous is not that some men are stronger, but that everyone is roughly equal. Even the weakest, he noted, can kill the strongest by a hidden trap or by ganging up with others. From this rough equality, what conclusion did Hobbes draw about how each person should treat the rest?
answer: That no one is ever safe, so each has reason to strike first
choices: That no one is ever safe, so each has reason to strike first
That each should seek a protector among the strongest men
That the weak will always band together and rule the strong
That equality breeds respect, so people leave each other be
context: Hobbes' engine is equality, not inequality: 'the weakest has strength enough to kill the strongest, either by secret machination, or by confederacy with others.' Because anyone can be killed even in sleep, the safest move is to strike first. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch.13; SEP 'Hobbes's Moral and Political Philosophy'.

question: John Locke did not think people without government live in terror; he thought they live in a workable peace spoiled by one flaw. The trouble, he said, is that when someone wrongs you, you decide your own case and carry out the punishment yourself, and self-love makes people partial to themselves and their friends. What one thing did Locke say government exists to supply?
answer: An impartial judge to settle disputes between equals
choices: An impartial judge to settle disputes between equals
An all-powerful king whose every word becomes law
An army strong enough to frighten men into obedience
A shared religion to bind the people in conscience
context: For Locke the state of nature fails not from war but from bias: each person is judge and executioner of the law of nature, and 'passion and revenge' carry them too far. Government supplies the missing thing, an impartial judge. Source: Locke, Second Treatise (1689), Sec.13, 124-126; Founders' Constitution (U. Chicago).

question: Jean-Jacques Rousseau imagined the precise moment civilization went wrong: the first man who fenced off a patch of ground, called it his own, and found people gullible enough to believe him. Rousseau then imagined a second man who could have spared the human race countless crimes, wars, and murders. What did Rousseau say that second man should have done?
answer: Pulled up the stakes and cried that the earth belongs to all
choices: Pulled up the stakes and cried that the earth belongs to all
Killed the first man on the spot and burned his fences down
Quietly fenced off even more land before anyone else could
Knelt and begged the first man to share his harvest fairly
context: Rousseau: 'The first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, bethought himself of saying This is mine... was the real founder of civil society.' He added that whoever pulled up the stakes and cried 'the fruits of the earth belong to us all, and the earth itself to nobody' would have spared mankind 'crimes, wars and murders.' Source: Rousseau, Discourse on Inequality (1755), Part 2 (marxists.org).

question: Thomas Hobbes anticipated an obvious objection: people without government are not actually fighting every minute of every day, so how can he call their condition a state of war? He answered with the weather: foul weather, he said, is not one or two showers but a stretch of days inclined to storm. By that comparison, what did Hobbes mean the state of war really is?
answer: A standing readiness to fight, even when no blow is struck
choices: A standing readiness to fight, even when no blow is struck
A war of words and threats that never turns physical
A clash that erupts only now and then, like a storm season
A punishment from God that no human action can prevent
context: Hobbes: the nature of war 'consisteth not in actuall fighting, but in the known disposition thereto,' just as foul weather lies not in a shower but 'in an inclination thereto of many dayes together.' War is a climate, not a battle. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch.13 (Wikisource).

question: Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau each began from the identical starting point, a human being with no government over him at all, yet reached three opposite verdicts: a war of all against all, a rough but workable order, and a lost peaceful paradise. What did that three-way split suggest each man's verdict was secretly driven by?
answer: His own politics, read back into pre-political man
choices: His own politics, read back into pre-political man
His private fear of the rulers of his own day
His nation's recent history of war or revolution
His religion, which fixed how good he thought people were
context: The thought-experiment does not settle human nature; the same blank slate yields terror, rough order, or lost innocence depending on the thinker. The lesson the topic draws: your picture of pre-political man IS your politics. Source: Britannica 'State of nature: political theory'; IEP 'Social Contract Theory'.

question: A sculptor presses two halves of clay together and a statue stands before her. The very same clay, in the very same spot, is also just a lump. The next day she squashes the whole thing flat. Afterward she points to the flat slab and asks her apprentice: in the squashing, what got destroyed?
answer: The statue, because a flattened slab is no longer a statue
choices: The lump, because pressing the clay flat scatters it into loose bits
Nothing at all, because rearranging one clay object cannot kill anything
The statue, because a flattened slab is no longer a statue
Only a passing shape, because shape is not the sort of thing that can die
context: This is the forcing wedge of the whole puzzle: the lump can survive being squashed, the statue cannot. So in the very same spot, the lump and the statue seem to have different futures. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Material Constitution'.

question: Plutarch tells how the Athenians kept Theseus's ship for centuries by replacing each rotting plank, one at a time, until not a splinter of the original wood was left. Then Thomas Hobbes sharpened the riddle: gather every discarded old plank and build a second ship out of them. After Hobbes's twist, what is the trouble?
answer: Both ships have a real claim to be Theseus's, yet they cannot both be it
choices: The repaired ship is now younger than the wood that it is built from
Both ships have a real claim to be Theseus's, yet they cannot both be it
The newer planks come from a different forest than the first ones did
The Athenians own two ships but can afford to keep only one of them
context: Legend: Plutarch recorded the plank-swapping puzzle in his 'Life of Theseus'; Hobbes added the rebuilt second ship. The continuously-repaired ship and the original-material ship each have a genuine claim to the name. Sources: Plutarch via Britannica; Hobbes addition via Live Science.

question: A philosopher lays down a 300-year-old rule from Leibniz: if a thing A truly IS the very same thing as B, then absolutely everything true of one must be true of the other — not a single difference allowed. He then notes that the lump of clay can survive being squashed flat, while the statue cannot. What does that one difference force him to conclude?
answer: The statue is not the same thing as the lump, though they share all their matter
choices: The lump and the statue must both be illusions, since the two of them disagree
Leibniz's old rule simply fails here, because shared matter can break the rule
The statue really is the lump, and surviving the squash was only an illusion
The statue is not the same thing as the lump, though they share all their matter
context: The rule is Leibniz's Law, the Indiscernibility of Identicals: if A is B, they share every property without exception. One genuine difference (surviving the squash) is enough to prove the statue and the lump are not identical, even made of the exact same stuff in the exact same place. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Identity' and 'Material Constitution'.

question: Long before any clay statue, the Stoic Chrysippus posed a grislier version. Dion is a whole man; 'Theon' is the name for just Dion-minus-his-left-foot. Yesterday they were plainly two. Now Dion's left foot is amputated, and the man left over is made of the very same matter as Theon, in the same spot. Chrysippus gives a startling verdict about who survives. Which one does he say perishes?
answer: Theon, the foot-less part, even though Theon itself lost nothing at all
choices: Dion, the whole man, because he is the one who actually lost a body part
Theon, the foot-less part, even though Theon itself lost nothing at all
Both of them, because the amputation destroys the original pair at once
Neither of them, because the matter that is left over is exactly the same
context: Chrysippus (c. 280–207 BC) ruled that Theon, who lost nothing, is the one who perishes, while the whole man Dion lives on after losing the foot. We know the puzzle because Philo of Alexandria wrote it down. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Chrysippus'.

question: Once you allow that a statue and a lump are two objects sharing one spot, why stop at two? Philosophers conjure a whole zoo of extra objects there, each defined by some passing condition: one that exists only while the statue stands indoors, one only while it sits in the light, one only while the sculptor happens to be eating dinner. Ernest Sosa warned that this opens an “explosion of reality.” On his warning, what would even the barest flutter of the smallest leaf then do?
answer: Create and destroy a fresh swarm of objects in that same instant
choices: Create and destroy a fresh swarm of objects in that same instant
Leave every real object untouched, since one leaf is far too slight to matter
Snuff out the statue while leaving the lump of clay unharmed
Become a brand-new object that coincides with the statue itself
context: Ernest Sosa (1987) called this the 'explosion of reality,' warning that 'the barest flutter of the smallest leaf' would then create and destroy infinitely many things at once. The phantom objects — the 'instatue,' 'litstatue,' 'dinnerstatue,' each defined by a passing condition — are a reductio against admitting coincident objects at all. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Material Constitution' (citing Sosa 1987); Moyer, 'Statues and Lumps'.

question: Suppose you settle on the answer that the statue and the lump are two different objects sharing one spot. They are built from the very same particles, arranged in the very same way. Critics call the trouble that follows the deepest unhealed wound in the whole puzzle. Why is it so damaging?
answer: Their matter is identical, so nothing is left over to explain their split fates
choices: Same particles must mean a single object, so the honest count is really one
The particles never hold still, so neither object lasts even a single instant
Their matter is identical, so nothing is left over to explain their split fates
Surviving a squash is not a real property, so the wedge never proved anything
context: This is the grounding problem: if statue and lump are physically identical down to every particle, their different survival conditions seem to float free, grounded in nothing. It is widely regarded as the deepest wound to the two-object view. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Material Constitution'; Moyer, 'Statues and Lumps'.

question: A knight is angry at a rival knight he is too afraid to challenge. So he stuffs a scarecrow with straw, props it up in the yard, shouts his rival's name at it, and beats it to pieces with his sword while a crowd cheers. He struts off claiming he won. What is the obvious problem with his "victory"?
answer: He beat up a fake stand-in, so the real rival is untouched and never fought
choices: He beat up a fake stand-in, so the real rival is untouched and never fought
He should have used a wooden dummy that could take a harder beating
He needed a bigger crowd to make the win against his rival count
He picked a fight he was always going to win and learned little from it
context: This is the literal picture behind the fallacy called the STRAW MAN: a straw man is a doll or scarecrow stuffed with bound straw, a fake person you can knock over without it fighting back. To 'knock down a straw man' means you build a flimsy fake version of your opponent and topple THAT instead of the real one. Source: etymonline.com/word/straw man (scarecrow sense, 1590s) + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man ('knock down a straw man').

question: Will says the country should spend more on schools and hospitals. Warren shoots back: "I can't believe Will hates his own country so much that he wants to leave us defenceless by gutting the army!" What did Warren actually argue against?
answer: A position Will never put forward, swapped in because it is easier to knock down
choices: A position Will never put forward, swapped in because it is easier to knock down
A genuine call to move money from the army over to schools and hospitals
A weighing of whether schools and hospitals truly matter more than defence does
A buried motive, hidden under Will's words, to see the army shrink over time
context: This is the classic textbook example of the STRAW MAN fallacy: 'You misrepresented someone's argument to make it easier to attack.' Warren refutes a position Will never took (cutting military spending), so even a perfect rebuttal proves nothing about what Will really said. Source: yourlogicalfallacyis.com/strawman (the Will/Warren example, verbatim).

question: A lawmaker proposes adding background checks before someone can buy a gun. Her opponent stands up and tells the crowd: "She wants to take ALL your guns away!" She never proposed taking anyone's guns. Why is the opponent's reply unfair, even though it fires up the room?
answer: He swapped her modest proposal for an extreme one that is easier to attack
choices: He swapped her modest proposal for an extreme one that is easier to attack
He should have let her finish before raising any of his own objections
He used a scary tone instead of calmly explaining the checks to voters
He brought up guns at all when the real debate was about public safety
context: A common political STRAW MAN: the modest real position (background checks) gets inflated into an extreme one (total confiscation) that is far easier to attack and was never actually said. Inflating a position is one of the most frequent forms of the move. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man + helpfulprofessor.com/straw-man-fallacy-examples (gun-control inflation example).

question: In a debate, one speaker says only: "I don't think we should spend EVEN MORE on the military than we already do." The other instantly replies: "So you want to leave our whole country defenseless and wide open to invasion!" How did the second speaker twist the first one's point?
answer: He grabbed the worst-case reading instead of the modest thing actually said
choices: He grabbed the worst-case reading instead of the modest thing actually said
He answered a budget question with an emotional appeal about invasions
He forgot that the military budget was already very large to begin with
He changed the subject to invasion when the topic was overall spending
context: Another textbook STRAW MAN shape: the reply seizes one exaggerated worst-case reading ('defenseless, open to invasion') instead of the actual claim (just: not MORE money). Source: scribbr.com/fallacies/straw-man-fallacy + helpfulprofessor.com/straw-man-fallacy-examples (defense-budget example).

question: The first speaker argues that a small town should repair its one cracked bridge before it builds anything new. The second speaker fires back with a crushing case proving the town could never afford to rebuild all of its bridges at once, and the crowd roars. What has the second speaker actually accomplished against the first?
answer: An empty win, since he toppled a target his rival never set up in the first place
choices: An empty win, since he toppled a target his rival never set up in the first place
A real win, because his case against rebuilding everything at once was thorough and correct
A fair tie, since each speaker landed one strong point about the town and its repairs
A small win, because sounding confident in front of the cheering crowd counts for something
context: This is the core trick of the STRAW MAN: the illusion of victory comes from 'the covert replacement' of the real proposition (fix the one cracked bridge) with a different, weaker one (rebuild ALL bridges at once), then refuting the substitute. The first speaker only argued for repairing a single bridge, so demolishing the 'all the bridges' version proves nothing about what was actually said. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (verbatim: 'creates the illusion of having refuted... through the covert replacement of it with a different proposition').

question: Spell out the exact trick. Person One asserts a claim, call it X. Person Two does not argue against X. Instead Person Two argues against a different claim, Y, that only LOOKS similar to X, and beats Y soundly. Even if Person Two demolishes Y perfectly, why has Person One's real claim survived?
answer: Because Person Two aimed at the look-alike claim and never landed a blow on the real one
choices: Because Person Two aimed at the look-alike claim and never landed a blow on the real one
Because a claim can only be proven false once its own author admits defeat
Because beating any claim at all leaves the truth of its conclusion untouched anyway
Because Person Two's attack on Y was simply too weak to count as a real refutation
context: This is the formal shape of the STRAW MAN, spelled out: Person 1 asserts X; Person 2 argues against a superficially-similar proposition Y, as though beating Y were beating X. The bug is that Y is NOT X, so even a flawless demolition of Y leaves X standing untouched. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (verbatim argument pattern '1. Person 1 asserts proposition X. 2. Person 2 argues against a superficially similar proposition Y...').

question: The straw man builds a flimsy fake of your opponent's case and topples that. Suppose you want the honest opposite, a win you can actually trust. You face an opponent whose argument has real weak spots in it. What is the fair-play opposite of building a straw man?
answer: Rebuild their case in its strongest possible form, then beat that version
choices: Rebuild their case in its strongest possible form, then beat that version
Patch their weak spots quietly and let the repairs pass as their own work
Allow only the version of their case that you decide is fair to debate
Hold back any clear verdict on whether their case is any good at all
context: The virtue opposite of the straw man is STEELMANNING: build a STEEL man, the strongest, most armored form of the other side, then reply to THAT. Straw is weak and burns; steel is strong and holds. You only get to claim victory if you beat the best version, not the worst. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (steel man section: 'addressing the strongest form of the other person's argument') + lesswrong.com 'The case for using the term steelmanning'.

question: In 1520 the monk Martin Luther fired back at the critics attacking his writings. He complained that they would not fight his real arguments: "They assert the very things they assail, or they set up a man of straw whom they may attack." When Luther accused them of setting up a "man of straw," what was he saying they did?
answer: Invented a fake, weaker version of his view and fought that instead
choices: Invented a fake, weaker version of his view and fought that instead
Quoted his real words exactly but then refused to answer them at all
Agreed with his actual argument while pretending loudly to oppose it
Accused him of heresy without ever reading a single page he wrote
context: Martin Luther coined the image in print in 1520, complaining his critics did exactly this. One of the earliest recorded uses of 'man of straw' in an argument is a man accusing his enemies of inventing a fake Luther to beat up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (quoting Luther, 1520, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church).

question: The Greek thinker Aristotle catalogued this dodge in his work Sophistical Refutations, grouping it with the sham tricks that only LOOK like real refutations. He warned that the move beats a distorted, weaker version of the opponent's position rather than the real one. According to Aristotle, what makes such a refutation worthless?
answer: It answers a claim the opponent never made, so it settles nothing about the real one
choices: It answers a claim the opponent never made, so it settles nothing about the real one
It leans on insulting the opponent personally instead of facing the argument
It hides an undefined middle term that secretly shifts meaning partway through
It stirs up the crowd's emotions in place of offering any reason at all
context: Aristotle described this move roughly 2,300 years ago in Sophistical Refutations as a refutation that misses the opponent's real position by attacking a distorted or weaker version (a form of irrelevant refutation, ignoratio elenchi). Because it answers a claim the opponent never actually made, even a flawless takedown settles nothing about the real position. The distractors name OTHER fallacies a person might confuse this with (a personal attack, an undefined middle term, an appeal to emotion), but none of those is the flaw Aristotle pins on this particular dodge. Source: iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ (Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations) corroborated by grokipedia 'Straw_man_rhetorical_device'.

question: A blogger known as Black Belt Bayesian gave steelmanning its sharpest motto: if you only care about WINNING a dispute, you will refute your opponents' arguments. But if you care about producing truth, you will do something stranger first. According to the motto, what does the honest truth-seeker do before answering the other side?
answer: Fixes the opponents' arguments for them, repairing the case before replying
choices: Fixes the opponents' arguments for them, repairing the case before replying
Refuses to reply until the opponents first admit their argument is weak
Declares the dispute unwinnable so that nobody has to be proven wrong
Restates only the strongest point the opponents already made out loud
context: The full motto from blogger 'Black Belt Bayesian': 'If you're interested in being on the right side of disputes, you will refute your opponents' arguments. But if you're interested in producing truth, you will fix your opponents' arguments for them.' The honest thinker repairs the other side before answering it. Source: wordspy.com/words/steel-man + skepticink.com/incredulous 'Against Steelmanning' (quoting Black Belt Bayesian).

question: The hardest straw man to catch is not a crude lie. The clever version takes an argument and stretches it just slightly past what the person meant, slipping in an "all" or a "never" or a worst case, then crushes the stretched version so the audience believes the original fell too. Why does this stretch-then-crush move slip past listeners who would have caught a plain lie?
answer: The stretched version began from something the person truly said, so it looks honest
choices: The stretched version began from something the person truly said, so it looks honest
The stretch is so tiny that the speaker can later deny exaggerating at all
The crushed version sounds so close to the original that no one rechecks it
The audience never learns whose argument was being stretched in the first place
context: The subtle, advanced STRAW MAN is exaggerate-then-refute: take a real position, stretch it slightly past what the person meant (add an 'all', a 'never', a worst case), demolish the stretched version, and let the audience think the real one fell too. It is hardest to catch precisely because it starts from something true, so the small stretch slips past unnoticed. Source: yourlogicalfallacyis.com/strawman ('By exaggerating, misrepresenting, or just completely fabricating someone's argument...') + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (exaggeration as a primary method).

question: Steelmanning has a serious philosophical ancestor. In 1959 the philosopher Neil Wilson named a rule for honest interpretation, later built into a full method by Quine and Davidson, that tells you how to read a confusing or clumsy speaker before you judge what they said. What does Wilson's rule tell the listener to do?
answer: Read their words in the most reasonable and consistent way the words can bear
choices: Read their words in the most reasonable and consistent way the words can bear
Read their words at face value, fixing nothing and forgiving no slip of phrasing
Read their words with suspicion, hunting first for the trap hidden inside them
Read their words as they were most likely heard by the crowd first addressed
context: Steelmanning's serious philosophical ancestor is the PRINCIPLE OF CHARITY, named by philosopher Neil L. Wilson in 1959: interpret a speaker's words in the most rational, coherent way possible before judging them. W.V.O. Quine (Word and Object, 1960) and Donald Davidson built it into a rule of interpretation; Davidson: 'We make maximum sense of the words and thoughts of others when we interpret in a way that optimises agreement.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_charity (Neil L. Wilson 1959 'Substances without Substrata'; Quine 1960; Davidson).

question: Two debaters each beat their opponent's argument. Mara quietly trims her opponent's case down to its shakiest claim and refutes that. Jonah instead patches every hole in his opponent's case, adds the strongest point they forgot to make, and refutes THAT improved version. A judge says only one of them has truly proven the opponent wrong. Which one, and why?
answer: Jonah, because he beat the strongest possible version, leaving no better form to fall back on
choices: Jonah, because he beat the strongest possible version, leaving no better form to fall back on
Mara, because she won faster, and the quicker refutation is always the cleaner one
Neither, because beating an argument can never prove its conclusion actually false
Both equally, since each one refuted the case in front of them, which is all debate asks
context: This is how to tell the two apart: a STRAW MAN makes the other side dumber so you can win cheap; a STEEL MAN makes the other side smarter so that if you still win, the win is real. Mara refuted a shrunken version, so a stronger form of her opponent's case is still standing; Jonah refuted the strongest possible version, so there is no better form left to rescue it. Same battlefield, opposite ethics: one builds a scarecrow to torch, the other forges armor for the enemy first. Source: synthesis of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (steel man = strongest form) + lesswrong.com 'The case for using the term steelmanning' (steelman improves beyond the original to test whether the position is TRUE).

question: A boy stands safe at the window while a thunderstorm splits the sky over the valley. He should be frightened, yet he cannot look away — and the thrill he feels is nothing like the gentle pleasure of a tidy flowerbed. How does this thrill differ from simply finding the flowerbed pretty?
answer: It mixes delight with dread before something vast and overpowering — the pretty soothes, but this overwhelms
choices: It mixes delight with dread before something vast and overpowering — the pretty soothes, but this overwhelms
It is the very same pleasure the flowerbed gives, only far stronger — the storm is just bigger and louder still
It is plain terror dressed up as enjoyment — for deep down, no one truly likes to feel afraid at all
It is simple relief at being safe indoors — a comfort that sharpens as the weather outside grows worse
context: This braided feeling of awe and dread before the vast or violent is called the SUBLIME — beauty's overwhelming cousin. The beautiful (a flowerbed) soothes; the sublime (a thunderstorm) overwhelms. They are not the same thing, only stronger versions of each other. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 18th Century British Aesthetics; Philosophy Break, Burke on the Sublime.

question: A monstrous wave rears over the bay. To the sailor it swallows, it is pure horror; to the painter who stands watching it from the headland, it is one of the grandest sights of her life. The wave is exactly the same wave for both. What makes the difference between their two reactions?
answer: The painter is in no real danger, so a power that would kill the sailor can only thrill her
choices: The painter is in no real danger, so a power that would kill the sailor can only thrill her
The painter is simply braver than the sailor, and courage turns any horror into a pleasure
The painter has trained her eye on art, and skill turns a frightful scene into a fine one
The painter cares little for the sailor, and that coldness lets her enjoy a dreadful sight
context: Edmund Burke (1757) made distance the key: 'When danger or pain press too nearly, they are... simply terrible; but at certain distances... they are delightful.' Drowning in the sea is terror; watching the raging sea from shore is the sublime. Kant agreed — the same hurricane is terror to the man in it and a glory to the man in shelter, because his position changed, not the storm. Source: Burke, A Philosophical Enquiry (1757); Kant, Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790).

question: Edmund Burke argued that a pretty thing and a fearsome thing are simply not the same kind of thing, and drew up two opposed lists to prove it. On one side he set the small, the smooth, the delicate, the bright. What did he pile onto the OTHER side — the side of the sublime?
answer: The vast, the rugged, the powerful, the dark
choices: The vast, the rugged, the powerful, the dark
The neat, the gentle, the polished, the warm
The rare, the costly, the ancient, the foreign
The useful, the orderly, the simple, the plain
context: Edmund Burke (1757) thought the beautiful and the sublime rest 'on foundations so different, that it is hard... to think of reconciling them in the same subject.' The beautiful is small, smooth, delicate, bright; the sublime is great, rugged, powerful, obscure and dark. For Burke, sheer endlessness was the surest trigger of all — 'Infinity has a tendency to fill the mind with that sort of delightful horror... the truest test of the sublime.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 18th Century British Aesthetics; Burke, A Philosophical Enquiry (1757).

question: Before the 1700s, painters mostly chased pretty, orderly scenes — tidy gardens, calm harbors, gentle hills. Then the idea of the sublime gave a whole generation of Romantic painters and poets permission to chase something else entirely, and they ran toward it. What did the sublime send them chasing instead?
answer: Storms, towering cliffs, and crumbling ruins — the vast and the overwhelming
choices: Storms, towering cliffs, and crumbling ruins — the vast and the overwhelming
Portraits of kings and saints, painted in gold leaf and the very richest of colors
Crowded city markets, full of merchants haggling loudly over their wares
Great battle scenes, with cavalry and cannon-smoke filling the whole canvas
context: The sublime became the secret engine of Romanticism, freeing artists to chase storms, cliffs and ruins instead of tidy gardens. The poet William Wordsworth described 'the mind trying to grasp at something towards which it can make approaches but which it is incapable of attaining' — the exact reach-and-fail the sublime is built on. The idea is far older than the Romantics: the first treatise 'On the Sublime' is credited to 'Longinus' in antiquity, where it meant lofty, soaring language that strikes a listener with awe. Source: Philosophy Break, Burke on the Sublime; Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Sublime, the.

question: The philosopher Immanuel Kant asked why a violent mountain storm, watched from safety, should thrill us rather than merely frighten us. His answer pointed not at the storm at all, but back at the watcher. Kant said the storm makes us discover something in ourselves. What did Kant say we discover?
answer: A greatness within us — a courage and strength of mind that no storm could ever crush
choices: A greatness within us — a courage and strength of mind that no storm could ever crush
A smallness within us — a deep humility that puts our everyday vanity firmly in its place
A kinship with nature — a sense that the wild storm is somehow our own true home
A hidden dread within us — a fear of death that we usually keep carefully buried
context: Immanuel Kant (1790) called this nature's overwhelming MIGHT the 'dynamically sublime' — overhanging rocks, thunderclouds, volcanoes, hurricanes, the boundless heaving ocean. His twist: such sights do not humble us, they ELEVATE us. They 'raise the soul's fortitude above its usual middle range and allow us to discover in ourselves... [the] courage that we could be a match for nature's seeming omnipotence.' The thrill is secretly the discovery of a greatness in OURSELVES that no avalanche can crush. Source: Kant, Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790).

question: Try to truly picture the whole night sky — every star, the full size of the universe — and your imagination stalls: you simply cannot hold it all as one image, and it feels like defeat. Immanuel Kant said that at this exact moment of failure, something in the mind rescues us and turns the defeat into a strange triumph. What did Kant say performs that rescue?
answer: Reason, which can still think the infinite as a single whole even when the eye cannot
choices: Reason, which can still think the infinite as a single whole even when the eye cannot
Memory, which stores the stars one by one until at last the whole of the sky is held
Faith, which trusts that some far greater being holds the whole that we never could
Habit, which slowly dulls the shock until the vastness no longer troubles us at all
context: Immanuel Kant (1790) called this the 'mathematically sublime' — not might but sheer SIZE, 'that in comparison with which everything else is small.' The imagination buckles trying to hold the infinite as one picture; that failure is the displeasure. But then our REASON can still think the whole of it as a single idea — so the defeat flips into a triumph, revealing a power in our own minds 'superior to nature.' That flip from crushed to exalted IS the feeling of the sublime. Kant said giant human-made things do it too — the pyramids, St. Peter's in Rome — too big for the eye to take in at one look. Source: Kant, Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790); 1000-Word Philosophy, Kant's Theory of the Sublime.

question: Abraham Lincoln told a fellow stagecoach passenger that every good deed is really done out of selfishness. Just then they passed an old sow shrieking as her piglets drowned in a muddy slough. Lincoln leapt out, ran back, and lifted the little pigs onto the bank. When his companion asked where the selfishness was in that, Lincoln said he would have had no peace of mind all day if he had left the sow suffering. A philosopher reading the story spots the flaw in Lincoln's reasoning. What is it?
answer: Lincoln felt that relief only because he already wanted the pigs to be safe, so his real aim was something beyond his own good feeling
choices: Lincoln felt that relief only because he already wanted the pigs to be safe, so his real aim was something beyond his own good feeling
Lincoln cannot prove what his motive was, since no one can ever truly know why another person chooses to act
Lincoln saved the pigs on impulse, and an impulsive act is neither selfish nor unselfish but simply automatic
Lincoln helped the pigs only because a witness was watching, so the deed reveals social pressure rather than real kindness
context: This is the classic 'everyone is selfish' move, and the catch was pointed out by philosopher Joel Feinberg. The good feeling Lincoln got was the RESULT of the rescue, not its target; he could only feel relieved because he had first wanted the pigs spared. That prior wanting is a desire for something other than his own emotional state, which is exactly what 'all acts are selfish' claims is impossible. The anecdote is widely reprinted from the Springfield Monitor. Source: Joel Feinberg, 'Psychological Egoism' (faculty.fiu.edu/~hauptli/Feinberg'sPsychologicalEgoism.html).

question: A friend insists that absolutely everything is mysterious. You point out that how blood moves through the body is well understood and no mystery at all. He replies that even blood flow still holds things left to learn, so it counts as mysterious too. By the time he is done, nothing in the world could ever be called non-mysterious. Why does that very success ruin his point?
answer: Once the word stretches to cover everything, it no longer divides anything, so calling a thing mysterious tells you nothing at all
choices: Once the word stretches to cover everything, it no longer divides anything, so calling a thing mysterious tells you nothing at all
He has confused two senses of the word, using mysterious to mean both unknown and merely complicated at the same time
He offered only blood flow as proof, and a single example can never establish a claim about absolutely everything
He assumed what he set out to show, treating the conclusion that all is mysterious as a premise of his own argument
context: A word like 'mysterious' earns its meaning by drawing a line, with mysteries on one side and plain known things on the other. Stretch it to swallow even well-charted facts and the line disappears; if the origin of the universe and the sum 3 x 4 = 12 are equally mysterious, the word divides nothing and says nothing. This is the suppressed correlative, also called the fallacy of lost contrast. The 'mysterious' version comes from Alexander Bain, the first Regius Professor of Logic at Aberdeen, who used it as a clean non-political illustration of the same trick as 'everyone is selfish.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Suppressed correlative'; Alexander Bain, Logic (19th c.).

question: In a debate, one side declares that real freedom is obeying the just laws of the state, so a citizen sitting in prison for breaking those laws is more free than ever. The warm feeling the word freedom carries now attaches to confinement, and anyone who accepts the wording has lost the argument before it began. Why has no actual case been made here?
answer: The verdict was packed into the definition itself, so renaming obedience as freedom settles the dispute by fiat rather than by any reasoning
choices: The verdict was packed into the definition itself, so renaming obedience as freedom settles the dispute by fiat rather than by any reasoning
The two sides are using freedom in different senses, and a debate cannot proceed until they first agree on one shared meaning
The claim cannot be tested against any experience, and a statement no evidence could ever count against is saying nothing
The argument leans on the feelings the word stirs, and an appeal to emotion can never settle a question about politics
context: This is the persuasive definition, the slipperiest cousin of the suppressed correlative. The trick keeps a word's emotional glow while quietly swapping what it describes, so the listener's good feeling about 'freedom' transfers to obedience unquestioned. Charles Stevenson catalogued the move with examples like calling imprisonment 'true freedom' and a wartime massacre 'pacification,' and summed it up: 'To choose a definition is to plead a cause, so long as the word defined is strongly emotive.' A definition that decides the dispute by decree has not proven anything; it has only renamed the goalposts. William Frankena later named the wider error the 'definist fallacy.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Persuasive definition'; Charles Stevenson, 'Persuasive Definitions,' Mind (1938).

question: A teacher writes two sentences on the board: 'Every human being is mortal' and 'Socrates is a human being.' She asks what, if anything, the class is now stuck with. Once you grant both of those sentences, what happens to the claim that Socrates is mortal?
answer: You are forced into it — you cannot grant both and still deny it
choices: You are forced into it — you cannot grant both and still deny it
You may take it or leave it — the two sentences leave it open
You can accept it only after confirming Socrates was a real person
You must reject it, since two sentences can never settle a third
context: This is the textbook syllogism: grant the two premises and the conclusion is forced — you cannot consistently accept both and deny that Socrates is mortal. It is the marquee demonstration that some conclusions follow of necessity. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle: Logic' (iep.utm.edu/aristotle-logic) and Wikipedia, 'Syllogism.'

question: Elizabeth tells you one true thing about her garage: she owns either a Honda or a Saturn, and nothing else. A moment later she adds, also truthfully, that she does not own a Honda. From just those two facts, what do you now know for certain about her car?
answer: It is a Saturn — ruling the one option out leaves the other forced
choices: It could still be either — she never actually said which one she owns
It is a Saturn — ruling the one option out leaves the other forced
It is a Honda, since that was the first option she happened to name
Nothing for certain — owning a car is not the same as garaging it
context: This is the disjunctive syllogism: rule one option out and the remaining one is forced. It shows validity is not only Aristotle's 'All/Some' categorical forms — eliminating possibilities is its own airtight move. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Validity and Soundness' (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: Look at how this argument hangs together: 'All Greeks are men; all men are mortal; therefore all Greeks are mortal.' One word does the secret work — it appears in both of the first two sentences, joins the two ends of the argument, then vanishes from the conclusion. Which word is that connecting hinge?
answer: men
choices: men
Greeks
mortal
therefore
context: That hinge is the middle term: it appears in BOTH premises, bridges Greeks to mortality, then drops out of the conclusion once it has done its job. No shared middle term, no syllogism. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle: Logic' (iep.utm.edu/aristotle-logic) and Wikipedia, 'Syllogism.'

question: A kid argues: 'All basketballs are round; the Earth is round; therefore the Earth is a basketball.' Notice that all three sentences are actually true — yet the conclusion is plainly silly. Even with every sentence true, did the conclusion really HAVE to follow from the first two?
answer: No — its truth is a lucky coincidence, the sentences never forced it
choices: Yes — once the sentences are true, the conclusion is locked in tight
Yes — any argument built from true sentences is automatically airtight
No — its truth is a lucky coincidence, the sentences never forced it
No — but only because the Earth is not a perfect geometric sphere
context: Here every sentence is true AND the conclusion is true, yet the argument is invalid — the conclusion's truth is a coincidence the form never forced. True sentences do not make a good argument. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Validity and Soundness' (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: A logic teacher writes 'All M are P; all S are M; therefore all S are P' on the board, using bare letters where real words would go, and challenges the class to break it. No one can. One student asks the sharp question: with not a single real subject named anywhere, what is it that we are even judging when we call an argument like this a good one?
answer: The arrangement of its terms — judged without knowing whether one sentence is true
choices: The arrangement of its terms — judged without knowing whether one sentence is true
The truth of its premises — a good argument needs true starting sentences
The fame of the example — Aristotle's own cases are the reliable ones
The order you read it in — premises first, then the conclusion last
context: Validity lives in the SHAPE, not the topic. The form 'All M are P; all S are M; therefore all S are P' is judged by the arrangement of its terms alone — which is why you can check whether an argument is valid without knowing whether a single one of its sentences is true. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Logic' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-logic) and IEP, 'Validity and Soundness.'

question: Logicians say an argument is 'valid' when its form makes one particular situation flat-out impossible. You can have a valid argument whose premises are false, or whose conclusion you doubt — but there is exactly one combination its form forbids. Which situation can a valid form never allow?
answer: Every premise true while the conclusion is false
choices: Every premise false while the conclusion is true
A conclusion that states something the premises did not
Premises about a topic the conclusion never mentions
Every premise true while the conclusion is false
context: A valid argument is one whose form 'makes it impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion nevertheless to be false.' Validity is a guarantee — IF the premises are true, the conclusion is locked in. It does not promise the premises actually are true. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Validity and Soundness' (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: A debater shows you an argument with a flawless valid shape, then grins: 'But valid only means the SHAPE is good — it never promised the argument actually proves anything TRUE.' Logicians keep a stronger word for an argument that doesn't just reason well but truly settles its conclusion as true. Beyond a valid shape, what must such an argument have?
answer: Its premises must all actually be true, not merely well-arranged
choices: Its conclusion must be something nobody has ever doubted before
Its premises must all actually be true, not merely well-arranged
It must use Aristotle's letters rather than ordinary everyday words
It must contain exactly two premises and one single conclusion
context: That stronger property is soundness: an argument is sound if and only if it is BOTH valid AND all its premises are actually true. Validity = the shape is good; soundness = the shape is good and the inputs are true. Only a sound argument actually proves its conclusion. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Validity and Soundness' (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: Aristotle replaced names like 'Socrates' and 'Greeks' with bare letters — A, B, C — so an argument's SHAPE could be studied on its own. Historians call this single stroke the birth of a tool we still use everywhere — in algebra, in code, in logic. What did Aristotle invent here?
answer: The variable — a placeholder letter that stands for any term at all
choices: The alphabet, repurposed from speech into a system of writing
The conclusion, a sentence drawn from the sentences set before it
The variable — a placeholder letter that stands for any term at all
The premise, a starting claim that an argument is then built upon
context: Aristotle was the FIRST thinker to use schematic letters as variables — A, B, C standing in for any terms — so an argument could be studied as a pure shape independent of its subject matter. This single invention is what made formal logic possible: the birth of the variable. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Logic' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-logic).

question: Aristotle sorted every basic statement into four kinds: 'All S are P,' 'No S are P,' 'Some S are P,' and 'Some S are not P.' Later logicians tagged them with the letters A, E, I, and O — and all four letters were lifted straight out of just two Latin words. Which pair of Latin words secretly supplied the four letters?
answer: AffIrmo and nEgO — 'I affirm' yields A and I, 'I deny' yields E and O
choices: AffIrmo and nEgO — 'I affirm' yields A and I, 'I deny' yields E and O
Universalis and Particularis — Latin for the 'all' claims and the 'some' claims
Subjectum and Praedicatum — Latin for a statement's 'subject' and its 'predicate'
Aristoteles and Organon — the logician himself and the title of his logic books
context: A = 'All S are P' (universal affirmative), E = 'No S are P' (universal negative), I = 'Some S are P' (particular affirmative), O = 'Some S are not P' (particular negative). The labels come from Latin AffIrmo ('I affirm,' giving A and I) and nEgO ('I deny,' giving E and O). Source: Wikipedia, 'Syllogism' and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Medieval Theories of the Syllogism.'

question: Centuries before flashcards, medieval students memorized the valid argument forms by chanting a string of made-up names — 'Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio.' The oldest version survives in William of Sherwood's 13th-century logic book. The names were nonsense words, yet each one secretly stored its whole argument. What was hidden inside each name that made it a memory device?
answer: Its vowels — read in order, they named the three statement-types in that form
choices: Its first letter — this pointed to which figure the argument belonged in
Its length — longer names flagged the arguments that were harder to prove
Its rhyme — names that rhymed with each other shared the same conclusion
Its vowels — read in order, they named the three statement-types in that form
context: In each made-up name the VOWELS encode the argument's three statements in order: Barbara = A, A, A; Celarent = E, A, E. The oldest surviving version is in William of Sherwood's 13th-century 'Introductiones in Logicam.' Students literally sang the shapes of valid reasoning. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Medieval Theories of the Syllogism' and Medieval Logic & Semantics, 'Syllogism Mnemonics.'

question: Consider this argument: 'All toasters are made of gold; everything made of gold is a time-travel device; therefore all toasters are time-travel devices.' Every line is plainly false, and the conclusion is absurd — yet logicians insist the REASONING is perfectly valid. How can an argument deserve to be called valid when not one of its sentences is true?
answer: Validity guards only the link from premises to conclusion, not the facts
choices: It cannot — an argument with all-false sentences is never truly valid
Validity guards only the link from premises to conclusion, not the facts
It is valid only because all three of its sentences are false together
Validity here just means the sentences are short and easy to follow
context: A perfectly VALID argument can have false premises AND a false conclusion — the SHAPE is valid even when every line is absurd. Validity protects the inference, not the facts. (This is the mirror image of the basketball case, where true sentences gave an invalid argument.) Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Validity and Soundness' (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: Here is an argument that FEELS just like the Socrates one: 'All cats are mammals; all dogs are mammals; therefore all cats are dogs.' Both starting sentences are true, and the three-line shape looks right — but the conclusion is false. The word 'mammals' sits in both premises, yet the argument still fails. Why does it collapse?
answer: The shared word 'mammals' sits above both cats and dogs but never joins them to each other
choices: The shared word 'mammals' sits above both cats and dogs but never joins them to each other
The shared word 'mammals' is too broad a category to settle any narrower conclusion
The premises link through 'mammals' but should have shared 'cats' or 'dogs' instead
The conclusion runs the link backwards, treating every mammal as if it were a cat
context: This is the undistributed-middle look-alike, the bridge to the fallacy ladder. Both premises are true and it feels like a syllogism, but it is invalid: putting cats and dogs each UNDER 'mammals' never joins them to each other, so the shared middle term proves only that both are mammals, not that one is the other. A valid-LOOKING shape is not a valid shape. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle: Logic' and Philosophy Institute, 'Common Fallacies in Categorical Syllogisms.'

question: In 1879 a slim book — Gottlob Frege's 'Begriffsschrift' — finally pushed past Aristotle's account of valid form and launched modern logic. Before that, the philosopher Kant had calmly pronounced the whole subject finished and perfect. What is the astonishing fact about Aristotle's logic that Frege's book finally brought to an end?
answer: It had stood essentially unchanged AS logic itself for two thousand years
choices: It had stood essentially unchanged AS logic itself for two thousand years
It had been patched and rebuilt by a fresh thinker in every single century
It had survived only as a curiosity, never once used in a real argument
It had been written down by Aristotle but kept secret until Frege's day
context: Aristotle's syllogistic ruled Western thought for over two thousand years — it was 'logic' itself until 1879, when Gottlob Frege's 'Begriffsschrift' (Concept-Script) launched modern predicate logic and went beyond it. Kant had even declared logic a finished science. One man's account of valid form stood essentially unimproved for two millennia. Source: Wikipedia, 'Syllogism' (Frege, Begriffsschrift 1879) and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Logic.'

question: Roman followers of Epicurus took a single Greek word and turned it into four short sentences you keep in your head to calm a worried mind. But that word, 'tetrapharmakos', already meant something else in ordinary life long before the philosophers borrowed it. What did it first name?
answer: A salve of beeswax, pine resin, pitch and animal fat, rubbed onto open cuts
choices: A salve of beeswax, pine resin, pitch and animal fat, rubbed onto open cuts
A battle line that locked four soldiers shield-to-shield in one tight square
A four-string lyre that wandering poets carried to accompany their verses
A four-herb spice blend that cooks worked into roasting meat for a feast
context: A 'tetrapharmakos' (four-drug) was a real ancient wound-salve of beeswax, pine resin, pitch and fat (usually pork fat), noted in Galen's 'On the Properties of Simples'. Roman-era Epicureans borrowed the pharmacist's word for a four-line ointment for the anxious SOUL: four sentences memorized the way you'd keep a salve in your kit, aiming at 'ataraxia', freedom from disturbance. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tetrapharmacum' / 'Tetrapharmakos'.

question: Epicurus taught that fearing death is wasted worry: death is the end of all sensation, and where nothing can be felt, nothing good or bad is left to suffer. He compressed the whole argument into one famous line. What was it?
answer: While I am still here death is not, and once death comes I am no longer here
choices: While I am still here death is not, and once death comes I am no longer here
Death is owed to nature like a debt, and a debt once paid can trouble no one
Death takes only the body, and what it cannot touch is the part worth keeping
Death ends a long journey, and no traveller fears the inn where the road stops
context: This is the second of Epicurus's four cures. His own words: 'So long as we exist death is not present, whereas when death is present we do not exist.' Principal Doctrine 2 adds: 'Death is nothing to us; for that which is dissolved is devoid of sensation, and that which is devoid of sensation is nothing to us.' The self and its death never overlap, so death can never be experienced as harm. Source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (trans. Saint-Andre); Principal Doctrine 2 in Diogenes Laertius Book X.

question: The first of Epicurus's four cures is 'don't fear the gods.' But he was no atheist — he insisted the gods are real. A student presses him: if the gods exist, why shouldn't I dread their punishment? What reasoning does Epicurus give to dissolve the fear?
answer: A god so perfect is troubled by nothing, so it feels no anger and never punishes
choices: A god so perfect is troubled by nothing, so it feels no anger and never punishes
The gods are far too distant and too many to keep track of one small human life
The gods reward the good and strike only the wicked, so a decent person need not worry
No one has ever returned from the gods to report a punishment, so the threat is unproven
context: Note the subtlety the cure turns on: NOT 'the gods don't exist' (Epicurus says they DO), but that a blissful, indestructible being meddles with nothing. Principal Doctrine 1: 'That which is happy and imperishable neither has trouble itself, nor does it cause it to anything; so that it is not subject to feelings of either anger or gratitude; for these feelings only exist in what is weak.' No anger means no punishment to dread; no gratitude means no favours to chase. Source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrine 1 (Diogenes Laertius Book X); Letter to Menoeceus.

question: The last of Epicurus's four cures promises that 'the terrible is easy to endure.' He backs the boast by claiming pain comes with a built-in limit that makes any suffering survivable. What is the limit he claims?
answer: If pain is intense it burns out fast, and if it drags on for long it stays mild
choices: If pain is intense it burns out fast, and if it drags on for long it stays mild
If pain is met in good company it shrinks, and borne alone it grows past bearing
If pain is met with the right attitude it fades, and resisted head-on it deepens
If pain strikes the young it passes quickly, and the old must outlast it slowly
context: This is the fourth cure. Principal Doctrine 4: 'Pain does not abide continuously in the flesh, but in its extremity it is present only a very short time... long diseases have in them more that is pleasant than painful to the flesh.' The pay-off: no suffering is BOTH unbearable AND endless. The sharpest pain is brief; whatever lasts must be mild enough to live with. Source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrine 4 (trans. in Diogenes Laertius Book X).

question: A Texan with terrible aim empties his rifle into the broad side of a barn, then struts into town and swears he never misses a shot, pointing back at a tight bullseye ringing a cluster of holes on the wall. A real marksman with no skill at all could fire into a blank wall and brag the very same way. What lets the Texan pull off the trick?
answer: He drew the bullseye around the holes only after the shots landed, so it fits whatever spray a wild rifle leaves
choices: He drew the bullseye around the holes only after the shots landed, so it fits whatever spray a wild rifle leaves
He fired so many rounds that pure luck alone was bound to drop at least one of them dead center on the wall
He stood so close to the barn that even a wildly aimed shot could hardly help but strike somewhere near the middle
He waited for a dead-still day so no breeze could pull a single one of his shots off the line he had called aloud
context: This barn scene is the namesake of the 'Texas sharpshooter fallacy.' The cluster looks like skill only because the bullseye was chalked AROUND it after the shots landed; any wall would do. Source: Fallacy Files (fallacyfiles.org/texsharp.html); Wikipedia: Texas sharpshooter fallacy.  (Legend.)

question: A shooting coach watches the barn-painter brag and says the man broke the one rule that tells a real marksman from a fraud. Three onlookers each guess which rule he means. Which one names the rule the painter actually broke?
answer: You must fix the target before you fire, so a hit only counts if you called it in advance
choices: You must fix the target before you fire, so a hit only counts if you called it in advance
You must report your aim point to a witness aloud before each shot leaves the barrel
You must gather a fresh round of shots before drawing any conclusion from the first batch
You must count every shot that misses, not only the ones that land near each other
context: A prediction is only evidence if it is locked in BEFORE the data; the same rule that separates a real marksman from a fraud separates real science from fooling yourself. A target drawn after the shots land can always be made to fit, so it carries zero weight. Source: Fallacy Files (fallacyfiles.org/texsharp.html); Wikipedia: Texas sharpshooter fallacy.

question: A con artist sends out free stock predictions month after month. A small group of strangers watches him call the market right every single time, becomes certain he has a rare gift, and gladly hands him their life savings. To that lucky group his record looks utterly flawless. What is really going on?
answer: Each of them got only the calls that came true; thousands of others got the wrong calls and were quietly dropped
choices: Each of them got only the calls that came true; thousands of others got the wrong calls and were quietly dropped
Each of them paid a small monthly fee, so the swindler made his money whether the picks won or lost in the end
Each of them saw glowing testimonials that he had cherry-picked from a few real clients who had once gotten lucky
Each of them received the picks a little late, so there was never any time to check them before the market moved
context: This is the Texas sharpshooter built on hidden losers: the 'bullseye' is painted around the few survivors while every miss is discarded out of sight, invisible to the winners. Source: ClearerThinking, 'What is survivorship bias' (clearerthinking.org); Wikipedia: Texas sharpshooter fallacy.

question: For centuries, fans of the writer Nostradamus have called him a great prophet, pointing to verse after verse that seems to foretell a famous disaster. His hundreds of verses are deliberately vague and gloomy, and most of them never matched anything at all. A skeptic says the fans have it exactly backwards. What is the trick that lets almost any event look 'predicted' by a Nostradamus verse?
answer: The fans wait for the event, then go find a verse to fit it, ignoring the hundreds that foretold nothing
choices: The fans wait for the event, then go find a verse to fit it, ignoring the hundreds that foretold nothing
The fans mistranslate the old French, so a clever reader can bend any line to mean almost anything at all
The fans count a near-miss as a hit, so a verse only roughly close to the event still gets called correct
The fans pass the verses around so fast that a 'prediction' spreads and convinces people before any check
context: Nostradamus is a centuries-old sharpshooter machine: the 'prophecy' is the bullseye chalked around an event that already happened, with every failed verse quietly ignored. (Often-repeated skeptic claim; treat as legend.) Source: Skeptic's Dictionary; Britannica, 'Nostradamus and His Prophecies.'

question: During World War II, Londoners were certain the German V-1 flying bombs were being aimed on purpose, pounding some districts hard while sparing others where spies were rumored to live. In 1946 the actuary R.D. Clarke gridded the whole city into small squares and counted exactly how many bombs fell in each. When his count came back, what did it reveal about the 'targeting' Londoners felt so sure of?
answer: The bunched-up districts were just what blind chance produces, with no sign of any deliberate aim
choices: The bunched-up districts were just what blind chance produces, with no sign of any deliberate aim
The Germans really had been aiming, though their guidance was far too crude to hit the marks they chose
The spared districts truly were protected, because the rumored spies had quietly bribed the bomb crews
The bombs had fallen in a near-perfect even spread, so every district that felt singled out had miscounted
context: The 'targeting' was the Texas-sharpshooter illusion painted onto chance. Clarke's hits matched a random Poisson scatter almost perfectly (a chi-squared fit of p=0.88), so the bunched districts were exactly what randomness predicts. Source: R.D. Clarke (1946) via Significance/OUP, 'The Flying Bomb and the Actuary.'

question: Surgeon and writer Atul Gawande described a frightened neighborhood that counts up several cancer cases among nearby homes and becomes sure something local must be poisoning them. Gawande warned that their case is built the same way the barn-painter builds his. Where exactly does the neighborhood's reasoning go wrong?
answer: They mark the boundary around the sick homes only after spotting them, so a cluster is guaranteed either way
choices: They mark the boundary around the sick homes only after spotting them, so a cluster is guaranteed either way
They trust their own count over the official maps, which would have shown the cases spread far apart
They assume cancer must be contagious, when in plain truth it cannot pass from one neighbor to the next
They notice only the worst cases and forget the milder ones, which makes the small cluster look far larger
context: Gawande named this trap for the public in 'The Cancer-Cluster Myth' (The New Yorker, Feb 8, 1999). The line is drawn around the cases after they appear, exactly like the sharpshooter's target. Of thousands of U.S. cancer-cluster scares investigated, not one has convincingly identified an environmental cause. Source: Atul Gawande, The New Yorker, 1999; Skeptic's Dictionary.

question: A scientist notices that several illnesses have bunched together in one spot, just as the barn-painter noticed his cluster of holes. When the physician John Snow saw cholera deaths bunched around one London water pump, he did not stop there and call the pump guilty. What did Snow do next that a sharpshooter never would?
answer: He went and gathered fresh evidence the cluster alone could not give, tracing which homes drank from a tainted supplier
choices: He went and gathered fresh evidence the cluster alone could not give, tracing which homes drank from a tainted supplier
He measured the cluster precisely and named the pump as the cause once the death count around it was exact
He went looking for the same bunching near other pumps and waited until a second cluster matched the first one
He trusted the cluster because it was so large, since a bunch of deaths that big could not happen by mere chance
context: Noticing a chance cluster is fine; the fallacy is treating the cluster you noticed as its own proof. Snow did not stop at the bunching around the Broad Street pump -- he went out for fresh, independent evidence, tracing which households drank from which water company so the new data could confirm or kill the hunch. As the Fallacy Files puts it, a cluster 'is the basis not for a causal conclusion, but for the formation of a causal hypothesis which needs to be tested.' Source: Fallacy Files (fallacyfiles.org/texsharp.html); Wikipedia: Texas sharpshooter fallacy.

question: In 1993 a Swedish team studied people living near power lines and checked them against more than 800 different medical conditions at once. One result jumped out: childhood leukemia looked about four times higher, and it made headlines. A statistician warned the headline was a sharpshooter's trick. Why does checking 800 conditions all at once turn a scary 'hit' into noise?
answer: With 800 chances, a few will look striking by luck alone, and the alarm was raised around whichever one jumped
choices: With 800 chances, a few will look striking by luck alone, and the alarm was raised around whichever one jumped
With 800 conditions, the study grew too costly to finish, so the leukemia result was never properly counted
With 800 conditions, the power lines truly caused many of them, but only leukemia was reported to the press
