With 800 conditions, the people near the lines were simply sicker overall, which inflated every single number
context: Checking hundreds of things guarantees a few false 'hits'; the bullseye gets painted around whichever number jumps, and here follow-up studies found no real link. Scientists call painting the target afterward 'HARKing' -- Hypothesizing After the Results are Known. Source: Wikipedia: Texas sharpshooter fallacy (Feychting and Ahlbom, 1993 Swedish power-line study).

question: A carpenter builds a wooden chair. It wobbles, the legs are slightly uneven, and one day it will rot. Yet you instantly know it is a chair, matching it against an idea of a perfect chair no carpenter ever made and you have never seen. A philosopher makes a startling claim about which chair is MORE real: the wobbly one you sit in, or the one no one ever built. What does he claim?
answer: The perfect chair you never see is more real than the wooden one you touch
choices: The perfect chair you never see is more real than the wooden one you touch
The wooden chair is more real, since the perfect chair is just a fiction
Both chairs are equally real, just known in two separate ways
The perfect chair is only a label the mind invents from many wooden ones
context: This is Plato's central reversal in the Theory of Forms: the perfect, unchanging original (the Form) outranks in reality the changing thing you can touch. 'Form' just means the perfect, eternal original of a thing, grasped by the mind, while sensible things are imperfect, perishable copies that 'strive to be such as the Forms are.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology.'

question: A bowling ball, a basketball, and a circle chalked on a blackboard are three completely different things, yet all three are round. A philosopher says this one shared feature points to a single thing standing behind every round object in the world. What does he say all round things take part in?
answer: One single Roundness itself, which every round thing copies
choices: One single Roundness itself, which every round thing copies
One single word we attach once we notice things look alike
One single curve that lives inside each ball and nowhere else
One single habit of the eye that lumps curved edges together
context: This is Plato's 'one over many' move: whenever many different things share the same feature, he posits one perfect original, the Form, that they all share in or 'participate' in. Roundness itself stands behind every round thing. Source: SEP, 'Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology,' summarizing Phaedo 100c.

question: Socrates asks a young friend whether justice itself, and beauty itself, are real things, and then asks, Have you ever seen any of these with your eyes? The friend admits he never has. Socrates says you grasp them another way entirely. By what does he say you grasp justice and beauty themselves?
answer: By the mind alone, since they are real but never met by the eyes
choices: By the mind alone, since they are real but never met by the eyes
By the eyes over time, after watching many fair and unfair deeds
By feeling, since justice and beauty are stirrings in the heart
By agreement, since a whole town decides what counts as just here
context: Plato's everyday examples of Forms are abstract properties, not objects: Justice, Beauty itself, Equality, the Good. In the Phaedo, Socrates argues these are real yet invisible, grasped only with the mind. Source: Phaedo 65c-65d (Fowler trans.), via SEP, 'Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology.'

question: Plato pictures three makers. God makes one true Bed in nature. A carpenter looks toward that Bed and builds a wooden bed you can lie on. Then a painter sets up an easel and paints the carpenter's bed. Plato ranks all three by how far each maker's bed stands from the truth. Where does the carpenter's wooden bed fall?
answer: One step below the true Bed, a copy that the painter in turn copies all over again
choices: One step below the true Bed, a copy that the painter in turn copies all over again
Furthest from the truth, since wood rots while a painted bed can outlast it for ages
Level with the true Bed, since both God and the carpenter make real beds you can use
Truest of the three, since a solid bed beats both a bare idea and a flat picture of one
context: In Republic Book 10 Plato ranks three beds: God's true Bed, the carpenter's copy of it, and the painter's copy of the copy. The painter's work is 'thrice removed from the king and from the truth,' which places the carpenter's wooden bed one step down from the original. Source: Plato, Republic Book 10 (Jowett trans.), Wikisource; Perseus 597.

question: Two sticks look exactly equal in length. But tilt your head, and one looks longer; hand them to a different person, and they call them unequal. Socrates notes the sticks can seem both equal AND unequal, yet Equality itself can never seem unequal. Why does he say this gap PROVES the perfect Equal is something separate from any pair of sticks?
answer: Because the sticks can fail to be equal but the perfect Equal never can, so they cannot be the same thing
choices: Because the sticks can fail to be equal but the perfect Equal never can, so they cannot be the same thing
Because a careful measurement of the sticks would settle the matter once and for all without any dispute
Because a true ruler with finer markings than the eye could tell the two sticks apart at last
Because two viewers would eventually agree on the sticks if they simply held them the very same way
context: The equal-sticks argument (Phaedo 74): Socrates says there is 'such a thing as equality... not one piece of wood equal to another... but something beyond that, equality in the abstract.' Because the sticks can appear unequal but Equality itself never can, the sticks 'fall very far short' of the perfect Equal, which he takes as proof the Form is separate from its copies. Source: Plato, Phaedo p.74 (Fowler trans.), Perseus Digital Library.

question: No two sticks in the world are ever PERFECTLY equal, yet every child has the idea of perfect equality anyway. Socrates argues you could not have gotten this idea from the imperfect things around you. So where, he says, must your soul have met perfect Equality, leaving the sticks merely to REMIND you of it?
answer: Before birth, so that learning is really remembering what the soul once saw
choices: Before birth, so that learning is really remembering what the soul once saw
In early childhood, by being patiently taught the word equal by elders
In a flash of pure invention, since the mind can dream up what it lacks
Nowhere at all, since the idea is just a blur of every pair you have seen
context: This is Plato's doctrine of recollection (anamnesis, Phaedo 72e-77a): since deficient copies could never give us the idea of the perfect Equal, the soul must have seen the Forms directly before birth, and the copies merely remind us of them, so 'learning is no other than recollection.' Source: Phaedo 72e-77a, via SEP and IEP 'Plato: Phaedo.'

question: A beautiful face is also plain from a bad angle; a just act in one city is called unjust in another. Such things, Plato says, can be both a thing and its opposite, so the most we can have about them is shifting opinion. Real knowledge, he argues, needs a different sort of object. WHY can a thing that is both F and not-F never be an object of real knowledge?
answer: Because a thing that turns into its own opposite gives the mind nothing fixed to lock onto and know
choices: Because a thing that turns into its own opposite gives the mind nothing fixed to lock onto and know
Because only a fact that enough wise people have agreed upon can ever rise to the level of knowledge
Because only a thing you can measure to the exact number can be known without any room for dispute
Because only a memory vivid enough to resist all later doubt can count as real knowledge of a thing
context: Plato's 'two worlds' argument (Republic 479a-480a): sensible things that can be both F and not-F are objects of mere opinion, while the Forms, each simply and only itself, are the objects of real knowledge. Knowledge and the changeable cannot share the same objects, so the Forms must be a separate, higher class of thing. Source: Republic 479a-480a; SEP, 'Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology.'

question: Plato draws a comparison. In the visible world the sun does two jobs at once: its light lets your eye SEE things, and its warmth lets those things GROW and live. He says one single Form does both jobs in the realm of the mind. Which Form does he crown as this sun of the mind?
answer: The Good, which Plato sets above every other Form
choices: The Good, which Plato sets above every other Form
Beauty, which a lover may chase from face to face
Equality, which two leaning sticks can only fall short of
Justice, which no single city has ever fully reached
context: The Sun analogy (Republic VI, ~508-509): just as the sun lets the eye see things and gives them life, the Form of the Good lets the mind know the Forms and is the source of their very being. 'What gives truth to the things known and the power to know to the knower is the Form of the Good.' Source: Republic 508c-509b; Wikipedia 'Analogy of the Sun'; SEP.

question: Plato pictures prisoners chained in a cave since birth, facing a blank wall where shadows are thrown. One prisoner is freed, stumbles past the fire that cast the shadows, and is dragged up into the blinding daylight outside. For his whole life he had taken the shadows on the wall for one thing. What had the shadows been to him?
answer: The whole of reality, when they were only flickering copies of real things
choices: The whole of reality, when they were only flickering copies of real things
A message from the gods, when the moving shapes carried no meaning at all
Cruel theater staged by jailers, when no one had chained him there to fool him
His own reflection cast back, when the bare wall in truth showed him nothing
context: In the Allegory of the Cave (Republic 514a-520a), the freed prisoner's climb from shadows to firelight to the sun pictures the soul's ascent from copies to the Forms. The prisoners' error is taking the shadows, mere copies, for the whole of reality, the same mistake Plato says we make when we treat sensible things as the only real ones. Source: Republic 514a-520a; Wikipedia 'Allegory of the cave'; SEP.

question: Plato keeps raising the Form of the Good above the other Forms. The Good, he writes, is the source that gives every other Form both its truth and its very being. Yet in the same breath he refuses to call the Good just one more being among the rest. So is the Good the highest being there is, or something that is not a being at all?
answer: Not a being at all, but the source that stands above being and lets everything else be
choices: Not a being at all, but the source that stands above being and lets everything else be
The highest being there is, simply the grandest item on the list of things that exist
The fullest being of all, so packed with reality that nothing else can possibly outrank it
Beyond all knowing, a thing so dark that not even the most trained mind can point at it
context: Plato pushes the Good past the other Forms: it 'is not itself a state of being but something transcending far beyond it in dignity and power' (epekeina tes ousias, 'beyond being,' Republic 509b). It is the source of being and knowledge, yet stands above the very being it grounds. Source: Republic 509b; Wikipedia 'Analogy of the Sun.'

question: Young Socrates says large things are large because they share in one Form, Largeness. The aged philosopher Parmenides springs a trap: if Largeness explains the large things, and Largeness is itself large, then the large things PLUS Largeness now share something, so you need a SECOND Largeness to explain that group, then a third. What has Socrates accidentally built?
answer: An endless tower of ever-higher Forms, when the Form was meant to STOP such a chain
choices: An endless tower of ever-higher Forms, when the Form was meant to STOP such a chain
A perfect proof that Largeness is real, since every step keeps pointing back to it
A clever way to measure size, by counting how many Forms a thing must share in
A single highest Largeness, above which Parmenides agrees nothing more can stand
context: This is the Third Man Argument (Parmenides 132a-b): the Form meant to stop the regress instead launches an infinite tower, since each new shared largeness demands yet another Largeness to explain it. Aristotle later nicknamed it the 'Third Man' (triton anthropos). Notably, Plato wrote this devastating objection to his own theory himself. Source: SEP, 'Plato's Parmenides'; Aristotle, Metaphysics 990b17.

question: Parmenides presses his hardest objection on young Socrates. Suppose the Forms are truly SEPARATE from our world, perfect and apart, touching only one another. Parmenides draws a chilling conclusion from this clean separation. What does perfect separateness cost us?
answer: We could never know the Forms, since our minds reach only things here and never cross over to where the Forms sit
choices: We could never know the Forms, since our minds reach only things here and never cross over to where the Forms sit
We could never copy the Forms, so the chairs and beds of our world could not be likenesses of them after all
We could never doubt the Forms, since their flawless perfection would silence every question we might raise
We could never count the Forms, since a realm sealed away admits no number we could ever assign to it
context: This is the 'Greatest Difficulty' (Parmenides 133a-134e): if the Forms are truly separate, Forms relate only to other Forms and human knowledge relates only to things in our world, so making the Forms perfectly transcendent threatens to put them forever out of human reach. Source: SEP, 'Plato's Parmenides,' 133a-134e.

question: Parmenides has just battered the theory of Forms with objection after objection. Young Socrates looks ready to give the whole thing up. But Parmenides stops him with a warning: deny that for each thing there is a character that is always the same, he says, and you will destroy something precious altogether. What does he warn that dropping the Forms would wreck?
answer: The power of disciplined argument itself, leaving the mind nothing steady to reason about
choices: The power of disciplined argument itself, leaving the mind nothing steady to reason about
The reputation of Socrates himself, who had staked his good name on the Forms in public
The unity of the city itself, since shared Forms were what held the citizens in agreement
The memory of the soul itself, which had recollected the Forms from before it was born
context: Even while demolishing the theory, Parmenides warns that abandoning Forms is worse: deny 'that for each thing there is a character that is always the same' and you 'destroy the power of dialectic entirely' (135b-c). Plato signals the Forms may be flawed but indispensable, since you cannot do philosophy without something stable to think about. Source: Plato, Parmenides 135b8-c2, via SEP, 'Plato's Parmenides.'

question: Tomas sits with his classmate Dmitri every day, but only on the days the homework is hard. On easy days, and after the final exam is over, he never seeks Dmitri out at all. What holds the two of them together?
answer: The use Dmitri is to him, which is all the bond rests on
choices: The use Dmitri is to him, which is all the bond rests on
A real care for who Dmitri is, the kind that outlasts school
The good times they share, which fade as the two drift apart
A quiet rivalry, since each wants to beat the other in class
context: Aristotle calls this a friendship of utility: the two 'do not love each other for themselves but in virtue of some good which they get from each other.' Once the usefulness is gone, the bond dissolves. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Philosophy of Love' (iep.utm.edu/love).

question: Priya seeks out her neighbor Kofi any time she is bored, because he is hilarious and quick-witted and always turns a dull afternoon into a good one. If he ever lost his spark, she admits, she would simply stop coming around. What is her bond with Kofi built on?
answer: How fun he is to be around, more than the person he is underneath
choices: How fun he is to be around, more than the person he is underneath
How good a person he is, which she admires and wants near her
How useful he is, doing favors she could never manage alone
How much he needs her, which makes her feel responsible for him
context: Aristotle calls this a friendship of pleasure. We like witty, charming people 'not for their character... but because they find them pleasant,' and the bond lasts only as long as the fun does. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Ethics (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-ethics).

question: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle argues that people find exactly three things lovable, and so there turn out to be exactly three kinds of friendship, one for each. Two of them rest on something the friend provides. What are the three?
answer: The useful, the pleasant, and the good person himself
choices: The useful, the pleasant, and the good person himself
The honest, the loyal, the brave, taken all together
The equal, the elder, and the one you look up to
The kin, the neighbor, and the stranger you take in
context: Aristotle's exact line: 'The kinds of friendship accordingly are three, being equal in number to the motives of love.' You are someone's friend because they are useful, because they are fun, or because you genuinely value the person they are. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII (F.H. Peters trans., Standard Ebooks).

question: Aristotle holds that most friendships rest on something that can change, so they last only as long as that thing does. But he singles out one kind that holds steady for a whole life. What does that lasting kind of friendship rest on?
answer: The good character of the two friends themselves
choices: The good character of the two friends themselves
The steady stream of favors they trade back and forth
The laughs and good times they keep finding together
The long stretch of years they have known each other
context: This is friendship of virtue, the bond between two good people who wish each other well for the other's own sake. Aristotle: 'their friendship lasts as long as they are good, and goodness is an enduring thing.' Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Ethics.

question: Aristotle says there is a simple way to find out which of your friends came for you and which came only for what you gave them: stop being useful or entertaining, and watch. What does Aristotle say the friend who came for the benefit does?
answer: Falls away, since the bond was never about you at all
choices: Falls away, since the bond was never about you at all
Lingers a while, then returns only when he needs something
Acts as if nothing has changed, hiding the loss
Becomes an enemy, bitter over the wasted time
context: Aristotle says utility and pleasure friendships are 'easily dissolved... for if they cease to be pleasant or useful to one another, their love ceases.' Only the friend who stays for the person, not the benefit, was a true friend. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII (Peters trans., Standard Ebooks).

question: Aristotle reaches for a single short phrase to capture how completely two true friends are bound together, so closely that what touches one touches the other. It is a line that has echoed for over two thousand years. How does Aristotle describe a true friend?
answer: A second self
choices: A second self
A guiding star
A safe harbor
A kindred spirit
context: The famous line, also rendered 'a friend is another self.' You care about a true friend exactly as you care about yourself; the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy echoes the poetic version, perfect friendship as 'one soul in two bodies.' Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book IX (Standard Ebooks, Peters trans.); IEP (iep.utm.edu/love).

question: Aristotle watches a man admire a famous stranger from afar and genuinely hope that stranger does well in life, though the stranger has no idea the man exists. Aristotle calls this real goodwill, but insists it is not yet friendship. Why does Aristotle say it falls short of friendship?
answer: Goodwill is only the seed; friendship is the grown thing, needing time and a bond returned
choices: Goodwill is only the seed; friendship is the grown thing, needing time and a bond returned
Goodwill is selfish at root; friendship must instead spring from cold and willed duty alone
Goodwill is far too mild; friendship must instead burn with a fierce and consuming passion
Goodwill is owed to all alike; friendship is instead owed only to ones own flesh and blood
context: Aristotle: 'well-wishing is the germ of friendship, in the same way as pleasure in the sight of a person is the germ of love.' Goodwill is the seed; real friendship is the grown thing that needs shared time and mutual awareness. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book IX (Standard Ebooks, Peters trans.).

question: In 399 BC the city of Athens dragged the 70-year-old philosopher Socrates before a citizen court on two charges. What did Athens accuse him of doing?
answer: Corrupting the young men and refusing to honor the city's gods
choices: Corrupting the young men and refusing to honor the city's gods
Plotting with Sparta to topple the Athenian democracy by force
Stealing from the city treasury and bribing jurors at earlier trials
Selling Athenian battle plans to merchants from rival Greek cities
context: The indictment charged corrupting the youth and impiety -- not believing in the gods the city believed in, and introducing new divinities. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Plato, Apology.

question: On trial for his life and facing death, Socrates told the Athenian jury he would rather die than give up questioning himself and others about how to live well. A life that is never questioned about goodness, he said, is what?
answer: Not worth living for a human being
choices: Not worth living for a human being
The safest and happiest kind of life
The proper life for an obedient citizen
A life the gods reward after death
context: "The unexamined life is not worth living" (Apology 38a) -- a life never questioned about virtue is not worth a human being's living. Source: Plato, Apology 38a; classics.mit.edu.

question: The jury found Socrates guilty, and under Athenian law he now had to propose his own punishment. Instead of begging for mercy or a small fine, the 70-year-old offered something outrageous. What did Socrates say he deserved?
answer: Free meals for life at the city's table, the honor reserved for its heroes
choices: Free meals for life at the city's table, the honor reserved for its heroes
A quiet life of exile, banished to the countryside far from Athens
A heavy fine in silver, paid out steadily over the coming years
A public whipping in the marketplace to satisfy his three accusers
context: Asked to name his penalty, Socrates said his true reward was free meals for life in the Prytaneum -- the honor given to Olympic champions and city heroes -- not a punishment at all. Source: Plato, Apology 36d-37a; Diogenes Laertius II.42.

question: Socrates warned the Athenian court that putting him to death would not help the city. He pictured Athens as a great, lazy horse, too big to bother moving, and himself as a small biting fly that stung it awake all day. If they swatted the fly, he said, what would happen to the city?
answer: It would simply doze back off to sleep
choices: It would simply doze back off to sleep
It would finally be free to grow strong
It would be punished by the angry gods
It would turn its anger on his accusers
context: Socrates compared himself to a gadfly sent by god to sting the sluggish city awake; kill him, and Athens would fall back asleep. Source: Plato, Apology 30e-31a; classics.mit.edu.

question: Socrates told the jury his whole strange life began with one trip to the oracle at Delphi: his friend Chaerephon went and asked the priestess about Socrates, and she gave an answer Socrates spent the rest of his days testing. What did the priestess at Delphi declare about Socrates?
answer: That no man alive was wiser than he
choices: That no man alive was wiser than he
That only the gods were wiser than he
That his wisdom would one day destroy him
That he was wise but had grown too proud
context: Chaerephon asked the Delphic oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the Pythian priestess answered that no man was wiser. Source: Plato, Apology 21a; classics.mit.edu.

question: The court hinted it would spare Socrates if he simply promised to give up philosophy and live out his old age in silence. The 70-year-old threw the bargain back in their faces. What did Socrates tell the jury he would do?
answer: Keep teaching and questioning people, as long as he had breath
choices: Keep teaching and questioning people, as long as he had breath
Leave the city of Athens quietly and never set foot there again
Pay over whatever fine the court chose to set against him
Beg the gods to forgive him and turn the city to mercy
context: "I shall obey God rather than you, and while I have life and strength I shall never cease from the practice and teaching of philosophy." Source: Plato, Apology; famous-trials.com/socrates; classics.mit.edu.

question: Condemned to death, Socrates did not rage or weep. He told the jurors the hour had come for them to part ways -- he to his death, they back to their lives -- and as for which path was the better one, he gave a calm answer. What did Socrates say about who was better off?
answer: Only god knows which of them is better off
choices: Only god knows which of them is better off
He was the lucky one, and they were the doomed ones
They were the lucky ones, and he was the doomed one
No one is ever truly better off after a trial
context: "The hour of departure has arrived... I to die, and you to live. Which of these two is better only God knows." Source: Plato, Apology 42a; classics.mit.edu.

question: The oracle had called Socrates the wisest man, which puzzled him, since he felt he knew nothing worth knowing. After questioning Athens' proudest experts, he decided he WAS a little wiser -- but only in one strange way. What made Socrates wiser than the men who were sure of themselves?
answer: He alone admitted he did not know what he did not know
choices: He alone admitted he did not know what he did not know
He had read far more books than any of them
He had won more public debates than any of them
He had been singled out and blessed by the oracle
context: "I am better off than he is -- for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know." Source: Plato, Apology 21d; classics.mit.edu.

question: Allowed to question his accuser Meletus in open court, Socrates sprang a trap. Meletus had sworn under oath that Socrates was an atheist who believed in no gods whatsoever. Yet the same indictment charged Socrates with inventing strange new divinities of his own. Socrates fastened on what those two sworn charges did to each other. What did he tell the court?
answer: Teaching new divinities means believing in divine things, so the atheism charge falls apart
choices: Teaching new divinities means believing in divine things, so the atheism charge falls apart
Each sworn charge held true on its own, so together they only doubled his guilt against him
Meletus had plainly mistaken him for the nature-philosophers who denied the gods of Athens
The oath bound Meletus to the first charge, so the second one no longer counted against him
context: Socrates trapped Meletus in a contradiction: a man charged with introducing NEW divinities must believe in divine things, which flatly contradicts the sworn charge that he believes in no gods at all. Source: Plato, Apology 26c-27a; Stanford Encyclopedia: Socrates.

question: Socrates told the jurors he had no fear of death at all, which startled them. Everyone around him treated dying as the worst thing that could ever happen to a person. But Socrates asked how any of them could be so certain of that. So when a man dreads death, Socrates argued, what is he really doing?
answer: Claiming to know death is bad, when no living person can know that
choices: Claiming to know death is bad, when no living person can know that
Simply valuing his own life, which is only right and natural
Fearing the pain of dying, rather than death itself
Trusting that the gods will step in to protect the innocent
context: "The fear of death is indeed the pretense of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being a pretense of knowing the unknown." Source: Plato, Apology 29a; classics.mit.edu.

question: Socrates had been convicted by a fairly close vote -- a swing of just thirty jurors would have freed him. Then, asked to name his own punishment, he demanded free meals for life as a hero's reward instead. When the jury voted a second time, this time on the death penalty, the count shocked his friends. What had happened on the second vote?
answer: Even more jurors turned against him than had voted to convict
choices: Even more jurors turned against him than had voted to convict
The jury softened, and many of them switched to spare his life
The presiding judges grew confused and threw the whole case out
His accusers lost their nerve and backed off the demand for death
context: His mocking "free meals" proposal enraged the jury: about eighty MORE voted for death than had voted to convict. Source: Diogenes Laertius II.42 ("an accession of eighty fresh votes"); famous-trials.com.

question: Many Athenians blamed Socrates for the city's wounds: two of his former students, Critias and Alcibiades, had betrayed Athens -- Critias as a leader of the murderous Thirty Tyrants, Alcibiades as a traitor-general. Yet the prosecutors never charged Socrates with those crimes, and attacked his religion instead. Why did they steer clear of the real grievance?
answer: A recent amnesty made it illegal to charge him for those old political ties
choices: A recent amnesty made it illegal to charge him for those old political ties
Both of his former students had already been pardoned by the court
No one could prove the two traitors had ever studied with Socrates
The betrayals had taken place too far away from the city of Athens
context: After the Thirty Tyrants fell, a 403 BC amnesty barred prosecuting Socrates directly for his ties to Critias and Alcibiades -- so the case was built on impiety instead. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; famous-trials.com.

question: You swore to yourself you would not check your phone during study time, yet your hand keeps creeping toward it. You want to grab it AND you want to keep your word, both at the same instant. Plato argued this ordinary tug-of-war could not happen unless the human mind had a certain structure. What structure?
answer: It is not one simple thing, but several drives that can pull against each other at once
choices: It is not one simple thing, but several drives that can pull against each other at once
It secretly never wanted to study, and the honest move is to admit that to yourself
It is ruled by whichever urge feels strongest, and that urge is always the real you
It can only want one thing at a time, so the felt struggle must be a kind of illusion
context: This is Plato's Principle of Opposites (Republic 439): the same thing cannot do opposite things at once in the same respect, so if part of you reaches while part of you holds back, you must be made of distinct parts pulling against each other. His own example is a thirsty man who refuses to drink — appetite says 'drink,' reason says 'no.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Ethics and Politics' (Rep. 436b, 439).

question: To picture the human mind, Plato has Socrates describe a chariot: a driver gripping the reins behind a team of two winged horses. The driver stands for the reasoning, steering part of you. In Plato's image, what do the two winged horses themselves stand for?
answer: The two pulling urges the driver must steer: a calm obedient drive and a wild stubborn one
choices: The two pulling urges the driver must steer: a calm obedient drive and a wild stubborn one
The body and the soul, which travel together but forever want to fly apart from each other
A good angel and a bad angel, who whisper their advice into the driver's two opposite ears
The past and the future, each one dragging the driver away from the living present moment
context: From the Phaedrus: 'Let the figure be composite — a pair of winged horses and a charioteer' (246a-b). The two horses are opposites in nature, 'one of the horses is noble and of noble breed, but the other quite the opposite in breed and character' (246b) — one obeys, one fights the reins. This is Plato's picture of the divided self. Legend/myth told by Socrates. Source: Plato, Phaedrus 246a-b (Perseus, Jowett trans.).

question: In his Republic, Plato argues the human soul has three parts, and each part hungers for a different kind of thing. One part loves truth and wisdom. Another part craves food, drink, sex, and money. What does the THIRD part love most?
answer: Honor and victory; it swells with pride and burns with anger whenever it is slighted
choices: Honor and victory; it swells with pride and burns with anger whenever it is slighted
Comfort and safety; it flinches from every danger and seeks only an easy quiet rest
Beauty and music; it is moved to tears by a fine song or the sight of a lovely face
Company and friends; it cannot bear to be left on its own for very long at a stretch
context: Plato's three parts are the rational part (loves truth and wisdom), the appetitive part (craves food, drink, sex, money), and the spirited part (loves honor and victory, and feels anger and indignation). The Greek names, kept here only as context, are logistikon, epithumetikon, and thumoeides. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Ethics and Politics in The Republic'; IEP, 'Plato'.

question: Plato says a person is just, or rightly ordered, when the three parts of the soul each do their own proper work. Reason should rule; appetite should obey. What, then, is the proper work of the third part, the spirited drive that loves honor?
answer: To serve as reason's ally, enforcing reason's decisions against the pull of appetite
choices: To serve as reason's ally, enforcing reason's decisions against the pull of appetite
To serve as the tie-breaker, casting the deciding vote when reason and appetite disagree
To stay quiet and asleep, since a truly calm person feels no anger or wounded pride at all
To take the lead over both, since the love of honor is the noblest of the three soul-drives
context: This is the payoff the chariot pictures: reason drives, using the obedient good horse (spirit) to control the unruly bad horse (appetite). Justice in the soul is 'each part doing its own work' and not meddling — reason rules, spirit is reason's ally enforcing its decisions, appetite obeys (Republic 441-442). Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Ethics and Politics' (Rep. 441d-442c).

question: In Plato's Phaedrus, the charioteer of the soul faces a crisis: the wild dark horse bolts, hauling the whole team toward what it lusts after. To break it, the driver yanks the reins back so violently that he bloodies the beast's mouth and slams its haunches to the ground. After this is repeated many times over, what at last becomes of the wild horse?
answer: It is humbled at last, and at the mere sight of beauty it trembles with fear and obeys
choices: It is humbled at last, and at the mere sight of beauty it trembles with fear and obeys
It tears free of the reins completely and gallops away, lost to the driver for good
It collapses dead from the punishment, leaving the driver with his one good horse
It grows to love the whip itself, and turns wilder with every fresh blow it is dealt
context: The most violent beat of the scene (254e): the charioteer hauls the bit back so hard he 'covers his scurrilous tongue and jaws with blood' and 'forces his legs and haunches to the ground.' The bad horse — crooked, dark, bloodshot-eyed, friend of insolence and pride, 'hardly obedient to whip and spurs' (253e) — is finally broken to obedience. Legend/myth told by Socrates. Source: Plato, Phaedrus 254e, 253e (Perseus).

question: Plato's winged chariots are not racing for sport. They climb behind the gods all the way to the rim of heaven, straining for a single glimpse of something. Souls that fail to see it lose their wings and tumble back to earth into mortal bodies. What are the souls struggling to glimpse?
answer: A colorless, formless realm of true being, where justice and wisdom themselves dwell
choices: A colorless, formless realm of true being, where justice and wisdom themselves dwell
The faces of the loved ones who have died and gone on ahead of them into the sky
A great throne where the chief of the gods sits weighing every soul that draws near
The far edge of the world itself, past which no chariot has ever managed to travel
context: The souls follow the gods up to glimpse 'the heaven which is above the heavens' — the 'colorless, formless, intangible essence' of true being, where justice, temperance, and knowledge themselves live (247c-d). The soul's wings are nourished by beauty, wisdom, and goodness and wither without them; souls that fail to see fall to earth into bodies (246e, 248c). Legend/myth told by Socrates. Source: Plato, Phaedrus 247c-d, 246e, 248c.

question: A runaway tram is hurtling down the track toward five workmen who cannot get clear in time. You stand at the switch. You can do nothing and let the five die, or throw the switch to send the tram onto a side track where one workman is working -- and he will be killed instead. Asked what to do, almost everyone gives the same answer. Which is it?
answer: Throw the switch, because one death is a smaller loss than five.
choices: Throw the switch, because one death is a smaller loss than five.
Do nothing, because you must never be the direct cause of a death.
Do nothing, because the five were on the track first and have priority.
Throw the switch, but only if the lone workman agrees to it first.
context: Philippa Foot first posed this runaway-tram case in 1967, in an essay on the doctrine of double effect. Roughly nine in ten people say turn it. Her exact setup: the driver 'can only steer from one narrow track on to another; five men are working on one track and one man on the other.' This is the scene the whole puzzle is built on. (Foot 1967, quoted in Britannica and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.)

question: A runaway trolley races toward five people on the track below. You stand on a footbridge above, beside a very large stranger whose body could stop the trolley. You can save the five only by shoving him off the bridge to his death. A friend says this must be fine, since it is the very same trade as a switch -- one dies, five live. Yet almost everyone recoils from the push. Why does that recoil bite against his argument?
answer: Two acts with the very same outcome can still differ in whether they are allowed.
choices: Two acts with the very same outcome can still differ in whether they are allowed.
A shoved body is far less sure to stop a trolley than a pulled switch is to divert one.
You owe nothing to five strangers you have never once met, so no rescue was required.
The stranger never agreed to take part, but the side-track workman somehow had agreed.
context: This is the Footbridge case, the most famous fork in the whole debate; Judith Jarvis Thomson introduced it in her 1985 paper 'The Trolley Problem' (Yale Law Journal 94). The friend reasons purely by the body count -- same net result, so same verdict. The near-universal recoil from the push, by people who would gladly throw a switch, is evidence that an act's outcome is not the whole of what makes it permissible. WHY the two acts differ -- doing versus allowing, means versus side-effect, your own hands on a body -- is exactly what the higher rungs take up. (Thomson 1985.)

question: A surgeon has five patients who will die today: two need a lung, two a kidney, one a heart. A healthy young man strolls in for a check-up and matches all five. The surgeon could quietly cut him up and parcel out his organs -- one death, five saved, the same gain as turning the trolley. Almost everyone says the surgeon may NOT do it, though they would turn the trolley. What does that flat 'no' show?
answer: Saving five at the cost of one is not always allowed; the body count alone cannot decide it.
choices: Saving five at the cost of one is not always allowed; the body count alone cannot decide it.
The surgeon cannot really be sure the young man would match every one of the five patients.
Doctors are bound by professional oaths that an ordinary passing bystander never had to swear.
Five strangers' lives can never outweigh the single person standing right in front of you.
context: Foot raised a transplant case in 1967; Thomson sharpened it into this surgeon in 1985. Her report: 'Everybody to whom this hypothetical case has been put says, No, it would not be' permissible. Same arithmetic as the trolley, opposite verdict -- which is exactly why 'five over one' cannot be the whole story.

question: Philippa Foot paired her runaway tram with a second case. A mob threatens to slaughter a town district unless a culprit hangs for a crime. The criminal is unknown, but a judge could frame and execute one innocent man to appease the mob -- the same grim one-for-five trade as turning the tram. The driver may turn; almost everyone says the judge may NOT. What distinction did Foot build the pair to draw out?
answer: The driver redirects a harm already loose, while the judge works up a death from nothing.
choices: The driver redirects a harm already loose, while the judge works up a death from nothing.
The driver acts in a split second of pressure, while the judge has all the time he wants.
The driver answers only to himself, while the judge betrays an oath to shield the innocent.
The driver risks one bystander, while the judge knowingly kills a man he is sure is innocent.
context: Foot's framing-judge case sits beside the tram in her 1967 essay as a matched pair: identical arithmetic, opposite verdict. The distinction she drew from the contrast is between actively DOING a harm and merely ALLOWING one -- the driver deflects a danger already loose, while the judge manufactures a brand-new death to feed the mob. (Foot 1967, quoted in Wikipedia 'Trolley problem' and Britannica.)

question: In Philippa Foot's original tram case the hero is the DRIVER -- already at the controls of a deadly machine bearing down on five men. Judith Jarvis Thomson rewrote it so that you are just a passer-by who happens to stand next to a track-side lever, with no connection to the runaway trolley. People still feel it is fine for the passer-by to throw the lever, killing one to save five. What did Thomson's change prove about the puzzle?
answer: Turning is not made all right by the driver's special job; the act of redirecting itself is what people accept.
choices: Turning is not made all right by the driver's special job; the act of redirecting itself is what people accept.
A driver who first set the deadly danger in motion carries far more blame than a stranger who merely watches.
Bystanders feel free to act here mainly because no one will ever afterward learn that they were involved.
Once you are merely standing beside a track-side lever, the law treats you in exactly the way it treats the driver.
context: This is Thomson's 'Bystander at the Switch' (1985). By stripping away the driver's special role and keeping the same verdict, she showed the puzzle was never about the driver's duty -- it is about the act of diverting harm itself. (Thomson 1985; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doing vs. Allowing Harm.')

question: Survey researchers put the two trolley scenes to ordinary people. In the first, you flip a switch to divert the trolley, killing one workman to save five. In the second, you shove a large man off a footbridge to stop it, killing him to save five. The result is identical either way -- one dead, five alive, four lives saved. What did the surveys find when the only thing that changed was switch versus shove?
answer: About nine in ten would flip the switch, but a clear majority refuse to push the man.
choices: About nine in ten would flip the switch, but a clear majority refuse to push the man.
Roughly equal numbers of people approved of flipping the switch and of pushing the man.
Most people refused to act at all once they were told a death was guaranteed either way.
A small majority were willing to push the man but balked at flipping the deadly switch.
context: This cliff between flipping a switch and pushing a person -- identical outcomes, opposite choices -- is the empirical heart of the trolley problem. (Survey results summarized at Wikipedia's 'Trolley problem' and The Conversation, 'The trolley dilemma: would you kill one person to save five?')

question: Alongside the tram driver and the framing judge, Philippa Foot's 1967 discussion adds a third figure: the pilot of a doomed airliner that is going to crash no matter what. The pilot can aim the wreck away from a crowded district toward an emptier one, so that fewer people die. Most people find this, like turning the tram, permissible. What do the driver and the pilot share that the surgeon and the bridge-pusher do not?
answer: Each one redirects a harm already on its way, instead of using a person's body as the thing that absorbs it.
choices: Each one redirects a harm already on its way, instead of using a person's body as the thing that absorbs it.
Each one merely lets the deaths happen, while the surgeon and the pusher are the only ones who truly cause them.
Each one harms only strangers, while the surgeon and the pusher both harm a person they have actually met.
Each one acts on a fast-moving machine, while the surgeon and the pusher act calmly with their own hands.
context: Foot's pilot is the third of her paired cases. The driver and pilot DEFLECT a threat that is already coming; the surgeon and the pusher INTRODUCE a person to absorb the harm. That deflect-versus-use line is the heart of her answer. (Foot 1967, summarized at the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Britannica.)

question: Why may the bystander turn the trolley, killing one, when the surgeon may not cut up one patient to save five? Philippa Foot argued the deepest difference is not the arithmetic but the KIND of act: at the lever you redirect a danger already on its way, while the surgeon takes a healthy person and makes his body the thing that absorbs the harm. On her view, which principle separates the two cases?
answer: Doing a harm is generally worse than merely allowing one, so the duty not to kill outranks the duty to save.
choices: Doing a harm is generally worse than merely allowing one, so the duty not to kill outranks the duty to save.
Whatever single course of action ends up saving the most lives is the right one to take in both cases alike.
A harm that you inflict from up close is always worse than the very same harm you inflict from a distance.
You owe nothing whatever to strangers, so neither one of the two rescues can ever truly be required of you.
context: This is Foot's doing-versus-allowing answer: a negative duty (do not kill) generally outranks a positive duty (save the five). The contested claim the bank presents -- without ruling on it -- is that killing-as-a-means is a different moral act from letting-die, not just a worse score on a body count. A competent utilitarian who picks the most-lives option is not thereby wrong; this is a live dispute. (Foot 1967; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doing vs. Allowing Harm.')

question: Judith Jarvis Thomson offered a sharper test for why the footbridge feels different from the switch. Imagine the victim simply vanishes an instant before you act. On the bridge, if the large man disappears, your plan collapses -- the trolley rolls on and the five die. At the switch, if the lone workman disappears, the five are still saved and you are glad. Thomson said this 'vanish' test marks the real moral line. What line does it draw?
answer: On the bridge his death is your MEANS of saving them; at the switch it is only a foreseen side-effect of it.
choices: On the bridge his death is your MEANS of saving them; at the switch it is only a foreseen side-effect of it.
On the bridge you act with your own bare hands, while at the switch a machine carries out the actual killing.
On the bridge you are made wholly certain of the death, while at the switch it always remains only a risk.
On the bridge an innocent stranger dies, while at the switch a workman who knew his job's dangers dies.
context: Thomson's exact wording: someone 'uses the one to save the five only if, had the one gone out of existence just before the agent started, the agent would have been unable to save the five.' If you NEED the death, it is your means; if you would be glad it didn't happen, it is a side-effect. This is the doctrine of double effect, made into a clean test. (Thomson 1985; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.)

question: Take the footbridge case and change one detail: the large man on the bridge is the very person who tied the five victims to the tracks and set the danger in motion. The physics is unchanged -- his body still stops the trolley, still one death for five saved. Now many people who refused to push an innocent stranger say go ahead and push HIM. What does this shift reveal about the original recoil from pushing?
answer: The reluctance was never pure arithmetic; who deserves the harm was quietly doing part of the work.
choices: The reluctance was never pure arithmetic; who deserves the harm was quietly doing part of the work.
People will end up pushing a stranger off the bridge whenever they grow angry enough at him.
The villain gave up every claim to his own life the moment he chose to commit any crime at all.
Pushing only ever felt wrong in the first place because the large stranger was a total unknown.
context: This is the 'Fat Villain' variant, usually discussed as a thought experiment rather than a settled result. Holding the math fixed while changing only the victim's guilt shifts the verdict, which shows the gut reaction was tracking desert, not just the body count. (Variant described at Wikipedia 'Trolley problem' and EBSCO Research Starters.)  (Legend.)

question: Judith Jarvis Thomson built a case to trap the easy answer. It is the ordinary switch case, but the side track curves around and LOOPS back to rejoin the main track ahead of the five. The lone workman on the loop is large enough that his body alone stops the trolley before it comes back around. Pull the lever and you still kill one to save five. People who happily flip the plain switch find this one queasier -- and Thomson argued it now does the very thing the footbridge push does. What has the lever-pull become here?
answer: His being struck is now the thing that saves the five, so the lever-pull works through his death, not past it.
choices: His being struck is now the thing that saves the five, so the lever-pull works through his death, not past it.
A short extra loop of track is far too slight a change to count, so the lever-pull stays exactly as fine as before.
His body merely shortens the wait, so the lever-pull saves the five whether or not the trolley ever reaches him.
The rail curves back on itself, so the lever-pull leaves you answerable for every death anywhere along the line.
context: Thomson's Loop case (1985). Once his body is what stops the trolley, the lever-pull relies on his death exactly as the footbridge push does -- yet, she wrote, we 'cannot really suppose that the presence or absence of that extra bit of track makes a major moral difference.' The clean means-versus-side-effect line suddenly wobbles. (Thomson 1985, pp. 1402-1403.)

question: Judith Jarvis Thomson proposed that you may redirect a threat so it harms fewer people, but only when the act itself violates no one's rights -- merely steering a trolley breaks no right, while shoving a man off a bridge infringes a 'stringent' one. Then she turned on her own answer, asking: if no one were on the straight track and the bystander turned the trolley onto a lone workman, wouldn't that infringe HIS right too? Why does her own question threaten her solution?
answer: If turning onto one man already violates his right, then 'five need saving' cannot strip the surgeon's victim of his.
choices: If turning onto one man already violates his right, then 'five need saving' cannot strip the surgeon's victim of his.
It shows the bystander really had no right to lay even a single hand on the track-side lever in the very first place.
It proves the lone workman out on the side track must have somehow consented to the danger just by working there.
It means the runaway trolley simply ought to be left entirely alone to carry on its way toward the original five.
context: Thomson's rights answer drew the line at whether your hands commit a rights-violating act, not at the body count. But by pressing whether even the plain diversion infringes the one man's right, she left the puzzle genuinely open -- a feature, not a bug. The bank presents the dispute without resolving it. (Thomson 1985, pp. 1404, 1409, 1411.)

question: Joshua Greene and his colleagues slid people into a brain scanner and posed the trolley dilemmas. The lever-flip mostly lit up the brain's cool reasoning regions, while the footbridge shove instead set the emotional regions firing -- the amygdala among them. Greene proposed that one particular feature of the shove is what trips that fast emotional alarm. Which feature did he point to?
answer: It is up close and personal -- your own hands pushing directly against a living person's body.
choices: It is up close and personal -- your own hands pushing directly against a living person's body.
It is unbearable to watch -- you must see the man's face the whole way down to his death.
It is a betrayal of trust -- the man stood beside you on the bridge as if you were no threat.
It is degrading to do -- you reduce a living man to a mere heavy weight thrown at a problem.
context: Greene's 2001 fMRI study (Science 293) gave the gut recoil a measurable neural signature. His proposed trigger was that the push is 'up close and personal' -- personal force, your own hands on a body -- which fires emotion in a way the impersonal switch does not. It does not settle which choice is RIGHT; it describes what the brain is doing, and it became the foundation of dual-process theory in moral psychology. (Greene et al. 2001, pp. 2105-2108.)

question: Alan Turing thought the question 'Can machines think?' led nowhere, because nobody could agree on what the word 'think' even means. So he refused to argue it. Instead of trying to settle that word-puzzle, what did Turing propose doing?
answer: Run a test where a judge swaps typed notes with a hidden machine and a hidden person, and tries to tell them apart
choices: Run a test where a judge swaps typed notes with a hidden machine and a hidden person, and tries to tell them apart
Open up the machine to check whether its inner workings look anything like the wiring of a real living human brain
Time the machine on long columns of arithmetic against a fast, well-trained human clerk
Simply wait for machines to grow powerful enough that the whole question would quietly answer itself
context: Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (in the journal Mind) calls the bare question 'Can machines think?' too vague to settle, and swaps in a concrete test instead -- the substitution itself is the famous idea. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Turing Test'; Turing 1950, Mind 59:433-460.

question: In Turing's test, the judge and the hidden contestant trade only typed messages, the way you would chat with a stranger online. Of all the ways the two could have talked, Turing chose plain typing on purpose. What was his reason for that choice?
answer: A clumsy voice or a metal face could give the machine away, but on the page the words alone are judged
choices: A clumsy voice or a metal face could give the machine away, but on the page the words alone are judged
Spoken words vanish, so only a typed record would let the judge pore back over the whole long chat
With typed lines, several judges in separate rooms could all follow exactly the same conversation at once
Typing handed the machine a useful little stretch of extra time to think out and compose each reply
context: The typed channel was a teletype; with no sight or sound, the machine's voice or body cannot betray it, so only the words are tested. Source: Turing 1950, section 1 'The Imitation Game'; plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-test/.

question: Turing borrowed his test from an old party game with no machines in it at all: a man and a woman hide in another room, and a questioner passes them written notes trying to work out which one is the man -- while the man secretly lies to throw the questioner off. What was Turing's twist on this game?
answer: Slip a machine into the place of one hidden player, then ask whether the questioner is fooled just as often
choices: Slip a machine into the place of one hidden player, then ask whether the questioner is fooled just as often
Let the questioner give up on the notes and finally walk in to meet both of the hidden players face to face
Make the woman, rather than the man, the player who tries to deceive and mislead the questioner
Hand the questioner a secret helper who quietly whispers hints about which guess is the right one
context: Turing opens with the party 'imitation game' -- man (A), woman (B), interrogator (C) reading typed notes, the man lying -- then asks: put a machine in A's chair, and is C fooled as often? Source: Turing 1950, section 1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_Machinery_and_Intelligence.

question: In Turing's imagined transcript, a judge tries to trip up the hidden machine by ordering it: 'Write me a sonnet about the Forth Bridge.' A real poem might be too tall an order. Turing has the machine answer 'Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.' Why was that reply a clever way to seem human?
answer: Brushing off a hard request the way a real person might is itself convincing -- people duck tasks too
choices: Brushing off a hard request the way a real person might is itself convincing -- people duck tasks too
It quietly proved the machine really could have written the sonnet but was choosing to stay modest about it
It bought the machine a full thirty seconds to secretly compose a sonnet away in the background
It flattered the judge into deciding that the great bridge was simply too grand a subject for a poem
context: From Turing's sample dialogue: 'Q: Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge. A: Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.' Convincingly ducking a hard task is itself a way to pass. Source: Turing 1950, section 1 sample interrogation; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_Machinery_and_Intelligence.

question: Joseph Weizenbaum built a 1966 program called ELIZA that merely echoed your own words back as a therapist's questions ('Tell me more about your mother') -- it understood nothing at all. Yet his own secretary, who KNEW perfectly well it was only a program, did something that startled him. What did she do?
answer: Asked him to step out of the room so that she could carry on talking with the program in private
choices: Asked him to step out of the room so that she could carry on talking with the program in private
Flatly refused to use it at all, insisting the typed replies felt far too cold and mechanical for her
Grew bored of it after a single afternoon and went straight back to her ordinary work
Set about trying to teach it brand-new words so that it could give her wiser and better advice
context: Weizenbaum's 1966 ELIZA, running its DOCTOR script, only mirrored your words as a Rogerian therapist's questions and understood nothing -- yet his secretary, who knew it was a program, asked him to leave so she could talk to it privately. Behavior fooled people; understanding was not there. Source: Joseph Weizenbaum 1966, CACM; nation.ai/eliza-the-story-of-the-pioneering-ai-chatbot.

question: John Searle imagined himself locked in a room, knowing not one single word of Chinese. Chinese notes slide under the door; he looks up each symbol by its shape in a giant rulebook and copies out whatever reply it tells him to. His answers come out flawless, so the people outside are sure a fluent Chinese speaker sits within. What did Searle conclude this shows about the typed-conversation test?
answer: Following a rulebook can produce the right output while the meaning never reaches him, so passing shows only behavior, never a mind
choices: Following a rulebook can produce the right output while the meaning never reaches him, so passing shows only behavior, never a mind
He clearly does understand after all -- nobody could reply that fluently by mere rote, so passing must prove a real mind at work behind it
The one who truly understands the Chinese is whoever wrote that rulebook, never the man inside following its printed instructions
Given enough years shut inside that room, the man would slowly start to pick up real Chinese from the symbols he keeps handling
context: John Searle's 1980 Chinese Room: the man matches symbols by their SHAPE and sends back perfect Chinese while understanding none of it -- his slogan, 'syntax is not sufficient for semantics.' So passing a behavioral conversation test (what Searle calls Weak AI, mere simulation) need not be real thinking (Strong AI). A functionalist who holds the opposite -- that flawless behavior just IS understanding -- rejects Searle here; the question keys his reasoning, not a verdict on who is right. Source: John Searle 1980, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs', Behavioral and Brain Sciences; plato.stanford.edu/entries/chinese-room/.

question: In 2014, on the 60th anniversary of Turing's death, a chatbot fooled a third of its judges into thinking it was a human, and its makers announced it had finally passed the test. But critics dismissed the win as a trick: the bot pretended to be 'Eugene Goostman,' a 13-year-old boy from Ukraine. Why did that disguise make the victory look hollow?
answer: A foreign kid's clumsy English and dodged questions get forgiven as a child's, masking how limited the bot is
choices: A foreign kid's clumsy English and dodged questions get forgiven as a child's, masking how limited the bot is
Under the contest's own posted rules a 13-year-old is simply far too young to count as a valid contestant at all
The judges had been told the boy's exact age beforehand, and that hint quietly broke the test's secrecy
Ukrainian turned out to be a language not one of the judges on the panel happened to be able to read
context: At a Royal Society event on 7 June 2014, a chatbot posing as 13-year-old Ukrainian 'Eugene Goostman' convinced 33% of judges and was declared to have cleared Turing's 30% bar -- but critics noted the boy persona was a cheat, since broken English and dodged questions get excused as a kid's. Source: University of Reading press release, 8 June 2014; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Goostman.

question: A class votes on where to go for the year-end trip. No rule is broken, and the one kid who wanted somewhere else is never punished. But for weeks the others stop saving him a seat, stop picking him, and go quiet when he walks up, until he wishes he'd just gone along. A teacher tells him, 'No law was broken here, so nobody coerced you.' What is the strongest reply?
answer: They broke no rule against him, yet their cold shoulder pressed as hard as any punishment.
choices: Since no one was actually punished, the boy only imagined that anything was truly wrong.
The vote itself was run unfairly, so the real problem lies in how the trip got chosen.
They broke no rule against him, yet their cold shoulder pressed as hard as any punishment.
Coercion can only ever happen when a government or an official is the one applying it.
context: This is the heart of the 'tyranny of the majority': a crowd can crush a person through disapproval alone, with no law and no ruler. J.S. Mill warned in On Liberty (1859) that protection against the magistrate 'is not enough; there needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling.' Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859), Ch. 1 — econlib.org/library/Mill/mlLbty.html.

question: A town disapproves of how a man spends his evenings alone in his own home. It offends their taste, though it harms no one but, at most, himself. They want to use the law to make him stop. John Stuart Mill argued there is exactly one thing that ever justifies the community in overriding a person's freedom against his will. What is it?
answer: To stop him from doing real harm to the other people around him.
choices: To shield him from the results of his own freely made choices.
To uphold the shared moral standards the town has long held dear.
To keep him from setting a poor example for the watching young.
To stop him from doing real harm to the other people around him.
context: Mill's harm principle: 'the sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection.' The majority may coerce you only to prevent harm to others — never merely because it dislikes how you live. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859), Ch. 1, as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Stuart Mill — plato.stanford.edu/entries/mill/.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville pictured how a democratic majority silences a person who thinks differently — not with a jail cell, but with a speech. 'You are free to think differently from me,' it says, 'but if such be your determination, you are henceforth an alien among your people. Your fellow-creatures will shun you like an impure being. Go in peace! I have given you your life, but...' How does Tocqueville have the majority finish the threat?
answer: it is an existence incomparably worse than death.
choices: the gates of this town are closed to you forever.
it is an existence incomparably worse than death.
your own children will answer for what you believe.
no honest trade will ever be open to you again.
context: Tocqueville's point is that democratic tyranny spares the body and destroys the man socially — it leaves you alive but makes you a stranger among your own people. He called it the refinement of despotism: 'Fetters and headsmen were the coarse instruments which tyranny formerly employed; but the civilization of our age has refined the arts of despotism.' Source: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. I (1835) — marxists.org/reference/archive/de-tocqueville/democracy-america/ch15.htm.

question: John Stuart Mill granted that a cruel king or magistrate is a real danger. Yet he argued that the tyranny of majority opinion — with no ruler and no law behind it — can be the MORE formidable of the two. According to Mill, what makes a tyranny that has no tyrant harder to bear than one that does?
answer: It leaves fewer ways out, reaching down into the smallest details of daily life.
choices: It leaves fewer ways out, reaching down into the smallest details of daily life.
It can call on far larger armies than any single king has at his own command.
It shifts its demands far too quickly for any one person to keep pace with them.
It conceals who is to blame, so no revolt can ever be aimed at any one person.
context: Mill's full line: society practising its will against the individual 'practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression, since... it leaves fewer means of escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself.' A tyranny with no tyrant and no law is harder to flee than one with both. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859), Ch. 1 — econlib.org/library/Mill/mlLbty.html.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville warned that a democratic majority holds a power subtler than punishing the people who disagree with it. The crowd's deeper power, he said, works on the citizen who never disagrees at all — it reaches him before he has formed a single view of his own. What is this quieter power Tocqueville is describing?
answer: It supplies people with ready-made opinions, sparing them the work of ever thinking.
choices: It slowly rewrites the public memory until older, rival ideas are simply forgotten.
It supplies people with ready-made opinions, sparing them the work of ever thinking.
It makes independent thought so exhausting that people gladly let others feel for them.
It fills every quiet hour with chatter, leaving no still moment in which to reflect.
context: From the second volume: 'In the United States the majority undertakes to supply a multitude of ready-made opinions for the use of individuals, who are thus relieved from the necessity of forming opinions of their own.' The crowd doesn't only punish dissent — it spares you the labor of thought, which is how it quietly produces sameness. Source: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. II (1840) — gutenberg.org/files/816/816-h/816-h.htm.

question: Some argued that once the majority rules, its will should reach as far as it likes — a free people can hardly tyrannize itself. Alexis de Tocqueville refused to grant it. He had called unlimited power a bad and dangerous thing in itself, and would not bow to a crowd merely because it was large. On what ground does Tocqueville reject letting the majority's power grow without limit?
answer: Because the danger lies in the sheer size of the power, not in whose hands grip it.
choices: Because a vast crowd shifts its aims too quickly for its power to stay just.
Because the danger lies in the sheer size of the power, not in whose hands grip it.
Because a large crowd is more easily stirred to cruelty than a single ruler is.
Because power that great will always burst past the limits meant to hold it.
context: Tocqueville's objection is to OMNIPOTENCE itself, not to who holds it: 'unlimited power is in itself a bad and dangerous thing... God alone can be omnipotent, because His wisdom and His justice are always equal to His power.' Since no human's justice ever equals such power, total power is unsafe in any human hands — a majority of millions as much as a single despot. The number of hands on the lever does not make absolute power safe. Source: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. I (1835) — marxists.org/reference/archive/de-tocqueville/democracy-america/ch15.htm.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville feared a gentler ruin for democracies than jackboots and secret police. He pictured a vast, mild power standing over the citizens, covering society 'with a net-work of small complicated rules,' that 'does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people.' To what does he compare the people left under such a power?
answer: A flock of timid, industrious animals, with the government as its shepherd.
choices: A garden of pruned hedges, kept neat by an unseen and tireless hand.
A courtroom of silent jurors who long ago stopped hearing the case.
A vast machine whose gears turn smoothly only while no one looks inside.
A flock of timid, industrious animals, with the government as its shepherd.
context: This is Tocqueville's 'soft despotism': not chains, but a smothering, shepherding gentleness that reduces 'each nation... to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.' The danger is not cruelty but comfort — a power that manages you so thoroughly you forget how to govern yourself. Source: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. II (1840) — oll.libertyfund.org/quotes/tocqueville-warns-how-administrative-despotism-might-come-to-a-democracy-like-america-1840.

question: In the marketplace, Nietzsche's prophet Zarathustra cries: "I teach you the Superman. Man is something that is to be surpassed." The crowd assumes he means a mighty being who already exists somewhere. Zarathustra corrects them. In his teaching, where does the Superman come from?
answer: Humanity has to create him for itself, as a goal to grow toward
choices: Humanity has to create him for itself, as a goal to grow toward
He is a perfect race, bred to be born already fit to rule the weak
He is a god who will descend once enough people have prayed for him
He is the strongest warrior, whom the greatest city will one day crown
context: Nietzsche introduces the Ubermensch (the "Superman" or "overman") in the Prologue of Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883) not as a being that exists, but as a goal humanity must make of itself. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Prologue (Project Gutenberg).

question: Zarathustra describes the opposite of the Superman: the "last man," a cozy, blinking little person who has given up all striving and murmurs, "We have discovered happiness." Zarathustra expects the crowd to recoil in disgust. Instead they shout back at him. What do they demand?
answer: "Give us this last man! You can keep the Superman!"
choices: "Give us this last man! You can keep the Superman!"
"Give us the Superman now, and burn the last man!"
"Teach us to fight, so none of us stays a last man!"
"Leave us in peace; we want neither of your two men!"
context: The "last man" is Nietzsche's warning picture of a future that chooses comfort over greatness -- and the crowd proves his point by begging for exactly that. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Prologue (Project Gutenberg); cross-checked against Eternalised, "Nietzsche: The Ubermensch."

question: Nietzsche maps the road to one's own values as three changes of spirit. The second is a lion that faces a dragon whose every scale glitters "THOU SHALT" -- every rule handed down by others. The lion roars a defiant "I WILL" and tears those old commands off itself. What has that roar actually won the lion?
answer: Freedom FROM the rules that others laid on it -- the right to refuse them
choices: Freedom FROM the rules that others laid on it -- the right to refuse them
The power to make other people obey its own "I WILL" instead of the old rules
A lasting peace in which it need never face the great dragon again
The dragon's respect, so the beast now serves the lion as a loyal guard
context: In "The Three Metamorphoses," the lion's "I WILL" wins freedom FROM the dragon's inherited "THOU SHALT" -- but that is freedom-from, the right to refuse, not yet the power to build anything new. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, "The Three Metamorphoses" (Project Gutenberg).

question: Zarathustra has just preached the overman to the marketplace crowd. A listener asks him where a person should place his deepest hope -- on a glory waiting in some life after this one, or somewhere else. How does Zarathustra answer?
answer: "Remain faithful to the earth" -- find your hope here, not in any world to come
choices: "Remain faithful to the earth" -- find your hope here, not in any world to come
"Look to the heavens" -- this life is only a test for the reward that follows it
"Trust the wisest among you" -- let a great teacher tell you what to hope for
"Wait for the crowd's love" -- hope lies in the cheers of those around you
context: "Remain faithful to the earth, and believe not those who speak unto you of superearthly hopes!" ties the overman's task to this life, not a promised heaven -- the overman makes meaning here rather than waiting for a reward after death. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Prologue (Project Gutenberg); cross-checked against Eternalised.

question: After the lion has torn down the old inherited commands, Nietzsche says the spirit must change a third time -- into a child, "a self-rolling wheel... a holy Yea." Tearing things down was the lion's work, and the lion could go no further. What does becoming this child finally let the spirit DO?
answer: Begin anew and bring its own values into being, out of nothing
choices: Begin anew and bring its own values into being, out of nothing
Faithfully obey whichever fixed law it judges to be wisest of all
Restore the best of the old commands the lion was too rash to keep
Refine and polish the inherited rules until they are flawless at last
context: Nietzsche calls the child "innocence... and forgetfulness, a new beginning, a game, a self-rolling wheel, a first movement, a holy Yea." Tearing the old values down (the lion) is not enough; creating new ones needs the child's fresh "yes." Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, "The Three Metamorphoses" (Project Gutenberg).

question: After World War II the scholar Walter Kaufmann spent years fighting to reclaim Nietzsche, whom the Nazis had loudly paraded as the prophet of their 'master race.' Kaufmann argued they had grasped the overman by the wrong end entirely. What did Kaufmann say Nietzsche's overman truly is?
answer: A person who masters and remakes himself, owing nothing to bloodline or birth
choices: A person who masters and remakes himself, owing nothing to bloodline or birth
A person who keeps the old moral law so faithfully that no saint outdoes him
A person who, wanting nothing further, has settled into his own comfort and ease
A person whose pure descent makes him fit from birth to rule over lesser men
context: Walter Kaufmann's Nietzsche: Philosopher, Psychologist, Antichrist (1950) rehabilitated Nietzsche after WWII. The Nazis had paraded the overman as a biological master race born to rule; Kaufmann showed they had grasped it by the wrong end -- the overman is a self-shaping individual who overcomes and remakes himself and creates his own values, NOT a racial type or conqueror -- and that Nietzsche himself despised antisemitism and nationalism. Source: Walter Kaufmann (Princeton); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Nietzsche’s Moral and Political Philosophy."

question: Nietzsche names a coming crisis: "God is dead." Once the old God-given rules no longer hold belief, he warns, most people will not rise to make their own meaning -- they will slide somewhere far emptier. Where, Nietzsche fears, does the herd actually drift when the old certainties die?
answer: Into deciding nothing is true or matters, and quietly ceasing to care
choices: Into deciding nothing is true or matters, and quietly ceasing to care
Into forging fresh values from themselves, owing nothing to God or soul
Into letting the strongest impose their will as the new law for everyone
Into trusting that science and progress will hand them new values in time
context: With the old God-given values collapsed, Nietzsche fears most people meet nihilism the easy way -- the herd and the "last man" slump into comfort and the sense that nothing matters.
