Only the overman takes the hard way: forging new values with no God or soul to lean on. The keyed answer is the herd’s drift, not the overman’s climb. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Friedrich Nietzsche."

question: In a real neurological case study, a patient with damage to the brain's planning system declared: "Money is green, and trees are green — so money must grow on trees." Both premises are true. Name the single thing that makes the leap collapse.
answer: Greenness is just a trait money and leaves happen to share, and a shared trait links nothing — being green never makes a dollar a leaf
choices: The patient quietly confused the color green with the slang "green" meaning cash, and the whole inference rests on that one hidden pun
"Grows on trees" is plainly only a figure of speech, not a literal claim, so the conclusion was never the kind of thing you could test
Greenness is just a trait money and leaves happen to share, and a shared trait links nothing — being green never makes a dollar a leaf
Money and leaves clearly belong to different sizes of category, and one can simply never reason from a small group up to a larger one
context: Formalized, the reasoning is "All leaves on trees are green things; all US paper money is green things; therefore all US money is leaves on trees." The shared middle (green) touches both but connects neither. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle (dysexecutive syndrome case); FallacyFiles.org/undismid.html.

question: "All students carry backpacks. My grandfather carries a backpack. So my grandfather is a student." The premises are airtight, yet the conclusion is absurd. The first premise placed students INTO the backpack crowd — but what did it never tell you, the gap the argument silently leaps?
answer: That the backpack crowd is all students — grandfather and the students could sit in separate, unconnected corners of the people who carry backpacks
choices: That the backpack crowd is all students — grandfather and the students could sit in separate, unconnected corners of the people who carry backpacks
That grandfather's backpack and the students' backpacks are really the same kind of bag, which the argument needs but never bothers to check
That carrying a backpack is the very thing that makes a person a student, a hidden rule the conclusion is quietly leaning the whole way on
That every last student without exception owns a backpack, since a single bare-shouldered student would already be enough to sink the first premise
context: This is what logicians mean by an undistributed middle term: the shared category (backpack-carriers) is never used to make a claim about EVERY member of it. The premise ran from students to backpacks, never from backpacks back to students. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle (grandfather/backpack example, verbatim).

question: In the 1960s some opponents of the civil-rights movement argued that the Communist Party also backed civil rights, so backing civil rights was "tantamount to supporting communism." Strip it to its skeleton — "Communists support X; this person supports X; therefore this person is a communist" — and say precisely where the smear breaks.
answer: Sharing a single stance with a group never makes you a member of it — many separate people can back the very same cause for their own reasons
choices: Communists backing a cause is really evidence the cause is a good and worthy one, so the argument draws exactly the wrong conclusion from it
The argument never once pins down what "communism" is supposed to mean, and without a precise definition no claim about who counts can be judged
Political labels keep drifting in meaning across the decades, so a charge of communism raised back in the 1960s cannot fairly be pressed today
Sharing a single stance with a group never makes you a member of it — many separate people can back the very same cause for their own reasons
context: This is the engine of "guilt by association," a real-world dress of the undistributed middle: one shared trait is treated as if it transferred group membership. The pedagogical point is the logical move, not a verdict on the politics. Source: Wikipedia, Association fallacy; Simple English Wikipedia, Guilt by association; FallacyFiles.org/guiltbya.html.

question: In Edgar Allan Poe's 1844 detective story "The Purloined Letter," the sleuth Dupin mocks the police Prefect for assuming a clever man must be a fool: "All fools are poets; this the Prefect feels; and he is merely guilty of a non distributio medii in thence inferring that all poets are fools." What blunder did Dupin just pin on the Prefect, in plain terms?
answer: Letting a one-direction overlap quietly run backwards — a trait that points one way got treated as if it pointed both ways
choices: Insulting both poets and fools alike all while he quietly dodges the actual question of who had really stolen the missing letter
Letting a one-direction overlap quietly run backwards — a trait that points one way got treated as if it pointed both ways
Trusting his own gut feeling ("this the Prefect feels") instead of the hard physical evidence sitting right there in front of him
Reversing cause and effect — deciding that writing poetry is the very thing that turns an otherwise clever man into a fool
context: "Non distributio medii" is the fallacy's Latin name — Poe used it as a punchline. The Prefect assumed that since fools are poets, the poet-minister must be a fool; sharing a trait one direction does not carry it back the other. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle (quoting Poe, "The Purloined Letter," 1844).

question: "All students carry backpacks; Grandfather carries a backpack; so Grandfather is a student" is a textbook fallacy. Yet keep the very same three sentences and change only which fact serves as the bridge, and it becomes ironclad. Which single swap flips the verdict from invalid to valid?
answer: Make "Grandfather is a student" a premise instead of the conclusion, and then conclude that "Grandfather carries a backpack"
choices: Swap the two premises with each other, leaving the conclusion "Grandfather is a student" exactly as it already stood at the end
Change the first premise to read "All students are backpack-carriers," so the claim is just reworded and the gap stays open
Replace the word "all" with the word "some" in the first premise, so the claim no longer overreaches past what is known
Make "Grandfather is a student" a premise instead of the conclusion, and then conclude that "Grandfather carries a backpack"
context: Fixed: "All students carry backpacks; Grandfather IS a student; therefore Grandfather carries a backpack" — valid. Now the shared term "students" spans an entire side, so the bridge holds. This is the form medieval logicians nicknamed "Barbara." Same three sentences, one swap, opposite verdict. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle; philosophy.lander.edu/logic/middle_fall.html (Barbara = AAA-1).

question: Translate any "shared-category" syllogism out of Aristotle's term-logic into modern if-then logic and, the encyclopedia notes, every one turns into the SAME well-known conditional error. The classic case: "If it rains, the ground is wet; the ground is wet; therefore it rained." Name the conditional mistake these category-overlap fallacies secretly are.
answer: Spotting the result and then leaping back to one single possible cause, as if only rain could ever have left the ground wet
choices: Denying the cause itself and then ruling the result out for good, as if no rain simply had to mean the ground would stay dry
Treating one lone event as a standing rule, so a single rainy afternoon swells into "it always rains here in this place"
Spotting the result and then leaping back to one single possible cause, as if only rain could ever have left the ground wet
Seeing two things turn up together and then declaring that one of them simply must have caused the other
context: A sprinkler, dew, or a hose could leave the ground wet too — so wet ground does not prove rain. Wikipedia states it directly: "all cases of the fallacy of the undistributed middle are, in fact, examples of affirming the consequent or denying the antecedent." Two classic fallacies, one underlying mistake — the wet ground (the consequent) is affirmed, but it has other possible causes. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle (first-order-logic note, verbatim).

question: Aristotle argued the whole cosmos must be set going by a first cause that itself never moves at all. How, then, did Aristotle say this perfectly still first cause manages to set everything else in motion?
answer: By being desired and loved, the way a beloved draws a lover toward them
choices: By being desired and loved, the way a beloved draws a lover toward them
By radiating a warmth that thins the heavens above and makes the spheres rise and turn
By breathing a divine spirit into matter so that each thing strains toward its proper place
By appointing countless lesser gods, each to keep a single sphere wheeling
context: This is the striking move of Aristotle's Unmoved Mover. A pushing cause would have to move to do its pushing, so the truly unmoved cause must work some other way: it draws things by being wanted. W.D. Ross renders Metaphysics XII.7 (~1072b): 'The final cause, then, produces motion as being loved, but all other things move by being moved.' The cosmos reaches toward the first mover the way a lover reaches toward a beloved, while the mover stays perfectly still. Note for the older reader: this is Aristotle's argued-for first PRINCIPLE of motion, not a verdict on whether the God of any religion exists. Source: Aristotle, Metaphysics Bk XII (Lambda) ch.7, ~1072b, W.D. Ross translation (classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/metaphysics.12.xii.html).

question: Aristotle reasoned that his first mover is a perfect, unchanging mind that never stops thinking. He argued that whatever such a mind dwells on must be the very best thing there is, because a lesser object would make the mind itself something less than perfect. Following that rule to its end, what did Aristotle conclude this supreme mind eternally thinks about?
answer: Itself, in one unbroken act of thought thinking about its own thinking
choices: Itself, in one unbroken act of thought thinking about its own thinking
The fate of every living creature, guiding each one to its proper end
The turning of the heavens, holding every sphere on its appointed path
The perfect Forms, which it gazes on as the changeless patterns of all things
context: If the best thing a perfect mind can contemplate must be the best thing there is, and that mind is itself the most excellent thing, then it can only contemplate itself. Ross renders Metaphysics XII.9 (~1074b): 'it must be of itself that the divine thought thinks (since it is the most excellent of things), and its thinking is a thinking on thinking.' Aristotle's first mover spends its whole existence in this single act of self-contemplation. (The 'perfect Forms' distractor borrows Plato's idea, which Aristotle did not place inside his first mover this way.) Source: Aristotle, Metaphysics Bk XII ch.9, ~1074b, W.D. Ross translation (classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/metaphysics.12.xii.html).

question: Aristotle traced motion back from mover to mover and argued the series cannot run backward forever with no starting point. What was his reason it must end in something that moves others while itself being moved by nothing?
answer: Each in-between mover only relays motion it was handed, so a line of them never explains where it began
choices: Each in-between mover only relays motion it was handed, so a line of them never explains where it began
An endless stretch of past time is impossible, so the whole series must have had a first moment
Each cause is slightly weaker than the one before, so an infinite chain would have died out by now
Only something that could freely choose was able to start a universe that did not have to exist
context: An intermediate mover both is-moved and moves, so it only relays motion it received; a chain made of nothing but relays leaves the original source unaccounted for. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy renders Aristotle: 'since what is moved and moves something is something medial, there is something that moves without being moved, being eternal, substance, and activity.' Centuries later Thomas Aquinas' 'First Way' (Summa Theologica I, q.2, a.3) inherits this no-infinite-regress structure — though SEP notes Aquinas shifts his emphasis toward a SUSTAINING cause and contingency rather than merely a first push, so the link is one of inherited reasoning, not an identical argument. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Metaphysics' (Lambda.6-7) (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-metaphysics/); cf. 'Cosmological Argument' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmological-argument/).

question: Uddalaka Aruni hands his son Svetaketu a lump of salt and tells him to drop it in a cup of water and leave it overnight. By morning the salt has vanished — Svetaketu reaches in but cannot pick it out. So his father tells him to sip the water from the top, then the middle, then the bottom. What does sipping at every level reveal?
answer: It is in every drop, unseen but everywhere — the one hidden essence inside all things
choices: It is in every drop, unseen but everywhere — the one hidden essence inside all things
It has sunk and settled at the very bottom, the way the heaviest things always do
It is gone past recovery — whatever dissolves into the world cannot be drawn back out
It changed nothing at all, which shows the salt was never really in the cup
context: The salt has not disappeared — it has spread through every drop, invisible but present everywhere. Uddalaka's point: just as you cannot see the salt yet taste it throughout, an invisible subtle essence pervades all things, and that essence is your own deepest self. This is the famous salt-in-water lesson of the Chandogya Upanishad (6.13), one of the oldest Upanishads (roughly 800-500 BCE). Source: https://hridaya-yoga.com/knowledge/upanishads/tat-tvam-asi-you-are-that-chandogya-upanishad/ (Chandogya Upanishad 6.13).

question: The word Upanishad is built from three small Sanskrit pieces: upa, ni, and sad. Read literally, those three words name a plain physical action — and that action is exactly how this knowledge was meant to be handed on. Put together, what do the three pieces literally describe?
answer: Sitting down near — a pupil seated close beside the teacher
choices: Sitting down near — a pupil seated close beside the teacher
Singing aloud — the verses chanted over and over at dawn
Writing it down — the words copied onto dried palm leaves
Walking the path — the long road a seeker has to travel
context: 'Upanishad' means 'sitting down near': upa (near) + ni (down) + sad (to sit) — a student seated close to the teacher to receive a secret doctrine (rahasya). Tradition counts 108 Upanishads, of which about 13 are the 'principal' ones; the earliest, like the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya, date to roughly 800-500 BCE. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Upanishad

question: Svetaketu studied the sacred Vedas for twelve years and came home at twenty-four — well taught, and very pleased with himself. His father Uddalaka empties that pride with a single question: have you ever asked for the teaching by which we hear what cannot be heard, and know what cannot be known? Svetaketu admits he has not. What had all those years of study left out?
answer: The one knowledge that, once you have it, lets you know everything else
choices: The one knowledge that, once you have it, lets you know everything else
The right way to pronounce the oldest and most difficult hymns
The names and the duties of all the gods in their proper order
The strict fire-rules a household priest must never once break
context: This is the opening move of the whole teaching (Chandogya Upanishad 6.1). Svetaketu had mastered the texts but never sought the single knowledge of the underlying Self — the knowledge that, like knowing what clay is, lets you understand everything made of it. His father's question deflates his book-learning and begins the lesson that ends in 'tat tvam asi,' thou art that. Source: https://vivekavani.com/svetaketu-thou-art-that-chandogya-upanishad/ (Chandogya Upanishad 6.1).

question: After every example — salt dissolved in water, rivers losing their names in the sea, the unseen sap that keeps a whole tree alive — Uddalaka Aruni turns to his son Svetaketu and repeats the same three Sanskrit words. That one short line became the most famous phrase in all the Upanishads, the line this whole teaching is built around. Which three words does he keep repeating?
answer: Tat tvam asi — thou art that
choices: Tat tvam asi — thou art that
Neti, neti — not this, not this
Aham brahmasmi — I am Brahman
Prajnanam brahma — consciousness is Brahman
context: The refrain is 'tat tvam asi' — 'thou art that' — Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7, repeated to close nine sections (through 6.16.3). It is the line the whole topic builds toward: Atman (the innermost self, literally 'breath') is declared identical to Brahman (the one ground of all being, from the root brh, 'to grow, expand'). The three distractors are also real 'great sayings' (Mahavakyas) or famous Upanishadic phrases — 'aham brahmasmi' (I am Brahman, Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10), 'prajnanam brahma' (consciousness is Brahman, Aitareya 3.3), and Yajnavalkya's 'neti, neti' (not this, not this) — but only 'tat tvam asi' is the line Uddalaka repeats to Svetaketu. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mah%C4%81v%C4%81kyas (Tat Tvam Asi, Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7).

question: One of the most haunting pictures in the Upanishads, from the Mundaka: two birds with lovely wings cling to a single tree as close companions. One bird feasts on the tree's fruit; the other never touches it and sits perfectly still. The sages say these are not two creatures at all, but two sides of you. Which two sides?
answer: The self that tastes your joy and sorrow, and the self that stays untouched
choices: The self that tastes your joy and sorrow, and the self that stays untouched
The body that one day dies, and the soul that slips free of it at death
The child who acts on impulse, and the grown-up who learns to wait
The waking mind that labors, and the sleeping mind that drifts in dreams
context: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1 (echoed in the Svetasvatara): 'Two birds, beautiful of wing, close companions, cling to one common tree. One eats the sweet fruit; the other eats not but watches his fellow.' The eating bird is the self caught up in pleasure and pain; the watching bird is the witnessing Self that is never touched by any of it — the same Atman the rest of the teaching points to. Source: https://sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe15/sbe15020.htm (Mundaka Upanishad III.1.1).

question: Ask an ancient Indian thinker 'what is a person, deep down?' and you started a real fight. The Buddhists gave one answer, the Nyaya logicians a second, and the sages of the Upanishads a third — and they could not all be right. Which of these is the Upanishads' own teaching about the self?
answer: Beneath all the separate people there is a single Self, and each of us is it
choices: Beneath all the separate people there is a single Self, and each of us is it
There are many real selves, each one a separate and distinct individual
There is no permanent self — a person is only a bundle of changing processes
The self is real, but only a small part of the divine, never the whole
context: The Upanishadic answer is one Self, and you are it — but it was always a position among rivals, with no verdict declared here. The Buddhists deny any permanent self (anatman: a person is just a bundle of processes); the Nyaya-Vaisheshika philosophers hold there are many separate, distinct individual selves; and within Vedanta itself Ramanuja's 'qualified non-dualism' says the self is real but only a genuine PART of Brahman, against Shankara's full identity. Source: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/personhood-india/ (Stanford Encyclopedia: Personhood in Classical Indian Philosophy).

question: The Upanishads reached Europe by an astonishing road. Around 1657 the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh — eldest son and chosen heir of the emperor who built the Taj Mahal — had fifty of them translated into Persian, naming the collection 'the Greatest Secret.' Two years later his younger brother Aurangzeb seized the throne and had him put to death. On what charge was the prince killed?
answer: Heresy, for chasing forbidden ideas
choices: Heresy, for chasing forbidden ideas
Treason, for plotting against the crown
Theft, for robbing the royal treasury
Cowardice, for fleeing his own troops
context: Dara Shikoh (1615-1659), son of Shah Jahan, had 50 Upanishads translated into Persian as the 'Sirr-i-Akbar' ('the Greatest Secret'), seeking a shared mystical core between Islam and Hinduism; his brother Aurangzeb had him executed for heresy in 1659. That Persian version, rendered into Latin by Anquetil-Duperron as the 'Oupnek'hat,' is how the Upanishads reached the West — Arthur Schopenhauer read it and wrote, 'It has been the solace of my life; it will be the solace of my death.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirr-i-Akbar (Dara Shikoh, 1615-1659).

question: Zhuangzi tells of Crippled Shu, a man whose chin is buried in his navel, whose shoulders rise above his head, and whose thighs press against his ribs. When recruiting officers sweep through the village, seizing every able-bodied man for the army, what becomes of Shu?
answer: He strolls among them untouched, passed over as no use to anyone.
choices: He strolls among them untouched, passed over as no use to anyone.
He is marched off with the rest to fight on the front lines.
He flees to the hills and hides until the recruiters have gone.
He is made to cook and carry for the soldiers instead.
context: In Zhuangzi's parable (Ch. 4, 'In the World of Men'), Crippled Shu's twisted body is what saves him: waved off as a useless invalid while abler men are dragged to war, he even collects the grain and firewood handed out to the disabled. His 'useless' frame protects his life exactly as the giant tree's uselessness protects its trunk. Legendary parable. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi Ch. 4 (terebess.hu/english/chuangtzu.html).

question: Carpenter Shih passes a giant oak — too gnarled for boats, coffins, or beams — and sneers that it is a worthless tree. That night the oak comes to him in a dream to defend itself. What is the oak's reply?
answer: Good timber would have meant the axe ages ago; uselessness is the very reason it grew so old and vast.
choices: Good timber would have meant the axe ages ago; uselessness is the very reason it grew so old and vast.
Beauty needs no excuse; a tree is for its shade and its shadow, not for what a saw can make of it.
Every living thing has a hidden purpose; the carpenter simply lacks the eye to see this old tree's.
A craftsman who scorns his timber will soon find his hands idle; such contempt is its own punishment.
context: This is the turn that flips the whole parable. The oak points to the cherry, pear, and orange trees, whose good fruit gets their limbs torn off so they never live out their years — then delivers its punchline: 'I've been trying a long time to be of no use, and though I almost died, I've finally got it. This is of great use to me. If I had been of some use, would I ever have grown this large?' Note the near-miss: the oak does NOT claim a secret hidden use — it claims its having NO use is the point. Legendary parable. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi Ch. 4 (terebess.hu/english/chuangtzu.html).

question: Hui Tzu needles his friend Zhuangzi: your ideas are a giant stink-tree — too knotted for any carpenter, big and good for nothing, just like your words. Zhuangzi answers with two animals. He names the wildcat: quick and clever, it crouches and springs, darting east and west to seize its prey. Then the great yak, vast as a cloud across the sky, too huge to catch so much as a mouse. Why does Zhuangzi answer the jab with these two animals?
answer: Cleverness and use are what get the wildcat killed in a trap; being big and useless is exactly what keeps the yak safe.
choices: Cleverness and use are what get the wildcat killed in a trap; being big and useless is exactly what keeps the yak safe.
A real friend tests your ideas rather than flattering them; Hui Tzu's mockery is a gift, not an insult.
Each creature has a nature suited to its own kind; the darting cat is no worse than the yak, only different.
The truly wise man takes the best of both creatures: he joins the cat's quick speed to the yak's great strength.
context: In Chapter 1 ('Free and Easy Wandering'), Hui Tzu's 'big and useless' tree is meant as an insult to Zhuangzi's impractical philosophy; Zhuangzi turns it into the whole point. The clever wildcat that darts after prey lands in the hunter's net and dies; the enormous, useless yak comes to no harm. His advice for the stink-tree follows the same logic: plant it in 'Not-Even-Anything Village,' nap under it — 'Because it has no use, how could it come to grief?' Legendary parable. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi Ch. 1 (terebess.hu/english/chuangtzu.html); Christopher Tricker trans. (thecicadaandthebird.com/the-large-tree).

question: Imagine a being so good at turning food into joy that one apple gives it 100 units of pleasure, while the same apple gives an ordinary person only 1 unit. A rule says: hand out resources however produces the biggest total-happiness number. A person at the table asks who should get the apples, the bread, everything. What does that rule's arithmetic demand?
answer: Give every apple and every resource to the one being, and let everyone else go without
choices: Give every apple and every resource to the one being, and let everyone else go without
Split the apples evenly so each person and the being receive an equal, fair share
Give the food to whoever is hungriest right now, no matter how much joy results
Give a little to the being and divide the large remainder among the ordinary people
context: This is the standard illustration of Robert Nozick's 'utility monster.' Pure total-happiness math has no built-in floor protecting individuals: if one being converts resources into pleasure far more efficiently, the biggest sum always points its way. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_monster.

question: Robert Nozick, testing the rule 'always act to maximize total happiness,' imagined a being that squeezes far more pleasure out of every resource than anyone else can. He warned that the rule would then keep diverting everything toward that one being. In his 1974 book he named the unsettling endpoint the rule seems to demand of everyone else. What did Nozick say the theory requires of the rest of us?
answer: That we all be sacrificed in the monster's maw, to push total happiness higher
choices: That we all be sacrificed in the monster's maw, to push total happiness higher
That we each surrender a fixed share of property to fund the common good
That we ignore the being entirely and split resources among ordinary folk
That we vote on the fairest division and abide by what the majority chooses
context: Nozick's exact phrase, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974, p. 41): the theory 'seems to require that we all be sacrificed in the monster's maw, in order to increase total utility.' He called such a being a 'utility monster.' Source: Nozick (1974); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_monster.

question: Utilitarianism advertises itself as fair to all: everyone's happiness counts, and everyone counts for exactly one. Robert Nozick argued that the utility monster exposes this as a disguise. Because one being's pleasure can outweigh the pain of thousands, he said the proud slogan quietly turns into something colder. What did Nozick claim 'everyone counts for one' really collapses into?
answer: Whoever converts resources into happiness best wins, and the rest count for nothing
choices: Whoever converts resources into happiness best wins, and the rest count for nothing
Whoever holds the most power sets the rules, so the strong always outvote the weak
Whoever suffers the most deserves the most aid, since their need outranks all others
Whoever owns property may keep it, because no one can be forced to share with others
context: Nozick's deeper jab: the monster shows the theory is not really egalitarian despite counting everyone equally. 'Everyone counts for one' becomes 'whoever turns resources to utility best wins.' It is a stress-test exposing the lack of a side-constraint protecting each person, not a declared knockout. Source: Nozick (1974); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_monster.

question: Derek Parfit pictured a slow slide from a thriving world down to a vast, crowded one, adding ever more people at ever-lower quality. As the population swells and quality drops, he said the finest things vanish one by one: first Mozart's music is gone, then Haydn's, then Venice is destroyed. He gave a single grim two-word phrase for the last things left in that final, barely-living world. What survives there?
answer: Muzak and potatoes
choices: Muzak and potatoes
Bread and shelter
Silence and ash
Numbers and noise
context: Parfit's image in Reasons and Persons (1984): the swarm-world Z is billions of lives each only just barely worth living, and the total-happiness sum 'prefers' it to the smaller flourishing world. He named this the Repugnant Conclusion and judged it unacceptable. Source: Parfit (1984); plato.stanford.edu/entries/repugnant-conclusion.

question: Derek Parfit built his Repugnant Conclusion as a chain of whole worlds. From a flourishing world A, add a separate group of new people, each with a life worth living, to reach a world A+. Then redistribute into a larger world B. Run those same two moves over and over, and you slide down to world Z: billions of lives each only barely worth living. Critics have hunted for the false step ever since. Which choice correctly locates where the chain can be cleanly broken?
answer: The whole chain is the culprit; no single link breaks because each one is separately defensible
choices: The whole chain is the culprit; no single link breaks because each one is separately defensible
The mere-addition step is the culprit; bringing extra people into being is never a value-neutral act
The redistribution step is the culprit; shifting to a bigger world cannot count as a change for the better
The repetition is the culprit; one pass is harmless, so a critic just forbids running it twice
context: This is the 'Mere Addition Paradox': A then A+ then B and onward to Z. Each individual move looks defensible, yet the chain lands on the repugnant Z, and the difficulty is precisely that no single step is obviously the villain. Real critics attack the chain not at one step but at a hidden assumption (for example, that 'better than' must be transitive). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mere_addition_paradox; utilitarianism.net/population-ethics.

question: Faced with the Repugnant Conclusion, some philosophers switch the goal from 'maximize total happiness' to 'maximize AVERAGE happiness,' hoping to block the swarm of barely-living billions. But this fix breeds a fresh monster of its own. A defender of the total view points out what the average rule would 'prefer' over ten billion people who are all extremely happy. What does maximizing the average end up favoring?
answer: A single blissful individual whose happiness is just a hair higher than each of the ten billion's
choices: A single blissful individual whose happiness is just a hair higher than each of the ten billion's
A small population kept deliberately tiny, so its scarce resources never have to be shared at all
The very swarm of barely-living billions it was meant to rule out, now reached by a different route
An equal split of happiness among all ten billion, which is just what basic fairness recommends here
context: Every escape route buys a new monster. The average view implies one supremely happy person beats ten billion who are all extremely happy but slightly less so; the average and 'critical-level' views also hit the 'Sadistic Conclusion,' where adding suffering lives can come out better than adding many decent ones. Gustaf Arrhenius's impossibility theorems prove no theory escapes every such result at once. Source: utilitarianism.net/population-ethics.

question: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome as emperor while wars, plague, and revolts battered the empire, and he kept a private notebook to steady himself. From Plato he borrowed one mental exercise for whenever a trouble felt overwhelming. What was the exercise?
answer: Rise above it in his mind, look down until his city is a speck, and let the trouble shrink with it
choices: Rise above it in his mind, look down until his city is a speck, and let the trouble shrink with it
Talk the trouble down by deciding it was never bad in itself, only his judgment of it
Throw himself into hard labor until the bad feeling had worn itself away
School himself to take it as the gods' own will and feel nothing about it at all
context: Marcus Aurelius (Roman emperor 161-180 CE) credits Plato in Meditations VII: one who discourses about men 'should look also at earthly things as if he viewed them from some higher place.' The exercise is literally a change of vantage point — rise above and look down so the swarming whole churns below and your one grievance becomes a speck in it. SEP notes he wrote the Meditations on military campaign during wars, rebellions, and plague — a man running an empire under siege, not a monk free of problems. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VII (George Long trans.); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Marcus Aurelius'.

question: Marcus Aurelius, looking down in his mind on the countless herds of men far below, turned the same thought against his own pride. What exact thought did he use against it?
answer: That most men do not even know his name, and those praising him now will soon blame him
choices: That most men do not even know his name, and those praising him now will soon blame him
That a good name, once earned, is the one possession that death cannot take
That the throne would pass to another soon, and the next man would undo all his work
That every emperor before him was already dust, his statues crumbling and forgotten
context: In Meditations IX.30 Marcus writes: 'Look down from above on the countless herds of men' — then aims the zoom-out at pride, adding 'how many know not even thy name, and how many will soon forget it, and how they who perhaps now are praising thee will very soon blame thee, and that neither a posthumous name is of any value, nor reputation.' So the practice deflates ego as much as worry. The keyed answer is his own line; the noble-sounding rival ('a good name death cannot take') is exactly the belief he rejects here. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IX.30 (George Long trans.).

question: Marcus Aurelius shrank the biggest things he could name down to almost nothing — even Mount Athos, a whole mountain, he reduced to a small clod of dirt. Pushing the same move, what did he call all the sea?
answer: A single drop
choices: A single drop
A thin trickle
A shallow puddle
A faint spray
context: Meditations VI.36: 'Asia, Europe are corners of the universe; all the sea a drop in the universe; Athos a little clod of the universe; all the present time is a point in eternity.' Named things — whole continents, the sea, even Mount Athos — each crushed to a corner, a drop, a clod. If a mountain is a clod of dirt, the whole sea is only a single drop, and your problem is smaller still. The passage ends 'All things are little, changeable, perishable,' making it the twin of memento mori: the cosmic height shrinks the world, death shrinks the self, and both cut a swollen problem down to size. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VI.36 (George Long trans.).

question: Rene Descartes holds a piece of beeswax fresh from the comb: it smells of flowers, tastes of honey, is hard and cold, and rings when he taps it. He carries it to the fire. The smell and taste vanish, the color shifts, it loses its shape, swells, turns to hot liquid, and no longer makes a sound when struck. Not one of those first qualities survives. What does Descartes insist is true of the puddle that remains?
answer: It is the very same wax he started with
choices: It is the very same wax he started with
It has become a completely different thing
It was never really wax in the first place
It is now only the idea of wax in his mind
context: From Descartes' Meditation II (1641). His own words: 'But is it still the same wax? Of course it is; no-one denies this.' This is the hinge of the whole wax argument: every single thing the five senses reported about the wax changed by the fire, yet you still grasp it as one and the same wax. Something held it steady that none of the senses delivered. Source: Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy II (Cottingham trans.); IEP, 'Rene Descartes.'

question: Descartes points out that before and after melting, his eyes, tongue, nose, fingers, and ears each reported different things about the wax. Yet he never once doubted it was one and the same wax the whole time. He asks: which power of his actually held onto 'the wax' as a single thing through all that change?
answer: His understanding, which the senses cannot supply
choices: His understanding, which the senses cannot supply
His eyesight, the clearest of his five senses
His sense of touch, pressing on the warm wax
His five senses, adding up all their reports
context: This is the rationalist core of the argument. Since the senses each reported one thing before and a different thing after, but 'the wax' stayed one thing, what fixes it as the same cannot be any sense; Descartes says its nature 'is perceived by the mind alone... a purely mental scrutiny.' Real knowing, for Descartes, is by reason, not the senses. The empiricists John Locke and David Hume read the very same melting wax the opposite way (see the later rungs). Source: Descartes, Meditation II (Cottingham trans.); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology.'

question: From his window Rene Descartes watches figures crossing the square below and would normally say, 'I see the men themselves.' Then he stops himself: looking down, he really catches sight only of hats and coats, which (he notes) could just as well be hiding clockwork machines. He is still sure they are men. So what is truly doing the work he had credited to his eyes?
answer: His judgment, concluding that men wear the coats
choices: His judgment, concluding that men wear the coats
His eyesight, which plainly shows him the men
His memory of other men he has seen before
His imagination, picturing men inside the coats
context: Descartes' famous window scene: 'do I see any more than hats and coats which could conceal automatons?' He concludes that 'something which I thought I was seeing with my eyes is in fact grasped solely by the faculty of judgment.' It is the same lesson as the wax: ordinary speech ('I see the men,' 'I see the wax') credits the eyes for work the mind quietly does. An automaton is a self-moving machine, like clockwork. Source: Descartes, Meditation II (Cottingham trans.).

question: Someone might grant Rene Descartes that the five senses don't grasp the wax, yet insist the imagination does, since we can picture the warm wax taking a new shape. Descartes blocks this too: the wax, he says, can be squashed, stretched, and bent into endlessly many shapes. Given that, what does Descartes conclude must be what grasps the wax?
answer: The pure intellect, since imagining holds only a limited stock of shapes
choices: The pure intellect, since imagining holds only a limited stock of shapes
The imagination, since it can run through the shapes one by one
The senses after all, since touch follows each new shape
The memory, since it stores every shape the wax has taken
context: Descartes rules out the imagination, not just the senses: 'the wax can be extended and moved in more ways than can be imagined,' so 'I could not even understand through the imagination what this piece of wax is.' Picturing runs out at a finite stock of shapes; the intellect grasps the wax as capable of change without end. Source: Wax argument (quoting Meditation II), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_argument; SparkNotes, Meditations, sec. 4.

question: Strip away everything the senses first reported about Rene Descartes' wax (the honey smell, the color, the hardness, the ringing sound), since by the fire every one of them changed. Descartes asks what is LEFT that his mind still holds onto as 'the wax' all the way through. What does he say that leftover really is?
answer: A thing that takes up room in length, breadth, and depth
choices: A thing that takes up room in length, breadth, and depth
A fixed weight that the melting could never change
The single name 'wax' that we keep giving it
A pattern of particles far too small to see
context: What the intellect holds onto is just what survives melting: the wax's being an extended thing (length, breadth, depth) that is flexible and changeable. Descartes calls this 'extension,' and says it 'is not perceivable by the senses but by the mind alone.' For him, extension (not honey-smell or hardness) is the real nature of any physical body. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rene Descartes'; Wax argument, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_argument.

question: The wax study, Rene Descartes says, was never really about wax. Each time he judges anything about it (that it persists, that it is one lump), the act of judging proves something to him even more surely than the wax itself does. What does Descartes claim he ends up knowing MORE certainly than he knows the wax?
answer: That he himself exists as a thinking thing
choices: That he himself exists as a thinking thing
That God placed the wax before him
That his own body is sitting by the fire
That other minds are watching the same wax
context: The wax is really a SECOND proof of Meditation II's true thesis: that the mind is better known than any body. Every judgment about the wax teaches Descartes even more certainly about his own thinking self: 'I am aware of my own self in a truer and more certain way than I am of the wax, and also in a much more distinct and evident way.' The rival certainties offered here are all things a thinker might claim to know, but they are not what Descartes singles out at this point of Meditation II: the existence of God is not established until Meditation III, and his own body and other minds remain exactly the things still in doubt; only his own existence as a thinking thing is secured. The empiricists disputed all of this: John Locke held the mind is a blank slate with no innate ideas (every idea, even extension, must enter through the senses), and David Hume held that the wax's felt 'sameness' is no intellectual discovery at all but just a HABIT of associating sense-impressions, dissolving Descartes' sharp split between intellect and senses. Source: Descartes, Meditation II (Cottingham trans.); IEP, 'Rene Descartes'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rationalism vs. Empiricism.'

question: Friedrich Nietzsche wrote a line so famous that people still quote it on gym walls: that whatever hardship you live through and come out the other side of does something to you. According to Nietzsche, what does surviving hardship do to a person?
answer: It makes them stronger
choices: It makes them stronger
It makes them gentler
It makes them wiser
It makes them safer
context: Nietzsche wrote 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' as aphorism 8 of 'Maxims and Arrows' in Twilight of the Idols (1888), under the heading 'Out of life's school of war.' It captures his bigger idea: resistance and hardship, once you overcome them, are exactly what build you up. Source: Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, 'Maxims and Arrows' no. 8 (1888); Wikipedia 'What does not kill me makes me stronger'.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche said the test of whether something is GOOD is one specific feeling it stirs in a person -- the same feeling an artist gets finishing a brutal painting, or an athlete gets pushing past her own record. What feeling did Nietzsche say marks a good action?
answer: A heightened feeling of power
choices: A heightened feeling of power
A deep feeling of calm and rest
A warm feeling of being admired
A settled feeling of being safe
context: This is Nietzsche's everyday handle for his idea. In The Antichrist section 2 he wrote: 'What is good? Everything that heightens the feeling of power in man, the will to power, power itself.' His test of a good action is whether it makes you grow by overcoming a limit: the artist finishing a work, the athlete pushing past a record, the thinker cracking a problem. Source: Nietzsche, The Antichrist, sec. 2, quoted in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche surprised his readers by claiming that real strength could live in a kind of person almost nobody would call powerful. Which sort of person did Nietzsche single out as secretly strong?
answer: Calm, mild people content with an ordinary life
choices: Calm, mild people content with an ordinary life
Bold rebels who openly defy the crowd
Restless strivers who can never sit still
Hardened people who have suffered terribly
context: In a private notebook Nietzsche wrote that he found strength 'in simple, mild, and pleasant people, without the least desire to rule.' It is a direct clue that the power he meant is NOT lording over others, which is exactly how his sister and later the Nazis misread him. Source: Nietzsche (Nachlass note), quoted in Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: Most thinkers had taught that the deepest thing driving every living creature is the urge to stay alive. In Beyond Good and Evil, Friedrich Nietzsche made a startling reversal: he claimed staying alive is not the real goal at all, only a side-effect of something deeper. What did Nietzsche say the deeper drive really is?
answer: The urge to discharge strength and grow
choices: The urge to discharge strength and grow
The urge to feel as much pleasure as it can
The urge to be loved and admired by others
The urge to rest and escape all suffering
context: Beyond Good and Evil section 13: 'A living thing seeks above all to DISCHARGE its strength -- life itself is WILL TO POWER; self-preservation is only one of the indirect and most frequent RESULTS thereof.' The basic drive is to grow and exert strength; merely surviving is just a side-effect. Source: Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, sec. 13.

question: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Friedrich Nietzsche has Life itself speak aloud to argue that the deepest drive in a creature cannot simply be the urge to keep existing. Life points to one plain fact about living things as proof. What fact does Life offer to show that bare survival is not the deepest drive?
answer: Creatures will risk death for what they prize more
choices: Creatures will risk death for what they prize more
Creatures all grow old and die in the end anyway
Creatures often act against their own interests
Creatures crave pleasure even more than safety
context: In the chapter 'On Self-Overcoming,' Life tells Zarathustra the drive is 'not will to life but ... will to power.' The proof: even living things will risk life for something they value more, and that very valuing is the will to power talking. Survival cannot be the deepest drive if a creature will gamble it away. Source: Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 'On Self-Overcoming' (1883), quoted in LitCharts and Wikipedia 'Will to power'.

question: There is a notorious book titled 'The Will to Power' that carries Friedrich Nietzsche's name and is often sold as his crowning masterpiece. Yet scholars warn readers about one shocking fact concerning how that book came to exist. What is the truth about it?
answer: Nietzsche never finished such a book himself
choices: Nietzsche never finished such a book himself
Nietzsche wrote it in a single feverish month
Nietzsche published it under a false pen name
Nietzsche dictated it after he had gone blind
context: Nietzsche planned a project called 'The Will to Power' but ABANDONED it by August 1888, then collapsed into insanity in January 1889. The famous 'book' was stitched together from his leftover notebooks AFTER his collapse; he never finished or published it. Source: Wikipedia 'The Will to Power (manuscript)'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche's 'will to power' is endlessly misread as a craving to dominate other people. Scholars say that misses his real point entirely, and that several other tempting readings miss it too. On the corrected reading, the power Nietzsche most admired is aimed at what?
answer: Mastering and remaking your own self
choices: Mastering and remaking your own self
Outdoing everyone you compete against
Grabbing as much pleasure as life allows
Holding on to what already belongs to you
context: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Life calls itself 'that which must always overcome itself.' This is the heart of the corrected reading: the power Nietzsche admires is power over YOURSELF -- the self disciplining and remaking the self -- not power over other people, not pleasure, and not mere self-protection. Source: Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 'On Self-Overcoming'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: Scholars sharpen Friedrich Nietzsche's idea by describing two ways a strong drive inside one person can handle the weaker drives. One way simply crushes a weaker drive and wipes it out. Nietzsche prized the OTHER way, which leaves the weaker drives intact. On that prized way, what becomes of those weaker drives?
answer: It disciplines them and puts their energy to work
choices: It disciplines them and puts their energy to work
It frees each one to follow its own urges
It bargains with them and splits the power
It tolerates them but starves them of attention
context: Scholars contrast 'tyranny' (a dominant drive crushes and erases what it rules) with 'mastery' (the stronger drive lets the weaker ones still find expression but disciplines and redirects them). Nietzsche prizes mastery: ordering your own conflicting drives into a coherent whole, like an artist composing. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche (citing John Richardson's reading).

question: Two scholars, Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari, produced the proper critical edition of Friedrich Nietzsche's papers and branded the popular book 'The Will to Power' a 'historic forgery.' But they were NOT charging that his sister had faked his handwriting or invented quotations he never wrote. What was their actual charge against her?
answer: She rearranged his real notes to push a false slant
choices: She rearranged his real notes to push a false slant
She rendered his rough German into smoother prose
She destroyed the notebooks so no one could check
She dated the notes years later than he wrote them
context: Colli and Montinari called the assembled book a 'historic forgery' not because the notes were fake -- Nietzsche wrote every one -- but because his sister Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche and his friend Peter Gast rearranged and spliced the genuine fragments to push their own nationalist, antisemitic slant, hiding the cut-and-paste from readers. The deception was the arrangement, not the words. Source: Wikipedia 'The Will to Power (manuscript)'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: The poet John Keats, in an 1819 letter to his brother George, refused to call the world a vale of tears. Instead he told George to picture it as a schoolroom full of children learning to read — a place whose very pains and troubles exist to school a raw, unformed intelligence into something far greater. He called it 'a system of Salvation which does not affront our reason.' What name did Keats give the world?
answer: 'The vale of Soul-making'
choices: 'The vale of Soul-making'
'The school of hard knocks'
'The best of all possible worlds'
'The valley of the shadow'
context: Keats wrote: 'Call the world if you please "The vale of Soul-making"... Do you not see how necessary a world of Pains and troubles is to school an Intelligence and make it a soul?' A century and a half later the philosopher John Hick borrowed the exact phrase for his answer to the problem of evil. Source: John Keats, Letter to George and Georgiana Keats, 1819; John Hick, Evil and the God of Love (1966).

question: A skeptic challenges a believer: 'If your God is all-powerful, why didn't He just make people who always freely do the right thing? No evil, but everyone still free.' The believer, defending free will, answers that this is not a job an all-powerful being failed to do — it is no job at all. Which reasoning move is the believer making?
answer: If God causes a person's right choice, it is no longer free — so even omnipotence cannot guarantee free people who never sin
choices: If God causes a person's right choice, it is no longer free — so even omnipotence cannot guarantee free people who never sin
God could have made such people but chose not to, because watching us struggle teaches Him about His own creation
An all-powerful being is bound by no rules of logic at all, so the demand for any reason simply does not apply to God
People really do always choose good in some other world God made, so the evil in this world is only an illusion
context: This is the heart of Alvin Plantinga's Free Will Defense. On the libertarian view of freedom, 'it is impossible even for an omnipotent being to make it the case that someone freely chooses to do what is right' — if God determines the choice, it stops being free. So the absence of a guaranteed all-good free world is not a limit on God's power but a feature of what 'free' means. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Problem of Evil'; Alvin Plantinga, God, Freedom, and Evil (1974).

question: John Hick rejected the idea that God should have made a painless, comfortable world. He argued the world is hard on purpose: a place 'where the heart must feel and suffer in a thousand diverse ways.' What did Hick claim a person GAINS from a world like that, which a person in an easy, painless world never could?
answer: Goodness slowly built up through real struggle, which is worth more to the Creator than goodness handed out ready-made
choices: A guaranteed reward in the afterlife, paid out in exact proportion to how much pain the person endured during life
Goodness slowly built up through real struggle, which is worth more to the Creator than goodness handed out ready-made
Solid proof that God exists, since only a real God would design a world this demanding for the creatures He loves
Freedom from ever having to make a hard choice again, since all the real struggle is finished once and for all
context: Hick's soul-making theodicy goes further than merely defending consistency — it offers a positive purpose for evil. Human goodness 'slowly built up through personal histories of moral effort,' he wrote, 'has a value in the eyes of the Creator' that effortless, ready-made goodness lacks. The hardship is the price of a deeper kind of virtue. Source: John Hick, Evil and the God of Love (1966); IEP, 'Hick, John'.

question: The philosopher J. L. Mackie thought the believer's appeal to free will failed, and he pressed it with one sharp question. He agreed that genuine freedom is worth having and that God was right to give it. Granting all of that, he still asked what an all-powerful God could have arranged differently. What was Mackie's exact challenge?
answer: Why could God not have made people who, while still free, always happen to choose the good?
choices: Why could God not have made people who, while still free, always happen to choose the good?
Why could God not have stepped in to stop each evil choice the very moment before it was made?
Why could God not have left people free in small matters while settling the weighty choices Himself?
Why could God not have made the good so plainly rewarding that no free person would ever pick evil?
context: Mackie's 1955 line is famous: 'If God has made men such that in their free choices they sometimes prefer what is good and sometimes what is evil, why could he not have made men such that they always freely choose the good?' If even one free agent always choosing good is possible, he argued, an omnipotent God should have been able to make a whole world of them. Plantinga's Free Will Defense was built to answer exactly this. Source: J. L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence,' Mind (1955), p.209; IEP, 'Logical Problem of Evil'.

question: Augustine of Hippo taught that humanity began perfect in the garden of Eden and then FELL into sin through Adam's choice. The rival tradition behind John Hick, named for the early bishop Irenaeus of Lyon (c.130-c.202), placed the perfect human somewhere else on the timeline. Where did Irenaeus put it?
answer: At the END — humans began immature and are still growing up toward a perfection that lies ahead of them
choices: At the very start too — humans began perfect, fell, and the whole story since is the long climb back to Eden
At the END — humans began immature and are still growing up toward a perfection that lies ahead of them
Nowhere real — there was no perfect past and there will be no perfect future, only endless change
In God alone — humans were never built to reach perfection, and reaching for it was itself the first sin
context: Hick's theodicy is called Irenaean, after Irenaeus of Lyon (c.130-c.202), and it flips the Augustinian timeline from decay to development. Augustine: humans began perfect and fell. Irenaeus and Hick: humans began immature and are still mid-journey, growing toward a perfection that lies ahead, not behind. A hard world is the workshop for that growth. Source: IEP, 'Hick, John'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: The Free Will Defense traces evil to the misuse of human freedom — but a critic raises an earthquake that buries a village, or a child's cancer, which nobody chose. Plantinga did not concede the point. Drawing on an idea from Augustine, he offered one suggestion in reply. What did he suggest?
answer: That it is at least possible such evils trace to the free choices of nonhuman persons, like Satan and fallen angels
choices: That it is at least possible such evils trace to the free choices of nonhuman persons, like Satan and fallen angels
That it is at least possible such evils are unintended fallout of free human acts, spread across the long ages
That it is at least possible God allows such evils so free human courage and compassion have something real to answer
That it is at least possible such evils only seem authorless, each in fact following some free choice we cannot trace
context: This is the purest illustration of a defense's possibility-only strategy. Following Augustine, Plantinga raises the possibility that natural evils — earthquakes, plagues, disease — are the work of free supernatural persons such as Satan and fallen angels. He stresses he is NOT asserting this is true; only that it is logically POSSIBLE, which is all a defense (as opposed to a full theodicy) needs to fold natural evil back under 'evil that traces to a free will.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Problem of Evil'.

question: Alvin Plantinga's boldest device imagines a possible person with a strange property: in EVERY possible world where that person exists and is genuinely free, there is at least one choice on which they would freely go wrong. Plantinga then dares to suppose this might hold of every possible person at once. If it is even possible, what follows for God?
answer: Whichever free creatures God tries to create, He still cannot get a world holding moral good with no moral evil at all
choices: Whichever free creatures God tries to create, He still cannot get a world holding moral good with no moral evil at all
Whichever free creatures God tries to create, the blame for their wrongdoing rests on them, never on the God who made them
Whichever free creatures God tries to create, a world with far less evil than ours was still well within His reach
Whichever free creatures God tries to create, the total amount of evil is fixed in advance, beyond even His control
context: This is 'transworld depravity.' Plantinga's further claim — that it is POSSIBLE every creaturely essence suffers from it — is all his defense needs. If possible, then even an omnipotent God who wants free creatures cannot guarantee a sinless world, because every candidate person would freely go wrong somewhere. He insists only that this is possible, not that it is actually true. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Problem of Evil'; Alvin Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity (1974).

question: Marilyn McCord Adams says soul-making theodicies 'teeter on the rock' of cases like a fawn that burns slowly to death, alone, in a forest fire no human ever sees. Adams demands MORE of God than merely outweighing such a horror with greater goods enjoyed by others elsewhere. What further thing does she insist God must do?
answer: Redeem the horror within the sufferer's own life, weaving it into a whole that is good for THAT very being
choices: Redeem the horror within the sufferer's own life, weaving it into a whole that is good for THAT very being
Prevent every such horror in advance, so that no creature is ever allowed to suffer this way at all
Pay the sufferer back afterward with a reward in proportion to exactly how much it was made to suffer
Track down and punish whoever or whatever was the cause, so that the suffering does not go unanswered
context: Adams pushes a demand stronger than either defense: God must not merely BALANCE OFF evil with greater goods elsewhere, but DEFEAT it — integrate the horror into the sufferer's OWN life as part of a whole that is incommensurably good for THAT person (following Roderick Chisholm's balancing-off vs. defeat distinction). A ledger where my agony is outweighed by someone else's joy is not enough; the evil has to be redeemed within my own story. She concedes soul-making theodicies 'at least teeter on the rock of horrendous evils.' Source: Marilyn McCord Adams, Horrendous Evils and the Goodness of God; Roderick Chisholm, 'The Defeat of Good and Evil'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A huge, heavy young student sat almost totally silent in class, so his quicker-tongued classmates decided the big quiet one must be slow and pinned a mocking animal nickname on him. What barnyard insult did the boys hang on young Thomas Aquinas?
answer: The dumb ox
choices: The dumb ox
The fat goose
The lazy mule
The plodding hog
context: The nickname fit two ways at once: Thomas really was famously tall and bulky, and he really did sit near-silent while quicker classmates assumed the big quiet boy was dim. The bellow that followed proved them all wrong. Source: English Dominicans (english.op.org), 'Our brother, the Dumb Ox'; World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: Thomas Aquinas sat silent while classmates mocked him as a dumb ox. His teacher Albert the Great overheard the jeering and snapped back a prophecy about the big quiet boy. What did Albert say this ox would one day do?
answer: Give a bellow heard across the whole world
choices: Give a bellow heard across the whole world
Gore the proudest of them with his horns
Outwork every clever boy in the room
Plow a straighter furrow than their tongues
context: Albert's exact retort: 'We call him the dumb ox, but one day he will give such a bellowing in his teaching that it will be heard throughout the whole world.' It came true. Source: English Dominicans (english.op.org), 'Our brother, the Dumb Ox'; World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: Thomas Aquinas, youngest son of a wealthy noble family, threw away a comfortable future as a rich abbot to join the penniless begging friars. His outraged brothers ambushed him on the road, hauled him back to the family estate, and set out to break his will. What did they do to him there?
answer: Locked him in a tower for about a year
choices: Locked him in a tower for about a year
Disowned him and burned all his books
Shipped him off to a far-away war
Married him to a noble daughter
context: Thomas's parents had groomed him to become the rich abbot of Monte Cassino, where his great-uncle had ruled; when he chose the Dominicans, his brothers held him roughly a year in the family tower to break him. It did not work. Source: Wikipedia: Thomas Aquinas; World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: When Thomas Aquinas died at Fossanova abbey, the monks there feared the Dominican friars would come and carry off his holy body to claim the relics. To keep the holy remains for themselves, the monks did something drastic to the corpse before anyone could arrive. What did they do?
answer: Boiled it down to clean bones
choices: Boiled it down to clean bones
Sealed it inside a stone wall
Buried it under the chapel floor
Salted and dried it for keeping
context: The Cistercians at Fossanova cut off his head, hid it, and boiled the body down to bones so they could keep the relics. The fight over Thomas's remains then dragged on for almost a century. Source: Wikipedia: Canonization of Thomas Aquinas; The Medieval Review (scholarworks.iu.edu), review of Rasanen, 'Thomas Aquinas's Relics'.

question: Besides his mountains of philosophy, Thomas Aquinas was asked to compose the worship for the new feast of Corpus Christi, and he wrote hymns still sung centuries later. For this towering body of sacred work the Church later gave him an honorary title. What was Thomas named?
answer: The Angelic Doctor
choices: The Angelic Doctor
The Silent Master
The Ox of Aquino
The Last Apostle
context: Around 1264 Thomas wrote the great Eucharistic hymns 'Pange Lingua' and 'Tantum Ergo.' He was canonized a saint on July 18, 1323, and is honored as the Angelic Doctor. Source: Wikipedia: Thomas Aquinas; World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: To break the will of Thomas Aquinas while his brothers kept him captive in the family stronghold, they sent a hired woman into his room to seduce him out of his vow. Thomas leaped to the fireplace and, the story goes, drove her out the door with a single weapon he snatched up. What did he grab?
answer: A burning log from the fire
choices: A burning log from the fire
A heavy iron poker
A pot of boiling water
A handful of hot ash
context: Told as legend: Thomas snatched a burning log, chased the woman out, and scorched a cross onto the wall with the firebrand; the tale adds that two angels then girded him with a 'girdle of chastity.' Source: World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas; Wikipedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: Dining as an honored guest at the table of King Louis IX of France, Thomas Aquinas fell silent mid-meal, lost in an argument in his own head. Suddenly his huge fist crashed down so hard the goblets jumped, and he shouted out loud. What did Thomas cry out?
answer: And that will settle the Manichees!
choices: And that will settle the Manichees!
And that will silence the Arians!
And that refutes the Pelagians!
And that finishes off the Averroists!
context: The Manichees were an old heresy Thomas had been mentally arguing against. Instead of taking offense, King Louis IX quietly sent scribes over to write the argument down before Thomas forgot it. Source: G.K. Chesterton, 'St. Thomas Aquinas' (ccel.org); Thomistic Philosophy Page (aquinasonline.com).

question: Thomas Aquinas leaned so heavily on one ancient Greek thinker that he rarely used the man's name, calling him simply "the Philosopher," and he worked to show that this pagan's logic and Christian faith could not truly contradict each other. Which thinker did Thomas mean?
answer: Aristotle
choices: Aristotle
Socrates
Plato
Pythagoras
context: Thomas first met the newly translated Aristotle at the University of Naples around age 14 and brought 'the Philosopher' into the heart of Christian thought, arguing reason and faith cannot truly conflict. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Thomas Aquinas; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas.

question: The Summa Theologiae of Thomas Aquinas runs to millions of words and stands among the most demanding works in all of philosophy. Yet Thomas had a surprising group of readers in mind when he sat down to write it. Who did he actually write this colossal book for?
answer: Beginners just starting theology
choices: Beginners just starting theology
Bishops settling church disputes
Kings ruling Christian realms
Monks set to copy it by hand
context: The Summa was meant as a beginners' textbook for students just starting theology. Thomas left it unfinished, breaking off in the middle of the section on the sacraments. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Thomas Aquinas; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas.

question: On December 6, 1273, while saying Mass, Thomas Aquinas had an overwhelming experience and abruptly laid down his pen for good. When his secretary Reginald begged him to finish the great Summa, Thomas compared his whole life of writing to one worthless thing. To what did he liken all his work?
answer: Straw
choices: Straw
Dust
Smoke
Sand
context: His words to Reginald: 'All that I have written seems to me like straw compared with what has now been revealed to me.' He never wrote again. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas; Diocese of Covington, 'Thomas Aquinas' Mystical Experience'.

question: Thomas Aquinas died at only about 48 in 1274 while traveling to a great church council. A freak accident on the road left him hurt, he fell ill, and he died soon after; a 2025 medical study points to that mishap as the cause of his death. What was the accident?
answer: He struck his head on a fallen branch
choices: He struck his head on a fallen branch
His horse threw him onto sharp rocks
A runaway cart rolled over his leg
He slipped while crossing a cold river
context: He was riding to the Second Council of Lyon when he struck his head on the branch of a fallen tree; a 2025 medical study concluded the blow likely caused the chronic brain bleed that killed him at Fossanova Abbey on March 7, 1274. Source: Wikipedia: Thomas Aquinas; Medievalists.net (2025), 'Thomas Aquinas died from head trauma, study suggests'.

question: A story tells that a voice from the crucifix once spoke to Thomas Aquinas: "You have written well of me, Thomas. What reward will you have?" Of all the rewards he might have asked for, Thomas named just one. What did he ask for?
answer: God himself, and nothing else
choices: God himself, and nothing else
A long and healthy life
The Summa finished at last
Wisdom beyond all other men
context: Reported as legend: Thomas answered, 'Nothing but yourself, Lord.' The account is traditional testimony rather than documented fact. Source: Catholic Answers (catholic.com), 'When St. Thomas Aquinas Likened his Work to Straw'; Diocese of Covington.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville warned that a democracy could fall under a gentle, all-managing power that handles every part of life for its citizens. He drew a sharp contrast: a good parent raises a child toward independence, but THIS power, he said, does the opposite on purpose. What is its aim, in his image?
answer: To keep its citizens in perpetual childhood, so they always need it
choices: To keep its citizens in perpetual childhood, so they always need it
To work its citizens to exhaustion, so they cannot resist its orders
To free its citizens from labor, so they may pursue higher learning
To split its citizens into ranks, so each one knows their station
context: Tocqueville's own line: the tutelary power 'would be like the authority of a parent if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks, on the contrary, to keep them in perpetual childhood.' A good parent works to become unneeded; this state works to stay needed forever. Democracy in America, Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6 ('What Sort of Despotism Democratic Nations Have to Fear'). Source: Pioneer Institute and Wikisource (en.wikisource.org/wiki/Democracy_in_America/Volume_2/Book_4/Chapter_6).

question: Alexis de Tocqueville said the rulers of a mild, over-helpful democratic state would not be the cruel tyrants of old history. When he pictured the soft manners and small wants of people in his day, he wrote that in their rulers they would find not tyrants but something else. What kind of ruler did he fear instead?
answer: Schoolmasters, who endlessly grade and correct them
choices: Schoolmasters, who endlessly grade and correct them
Merchants, who buy and sell them like any goods
Generals, who drill and march them into order
Priests, who weigh and absolve them of their sins
context: Verbatim: 'When I think of the small passions of men of our day, the softness of their mores... I do not fear that in their chiefs they will find tyrants, but rather schoolmasters.' Not a master with a whip, but a teacher who never stops grading you. This sentence (Mansfield and Winthrop translation) is the root of the 'benevolent schoolmasters' phrasing. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_tyranny and lawliberty.org.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville asked how a soft, tutelary state actually holds a free people down, since it rules with no chains and no terror. His answer was not one great shackle but something far finer, spread thin across the whole surface of society. What does this state lay over its people to bind them?
answer: A network of small, complicated rules, minute and the same for all
choices: A network of small, complicated rules, minute and the same for all
A creed of fixed beliefs that everyone must recite each morning
A wall of armed watchmen who pen the citizens inside the city
A ladder of strict ranks that fixes each citizen in their place
context: Verbatim: the soft power 'covers the surface of society with a network of small complicated rules, minute and uniform, through which the most original minds and the most energetic characters cannot penetrate, to rise above the crowd.' Not one heavy chain but a fine mesh of tiny regulations that quietly flattens everyone to the same level. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org) and Wikipedia 'Soft despotism'.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville described exactly how a mild despotism works on a person's will. He noted that this power does not break a man's will the way an old tyrant would; instead it softens, bends, and guides it. So what does it mainly do to him, day to day?
answer: It constantly restrains him from acting, so choices are never born
choices: It constantly restrains him from acting, so choices are never born
It steadily flatters his vanity, so pride governs his every step
It openly punishes his mistakes, so fear governs his every step
It quietly watches his movements, so shame governs his every step
context: Verbatim: 'men are seldom forced by it to act, but they are constantly restrained from acting,' and 'it does not break men's will, but softens, bends, and guides it.' The mechanism is prevention, not command: it rarely makes you do things, it quietly keeps you from doing things, so the choice is stopped before it is ever made. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via Wikipedia 'Soft despotism' and Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org).

question: Alexis de Tocqueville gave a final image for where comfort-by-the-state ends up. He said this power does not tyrannize; it compresses, drains, and dulls a people until the whole nation sinks into one low condition, with the government set over it. What does he say the people become?
answer: A flock of timid, industrious animals, with the government as shepherd
choices: A flock of timid, industrious animals, with the government as shepherd
A gang of broken, starving prisoners, with the government as warden
A line of weary, footsore soldiers, with the government as general
A house of meek, flattering servants, with the government as master
context: Verbatim closing image: the power 'does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people, till each nation is reduced to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.' The endpoint of being tended by a kindly state is not slaves in chains but contented sheep. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via City Journal / Daniel Klein (city-journal.org) and Online Library of Liberty.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville faced a puzzle: why would a free people accept being led about like toddlers in leading-strings? He answered that each man accepts it because of who, in a democracy, he believes holds the other end of his cord. Whose hand is it, that makes the leash feel like freedom rather than bondage?
answer: The whole body of the people holds the end of his chain
choices: The whole body of the people holds the end of his chain
His own elected representatives hold the end of his chain
The fellow citizens of his own town hold the end of his chain
The shifting will of the majority holds the end of his chain
context: Verbatim: 'Every man allows himself to be put in leading-strings, because he sees that it is not a person or a class of persons, but the people at large who hold the end of his chain.' Tocqueville's point is precise: not your representatives, not your town, not a ruling faction, but the WHOLE people, so the chain feels like self-rule rather than bondage. 'Leading-strings' were the cords used to keep a toddler from falling, his deliberate perpetual-childhood image again. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via libertyfreedom.wordpress.com.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville coined a biting epigram for how voting fits inside this soft despotism. Under this system, he said, the people lean on the state nearly all the time, but they break free for one brief act before sinking back. What, in his line, do they do in that single free moment?
answer: They shake off dependence just long enough to select their master
choices: They shake off dependence just long enough to select their master
They crowd the square just long enough to air their grievances
They open the laws just long enough to learn their own rights
They take up arms just long enough to frighten their officials
context: Verbatim: 'By this system the people shake off their state of dependence just long enough to select their master, and then relapse into it again.' Election day is the one day you are free, and you spend that freedom choosing the hand that holds your chain, then return to dependence. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via libertyfreedom.wordpress.com and Wikipedia 'Soft despotism'.

question: Leo Tolstoy pointed to a boy who meets a wolf in the woods and later tells the story — the quiet path, the yellow eyes, the gap closing between them — to settle one big question: what makes a thing a work of art at all?
