answer: Passing a feeling you have truly lived through on to others
choices: Skilled imitation of how things truly look in nature
The making of something beautiful and pleasing to behold
Whatever an artist chooses to call art, simply by saying so
Passing a feeling you have truly lived through on to others
context: Leo Tolstoy (1828-1910) rejected the idea that art is beauty, pleasure, or skill. In What Is Art? (1897) he defined it as communication: 'one man consciously, by means of certain external signs, hands on to others feelings he has lived through, and that others are infected by these feelings and also experience them.' The boy-and-the-wolf is his own handle for it: a feeling genuinely lived through and passed on so listeners catch it IS art. (The 'whatever an artist calls art' option is Duchamp's rival view, where merely designating a urinal as art makes it art — exactly what Tolstoy denies; he demands the work actually transmit a real feeling.) Source: Leo Tolstoy, What Is Art?, chs. 5 and 15 (marxists.org/archive/tolstoy/1897/what-is-art); IEP, Aesthetics (iep.utm.edu/aestheti).

question: Leo Tolstoy measured every work of art by a single test: does it truly carry a feeling from its maker into those who receive it? Applying that test to Beethoven's Ninth Symphony — one of the most revered works in all of music — he reached a verdict that stunned the cultured world, ranking it as 'bad art.' What was Tolstoy's complaint against the Ninth?
answer: It was long, confused, and artificial, past any ordinary listener's grasp
choices: It merely imitated older symphonies instead of breaking new ground
It was long, confused, and artificial, past any ordinary listener's grasp
It was too plain and simple to deserve such towering fame
Its grandeur dazzled the senses but bypassed the mind
context: On Tolstoy's test, what counts is whether a work infects an audience with real feeling and unites them in it — fame and technical brilliance count for nothing. Of Beethoven's Ninth he wrote: 'I am unable to imagine to myself a crowd of normal people who could understand anything of this long, confused, and artificial production,' concluding that 'this work belongs to the rank of bad art.' This is why he could rank a humble folk song that genuinely moves people ABOVE an elaborate masterpiece that transmits nothing. Presented as Tolstoy's position, not a verdict on Beethoven. Source: Leo Tolstoy, What Is Art? (ch. 13); readersquest.wordpress.com/2011/08/14/what-art-isnt-tolstoy-disses-beethoven-and-wagner.

question: Leo Tolstoy taught that sincere feeling, not polish or fame, is what makes real art. The man the world ranks among its greatest novelists then aimed that same test at the very books that made his name, War and Peace and Anna Karenina. By his own theory, what verdict did Tolstoy reach about his masterpieces?
answer: Branded them bad art — upper-class vanity that united no one in feeling
choices: Branded them bad art — upper-class vanity that united no one in feeling
Praised them as his one success at infecting plain readers with feeling
Judged them weak in craft yet honest in the feeling they carried across
Ranked them his finest art for binding readers of every class in feeling
context: Tolstoy ranked the SINCERITY of the artist — the force with which he himself actually feels what he passes on — as the most important of the three things that give art its power. He applied this so strictly that he disowned his own masterpieces, War and Peace and Anna Karenina, as 'bad art': products of upper-class vanity that, in his judgment, failed to bind people together in shared feeling. The author the world calls one of its greatest condemned his own most famous novels by his own theory. (War and Peace and Anna Karenina are the novels at issue; both are Tolstoy's own.) Presented as Tolstoy's own position, no verdict. Source: thecollector.com/leo-tolstoy-what-is-art; readersquest.wordpress.com/2011/08/14/what-art-isnt-tolstoy-disses-beethoven-and-wagner.

question: A father tells his son, "Don't lie." The boy shoots right back, "But YOU lied yesterday!" And it's true — the father did lie yesterday. Has the boy shown that lying is actually okay?
answer: No — "don't lie" is sound advice no matter who happens to be saying it
choices: No — "don't lie" is sound advice no matter who happens to be saying it
Yes — a rule that its very own maker openly breaks can't bind anyone else
Yes — the father lost the right to give that advice the moment he broke it
No — but only because a parent outranks a child, so the boy is bound to obey
context: This is the classic 'tu quoque,' Latin for 'you too' — the appeal to hypocrisy. The father's hypocrisy is a real and separate charge, but it does nothing to the advice itself: 'don't lie' is good counsel whether or not he follows it. Catching a hypocrite is satisfying; it is not a refutation. Source: finmasters, Tu Quoque Fallacy (finmasters.com/tu-quoque-fallacy); Your Logical Fallacy Is: tu quoque (yourlogicalfallacyis.com/tu-quoque).

question: A man who smokes a pack a day warns his nephew, "Smoking will kill you — don't ever start." The nephew laughs: "You smoke, so your warning means nothing." Is the nephew right that the warning means nothing?
answer: No — smoking is deadly or not because of the world, not because of the speaker
choices: No — smoking is deadly or not because of the world, not because of the speaker
Yes — a warning from a person who plainly ignores it carries no weight at all
Yes — the uncle would have to quit first before his warning could really count
No — but the warning only counts if the uncle is genuinely sorry he ever started
context: The sharpest form of the point: a smoker who tells you smoking is deadly is still telling the truth. Whether a person practices what they preach has zero bearing on whether the claim is true — a claim is true or false because of how the world actually is, not because of who happens to say it. Philosopher Douglas Walton uses this very smoking example to illustrate the tu quoque (appeal to hypocrisy). Source: Wikipedia, Tu quoque (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tu_quoque); finmasters, Tu Quoque Fallacy.

question: During an argument, the moment Mara is criticized she snaps back, "Well, YOU do the exact same thing!" It is a slick comeback. As a way of MEETING the criticism aimed at her, what did it actually accomplish?
answer: It got her off the hook by turning everyone's attention onto her critic
choices: It got her off the hook by turning everyone's attention onto her critic
It proved the criticism of her was false by finding some flaw in her critic
It made both of them equally guilty, so the original criticism cancelled out
It settled the whole dispute, since neither side could claim the high ground now
context: This is why tu quoque works as a red herring: it answers a criticism with a criticism, so the original point never has to be defended. The move 'takes the heat off' the person who should be answering and shifts the spotlight onto the accuser instead. Spotting that swap — criticism dodged, not met — is the whole skill. Source: Your Logical Fallacy Is: tu quoque (yourlogicalfallacyis.com/tu-quoque).

question: Caught cheating on a test, Leo shrugs and says, "Well, half the class cheats too!" An old proverb fits his move — the pot calling the kettle black — and so does its cousin, "two wrongs don't make a right." What error do both proverbs put their finger on?
answer: Using another person's wrongdoing as if it cleared you of your own
choices: Using another person's wrongdoing as if it cleared you of your own
Judging a person by their looks instead of by what they have actually said
Believing a claim only because a very large crowd already believes it too
Accepting an idea just because some famous expert happened to endorse it
context: Both sayings name the same family of mistake as tu quoque: treating one party's bad behavior as a defense of another's. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy files both 'Tu Quoque' and 'Two Wrongs Do Not Make a Right' under the ad hominem fallacies — moves that shift attention to the person instead of answering the claim. The other three options are different fallacies (attacking looks, bandwagon, appeal to authority). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (iep.utm.edu/fallacy).

question: Philosopher Douglas Walton built a textbook case: a parent argues that smoking causes chronic disease, so the child shouldn't smoke. The child fires back, "You smoke yourself — so much for your argument!" Walton ruled the child's reply does NOT defeat the argument. Pinpoint where the reply misfires.
answer: The child attacked how the parent lives but left the parent's actual reasons untouched
choices: The child attacked how the parent lives but left the parent's actual reasons untouched
The parent is the adult, so the parent's word automatically settles the whole matter
The child changed the subject, and changing the subject always means the child lost
Only a lifelong non-smoker may argue against smoking, so the child cannot do it either
context: From Douglas Walton's 'Ad Hominem Arguments' (1998). Walton's verdict is precise: the parent's argument rested on a reason — smoking causes chronic disease — and the child never laid a finger on that reason. Instead the child aimed at the parent's habits, which were no part of the support in the first place; so the argument is left standing. The parent's inconsistency is a real but separate charge, not a hole in the reasoning. Note the wrong grounds: appealing to the parent's authority and treating any subject-change as an automatic loss are themselves shaky moves. Source: Douglas Walton, Ad Hominem Arguments (1998), cited in Wikipedia, Tu quoque and Ad hominem (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_hominem).

question: In a 1611 London stage comedy, the star clown Thomas Greene played a fool named Bubble who blurted one Latin tag — "the same to you" — whenever anyone insulted him. Audiences loved that running gag so much that something happened to the comedy itself. What did its popularity do?
answer: The playhouse renamed the whole comedy after Bubble's catchphrase
choices: The playhouse renamed the whole comedy after Bubble's catchphrase
The playhouse hired a second clown to share Bubble's best lines
The playhouse barred children from the rowdiest of its performances
The playhouse moved the comedy to a far larger stage across town
context: The catchphrase entered English straight off the stage. Bubble's repeated 'Tu Quoque' ('the same to you') so delighted audiences that the playhouse renamed the whole comedy 'Greene's Tu Quoque, or The City Gallant.' It was such a hit that within a year the catchphrase ate the title — by summer 1612 court records call it simply 'Tu Coque,' and Queen Anne's Men staged it at the Red Bull Theatre. Source: Wikipedia, Greene's Tu Quoque (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greene's_Tu_Quoque); Folger Early Modern English Drama (emed.folger.edu/gtq).

question: Sean O'Conaill, a history teacher in Northern Ireland during the Troubles, grew tired of one debating habit: every time someone's side was accused of an atrocity, a defender answered by pointing at the OTHER side's atrocities instead. In a 1974 newspaper letter he gave that dodge a homemade nickname. What did he call the people who do it?
answer: "the Whatabouts"
choices: "the Whatabouts"
"the Tu-Quoquers"
"the Mudslingers"
"the Deflectors"
context: This coinage is the root of 'whataboutism' — the political-scale version of tu quoque, deflecting a charge by pointing at the accuser's own faults ('What about YOU?'). O'Conaill's letter about 'the Whatabouts' ran in The Irish Times on 30 January 1974. Journalist Edward Lucas later revived the word in The Economist (2007-2008), pinning it on Soviet propaganda technique. Source: Wikipedia, Whataboutism (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whataboutism); lexicographer Ben Zimmer's attribution cited therein.

question: All through the Cold War, whenever the United States accused the Soviet Union of crushing human rights, Soviet officials had a stock reply that never once defended the Soviet record — it just pointed back at some sin of America's instead. One particular comeback became famous enough to be quoted for decades as a punchline. Which was it?
answer: "And you are lynching Negroes"
choices: "And you are lynching Negroes"
"And you are poisoning your skies"
"And you are starving your poor"
"And you are burning the world"
context: In Russian, 'А у вас негров линчуют' ('A u vas negrov linchuyut'). It is the textbook example of whataboutism: instead of answering for Soviet abuses, the reply changed the subject to American racism. The Soviets had real ammunition — the 1931 Scottsboro Boys trial fueled propaganda like Dmitri Moor's 1932 poster 'Freedom to the Prisoners of Scottsboro!' — but pointing at America's sins never defended their own record. Source: Wikipedia, And you are lynching Negroes (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And_you_are_lynching_Negroes).

question: People treat the "but you lynch black men" comeback as a Soviet invention, the Kremlin's pet reply to American criticism. Yet the very same dodge was already a Russian reflex a full generation before any Communist ran the country. Who is the earliest famous user of it?
answer: A Tsarist minister, waving away a deadly anti-Jewish pogrom in his own empire
choices: A Tsarist minister, waving away a deadly anti-Jewish pogrom in his own empire
A Slavophile editor, shrugging off a deadly anti-student riot in the capital
An Okhrana police chief, excusing a bloody crackdown on striking factory workers
An imperial governor, dismissing a deadly riot out in the Caucasus mountains
context: The lynching deflection predates the USSR. After the 1903 Kishinev pogrom, Tsarist interior minister Vyacheslav von Plehve compared the rioters to Americans 'when they lynch negroes.' Two years later, in a 1905 Century magazine interview, novelist Leo Tolstoy jabbed that America 'lynch[es] negroes, form[s] trusts, and adopt[s] imperialism.' The move was an old Russian reflex long before it became Soviet routine. Source: Wikipedia, And you are lynching Negroes (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And_you_are_lynching_Negroes), citing von Plehve (1903) and Tolstoy's 1905 interview.

question: Pointing out "you do it too" isn't always a cheap dodge — sometimes it exposes a real hypocrisy. A critic blasts your country for jailing dissidents but stays totally silent when his own ALLY jails dissidents the very same way. You point that out. The test of whether your reply is fair turns on one thing. Which?
answer: Whether you held both sides to the same standard or just changed the subject
choices: Whether you held both sides to the same standard or just changed the subject
Whether your country's own jailings happened to be milder than the ally's were
Whether the critic ends up looking even more foolish than you do by the end
Whether the audience watching the whole exchange already agrees with your side
context: This is the line between fair hypocrisy-spotting and the fallacy. Pointing at 'you too' is legitimate only when it exposes a genuine double standard — the same criterion applied to comparable cases, allies and enemies alike. It collapses into tu quoque the instant it's used to avoid defending your own claim. The test: is it the same standard applied consistently, or just a change of subject? Source: Wikipedia, Whataboutism (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whataboutism), on selective application of the same criterion to comparable situations.

question: Suppose you catch a critic in a genuine double standard — he condemns your country for jailing dissidents yet excuses his ally for doing exactly the same. Catching him is fair game. But here's the subtle part: even after you've exposed his hypocrisy, what does it actually tell you?
answer: His motive — it shows his bias, yet the charge against your country may still be true
choices: His motive — it shows his bias, yet the charge against your country may still be true
Nothing at all — a proven hypocrite's every last claim collapses with his credibility
Victory — exposing his double standard wipes out the charge he had made against you
His guilt — his silence about the ally proves your own country must be in the clear
context: The deep point that survives even a fair catch: exposing a double standard reveals the critic's MOTIVE — it tests whether he actually believes his principle or is just wielding it as a weapon. But motive is not truth. The original charge against your country stands or falls on the facts, not on the critic's hypocrisy. To think 'he's a hypocrite, therefore his charge is false' is to commit the very tu quoque you just caught him needing. Source: Your Logical Fallacy Is: tu quoque (yourlogicalfallacyis.com/tu-quoque); discussion summarized in Wikipedia, Whataboutism.

question: A boy wants to grow up brave and fair, and asks Aristotle how. Aristotle answers with a craftsman: a person becomes a builder by building houses, and a lyre-player by playing the lyre. By that same logic, how does the boy become brave and just?
answer: By repeatedly doing brave and just acts himself
choices: By repeatedly doing brave and just acts himself
By studying what bravery and justice truly are
By being born with a brave and just nature
By admiring brave and just people from afar
context: Aristotle's central craft image: 'men become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.' The skill is in the doing, not the knowing -- character is trained by repeated action. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle claims it matters enormously which habits a person starts building back in childhood. How much difference, he says, does that early practice make to the adult one becomes?
answer: It makes all the difference in the world
choices: It makes all the difference in the world
It makes only a small difference at most
It makes no real difference either way
It makes a difference that fades with age
context: Aristotle: 'It makes no small difference, then, whether we form habits of one kind or of another from our very youth; it makes a very great difference, or rather all the difference.' The habits you practice as a kid lay down the character you carry as an adult. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: To prove good character is not something you are simply born with, Aristotle points to a stone. A stone naturally falls downward, he says, and you could throw it upward ten thousand times and it would never learn to rise on its own. What follows about virtue?
answer: Habit can train virtue into us, so it is not fixed by nature
choices: Habit can train virtue into us, so it is not fixed by nature
Virtue is locked in at birth, just as the stone is locked
Virtue is a gift the gods grant to only a lucky few
Virtue rises within us the way the stone falls down
context: Aristotle: 'the stone which by nature moves downwards cannot be habituated to move upwards, not even if one tries to train it by throwing it up ten thousand times.' Things fixed by nature can't be retrained by habit -- but virtue CAN be trained by habit, so virtue is not fixed by nature. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle has already said we become builders by building and lyre-players by playing. Now he asks where justice itself gets trained into a person. As Aristotle tells it, what is it that actually makes someone just rather than unjust?
answer: Doing fair or unfair acts toward the people around us
choices: Doing fair or unfair acts toward the people around us
Grasping the true definition of what justice means
Inheriting a just temperament from a just parent
Facing one great trial that proves what we are made of
context: Aristotle: 'by doing the acts that we do in our transactions with other men we become just or unjust.' Justice is not built by reflection or inherited by blood -- it is forged in the ordinary back-and-forth of how we treat the people around us, one fair or unfair act at a time. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle points out that the Greek word for moral character, ETHIKE, is just a slight bend of another everyday Greek word. Which word did it grow out of?
answer: ETHOS, meaning habit or custom
choices: ETHOS, meaning habit or custom
LOGOS, meaning reason or word
PATHOS, meaning feeling or suffering
NOMOS, meaning law or convention
context: Aristotle: 'moral virtue comes about as a result of habit, whence also its name (ethike) is one that is formed by a slight variation from the word ethos (habit).' The very word 'ethics' grew out of the word for 'habit' -- the etymology is itself the lesson. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: A soldier learns to hold the line; a man learns to push the rich feast away. Aristotle says there is a telltale sign that reveals whether a brave or temperate character has truly been built in someone, rather than merely forced. What is that sign?
answer: Whether doing the right thing has started to feel pleasant
choices: Whether doing the right thing has started to feel pleasant
Whether the right act still costs them a hard inner struggle
Whether they must talk themselves into it each time
Whether they act well only when someone is watching
context: Aristotle: 'We must take as a sign of states of character the pleasure or pain that ensues on acts.' The trained-up brave person no longer dreads standing firm and the temperate person stops longing for the pleasure given up -- enjoying the virtuous act is the mark that the skill is built, not merely attempted. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.3 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle gives a surprising reason for studying ethics at all. The point, he says, is not to settle in our minds what virtue is, since that alone would be useless. A harpist is not made by understanding music. So what is the real aim of the whole inquiry?
answer: To become good by actually doing good acts
choices: To become good by actually doing good acts
To teach virtue to others through clear lessons
To honor the wise thinkers who came before us
To enjoy the pleasure that thinking deeply brings
context: Aristotle: 'we are inquiring not in order to know what virtue is, but in order to become good, since otherwise our inquiry would have been of no use.' You don't become honest by understanding honesty -- you become honest by doing honest things, the way a harpist learns by playing, not by knowing the theory. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.2 (Ross translation).

question: A boy wants to be brave but feels terror every time he should stand up to a bully, so he keeps quiet and tells himself he'll be braver once he understands courage better. Aristotle says he has it backwards. According to Aristotle, how does a person actually become brave?
answer: By doing brave acts over and over until courage becomes his settled character.
choices: By doing brave acts over and over until courage becomes his settled character.
By studying what courage is until he grasps its true definition.
By being born with a bold temperament that fear can never shake.
By waiting for one great danger that calls his hidden courage out.
context: Aristotle's habituation argument: we get virtues like crafts. 'Men become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts... brave by doing brave acts.' A virtue is a trained disposition (a hexis), not a fact you memorized. Nicomachean Ethics Bk II, ch.1 (1103a31-b2), Ross trans. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Aristotle's Ethics' section 4.

question: Most people, Aristotle observes, decide the good life just means piling up pleasure and enjoyment. He thinks they aim far too low, and gives the chase after pleasure a cutting label that names what kind of life it really is. What did Aristotle call the life of heaped-up pleasure?
answer: A life fit for cattle, suitable to beasts.
choices: A life fit for cattle, suitable to beasts.
A life unworthy of a free citizen.
A life chained to the opinions of the crowd.
A life of borrowed and fading joys.
context: Aristotle states hedonism as a serious, widely held rival before answering it: 'Most men... identify the good, or happiness, with pleasure,' and are 'quite slavish in their tastes, preferring a life suitable to beasts.' He sets pleasure-seeking up as the genuine competitor to flourishing. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.5 (1095b16-20), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: Aristotle describes a person who knows perfectly well that something is wrong, agrees it's wrong, and then gets dragged into doing it anyway by his own appetite. To capture this gap between knowing and doing, Aristotle compares such a person to a particular kind of city. What is that city like?
answer: A city with good laws on the books that it never bothers to enforce.
choices: A city with good laws on the books that it never bothers to enforce.
A city whose citizens keep the laws only while a magistrate is watching.
A city that enforces its laws harshly, but on all the wrong people.
A city that debates each law so endlessly it ends up passing none.
context: Aristotle's image for akrasia (weakness of will): the weak-willed person 'is like a city which passes all the right decrees and has good laws, but makes no use of them.' You have the law on the books; you just don't enforce it on yourself. So virtue isn't only knowing the good -- it's acting on it when desire pulls the other way. Nicomachean Ethics Bk VII, ch.1-3 (1145b-1152a), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: A girl has one wonderful afternoon -- sun, friends, a win -- and announces her life is now a happy, flourishing one. Aristotle answers that the good life is an activity stretched across a whole lifetime, and seals the point with a line about the seasons. How did Aristotle put it?
answer: One swallow does not make a summer, nor one day a happy life.
choices: One swallow does not make a summer, nor one day a happy life.
A single bright morning cannot promise a cloudless year.
One ripe fruit does not prove the whole tree is sound.
A calm hour at sea is no guarantee against the coming storm.
context: Aristotle's keystone line on flourishing (eudaimonia): 'For one swallow does not make a summer, nor does one day; and so too one day, or a short time, does not make a man blessed and happy.' The good life is an activity sustained over a complete life, not a pleasant moment you can have on a Tuesday -- the direct answer to the pleasure-seeking rival. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.7 (1098a18), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: A young soldier boasts that fear is a soldier's only enemy, so the man who feels none at all must be the bravest of them. Aristotle held that every virtue stands as a middle between two opposite vices. How would Aristotle answer the boast?
answer: Feeling no fear is one of the two vices itself, the deficiency that misses courage as surely as cowardice does.
choices: Feeling no fear is one of the two vices itself, the deficiency that misses courage as surely as cowardice does.
Feeling no fear is the success courage aims at, the full removal of the one thing that defeats a soldier.
Feeling no fear settles nothing about courage, since courage is judged by the deed and never by the feeling behind it.
Feeling no fear is simply a man's inborn nature, a thing neither to be praised as a virtue nor blamed as a vice.
context: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, with courage as the example: virtue sits between a too-much and a too-little. The coward fears too much and flees; the rash man fears too little and charges. Courage is the mark between them -- so feeling NO fear is not the height of courage but an overshoot, missing the target on the far side just as cowardice misses it on the near side. It is the amount the situation calls for, 'relative to us,' not a quantity to be minimized. Nicomachean Ethics Bk III (1115b24-1116a) + Bk II (1106a26-b28), Ross trans. SEP section 5.

question: Aristotle wants to find the good FOR a human being, so he reasons by analogy. A flute-player has a job, and a good flute-player does that job well; the eye, the hand, the foot each have work they do well. So, he asks, does the whole human being have some work that is peculiarly its own? What did Aristotle single out as the special work of a human being?
answer: Reasoning, which the good person does well over a lifetime.
choices: Reasoning, which the good person does well over a lifetime.
Growing and feeding, which keeps the body alive and thriving.
Sensing the world, which all the animals share in common.
Winning honor, which the best citizens pursue above all.
context: Aristotle's function (ergon) argument: 'just as for a flute-player... the good and the well is thought to reside in the function, so would it seem to be for man.' Plants merely grow, animals merely sense; what is peculiarly human is reason. So 'human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue.' The good flute-player plays well; the good human reasons well. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.7 (1097b25-1098a18), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: Aristotle weighs the life devoted to winning honor as a candidate for the good life, and rejects it. Why, then, did Aristotle judge that honor falls short and cannot be the highest good?
answer: It depends on the people who bestow it, not on the one who has it.
choices: It depends on the people who bestow it, not on the one who has it.
It corrupts the soul of anyone who comes to crave it.
It fades the instant a greater hero appears to outshine you.
It costs more to keep than the holder can ever truly afford.
context: Aristotle maps three lives -- pleasure, honor (the political life), and contemplation. He faults honor because 'it seems to depend on those who bestow honor rather than on him who receives it,' and a final good can't be so easily taken away. The test: is it self-sufficient and properly yours? Only the activity of your own excellent reason passes. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.5 (1095b14-1096a5), Ross trans. SEP section 3.

question: Two officers are equally brave and equally well trained, and both face the same hard choice: hold a crumbling line or fall back to save the men. One reads the moment exactly right and acts well; the other, just as well-meaning, blunders. Aristotle says one capacity separates them. Which capacity is it?
answer: The judgment to deliberate well about what to do in this very case.
choices: The judgment to deliberate well about what to do in this very case.
The settled habit of wanting and feeling the right things in the soul.
The grasp of universal truths that hold always and everywhere alike.
The quick wit for finding the means to whatever end one happens to please.
context: Aristotle's phronesis (practical wisdom): 'ethical virtue is fully developed only when it is combined with practical wisdom.' It can't be had by learning general rules -- no rulebook tells you how much fear courage needs against THIS enemy on THIS day. Two equally good-charactered, equally trained people can face the same fork and one lands rightly; the difference is the trained judgment that reads the unrepeatable particular. Nicomachean Ethics Bk VI (1144b14-17), Ross trans. SEP sections 9-10.

question: King Priam of Troy was prosperous, blessed, and powerful for most of his long life -- and then, in old age, watched his city burn and his sons cut down before he himself died wretchedly. Aristotle uses Priam to defend a hard claim about whether we should call any living person happy. What does the fall of Priam show, on Aristotle's view?
answer: A disaster at the end can unmake a life, so flourishing is judged over the whole of it.
choices: A disaster at the end can unmake a life, so flourishing is judged over the whole of it.
The gods envy great kings and topple them precisely when they stand highest.
No one is ever truly happy, since every life ends in loss and death.
A virtuous soul stays untouched, so even ruin cannot dim a good man's happiness.
context: Aristotle raises Solon's saying -- 'must we... see the end?' -- with Priam as his case: 'the most prosperous may fall into great misfortunes in old age, as is told of Priam in the Trojan Cycle; and one who has... ended wretchedly no one calls happy.' Because flourishing is the shape of a whole life, a late catastrophe can unmake it -- which is just why one good moment can't make it. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.9-10 (1100a), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: Aristotle sketches his 'great-souled' man -- the person who thinks himself worthy of great things and truly is, who gladly gives help but is ashamed to receive it. Then he describes, almost comically, how such a man physically carries himself. According to Aristotle, how does the great-souled man move and speak?
answer: With a slow step, a deep voice, and a level, unhurried way of speaking.
choices: With a slow step, a deep voice, and a level, unhurried way of speaking.
With a quick stride, a ready laugh, and a warm word for every passer-by.
With a stiff bearing, a cold stare, and a clipped command for his servants.
With a restless pace, a sharp tongue, and an eye always on the door.
context: Aristotle's character sketch of megalopsychia, greatness of soul: 'a slow step is thought proper to the proud man, a deep voice, and a level utterance; for the man who takes few things seriously is not likely to be hurried.' He calls this virtue 'a sort of crown of the virtues; for it makes them greater, and it is not found without them.' Nicomachean Ethics Bk IV, ch.3 (1123b-1125a), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: Aristotle has just argued that the very best activity of human reason is contemplation, the godlike activity. He then turns to ask how high a person should set his sights in a single mortal life. What does Aristotle exhort us to do?
answer: Strain every nerve to make ourselves immortal and live by the best thing in us.
choices: Strain every nerve to make ourselves immortal and live by the best thing in us.
Submit gladly to our mortal limits and find peace in an ordinary life.
Seize every pleasure the brief span allows, since death undoes us all.
Win the lasting fame that lets a great name outlive the body's death.
context: Aristotle's capstone on contemplation (theoria), the godlike activity: 'we must not follow those who advise us, being men, to think of human things... but must, so far as we can, make ourselves immortal, and strain every nerve to live in accordance with the best thing in us.' Against the respectable counsel to keep one's thoughts on mortal things, he charges us to aim at the highest thing in us. Nicomachean Ethics Bk X, ch.7-8 (1177b31-1178a8), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: Aristotle does not call pleasure bad, and he refuses to answer the pleasure-seeker with a sneer. Instead he offers a fair picture: pleasure is not the goal you chase but something that rides along with a fine activity done well, crowning it without being the point of it. To capture how pleasure 'completes the activity,' what image did Aristotle reach for?
answer: The bloom that rests on those in the flower of their age.
choices: The bloom that rests on those in the flower of their age.
The warmth that fills a room in the strength of its fire.
The fragrance that rises from a rose in the height of its season.
The shine that lies on a blade in the prime of its use.
context: Aristotle's mature, fair reply to hedonism: pleasure isn't the goal but it isn't bad. Test it -- add wisdom to a life of pure pleasure and it improves, so pleasure can't be the complete good. His positive view: pleasure 'completes the activity... as the bloom of youth does on those in the flower of their age.' Chase the good activity and the right pleasure rides along with it. Nicomachean Ethics Bk X, ch.2-4 (1172b23-35, 1174b31-33), Ross trans. SEP section 8.

question: Mara finds a fat wallet on the sidewalk, thick with cash and an ID card, and no one is watching. She wants to do the right thing, but she is tempted, and the people she could ask would each tell her something different. Her grandmother once gave her a trick for hard choices: when you are torn, ask one single question and follow wherever its answer leads. Which question is the one Mara's grandmother taught her to ask?
answer: ''What would a person of good character do here?''
choices: ''What would a person of good character do here?''
''What would most ordinary people do in my place?''
''Which choice would make me look best to others?''
''What did I once promise my parents I would do?''
context: This is the virtue move: decide by picturing an excellent person and doing as they would. It points at the PERSON acting, not at a rule or an outcome. As the IEP puts it, where the other approaches 'concern themselves with the right action, virtue ethics is concerned with the good life and what kinds of persons we should be.' The wrong choices are real but different measures -- what is NORMAL (most people), what wins APPLAUSE (looking good), or a personal RULE (a promise) -- none of which is the same as asking what a genuinely good person would do. Source: IEP, Virtue Ethics (iep.utm.edu/virtue/).

question: A man visits his friend in the hospital. As he sits down she smiles, glad he came -- until he tells her the truth: he came only because visiting a sick friend is his DUTY, the thing one is supposed to do. Her smile fades. To someone who measures goodness by a person's character, why did that honest little confession spoil the visit?
answer: A real friend comes because he cares about HER, not because a rule says so
choices: A real friend comes because he cares about HER, not because a rule says so
He should have kept his true reason hidden so the visit still felt warm
Visiting out of duty is fine, but saying it out loud was simply rude
Sick people need cheering up, and his gloomy mood only made her worse
context: The deed looks identical either way -- a man at a bedside -- but the virtue view cares about the motive behind it. A good friend shows up out of genuine care for the person, so 'I'm only here out of duty' guts the very thing that made the visit good. The SEP uses this case: the agent 'will rather lessen the impact of his visit on her if he tells her... that he is doing it because it is his duty.' The poet Schiller mocked the same gap -- doing good gladly, not through gritted teeth, is the mark of real virtue. Source: SEP, Virtue Ethics (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-virtue/).

question: Most people think courage has just one opposite -- cowardice, the failure to act when you are afraid. Aristotle said every virtue sits between TWO faults, not one. If cowardice -- fleeing every danger -- is one of courage's opposites, what is the OTHER fault courage steers between?
answer: Recklessness -- rushing at every danger with no fear to check him
choices: Recklessness -- rushing at every danger with no fear to check him
Cruelty -- taking plain pleasure in the pain a fight does to others
Stubbornness -- refusing to retreat even when the cause is plainly lost
Vanity -- craving the loud applause that daring deeds win from a crowd
context: This is Aristotle's 'golden mean': each virtue is a midpoint flanked by two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage sits between cowardice (too much fear, flees every danger) and recklessness (too little fear, charges every danger). The surprise for most people is that the daredevil is failing at courage just as the coward is. The wrong choices are all genuine vices, but none is the fault that sits opposite cowardice on the fear scale. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Bk II; Britannica, 'Golden mean'.

question: Aristotle asked how a person comes to be brave -- not as a fine idea, but in real life, in flesh and blood. He thought most people guess wrong about it, reaching for the answer that flatters them. His own answer was plain, almost humble, and easy to overlook. On his view, how does a person truly become brave?
answer: By doing brave things over and over until courage becomes his habit
choices: By doing brave things over and over until courage becomes his habit
By being born with a naturally fearless and bold temperament
By studying what courage is until he grasps it completely
By facing one truly great danger that transforms him all at once
context: Aristotle, verbatim: 'men become builders by building... so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.' Character is built by practice, like a craft -- which is why the Greek word for moral virtue, 'ethike,' is a slight variation on 'ethos,' meaning habit. Bravery is a muscle grown by acting bravely, not a gift you are simply born with, nor a fact you can learn by study alone. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Bk II.1 (1103a-b).

question: A merchant never lies to his customers, never short-changes them, never breaks a deal. But ask him WHY and he answers plainly: ''Honesty is just the best policy -- it's good for business, and the day it stops paying, so will I.'' To a thinker who treats a virtue as a deep, settled trait of character, why does this careful man still NOT count as an honest person?
answer: His fairness is just a strategy, so honesty's wholehearted commitment is missing
choices: His fairness is just a strategy, so honesty's wholehearted commitment is missing
He simply has not yet been honest for long enough to count as the real thing
He keeps to his bargains too strictly, leaving no room for mercy or kindness
He boasts about his honesty aloud instead of just quietly living it out
context: A virtue isn't a string of tidy acts -- it is a deep, wholehearted trait. The SEP makes exactly this point: 'an honest person cannot be identified simply as one who does not cheat. If such actions are done merely because the agent thinks that honesty is the best policy... they are not the actions of an honest person.' His deals merely happen to look honest; the moment lying paid better, he would lie -- so the settled character is missing. The other diagnoses are real-sounding but wrong: it is not a matter of time served, of being too strict, or of talking too much. Source: SEP, Virtue Ethics (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-virtue/).

question: Your friend runs into your house and hides, terrified. A moment later a killer pounds on the door and demands to know where she went. Three thinkers argue over what to do. One insists lying is always forbidden -- you must tell the truth even now. Another tallies a lie against a life and says lie to save her. The third asks what a person who is at once deeply honest AND deeply compassionate would do in this exact scene. Where does that third thinker most likely land?
answer: Lie to the killer, since a good person's honesty was never a duty to doom the innocent
choices: Lie to the killer, since a good person's honesty was never a duty to doom the innocent
Tell the killer the truth, because a truly honest person speaks no falsehood ever
Stay silent and refuse to answer, keeping his own hands clean of any lie at all
Flip a coin, since no rule could ever settle so impossible a clash of two duties
context: This is the classic case where the three moves split. The rule-move (Kant's famous 'murderer at the door') says never lie -- tell the truth even here. The results-move weighs the lie against the life and lies to protect her. The virtue-move asks what a person who is BOTH honest AND compassionate and courageous would do, and most virtue ethicists land on the protective lie: honesty is a trait of good character, not a suicide pact. Even virtue ethics admits the real pull -- 'honesty points to telling the hurtful truth, kindness and compassion to remaining silent or even lying.' A competent thinker could defend the rigid-truth view; this asks only where the character-first reasoning points. Source: SEP, Virtue Ethics; Varden, 'Kant and Lying to the Murderer at the Door'.

question: Seneca taught that a wise person would rather be good and in chains than wicked and living in a palace. His reason: there is one thing fortune can never steal from you, no matter how much else it takes. What did he mean?
answer: Your own good character is the one possession nobody can take from you
choices: Your own good character is the one possession nobody can take from you
A clear conscience will always win back the riches you have lost
The gods reward chained prisoners who refuse to complain about pain
A wicked ruler is secretly more miserable than any of his prisoners
context: This is the emotional hook of Stoic ethics. Seneca wrote that the only possession the wise person truly has is virtue, 'and of this they can never be robbed; of all else they have merely the use on loan.' Health, money, and status are borrowed; your character is the one thing fully your own. Source: Seneca, On the Supreme Good (Letters), corroborated by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Seneca, https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/seneca/

question: The Roman general Regulus was captured by Carthage and sent home on his sworn word, told to argue for a prisoner swap and then return. Standing before the Roman Senate, what did Regulus actually do?
answer: He urged the Senate to refuse the swap, then returned to Carthage to die
choices: He urged the Senate to refuse the swap, then returned to Carthage to die
He begged the Senate to ransom him at any price they could afford
He revealed Carthage's battle plans and was made a Roman consul
He broke his oath, stayed in Rome, and lived out his days in peace
context: Marcus Atilius Regulus became the Stoics' favorite real-life proof that virtue is the only good. Sent to argue FOR the prisoner exchange, he argued AGAINST it as bad for Rome, then kept his oath and went back to Carthage to be tortured to death — choosing honor over his own life and freedom. Later Roman tradition embellished the death (eyelids cut off, sealed in a spiked barrel); historians treat those details as legend, but the choice to return is the point. Source: Cicero, De Officiis 3.99-109, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Officiis

question: A young Stoic asks her teacher: if only good character makes a life truly good, should she just stop caring whether she is healthy or sick, rich or poor? Her teacher says no — that misunderstands the teaching. How does he correct her?
answer: Health and wealth are worth pursuing, but they never make a life good or bad
choices: Health and wealth are worth pursuing, but they never make a life good or bad
Health and wealth are illusions, so a wise person ignores them completely
Health and wealth are evils that a truly good person learns to reject
Health and wealth matter most, and good character is a bonus on top
context: The crucial nuance: the Stoics did NOT say 'care about nothing.' They called health, wealth, and reputation 'indifferents' (Greek adiaphora), and they RANKED them. Life, health, beauty, strength, and good repute are 'preferred' indifferents — according to nature, worth pursuing — while disease, pain, and poverty are 'dispreferred.' A Stoic still chases health; it just doesn't decide whether the life is GOOD. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Stoicism (Diogenes Laertius 58A), https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/stoicism/

question: The Stoic Antipater compared the good life to an archer aiming at a distant target. A sudden gust can carry even a perfect shot wide of the mark. So Antipater asked: should we measure the archer by the arrow or by the man? Where did he locate the archer's real success?
answer: In how well he aimed and released, whether or not the arrow lands
choices: In how well he aimed and released, whether or not the arrow lands
In whether the arrow finally strikes the center of the mark
In picking a target so near that no gust could ever reach it
In waiting to loose the arrow until the air is perfectly still
context: Antipater's archer is a picture of the whole Stoic system. 'One's ultimate aim is to do all in one's power to shoot straight.' Whether the arrow actually hits is, in Stoic terms, 'to be selected but not sought' — a preferred outcome, but not what your happiness rests on. You control your aim and release (your virtue); you do not control the wind (fortune). Source: John Sellars, 'Stoicism and the Art of Archery,' Modern Stoicism (Cicero attributing the image to Antipater via Cato), https://modernstoicism.com/stoicism-and-the-art-of-archery/

question: Cicero argued that wealth, health, and pleasure cannot be what makes a person good. A young listener objects: surely there is SOME reason those things fall short of being the real good. Which reason did Cicero actually give?
answer: Even a thoroughly wicked man can possess all of them in full
choices: Even a thoroughly wicked man can possess all of them in full
They always slip away in time, while good character lasts for life
Good men deserve them, and wicked men only seem to enjoy them
They corrupt whoever holds them, whether that person is good or wicked
context: This is the argument behind the first of Cicero's six 'Stoic paradoxes' (Paradoxa Stoicorum, 46 BC): only the morally good is good. The logic is clean — since a totally evil person can have wealth, health, and pleasure to the brim, those things can't be what makes a life or a person good. Only something a wicked man cannot have while staying wicked qualifies as the real good: virtue. (The other answers are real rival lines people have offered — externals are impermanent, the good deserve them, externals corrupt — but Cicero's own move was the possession-by-the-wicked point.) Source: Wikipedia, Paradoxa Stoicorum (summary of paradox 1), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradoxa_Stoicorum

question: Picture a genuinely good man stretched on the torturer's rack. Aristotle's school and the Stoics clashed over one question about him: can a person in that condition still be living a happy life? The Stoics gave an answer that scandalized their rivals. What was the Stoic claim?
answer: His good character by itself is enough to make him fully happy there
choices: His good character by itself is enough to make him fully happy there
His happiness merely pauses until the torture has run its course
His happiness shrinks in proportion to how much pain he must endure
His happiness holds only while the gods stay favorably disposed to him
context: This is the sharpest dividing line in ancient ethics. Aristotle's school, the Peripatetics, held that virtue is necessary for happiness but NOT sufficient — you also need a decent share of external goods. The Stoics said virtue alone is enough; fortune adds nothing real. Cicero pushed it to the limit (De Finibus 3.42): even mutilated and searing with pain on the rack, the virtuous person is 'maximally happy.' Chrysippus said the sage would stay happy even inside the bull of Phalaris, the bronze furnace the tyrant used to roast victims alive. A defensible, demanding claim — and one Aristotle's heirs rejected. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Stoic Ethics, https://iep.utm.edu/stoiceth/; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Stoicism (Cicero, De Finibus 3.42), https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/stoicism/

question: A New York art show in 1917 advertised a radical promise: no jury, no rejections — pay the fee and your work is shown. Marcel Duchamp, who sat on the show's own board, decided to test that promise: he bought a plain factory-made porcelain urinal, laid it on its back, signed it 'R. Mutt 1917,' and titled it 'Fountain.' How did the board respond to a piece its own no-rejection rule said it had to hang?
answer: They hid it from view and refused to display it
choices: They hid it from view and refused to display it
They hung it in the place of honor at the entrance
They displayed it but printed an apology beside it
They asked Duchamp to repaint it before showing it
context: The board hid 'Fountain' and refused to show it despite its own 'no rejections' rule; Duchamp, on the board himself, resigned in protest. The submission was signed 'R. Mutt' so the committee did not know it was his. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fountain (Duchamp)'; Philadelphia Museum of Art press release, 'Marcel Duchamp and the Fountain Scandal'.

question: Marcel Duchamp once bolted a bicycle wheel onto a kitchen stool, and another time bought a snow shovel and simply hung it up with a title — declaring each one his own art, though he had shaped none of it with his hands. He coined a single word for these everyday objects he lifted into the world of art. What did he call them?
answer: Readymades
choices: Readymades
Found art
Collage
Assemblage
context: Duchamp coined 'readymade' for ordinary objects he chose and titled rather than crafted: the 1913 'Bicycle Wheel' on a stool, a 1914 'Bottle Rack,' and a 1915 snow shovel titled 'In Advance of the Broken Arm.' The distractors are real art terms a kid could confuse it with — found art, collage, and assemblage all use everyday or found objects, but 'readymade' is Duchamp's own word for an unaltered object promoted to art by his choice alone. Source: Tate, 'Readymade'; MoMA, 'Marcel Duchamp and the Readymade'.

question: Two years after the urinal, Marcel Duchamp pulled the same stunt on the most worshipped painting in France. He took a cheap postcard of the Mona Lisa and, with a few pencil strokes, altered her famous face before giving the result a rude title. What did he add to her?
answer: A moustache and a goatee
choices: A moustache and a goatee
A blindfold and a tear
A halo and a crown
A scar and an eyepatch
context: The 1919 piece is titled 'L.H.O.O.Q.' — read aloud letter by letter in French the title sounds like a crude pun. Defacing France's most sacred painting was the same move as the urinal: treating a worshipped object as raw material to provoke the art establishment. Source: Wikipedia, 'L.H.O.O.Q.'; Norton Simon Museum; MoMA.

question: The original 1917 'Fountain' does not exist anymore. After the board hid the urinal away, it was soon lost or thrown out as trash, and every 'Fountain' standing in a museum today is a later replica. Only one record of the real object survives, made by Alfred Stieglitz at his New York gallery. What is it?
answer: A single black-and-white photograph
choices: A single black-and-white photograph
A wax mold cast from the original urinal
A careful pencil drawing of the piece
A signed written description of it
context: Stieglitz photographed the urinal on a pedestal in front of a Marsden Hartley painting at his gallery '291.' The original was then lost or discarded; that one photo is the only record of the actual 1917 object, and every museum 'Fountain' is a later replica. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fountain (Duchamp)'; Philadelphia Museum of Art press release.

question: In a December 2004 poll, five hundred British art experts voted 'Fountain' — Marcel Duchamp's discarded factory urinal — the single most influential artwork of the entire twentieth century. It even outranked Andy Warhol's silkscreened 'Marilyn.' But the painting it pushed into second place, the runner-up a thrown-out urinal beat for the top spot, was a far more famous canvas. Which masterpiece did it edge out?
answer: Pablo Picasso's 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon'
choices: Pablo Picasso's 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon'
Salvador Dali's 'The Persistence of Memory'
Henri Matisse's 'The Dance'
Jackson Pollock's 'Autumn Rhythm'
context: In the December 2004 poll (run around the Turner Prize), 500 British art-world professionals voted 'Fountain' the most influential artwork of the twentieth century, beating Picasso's 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' and Warhol's 'Marilyn Diptych.' A discarded urinal outranked the century's most famous paintings. Source: Artforum news; Salon.com, 'The most influential piece of modern art' (Dec 2004); Wikipedia, 'Fountain (Duchamp)'.

question: A 'Fountain' replica in a Paris museum has been attacked twice by the same man, the performance artist Pierre Pinoncelli — once he urinated into it, and in 2006 he chipped it with a hammer. Hauled before a Paris court that fined him 214,000 euros, he insisted his hammer-blow had a respectable artistic meaning. How did he explain it to the judge?
answer: A wink at Dadaism Duchamp would have loved
choices: A wink at Dadaism Duchamp would have loved
A blow struck for the museum's underpaid guards
A holy man's stand against an unclean idol
A stunt to force the lost urinal to be hunted down
context: Pinoncelli urinated into and struck the piece in Nimes in 1993, then chipped it with a hammer at the Pompidou Centre on 4 January 2006. He told the court it was 'a wink at Dadaism' that Duchamp himself would have loved; a Paris court fined him 214,000 euros with a three-month suspended sentence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pierre Pinoncelli'; CBC News; NYT (Alan Riding, 7 Jan 2006).

question: When the board rejected the urinal, Marcel Duchamp and his friends fought back in their magazine with an unsigned editorial. It brushed aside the obvious complaint — that Duchamp had not built the urinal with his own hands — by insisting that building it was never the point. According to that editorial, what was the real creative act?
answer: That he chose it
choices: That he chose it
That he paid for it
That he signed it
That he hid it
context: The editorial 'The Richard Mutt Case' in The Blind Man no. 2 (May 1917) carries the founding sentence of conceptual art: 'Whether Mr. Mutt with his own hands made the fountain or not has no importance. He CHOSE it.' The choosing, not the making, was the art. Source: The Blind Man no. 2 (May 1917); University of Iowa International Dada Archive; Tate.

question: At the 1917 show the directors argued bitterly over whether the urinal could really be let in. One director pressed the hard case: by their own no-jury rule, would they then be forced to hang a pile of horse manure if an artist submitted it? Walter Arensberg gave a blunt answer. What did he say?
answer: Yes — by their own rules, they would
choices: Yes — by their own rules, they would
No — manure is filth, not an object
Yes, but only if it were arranged artfully
No — only factory goods could ever qualify
context: Among roughly 2,500 works by about 1,200 artists, the directors fought over the urinal; asked whether their no-jury rule would force them to hang horse manure too, Walter Arensberg answered that yes, it would. President William Glackens dismissed the piece as 'suppressed adolescence,' and the conservatives voted it down. Source: Artforum, 'The Big Show: The First Exhibition of the Society of Independent Artists, Part I'.

question: The magazine editorial defending 'Fountain' ended on a barb aimed straight at America's idea of itself. It granted that America had produced real works of art after all — then named two unglamorous, everyday things as that art. Which two things did it crown as America's only art?
answer: Her plumbing and her bridges
choices: Her plumbing and her bridges
Her skyscrapers and her railroads
Her cathedrals and her statues
Her warships and her factories
context: 'The Richard Mutt Case' closed: 'The only works of art America has given are her plumbing and her bridges.' The joke cuts both ways — calling a urinal art, and calling American plumbing the country's real art. Source: The Blind Man no. 2 (May 1917), closing line.

question: A philosopher asked a sharp question: a urinal in a gallery is art, but the very same urinal in a hardware store is not — so what makes the difference, when the two objects are identical? He concluded that whatever makes one of them art is not a property you could ever point to in the object itself. Where did he say it lives instead?
answer: In the surrounding theory and history of art
choices: In the surrounding theory and history of art
In the years of training the artist put in
In the steep price a collector would pay
In the private intention locked in the maker
context: Arthur Danto, in 'The Artworld' (1964), argued that seeing something as art 'requires something the eye cannot descry — an atmosphere of artistic theory, a knowledge of the history of art.' On this view the theory, not the thing, makes it art. The distractors name rival theories of art (skill, market value, the artist's expression). Source: Arthur Danto, 'The Artworld,' Journal of Philosophy (1964); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Definition of Art'.

question: When the urinal forced the question 'what is art?', one thinker reached for an analogy. Think of the word 'game,' he said: board games, ball games, and solitaire need not share any one feature — just a web of overlapping likenesses. Art, he claimed, is a word like that. So when a shocking new case like the urinal turns up, what does HE conclude we are really doing when we call it art?
answer: Deciding whether to stretch the word to cover it
choices: Deciding whether to stretch the word to cover it
Spotting the hidden essence it shares with all art
Placing it inside art's long history and theory
Accepting that an art institution has crowned it art
context: Following Wittgenstein, Morris Weitz argued in 'The Role of Theory in Aesthetics' (1956) that art is an 'open concept' with no shared essence, only overlapping 'family resemblances' like games. Each new case forces us to decide whether to extend the word 'art,' not to discover a hidden rule. The distractors are rival answers a different thinker would give — that we detect a hidden essence (the essentialist view Weitz rejects), that we place it inside art's history and theory (Danto), or that an art-world institution has conferred the status (Dickie). Source: Morris Weitz (1956); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Definition of Art'.

question: A painter hunts for a beautiful subject. Marcel Duchamp said he picked his readymade objects in the exact opposite spirit. He even warned that you must not let yourself look too long: give the object two weeks, he said, and its look would start to work on you — and that would ruin everything. So how did Duchamp say a readymade had to be chosen?
answer: With no taste reaction at all
choices: With no taste reaction at all
With an eye for its beauty
With a craving to shock people
With an eye to its usefulness
context: Duchamp said the choice rested on 'a reaction of visual indifference, with at the same time a total absence of good or bad taste' — pick before any liking or hating sets in. He warned you 'had to beware of its look': wait fifteen days and you'd start to like or hate it. It is the opposite of how a painter chooses a beautiful subject, and the opposite of merely seeking shock. Source: Marcel Duchamp, 'Apropos of Readymades,' Art of Assemblage symposium, MoMA, 19 October 1961.

question: Will flips a coin, and before it lands he announces with total confidence that it will come up tails -- on no particular hunch, just a feeling. It lands tails. He believed it, and he turned out right. Did Will KNOW the coin would land tails?
answer: No -- he had no real reason, so being right was just luck, not knowing.
choices: No -- he had no real reason, so being right was just luck, not knowing.
Yes -- he believed it and it came true, which is all that knowing takes.
Yes -- calling a coin flip correctly is a clear case of knowing.
No -- he should have studied the coin more closely before calling it.
context: This is the Stanford Encyclopedia's own coin-flip scene. A belief can be true and sincerely held yet still fail to be knowledge: 'such a lucky guess, intuitively, can't count as knowledge.' The missing ingredient is justification -- a good reason. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Analysis of Knowledge' (coin-flip example), https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/knowledge-analysis/

question: Maya's textbook says the heart has four chambers, and it is correct -- but Maya skimmed straight past that line, never took it in, and if you asked her she'd shrug and say she has no idea. The true fact sat right there on the page. Can Maya be said to KNOW the heart has four chambers?
answer: No -- you can't know something you don't even believe, however true it is.
choices: No -- you can't know something you don't even believe, however true it is.
Yes -- the fact was printed in her own book, so the knowledge was hers.
Yes -- a true statement counts as known once it is written down somewhere.
No -- a school textbook isn't a reliable enough source to ground knowing.
context: This is the quietest of the three ingredients: belief. 'Knowledge is a kind of belief. If one has no beliefs about a particular matter, one cannot have knowledge about it.' A truth you have never actually taken in is not yet something you know. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemology' (belief condition), https://iep.utm.edu/epistemo/

question: Before Copernicus, every careful astronomer studied the night sky, reasoned from the best evidence they had, and concluded the Sun goes around the Earth. They were sincere and rigorous -- and wrong. However well they argued for it, could those astronomers be said to have KNOWN the Sun circles the Earth?
answer: No -- a belief that is false can never be knowledge, however good the reasons for it.
choices: No -- a belief that is false can never be knowledge, however good the reasons for it.
Yes -- they reasoned carefully from real evidence, and that is what knowing means.
Yes -- it counted as knowledge back then and only stopped being so later on.
No -- they ought to have gathered far more evidence before concluding it.
context: This is the truth condition, and it is 'factive': 'If a belief is not true, it cannot constitute knowledge.' You can reason carefully from real evidence and still be wrong (human fallibility), and a well-justified false belief never counts as knowing. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemology' (truth/factivity condition), https://iep.utm.edu/epistemo/

question: Two students both write that the library closes at 8. Dev checked the posted hours this morning; Ben just guessed a number that happened to be right. Both wrote the truth. What does Dev have that Ben doesn't -- the thing that makes Dev's belief actual knowledge?
answer: A good reason for it -- he based it on evidence, not on a hunch.
choices: A good reason for it -- he based it on evidence, not on a hunch.
A stronger feeling of certainty that his answer was the right one.
More years of schooling standing behind the answer he gave.
A sharper memory for numbers than Ben happened to have.
context: This is justification, the ingredient doing the heavy lifting. A belief is justified when it is 'based on evidence and reasoning rather than on luck or misinformation.' Dev and Ben hold the same true belief, but only Dev came by it 'in the right way' -- which is exactly what separates knowing from a lucky guess. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemology' (justification condition), https://iep.utm.edu/epistemo/

question: Bertrand Russell pictured a man who glances at a clock to learn the time. The clock looks reliable but in fact stopped exactly twelve hours ago -- and the man happens to look at the one moment in the day when its frozen hands show the correct time. He now believes the right time. Russell says he still does NOT know it. Why not?
answer: His reason was no good -- a stopped clock doesn't track the time, so being right was luck.
choices: His reason was no good -- a stopped clock doesn't track the time, so being right was luck.
His glance was too quick -- a fast look at a clock can never really count as knowing.
Knowing the time always takes more than one clock to properly confirm it.
A clock shows only clock-time, which is never quite the same as the real time.
context: The most famous 'right by accident' picture. The man's belief is true and he holds it, yet 'he cannot be said to have knowledge' -- he came by the truth 'by luck' rather than 'as the result of honest toil,' because a stopped clock is no real link to the time. Source: Bertrand Russell, 'Human Knowledge: Its Scope and Limits' (1948); summary at The Philosphere, https://philosphere.blog/2018/03/28/russell-and-the-stopped-clock/

question: Socrates imagines two guides leading you to the city of Larissa. One has walked the road many times and KNOWS it. The other has never set foot on it but happens to hold a correct opinion about which way to go. As guides for actually getting you there, how do the two compare?
answer: They get you there equally well -- a right opinion guides the trip as surely as knowledge.
choices: They get you there equally well -- a right opinion guides the trip as surely as knowledge.
Only the guide who truly knows the road gets you there; the other is bound to stray off.
The guide with mere opinion actually gets you there quicker by trusting his own gut.
Neither one can be trusted, since real guidance demands having mapped the whole route.
context: Plato's road-to-Larissa puzzle: 'a person who had a right opinion about the way, but had never been and did not know, might be a good guide also.' Since a true opinion guides action just as well as knowledge, it raises the real question -- why is knowledge worth more? Source: Plato, Meno 97 (Jowett translation), http://classics.mit.edu/Plato/meno.html

question: Socrates compares a true opinion to a statue made by the legendary craftsman Daedalus -- statues so lifelike they would walk away on their own unless tied down. A true opinion, he says, is just as ready to slip out of the mind. What, in his picture, finally fastens it in place and turns it into lasting knowledge?
answer: Working out the reason why it is true, which ties it down so it stays.
choices: Working out the reason why it is true, which ties it down so it stays.
Repeating it over and over until it is burned into memory for good.
Hearing it confirmed by someone wiser who has already learned it.
Writing it down carefully so the mind can never misplace it again.
context: Plato's answer to the Larissa puzzle (Meno 97-98), told through the legend of Daedalus's walking statues. True opinions 'run away out of the human soul, and do not remain long... until they are fastened by the tie of the cause.' Tie a true opinion down by working out WHY it is true and it becomes stable knowledge -- which is why the reason makes knowledge prized above mere correct opinion. (Daedalus's self-walking statues are legend.) Source: Plato, Meno 97-98 (Jowett translation), http://classics.mit.edu/Plato/meno.html

question: Friedrich Nietzsche is instantly recognizable in old photographs for one feature: a giant bushy mustache drooping right over his mouth. He even made a joke about how rarely he had to groom it, because it grew back so slowly. What did Nietzsche claim about his mustache?
answer: He could only shave it once a week
choices: He could only shave it once a week
He had never once trimmed it
He waxed it fresh every morning
He dyed it a different color each day
context: In every surviving photo of the adult Nietzsche, the same enormous 'walrus' mustache droops over his mouth above clean-shaven cheeks and chin. He reportedly joked that it took so long to grow back he could only shave once a week. Source: Nietzsche's Body (nietzschesbody.com/mustache) and The History of Hair.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche was born in 1844, the son of a village pastor. When Friedrich was not yet five, his father died of a brain ailment, and a baby brother died soon after. Friedrich grew up the only boy in a house full of women. Which women raised him?
answer: His mother, sister, grandmother, and aunts
choices: His mother, sister, grandmother, and aunts
His grandmother, two aunts, and a governess
His stepmother, two cousins, and a nanny
His mother, an aunt, a cousin, and a nun
context: Nietzsche was born October 15, 1844 in the tiny Prussian village of Rocken, son of the Lutheran pastor Karl Ludwig Nietzsche. When his father died in July 1849 of a brain ailment (and a baby brother died soon after), Friedrich was left the only male in a house of women: his mother, his sister Elisabeth, his grandmother, and his aunts. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nietzsche's Life and Works; IEP: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: On a January morning in 1889, in the Italian city of Turin, Friedrich Nietzsche saw a cab driver in the square whipping a stubborn horse that would not move. According to the famous story, Nietzsche did something startling before he collapsed and lost his sanity for good. What did he reportedly do?
answer: Threw his arms around the horse's neck, sobbing
choices: Threw his arms around the horse's neck, sobbing
Bought the horse from the driver to set it free
Calmly sat and sketched the whole scene in ink
Challenged the cab driver to a fight then and there
context: On the morning of January 3, 1889, in the Piazza Carlo Alberto in Turin, Nietzsche reportedly ran to a horse being flogged, threw his arms around its neck sobbing to protect it, and collapsed. He never recovered his sanity. The horse detail is third-hand and may be embellished, but the Turin breakdown of Jan 3, 1889 is firmly documented. Source: IEP: Friedrich Nietzsche; Los Angeles Review of Books: 'Nietzsche's Horse'.  (Legend.)

question: In 1869 the University of Basel gave Friedrich Nietzsche a full professor's chair in classical philology before he had even finished his doctoral dissertation. His old teacher Ritschl said he 'will simply be able to do anything he wants to do.' What made this appointment so astonishing?
answer: He was the youngest person ever to hold that chair
choices: He was the youngest person ever to hold that chair
He was offered the chair without any interview
He had not yet published a single book
He was paid more than any other professor there
context: Nietzsche became a full professor of classical philology at Basel in 1869 at age 24, the youngest person ever appointed to that chair, and was given the post before finishing his doctoral dissertation. His teacher Ritschl said he 'will simply be able to do anything he wants to do.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: By 1879 Friedrich Nietzsche was so tormented by blinding migraines, vomiting, and failing eyesight that at age 34 he gave up his Basel professorship and lived on a small pension. Yet what happened to him in the years after he stopped teaching surprised everyone. What was it?
answer: Free of teaching, he wrote more than ever before
choices: Free of teaching, he wrote more than ever before
His health recovered almost as soon as he rested
He took a wealthy widow as a patron and married
He begged the university to take him back at once
context: Tormented by migraines, vomiting, and failing eyesight, Nietzsche resigned his Basel chair in 1879 at age 34 and lived on a modest pension. Paradoxically, freedom from teaching set off his most prolific writing. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche and Nietzsche's Life and Works.

question: After he left his professorship, Friedrich Nietzsche had no settled home. He drifted through cheap boarding houses, spending summers high in the Swiss Alps and winters by the Mediterranean. Why did this sick, lonely man keep moving with the seasons like this?
answer: He was chasing climates that might ease his pain
choices: He was chasing climates that might ease his pain
He was fleeing creditors he owed money
He was on a long lecture tour of Europe
He was hunting for a lost family fortune
context: After Basel, Nietzsche became a homeless wanderer, moving with the seasons through cheap boarding houses: summers in the Swiss Alps at Sils-Maria, winters on the Mediterranean in Genoa, Nice, Rapallo, or Turin, chasing climates that might ease his pain and give him solitude to write. Source: IEP: Friedrich Nietzsche; SEP: Nietzsche's Life and Works.

question: In August 1881, while walking beside Lake Silvaplana in the Swiss Alps, Friedrich Nietzsche was struck by one of his most famous ideas. He stopped beside a great pyramid-shaped rock and scribbled a few words marking the exact spot. What did that note say?
answer: '6,000 feet beyond man and time!'
choices: '6,000 feet beyond man and time!'
'Here the long thought first seized me.'
'On this stone the gods spoke to me.'
'Let no living soul disturb this place.'
context: The idea of eternal recurrence struck Nietzsche in August 1881 while walking by Lake Silvaplana near Sils-Maria; he stopped beside a huge pyramidal rock near Surlei and scribbled '6,000 feet beyond man and time!' Source: Aeon: 'The mysticism of Nietzsche's doctrine of the eternal return'; Nietzsche's Ecce Homo.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche wrote his strange, poetic masterpiece 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra' not slowly but in sudden explosions of work. In early 1883, staying in the town of Rapallo, he composed the entire first part in one furious stretch. How long did that first part take him?
answer: Just ten days
choices: Just ten days
A single afternoon
Almost seven years
Exactly one month
context: Nietzsche wrote each part of 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra' in furious ten-day bursts; he composed Part One in just ten days while staying in Rapallo in early 1883. Source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Wikipedia); Nietzsche's Ecce Homo.

question: The book 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra' would one day sell in the millions, but in Friedrich Nietzsche's own lifetime almost no one read it. He had to pay out of his own pocket just to get it printed. How many copies of its fourth part were ever printed while he lived?
answer: Only about forty
choices: Only about forty
Only about a dozen
Only about a hundred
Only about four hundred
context: Almost nobody read Nietzsche in his lifetime. He paid out of his own pocket to print 'Thus Spoke Zarathustra'; of Part Four only about forty copies were ever printed, which he gave to a handful of friends. The book that later sold millions was virtually unknown while he lived. Source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Wikipedia); Britannica: Thus Spake Zarathustra.

question: In 1882 Friedrich Nietzsche fell for a brilliant young woman named Lou Salome and proposed marriage to her twice that spring; she refused both times. That same year the three of them staged a now-famous photograph in Lucerne. How were Nietzsche and his friend posed in that picture?
answer: Harnessed to a cart while Salome held a whip
choices: Harnessed to a cart while Salome held a whip
Kneeling in prayer before a stone altar
Dueling each other with wooden swords
Asleep under a tree by a mountain lake
context: In 1882 Nietzsche staged a famous photo in Lucerne: he and his friend Paul Ree harnessed to a small cart while the brilliant young Lou Salome sat on it brandishing a whip (decorated with lilac sprigs). He proposed to her twice that spring; she turned him down both times. Source: Darwinian Conservatism: 'Nietzsche Under Lou Salome's Whip'; NECSUS: 'When Lulu met the Centaur'.

question: In the days right after his collapse in Turin, Friedrich Nietzsche mailed a flurry of deranged letters to old friends like the historian Jacob Burckhardt, full of wild boasts about who he believed he had become. Most chilling were the two names he signed at the bottom. How did Nietzsche sign these final letters?
answer: As 'Dionysus' and as 'The Crucified'
