choices: As 'Dionysus' and as 'The Crucified'
As 'The Kaiser' and as 'God Himself'
As 'Apollo' and as 'The Redeemer'
As 'Napoleon' and as 'King of Europe'
context: In the days after his collapse, Nietzsche mailed deranged 'madness letters' (Wahnbriefe), signing them 'Dionysus' or 'The Crucified.' To Jacob Burckhardt he wrote, 'I have had Caiaphas put in fetters; last year I was crucified by the German doctors in a very drawn-out manner.' Source: Friedrich Nietzsche (Wikipedia); fnietzsche.com: Mental breakdown and death 1889-1900.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche's father had died young of what doctors called a 'softening of the brain.' Through his life Friedrich carried a private dread that he had inherited the same doom. How did that fear turn out?
answer: It came true when his own mind finally collapsed
choices: It came true when his own mind finally collapsed
It proved groundless; he stayed sharp into old age
He escaped it but died young in a mountain accident
He outlived the fear and made his peace with it
context: Nietzsche's father died young of a 'softening of the brain,' and Friedrich lived in dread that he had inherited the same doom, a fear that proved horribly prophetic when his own mind gave way at 44. Source: pages.hmc.edu: 'Nietzsche's Life in Outline'; Carl Ludwig Nietzsche (Wikipedia).

question: In his last sane book, an autobiography from 1888, Friedrich Nietzsche gave his chapters titles like 'Why I Am So Wise' and 'Why I Write Such Good Books.' In it he made a famous prediction about how the world would one day react to him. How did Nietzsche put it?
answer: 'I am no man, I am dynamite.'
choices: 'I am no man, I am dynamite.'
'My name will outlast every king and empire.'
'They will raise me statues in every city.'
'I shall die quietly, soon forgotten by all.'
context: In his last sane book, the defiantly titled autobiography 'Ecce Homo' (1888), with chapters like 'Why I Am So Wise' and 'Why I Write Such Good Books,' Nietzsche predicted his own explosive legacy: 'I am no man, I am dynamite.' Source: Ecce Homo (Wikipedia); Wikiquote: Ecce Homo.

question: After Friedrich Nietzsche went mad, his sister Elisabeth took control of his papers and ran an archive in his name. She stitched his scattered notes into a book called 'The Will to Power' and bent his ideas to serve her own politics. What did her meddling ultimately do to her brother's name?
answer: It tied his name to the Nazis he would have despised
choices: It tied his name to the Nazis he would have despised
It cast him as a gentle prophet of universal peace
It made him the darling of the German church
It got his books dismissed as a madman's ravings
context: Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche seized his manuscripts, ran the Nietzsche-Archiv from Weimar, and stitched his notes into 'The Will to Power,' bending the meaning toward her own anti-Semitic, German-nationalist views. She later courted Mussolini and Hitler, helping fasten her brother's name to the Nazis he would have despised. Source: Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche (Britannica); TIME: 'Her Brother's Keeper'.

question: The Laws of Athens confront Socrates in his prison cell. They claim that any citizen who, once grown and having seen how the city runs, still chooses to keep living there has by that very choice committed himself to something. According to the Laws, what had Socrates committed himself to by never leaving Athens?
answer: Obeying whatever the city lawfully commands him
choices: Obeying whatever the city lawfully commands him
Paying back the taxes owed for his years there
Keeping the vow of silence sworn to the elders
Teaching philosophy only inside the city walls
context: In Plato's Crito, the personified Laws of Athens tell Socrates that a citizen who, once grown and having seen the ways of the city, chooses to stay has entered into an implied contract to obey them. This is the 2,400-year-old root of the love-it-or-leave-it argument, and the very move Hume would later attack. (Plato, Crito, Jowett trans., gutenberg.org/files/1657)

question: David Hume mocked the idea that a person who stays in a country has thereby freely agreed to obey its rulers. He likened that person to a man who was carried aboard a ship while fast asleep, and who now cannot escape the captain except by jumping overboard far out at sea. What point was Hume making with this picture?
answer: No real choice is free when the only way out is to perish
choices: No real choice is free when the only way out is to perish
A sleeping man can never be held to any bargain at all
A ship captain wields more rightful power than a king
People who stay home have simply never dared to leave
context: David Hume, 'Of the Original Contract' (1748): we may as well say a man consents to the captain by staying aboard a ship he was carried onto asleep, though he must leap into the ocean and perish the moment he leaves. Staying when leaving means death is no free choice, the most famous demolition of tacit consent. (davidhume.org/texts/empl2/oc, OC 24)

question: John Locke drew a line between two ways of agreeing to a government. One is express consent: a man swears an oath and becomes a full member. The other is tacit consent: a man merely uses the country, even just walking its public roads, and is thereby silently bound to obey. A road-using stranger, bound only by this second, quieter kind of duty, one day packs up and crosses the border for good. What did Locke say became of his duty to obey?
answer: The duty ended the moment he stopped using the country
choices: The duty ended the moment he stopped using the country
The duty passed down unbroken to his own children back home
The duty hardened into a debt he could never fully repay
The duty transferred at once to whatever land he entered next
context: John Locke, Second Treatise of Government §121: the obligation one is under by such enjoyment 'begins and ends with the enjoyment.' A road-using stranger is bound only while he uses the country; cross the border and the duty lapses. Express consent, by contrast, made you a permanent member for life, the escape hatch Hume pounced on. (§119 stretched tacit consent as far as 'barely travelling freely on the highway.') (marxists.org/reference/subject/politics/locke/ch08.htm)

question: A defender of the social contract tells the poor man who hates his government a simple thing: if you have not packed up and left, then by staying you have consented to it. David Hume answers by pointing at a peasant who speaks no foreign tongue, knows no foreign ways, and lives only on the small daily wages he scrapes together at home. Why did Hume say calling that man's staying a free consent was a sham?
answer: A man chained to home by need has no real freedom to go
choices: A man chained to home by need has no real freedom to go
A peasant who pays his taxes has already consented in full
The rich and poor alike can emigrate whenever they please
Only a man who has traveled abroad can judge his own land
context: David Hume, 'Of the Original Contract' (1748): can we seriously say a poor peasant or artisan has a free choice to leave his country, when he knows no foreign language or manners and lives from day to day on the small wages he acquires? The rich can emigrate; for the poor, consent-by-not-leaving is hollow. (davidhume.org/texts/empl2/oc, OC 24)

question: Robert Nozick imagined a neighborhood of 365 houses that sets up a public-address system playing music and readings all day. Each household is assigned one day a year to run it, and your name is on the list. You never signed up, but on hot evenings you have sometimes opened your window to enjoy a song drifting in. When your assigned day arrives, are you obligated to take your turn? What did Nozick conclude?
answer: No — merely benefiting from a group effort creates no such duty
choices: No — merely benefiting from a group effort creates no such duty
No — the music was too faint to count as a real benefit to you
Yes — anyone who hears the music must repay it by serving
Yes — opening your window was a silent promise to take part
context: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974): his loudspeaker case argues that benefiting from a scheme you never joined does not obligate you to do your part. His underlying principle: you may not foist a benefit on someone unasked and then grab payment for it, which is exactly how a citizen can describe state services. A direct counterexample to the fair-play ground of obligation. (via SEP & IEP: Political Obligation)

question: One old answer to why you must obey is gratitude: the state raised and protected you, so you owe it obedience the way a child owes a parent. The philosopher A. John Simmons replied that genuine gratitude is owed only to a benefactor who freely gives something up for you, and argued that a government does not really fit that description. On what ground did Simmons say a government earns no such gratitude?
answer: Its officials are paid and its services run on your own taxes
choices: Its officials are paid and its services run on your own taxes
Nobody can ever owe a debt of gratitude to a total stranger
A child, too, owes a careless parent no thanks whatsoever
Gratitude felt under pressure is never real gratitude at all
context: A. John Simmons: gratitude is owed only for a voluntary sacrifice, but government officials are paid and public goods are taxpayer-funded, so the state makes no real sacrifice. He adds that even if a debt existed, benefactors 'are not specially entitled to themselves specify what shall constitute a fitting return', so the state cannot dictate that gratitude take the form of obedience. (via IEP: Political Obligation)

question: The philosopher A. John Simmons worked through every classic ground for a duty to obey the law — tacit consent, fairness, gratitude, belonging — and concluded that not one of them succeeds for the ordinary citizen. From that finding Simmons drew a careful conclusion about the ordinary person's relation to the law. What did he conclude?
answer: You may still obey, just never merely because it is the law
choices: You may still obey, just never merely because it is the law
The law binds you only when it commands what is right
No one anywhere has ever had any reason to follow a law
Obedience is owed only to rulers chosen by a fair election
context: This is A. John Simmons' philosophical anarchism: every proposed ground (consent, fair play, gratitude, membership) fails, so there is no general moral duty to obey the law as such. Only those who explicitly swore an oath are bound. Crucially it is not a claim that the state is evil or that you should resist it; you might still obey for other reasons, just not because 'it's the law.' The 'binds only when it commands what is right' distractor is a different position (natural-law obedience), not Simmons' move. (via SEP: Political Obligation)

question: W.K. Clifford opens an 1877 essay with a shipowner who suspects his old emigrant ship is no longer seaworthy. The doubts gnaw at him, but he pushes them down -- she has crossed safely so many times before -- until they fade and he watches her sail with a light heart. She sinks in mid-ocean with all aboard. Clifford says the man did wrong even before she sailed. Where exactly is the wrong?
answer: In coming to believe the ship was safe when his evidence gave him no right to believe it.
choices: In coming to believe the ship was safe when his evidence gave him no right to believe it.
In failing to spend the money that the long-overdue repairs to the old ship would have cost.
In sending strangers to sea on a voyage he himself would never have dared to take with them.
In standing to collect the insurance money if the ship he privately doubted happened to go down.
context: This is W.K. Clifford's evidentialist position -- the foil William James sets out to answer. The shipowner 'had a sincere and comfortable conviction that his vessel was thoroughly safe'; the guilt is in HOW he reached it, not in the deaths. The recognition skill is to locate the wrong in the believing-past-the-evidence, not in the disaster that followed. Source: W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877), infidels.org/library/historical/w-k-clifford-ethics-of-belief/.

question: William James points out that a whole train car of passengers, each one brave enough alone, will be robbed by a couple of highwaymen -- because each passenger fears that if HE moves first, he will be shot before anyone backs him up. James says that if every passenger believed the whole car would rise at once, each one would rise, and the robbery would never even be tried. What point about belief is James making with the train?
answer: That for some things, believing it first is what makes the thing become true at all.
choices: That for some things, believing it first is what makes the thing become true at all.
That a crowd will always act more bravely together than any one person acts alone.
That fear spreads through a group far faster than courage can ever manage to spread.
That a belief is worthless until the hard evidence for it has actually come in first.
context: James's line is 'faith in a fact can help create the fact.' Some truths -- trust, cooperation, that the car will rise with you, that someone will love you -- only come true if you believe ahead of the proof. The train robbery is his most retellable case that belief can rightly run in front of the evidence. Source: William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896), Project Gutenberg gutenberg.org/files/26659/26659-h/26659-h.htm.

question: Around 1870 a young William James, about twenty-eight, was sunk in years of depression and panic, half-convinced that his own will -- and even his God -- might be illusions. After reading the philosopher Charles Renouvier on free will, he wrote one line in his diary that he later credited with pulling him out of the pit. What was the vow he wrote down?
answer: That the very first act of his free will would be to believe in free will.
choices: That the very first act of his free will would be to believe in free will.
That he would obey cold reason alone and never again trust a mere feeling.
That he would wait for solid proof of his freedom before daring to act on it.
That he would surrender the whole question of his will to God's keeping.
context: James's diary, April 30, 1870: 'My first act of free will shall be to believe in free will.' He performed the will-to-believe move on himself decades before he gave it a name in his 1896 lecture -- choosing to act as if free, and crediting that choice with his recovery. Source: William James diary, recounted in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'James,' iep.utm.edu/james-o/.

question: W.K. Clifford treated knowing as a single duty: avoid believing anything on insufficient evidence, full stop. William James answered that a knower has TWO separate duties, not one -- 'we must know the truth; and we must avoid error' -- and that they can pull apart. Clifford, James said, obeys only the second and dreads being duped above all. On James's view, what does that one-sided caution cost a person?
answer: It can make you miss a real truth, since refusing every risky belief is itself a choice.
choices: It can make you miss a real truth, since refusing every risky belief is itself a choice.
It slowly trains the mind to doubt even a truth that is already perfectly well established.
It leaves a person unable to act at all until perfect certainty has finally arrived.
It hands every hard question over to whoever happens to feel the most sure about it.
context: James grants he too has 'a horror of being duped,' but adds that 'worse things than being duped may happen to a man.' Clifford guards only against error; James insists gaining truth is a second, separable duty, and that locking down to dodge ALL error can quietly forfeit a truth you could have had. This is the crux of the fork -- presented without a verdict; a careful evidentialist is not thereby wrong. Source: William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896), Project Gutenberg gutenberg.org/files/26659/26659-h/26659-h.htm.

question: William James, in his 1901-02 Edinburgh lectures, studied religion as raw human experience rather than doctrine, and sorted believers into two kinds. The 'healthy-minded' feel life's native goodness and live at ease in it. The 'sick soul' must pass through despair before reaching any peace. Many would call the second type simply gloomier. What did James insist the sick soul does instead?
answer: Sees more of life than the healthy-minded, including the bitterness the cheerful miss.
choices: Sees more of life than the healthy-minded, including the bitterness the cheerful miss.
Recovers a far deeper and steadier joy once the long bout of despair finally lifts.
Draws closer to the divine than the sunny, untroubled believer ever manages to come.
Feels life's blows more sharply than the healthy-minded only for want of strong nerves.
context: From The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902). James defined religion as 'the feelings, acts, and experiences of individual men in their solitude,' and argued the sick soul is not just sadder but more clear-eyed: 'unsuspectedly from the bottom of every fountain of pleasure... something bitter rises up.' He treats that darker vision as real data about the human condition, not a defect. Source: The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), summarized in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'William James,' plato.stanford.edu/entries/james/.

question: William James held that your passional nature may tip a belief only for a 'genuine option' the evidence cannot decide. He says 'be an agnostic or be a Christian' was a genuine option for his New England audience, but 'be a theosophist or be a Mohammedan' was not. What separates the two pairs for that audience?
answer: Whether each side is a live, tempting possibility for the particular person facing it.
choices: Whether each side is a live, tempting possibility for the particular person facing it.
Whether there is solid historical evidence on record for at least one of the two faiths.
Whether the two named options actually contradict each other or could both be true at once.
Whether the person has had enough time to study both faiths before having to choose between them.
context: This is the first of the three conditions James packs into a 'genuine option.' LIVE: each side must be a real, tempting candidate for the actual person -- 'be a theosophist or a Mohammedan' had no pull on his New England readers, so it was a 'dead' option for them, however live it might be for someone raised differently. The full lock has three parts at once: LIVE, plus FORCED (no fence to sit on -- you cannot abstain), plus MOMENTOUS (a big, unique, irreversible stake). Only when a choice is all three AND the evidence cannot settle it does James allow feeling to decide. Source: William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896), Project Gutenberg gutenberg.org/files/26659/26659-h/26659-h.htm.

question: A reader assumes William James is just reviving Pascal's bet -- believe because the possible payoff is infinite. James rejects the comparison. To show why, he imagines the Mahdi pressing the very same infinite-reward wager on a Western reader -- accept Islam or risk eternal loss -- and notes that on that reader it would simply fall flat. What makes James's own argument unlike Pascal's bet?
answer: It works only on an option that already grips the believer, where Pascal's never did.
choices: It works only on an option that already grips the believer, where Pascal's never did.
It demands far more certainty before believing than Pascal's cautious wager ever required.
It applies to any high-stakes gamble in life, while Pascal's bet was about religion alone.
It leans on the heart's pull where Pascal's wager runs on a cold weighing of the odds.
context: James wrote that 'unless there be some pre-existing tendency to believe in masses and holy water, the option offered to the will by Pascal is not a living option.' He mocks the move by having the Mahdi run the identical logic -- 'weigh your infinite gain if I am genuine against your finite sacrifice if I am not' -- which 'he would vainly use it on us, for the hypothesis he offers us is dead.' James's argument needs a genuinely live option the intellect cannot settle, never a cold infinite-payoff calculation. Source: William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896), Project Gutenberg gutenberg.org/files/26659/26659-h/26659-h.htm.

question: Mary Wollstonecraft asked her readers' pardon for an unusual choice. Most writers of her day, she said, addressed women as charming creatures kept 'in a state of perpetual childhood, unable to stand alone.' She refused to. How did she choose to address grown women instead?
answer: As reasoning adults responsible for themselves
choices: As reasoning adults responsible for themselves
As charming favorites whose moods must be humored
As fragile minds to be guarded from unsettling ideas
As gentle souls owed an easier standard than men
context: This line opens A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792): she would treat women 'like rational creatures, instead of flattering their fascinating graces, and viewing them as if they were in a state of perpetual childhood.' Her whole case starts here — stop addressing women as charming pets to be indulged, and start addressing them as reasoning adults. The 'perpetual childhood' charge is that ornamental upbringing keeps women from ever learning to stand on their own. Source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Introduction (marxists.org).

question: Mary Wollstonecraft pictured a girl taught from infancy 'that beauty is woman's sceptre' — her one source of power. The mind, she wrote, then 'shapes itself to the body.' What does she say a mind raised that way comes to want?
answer: To beautify its confinement rather than escape it
choices: To beautify its confinement rather than escape it
To win every rival girl's envy rather than her friendship
To be shielded from hard study rather than strained by it
To trade its looks for a husband before they fade
context: Wollstonecraft's full image: the mind, 'roaming round its gilt cage, only seeks to adore its prison.' Make beauty a girl's only 'sceptre' (her only source of power) and her mind learns to ornament its own confinement rather than reach past the bars. Source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Ch. 4 (primary text; quoted via LitCharts).

question: Mary Wollstonecraft compared a girl trained only to be pretty to a flower 'planted in too rich a soil.' Such blooms, she wrote, 'please a fastidious eye,' then 'fade, disregarded on the stalk.' What did she say this ornamental upbringing does to the girl?
answer: Her real powers wither unused while she is still young
choices: Her real powers wither unused while she is still young
Her looks fade faster than a girl never praised for them
She poisons the soil for every girl planted after her
She hardens into someone too proud to be of any use
context: The hothouse-flower image: in too-rich soil 'strength and usefulness are sacrificed to beauty,' and the showy bloom wilts 'long before the season when they ought to have arrived at maturity.' Train a girl only to be lovely, Wollstonecraft argues, and her true powers waste away before she ever comes into them. Source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Introduction (marxists.org / gutenberg.org).

question: A schoolmaster defends keeping girls unread and unquestioning: it preserves their innocence, he says. Mary Wollstonecraft answered that if women are not 'a swarm of ephemeron triflers,' there is no reason 'they should be kept in ignorance under the specious name of innocence.' What is the move she exposes in the word 'innocence' here?
answer: It dresses up a forced lack of learning as a virtue
choices: It dresses up a forced lack of learning as a virtue
It mistakes being chaste for being unschooled
It assumes a girl can stay pure through any amount of study
It treats every triviality a girl enjoys as a sign of grace
context: This is the substantive collapse Wollstonecraft catches: calling a girl's enforced ignorance 'innocence' is a flattering relabel that makes a deprivation look like a virtue she chose. 'Ephemeron triflers' means short-lived, flighty creatures — she refuses to accept that women are that by nature. The move being named here is the flattering-relabel (giving a bad thing a pretty name); the label goes in context, not the answer. Source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Ch. 2 (gutenberg.org).

question: A tutor points to how little the women he knows have read, and calls it proof their minds are the weaker sex by nature. Mary Wollstonecraft had already met this argument head on. What did she say the women's ignorance actually proved?
answer: Only that they had been denied a real education
choices: Only that they had been denied a real education
That nature had fitted them for feeling, not reasoning
That the law, not the mind, held them back
That husbands gained too much to let them learn
context: Wollstonecraft's foundational claim — the heart of equity feminism: women only SEEM intellectually lesser because they are denied real education, so the defect is in the schooling, not the mind. As she opens the book, 'the neglected education of my fellow creatures is the grand source of the misery I deplore.' The tutor reads the symptom (light reading) as the cause (weaker nature); she points to the schooling withheld. Source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Introduction (marxists.org).

question: Mary Wollstonecraft argued that 'blind obedience is ever sought for by power,' and so 'tyrants and sensualists are in the right when they endeavour to keep women in the dark.' By her own account, why do both of them fight to keep women uneducated?
answer: Both lose their hold once she can think for herself
choices: Both lose their hold once she can think for herself
Both fear being out-argued by an educated woman
Both profit from the cheap labor an ignorant woman gives
Both were shamed by a learned woman earlier in life
context: Her words: 'the former only want slaves, and the latter a play-thing.' Strengthen and enlarge a woman's mind and blind obedience ends — which is exactly why those who want a slave (the tyrant) or a plaything (the sensualist) work to keep women uneducated. The deprivation isn't an accident; it serves someone's grip, and a mind that can reason for itself slips that grip. Source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Ch. 2 (marxists.org).

question: Rousseau warned that educating women like men would only cost men their power: 'the more they resemble our sex the less power will they have over us.' Mary Wollstonecraft seized on the line — 'This is the very point I am at' — and named the power she actually wanted women to win. Which was it?
answer: Mastery of themselves, not sway over men
choices: Mastery of themselves, not sway over men
A seat in public office, not just the home
The right to refuse a marriage, not to command one
Authority over their own daughters, not their husbands
context: Her exact reply: 'I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.' This is the heart of equity feminism — the aim is self-command, not a sex war or rule over the other sex. She turns Rousseau's fear back on him: yes, educated women lose their hold over men, and that is the point. Source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (primary text; passage confirmed via multiple quote indexes).

question: Mary Wollstonecraft answered the fear that a woman who learned to think for herself would abandon her family. What did she say a real education makes of a woman at home?
answer: A wife and mother her family is the stronger for
choices: A wife and mother her family is the stronger for
A companion her husband must reason with as an equal
A teacher her own children learn their first lessons from
A manager who runs the household by her own judgment
context: Wollstonecraft frames educated women as a gift to the family, not a threat to it: 'Make women rational creatures, and free citizens, and they will quickly become good wives and mothers' — since (in her words elsewhere) the marriages people form are 'the cement of society.' Equal treatment strengthens the home rather than emptying it. This line is widely attributed to her conclusion; the exact placement is reported via quote indexes rather than verbatim-located in the fetched Gutenberg excerpt. Source: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (Goodreads/Bookey quote indexes).

question: A teenager hears that the Daoist ideal is wu wei, often translated word-for-word as non-doing, and decides it means he can skip his chores and just do nothing. His grandfather warns that the translation is a trap. What does wu wei really call for?
answer: Acting smoothly and naturally, without strain or forcing
choices: Acting smoothly and naturally, without strain or forcing
Doing nothing at all and letting other people cope
Working as hard and as forcefully as a person can
Holding back from any action until you are certain
context: Wu wei (無為) is built from wu = 'not/without' and wei = 'do/strive,' so word-for-word it reads 'non-doing.' But the literal reading is the trap: it never meant inaction, passivity, or laziness. The Daoist sense is effortless, spontaneous RIGHT action — acting without strain or fighting the grain of things. As the IEP puts it, 'Daoism is not a philosophy of doing nothing... Those who wu wei do act.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wu_wei ; IEP, Daoist Philosophy, https://iep.utm.edu/daoismdaoist-philosophy/

question: Laozi points to something every child has seen at a river: water is the softest, most yielding thing there is, yet over time nothing is better at wearing down rock and grinding away what is hard. How does the gentle water defeat the solid stone?
answer: By flowing around it and never fighting it head-on
choices: By flowing around it and never fighting it head-on
By smashing it apart with one sudden hard blow
By turning itself harder than the stone it meets
By drying away so the stone cracks in the heat
context: This is the marquee image of wu wei, from Daodejing Chapter 78: 'There is nothing softer and weaker than water, and yet there is nothing better for attacking hard and strong things.' The weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard precisely because water does not force — it gives way and outlasts. Laozi adds a sting: everyone KNOWS this, yet almost no one can put it into practice. Source: Tao Te Ching Ch. 78, Wing-Tsit Chan (1963) trans., https://www.egreenway.com/taoism/ttclz78.htm

question: From the outside, a lazy man slumped on a couch and a Daoist master at rest can look exactly alike: both seem to be doing nothing. Yet only one is living out wu wei. What truly sets the master apart from the merely idle?
answer: When action is needed, the master acts well and easily; the idler still does nothing
choices: When action is needed, the master acts well and easily; the idler still does nothing
The master has risen above all action; the idler has merely grown bored of it
The master is secretly straining hard inside; the idler is relaxed all the way through
The master feels calm about resting; the idler feels guilty about resting
context: The related phrase wei wu wei (為無為) means 'doing not-doing' — action without forcing. The paradox dissolves once you see wu wei is not NO action but UNFORCED action. The lazy man and the master can look identical, but one is asleep and the other is the swimmer riding the current or Cook Ding's blade gliding through the gaps: ready, skillful, effortless. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wu_wei ; IEP, Daoist Philosophy, https://iep.utm.edu/daoismdaoist-philosophy/

question: Mencius tells of a farmer in Song who fretted that his grain grew too slowly, so he walked his whole field tugging each young sprout higher to help it along. Worn out, he bragged to his family about the hard day he had put in. When his son ran out to the field the next morning, what had all the tugging done?
answer: Every stalk he had pulled was withered and dead
choices: Every stalk he had pulled was withered and dead
The roots had spread and the field grew faster
The neighbors copied his clever new technique
The grain stood taller but the harvest soured
context: This is the classic anti-wu-wei parable (Mengzi 2A2): forcing growth does not speed it, it kills it — yet Mencius notes almost everyone meddles like this. The idiom 拔苗助長, 'pull up sprouts to help them grow,' is still proverbial in Chinese for ruining a thing by rushing it. Going with the grain means letting it grow in its own time. Told as a teaching parable. Source: Mengzi 2A2, http://schwitzsplinters.blogspot.com/2007/02/parable-of-farmer-of-song-mengzi-2a2.html  (Legend.)

question: Confucius, touring a gorge, watches a man plunge into a waterfall so violent that no fish can survive in it, and assumes the man means to drown himself. Downstream, the man strolls out unharmed and singing. Asked his secret method for riding the deadly current, the swimmer says he has none at all, only this. What does he do?
answer: He goes down with the whirlpools and rises where the water spouts up
choices: He goes down with the whirlpools and rises where the water spouts up
He holds one long breath and sinks to the still riverbed
He fights toward the bank with all the strength he has
He grips the rocks and hauls himself along hand over hand
context: From the Zhuangzi, 'The Swimmer at Lü Liang.' The man insists he has no special 'way': 'I go under with the whirlpools and emerge where the water spouts up, following the way of the water and never thinking about myself.' He survives the killing current by going WITH it rather than fighting it — the cleanest picture of wu wei in action. A Daoist parable. Source: Zhuangzi ch. 19 'Mastering Life,' https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat3/sub10/entry-5581.html  (Legend.)

question: In a tale from the Zhuangzi, Cook Ding carves up a whole ox for Lord Wenhui so gracefully that every stroke falls into rhythm, like steps in a dance. He has used the same knife for nineteen years on thousands of oxen, yet its edge is still as sharp as the day it was ground. How does Cook Ding keep an edge that should have worn out long ago?
answer: He slides the blade through the natural gaps between the joints
choices: He slides the blade through the natural gaps between the joints
He quietly hones the blade between each and every cut
He swings so hard the bone gives way before the edge can
He keeps every cut shallow so the edge never bites deep
context: This is the single most retellable wu-wei image. Cook Ding never hacks — he finds the openings between the joints and lets the blade slip through, never striking bone, so it never dulls. As he tells it: 'A good cook changes his knife once a year — because he cuts. A mediocre cook changes his knife once a month — because he hacks.' His own lasts nineteen years. Mastery is letting the work flow through you, not muscling it. A Daoist parable. Source: Zhuangzi ch. 3, Burton Watson trans., https://thedewdrop.org/2020/05/18/the-dexterous-butcher-zhuangzi/  (Legend.)

question: Laozi ranks rulers from worst to best: the worst is one the people despise, above him one they fear, above him one they love and praise, and at the very top a fourth and highest kind. This best ruler governs so quietly that the people hardly know he is there. When the work is done and all has gone well, what do these people say?
answer: We did the whole of this all by ourselves
choices: We did the whole of this all by ourselves
It was heaven favor that carried us through
Our chief minister managed every bit of it
Nothing much really changed under his rule
context: Daodejing Chapter 17. The hands-off sage governs so lightly that 'when the work is finished, the people all say, We did this ourselves.' This is wu wei applied to ruling: the great ruler succeeds precisely by NOT meddling, arranging things so they barely need doing — so the people credit themselves rather than the throne, a minister, or the heavens. Source: Tao Te Ching Ch. 17, https://www.wussu.com/laotzu/laotzu17.html

question: Laozi states the heart of wu wei as a riddle: the Dao does nothing, he says, and yet nothing is ever left undone. He promises that a ruler who truly held to this would see the whole realm prosper. By Laozi reasoning, how can doing nothing leave nothing undone?
answer: Stop meddling, and things complete themselves on their own
choices: Stop meddling, and things complete themselves on their own
Keep your effort hidden so that no one ever sees it
Do one small piece each day until it is all finished
Have other people carry out the work in your place
context: Daodejing Chapter 37: 'The Dao eternally does nothing (wu wei), yet nothing is left undone. If leaders and kings can hold to this, all things will transform of their own accord.' The non-forcing is not a gap in effectiveness — it IS the source of it. Stop tampering and the world rights itself; the meddling is what breaks things. Source: Tao Te Ching Ch. 37, https://www.egreenway.com/taoism/ttclz37.htm

question: For all his ease, Cook Ding does not just coast through the ox. When his blade reaches a knotted, tangled place where the joints lock tight, he changes how he works, right up until the whole piece falls apart like a crumbling clod of earth. At this hardest spot, what does the effortless master do?
answer: He slows right down and barely moves the blade at all
choices: He slows right down and barely moves the blade at all
He speeds up and powers straight on through the tangle
He sets that ox aside and begins fresh on another one
He sends for a heavy cleaver to smash the knot apart
context: This is the rung that corrects the deepest misread of wu wei: at the hard part Cook Ding is MOST careful, not least. He slows, watches, and barely moves the blade until — flop! — the whole thing 'comes apart like a clod of earth crumbling to the ground.' Then he stands holding the knife, completely satisfied. Watching, Lord Wenhui says he has learned how to care for life. Effortless does not mean thoughtless. A Daoist parable. Source: Zhuangzi ch. 3, Burton Watson trans., https://thedewdrop.org/2020/05/18/the-dexterous-butcher-zhuangzi/  (Legend.)

question: An old wheelwright in the Zhuangzi tells Duke Huan that shaping a wheel takes a feel earned only by doing it: chisel too slow and the blade slips without biting, too fast and it jams in the wood. After seventy years at the trade, what does the wheelwright confess about passing on this knack of his?
answer: He cannot teach it to his son, nor the son learn it from him
choices: He cannot teach it to his son, nor the son learn it from him
He can drill it into his son with enough years at the bench
A sharp apprentice could copy it just by watching him work
Any wheelwright picks it up once his hands grow strong enough
context: From the Zhuangzi, 'The Wheelwright.' Old Wheelwright Bian dares to call a sage's book 'the dregs of the men of old,' because the real skill lives in the hand: 'Not too slow, not too fast — I feel it in the hand and respond from the heart. The mouth cannot put it into words. There is a knack in it I cannot teach my son, and my son cannot learn from me.' Wu wei as embodied feel — it can be earned through practice but never forced or fully spoken. A Daoist parable. Source: Zhuangzi ch. 13, A.C. Graham trans., https://www.asianstudies.org/publications/eaa/archives/the-wheelwright-and-the-butcher-master-zhuangs-recipe-for-mindful-living/  (Legend.)

question: Xunzi taught that warped wood, left alone, stays warped: only a steaming press and a whetstone make it straight and sharp. He insisted people are exactly the same. What was his claim about human goodness?
answer: Goodness must be worked into a person from outside, by training; it is not born in us
choices: Goodness must be worked into a person from outside, by training; it is not born in us
Goodness is a sprout already inside each person, needing only water and sun to grow it
Goodness is fixed at birth by fate, so no effort can ever add it or take it away again
Goodness is breathed into each person by Heaven as a reward for their parents' virtue
context: Xunzi (Xun Kuang, c.310-c.220 BCE) ranks as the third great classical Confucian. His signature image, in Burton Watson's translation: warped wood must be 'laid against a straightening board, steamed, and bent into shape before it can become straight; blunt metal must be ground on a whetstone before it can become sharp.' The craft (steaming, the press, the grindstone) is what MAKES the wood straight; in the same way ritual and effort make a person good. He set this squarely against Mencius, who held goodness is already inside us -- a live, still-debated fork. Source: Facts and Details (Burton Watson trans.), https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat3/sub69/entry-5567.html

question: A potter sits at the wheel and a smooth jar rises out of a shapeless lump of clay. Xunzi used this scene to settle one stubborn question about that finished jar.
answer: The potter shaped it; no jar was hiding in the clay, waiting to grow out on its own
choices: The potter shaped it; no jar was hiding in the clay, waiting to grow out on its own
The clay was always secretly a jar, and the potter only freed the shape it already held
The clay made a finer jar than any plan, because it was left to choose its own true form
The clay resents the wheel and will, given time, slump back into a shapeless lump again
context: Xunzi (Burton Watson trans.): 'A potter molds clay and makes a vessel, but the vessel is the product of the conscious activity of the potter, not essentially a product of his human nature. The sage stands in the same relation to ritual principles as the potter to the things he molds.' Goodness, on this view, is a vessel, not a seed -- it is achieved through deliberate effort (what Xunzi calls wei, artifice), never simply inherited from the nature one is born with (xing). Source: Burton Watson, Xunzi: Basic Writings, via Wabash Center lecture notes, https://www.wabashcenter.wabash.edu/syllabi/g/gier/308/xunzi.htm

question: Xunzi asked a blunt question about prayer: you pray for rain, and it rains, so why did it rain? His startling answer explained why he thought fixing human nature was entirely up to people.
answer: Because the sky is just plain Nature with no care for us, so the rain falls for no reason at all
choices: Because the sky is just plain Nature with no care for us, so the rain falls for no reason at all
Because Heaven heard the prayer and rewarded the faithful, which proves the cosmos cares for the good
Because the rain was always coming, and the prayer merely lets people feel they had caused it
Because the ritual of prayer itself stirs the clouds, which is exactly why ritual must never be skipped
context: Xunzi treated Heaven (Tian) as regular Nature, not a moral rewarder: 'Heaven does not suspend winter because people dislike cold; earth does not contract its breadth because people dislike traveling great distances.' On prayer (Watson): 'You pray for rain and it rains. Why? For no particular reason, I say.' Because the cosmos will not fix human nature, the whole burden of straightening falls on human culture and effort. Sources: Facts and Details (Burton Watson trans.), https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat3/sub69/entry-5567.html ; IEP: Xunzi, https://iep.utm.edu/xunzi/

question: Xunzi spotted a quiet clue in the carpenter's shop: someone, at some point, had to invent the straightening board and the plumb line. Why did Xunzi think a tool's mere existence proved anything at all?
answer: You only ever build such a tool for things that come out crooked, so its existence betrays the bend
choices: You only ever build such a tool for things that come out crooked, so its existence betrays the bend
You can see this tool is beautifully made, so its existence proves that people are born loving beauty
You find that just anyone at all can use the tool, so it proves all people start out equally skilled
You notice the tool itself slowly wears out, so it proves that even good materials must decay in time
context: Inverted into one line (Sources of Chinese Tradition, vol.1 p.182): 'The straightening board was created because of warped wood, and the plumb line came into being because of things that are not straight. Rulers are established and ritual and rightness are illuminated because the nature is evil.' The existence of correcting tools is itself the proof the raw material was crooked -- we only invent straighteners for things that need straightening. Source: Wikiquote: Xun Zi, citing de Bary & Bloom, Sources of Chinese Tradition (1999) vol.1, p.182, https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Xun_Zi

question: Xunzi named his great rival and broke with him out loud: Mengzi says that when people learn, it reveals the goodness already in their nature; I say this is not so. Each man pictured learning as a different craft. What was Xunzi's picture of it?
answer: A carpenter forcing a bent board flat against a press, making straight what came out crooked
choices: A carpenter forcing a bent board flat against a press, making straight what came out crooked
A gardener watering a young seedling, coaxing out a goodness that was already there sprouting
A merchant trading his wares at the market, swapping ignorance for knowledge at a fair price
A soldier drilling long hours for battle, hardening a body that was already strong to begin with
context: Xunzi quotes and rejects his rival by name (ch.23): 'Mengzi says: When people engage in learning, this manifests the goodness of their nature. I say: This is not so.' Mencius's optimistic picture is gardening -- learning waters sprouts of virtue already inside you. Xunzi's is carpentry -- learning is the press-frame bending a board that was never straight to begin with. The Mencius-Xunzi quarrel over human nature is one of the great unsettled debates of Chinese philosophy. Sources: Philosophy Break, 'Mengzi vs. Xunzi On Human Nature', https://philosophybreak.com/articles/mengzi-xunzi-on-human-nature-are-we-good-or-evil/ ; SEP: Xunzi, https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/xunzi/

question: Xunzi pointed to one ordinary act as his proof: a hungry younger brother lets his older brother take the first share of the food. That single act, he argued, exposes where such behavior really comes from.
answer: It cuts against what hunger makes you do, so it can only be the fingerprint of teaching
choices: It cuts against what hunger makes you do, so it can only be the fingerprint of teaching
It is exactly what hunger makes you do, which proves that kindness is a natural human instinct
It happens only between brothers, which proves goodness is confined within one's own family
It pleases the watching father, which proves people only ever behave well while being watched
context: Xunzi (Burton Watson trans.): 'For a son to yield to his father, and a younger brother to yield to his elder brother... these two acts are contrary to the nature and counter to the emotions.' Yielding the first share when you are hungry is NOT what raw nature would do; that a person does it anyway is, to Xunzi, the fingerprint of teaching and ritual, not of inborn instinct. Source: Facts and Details (Burton Watson trans.), https://factsanddetails.com/china/cat3/sub69/entry-5567.html

question: Xunzi made a startling claim: even the lowliest man in the street can become a Yu, the great sage-king himself. By what route, Xunzi said, does such an ordinary person actually reach sagehood?
answer: By long, piled-up effort that never stops, since crooked wood is still wood and can be bent straight
choices: By long, piled-up effort that never stops, since crooked wood is still wood and can be bent straight
By a single instant of sincere wishing, since the full goodness of a great sage already sits inside him
By no route at all, for in the end sagehood is fixed by noble birth and can never once be earned
By casting off ritual and its burdens, and simply letting his natural feelings run as they will
context: The democratic kicker that Xunzi was no pessimist, though critics painted him as one (Watson): 'The man in the street can become a Yu' -- anyone, however lowly, can become the sage-emperor Yu by long accumulated effort, one who 'concentrates his mind, unifies his will... continues his efforts over a long period of time, accumulating good acts without stop.' Crooked wood is still wood: with enough art and patience ANY person can be straightened all the way to sagehood. The doctrine is demanding, not despairing -- and the opposite of casting off ritual. Sources: Burton Watson, Xunzi: Basic Writings, via SEP: Xunzi, https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/xunzi/ ; Wabash lecture notes, https://www.wabashcenter.wabash.edu/syllabi/g/gier/308/xunzi.htm

question: Xunzi threw the optimists' own logic back at them. If human nature really were good all on its own, he argued, then one stubborn fact true of every society on earth would become impossible to explain. Which fact?
answer: That every culture takes the trouble to build laws, teachers, and rites it would not have needed
choices: That every culture takes the trouble to build laws, teachers, and rites it would not have needed
That every culture passes down stories of a lost golden age when people were perfectly happy
That every culture fears its own death and raises elaborate tombs and monuments for its dead rulers
That every culture seems to invent music and dance long before it ever invents writing
context: Xunzi's steel-man clincher (IEP): if people really were good by nature, 'there would be no need for ritual and social norms -- the sages would not have had to create them,' because everyone would already behave well on their own. The very fact that every culture builds laws, teachers and rites is, to him, evidence that the raw material needed correcting. This keeps the Mencius-Xunzi fork genuinely live: a serious argument, not the grumbling of a pessimist. Source: IEP: Xunzi, https://iep.utm.edu/xunzi/

question: Zeno of Citium was a rich merchant whose ship sank off the coast of Athens, swallowing his entire cargo and leaving him stranded and ruined far from home. Most men would have cursed that day forever. Yet years later Zeno had a surprising way of describing the very shipwreck that had destroyed his fortune. What did he say about it?
answer: That he made a prosperous voyage on the day he was wrecked
choices: That he made a prosperous voyage on the day he was wrecked
That the gods had cursed him for some forgotten crime
That he would rebuild his fleet and sail out twice as rich
That no honest trader should ever trust the open sea
context: 'I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered shipwreck.' Being ruined drove Zeno into philosophy in Athens, and he counted the wreck as the luckiest thing that ever happened to him; another version has him thank Fortune for driving him to philosophy. He went on to found the school later called Stoicism. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.1-2, via attalus.org and worldhistory.org/article/741.

question: Shipwrecked and penniless in Athens, Zeno of Citium wandered into a bookseller's shop to pass the time and began reading the life of a long-dead philosopher, a barefoot Athenian who had roamed that same city questioning everyone about how a person ought to live, and who claimed he himself knew nothing. Zeno was so electrified he demanded to know where living men like that could be found. Whose life had he been reading?
answer: Socrates
choices: Socrates
Pythagoras
Thales
Homer
context: The book was the second book of Xenophon's Memorabilia, a portrait of Socrates, the Athenian who questioned everyone and professed to know nothing. Its account so moved Zeno that he asked where such men could be found, and from that question his own path in philosophy began. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.2-3, via attalus.org and worldhistory.org/article/741.

question: In an Athens bookshop, Zeno of Citium looked up from the book that had gripped him and begged the bookseller to tell him where living men as wise as the philosopher in his book could still be found. The bookseller glanced out at the street, pointed at a figure passing the door, and said that was the man to follow. Which of these passers-by did the bookseller single out as Zeno's teacher?
answer: The ragged Cynic who begged in the streets
choices: The ragged Cynic who begged in the streets
The grave geometer who charted the stars
The robed priest who served at the altar
The smooth orator who swayed the courts
context: The man passing the shop was Crates of Thebes, the leading Cynic philosopher of the day. The bookseller simply pointed and said 'Follow yonder man,' and Crates became Zeno's first teacher. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.2-3, via attalus.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeno_of_Citium.

question: Early in his search, Zeno of Citium asked an oracle what he should do to reach the best possible life. The answer came back as a grim little riddle: he should 'take on the color of the dead.' Instead of despairing, Zeno worked out a hopeful meaning and built his whole study around it. What did he decide the strange command was really telling him to do?
answer: Soak up the wisdom of long-dead writers by reading them
choices: Soak up the wisdom of long-dead writers by reading them
Give away his money and live as poor as a corpse
Master his fear so he could face his own death calmly
Put on the pale gray clothes that mourners wore
context: Zeno read the cryptic oracle as an instruction to study the ancient authors and absorb the wisdom of the long dead. The 'color of the dead' became his image for steeping himself in old books. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.2, via attalus.org; whatisstoicism.com/stoicism-resources/take-on-the-color-of-the-dead.

question: The word 'Stoic' has nothing to do with Zeno of Citium's name or with any belief he held. His followers were first nicknamed 'Zenonians.' But the name that finally stuck was taken from the spot in Athens where Zeno liked to pace back and forth while he taught his students. What kind of place was it that ended up naming the entire school?
answer: A roofed public porch beside the marketplace
choices: A roofed public porch beside the marketplace
A walled private garden behind his house
A marble temple high on the city hill
A shady grove out beyond the city walls
context: Zeno taught in the Stoa Poikile, the 'Painted Porch,' a roofed colonnade beside the Athenian agora decorated with murals of famous battles. The word 'Stoic' comes straight from stoa, Greek for that porch, not from any doctrine. Sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.5, via attalus.org; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoa_Poikile.

question: Plato's Academy and Aristotle's Lyceum schooled a chosen few behind walls and gates. Zeno of Citium chose instead to teach in a roofed public porch in the heart of Athens. The ancient record names the kind of people who stopped in the street to hear him. Which sort were remembered among Zeno's listeners?
answer: Merchants, slaves, and day laborers
choices: Merchants, slaves, and day laborers
Generals, envoys, and city magistrates
Actors, athletes, and festival crowds
Scribes, money-changers, and tax men
context: Because Zeno taught in an open public colonnade rather than a private walled school, anyone in the street, traders, slaves, and passers-by alike, could stop and listen for free, instead of only the elite the gated schools admitted. Sources: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Zeno_of_Citium; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoa_Poikile.

question: The young Zeno of Citium was painfully shy and hated being stared at, so his teacher Crates set out to break him of caring what strangers thought. Crates handed him a brimming pot of lentil soup and ordered him to carry it across the crowded marketplace. The instant Zeno tried to hide the pot in embarrassment, what did Crates do to him?
answer: Smashed the pot so soup poured down his legs
choices: Smashed the pot so soup poured down his legs
Snatched it back and ate it in front of him
Praised him aloud for finally obeying orders
Tipped it out and sent him home for more
context: Crates struck the pot with his staff, the lentil soup ran down Zeno's legs, and as the mortified young man bolted Crates called after him: 'Why run away, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you.' The lesson was to stop being ruled by other people's opinions. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.3, via perseus.tufts.edu and attalus.org.

question: Zeno of Citium was only a resident foreigner from Cyprus, yet over the decades he taught in Athens the city grew to trust him as it trusted few outsiders. The Athenians are even said to have handed Zeno one extraordinary mark of trust that a city guards above almost everything else. What did they reportedly give him?
answer: The keys to the city walls
choices: The keys to the city walls
A seat on the ruling council
Command of the city's soldiers
A share of the public treasury
context: During his life the city is said to have trusted this Cypriot foreigner with the keys to its walls, a remarkable honor for an outsider; and after his death a public decree proposed by Thraso granted Zeno a golden crown 'on account of his virtue and temperance' and a tomb in the Ceramicus at public expense. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.6, via attalus.org.

question: Legend tells that Zeno of Citium, leaving his school as a very old man, tripped on the way out and wrenched a toe. Taking even this tiny stumble as a kind of summons, the aged philosopher reacted in a way that stunned everyone who later heard the tale. According to the story, what did Zeno do right there after his little fall?
answer: Held his breath on purpose until he died
choices: Held his breath on purpose until he died
Called his students to carry him home
Cursed the gods for so petty an injury
Swore he would never teach another lesson
context: The story has Zeno, after tripping and breaking a toe, strike the ground with his hand, quote the line from the tragedy Niobe, 'I come; why call me so?', then hold his breath until he died. It is flagged as legend because even ancient and modern readers found the tale suspiciously theatrical, and the sources disagree on his age (Diogenes says 98, his pupil Persaeus said 72). Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.5-6, via attalus.org; worldhistory.org/article/741.

question: Achilles, the fastest runner alive, races a tortoise and spots it a head start. He reasons: to pass it, I must first reach the spot where it now sits. But by the time he arrives there, the tortoise has crawled a bit farther on. He reaches that new spot; it has crept farther still. Every time he closes a gap, a smaller fresh gap has opened. Where does this chain of reasoning lead?
answer: The fastest runner can never overtake the slowest creature
choices: The fastest runner can never overtake the slowest creature
Achilles wins easily once he takes his very first stride
The tortoise must eventually tire and let Achilles pass
Both racers reach the finish line at the exact same moment
context: This is the Achilles paradox. As long as you insist Achilles must close each gap one at a time, with a new gap always waiting, the argument forces the absurd conclusion that he never catches up at all. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zeno's Paradoxes' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/paradox-zeno/).

question: Achilles chases a tortoise given a head start, and a tricky argument lets him gain only by stopping at a string of marked points along the way. The unsettling part is that this string of required stops never runs out, no matter how close he gets. Why does the argument say there is always one more stop still ahead of Achilles?
answer: Each arrival leaves the tortoise a tiny new lead to chase down
choices: Each arrival leaves the tortoise a tiny new lead to chase down
Each arrival lets the tortoise sprint clear out of reach again
The rule sends him to the midpoint, then halves what is left
The rule keeps restarting him from his own starting line again
context: By the rule of the argument, Achilles may only aim for where the tortoise already was; but by the time he gets there, the tortoise has crept on and opened a small new lead. Every arrival manufactures the next gap, so the stops never run out. Source: Aristotle, Physics VI.9, 239b15, via Britannica, 'Achilles paradox' (britannica.com/topic/Achilles-paradox).

question: A thinker claims you can never walk across your own bedroom. His argument: before you reach the far wall, you must first get to the halfway point of the room. But before you reach that halfway point, you must first get to the quarter point. And before that, the eighth point, each new mark closer to where you stand. What does this argument say you face just to cross one ordinary room?
answer: Endlessly many separate distances you must clear
choices: Endlessly many separate distances you must clear
A single short walk that takes only a moment
A wall that quietly retreats as you step toward it
Exactly one halfway point and nothing more
context: This is the Dichotomy, also called the Racecourse. Aristotle's phrasing: 'that which is in locomotion must arrive at the half-way stage before it arrives at the goal.' Because the halving never stops, the walk seems to break into infinitely many pieces. Source: Aristotle, Physics VI.9, 239b11, via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A story, told 700 years after the fact and almost certainly invented, claims that Zeno of Elea was caught smuggling weapons to rebels against a tyrant. Hauled in and ordered to name his fellow plotters, Zeno said he would whisper the names. He leaned toward the tyrant's ear, and instead of speaking, did something the tale is remembered for. According to the legend, what did Zeno do at the tyrant's ear?
answer: Bit down and refused to let go until he was stabbed
choices: Bit down and refused to let go until he was stabbed
Quietly recited every conspirator's name in order
Begged for mercy and offered up a full confession
Whispered a riddle that no guard could untangle
context: Diogenes Laertius reports this roughly 700 years later, so it is legend, not history. It survives because it fits Zeno's reputation for refusing to yield ground. Source: Diogenes Laertius (3rd c. AD), via Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/Zeno_of_Elea/).

question: Zeno of Elea points at an arrow in mid-flight and argues it is not really moving. His reasoning: freeze the arrow at any single instant, and in that frozen instant it fills a space exactly its own size and crosses no distance at all. In that instant it looks no different from an arrow lying still. Time, he says, is just a string of such instants. What conclusion does Zeno draw about the flying arrow?
answer: It never truly moves at any point in its flight
choices: It never truly moves at any point in its flight
It moves fastest right at the top of its arc
It speeds up the longer it stays in the air
It moves only when nobody is watching it
context: This is the Arrow paradox. Aristotle's words: 'if everything when it occupies an equal space is at rest... the flying arrow is therefore motionless.' If the arrow is at rest in every single instant, and time is nothing but instants, Zeno says motion vanishes. Source: Aristotle, Physics VI.9, 239b30, via SEP and faculty.washington.edu/smcohen/320/ZenoArrow.html.

question: Zeno of Elea took up a strange fight. His teacher Parmenides had argued that all reality is one motionless whole and that the change we see is mere illusion, and crowds ridiculed the idea as obviously false. Instead of defending the motionless One head-on, Zeno trained his puzzles on the crowd's own everyday belief that many things exist and move. What was Zeno trying to accomplish by going after that everyday belief?
answer: Show the crowd's own view collapses into knots worse than his teacher's
choices: Show the crowd's own view collapses into knots worse than his teacher's
Trade his teacher's One for a livelier world full of many moving things
Settle a private grudge by beating a famous athlete in a public footrace
Warn archers that a fired arrow never truly leaves the bowstring at all
context: Zeno granted the common-sense view that many things move, then showed it bred contradictions worse than Parmenides' One, defending his teacher by indirect attack rather than head-on. Aristotle credited him as the inventor of dialectic. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zeno of Elea' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/zeno-elea/).

question: Achilles seems trapped: he must close infinitely many shrinking gaps to catch the tortoise, so it looks like the chase has no end. Suppose the tortoise starts 10 paces ahead and Achilles runs ten times faster. Then the gaps he closes measure 10, then 1, then a tenth, then a hundredth, smaller and smaller forever. Here is the trick that dissolves the paradox: what is true of all those endlessly many shrinking gaps added together?
answer: They add up to a single finite distance
choices: They add up to a single finite distance
They add up to an infinitely long road
They never settle on any total at all
They each stay the same size as the first
context: The gaps sum to exactly 11 and one-ninth of a pace, reached in a finite time. Infinitely many shrinking steps can still add to one ordinary finishing point, so Achilles passes the tortoise right there. Source: John D. Norton, Univ. of Pittsburgh, 'Zeno's Paradoxes of Motion' (sites.pitt.edu/~jdnorton/teaching/paradox/chapters/Zeno/Zeno.html).

question: The Arrow argument says that at any single frozen instant the arrow crosses no distance and so is at rest, and that if it is at rest in every instant it never moves. Marc Cohen points out the argument leans its whole weight on the word 'rest,' and uses it in a way that does not actually hold. Where does the Arrow argument go wrong about being 'at rest'?
answer: Resting means holding a place over a stretch of time, not at a single instant
choices: Resting means holding a place over a stretch of time, not at a single instant
Resting and moving are really the very same state seen from different angles
An arrow can rest and move at the very same instant without contradiction
Resting is impossible for any object, so nothing is ever truly still
context: A durationless snapshot shows neither motion nor rest; both are facts about positions across an interval. So 'at rest at every instant' is a confusion, and 'therefore motionless' does not follow. Source: faculty.washington.edu/smcohen/320/ZenoArrow.html (Marc Cohen, Univ. of Washington); Aristotle's solution in Physics.

question: The room-crossing puzzle has a nastier twin aimed not at finishing a walk but at starting one. To take any step at all, the argument says, you must first cross the first half of it. But before that half, you must cross a quarter; and before that quarter, an eighth; and the demand keeps pushing earlier and earlier. Why does this version claim you can never even begin to move?
answer: There is no first stretch to cross, since a smaller one always comes before it
choices: There is no first stretch to cross, since a smaller one always comes before it
The far wall quietly slides away faster than a walker can ever approach it
Each half somehow takes longer to cross than the whole step it belongs to
A walker's first step would have to be infinitely long in order to count
context: This is the regressive form of the Dichotomy. The progressive form denies you can finish; this one denies you can start, because every candidate for 'the first bit to cross' has a smaller bit hiding before it. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zeno's Paradoxes' (iep.utm.edu/zenos-paradoxes/).

question: Aristotle answered the room-crossing puzzle with a distinction that calculus would not make precise for two thousand more years. He agreed a walk can be chopped into an unlimited number of ever-smaller pieces, yet he denied that this traps the walker, and claimed a body really can pass through unlimitedly many such pieces in a finite stretch of time. The distinction he leaned on turned on what 'unlimited' means here. What distinction was Aristotle drawing on?
answer: Divisions one could always go on making versus divisions ever actually finished
choices: Divisions one could always go on making versus divisions ever actually finished
Distances a person can plainly see versus distances far too small to see
Real motion of the body itself versus the motion of the surrounding air
Time measured out by a steady clock versus time as we feel it slipping past
context: Aristotle wrote 'it is possible for a thing to pass over a potentially infinite number of things in a finite time' (Physics 263b). He had the right instinct, separating a merely possible infinity of cuts from a finished one, but lacked the tools to compute the finite time. Source: Aristotle, Physics 263b2-5, via Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: For more than two thousand years no one could give an airtight answer to Zeno's runner, who seems forced to complete an endless task. The repair came in the 1800s, when Augustin-Louis Cauchy in 1821 and Karl Weierstrass after him finally put one slippery mathematical idea on rigorous footing for the first time, and that idea is exactly what Zeno's argument had been missing. Which idea did Cauchy and Weierstrass finally pin down?
answer: The limit an endless sum can be proven to settle upon
choices: The limit an endless sum can be proven to settle upon
The rule that any endless sum must grow without bound
The claim that no endless sum can have an exact value
The proof that space holds a smallest uncuttable length
context: Cauchy defined limits rigorously in 1821 and Weierstrass formalized continuity, together proving that a convergent infinite series settles on a definite finite value. That it took this nineteenth-century machinery to nail down shows Zeno's puzzle was genuine all along, not sophistry. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zeno's Paradoxes' (Cauchy 1821, Weierstrass 19th c.).

question: In a tale by the Daoist thinker Zhuangzi, a man named Zhuang Zhou dozes off and dreams he is a butterfly, flitting and fluttering about, happy and doing just as he pleases. Inside the dream, how aware is he of being Zhuang Zhou the man?
answer: Not at all aware -- he is wholly the butterfly and forgets the man
choices: Not at all aware -- he is wholly the butterfly and forgets the man
Dimly aware he is a man wearing the shape of a butterfly for fun
Aware something is off, though he cannot say quite what
Aware of his name but blank on the rest of his waking life
context: This total forgetting is the engine of the whole puzzle. In Burton Watson's translation: 'a butterfly flitting and fluttering around, happy with himself and doing as he pleased. He didn't know he was Chuang Chou.' Because the dreaming butterfly has no inkling of the man, when Zhuang Zhou wakes he cannot rule out that he is now a butterfly dreaming HE is a man. Source: Burton Watson trans., The Complete Works of Chuang Tzu, ch. 2 (terebess.hu/english/chuangtzu.html).

question: Zhuang Zhou wakes from dreaming he was a butterfly and finds himself, in Zhuangzi's words, "solid and unmistakable" -- clearly a man again. A friend tells him: you obviously KNOW you are awake right now, so there is nothing left to puzzle over. But inside the butterfly dream, everything had felt every bit as real. What is wrong with the friend's confident point?
answer: Feeling sure you are awake proves nothing, since a dream hands you that same sureness
choices: Feeling sure you are awake proves nothing, since a dream hands you that same sureness
You can always settle it by pinching yourself, which never works inside a dream
Butterflies enjoy their dreams far more deeply than any man ever enjoys his
Nothing -- once a person is plainly awake, no real puzzle about it remains
context: The friend mistakes a feeling for a proof. While Zhuang Zhou was the butterfly he was just as convinced he was the butterfly -- the dream delivers the very same sense of certainty that waking does, so that certainty can't be the thing that tells you which state you are in. The gem kids can feel: the dreamer was MORE content and equally sure, yet the text pointedly does not say the woken man is happier or more certain of being real. The pinch-test feels decisive but isn't -- a dream can perfectly well include a pinch that 'works.' Source: Burton Watson trans., Chuang Tzu ch. 2; original Chinese 栩栩然 'flitting and fluttering' (Wikipedia: Zhuangzi book).

question: Zhuangzi presses the butterfly puzzle further. One man dreams he is drinking wine, then weeps when morning comes; another dreams he is weeping, then wakes and cheerfully goes off hunting. Each man, while inside his dream, was fully convinced it was real. So why can a person not simply tell, right now, from the inside, that they are awake?
answer: Because being inside a dream feels every bit as real and clear-headed as being awake does
choices: Because being inside a dream feels every bit as real and clear-headed as being awake does
Because you can always reason logically when awake but never can while inside a dream
Because a dream is always blurry and faint, while waking life is sharp and vivid
Because only young children, never grown adults, are ever truly fooled by a dream
context: This is the 'great dream' passage. Watson: 'While he is dreaming he does not know it is a dream, and in his dream he may even try to interpret a dream. Only after he wakes does he know it was a dream. And someday there will be a great awakening when we know that this is all a great dream.' The killer detail is that you can reason clearly WHILE dreaming -- you might even sit and interpret a dream inside a dream -- so 'this feels real and I'm thinking straight' is exactly what a dream feels like too. A dream is not reliably blurry, and grown adults are fooled by their dreams every night. Source: Burton Watson trans., Chuang Tzu ch. 2 (terebess.hu/english/chuangtzu.html).

question: The butterfly dream is the closing line of the second chapter of the Zhuangzi. Earlier in that chapter, Zhuangzi argues that a single log is huge to an ant and tiny to an ox -- so big and small are not in the log itself, but in whoever is looking. Ending the whole chapter on the dream lets him stretch that very move to one last, startling place. Which?
answer: That even real-versus-dreamed is a line the viewer draws, not one the world itself carries
choices: That even real-versus-dreamed is a line the viewer draws, not one the world itself carries
That the dream proves the waking world is an illusion a wise person ought to escape
That a butterfly and a man are, deep down, one and the same kind of creature
That patient argument can at last settle which of the two states a person is really in
context: The chapter is titled 齊物論 (Qiwulun), 'Discussion on Making All Things Equal,' the philosophical heart of the whole book. It turns on the relativity of shi-fei (是非, 'this/not-this,' i.e. right/wrong) judgments: 'Any thing can be a this; any thing can be a that,' depending on where you stand. The log-to-ant-and-ox move says big and small live in the looker, not the log; the dream is the capstone -- if even waking-vs-dreaming is a line we draw rather than one the world supplies, then so is every other 'this is real / that is not' boundary. Note the dream does NOT say the waking world is a mere illusion to flee; it unsettles the boundary, it does not pick the dreaming side. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Zhuangzi (Qiwulun, shi-fei); IEP: Zhuangzi; Burton Watson trans. ch. 2.

question: The butterfly dream ends Zhuangzi's second chapter, and the last line is famous for how it handles the doubt it just raised -- man dreams butterfly, or butterfly now dreams man, with no way to tell which. Many a thinker would rush to settle such a riddle. What does Zhuangzi do with it in that closing line?
answer: He names the event the Transformation of Things and lets the doubt stand open
choices: He names the event the Transformation of Things and lets the doubt stand open
He proves, at last, that the waking man was the real one all along
He grants that the butterfly was the true self and the man only a dream
He brands the whole riddle a childish error and warns readers off it
context: Watson's final line: 'Between Chuang Chou and a butterfly there must be some distinction! This is called the Transformation of Things.' The Chinese is 物化 (wu hua), literally 'thing-transformation.' Zhuangzi ends not with an answer but by NAMING the phenomenon -- the question of which side is real is left standing open on purpose; he simply notes that one thing has flowed into another. Source: Burton Watson trans. ch. 2 + Wikipedia: Zhuangzi (book), Chinese term 物化 wu hua.

question: In the same chapter, Zhuangzi tells of Lady Li, a border guard's daughter seized as a war captive and carried off to a foreign court. At first she wept until her robe was soaked, sure her fate was a horror. But once she reached the palace and its comforts, she wondered why she had ever cried. Zhuangzi then asks: how do I know the dead do not wonder why they ever clung to life? What is his point in pairing her tears with that question about the dead?
answer: That being sure a state will be dreadful proves nothing until you have lived it
choices: That being sure a state will be dreadful proves nothing until you have lived it
That captives always come to love the courts of the men who captured them
That weeping is a sign a person has badly misjudged their true situation
That the dead can speak to the living and report what death is truly like
context: It is the same skeptical move as the butterfly, aimed now at a feeling we never question -- the preference for being awake and alive. Lady Li was CERTAIN her new state was a horror, then found it was bliss; so present certainty about which state is better is worthless evidence. Watson: 'How do I know that the dead do not wonder why they ever longed for life?' Source: Burton Watson trans., Chuang Tzu ch. 2.

question: In his second chapter, Zhuangzi says the people who bustle about so sure they are awake -- calling this man a ruler, that one a herdsman -- are themselves dreaming. Confucius is dreaming, he goes on; you who hear this are dreaming; and then he adds one more clause: "and when I say you are dreaming, I am dreaming, too." He even dubs his own claim the "Supreme Swindle." Why does tacking on that last bit about himself keep the whole thing from being a smug gotcha?
answer: Because his doubt now claims no solid ground for itself that it denies to everyone else
choices: Because his doubt now claims no solid ground for itself that it denies to everyone else
Because it quietly shows he believed all along that his own doubt was really false
Because it proves Confucius was the one rival thinker Zhuangzi truly admired
Because calling it a swindle admits he judged his own teaching to be worthless
context: Watson: 'Yet the stupid believe they are awake... Confucius and you are both dreaming! And when I say you are dreaming, I am dreaming, too. Words like these will be labeled the Supreme Swindle.' 'Supreme Swindle' renders 弔詭 (diao gui). A smug skeptic exempts himself -- everyone ELSE is fooled, but I see clearly.
